en: Preface to the Great Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment:
This commentary has existed from the Tang dynasty until the present for many years. Although it was carved onto wooden blocks in foreign lands, it has never been printed and circulated within China.

Copies were transmitted by hand, leading to errors through successive transcriptions—like the "crow" and "horse" characters mistaken for one another. Consequently, I obtained a printed edition from Goryeo and compared it with the manuscript.

I have personally collated this work. Having observed that there were mutual gains and losses among the various versions, I traced back to the original texts of the sūtras and śāstras from which they derived.

After three careful readings and detailed comparisons, I established a definitive standard before proceeding with the carving and writing. Wherever there was no corroborating evidence, I followed the printed edition.
As in the introduction, following the mention of Mount Weilu (Lushan) of the Jin dynasty, there appears to be an omission; thus, I have not dared to add anything arbitrarily.
Furthermore, where different characters are used, both having their own sources, I have likewise not dared to alter them at will.

For instance, the characters "dream" (*mèng*) and "sickness" (*huàn*) used in the *Jiěshí* differ from the character "illusion" (*huàn*) used in the *Lüejì*; in such cases, I have followed the *Cheng weishi lun* and the *Yuánrénlùn*.
Since this [manuscript] is identical to the printed edition, I have followed it here.

However, where there were errors due to scribal slips—such as the phrase "first explaining the title" being mistakenly written as "manifesting," or "having words and having meaning" being corrupted to "having principles"—these have all been corrected according to the manuscript.
Other instances that remain unsatisfactory are left as they are, pending further refinement. Dated the year of Wuma (1158) of the Shaoxing era.
The sixth day of the first month of spring. At Nengren Monastery in Kunshan, Pingjiang Prefecture, the śramaṇa Yìhé, refined and liberated, collated this at Xuān School.
His disciple Yuàntí: The Great Way is perfectly pervasive;
the great chiliocosm has no inherent substance. Once the six sense-faculties arise, the six elements combine to form shape, and delusive confusion fills [the mind].

Yet true wisdom is impaired; as empty appearances manifest, the real nature remains hidden. Consequently, it is as if one possesses a supreme treasure stored within one’s robes, yet has neither it nor its absence;

or as if one holds gold and iron in hand, yet fundamentally gains and loses them both. For this reason, the Tathāgata, who awakens to reality as it is, initiates his activity and bestows the Dharma upon the world.

Although he contemplates all with the four minds of equality, the three faculties of sentient beings differ; thus, he establishes teachings of gradual and sudden stages, while further opening up provisional means.
How could the moon at night intentionally settle its reflection only in a clear pond, or the morning sun have a partial intent to shine first upon a high mountain?

As for this *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, it reveals the true source instantaneously; thus, the Bhagavān preached it while dwelling in a pure land, as fully demonstrated in the preface to the commentary.
There is no need to labor over this point further. Yet, a paulownia tree is but a common wood, and a fine steed is indistinguishable from a hack; they are not the same as the [sage] of Bo.

Without Cai, the five musical notes would remain forever hidden; without Bole, the thousand-li steed would remain forever among the common herd. In the distant past, there were those who delved into the truth with chisels and drills;

in the present day, those who carve rhinoceros horn have merely multiplied their schools, yet none have achieved even a slight degree of correctness. My Venerable Master possesses the numinous power of a resonant jar and the brilliance of the radiant sun.

In silence, he received the Single Seal; by suspension, he penetrated all the scriptures. Thus it was that the four classes of practitioners were transformed together and the sevenfold assembly returned in sincerity. Half—

With a single verse he stilled the monkey of the mind; with a single phrase he tamed the horse of the intellect. He declined worldly glory and cast off his hair; he crushed arrogance and threw away the needle.

Those who admired his righteousness and followed his reputation rushed to his chamber like the wind, while those who harbored doubts and stored up misconceptions found their mists cleared by a cloudless sky.

This was my Master’s method for delivering sentient beings. As for those who fled from fame yet were drawn back by it, or who sought to obscure their virtue yet ended up attracting it—[this was the result].
As for his virtue: he was praised by the Emperor of Jin at Mount Weilü; he took temporary leave from his Dharma Master. The King of Men beheld him with his own eyes and realized the Way;

though he declined the purple robes three times, they were bestowed upon him again. He presented the White Dharma twice and was delighted to hear it. The lamp of the mind was lit within the Purple Palace; the mirror of the Dharma hung in the Yellow Abode.
The six palaces admired his virtue, hearing what they had never heard before; the three ministers submitted to his teachings, attaining what they had not attained before. Chan...
The mind is naturally still; it is not deluded by floating splendors. To speak eternally of being without fetters—who could be like this? This is my teacher’s non-abiding in fame and position.

As for his reaching the ultimate principle, exhausting the single flavor of the teachings, and excelling in the three schools, those who entered his gate numbered over a thousand, and those who ascended the hall filled the hundreds.
Each received the jewel from their topknot, and together they sipped the *amṛta* (clarified butter). Dividing the inexhaustible lamp, they spread like stars throughout China.
The Great Master, through his skillful attachments, recalled his old mountain; finding joy in a single peak, he sat therein and left behind all worldly affairs.

He repeatedly submitted petitions heard at the Northern Gate, requesting to return and hide away in the Southern Mountains. When the imperial decree was issued granting his request, the court officials came to escort him with due ceremony.
Thus, our Master was impartial toward the two benefits [of self and others]. As Confucius once said: "My will lies in the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals)."

Now the Great Master says: "My heart’s lineage is Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa). However, because we compete in debate, the wondrous meaning is eclipsed; the Dragon Canon is obscured by its profound texts.
Thus, the teachings that reveal the nature are buried, while the schools of names and characteristics flourish. For this reason, I shall reform old customs and establish new teachings:
I will suppress provisional methods and Hinayana, and uphold the Sudden and manifest the Perfect. This shall cause the constellations of the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha)..."
The images of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom are arrayed and manifest; how much more so for this volume, which is its primary doctrine.

For over twenty years, I have vowed to propagate it widely, repeatedly contemplating its profound significance. It is the crest-jewel of the Wheel-Turning King’s topknot, the heart-transmission of the Great Cloud Sūtra;

it is the family wealth of the Elder, personally handed down by the Coolness (Śīlabhadra). Therefore, relying internally upon wisdom-observation and externally upon sincere texts, I have aligned my own body and mind with the response.
The commentary consists of three fascicles. It organizes the entire sutra, synthesizing its divergences and connecting its beginning and end.
Its phrasing is concise, yet its principles are comprehensive. If one wishes to say it is brief, no meaning is omitted; if one wishes to say it is extensive, no word is superfluous.
It possesses the profound depth of "the mystery within mysteries" and the method of "reducing what is already diminished. How could this truly be merely a cultivation of the three [meanings]?
The essential meaning encompasses the five colors; as for the causes and conditions that give rise to the teaching, it explains the origins and circumstances of this specific scripture.

It classifies the divisions of the *pitakas* and *yānas*, revealing the ultimate destination of all teachings. Through the mutual manifestation of the provisional and the real, and the opening and closing of the three schools, when adherents contend, red and blue are clearly distinguished;
yet when they are harmonized and subsumed, water and milk suddenly become one. Its boundaries are profound and subtle, explaining the ultimate state of the One Mind.

Regarding this Dharma, the capacities of those to whom it is addressed encompass five categories of practitioners. To forget verbal explanations while cultivating the mind, one must clarify the discourse on realization and verification (*sākṣātkriyā*).

To expound and praise according to the text, one must first recount the origins of its translation and transmission. Thereafter, the title shall first be explained; its principle transcends all categories of verbal expression.
Subsequently, the verses shall be interpreted, so that their meaning may illuminate the text of this single fascicle. In explaining the Buddha-body, the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are not...

When clarifying the Pure Land, there is no distinction between self and others; when expounding the teaching, both mind and object vanish together; and among the audience, leaders and followers merge with one another.
This answers the original cause through three successive stages and brings forth the ultimate fruit as a single, perfectly luminous principle.

Thus, the thousand-fold flowers of meaning suddenly bloom within the literary garden, and the hundred rivers of Dharma-water entirely converge in the celestial lake. Truly, this is the exhaustion of all inquiry.

The Sūtras constitute the very backbone of the teachings. As for the two emptinesses, the eight consciousnesses, the severing of delusions, dependent origination, the four wisdoms of *bodhi*, and the six *pāramitās*—these exhaustively cover the source and flow of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) school.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the land of tranquil light, the chapter on the *tathāgatagarbha*, the eradication of the root of ignorance, the investigation into the foundation of craving, the attainment of Buddhahood through the ten minds, and the realization of suchness according to the five teachings—all these fully expound the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

This is the fundamental essence of our school from beginning to end. As for the commentary on the Mañjuśrī Chapter, it does not yet reach the point where both mind and objects are simultaneously extinguished.

In the explanation of the *Zhēnkōng Guān* (Contemplation of True Emptiness), at its initial stage, the sense organs and their objects are universally purified; by relying on the clarification of the spirit, phenomenal marks vanish, and through the process of investigation and reflection (*vitarka-vicāra*), the self is realized as empty.

This encompasses the profound principles of the Prajñā school. Furthermore, there is the analysis of the four great elements, the restraint of the six sense faculties, the wearying and subduing of the eight meditative absorptions, and the four... [text fragment].

The fruits of subduing and severing [afflictions], the fivefold ten wholesome actions, and the comprehensive regulation of the Great and Small Retreats constitute the framework for subduing the hidden storehouse (*guǐfáng*).
Dividing the *dharmadhātu* into three layers, the purport of the *Avataṃsaka* is manifested; opening two gates within the single mind, the intent of the *Awakening of Faith* is made clear.
In matters, he combined the two teachings, elucidating the profound pivot of Confucius and Laozi; in meditation, he united the two schools, furthering the traditions of Xiu and Neng.
This is the secret intent [of the teachings]. Now, as for the Śūnyatā deity, he manifests his body appearing daily; the Sūtra-piṭaka has been annotated so that its principles are clarified.
This enables those who seek the text to transcend the words and those who dwell in appearances to dissolve those appearances.

Were it not for the true mind and the ocean-like wisdom of Master Fashi—who refined his intellect and spirit and perfected both principle and teaching—how could the ocean of meaning remain inexhaustible when even a mere hair-tip is raised? Thus, in discourse...
With a single stroke of his brush, he spoke like a cascading river without impediment; such is this text. It fully encompasses the three faculties [of hearing, contemplation, and practice].
To read it and to study it, there is no one who will not benefit. Yet, fearing that the merit of reciting it a hundred times might be lacking, he relied upon explanatory commentaries (*transhishi*);

and lacking the learning of the Three Vehicles, he sought to cite explicit scriptures. With great compassion, he never grew weary of perfecting this work through detailed compilation, further composing the *Gishō* (Commentary on the Meaning) in ten volumes.
This work consists of eight fascicles, compiled into five volumes of separate texts, totaling over one thousand sheets of paper. It is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end.

Furthermore, since ancient times, various excerpts have been produced, most of which were compiled by later individuals; this has caused those within the scholarly tradition to remain subject to dispute. Now that I have provided my own commentary, what cause for doubt remains?

Moreover, regarding the methods of compilation used by various schools, they frequently cite separate texts and distinct interpretations; those who study according to these traditions merely follow established precedent.
Consequently, [the texts] have become either erroneous or corrupt. Now, although I cite the writings of others, my intention is to establish my own meaning;

I employ them merely as decorative embellishments and do not concern myself with a proliferation of categorical examples. Furthermore, when various commentaries cite passages as evidence, that which serves as evidence is the *meaning* (義), while the citation of the vermilion [text] is the *wording* (文).
As for the meaning, it may sometimes correspond exactly; however, the wording must certainly not be identical in every instance.
Failing to understand the principle of mutual correspondence, they merely cite isolated passages.

As the faculties and intelligence of later students and beginners gradually decline, they are unable to comprehend the profound meaning beyond the literal phrasing and imagery. Comparing the ancients with the present, such instances are numerous.

Now, the Great Master’s intention is as follows: The "pervasion of the school" (zongtong) is the Buddha-mind; its principle must be realized through direct realization. The "pervasion of teaching" (shuotong) consists of literary instruction; its value lies in its adaptation to the occasion.

As there are distinctions between superior and inferior capacities, he sets forth teachings of varying depth. As there are differences between partial and perfect principles, [he provides corresponding doctrines].

Thus, this treatise employs the texts of both the provisional and the ultimate; relying upon them, there is nothing that is obstructed or unpenetrated, and propagating them, there are no capacities that remain unreached.
Truly, it is like the skill of the master artisan Ban Chui, for whom every curve and straight edge is suitable timber, or the physician Bian Que, for whom every herb and tree is a medicine.

If one obtains their proper application, there is nothing that is not sincere truth. I, Yuanti, having received the great fortune of my past lives, have had the misfortune of encountering such a teaching in this lifetime, and have personally obtained the opportunity to hear it.
I have heard that I was personally granted his seal of approval. At Vulture Peak in past lives, I could never forget the grace of the tied jewel;
at Mount Heng in this life, I truly rejoice in the encounter with the gift of the chariot. Had I not received his instruction, I would have long harbored an inferior mind.

Now that I have obtained this guidance, I vow to fulfill my lifelong resolve. I fear that after a hundred or a thousand years, when the times change and people decline, errors and corruptions will increase further, and the profound...
The essential meaning has thus fallen into decline. It is my hope that the pure source shall not be severed and that there may be a reliable basis for study and practice.

Furthermore, I have set forth the origins of this matter in the preface to the *Chao* (Excerpts), striving to present the facts as they are. This work is plain rather than ornate and remains deficient in many respects; it is intended to await the wisdom of future sages.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Sub-commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll One (Part One of Two), composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.

In preparing to explain this entire body of commentarial text, there are four major sections: first, a general presentation of the fundamental intent; second, the expression of reverence and a request for divine assistance.

Third, the opening chapter explaining the text; fourth, the celebration and dedication. Within the first [section], there are four parts: first, revealing the principle; second, from "Our Buddha" onwards, clarifying the teaching;
third, from "Ei-pa-go" onwards, narrating the commentary; fourth, from "The Four Greats" onwards, judging the title. Within the first [of these four], there are again two parts.

First, the essence of the awakened mind is shown; subsequently, the awakened aspect of the mind is shown. Within the first [section], there are again two parts: first, distinguishing its essentials; second, the formal demonstration.
Within the former, there are again two parts: first, pointing to the source of the mind by way of the fruit-virtue; second, clarifying how cultivating the mind accomplishes that fruit-virtue.
In this current section, each instance first presents a category, followed by the formal clarification—namely, the four lines of the hexagram Qian.
Regarding these virtues, if one investigates their origin, they arise from the single qi (one-qi).

Just as the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity in the fruit of Buddhahood have their root in the single mind, so too, since that [Daoist] system begins with the single qi, those who practice refinement focus exclusively on the single qi.
Since the virtues of the Buddha are rooted in the single mind, it follows logically that one must cultivate the single mind in order to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.
In each of these sections, a precedent is first cited; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the commentary’s passage from “Yuánhéng” (Original Pervasion) to “begins with the One Qi,” this is the precedent cited within the preceding section.

That is to say, it cites the virtue of the Qian hexagram from the *Zhouyī* as the paradigmatic example. However, among the various classics that serve as the basis for the customs of this country, the ultimate limit is...

The *Zhouyi* (Book of Changes): "The myriad things reach their ultimate in the Way of Qian. (Among the myriad things of the world, none are greater than Heaven and Earth. Within this, Heaven governs through Earth; Heaven is honored and Earth is submissive.

The Way of Qian is Heaven; therefore, it is taken as a category. The principle for taking this [as a model] lies within the Confucian tradition; thus, the Way known through Confucian learning is cited to categorize the principle of ultimate awakening, so that it may be understood.
Once the style of the Confucian scholars has shifted, the grass under which the herd of deer lies will naturally bend. Remaining metaphors...
Trifling matters cannot be categorized as the True Dharma; it is here that the primary manifestation of the Virtue of Heaven (Qian-de) is found.

Now, since "Original, Auspicious, Beneficial, and Correct" (*yuan-heng-li-zhen*) constitutes the four virtues of Qian, we shall first clarify the Way of Qian. Qian is the name of a hexagram; it is the very first hexagram of the *Zhouyi*.

(As with the hexagram Qian, all things begin with Qian, and thus it is placed at the head. Therefore, the *Xici* says: "Qian knows the Great Beginning; Kun completes the creation of things. It is called—
Regarding the term "gua" (hexagram): the *Yiwei* states, "Gua means 'to hang' (*guà*). It refers to hanging up objects to display them to people; therefore, they are called gua.
However, while the structure of two lines may symbolize the qi of yin and yang, it does not yet constitute the images of the myriad things and cannot form a hexagram.
One must have three lines to symbolize the Three Powers (*sancái*), thereby depicting the images of heaven, earth, thunder, wind, water, fire, mountain, and lake.
This is what is called a "hexagram" (*gua*). Thus, the *Xici* says: "The eight trigrams are arrayed in order, and their images are contained therein.
However, with only three lines (*strokes*), there was not yet a full representation of the myriad things;

therefore, they were doubled to form six lines, thereby encompassing the forms and images of the myriad things and exhausting the capacities of heaven and earth. Thus, the hexagram is completed. This is the hexagram of Qian, which originally...
The Trigram Qian represents Heaven. Because Heaven is formed by the accumulation of various Yang energies, all six lines of this hexagram are Yang strokes (one long stroke constitutes a Yang line;

two short strokes placed opposite each other constitute a Yin line). Since this trigram images Heaven, yet it is not called "Heaven" but rather "Qian," it is because "Heaven" is the name for its fixed substance, while "Qian" is the designation for its substance-and-function (that is, the function of the substance).
Therefore, the *Saying on the Trigrams* states: "Qian is vigor. This means that—
The substance of Heaven functions through vigor. This means that when the Sage composed the *I Ching*, his primary aim was to instruct people;
he wished for them to emulate the function of Heaven rather than its substance. Therefore, he named it "Qian" (Heaven) rather than simply "Heaven. It is Heaven that takes vigor as its function.

Its operation never ceases; its responsive transformations are inexhaustible. This is the natural principle of Heaven. Therefore, the Sage constantly takes this spontaneity as his model to carry out human affairs;
he likewise responds to things and accomplishes tasks, acting without end, remaining ever-vigilant day and night, never for a moment becoming lax or weary.
Thus, he uses the celestial phenomena to instruct human conduct. Therefore, the Great Image says: "Heaven, by means of pure firmness..."

Therefore, it possesses the function of vigor. Now, the hexagram of pure Yang is drawn; this is used as a model for it, and thus it is called an "image. *Tianxing* (the movement of Heaven) is a term for motion. *Jian* (vigor) is a name for strength. It is the natural image of Heaven. Among all things that are vigorous, there is always decline and weariness; yet Heaven travels one degree each day.

This refers to the movement of the celestial body, which proceeds day and night without ceasing, beginning again after it has ended, never failing or retreating at any time. Liu Biao said: "Thus, 'Heaven' (*tian*) is the name of the substance, while 'Qian' (*gan*) is the name of the function.

'Vigor' (*jian*) is its definition. The Gentleman, accordingly, exerts himself with strength and does not cease. (This means using the image of the hexagram to encourage oneself so that one does not stop; hence it is called "vigor. [End of] the *Wenyan*.
[The Master] says: "The Qian hexagram begins by being able to benefit the world with its beautiful benefits, yet it does not speak of what it benefits.

How great it is! It further says: "How great is Qian! Its nature is firm and vigorous; its center (the second and fifth lines) is correct; its purity (the six yang lines) is its essence. (Essence refers to its spiritual vitality.)
Speaking in terms of phenomenal forms, it is pure yang and heaven; speaking in terms of human affairs, it is the sovereign and the father.
Because it occupies the position of supreme honor, it stands at the head of all hexagrams and constitutes the beginning of the principles of the *I Ching*.

"Great, capable, advantageous, and correct" (the text appears in the hexagram’s *ci*) refers to the functions of Qian; though its applications are manifold, they are subsumed within these four virtues, and thus these are selected. *Yuan* (Greatness).
"Qi" (初) signifies the beginning; "heng" (亨) signifies unimpeded flow; "li" (利) signifies harmony resulting in benefit; and "zhen" (貞) signifies completion and firmness.

This refers to the virtue of this hexagram: possessing the nature of pure yang, it is naturally able to initiate the birth of the myriad things through yang energy, thereby attaining unimpeded flow (*heng*);
it can cause the natures of things to be harmonious, each obtaining its own benefit (*li*), and remain firm and solid (*zhen*).
Ji. Because there is a beginning and an end, it is called the Four Virtues.
This means that the Sage should likewise model his conduct after this hexagram to practice the Way of Goodness, so as to bring all things to growth—this is Yuan (Primacy).

Furthermore, he should employ auspicious and beautiful matters to bring all things together, causing them to open and flow forth—this is Heng (Pervasive Success). Moreover, he should employ righteousness to harmonize all things, so that each may obtain [its proper place].
It is through principle that there is benefit. Furthermore, one must be firm and steadfast to carry out the task, ensuring that all things reach their completion;
this constitutes "permanence" (*zheng*). Therefore, the Sage models himself after the *Qian* hexagram and practices these four virtues, hence saying:

"Originality, Advantage, Benefit, and Permanence. The *Wenyan* says: [The Master is the seventh wing. Hereafter, the four virtues of *Qian* are discussed. However, the substance of *Qian* is the function of Heaven. The transformation and movement of Heaven and Earth occur spontaneously; because there is no...]

And thus existence arises. Heaven is originally without intention; how could it deliberately create the names *yuan*, *li*, *hen*, and *zhen*? It is only the Sage who entrusts these matters to them, designating this spontaneous efficacy as the four virtues of Heaven and transmitting this teaching to the world, so that future sovereigns may model themselves upon what Heaven does.
Therefore, the four virtues of Heaven were established to set forth the teachings. *Yuan* (benevolence, wood, spring) is the eldest of the good. Master Zhuang said:

"Heaven’s virtue of *yuan* first gives birth to the myriad things. Among all forms of goodness, nothing is greater than bestowing life. It is like the most profound kindness of parents, precisely because they are able to give birth to this body. Therefore, for one who fails to repay such kindness, there are three thousand offenses belonging to the five punishments."

Nothing is greater than unfiliality. If one repays this debt of gratitude, the blessing of filial piety is likewise the greatest in the world. Those who have been most filial since antiquity have all moved Heaven and shaken the earth; thus one knows that it is capable of producing human life, making it the highest good in the world.

Therefore, Buddhism says: "To build a thousand Buddha-lands is not as good as saving the life of a single person. Now, although all things each have their own place of origin, if one traces them back through successive stages to the very beginning, it is the Yang of Heaven (*qian*) that serves as the root of initial generation.

Thus, the merit of *qian* is named "Origin" (*yuan*). One thereby knows that the Origin is the foremost of all virtues. *Heng* (associated with the hexagram *li*, Fire, and the season of Summer) signifies the gathering of excellence. [Heaven] is able to bring forth and harmonize all things.

It causes them to gather together; thus it is said so. *Lì* (Harmony—Autumn) means the harmony of righteousness. (Heaven can benefit all things, causing each to attain its proper measure and achieve concord. *Zhēn* (Constancy—Winter) means the backbone of affairs.

(Heaven can, through the qi of central correctness, bring all things to completion, each attaining its own structural support. Master Zhuang’s intention was to clarify the virtue of Heaven by means of these four phrases:

*Yuán* [Origin] is the beginning of things and corresponds to Spring; *Hēng* [Pervasion] is thorough penetration and corresponds to Summer; *Lì* [Benefit] is the righteousness of harmony and corresponds to Autumn—since in autumn things are completed and each accords with what is appropriate; *Zhēn* [Constancy] is the backbone of affairs and corresponds to Winter—[when] things...)

The collection is completed; all matters have been successfully concluded. Among the five elemental energies (*wǔxíng*), only the energy of Earth (*tǔdì*) is lacking. For Earth presides over the four seasons; the movement of the four energies cannot be sustained without Earth. From this point onward, it clarifies how the person emulates Heaven by practicing these four virtues.

The superior man embodies benevolence (*rén*). (Because benevolence is the essence of Spring. He is sufficient to lead others. (By embodying the Way of benevolence and bestowing universal love upon all living beings, he is sufficient to be honored as a leader among men.

This is the emulation of Heaven’s primal virtue. His auspicious gatherings are sufficient to accord with ritual propriety (*lǐ*); his benefiting of things is sufficient to harmonize with righteousness (*yì*). (These may be understood by analogy. His steadfastness and solidity are sufficient...

It is used for accomplishing tasks. (Uprightness, correctness, firmness, and solidity cause things to reach completion; this means that all affairs are successfully managed. When a gentleman practices these four virtues—Greatness (Yuan), Benevolence (Ren), Pervasiveness (Heng), and Advantage (Li)—as well as Righteousness (Yi) and Firmness (Zhen)—these constitute the Four Virtues.

(Although "Wisdom" [Zhi] is not explicitly mentioned here, one must possess wisdom in order to practice these four matters. Furthermore, the *Qian Zuodu* states: "The two operations of Water and Earth both encompass Wisdom and Trustworthiness [Xin].

Therefore it is said: "Qian: Greatness, Pervasiveness, Advantage, and Firmness. (This concludes the section on King Wen’s composition of the *Yi*. Having finished the discourse on "Qian Yuan" and so forth, he wishes to have the gentleman take them as a model. Thus, by practicing the Four Virtues, one shares the same efficacy as Heaven; this is not merely the work of a sage.)

This is not so. When we speak of the "Junzi" (the superior person), it is because the Way of the *I Ching* establishes laws broadly for all to follow. If one were to restrict this to the Sage alone, I fear those below him would fail to reach [this standard]. Therefore, it speaks generally of the "Junzi," so that the feudal lords, high officials, and others may all practice it.

While it is the Sage who, in practicing it, can reach the ultimate limit, others each act according to their own capacity; there is a specific measure for each degree of attainment. Furthermore, as the hexagram *Qian* (Heaven) symbolizes Heaven, these four virtues are all considered the virtues of Heaven.

However, through the union of Yin and Yang, the two images complement one another, and both are capable of possessing virtue—not only the single hexagram *Qian*. For this reason, among the various hexagrams, there are also four virtues. Yet, the four virtues of the other hexagrams are all inferior to those of *Qian*; therefore, the hexagram *Qian* simply states the four virtues directly, with nothing further to be said. This is because...

One observes that the four virtues of Qian encompass everything without exception. In the other hexagrams, beneath these four virtues, there are further activities; because the four virtues vary in degree of excellence, they are supplemented by these additional matters. This is exemplified by the Kun hexagram, which states: "Kun:

Yuan, Hong, Li, and Zhen [the perseverance of the female horse]," and so forth, as seen in the pattern of the dozens of other hexagrams. Furthermore, the correlation of the four virtues with the six positions is all contained within the *Buke* (Supplementary Volume).

Now, when Qian is used as a metaphor for the Buddha, since Qian signifies unceasing movement and function—the quintessence of Yang energy—it is not like the Yin substance, which is characterized by stillness and quiescence.
Furthermore, just as the Buddha is the "Awakened One" and thus represents the wisdom of bodhi, he differs from the essence of nirvāṇa, which is mere quiescence.
As for the analogy of Yuan, Hen, Li, and Zhen to represent the [Buddha's] permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity:

although the functional activity of Qian (the Creative/Heaven) is vast and boundless, benefiting all things under heaven, its essential virtuous qualities consist only of these four; because it possesses these five constants [when including the underlying principle], it fully encompasses the Confucian tradition.

Because it possesses the five elements (encompassing all yin-yang arts, numerical divination, and the prognostication of fortune and misfortune). Because it possesses the four seasons (encompassing the entire circuit of the heavens). As explained above.
The virtues of the Buddha are likewise: although they are immeasurable and boundless, the virtues of his essential reality consist of only four.

As for this, form can indeed blind, but it can only blind the consciousness that confronts form. Now, the true mind is free from characteristics and does not confront form;
how then could form blind it? If one confronts form, form is immediately empty; who then is there to be blinded?

In the Daoist teachings, emptiness and stillness are taken as the Way, and the extinguishing of emotions and severing of intellect as cultivation. Therefore, upon observing forms or hearing sounds, one is immediately blind and deaf.

One has lost the Way. Now, the true mind is detached from inherent nature and does not stagnate in emptiness or nothingness; therefore, when seeing forms or hearing sounds, those sounds and forms cannot blind or delude it.
It is like a bright mirror manifesting forms: how could the forms obscure its brightness?

The four lines following "dwelling in birth and death" in the commentary concern the seventh [meaning], immutability. Within these two pairs of four lines, the first phrase in each pair indicates the principle (*dharma*), while the second phrase illustrates it through a metaphor.
The metaphor of the pearl in water illustrates its concealment during delusion; the metaphor of the moon in the sky illustrates its manifestation upon awakening.
The initial mention of the "stream of birth and death" refers to the beginningless cycle of birth and death that causes sentient beings to drift and drown.
Therefore, it is like a flowing stream; being boundless and bottomless, it is like the ocean. Nirvāṇa is the ultimate heaven (*paramārtha-deva*), in the sense of transcending to the further shore;
hence there is the expression "heaven with shores. Although *saṃsāra* consists of two types—segmented and transformative—[it is nonetheless like the ocean].

Now, we specifically take up the *pariccheda* (segmented) [birth-and-death], while its meaning also encompasses the *pariṇāma* (transformative). Although there are both Great and Small Vehicles within *nirvāṇa*, we now specifically take up the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the "pearl from a black dragon" (*li-zhu*): beneath the chin of a black dragon is a bright moon-like precious pearl whose radiance is transparent and penetrating.

Even when it is in the midst of the ocean, its radiance does not diminish; it is unlike a lamp or candle, which is extinguished upon entering the water. However, it cannot illuminate the entire ocean.
Because all that exists within it is [unified], it is called "Sole Radiance" (*duyao*). Although sentient beings dwell amidst birth and death, this spiritual mind remains clear and unclouded;
yet, they remain deluded and unaware of it, unable to penetrate all things. It simply shines forth as a solitary embodiment, like a pearl shining alone.
Thus, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty composed the inscription for the Great Master Bodhidharma, he expressed his intent at the outset by saying: "The vast ocean..."

Within it, there is the pearl of the black dragon, the color of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows. Neither gods nor men have seen it; neither men nor gods have recognized it. Our Great Master has obtained it.
"Cang" (Cang) describes the profound depth, vastness, and remote seclusion of water; it is like the azure blue of heaven, describing its loftiness and distance.
"Squatting on the shore of Nirvana": *Nirvāṇa* here is translated as "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*). All phenomena are empty; the mind is fundamentally...
Non-thought (*amanyana*) fuses into the single essence of true mind (*tathatā-citta*), for there is no separate clamor or agitation of birth and death;

thus, the true mind is perfect and entirely quiescent. "Sitting" (*ju*) refers to abiding in tranquility. Therefore, people of the time all called arrogance "sitting in haughtiness. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:

(Ma says: Yuan Rang was a man of Lu and an old acquaintance of Confucius. 'Yi' means to sit with legs spread; he waited for Confucius thus. The Master said: 'In youth he was neither respectful nor filial; as he grew older, he had nothing worthy of mention.'"
To grow old and not die is to be a thief. As for the "cassia orb," this refers to the moon; because there is a cassia tree within the moon, it is called the "cassia orb.
As for the "azure sky," this refers to the sky of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); because it is free from the clouds and mists of afflictions and karma, it is called "azure."
Since all phenomena are empty and quiescent, the fundamental awakening of the mind—the great wisdom-light—shines universally throughout the dharma-realm, free from all discrimination;
thus it is called "solitary and luminous. Yet, when the moon is in a clear sky, there is nowhere it does not illuminate;
therefore, when the mind is perfectly quiescent, it is like the moon in the heavens, unlike a pearl in the sea. Furthermore, as stated previously, the term "solitary" refers to the state of delusion.

It can only illuminate itself; it cannot universally illuminate all things. The present description of it as "solitary" refers to a clear autumn night when only the moon universally illuminates the world, such that the stars, lamps, and candles are all beyond comparison.
Thus, the wisdom of the essence-as-such is not comparable to the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣaṇika-bodhi*), which functions through duality and contrast.
"How great it is!"—these two phrases below refer to the eighth [point], "following conditions. "How great it is! is a term of reverent admiration; it follows the stylistic pattern of the *I Ching*.
Sometimes it appears above the object of admiration, as in: "How great is the Primordial Qian! All things receive their beginning from it," or "How great is Qian!

among all phenomena, there is nothing it does not penetrate thoroughly. Since its description cannot be exhausted, it is concluded with the praise: "How great it is!

Furthermore, wishing to describe its subsequent capacity to give rise to the myriad dharmas—its virtue of profound depth and vast breadth wherein essence and characteristics are mutually unimpeded—I therefore offer this designation and praise.

"How great it is! This refers to the fact that this mind, as the source from which the myriad dharmas arise, does not abide in its own nature but follows conditions to give rise to all the defiled and pure phenomena of the mundane world.
For now, we shall first clarify how delusion regarding this true mind results in the formation of tainted, defiled dharmas;
subsequently, we will rely on the commentary provided below to reveal that this mind is free from inversion and inherently possesses [virtues] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The sublime function of the merit of sand is such that its nature and characteristics are unimpeded; it is fundamentally a dharma free from outflows (*anāsrava*). Now, regarding the initial defilement:

although all sentient beings inherently possess this pure mind, from time immemorial they have been deluded by it and remain unaware of it (this refers to "fundamental non-awakening" in the Treatise, which is the meaning of independent ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) deluding the Truth;
as the Treatise says: "Because one does not know the Dharma of True Suchness as it truly is," etc.). Consequently, they falsely identify with the four great elements and their conditions.
[This] is for the sake of one's own body and mind (as the subsequent text states: "falsely identifying with the four elements," etc.). Thus, the secondary and tertiary branches arise successively.

These secondary and tertiary branches themselves consist of three levels: first, due to the aforementioned fundamental ignorance, various afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; second, due to these afflictions...
One creates various kinds of karma. Thirdly, because these are accomplished through karma, one undergoes the various sufferings of birth and death within the six realms.
The *Buddhanāmasūtra* states: "Isolated ignorance serves as the seed of affliction. It further states: "These three obstacles are mutually dependent;
because of afflictions, one gives rise to evil karma, and due to the causal conditions of evil karma, one obtains bitter fruits. Thus, [suffering] first arises from ignorance.
Regarding afflictions (*kleśa*): to briefly explain the coarse characteristics of afflictions, they consist solely of greed, anger, and delusion.
This means that once one has falsely identified the four elements and five aggregates as one's own body and mind, one naturally craves all matters of glory and pleasure, desiring to nourish them;

one becomes angry at all circumstances that oppose one's feelings, fearing they might cause harm; and through the state of delusion, one engages in various kinds of calculations and deliberations. As it is said:
The aforementioned afflictions all arise from delusion regarding the truth and attachment to the false. Second, as for creating karma from afflictions:

once greed and anger are intense and rampant, one immediately creates the ten unwholesome karmas and so forth; or, desiring the retribution of wealth and pleasure in future lives, one creates various wholesome karmas;

or, weary of the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower realms while rejoicing in the tranquility, subtlety, and detachment of the higher realms, one cultivates the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, which constitute immovable karma.
Because of delusion regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), both wholesome and unwholesome non-active karma are likewise tainted (*sāsrava*) karma.
Third, as for receiving retribution from karma: the retribution of sounds, echoes, forms, and shadows does not deviate by even a hair’s breadth.

If it is produced by prior unwholesome karma, there will be various painful retributions such as those of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; if it is produced by prior wholesome karma, there will be the four [rebirths].
The various pleasant retributions, such as the continents and the six heavens of the desire realm, are accomplished through prior immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*).
Thus, there arise various differentiated retributions, including the four dhyānas of the form realm and the four spheres of the formless realm;

these bodies that experience suffering and pleasure constitute the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of individual karma (*bhinnakarman*), while the superior or inferior environmental realms in which they dwell constitute the supporting retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of collective karma (*sādhāraṇakarman*). Following the passage "The myriad dharmas are false," the second section demonstrates the awakened aspect of the mind. This section has three parts: first, reconciling the delusive to reveal the true as a guiding pointer;
second, the circular inclusion of the aspects within the essence itself; third, a concluding praise of the awakened essence as transcending names and forms.
Now, the first point, "The Round Enlightenment of the Eye," corresponds to the first summary. The previous section stated that the myriad dharmas pervade both the defiled and the pure;
this section states that the myriad dharmas are first considered in terms of their defiled aspects. By realizing that the defiled are all empty, one then reveals the pure aspect.
The pure aspect and the fundamental nature are thus unimpeded. This passage shall be explained through a fourfold analysis: first, a comprehensive explanation; second, a systematic correlation.
The Chan School. (1) The threefold classification of its affiliations with various teachings; (2) the fourfold discernment of the texts employed.

First, to provide a detailed explanation of what is meant by "falsehood" (*xuwěi*): it refers to being deceptive and fraudulent. That which possesses only illusory appearances while lacking substantial reality is called "void" (*xū*).

To conceal its empty nature and falsely manifest a real state is called "deceit" (*mṛṣā*). Thus, the Treatise says that the three realms are deceptive. Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "arising through the convergence of conditions":
one should first ask, "How do we know that all phenomena are deceptive? The answer is: because they can only arise when a multitude of conditions converge;

therefore, it is said they "arise through the convergence of conditions. There are four types of conditions, namely: cause (*hetu*), [object (*ālambana*), dominant (*adhipati*), and immediate (*samanantara*)].

Conditions: the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). To explain them first by way of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are internal and external types.
The external is, for example, when a sprout arises from a grain seed, soil, water, human effort, and time; or when a vessel is produced from a lump of clay, a wheel, a string, and a potter.
The internal refers to the body, which arises with past karma that has already matured as the cause and the parents of this life as the condition.
Nothing whatsoever arises without depending upon internal causes and external conditions. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"There has never been a single phenomenon that does not arise from causes and conditions. The above explanation is still made in contrast to the tenets of the Hīnayāna school.

If one investigates the meaning of dependent origination by explaining it from its origin to its manifestations: the pure nature of the mind serves as the cause, and fundamental ignorance serves as the condition, giving rise to the three subtle states.

With the karmic consciousness as the cause and objective realms as the condition, the six coarse states arise. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the dharmas of arising are fundamentally non-existent":
since they belong to a multitude of conditions, they lack an inherent essence of their own. One should know that all dharmas of arising are thus devoid of self-nature.

They do not wait for extinction to be fundamentally non-existent; therefore, it is said that "the dharmas of arising are fundamentally non-existent. Thus, the preceding verse in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"Therefore, there is no dharma whatsoever that is not empty. It further says: "Dharmas are not born from themselves, nor are they born from another; they are not born from both together, nor without cause;
therefore, one knows them to be unarisen. The *Zhao lun* (Treatise by Sengzhao) states: "All dharmas are the convergence of conditions."

They arise through the convergence of conditions; thus, that which has not yet arisen does not exist. When conditions disperse, they cease. If they were truly existent, they would never cease to exist.
By this reasoning, although things currently appear to exist, their nature is eternally empty of itself. Even ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is inherently non-existent;

it is not made non-existent by being analyzed. Therefore, it is called "primordial non-existence" (*mūlābhāva*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the phenomena of arising are themselves the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
Because both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena exist, it is said that they are "originally non-existent.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "all is consciousness-only," one should first ask: if all things are originally non-existent, why do we currently perceive various phenomena?
Answer: Because [all things] are merely manifested by one’s own deluded mind and consciousness, it is said that "everything is consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

(When the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) conceives of external objects, it may conceive of them as non-existent while the objects appear to exist, or conceive of them as existent while the objects do not exist; thus one knows that what is conceived by consciousness has no fixed reality. This is illustrated by the fact that the five consciousnesses perceive the five sense-objects in the same way.

Therefore, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states: "Those characteristics of self and dharmas" (the self has various characteristics, and dharmas have various characteristics; these two categories of self and dharma encompass all phenomena in the world) all depend upon...

Internal consciousness (the substance of consciousness) manifests as the two divisions of seeing and appearance (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*), and based upon these, provisional designations arise (provisional names are established in accordance with provisional appearances).

This does not rely on the existence of a real self or dharmas apart from consciousness. Furthermore, it is said that "transformation" refers to the substance of consciousness (the self-verifying division, *svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). It "revolves" into what resembles the two divisions (the seeing and appearance divisions).

However, when the substance of contaminated consciousness arises, the cognition manifests in the semblance of the object and the subject. That which resembles the aspect of the object is called the appearance division; that which resembles the aspect of the subject is called the seeing division. Regarding this, there are two interpretations. The first states that the substance of consciousness is existent. The second... [text continues]

The two parts are non-existent; because they are non-existent yet appear as if existent, they are called "semblances. Second, it is said that the two parts also exist, for they are the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). What is meant by "semblance" is that they resemble the two parts [of subject and object] as if they were truly existent according to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

This is because both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) arise based upon self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Based on these two parts, the notions of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) are established, for those two have no basis apart from this.

The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* verse states: "Consciousness-only has no objective realm; because there are no external objects, there is deluded seeing. It is like a person with [defective] eyes..."
There is a visual impairment that causes one to see such things as hairs or a moon. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "All phenomena exist only through the distinctions created by deluded thought;
if one is separated from mental thought, then there are no signs of any objective realms. It further states: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. Question: If there are no external objects and these are merely false perceptions, [how can this be so?]
One should see forms at all times and in all places, or else not see them at all.

Why is it that the eye sees forms only at times and in places where forms exist, and does not see them at other times and in other places where no forms exist? Answer: It is like the objects and various things seen in a person’s dream;
although they are entirely non-existent, they nevertheless arise from mental conceptions. Yet, this does not prevent one from seeing that there are indeed things.
In some places one sees nothing; in other cases, one may see something first and later not see it, or not see it at first and later see it.

It is not that one sees in every place, nor is it that one sees for a long duration throughout one's entire life. Just as the mind and consciousness arise as the various phenomena, so too does what is non-existent appear as existent.

He asked again: "If that is so, why is it that many people, in the same place and at the same time, all see existence where there is existence, non-existence where there is non-existence, existence when it is time for existence, and non-existence when it is not? He replied:

"It is like hundreds of thousands of hungry ghosts who, by the power of their shared karma, simultaneously perceive pus, blood, and fierce fires in places where such things do not exist. How could these be clear, flowing river waters?"
Since there are no such things as actual fierce fires and so forth, we know that all things are solely mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that “consciousness is like an illusion or a dream,” one first asks:

If it is the case that various objects arise through the transformation of mind-consciousness, and although these objects do not exist, the mind-consciousness itself still exists, why was it previously stated that "all produced phenomena are fundamentally non-existent"? Is the conditioned mind-consciousness not itself a dependent origination (*pratyaya*)?
Is it a produced phenomenon? Therefore, the answer states: "Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream; it is also non-existent.
However, this same metaphor also appears in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, though its intended meaning differs. That text says:

"Due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination of self and phenomena, when the various consciousnesses arise, they transform into what resembles a self and phenomena. As for 'like an illusion or a dream,' it is because through the power of illusion and dreams, the mind resembles seeds."
The appearances of various external objects manifest; based on these, one clings to them as being real external objects.

His interpretation means that although the things seen in a dream-sickness do not exist, the dream-sickness itself is not non-existent, and thus it has the power to transform and give rise to illusory objects.
However, this interpretation is not correct according to the Niṣsvabhāvavāda (School of Non-characteristics) and the Dharmatā-vāda (Dharmatā School). Regarding the two metaphors, first, concerning...

Regarding the discourse on dream-objects: both the dream-thought and the dream-object are non-existent phenomena. If one were to say that one exists while the other does not, then the dream-thought and the perceived object would have to be distinct.
If they were distinct, the dream would not be the object, and the object would not be the dream.
When one awakens and the dream ceases, the object should still remain; it would be as when Zhuang Zhou, while asleep, dreamed that his body had become a butterfly, fluttering among flowers.
In the garden, if the butterfly were not a dream, and the dream were not the butterfly, then upon waking, when the dream has ceased, the butterfly ought to remain;
for the two things would then be distinct as real and illusory. Furthermore, if the butterfly were not a dream, it should be a real butterfly;

if the dream were not the butterfly, by what characteristic would it be defined? By this reasoning, although the dream-thought and the butterfly appear to differ as subject and object, they are in essence one.
In reality, they are one and the same entity. As for what is called a "dream," it is merely when Zhuang Zhou was asleep;
his fundamental mind-consciousness, due to being obscured and indistinct, suddenly and falsely manifested inverted perceptions and appearances such as butterflies and flower gardens.
These perceptions and appearances are what he called a "dream. Upon this single, false dream, there appear to be internal and external bodies and minds.

Furthermore, internally there is the thought of a butterfly; since this is entirely empty and non-existent, the body of the butterfly is but the appearance of a butterfly. Externally, there is the appearance of the flower garden.

Speaking according to the ultimate principle, the thought is the butterfly, and the butterfly is the thought. Since the appearance of the butterfly is entirely empty and non-existent, how could the thought of the butterfly alone be existent?
Moreover, the grasped appearance of the butterfly seems clearly to exist; yet since it is not truly existent, the grasping thought is likewise non-existent.
If it is clear that [the butterfly] appears as if existent, how could one allow it to be truly existent?

Furthermore, if the perceived image of the butterfly were to exist provisionally even while one has not yet awakened—despite its absence once one has awakened—then that very image of the butterfly being grasped should likewise exist during the time before awakening.
If this were so, then both the object and the mind would be co-existent; how then can you say "consciousness-only"? Now, let us exhaustively investigate the root and the branches through the Dharma.

This is the application of the analogy (*yoga*). That which is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) refers to the fundamentally existing, intrinsically pure, true mind of one who is deluded (analogous to Zhuang Zhou’s original mind while asleep).

Because they do not realize it for themselves (analogous to being in sleep), the three subtle and six coarse [transformations] appear (analogous to the appearance of the butterfly). These are what are termed "consciousness-only" (analogous to a dream). Regarding this class of delusion...

Above consciousness, there appears to be a distinction between the internal and the external (the internal corresponding to the thought of a butterfly, and the external corresponding to the appearance of a butterfly).

In reality, the object is the object of consciousness, and consciousness is the consciousness of the object (to unite with the butterfly is the thought; the thought is itself the butterfly). Thus, Master Fu said: "There has never been a mind without an object, nor has there ever been an object without a mind.
Each of these metaphors is clearly evident; let the wise reflect upon them carefully. In the provisional teachings, the Buddha spoke...

The principle of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) arises precisely because the intrinsically pure true mind has not yet been manifested, and thus remains contained within the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Therefore, objects are eliminated while the mind is preserved. It is only in the definitive sutras of the Final Teaching (*paryantadeśanā*) that the original enlightenment (*mūlapratibhāsa*) of the true mind is revealed, at which point it is said that both mind and objects are empty.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states: "In order to dispel the false attachment to the real existence of objects external to the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*)."

Therefore, it is said that "there is only consciousness. If one clings to the idea that consciousness truly exists as a substantial reality, such clinging is likewise a form of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), just as clinging to external objects is.

To explain this by means of the analogy of illness: suppose a person possesses naturally pure eyes, yet they are afflicted by cataracts caused by wind, heat, and so forth (the fundamental ignorance being like these cataracts).

A person without eyes would certainly not suffer from cataracts; likewise, those who lack the Buddha-nature would certainly not harbor deluded thoughts. Consequently, [the person with cataracts] perceives various forms and appearances of empty flowers.

(The six sense objects. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* explains the underlying intent as follows: "Although the flowers in the sky do not exist, the visual impairment that perceives those flowers is not non-existent.

The present meaning is precisely this: apart from the fundamental eye, there is no separate eye that perceives the flowers (just as apart from the nature of the true, pure mind, there are no distinct eight consciousnesses).
This "impairment" is a heat-vapor; how could such a heat-vapor perceive? Therefore, both the perceiver and the perceived are [merely manifestations].
It is false and illusory. It is merely because of cataracts that the fundamentally pure eye falsely perceives flowers; thus one knows that both objects and consciousness are empty.
It is merely because of delusion that within the truly pure mind one falsely perceives objects. One speaks only of the non-existence of consciousness, but not of the absence of delusion.
It is merely said that outside the fundamental eye there is no separate cataract-eye; it is not said that there is no cataract at all.

All other afflictions, such as those caused by wind, heat, or insanity, should be understood by this same analogy. Likewise, apart from the fundamental mind, there is no separate "mad mind" or the like.
Since the commentary states that all is but the one mind, it first asks: "If everything is like a dream and entirely non-existent, who is it that perceives this non-existence?
For instance, since ultimate truth is fundamentally without a perceiver of existence, perceiving existence is delusion;

yet if there is likewise no perceiver of non-existence, then perceiving non-existence should also be a form of delusion. Furthermore, although the dream of being a butterfly is unreal, there is still...
Regarding the person who dreams: although their consciousness (*vijñāna*) is unreal, there must nonetheless be one who gives rise to the thought.

Since the dream-butterfly was entrusted to Zhuang Zhou’s deluded consciousness, upon what, in turn, does that deluded consciousness depend for its arising? Therefore, the answer is given: it is simply the single mind.

Both the dream-image and the butterfly—these two aspects—are merely the single person, Zhuang Zhou, and not two distinct entities; likewise, deluded consciousness and the deluded object are both [the same].
The Dharma is likewise nothing other than the true *tathāgatagarbha*, the single mind; there are no two distinct dharmas.

How can it be that deluded consciousness and deluded objects are both the single mind? Answer: Therefore, the eyes, body, and the vessel-world, as well as the mind and its mental factors—all are empty;
there is nothing that is not the one true mind. All Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras state that "all phenomena are mind-only," which is precisely this meaning.
However, the expression "mind-only" (cittamātra) differs in its depth and subtlety.

If the Dharmalakṣaṇa school speaks of "mind-only," it means that the mind is merely the conditioned consciousness (*vijñāna*) which, through the accumulation of objective considerations, takes the discernment of objects as its characteristic;
this is what was referred to above as "all is representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). If the Dharmatā school speaks of "mind-only," it refers directly to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The mind is unconditioned and signless; it is free from all conceptualization and discrimination. Since even conceptualization and discrimination are but the single mind, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The suchness of the mind is the great universal essence of the one dharma-realm," and so forth, until:
"It is beyond the marks of speech and names, and free from the marks of mental objects; it is ultimately equal, without change or variation. It does not...
It can be destroyed; it is solely this single mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (suchness).

Regarding the statement here that "objects of cognition, discrimination, and so forth are also solely this single mind," this is, for example, like the teaching in the Dharma-character (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) school that all external objects are nothing but the eight consciousnesses. Question:
If this is so, do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas see nothing but the signless true mind, with no further objective realms and so forth?
The answer is that this is indeed the case according to the true principle. Thus, a sutra says: "To be free from all marks is precisely what is called the Buddhas, and so forth.

Once the grasping at the roots of false conceptualization, consciousness, sense objects, and environments is entirely exhausted, one achieves a body and wisdom that are pervasive and sovereign, wherein the realms of defilement and purity are unimpeded, as explained below in the section on the characteristics of awakening.

Regarding the phrase "one who knows through a tranquil mind": First, it was asked that since the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) is neither characterized by form, sound, fragrance, taste, and so forth, nor by the characteristics of conceptual discrimination, objective cognition, or likes and dislikes, one wonders what this true mind actually is.
What superior capacity does the self-substance of the true mind possess? How is it manifested as being definitively present? Whenever one intends to explain any dharma-gate, one must...

The *Śeṣam* (Explanatory Notes) clarifies the essential nature [of the mind], for it cannot be said that "the one mind" alone does not manifest its essential characteristics. The answer states: "It is quiescent yet capable of cognition.
"Quiescence" (*jì*) refers to the definitive essence; it signifies being firm, eternally settled, non-disturbing, and immutable—not the sense of a mere void or nothingness.
Therefore, a sutra says: "While all dharmas are empty and quiescent, this dharma is quiescent yet not empty."
If there were no substance of true mind, what could be said to be quiescent, and what could be said to be unmoving and unchanging?

That which knows is the substance itself that self-knows and self-awakens; it is luminously manifest and never obscured. One cannot discard it, nor can one grasp it. This is the meaning of its manifestation as the very substance itself;
it is not a matter of conceptual discrimination or inferential cognition. As for the previous mention of being "unruffled," "unmoving," and "unchanging," these merely describe—
Is this knowing quiescent and immutable? Quiescence is the quiescence of knowing; knowing is the knowing of quiescence.

Quiescence is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of knowing, while knowing is the functional activity (*vṛtti*) of the essential nature of quiescence. Therefore, the Great Master Qingliang said: "Spiritual knowing is unobscured, yet its nature and characteristics are profoundly still. He further stated:
"By means of the single mind in which knowing and quiescence are non-dual, one accords with the state where emptiness and existence are mutually fused."
The Middle Way. This sutra states: "Perfect Enlightenment universally illumines" (this is *jñāna*, knowing); "quiescent extinction is non-dual" (this is *śamatha*, stillness).

The *Yingluo jing* says: "Equal Enlightenment illumines stillness; Wondrous Enlightenment is stillness-illumination. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that in the fruit of Buddhahood there are no distinct qualities of form or sound;
only Suchness (stillness) and the Wisdom of Suchness (knowing) remain. Heze [Shenhui] said: "This is the very substance."

Through this, one knows by means of self-awareness; knowing thus, the essence is inherently quiescent. This is called "difficult to distinguish in explanation," for essence and function are of one accord.

In reality, it is said that within function there is constant quiescence, and within quiescence there is constant function. The single word "knowing" is the gateway to all wonders; the Buddha-dharma, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is established because of it.

The "Chapter on the Inquiry into Knowledge" (*Prajñā-prakarana*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the knowledge of the Buddha’s realm. There are two aspects to this knowledge of the Buddha’s realm.
Each is distinct. The verse answers, stating: "It cannot be known by consciousness, nor is it the domain of the mind; its nature is fundamentally pure. This is revealed to all sentient beings.
"Revealed to all sentient beings" is equivalent to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*’s teaching on the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for sentient beings.
Now, this true mind has two kinds of function: first, the function of self-nature; second, the function of application. Now...
"Knowledge" refers to the function of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because it is primordial self-cognition, it does not depend upon confronting external conditions.
"Application" refers to all conceptualizations, various forms of consciousness, differentiated wisdoms, and all activities performed to accomplish every task;

this is because they only manifest when necessarily confronted with conditions and are only able to bring about results through such dependence. It is like a great *maṇi* jewel... [text fragment ends].
The "Noble Jewel" (ni-bǎo) is able to manifest all forms and images, and can also produce whatever objects are required at will;

this is called its "functional application" (yìng-yòng). If there is no intention or wish, it does not produce anything, for it cannot manifest even with respect to objects that are not confronted by it.
The radiance of this jewel permeates through the interior of the garment, constantly shining of its own accord, whether confronting an object or not.
The object clarifies that there is neither increase nor decrease. This clarity is firm, solid, and translucent, being flawless both internally and externally.

Even though images may appear or disappear through various transformations, the clarity itself does not change; it remains eternally firm and pure. This is a metaphor for the tranquil essence of the mind.
"Firm and pure" means that the clarity itself is firm and pure. As for the various distinctions such as blue and yellow, this refers to the clarity responding to objects and being able to...
[This refers to] blue, yellow, and so forth.
The *Shu* (Commentary) identifies these as "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*), thereby concluding that they constitute the Dharma expounded by this sutra.

If, within the realm of quiescent awareness, one perceives only the signs of the body, mind, external objects, birth and death, and shifting transformations, as well as the signs of dull obstruction and moment-to-moment thought, then—

It is not called awakening. Therefore, the Treatise says: "All sentient beings are not called awakened because, amidst this body and mind, emptiness, existence, and so forth, they possess an awakening that is a cognizing mind;
yet it does not belong to any phenomena, being always able to know itself by itself. Although it resembles the aspect of awakening," [it is not true awakening].

Nor can it be called "perfect" (yuan), because phenomena such as emptiness and existence are not identical to awakening; for outside the awakened mind, emptiness, existence, and so forth still persist.
Therefore, it is not perfect. Now, this is truly because when one investigates and pursues the myriad dharmas from every angle, not a single dharma is found to possess a substantial essence;
there is only the one true mind, vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, with no other dharma existing apart from the mind.
All of this is the awakened mind; therefore, it is called "perfect" (*yuan*). Thus, the subsequent text says:

"Having realized that all illusions are extinguished, because the conditions for their shadows have vanished, one then attains directionless purity and boundless emptiness. Because the awakening is perfectly luminous, it reveals the purity of the mind;
because it is the awakening of all things. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "If there is a person who gives rise to true return..."

The source [of all things]—the empty space of the ten directions—vanishes all at once. It is further said: "Tranquil illumination encompasses empty space; yet when one returns to observe the world, it is like a dream.
Therefore, by now observing and investigating the myriad dharmas, one realizes they are illusory and like a dream, and that their fundamental nature is originally empty.
This is precisely what is called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). The preceding section concludes the detailed explanation.
Next, regarding the second part, the correlation with the Chan school: the first five phrases represent emptiness; the next phrase, "it is simply the one mind," represents stillness;
the following phrase represents knowing within stillness; and the final phrase serves as a general conclusion for the entire section.

Next, regarding the third classification that subsumes the various teachings: the first two phrases correspond to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, for by knowing that phenomena arise from conditions, one does not cling to a self or to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

The next two phrases belong to the Dharma-character school (*Faxiangzong*) of the Mahāyāna. The subsequent phrase, "consciousness is like a diseased dream," indicates that both mind and objects are entirely empty;
this belongs to the Destructive-appearance school (*Poxiangzong*) of the Mahāyāna. Combining these two schools constitutes the Initial Teaching (*Shijiao*).
Taking the latter three phrases together constitutes the Final Teaching (Jiao); taking only the latter three phrases individually constitutes the Sudden Teaching (Dun Jiao).

Furthermore, within these latter three phrases, the first corresponds to the Final Teaching, the next to the Sudden Teaching, and the final phrase establishes the core tenet of the sutra, which in meaning corresponds to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan Jiao).
Since this sutra merely shares a structural division with the *Avataṃsaka*, it is not specifically correlated [with the individual teachings].
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the characters employed for their application: indeed, every sentence and phrase in this section has its source of authority;

only the single phrase "the Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*) is a self-contained conclusion. This is because the *Treatise* states that "the three realms are false and illusory, being but the One Mind.
Now, by following upon the preceding mention of "myriad dharmas," one simply changes the character "three realms" (*sanjie*) to "myriad dharmas" (*wanfa*).

The statements regarding "arising through the convergence of conditions" and "original non-existence" (benwu) are precisely those found in Sengzhao’s *Zhao lun*. In the "Zongben yi" (Meaning of the Fundamental Basis) chapter of the *Zhao lun*, it is stated:
"Original non-existence, the true mark (*dharmatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the emptiness of nature—these are but one meaning: the convergence of conditions. It further explains:

"All dharmas arise through the convergence of conditions; since they arise through the convergence of conditions, they do not exist prior to their arising," and so forth (as cited above), continuing up to the section on existence.
Because its nature is eternally empty of itself, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Because it is empty of nature, it is called "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).

Since the dharma-nature is thus, it is called "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). True reality is itself non-existent; it is not made non-existent through deliberation. Therefore, it is said that dharmas are fundamentally unarisen.

The phrase "all is but mind" (yīqiè wéi xīn) is a common expression in the sūtras, śāstras, and commentaries of the Dharma-character school (Faxiang zong). The statement "all is consciousness-only, and consciousness is like one suffering from a dream" is from the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only).
The phrase "it is but one mind" is from the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith); it is simply that the character "only" (wéi) has been changed to the character "but" (dàn).
The commentary states: "Pervasive and full within purity, there is no room for anything else to enter below. Second, the characteristics of this essence are encompassed by its perfection.

This section has two parts: first, the two initial phrases eliminate faults; second, the possession of virtues. This is the first part. By tracing back the mind and objects to find both empty, one reveals the attainment of perfect, luminous awareness.
Since there is not the mark of a single speck of dust or a single thought, it is vast and all-pervading throughout the dharma-realm, pervasive and filling it to the brim.
It is full, without boundaries or limits, and is solely the awakening of a single flavor, wherein nothing is not pure. Therefore, the subsequent passage states:

"At that time, one immediately attains directionless purity; even from a single body to many bodies, from a single world to many worlds, throughout the entirety of space, all that exists within the three periods of time is perfectly encompassed by purity. Within this realm of pure awakening, there is no other..."
This is the nature of dharmas. Why is this? Because form contradicts emptiness, just as fire contradicts water. Water does not accommodate fire;
