therefore it is said that the center does not accommodate anything else. This is precisely the contemplation of true emptiness transcending all marks within the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm. Within this, one is properly engaged in the contemplation of total cessation and non-reliance.
Furthermore, one cannot say that form is identical to emptiness or not identical to emptiness, nor that emptiness is identical to form or not identical to form.
...and so forth. Therefore, it is further said: "To give rise to thoughts or stir the mind is to deviate from the essence of the Dharma, for it constitutes the loss of right mindfulness.
This is precisely the meaning of not admitting anything else. One should also say that to admit other things is to deviate from the essence of the Dharma;

this too belongs to the "gate of subsuming phenomena by principle" (*li duoshi men*) within the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai guan*). That text states: "Since phenomena already grasp principle, they cause the characteristics of phenomena to all..."
All things are exhausted; only the single truth manifests in equality, for apart from this truth, not even a fragment of a thing can be found.

Based on this, one infers upward that the myriad phenomena manifest as false and illusory, culminating in quiescent awareness. This is precisely the gate of manifesting the principle through the phenomena.
Furthermore, the contemplation of returning form to emptiness states: "It is truly because form is returned to emptiness that within emptiness there is necessarily no form."
Therefore, there is no room within it for anything else; this is the force of the textual flow of the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* (or *Uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī*).

As for the passage, "How could there be room for any other thing within this?"—the commentary states that because its virtues and functions are boundless, they are all of one single nature. This section has two parts: first, the principle (*dharma*).

The subsequent analogy: In the Dharma, the first two lines provide a general indication of the possession of all virtues; the latter four lines explain the non-obstruction between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
This means that if all phenomena—such as the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses—were substantially existent, they would contradict the nature of awakening.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Never has there been a single dharma that can enter into the dharma-nature. Now, because all things are pure, not even one [dharma] remains.

Because they are the very essence of even a single atom, all phenomena within infinite pure awakening are, without exception, each and every one the virtuous marks of the dharma-nature and the functional activity of its nature.
It is like a vessel made of gold: every single vessel is entirely gold.

It is like images in a mirror; every image is the mirror itself. Therefore, it is said that they all share the same nature (*ekalakṣaṇa*). This is the convergence of phenomena (*dharma*) back into principle (*li*). As for "virtuous function" (*guṇavṛtti*):

"virtue" refers to the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahattva*), and "function" refers to the greatness of function (*vṛttimahattva*); their sharing the same nature is the greatness of essence (*svabhāvamahattva*).
However, these virtuous functions fully encompass all phenomena—form, mind, objects, consciousness, time, place, teachings, meanings, practices, and stages.

This differs from other treatises which, in translating [the term], contrast it with deluded defilements as being fundamentally empty, thereby merely manifesting the virtues of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the term "boundless" (*ananta*), there are two meanings: first, the phenomena, teachings, and doctrines are more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, exceeding all limits; second, this...
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they have no limits; thus they are called "boundless.

The four lines following the commentary on the *Xingqi pin* (Chapter on the Arising of Nature) establish that nature and characteristics are mutually unimpeded and that principle and phenomena penetrate one another, such that phenomena do not differ from principle.

Principle is not different from phenomena, for they are mutually interfused. This means that although the nature of awakening has been subject to the errors of prior attachments and calculations, it is nevertheless able to manifest its entire substance as all dharmas.
It is like gold emerging from ore to become various vessels, or like a mirror appearing with myriad images once its defilements are exhausted.
Outside of this nature, there is not a single dharma that exists as a separate agent or object of arising; arising is solely the arising of the nature itself. Thus, the Jin translation [states]:
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*), and the *Huayan jianyao* contains the "Gate of the Arising of Nature.
Although it is taught that all conditions mutually assist and stimulate one another, within this gate, even dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) constitutes the arising of nature.

However, according to the teachings of the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*), True Suchness (*tathatā*) is exclusively quiescent and unchanging; its dependently originated phenomena are themselves conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) matter and mind. If these phenomena...
According to the teachings of the Nature School (Xingzong), the true nature is a penetrating, numinous clarity;

its entire substance is function, and thus its entire substance constantly constitutes all phenomena, while its entire substance is eternally quiescent in itself. This quiescence is the very quiescence of all phenomena;

it is not like empty space, which is a mere void of insentient stagnation. All phenomena are the phenomena of this total quiescence; therefore, they are not like those of the parikalpita (imagined) nature.
When one is obstructed and hindered by objects perceived through inverted views, the relationship between the object and the wisdom that perceives it remains distinct.

Although all phenomena (*dharmas*) are infinite in number, they are fully subsumed within form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). However, at the time of inverted attachment, form and the other phenomena are regarded as the five sense organs and the six sense objects, while the various states of mind and mental factors (*caitta*) are regarded as the emotional consciousnesses and their conceptualizations.
Now, because there is no longer any attachment to subject and object, [the distinction between them vanishes].

"Accomplishing boundless, wondrous realms and immeasurable wisdom"—these two phrases correspond to the "Gate of Establishing Phenomena Based on Principle" and the "Gate of Principle Manifesting as Phenomena.
The commentary states: "The characteristics [of phenomena] attain the nature, and body and mind become vast and open. This refers to the "Gate of Phenomena Being Pervasive According to Principle.
It means that since all phenomenal characteristics arise entirely from the nature (*dharmatā*), their arising is not different from the nature itself; thus, they follow whatever they rely upon.
The nature is vast and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Body and mind are quiescent and extinguished;

at the limit of fundamental equality, they are perfectly fulfilled throughout the ten directions, non-dual and compliant. It further states: "Because the awakened nature is all-pervading and perfect without boundaries.

One should know that the six sense organs pervade the Dharma-realm, as do the six sense objects, the four great elements, and the *dhāraṇī* gates—each and every one is said to pervade the Dharma-realm.

"Comparing it to the Sea-Seal [Samādhi] that transcends the great void" refers to the second metaphorical explanation. This means that when the fragrant ocean is clear and still, the myriad phenomena appear instantaneously;
likewise, because the pure *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) has as its very substance the arising of conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

In the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, among the ten types of samādhi gates, the first—the Perfectly Luminous Sea-Seal Samādhi Gate—states: "Or he manifests as a young boy..."
The forms of women, devas, nāgas, and asuras, even up to mahoragas—whatever they delight in, all are made visible.
The physical forms of sentient beings are each different; their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable.
All such things can be manifested through the majestic spiritual power of the Ocean Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). It is further said: "The ocean possesses a rare and extraordinary quality."
It is able to serve as the seal of equality for all things. Furthermore, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states:

"Just as the ocean universally manifests the bodies of sentient beings, it is for this reason called the 'Great Ocean. Bodhi universally seals all mental activities; therefore, Perfect Enlightenment is named 'Immeasurable.'"

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "Because within the bodies of all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and within the ocean of external forms, there are all reflected images, it is called the 'Great Ocean Seal' (*mahāsāgarāmudrā*).
The Bodhisattva is likewise; this is the Bodhisattva’s Ocean Seal Samādhi.
Qingliang explains this through ten meanings. First is the meaning of being able to manifest without mind. The commentary states: "There is no effortful application and no conceptual discrimination."
Therefore: (2) the meaning that there is nothing manifested in what is manifested. As the Sūtra says: "It is like light and shadows. The *Samantavyūha-parivarta* states:

"It universally manifests the mental activities, faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all sentient beings, yet there is nothing manifested. (3) The meaning that the manifestor and the manifested are not identical.
(4) The meaning that they are not different. As the Sūtra says: "Because the ocean can [manifest] and the manifested are different, they are not one; yet, apart from..."

Because a reflection cannot be found when sought within water, it is not different [from the water]. This demonstrates that the concentrated mind and the phenomena manifested therein are the characteristic of the very nature;
yet the subject and object remain distinct. They are the nature of the very characteristic; thus, object and self are non-dual. Regarding the meaning of the fivefold absence of coming and going:

the water does not go up to grasp [the image], nor does the object descend to approach [it], yet they are clearly manifested. The mind of samādhi is likewise: it manifests the myriad dharmas [within itself].
One's own mind does not come from anywhere; nor does the cloud-body of the *dharmakāya* ever depart for even a moment from the *dharmadhātu*.

These five preceding meanings are largely identical to the analogy of the mirror. Regarding the sixth meaning, "vastness," the Sūtra says: "Because it pervades the ten directions; because it universally encompasses all things without rejection.
This clarifies that the mind of samādhi extends throughout the *dharmadhātu*, such that the form and mind of sentient beings are all within this very mind.

Regarding "things" (*vastu*): their utility pervades the *dharmadhātu*, yet they do not depart from this mind. Seventh, the meaning of "universal manifestation": the Sūtra says that all things can be manifested;
the "Chapter on Manifestation" states that Bodhi universally seals all mental activities. This differs from "vastness" (*vaipulya*) in the following way:

This [first point] concerns that which is manifested; it does not distinguish between large and small. That [second point] concerns the capacity to manifest; its measure is universally pervasive. Furthermore, this [third point] concerns that which is manifested;

there is no category that is not manifested. That [fourth point] concerns the capacity to manifest; its measure is universally pervasive; there is no practice that is not cultivated. This is the meaning of the eightfold simultaneous manifestation. As the Sūtra says:

"Because they are manifested in a single thought-moment," meaning there is no sequence before or after, like a seal being impressed all at once. Ninth is the meaning of constant manifestation; it is not...

Just as a bright mirror has times when images appear and times when they do not, there are ten points regarding the meaning of "non-manifestation and manifestation. It is not like a bright mirror that manifests only when objects arrive before it;

for the Sūtra says that it manifests the images of the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*). While the fourfold army manifests only when facing the empty space, the images of the four continents manifest even without facing it.
Therefore, it is called "non-manifestation and manifestation. Because it does not depend upon facing [an object], it is therefore eternal.

This manifests the conditions of the three periods of time. Because it possesses the ten meanings mentioned above, it is called the "Ocean Seal" (Sāgarāmudrā). It is fully investigated by the Buddhas and is similar to that of the Bodhisattvas.
The commentary states: "That which transcends the great void" does so for two reasons. First, if one perceives space with the eyes, it still has form as its boundary.
Second, if one contemplates space with wisdom, it is a transformation of consciousness; it is merely the nature of awakening.

Because it constitutes only one portion of the meaning within [the totality]. Furthermore, because true awakening (bhūta-jñāna) integrates form, it is all-pervasive; because the great void cannot integrate form, it is not pervasive.
(Since it does not integrate, it is obstructed by characteristics. Thus, the *Buddhapiṭaka* states: "The void arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean."

Kuo says: *Śūraṅgama* laments the smallness of empty space; *Awakening of Faith* praises the vastness of the dharma-nature. This may be compared to the common saying that compares the ocean to the hoofprint of an ox.

The commentary’s phrase "vast and expansive" (*huāihuāi*) below concludes the third section, praising how the essence of awakening transcends names and forms. "Vast and expansive" means broad, great, and open.
Regarding the appearance of "distance" (*yuǎn*): The *Laozi* says, "The heavenly net is vast and wide; it is sparse yet nothing escapes it. (The net spread by Heaven is exceedingly vast;

though it is distant and seemingly loose, it minutely examines the good and evil of men, leaving nothing lost. The *Zhuangzi* says, "It is so vast that there is still room to spare. The *Lunyu* says, "The petty person does not know the mandate of Heaven and thus has no fear.
(The commentary notes: Because it is vast and sparse, they do not know to fear. △ Regarding "shimmering" (*huǎnghuǎng*): It refers to the intense brilliance of the sunlight.
"Radiant and brilliant" is the appearance of Heaven; "vast," "substantial," "quiescent," and "perfect" are its essence. "Resplendent," "active," "cognitive," and "awakened" are its function.
△ Regarding "transcending the realm of thought and deliberation": this refers to the inconceivable. Why is it called inconceivable?

Because it is beyond the reach of mind and speech. This means that while principle is perfect, words are partial; when words give rise to principle, the principle is lost. The Dharma is without marks.
Conceptualization. For when one thinks, confusion arises. The *Vajrasamādhi* states: "A thousand thoughts and ten thousand deliberations do not benefit the principle;

they merely cause agitation and disorder, causing one to lose the sovereign king of the mind. Thus, one knows that the sovereign king of the mind is cut off from the path of speech (for names are the pathways of speech), and its sphere of mental activity is extinguished (for marks are the sphere where the mind operates).
Therefore, an ancient worthy said: "The mouth wishes to discern, yet words fail; the mind intends to engage with objects, yet deliberation ceases."

When one ceases [discursive thought], one transcends far beyond the realm of words and images. As for the statement that "mind and speech cannot reach it": because phenomena (*dharma*) are nameless, speech cannot reach them;
because they are signless (*animitta*), the mind cannot reach them. This is because, with respect to the objects of perception, there are no fixed names or fixed signs;
thus, they are inconceivable by mind and mouth. Furthermore, there are three additional reasons why they are inconceivable: first, among persons, they transcend the ordinary and the small.

Furthermore, it is not the object of the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings, nor of the two types of wisdom that are not derived from the three types of insight (*prajñā*), nor of the wisdom born of retribution.
Third, it reveals the essence of the Dharma; even the Buddhas and bodhisattvas cannot fathom it, for it stands utterly alone. This is because this Dharma alone transcends words and thought.

Furthermore, this very expression "cutting off" is employed to dispel both speech and thought; for there is no state of non-speech that can serve as a point of reliance. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to non-discourse. How much more so, since the characteristics of speech are fundamentally quiescent?
When words are cut off, they too vanish; thus, speech and the absence of speech are both quiescent in their mutual dependence. What dharma is inconceivable?

It is the nature and characteristics of Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa), which are non-obstructive. Why is it inconceivable? Because it is pure even while being defiled. (All categories such as ordinary beings and sages, or the universal and the particular, should be treated accordingly.)

Furthermore, since it is neither a nature nor a characteristic, what use is there for inconceivable designations? Even with provisional names used as guides, one fears they are still difficult to master; moreover, if one now eliminates all traces and footprints, what benefit would this bring to sentient beings?

This is because the Dharma is revealed as transcending the emotions so that words may cease. That is to say, the essence of the Dharma is truly beyond the realm of thought and deliberation; if one were to cause it to abide within thought and deliberation, [it would fail its purpose].
One can never enter it through these means. Now, it is said that it transcends words and surpasses the intellect. Sentient beings then ask:

"If words are cut off and thought is stilled, how does one naturally enter by seeking beyond both words and mental images? Therefore, it is said that the Seven Patriarchs all spoke such words as "do not deliberate upon good or evil," and so forth.

The commentary states: "Our Buddha realized this," and so forth. This clarifies the teaching (*śāsana*). The text has two parts: first, a general account of the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching;
second, a specific account of the essential purpose (*abhiprāya*) of this sutra. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, elucidating the Buddha’s compassionate mindfulness;

second, describing the Buddha’s methods of transformation. Regarding the first section, the four lines clarify the Buddha’s compassionate mindfulness. "Our Buddha realized this": "this" refers to the aforementioned inconceivable, interpenetrating Dharma.
The Buddha realized this Dharma and attained unsurpassed peace and bliss.

Out of compassion for all sentient beings—who, though possessing this very Dharma of peace and bliss, are deluded by it and thus undergo groundless, false suffering—the Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha) said: "True bliss is inherently present, yet lost and unrecognized;
false suffering is inherently empty, yet acquired and unawakened. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that when the Buddha first attained [enlightenment]...
The reason the Buddha did not preach the Dharma for seven days was to manifest his own enjoyment of the Great Vehicle’s Dharma-joy.

Furthermore, having relinquished such sublime bliss, he preached out of compassion for sentient beings. Thus, one should know that what he realized was realized only as this, and what he preached was preached only as this. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle; according to the Dharma he has attained, adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, he delivers all beings by means of this."
I have given birth to the realization of the unsurpassed path, the Mahāyāna Dharma of equality.
If I were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is impossible for me. The commentary further exclaims, "How marvelous!

This refers to what is said in the "Appearance" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "O Son of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata. However...

Because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachments, one does not realize it. (The deluded thoughts of ordinary beings and the attachments of those of provisional and limited capacity both pertain to these two categories.
If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and unimpeded wisdom (*asaṅga-jñāna*) will manifest before one.

Then, the analogy of a single mote of dust containing a great thousand-fold world-system sutra is presented, followed by the application: "The wisdom of the Tathāgata is also like this; it is fully present within [all beings]."
Within the bodies of sentient beings, only the ignorant and foolish do not know or perceive it, and thus fail to obtain its benefit.
At that time, the Tathāgata universally observed all sentient beings and spoke these words: "How marvelous! How marvelous! (The word is repeated for this reason. These sentient beings—
"How is it that they possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata yet, being deluded, do not see it?

I shall instruct them in the Noble Path so that they may forever leave behind false conceptualization and, within their own bodies, perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, no different from that of a Buddha."

△ Regarding the third section, "Contemplating the Great Matter": When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, before he had yet turned the wheel of Dharma, he contemplated for a second and third time whether the wondrous Dharma he had realized could or could not be taught.
However, these words regarding the "three contemplations" carry two meanings.

First, according to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, this was spoken by the Buddha on the second seventh-day period after his initial enlightenment; during the first seven days, he had already engaged in preliminary contemplation.

That treatise judges that time is superior, because it was recited seven times on the second day after his attainment of enlightenment. (Question: If the first [period] were superior by way of its manifestation, why was it not recited during the first seven days?)

The commentary answers this as follows: During the first seven days, he engaged in contemplation regarding the causal practice (the wisdom capable of teaching) and its conditions (the capacities of those to be converted). This was because he intended to employ the sublime Dharma he had attained to suit the capacities of sentient beings; thus, it was a period of contemplative practice. [An objection is raised:
Since his original purpose was to attain enlightenment for the benefit of others, why did he contemplate for seven days? [The intent of the commentary’s response is:

While in the stage of the Dharmakāya, he perceives that there are those whose capacities can be converted and only then manifests in the world. Why, then, would further contemplation be necessary? [The answer is: It was to manifest his own enjoyment of the great Dharma-joy. This "Dharma-joy" is precisely the wisdom attained; as stated above, he realized this...
[This refers to] the unsurpassed joy of the Dharma. Why does he manifest his own joy of the Dharma? It is to cause sentient beings to increase their heart of love and reverence.

Furthermore, having relinquished such sublime joy, he speaks out of compassion for sentient beings (this corresponds to what was stated above: "pitying the delusion of beings"). The commentary states:

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* merely says "contemplation" (*cintā*), whereas here it says "three contemplations. This is because there is a textual basis externally and a doctrinal meaning internally. As for the presence of this meaning:

In contemplating and deliberating with thorough scrutiny, one must certainly reflect upon a matter three times before making it a standard for future conduct, as seen in such instances as the three requests and three prostrations.
Regarding external textual evidence, the *Analects* states: "Ji Wenzi would deliberate three times before acting."

The Master (Wenzi) heard this and said, "It is sufficient to reflect twice. (The note states: Wenzi was loyal and possessed virtuous conduct; in his undertakings he rarely erred, so it was not strictly necessary for him to reflect thrice.

Now, this statement is used to respond to the superior's previous remark regarding "twice sighing. As for the "two," the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I gazed at the tree and also walked about.
During the three periods of seven days, I contemplated such matters. (The present mention of "three reflections" refers to these three [periods]; three is...)
Seven days. He reflected upon such a great matter: "The wisdom I have attained is subtle and supreme—this is the 'great matter.
(This shall be fully cited from the original text later. Sentient beings have dull faculties; they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance. How can such as these be delivered?

(Therefore, it is said below that awakening is sometimes easy and sometimes difficult; at present, this refers only to the difficulty. Regarding the term "great matter," the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, act solely for..."
It is for the sake of one great cause and condition that [the Buddha] appears in the world;

that is to say, he appears in the world because he desires to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to attain purity therein, and so forth. The meaning will be explained below.

Below the phrase "having fully [attained] the ten powers," the commentary (*śūtra*) narrates the Buddha’s mode of transformation. This section has three parts: first, explaining the mind of benefit and salvation;

second, explaining the sudden and gradual [teachings] according to the capacity of beings; and third, explaining the characteristics of the sudden and gradual. Now, for the first part, these four lines explain the equality of the mind.

The word "already" (*ji*) means "having already"; it refers back to the preceding statement about "realizing this. That is to say, it refers to what was previously stated: "realizing this," as well as "the three types of contemplation," and so forth. "Already" [indicates that these have been established].

This concludes the subduing of Māra’s army by means of the ten powers (*daśabala*). Now, in order to manifest and expound the ritual for teaching and delivering sentient beings, the text returns to describe the signs of attaining enlightenment;

hence the word "already" (*ji*). "Complete" (*quan*) serves to distinguish these from the ten powers of a Bodhisattva, for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Bodhisattvas also possess ten powers.
The present mention of "complete" refers specifically to the Buddha-wisdom. Furthermore, at the time of subduing Māra, he entered into a state of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).

Regarding samādhi, it is not necessarily the case that it functions solely through the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*). Because its meaning lies in subduing adversaries, it should logically be called "power.

Even if one subdues them through compassion (*maitrī*), compassion is also a form of power (as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* speaks of the "power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness"). Nevertheless, the Tathāgata speaks only of the single power of the wisdom of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā-yathābhūta-jñāna-bala*).
This power has ten types of function; therefore, it is spoken of as being tenfold. As for the general name "power," it is that which is able to crush enemies.

Because it is the enemy and cannot be subdued or defeated; its ten distinct meanings are listed below. They are explained in detail in the Chapter on the Ten Powers within the *Puyan* (Universal Eye) section.
"Under the tree" refers specifically to beneath the Bodhi tree. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "That Bodhi tree was lofty, magnificent, and extraordinary;

its trunk was made of diamond (*vajra*) and its branches of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), and so forth. According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), the tree was [several hundred feet] high.
One hundred *chi* [in height]; this refers to the *pipala* tree. △ Regarding "capable of crushing Māra":

the *Sūtra on the Original Deeds* (*Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*) states that when Prince Siddhārtha was about to attain enlightenment, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree and resolved in his mind to subdue the Māra Pāpīyas. He emitted light that illuminated the three thousandfold world system.
Māra naturally heard the sound of verses being recited, which said: "The Prince desires to realize the Great Illumination; it shall empty your realm."
Pāpīyān immediately commanded his host of troops to proceed to the Bodhi tree, each displaying their own strength and manifesting terrifying forms—[such as] with swords, staves, and so forth.
The Prince, however, contemplated only the Dharma; his mind was undisturbed. [Consequently], the swords, stones, and mountains all became stuck.

Alternatively, he dwelt in emptiness and manifested lotus flowers and other forms, until finally Māra was defeated and the various devas rejoiced and offered praise. That very night, the Buddha attained the Way.
The details regarding the signs of his subduing Māra are found in a separate fascicle. Question: According to this account, the Buddha first subdued Māra and only thereafter attained the Way.
How can you maintain, in your commentary, that the Ten Powers occurred prior to the subduing of Māra? Answer: This merely follows the convenience of the textual arrangement.
This does not mean that the attainment of the Way occurs prior to the subduing of Māra. "Power" refers to that which is capable of subduing; "Māra" refers to that which is subdued.

Because it is that which subdues and that which is subdued, it is said: "Having perfected the ten powers, he is able to crush [them]," and so forth. Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "Thereupon, four minds arise": *yuan* (爰) is a particle used to introduce speech;
the *Erya* states, "*Yuan* means 'thereupon'. *Qi* (起) means to initiate or give rise to. The "four minds" refer to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which bestows happiness.

The four immeasurables—compassion (the uprooting of suffering), sympathetic joy (rejoicing in their attainment of happiness), and equanimity (regarding enemies and kin as equal)—are all immeasurable. From the bodhisattva’s first resolve until the attainment of Buddhahood, [they remain so].

One should constantly exercise these four minds to teach and transform sentient beings. Each of the four minds possesses three types of objects: namely, the object of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), the object of phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and the objectless (*anālambana*).
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, chapter fifteen, states: "Regarding the object of sentient beings: it is that which the World-Honored One’s loving-kindness takes as its object—namely, all sentient beings.
Because it is like taking one's parents, wife, children, and relatives as objects, it is called the 'object of sentient beings. Regarding the object of phenomena..."
Not seeing one’s parents, wife, children, or kinsmen, but seeing that all phenomena arise from conditions—this is called the object-condition (*dharmālambana*).
That which is without an object (*anālambana*) does not abide in the marks of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) nor the marks of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*); this is called being without an object.

Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise. Once the Buddha had subdued Māra and attained the Way, he gave rise to compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity out of pity for beings who were mired in delusion.

And thus provides salvation. △ Regarding the "Treasury of Jewels" (Ratnagarbha): In the seventh fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, while the Buddha was expounding upon permanence, bliss, self, and purity, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva asked:
"World-Honored One, do the twenty-five states of existence possess a self? The Buddha replied: "Good son, 'self' is the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; this is precisely what is meant by 'self.'"
This meaning is as follows: from the very beginning, this meaning has always been shrouded by immeasurable afflictions;
therefore, sentient beings are unable to perceive it. Good son, it is like a poor woman who has a store of pure gold within her house.
None of the members of her household, whether young or old, knew of it. At that time, there was a stranger who was skilled in expedient means.
He said to the poor woman, "I know an expedient means by which I can show you the treasure. The woman replied, "Even the members of my own household, young and old alike, do not know of it;
how could you possibly know? The man spoke again, "I am now certain that I can. The woman replied, "I too—"
"I wish to see it; please show it to me. The man immediately dug up a treasure of pure gold within his own house.
When the woman saw it, her heart was filled with joy; she conceived a sense of wonder and began to revere the man. "Good son, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this.
All sentient beings are unable to perceive it, just as that poor man could not see the treasure."
"Know this, son of good family. I now universally reveal to all sentient beings that their buddha-nature is obscured by various afflictions, just as that poor man cannot see his store of pure gold.
Today, the Tathāgata universally reveals to sentient beings the treasure-store of awakening, namely, the buddha-nature; and when sentient beings have seen this matter,"
Their hearts were filled with joy, and they took refuge in and looked up to the Tathāgata. The one of skillful means is the Tathāgata;
the poor woman is all immeasurable sentient beings; and the treasury of pure gold is the Buddha-nature.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle eighteen, further states: "Good son, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is the secret treasury of all Buddhas. Why is this so?"
Although the Buddhas possess the eleven divisions of the sūtras, they do not therein speak of the Buddha-nature, nor do they speak of the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not enter ultimate nirvāṇa; for this reason, this sūtra is called the Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata.
Because it is that which is not spoken of in the eleven divisions of the sūtras, it is called a "treasury" (kośa), just as when a person's seven treasures are not revealed to the outside.
It is for this reason that it is called a "treasury" (garbha). [The following is the analogy for the treasury: The treasury refers to future ages.
There will be wicked bhikṣus who store impure things and preach to the fourfold assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa," and so forth.
In the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, there are nine analogies. The wisdom of the Tathāgata, hidden within sentient beings, is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. This corresponds to the fifth analogy.
Furthermore, a sutra says: "For example, suppose a poor family possesses a treasury of rare jewels. The jewels cannot say, 'I am here.
Because they do not know it themselves and there is no one to tell them, they are unable to open this treasury of rare jewels. All sentient beings are likewise.
The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the great dharma-treasury, exists within their own bodies; yet they neither hear of it nor know it, remaining immersed in [delusion]."

Attached to the five desires, they transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing immeasurable suffering. For this reason, the Buddhas appear in the world to open for them the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata within their own bodies.
The meaning of the nine similes, along with the textual and semantic content of the remaining eight similes, are all explained extensively below in the Mañjuśrī Chapter.

The commentary states: "Below, regarding 'the head lost in confusion,' there are two [sections] concerning sudden and gradual according to the capacity of the vessel. Both metaphors illustrate that sentient beings lose sight of their original nature and mistakenly believe it to be fundamentally non-existent;
thus, they transmigrate through birth and death. These are the capacities (*māya*) transformed by the Buddha. There are two types of such capacities.
Therefore, two metaphors are presented. △ Regarding the phrase "deluded regarding one's head," the *Śrī-māyā-viśeṣa-vibhāga-sūtra* (Buddha-śikhara Sūtra), fascicle four, states:
Pūrṇa said, "I and the Tathāgata’s precious, awakened, perfect, bright, true, wondrous, and pure mind are non-dual and complete.

Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusive thoughts and have long remained in saṃsāra. Although I have now attained the fruit of sainthood, it is not yet ultimate. World-Honored One, all delusions..."
"Perfectly round, extinguished, solitary, wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata: for what reason do all sentient beings give rise to delusion?
How is it that they obscure their own wondrous clarity and undergo this drowning in saṃsāra? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unresolved."
Based on these manifest matters of the world, I now ask you again:

Have you not heard that in the city of Śrāvastī, a man named Yan-liao-da-duo suddenly one morning looked at his face in a mirror and became attached to the head in the reflection, seeing its eyebrows and eyes?
"Reproaching his own head, he does not see his face and takes it for a *chimei* (a mountain sprite). In a state of shameless madness, he runs about wildly. What do you think?
For what reason does this man run about wildly without cause? Pūrṇa replied, "This man’s mind is deranged; there is no other cause."
The Buddha said: "The wondrous enlightenment is perfectly luminous; it is fundamentally perfect, round, and wondrous. Since it is called delusion, how could it have a cause?

If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion? From various delusive thoughts they mutually depend upon one another, accumulating delusion upon delusion through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
Even though the Buddhas have revealed this, people still cannot turn back from it. Such a cause for delusion exists inherently because of delusion itself; one must recognize this delusion."

It has no cause; being false, it has nothing upon which to rely. Since there is not even arising, what is there to be extinguished? One who attains Bodhi is like a person awake recounting the events of a dream.
Even if the mind were sharp and clear, by what causes and conditions could one grasp objects within a dream?
How much more so when there is no cause and they fundamentally do not exist? It is like that person in the city, Yanjadatta; how could he have been terrified by any cause or condition?
He ran about his head. Suddenly his madness ceased. His head was not obtained from without; even if his madness had not ceased, what would have been lost?
Pūrṇa, the nature of delusion is thus. By what cause does it exist? You need only not follow after the three kinds of continuous succession—of worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings.
Because these three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise. Then, within your own mind, the *yāvadattha* (the "ever-running")...
The many states of madness will naturally subside; this subsiding is itself Bodhi. The supreme, pure, and luminous mind is coextensive with the Dharma-realm and is not obtained from others.
What need is there for arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization? Regarding the phrase "leaving one's father":

in the *Fa-hua* (Lotus Sutra), in the "Chapter on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Parable" (*Aupamya-parivarta*), Subhūti and the other three heard the unprecedented Dharma and understood it through these parables.

Explanation (this is a complete summary of the essential meaning): The general purport is as follows. Suppose there is a man who, in his youth, abandons his father and flees, dwelling for a long time in another country.
When he reached the age of fifty, having grown old and being further impoverished, he traveled in all directions in search of food and clothing.
Wandering by degrees, he eventually arrived at his native land. Meanwhile, his father had previously come seeking his son but had not found him; he settled in a certain city.

His family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable treasures and riches. The impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate.
From afar he saw his father seated upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet, surrounded by a respectful retinue of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders.
His body was adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold. The official...
The servants and attendants stood on his left and right, each holding a white fly-whisk. The impoverished son was terrified;

he regretted having come here and secretly thought with suspicion that this must be a king or a high minister. Fearing he would be coerced into service, he fled in haste. The elder recognized him from afar;
his heart filled with joy, he thought, "My wealth now has an heir," and he dispatched men to seize him. The impoverished son cried out in grievance, thinking to himself, "I am innocent."
He was imprisoned. The father, knowing his son’s lowly status, employed a stratagem by sending a haggard man who spoke to him slowly:
"There is work here; I will pay you double wages to hire you to clear away the filth. The father put on coarse, tattered clothes, took up a refuse-pitcher, and said, "Work diligently;
do not go elsewhere. I am like your father, and you are like my own son. He called him "son."

Although the impoverished son rejoiced, he still considered himself a hired laborer; thus, for twenty years, he was made to remove filth. Later, as they came to trust one another, he entered and left without hindrance;

nevertheless, his dwelling place remained in that same spot. When his father was near death, he summoned his son and assembled his kinsmen, kings, and ministers, entrusting him with his wealth and treasures.
Subsequently, according to the Dharma, it was said: "World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder is none other than [the Buddha]."
“Tathāgata, we are all sons of the Buddha... [and so forth]. Amidst birth and death, we have experienced various afflictions;

deluded and ignorant, we took pleasure in and were attached to inferior dharmas. Today, the World-Honored One has caused us to reflect and cleanse away the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all dharmas, enabling us to obtain the price of a single day’s labor for the sake of reaching nirvāṇa. Our hearts are filled with joy and contentment, and we consider this to be a great deal.”
The Buddha then set us aside and did not distinguish for us that we too possessed a share in the treasure-house of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
The World-Honored One taught the wisdom of the Tathāgata through skillful means;

we, having obtained a small nirvāṇa from the Buddha, considered it a great attainment and had no aspiration or pursuit toward this Mahāyāna. Furthermore, because the wisdom of the Tathāgata was intended for the sake of all bodhisattvas...
He has expounded [the Dharma], yet he himself has no aspiration for this. Why is that?

The Buddha, knowing that our minds delight in the lesser teachings, spoke to us according to our capacities through the power of skillful means; we did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha, but now we finally know it.
The World-Honored One is not stingy with the Buddha’s wisdom. If we had delighted in the Great Vehicle, the Buddha would have...
"Please preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for us. In this sutra, only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is taught; therefore, we say that originally we had no mind seeking anything.
Now, the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously. [Commentary: Regarding the ease and difficulty of awakening to existence:
"The one who lost his head" is like one whose mad mind has ceased; once it ceases, it is Bodhi—this is easy. "The one who abandoned his father" is...
For twenty years he removed filth, yet he remained in his original place, refusing to believe early on that this was the son of the elder;

thus, it is difficult [to lead him]. △ Regarding the phrase "the Immortal Garden" (*śrī-udyāna*) and so forth: it is because the preceding faculties possess the distinction between those who are easily awakened and those who are difficult to awaken.
The Buddha spoke of the distinction between the sudden teaching and the gradual teaching. "Xianyuan" (Garden of the Immortals) refers to Mṛgadāva (the Deer Park).
Because this was the dwelling place of sages of antiquity, the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) states:

After the Buddha had attained enlightenment, on the sixth seventh-day period, he went to the Deer Park of the Sages in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and delivered Ājñātakauṇḍinya. The Buddha proclaimed, "Come, bhikṣu!"
The Chapter on Precepts (*Śīla-skandha*) was thus initiated. The *Fǔfǎzàng jīng* (Scripture of the Attached Dharma-Treasury) states:

"The Buddha resided at the Abode of the Ancient Seers in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, where he first turned the Wheel of the Dharma for the five bhikṣus. The *Kāiyuán lù*, fascicle 13, also says: "It began at the Garden of the Seers and concluded at the Golden River.
Wang Bo’s preface to the *Sū lǜshī shū* (Commentary on Master Sū) states: "The Garden of the Seers was the origin of the foundation."

"Welcome" is used to harmonize sentient beings. The River of the Ganges (the Bodhi Tree) extinguishes traces by relying on the pure precepts as one's teacher. Regarding the "Site of Enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*):
in Sanskrit it is *bodhi*, which here means "enlightenment. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* states: "It is the ultimate, perfectly luminous great wisdom that is capable of realization."

A "site" (*dharmapada*) is the place of realization and awakening; it is located two hundred *li* west of Rājagṛha in Magadha, at the center of heaven and earth, beneath the Bodhi tree upon the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*).
According to the Dharma, all myriad practices constitute a site of enlightenment, for it is the place where principle and wisdom meet.
To demonstrate that what is taught accords with what has been realized, he speaks without moving from that very spot.
The Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). The Sudden Teaching begins with the *Avataṃsaka*. The sutra states: "Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Magadha, in the place of practice at the Bodhimanda, having just attained perfect enlightenment...
[surrounded] by as many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as there are motes of dust in ten worlds. *Commentary on the Arising of the Sudden and Gradual Teachings* (Shu jiao xing dun jian).

This refers to the fact that, for those of superior capacity who are easily awakened, he attained perfect enlightenment at the site of Bodhi and, without moving from that place, immediately established the Sudden Teaching.
For those of superior capacity who are difficult to awaken, he proceeded to the Abode of the Seers in Vārāṇasī and established the Gradual Teaching.
The beginning of the Gradual Teaching was the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths heard by the five bhikṣus; as for the middle three...
At that time, the five periods were taught sequentially, with each location being distinct, culminating in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*; these are all termed the "gradual teaching.
As for the "sudden teaching," it will be explained below. At the beginning of these two teachings, each was established in this one place;

thereafter, each came to have its own various locations, and at other times, they were not restricted to only these two places. Now, by pointing to these two places, we are merely discussing their original sources.
This marks the initial arising [of the teaching].

Below the passage "The Commentary gradually establishes the five periods," the third section clarifies the characteristics of the sudden and gradual [teachings]. Regarding the differences between the five periods:

after the Buddha first attained enlightenment and completed his three-week period of reflection, he proceeded to the Deer Park and various other residences; for twelve years, he preached various [teachings].
Conditioned phenomena arise dependently and are without self; however, the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) has not yet been taught.

This is called the "Teaching for the Initial Period," which refers to the one collection (*piṭaka*) of Hīnayāna sūtras, such as the Āgamas. During the second period, based on the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the emptiness of all phenomena was taught;
however, the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected natures (*pariniṣpanna*) were not yet said to exist. This is called the "Teaching of Emptiness," referring to the various schools [of Mahāyāna].

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* belong to this [second period]. During the third period, he taught the Mahāyāna of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), asserting that while objects are empty, consciousness exists;
this is called the Middle Way teaching, and includes such sūtras as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.

During the fourth period, he revealed the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision to all sentient beings, unifying the three vehicles into one vehicle, reconciling the provisional with the ultimate, and showing that all myriad virtues lead toward Bodhi; this is called the [One Vehicle] teaching.

The teaching to which he returned is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. During the fifth period, as he was about to enter nirvana, he taught that all sentient beings, even icchantikas, possess Buddha-nature;
that all who possess a mind will certainly become Buddhas; and that [the nature of Buddhahood] is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

This is called the Teaching of Constant Abiding; it is precisely the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. Because it brings a single class of practitioners to fulfillment from beginning to end, it is collectively termed the "Gradual Teaching.
Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "emptiness and existence manifest alternately": "alternately" (*die*) means in succession.

This refers to how, with respect to self and dharmas, mind and objects, or the ultimate and conventional truths, they are presented either sequentially or simultaneously, alternating and confronting one another. "Manifesting" (*zhang*) means to reveal all phenomena.

This is the meaning of emptiness and existence. Furthermore, regarding the objects and mind of the initial stage, there are two pairs of emptiness and existence: first, in the teachings of the first period, both object and mind exist;

second, in the teachings of the second period, both object and mind are empty (in these two, the former and latter are mutually alternating). Third, in the teachings of the third period, the object is empty while the mind exists (simultaneously alternating).
Regarding the ultimate and conventional truths, there are naturally four propositions: namely, in the teachings of the second period, the conventional exists while the ultimate is... [empty].

The teaching of the fourth and fifth periods is conventional emptiness (because it destroys the worldly notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity); it is true existence (because it reveals the supramundane permanence and so forth; thus the Sūtra says: "Emptiness is saṃsāra; non-emptiness is nirvāṇa").
Regarding the teaching of the third period, the fourfold two-truths (catuḥsatya-dvaya) view the preceding and succeeding stages as mutually empty and existent.

If one compares the teachings of the second and third periods: in the second period, both the ultimate and the conventional are empty; in the third period, both the ultimate and the conventional are existent. This is based on...

My teaching also consists of four propositions. That is to say: in the first period of instruction, for those of the initial vehicle of humans and devas, both the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) exist.
In the intermediate [period] of the Mahāyāna, both the self and phenomena are empty. Next, in the initial [period] of the Hīnayāna, the self is empty while phenomena exist.

Finally, in *nirvāṇa*, the self exists while phenomena are empty (for that sutra refutes the Hīnayāna notion of non-self and explicitly teaches the true self). Altogether, there are ten pairs of "emptiness" and "existence" mentioned above, all of which are based upon...

Regarding the Dharma, it is constrained by time; as phenomena alternate between concealment and manifestation, they are said to "alternately reveal" one another. (Although what follows further discusses the relative nature of emptiness and existence, those lacking the mental capacity need not be recounted here.

As for distinguishing the depth and shallowness of teachings that speak of emptiness or existence according to the various doctrinal systems: for example, when discussing external objects, if one compares the first and second periods of the teaching, the former asserts existence while the latter asserts emptiness;
thus, emptiness is profound while existence is shallow. However, if one speaks of the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)...

Regarding the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), there are two pairs of contrasts: namely, the comparison between the teachings of the second and third periods, and the contrast between emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhava*).

Emptiness is shallow and existence is deep. Furthermore, comparing the third with the fourth and fifth [periods], the former involves existence and the latter involves emptiness; here, emptiness is deep and existence is shallow.

If one speaks of the "self" (*ātman*), comparing the first and last [periods], the first three are said to be empty and the latter two are said to be existent; thus, emptiness is shallow and existence is deep. Moreover, regarding humans and devas...

It is said that [things] exist; the teachings of the first three periods state they are empty. There are varying depths to this emptiness. All other instances of depth and shallowness should be understood by analogy with this.

Because of this, various teachings may refute existence and praise emptiness, or disparage emptiness and praise existence; without grasping this intent, it is difficult to understand the words of the Sage.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Sudden [teachings] have no two truths," etc.: this merely reveals the Middle Way, the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). First...

The meaning of *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) has two interpretations. First, when the two are fused and clarified within the Middle Way, the identity of the ultimate and conventional truths (*satya*) as non-dual constitutes the primary meaning.
Thus, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna* (Renwang jing) states: "Regarding the truths, they are always dual (the ultimate and the conventional); regarding their realization, they are always one."

(Reality is precisely the conventional; the conventional is precisely reality. To penetrate this non-duality and enter the ultimate truth of the first principle—this is why the ancients said that when both truths are present, it is already a "brief excerpt" (*pi-chao*). Therefore, I have not supplemented it.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*,
Scroll One (Part I) / *Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll One (Part II),
completed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.
[Commentary: Regarding this present sutra, is it of the class of the Sudden [Teaching]? Below, the second major section specifically describes the tenet and purpose of this sutra.
This section has three parts: first, the presentation of the tenet; second, the formal description; and third, the conclusion regarding its excellence. This is the first part.

Now, since the Tripitaka does not exist apart from the two teachings of the Sudden and the Gradual, we must now point to their respective categories. As for the Gradual, it begins at the Deer Park and ends at the Crane...

Lin: From beginning to end, this gradually leads a certain class of practitioners; among these, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras represent the convergence of the provisional toward the ultimate.

Within the gradual teachings of the Mahāyāna, they are the final and culminating doctrines. Regarding the sudden, there are two types: first, the suddenness of the pedagogical method (*saṃdarśana-vidhi*).

This refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. First, at the time of his initial enlightenment, the Buddha taught the principle and phenomena, their origin and end, and their cause and effect all at once in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), thereby exhausting the ultimate principle and fully realizing the nature.

Second, there is the "sudden teaching according to capacity," which means that for ordinary beings who possess full afflictions yet have superior faculties, he suddenly points directly to the absolute Middle Way and true nature; this differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras, which involve a threefold progression.
The provisional teachings that dismantle existence can be reconciled; they merely manifest the single true nature of awakening.

This is evident in more than forty scriptures, such as the *Śrīmālā*, *Ghanavyūha*, *Vajrasamādhi*, *Tathāgatagarbha*, *Samantaprabhāgarbha*, and *Avataṃsaka* Sūtras, all of which contain little discussion of phenomenal circumstances.

They lack the expedient devices such as the three carts, the removal of filth, or the illusory city, which require reconciliation through causal conditions. Therefore, this sūtra is pointed out as being of the sudden teaching.

This belongs to the same category [as the previous]. It is a sudden revelation of the essence according to the capacity of the recipient, not a suddenness in terms of the formal method of transformation (*vyañjana*).
Since it is not a gradual teaching, it does not fall within the three periods or five periods.

"Below 'Therefore, the Tathāgata'... [The commentary] consists of two parts: first, the formal narration; second, the actual exposition. The text has three sections: first, the narration of the introductory section (*nidāna*); second, the narration of the main body (*śarīra*); third, the narration of the dissemination (*pariṇāmana*).
Now, for the first part, these four lines narrate the introductory section. Regarding "the land of tranquil light" (*sukhāloka-bhūmi*): Tiantai established four types of lands.

1. The Land of Mixed Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages (*pariṇāmanā-vikurvaṇa*). 2. The Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*). 3. The Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction (*sva-para-sambhoga*). 4.
The Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-dharmatā-bhūmi*; this is the *dharmatā*-land). The Land of Skillful Means is not found in the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Abhidharma) teachings;

it was established by Tiantai based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The ninety-fifth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The causes from previous lives of an Arhat..."
Regarding the body received through conditions, it must necessarily be extinguished according to its capacity. In what place is the Buddha-way accomplished? The answer is:

there is a pure buddha-field beyond the three realms where even the name of "affliction" does not exist. In that land, at the dwelling place of the Buddha, one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and fully accomplishes the Buddha-way.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "There are arhats; I [taught them] in other lands," and so forth.

The present sutra states: "Entering the Great Radiant Treasury of Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā*), in the correct reception of *samādhi*, and so forth, up to 'because of conforming to non-duality'—this is the Land of Tranquil Light.
Regarding "the single source of ordinary beings and sages," the text says:

"All Tathāgatas dwell in the majesty of light and maintain it" (since Buddhas question one another regarding this, it is the Dharma-nature land). "These sentient beings are the ground of pure awakening" (the meaning of which will be explained below). Regarding "manifestly receiving":
"Utilizing the body" refers to the enjoyment by others (*parabhogatā*). As the text states: "Because he manifests all pure lands within the non-dual realm.

Regarding "the principal and the associates gathering together": after the sūtra has enumerated the assembly of bodhisattvas, it concludes by stating that they, along with their retinues, all enter into samādhi and dwell together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma (the meaning of which is found in the lower portion of the commentary).

Below the section on Mañjuśrī, there are two parts: first, the introduction to the main body of the treatise; second, the actual exposition. This section has two sub-divisions: first, the authentic faith and understanding;

second, cultivation and realization based upon that understanding. Now, for the first part, there are eight phrases which clarify faith and understanding. "Mañju" is the correct Sanskrit term for Wen-shu (Mañjuśrī).
The meaning of his name and virtue is explained as follows in the sub-commentary (shū). △ Regarding "Great Being" (Mahāsattva): he is a Great Being of the Dharma-body.
△ Regarding "first asking about the original cause": "first" (sō) has the sense of being the very beginning. There are two senses of "first" here:
first, among all the bodhisattvas who had not yet asked, Mañjuśrī asks first; since no one had previously asked this, it is called "first. Second, regarding that which is asked...
This is the matter. It is the foremost dharma that must be understood within the Buddha-dharma.

Prior to this dharma, there is no other principle of cause and effect in the Buddha-dharma that can serve as the essential starting point. Regarding "The Original Arising" (*benqi*): it refers to the initial mind arising from the fundamental cause.

For further meanings, consult the subsequent commentary which introduces the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Awakening of Faith). [It explains] the realization of the two types of awakening and the arousal of the three minds.
The practice of the five elements is taught in such places as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the story of Sudhana. △ Regarding the term *bhagavat*: the *Buddhabhūmi Sūtra* states, "Thus have I heard:
at one time, the Bhagavat... The commentary says: "As for the term *bhagavat*, the word *bhaga* functions according to six meanings:

first, the meaning of sovereignty; second, the meaning of brilliance; third, the meaning of majesty; fourth, the meaning of renown; fifth, [the meaning of fortune]; sixth, [the meaning of destruction]."
The meaning of *śrī* (auspiciousness). The meaning of *bhaga* (noble excellence). As a verse says: "Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), splendor (*tejas*), and beauty (*darśanīyatā*);
fame (*yaśas*), auspiciousness (*śrī*), and noble excellence (*bhaga*)—one should know that these six distinct meanings are collectively termed *Bhagavān*.
In this way, all Tathāgatas possess the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) without exception; therefore, the Tathāgata..."
He is named Bhagavat. What is the meaning of this? It means that because all Tathāgatas are forever unbound by any afflictions (*kleśa*), they possess the sense of mastery (*vaśitva*).
Because they have been refined and purified by the intensely blazing great wisdom, they possess the sense of brilliance.
Because they are adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), they possess the sense of physical excellence. Thus, they are perfected in all supreme qualities.
Because there is nothing he does not know, it possesses the meaning of "renown. Because all the world approaches, makes offerings to, and praises him, it possesses the meaning of "auspiciousness.
Because he constantly exerts skillful means to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without ever wearying or ceasing, it possesses the meaning of "noble dignity.
Other meanings are found in separate volumes. △ Regarding "Supreme Honored One" (*Bhagavat*): it refers to the ultimate...
He is the Honored One (*bhadanta*). Furthermore, the myriad people serve the king; the king serves the Supreme Deity (*shangdi*), who is none other than the Heavenly Lord (*devendra*).
All the devas revere the Buddha, and the worthy sages of the Three Vehicles likewise attend upon the Buddha.

The Buddha is the most honored among all saints, just as the moon is supreme among the stars and the ocean is supreme among all streams. Therefore, he is called the Most Honored One (*zhizun*). △ Regarding "The Preface" (*shoushu*) at the beginning:
This is the initial presentation. Regarding the ultimate fruit, the Sūtra’s primary response begins by stating:

"Good son, the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gate called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), from which flow forth all pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and *pāramitās*, teaching them to Bodhisattvas.
This "Perfect Enlightenment" thus designated refers to the Great State (*mahā-sthāna*).

The fruit (phala). Its essence encompasses both the defiled and the pure; this refers to its existence within the Unsurpassed Dharma King. As it says below: "The beginningless illusory ignorance is all established from within this.
If one discusses the One Mind within the Middle [Treatise], it occupies the stage of the Great Position in the causal state and likewise encompasses both the defiled and the pure;
therefore, it is designated as the "mind of sentient beings," and its explanation includes the two meanings of awakening and non-awakening. As for what is called "ultimate" (niṣṭhā):
In this treatise, initial awakening (shijue) merges with original awakening (benjue); when the initial and the original are non-dual, it is called "ultimate.
Regarding the phrase in the *Commentary*, "one who illuminates this true essence":

the Sūtra states, "The ground of the original arising of all Tathāgatas" (this cites the preceding question), "all rely upon the perfectly illuminating, pure aspect of awakening" (the wisdom that illuminates) which "permanently severs ignorance, thereby attaining the Buddha-way" (this simultaneously indicates the meaning of extinguishing the forms of those dreams mentioned below, thereby establishing the foundation).
[The cause]. △ Regarding the phrase "extinguishing that dream-form," the Sūtra says: "What is ignorance? Good son, all sentient beings from time immemorial...
and so forth, until: "...this ignorance has no real substance. It is like a person in a dream;

while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found. (The "dreamer" is a metaphor for ignorance. Now, by means of this metaphor, [the text] demonstrates its extinction.)

Ignorance (which, combined with the preceding [section], constitutes the cause for the manifestation of the True Nature). The Commentary states: "Knowing that there is no self or person, who is it that undergoes transmigration? The Sūtra says:
"One who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment knows these to be like flowers in the sky; thus there is no transmigration, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death.

They are not non-existent because of being produced (it is not through the practice of contemplation that they cease to exist), but because their fundamental nature is non-existent (the self-nature of birth and death is originally non-existent)."

Below the section "Various Illusory Transformations," the second part concerns cultivation based on understanding (*prativedha-bhāvanā*). This text has three sections: first, a general explanation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*);

second, a specific explanation of contemplative practice; and third, the preparatory practices for the site of enlightenment (*maṇḍala-prayoga*). Within the first of these, there are again three parts: first, the accomplishment of contemplation being identical to that of the Buddha;

second, an inquiry and explanation regarding the source of delusion; and third, a brief differentiation of the stages (*bhūmi*). Here, we address the first point—contemplative accomplishment being identical to the Buddha—concerning "various illusions."

Regarding the phrase "The Transformation, etc.": This is the answer to the inquiry posed by Samantabhadra, intended to establish the fundamental application of the mind for the cultivation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

That is to say, Samantabhadra asks: "For one who cultivates the Mahāyāna, having heard this *Perfect Enlightenment*, how should they practice? (This question is raised by way of examining the practitioner's faculties.

"If those sentient beings know that [all things] are like an illusion, then their own bodies and minds are also illusions; how then can they use an illusion to further cultivate an illusion? (Illusion upon illusion...)

[He] asked: "If the nature of all illusions were to be completely extinguished, then there would be no mind. Who would then practice? [This addresses the question of who practices if all is annihilated;

the above points conflict with the characteristics of practice. If one has never practiced from the beginning, how can the mind of delusive appearances now be liberated? [This prevents the fault of not practicing. The Buddha replied:
"The various illusory transformations of all sentient beings are all produced from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*tathāgatagarbha*), just like..."

"Empty flowers arise from emptiness" (this is designated as the fundamental meaning). △ Regarding the commentary on "when illusion is exhausted, awakening is perfected": this contains two layers of meaning.

The first refers to the *Puxian* (Samantabhadra) chapter, which concerns the principle of employing the mind. The second refers to the *Puyan* (Universal Eye) chapter, where long-term engagement with objects through the employment of the mind correctly constitutes the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
As for the first meaning, the Sūtra says: "Who can extinguish illusory flowers? The nature of emptiness is indestructible. The multitude...
The illusory mind arises and returns to extinction based upon that very illusion. When all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind is unmoving.

Thus, to know that illusion is itself detachment requires no expedient means; to be detached from illusion is itself awakening, and there is no gradual progression. This is explained subsequently in the context of correct cultivation.

This is what the Buddha taught in the "Universal Eye" chapter: Bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect awakened mind should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions; they should first rely upon the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*.

Firmly maintain the prohibitive precepts, dwell peacefully among the assembly, and sit in meditative seclusion within a quiet chamber. Constantly contemplate that this body is a provisional combination of the four great elements which will eventually separate;
that the sense organs, objects, and conditions are provisionally named "mind. Ultimately, there is no such thing as an illusory body, an illusory mind, or illusory objects.

"Even the extinction of illusion is extinguished. This refers to the two characters "illusion-exhausted" (huàn-jìn) in the Commentary. Because the extinction of illusion is itself extinguished, that which is not illusion does not cease.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is gone, the brightness appears. It is also like a *maṇi* jewel and so forth.

This refers to the two characters "awakened-perfection" (jué-yuán) in the Commentary. △ Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "the mind penetrates and the Dharma pervades," the Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva and [the others]..."

Sentient beings of the world, because they realize that all illusions are but the extinction of reflected images, at that time attain purity that is directionless and boundless empty space, manifested by awakening (another interpretation:
it is only up to this point that the two characters "awakening-perfection" [覺圓] apply). Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the mind is revealed as pure;
because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are seen as pure, and so forth, even unto one body and many bodies, and one realm...

The many realms are entirely pure; this is all the penetration of the mind. (However, there is also the meaning of the penetration of phenomena here; because the phrasing of the commentary is narrow, it is included but not explicitly revealed.
Regarding the pervasiveness of phenomena, the Sūtra says: "Good son, the nature of awakening is all-pervasive, pure and unmoving, for it is perfect and boundless."

One should know that the six sense faculties pervade the *dharmadhātu*, and so forth (this refers to their mutual interpenetration). This continues up to the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates, which pervade the *dharmadhātu*, and so forth.
Finally, one comes to realize that sentient beings have been, from the very beginning, Buddhas. These are the two characters for "pervasion of phenomena" (*fàbiàn*).

[The meaning of] mental penetration (*xintōng*) inherently contains the pervasion of phenomena, yet the meaning of the pervasion of phenomena does not necessarily contain mental penetration. This is because the mind itself is the awakened mind and has nothing further to pervade; rather, it is simply that all phenomena are manifested in dependence upon the mind. When the mind is obstructed...

Therefore, while all phenomena possess their own distinct entities and boundaries, the mind-penetration (*cittapraveśa*) is without boundaries, and thus it is "pervasive" (*vyāpin*). However, the passage concerning sentient beings attaining Buddhahood belongs to this section;
in the present commentary, I have taken its essential meaning and will describe it later in the section on resolving difficulties, where it shall serve as the formal introduction to the inquiry.
A careful examination of this will make it clear.
From "The essence of mind is fundamentally Buddha" onwards, the text investigates and explains the source of delusion. As for the first two phrases:
they refer back to the previous statement regarding sentient beings attaining Buddhahood, citing it here to answer the objection raised by Vajragarbha. Vajragarbha’s objection was as follows:
"If all sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, why is there still the existence of all ignorance? If all ignorance were originally..."

There is. For what reason does the Tathāgata further say that he has been a Buddha from the beginning, and that the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the ten directions have fundamentally attained the Buddha-way, only to subsequently give rise to ignorance?
When will all Tathāgatas ever again produce afflictions (*kleśa*)? Now, to summarize the general meaning of the Buddha’s response:
it is as stated in passages such as "the mind is fundamentally the Buddha," which means that the essence of the true mind is fundamentally the Buddha. However, since beginningless time...
Since beginningless time, deluded thoughts have continued in succession; thus, one does not realize oneself to be the Buddha. Therefore, the Treatise states:
"All sentient beings are not called 'Awakened,' because from beginningless time their thoughts have continued in succession, never departing from deluded thought.

This is why it is called "beginningless ignorance" (*anādikālikā-avidyā*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Afflictions and bodhi both have no beginning. Thus, we know that since the beginningless past, sentient beings...
It has always been the Buddha; it has always been that one had not yet awakened. This does not mean that one first became a Buddha and only later gave rise to ignorance and so forth;
therefore, there is no fault of contradiction. It is simply because every thought-moment is fundamentally empty, and thus every mind is fundamentally the Buddha. As the Treatise says:

What is called the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought. This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is the Tathāgata’s impartial *dharmakāya*.
This teaching holds that the very nature of thought is fundamentally free from thought, and thus it is termed "freedom from thought.

Therefore, it is said: "By means of thought arising, one drifts along. To "drift" means to temporarily emerge within the realms of humans and devas; to "sink" means to fall into the three evil paths. (The *Wenlun xu* also says: "Chasing after...")

"Regarding the rising and sinking through delusion and awakening, I wonder if this is the same as that [other teaching]. Answer: Both the phrasing and the meaning differ. That [teaching] takes delusion as 'sinking' and awakening as 'rising. This [text], however, means that within delusion itself there is naturally rising and sinking.
