In this same way, because sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform, one employs all manner of piercing and urgent words. Thus...

One may enter the Vinaya; all [beings] are thereby tamed. Once the Truth of Origination—the accumulation of delusions and karma—is extinguished, the Truth of Suffering—old age, death, and so forth—is immediately severed.
Therefore, it is said that for the sake of old age, sickness, and death, he teaches the matters of taming.

If one speaks according to the non-obstruction of the provisional and the real, teaching the matters of taming means appearing in the world for the sake of old age, sickness, and death; teaching the Dharma realized is precisely for the sake of the One Great [Vehicle].
Thus, one transcends the world. Because afflictions and karma have been subdued, one realizes the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

Through this realization of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, both delusion and suffering vanish; they mutually condition one another in a reciprocal cycle. Although the commentary mentions only two characters, it encompasses these two aspects.

The first [interpretation] states: "Although the three vehicles are taught. The second [interpretation] states: "Although the dharmas realized and so forth are taught. Regarding the phrase "although the three vehicles are taught":

this refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the World-Honored One, fearing that those in the assembly might become suspicious upon hearing it said that the Buddha appears only to teach the Single Vehicle—wondering why he had previously, since the Deer Park, taught various other dharmas—therefore raised the example of how the Buddhas of the three periods of time, although they teach various [dharmas],...

All vehicles are but the One Vehicle. As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, have expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings;
these dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle. All these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, ultimately attain the knowledge of all modes. Thus it is said.
By the power of skillful means, [the Buddha] distinguishes and teaches three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Since it is stated that these various [teachings] all constitute the single vehicle, one knows that although there are three vehicles, this does not contradict the statement that they are "only" for that purpose.

Regarding the phrase "though it speaks of what is realized, etc.," this refers generally to the difficulty of transcending old age, sickness, death, and worldly suffering as taught in the *Anitya-sūtra*. Thus, in these two instances of doubt and difficulty, the term "only" (*kevalam*) is explained.
One passage: although it is said that the many are all one, this is merely because the one is described as being many. Regarding the term "distinct" (*bié*) in the commentary:
it refers exclusively to the causes and conditions for the arising of the single scripture, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), and does not discuss other scriptures;

hence it is called "distinct. This section has two parts: first, the enumeration of the numbers; second, the detailed explanation, beginning with the commentary on "The practice of causes has its basis. Regarding "the basis of practice": [text continues].
That is to say, all the *pāramitās* and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) are practices of the cause;

it is only through the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) that they become practices of realization and are termed the "correct cause. Therefore, the Sūtra points to the awakened mind as the root of all practices.
It is said that the pāramitās and other qualities flow forth from Perfect Enlightenment; this is fully contained in the chapter on Mañjuśrī, where one may consult the scriptural text.
The commentary provides a preemptive exposition of this point here.

The commentary on the section "The two [extremes] are extinguished" consists of two parts. First, the exposition of the meaning. Regarding the phrase "the extinction of bodhi and so forth," the subsequent text states:
"In the wondrous, perfect, enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas, there is fundamentally no such thing as bodhi or nirvāṇa;

furthermore, there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the failure to attain it. It further states: "Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are all equally like flowers in the sky."
Regarding the phrase "without beginning and without end" in the Commentary: Bodhi has no beginning, and afflictions have no end.

This differs from the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiang zong), which holds that bodhi has a beginning and afflictions have an end. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The mundane world is not destroyed; the supramundane does not exhaust.
Regarding the phrase "neither increasing nor decreasing," the treatise states: "All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas..."
The Buddha is without increase or decrease; he is not born in the past limit, nor does he perish in the future limit. He is ultimately eternal and constant.
From the very beginning, his nature has been spontaneously replete with all merits, namely, the great wisdom-light of his own essence, and so forth.
It is even called the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is said that there is neither increase nor decrease. Regarding the "ultimate fruit" (*niṣṭhā-phala*) mentioned in the commentary:

this sutra states later on that when obstructions are exhausted and vows fulfilled, one ascends to the pure Dharma-palace of liberation and realizes the wondrously adorned city of Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vajra-bodhi*).
This is precisely what the commentary refers to as the ultimate fruit. There are many such passages in the subsequent text, such as where it says: ... [text continues] ...
Because the three matters are perfectly realized, it is called ultimate nirvāṇa. Furthermore, it is said:

"If the obstacles of both phenomena and principle have been forever severed and extinguished, one immediately enters the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous perfect enlightenment, fulfilling bodhi and great nirvāṇa. It is also said:
"All obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment," whereby one knows that the marks of the fruit are obliterated and the truly perfect fruit is established.
...Furthermore, [the commentary] states "below," which refers to the second section of the text. This is the passage at the end of the "Universal Eye" chapter. It reads in full:
"If these Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age cultivate this mind until it achieves accomplishment, there is herein neither cultivation nor accomplishment.
Perfect Enlightenment shines universally; it is quiescent and non-dual. Within this, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of..."
It is said that the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya*) are like flowers in the sky:

arising and ceasing in confusion, neither identical nor distinct, neither bound nor liberated. Only then does one come to know that sentient beings have been enlightened from the very beginning, and that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*): it includes what was previously cited, namely that there is originally no bodhi and no nirvāṇa, and so on.
The *Wén* (Text). The categories of *wén* are also numerous; they must be further examined and explained.

Regarding the third section of the *Shū* (Commentary), "Decisive Selection" (*juézhé*), this refers to the definitive selection [of the path] that requires the realization of the principle through the Perfect and Sudden (*yuándùn*) approach and practice in accordance with that principle.

It excludes those who exclusively claim that one is inherently perfect and true from the beginning and thus does not require cultivation, as well as those who exclusively advocate for the severing of hindrances and the realization of truth [through gradual means].

Regarding "extinguishing the ordinary and becoming a sage" and "one who has awakened to the principle should practice," these meanings are fully contained within the *Benqi yindi shu* (Commentary on the Ground of the Original Vow).
This section consists of two parts: first, the explicit clarification of awakening and practice. As for the statement "Universal Worthy asks," the text says:
"All sentient beings who practice the Mahāyāna, having heard of this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment, how should they practice? World-Honored One."
If those sentient beings know that [all things] are like an illusion, then their own bodies and minds are also illusory. How can they use an illusion to cultivate an illusion?
If the nature of all illusions were completely extinguished, there would be no mind; who then would perform cultivation? Why, then, do you further say that cultivation is like an illusion?
If sentient beings fundamentally do not engage in cultivation, they will forever dwell within the transformations of birth and death.
Having never understood the realm that is like an illusion, how can the mind of discursive thought be liberated? Regarding the passage "The Buddha said," the text states:
"The various illusory transformations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

They are like flowers in the sky that appear from space; though the illusory flowers perish, the nature of space is not destroyed. The illusory minds of sentient beings likewise depend upon [this same source]."
Illusions are extinguished; when all illusions are utterly extinguished, the awakened mind is unmoving. It is further said: "One should remain far removed from all illusory and false realms;
even the act of distancing oneself from such illusions must be further transcended. This is like the analogy of drilling for fire and so forth. As a verse states:

Illusion arises from various perceptions; when illusion ceases, perception becomes perfected. The "Chapter on the Universal Eye" states: "Because illusory body, illusory mind, and illusory objects cease, even the cessation of illusion itself ceases.
Because the cessation of illusion has ceased, that which is not illusion does not cease. It is like polishing a mirror: when defilements are exhausted, clarity appears. It further states:
"Having realized all illusions, because the reflected images are extinguished, one then attains the purity that is without direction."
The boundless space is manifested by awakening; because awakening is perfectly luminous, it reveals the purity of the mind and so forth.
To say that one "should distance oneself" from these refers to the arising of illusory wisdom. "Illusory objects" refer to the illusions that are to be eliminated.
The phrase "the extinction of the illusory body, mind, and sense-objects" refers to the exhaustion of illusion.
Expressions such as "further distancing from distancing," "the extinction of the extinction of illusion," and so forth, all refer to the cessation of cognition (*jñāna*).

Expressions such as "the perfection of awakening," "that which is non-illusory and does not perish," "the exhaustion of defilements and the manifestation of clarity," and "that which is revealed by awakening" all refer to the perfect luminosity of the awakened mind. *Commentary:* However...

Now, below, two seals are set forth to define its essentials. The text has two parts: first, to reveal the reason for these essentials. The word "only" (*wei*) serves to distinguish those of perfect realization;
it refers to the essence of the true nature within the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). One knows that this true nature follows conditions to form illusory phenomena;
because conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all things are empty. This teaching ensures one does not sink into the extreme of non-cultivation. Now, there are those who merely...
To speak of emptiness and illusion while failing to realize that their essence is the numinous nature (lingxing) is, on the contrary, to deviate from cultivation.

Why is this? Because empty space cannot be removed or severed, nor can it be supplemented or augmented; therefore, emptiness cannot be cultivated. Furthermore, the flowers seen by one with cataracts have no substance that can be severed;
thus, they ultimately lack the principle of bearing fruit. Therefore, illusion cannot be cultivated. This is the loss of the true meaning when the Southern School discusses Chan.
There are many such individuals of this kind. Among those who study the sūtras and śāstras, there are those under the school of Bhāviveka in the Western Regions (India);

likewise, among those in this land (China) who practice the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*) but have not grasped their true meaning, there are also such types. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the followers of the Vaipulya establish a doctrine of emptiness and illusion;

the Western Regions classify them as non-Buddhists who merely affiliate themselves with the Buddha-dharma. Regarding the phrase "cultivating [the path] below" (*xiuxi xia*), it means not first seeking ultimate understanding.

They have realized their own minds, yet they do not know that all merits are inherently complete within them; they do not awaken to the fact that dependent origination is like an illusion, fundamentally empty.

Relying solely on the Buddha’s words, they resolve their minds and apply their intentions to practice. Since they do not seek the Buddha’s true intent and remain deluded regarding the four *siddhāntas*, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"One must not associate with those who study the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna. There are many such individuals within this school of the Chan gate.
Those who study the sutras and treatises are mostly followers of the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Faxiang) school and the Hīnayāna tenets.

Furthermore, there are those who do not consult or question spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and do not listen to the sutras and treatises, yet practice with a virtuous mind. Thus, the *Three Sages’ Contemplation* states:

"To have faith without understanding increases ignorance. Since they do not know that the inherent virtues of nature are fundamentally perfect and that all phenomena are empty and illusory, they consequently [cling to] existence.

It is attained. However, it merely binds together the causes and effects of the three realms. The commentary [states] "seemingly contrary yet conforming to what follows," which serves as a second conclusion to seal the meaning.

Within this, first we shall distinguish the reason for delusion. Regarding the phrase "seemingly contrary": since one has already attained sudden awakening to the fact that the nature-merit is inherently complete and that afflictions are fundamentally non-existent, one should not need to practice further.
Yet, because one relies on the accumulation of provisional practice to gradually sever delusions and perfect virtues, it is not called [sudden].
Sudden enlightenment is thus like the opposite. Regarding the term "conformity" (*fu*): it is like suddenly seeing a nine-story tower, yet ascending it step by step;

or suddenly giving birth to a child with all six sense-faculties complete, yet gradually growing up; or suddenly recognizing that one’s own body is that of a noble person, yet gradually learning benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and music.
Sudden insight into one's original nature and gradual cultivation are likewise so. Therefore, these two meanings are mutually... [correspondent].

"Fu" (符) means "conformity," signifying that things accord and do not contradict one another. Therefore, the very last part is precisely the seal of confirmation. The first line concludes; the second line confirms.
Within the conclusion, it may speak exclusively of the sudden, exclusively of the gradual, or speak of the sudden and gradual as distinct from one another—all of these are easy [to understand].
Only when it speaks of the two as non-contradictory is it difficult.

The Commentary, section four, exhaustively explains the following two parts: first, the direct elucidation; second, the manifestation of the essential point. Within the first part, there are three sections. The commentary states, "As for the Bodhisattvas...
and so forth, which is the first: the raising of a doubt. "Bodhisattvas" refers to Vajragarbha. The text further states:
"If all sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, why is there still the existence of all ignorance? If all ignorant sentient beings were originally [enlightened]..."

There is. For what reason does the Tathāgata further state that he has been a Buddha from the beginning, and that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) throughout the ten directions have fundamentally attained the path of Buddhahood, yet subsequently give rise to ignorance? When will all Tathāgatas ever again produce any afflictions (*kleśa*)?

The commentary states: There are three points here. First, it means that the real gives rise to the false. Second, it means that the false is described as being real. Third, it reiterates [the objection] and then grants it [as a concession].

Reproving him for his endless faults. △ The commentary states "The Buddha’s answer below" [referring to the following section], which secondly rebukes his doubts. The text says: "All manner of grasping and rejecting are entirely saṃsāra;
to discriminate Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) without having escaped saṃsāra is for that nature of Perfect Enlightenment to be identical with the cycle of transmigration.

The commentary explains: The phrase "all manner of grasping and rejecting" comprehensively encompasses all conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), and thus already includes the three statements of Vajragarbha.
This is a point of doubt and difficulty. Therefore, the Sub-commentary (*Sūtra*) states its intent: "This very discrimination is itself ignorance (*avidyā*). The remaining text is easy to understand.

Regarding the passage in the Sub-commentary beginning with "As when clouds move," the text says: "For example, by moving one's eyes, one can make still water appear to shake; or as when the eyes are fixed, a whirling firebrand appears to rotate.
It is likewise when clouds move and the moon seems to travel, or when a boat moves and the shore appears to shift. Good son, all..."

The spinning has not yet ceased. Since that object cannot even be found to exist as something previously stationary, how much less can the mind—which revolves in the defilements of birth and death—ever become pure?

By contemplating the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), one does not continue to spin and return [to delusion]. For this reason, you have given rise to the three delusions. Commentary:
Among the four metaphors, the first is due to the movement of the eyes; the still water appears to ripple like waves. Next, the visual consciousness is sluggish; it spins...
The wheel-form is produced by fire; the other two may be seen. For those who spin, the eyes are like clouds and boats; the objects are water, fire, the moon, and the shore.
△ Regarding the passage beginning with "But in a single thought-moment" (*xià*), this is Master Qingliang’s response to Emperor Shunzong concerning the essentials of the mind.
It further states: "The illuminating essence stands alone; both object and self are equally such. As for the term "a single thought-moment":

First, it refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature); second, it refers to the *paratantra* (dependent nature). Regarding the commentary’s phrase “like the disappearance of flowers when cataracts are cured,” the text states:

“For example, due to illusory cataracts, one falsely perceives flowers in the sky; if the illusory cataracts are removed, the flowers vanish from the sky. As for the word “etc. (*ādi*) in the commentary, there are two intended meanings.

First, it is equivalent to other passages because [the text] does not take [the metaphor] in its entirety. Second, it is equivalent to the subsequent metaphors; that is, the Buddha addresses this objection by providing two metaphors:

the metaphor of flowers in the sky illustrates the sudden realization that afflictions are fundamentally non-existent, while the metaphor of gold ore illustrates the gradual severing of delusions and habitual tendencies.
If one were to employ only the former metaphor, one would negate the characteristics of the causes and effects of delusion and awakening, thereby constituting a false view. If one were to...

By using the latter analogy, it would follow that the sentient beings' nature of awakening is originally impure, that they have lost the principle of true permanence, and that this would also constitute a false view;
therefore, two analogies are taught. Since the commentary mentions only one, the word "etc. (等) includes the other two as well. Regarding the passage on gold ore, it says:
"Good son, it is like smelting gold ore: the gold does not exist because of the smelting. Once it has become gold, it will never again become ore, even throughout an infinite duration."
At that time, the nature of gold does not perish; one should not say that it was originally unaccomplished. The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa) is likewise. [Commentary:
From "Sentient beings are themselves Buddhas" onwards, there are two parts, the second of which clarifies the essential point. This section has two sub-divisions.

First, the analysis of the reason for this, which consists of five successive layers of difficulty in finding such a person—namely, that they are difficult to know and difficult to believe, difficult to understand and difficult to realize, with each subsequent stage being more difficult.
Regarding the preceding [sections]. To address the general objection: because the ordinary and the noble are diametrically opposed, and because it is taught through many different approaches.

To explain the specific characteristics: the first means that one has not encountered a person who can teach; since vast eons have passed, there is no way to know it for oneself. As virtuous friends are difficult to meet, it is not easy to realize this.

The second means that one possesses the seeds of past affinities and only believes upon hearing it; furthermore, [this applies to] hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions [of beings].
Regarding the number [of such people]: there is not a single one who possesses past seeds or past conditions; therefore, even though they hear this teaching, it is difficult for faith to arise.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* praises those with faith, stating: "Not from one Buddha, nor two Buddhas... (and so forth).

This means that even if one were to have only the conditions but no seeds, or only the seed of hearing but no seed of faith, then even if one hears it in this life, it would be difficult to believe and realize. This does not need further discussion.
Whether one's faculties are sharp or dull must depend on the impressions left by hearing and faith in past lives; it is only through hearing again that understanding now arises.
Therefore, one must carefully select both the Dharma heard and the mind capable of faith, so as not to allow extraneous impressions to defile the ultimate Way.

Now, conditions belong to the person, while seeds belong to the Dharma. Based on these conditions and seeds, four permutations should be established: namely, there are cases where there are conditions but no seeds.

And so forth. If one has a karmic affinity for the person [who teaches], it is easy to have faith; if one possesses the seeds for the Dharma, it is easy to understand. This also applies to those who are naturally inclined toward faith.

The remaining phrases may be understood accordingly. "Four" refers to those who, upon merely hearing the meaning of a single gateway or a single layer of the Dharma, immediately believe, understand, and accept it, without having undergone any refutation, debate, or critical investigation.
Alternatively, if their past seeds were not originally deep or vast, then even if they do understand, it remains difficult.
This refers to the realm [of the teaching]. This realm is twofold. The first is non-awakening (*abodha*); this is the realm of the three phrases that Vajragarbha has raised as a challenge.
Even the mere meaning of these words is not yet understood, giving rise to doubt; let alone being able to resolve them through comprehensive explanation.

The second is that even if one were to awaken to this realm of doubt, it would still be difficult to achieve self-realization. "Self-realization" refers to the textual expressions as spoken by the Buddha; it is difficult to reach this level.

The term "object" (*viṣaya*) already contains two layers; when combined with the preceding three layers, they constitute five. "Rarely" (*han*) means infrequently. "Oligarchic" (*gua*) and "scarce" (*xian*) both mean few.

"Attaining" (*zhen*) means reaching. *Commentary:* Regarding the section beginning with "Now, this sutra," there are two parts that conclude its essential points. Within this, the first two lines conclude the relationship between sentient beings and the Buddha.
If explained according to their respective characteristics, this constitutes the arising of defilement and purity within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*shengmie men*).

These are all matters concerning the branches and offshoots. This is truly because, by merging their distinct characteristics into the single source of the mind, they are able to be mutually identical.
One should know that this mutual identity is precisely the exhaustion of the source. The following two lines clarify the essential point. Regarding the phrase "multitude of doubts":

although there are many doubts held by those seeking the Mahāyāna, when summarized, they are only two. The first is doubt regarding the Dharma, which obstructs the arousal of the bodhicitta; it refers to raising such a doubt as follows:
Regarding the essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma, is it one or many? If it were one, there would be no sentient beings; for whom then would the Bodhisattva arouse his great vow?
If it were many, then self and others would be distinct; how then could he give rise to the great compassion of identical substance (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*)?

Because of such doubts, one is unable to resolve to attain the mind [of enlightenment]. This is the second gate of doubt, which obstructs spiritual practice; namely, doubting the teaching-gate established by the Tathāgata.
Upon what do the multitude rely for practice? If all [dharmas] could be relied upon simultaneously, one could not enter [the path] all at once;
yet if one relies on only one or two, which should one follow and which should one abandon? Because of such doubts, they are unable to initiate practice.

Therefore, the Treatise establishes the dharma of "One Mind" to dispel that initial doubt, clarifying that the Mahāyāna Dharma consists solely of One Mind, and that apart from One Mind there are no other dharmas, existing only as the non-existent.

Clarify this: delusion regarding one's own single mind gives rise to various waves that circulate through the six realms. Although these waves of the six realms arise, they do not transcend the ocean of the single mind.
This is truly because the single mind moves and acts as the six realms; therefore, one can give rise to the vow for great salvation.

Because the six realms do not transcend the single mind, one is able to give rise to great compassion of identical substance (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*). Thus, by dispelling doubt, one attains the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Two gates are opened to dispel the second type of doubt: although the various practices of a bodhisattva are numerous, when first entering into cultivation, they do not transcend these two gates.
One cultivates the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) based on the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and one contemplates based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
Arising in practice: when calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are practiced in union, all myriad practices are complete.

By entering these two gates, one gains mastery over all gates. Dispelling doubts in this manner enables the arousal of cultivation. The intent of this commentary is likewise the same as that of the treatise:

namely, that through faith and understanding, the pure nature and the single mind possess both sentient beings and Buddhas; furthermore, one realizes their mutual identity. This is precisely the single mind wherein the two gates are fundamentally and ultimately unimpeded.
Since this meaning has been thoroughly mastered, all doubts are naturally purified and explained, leaving nothing obstructed.
Regarding the fifth section on "eliminating and severing" and so forth: ignorance and craving are the very root of saṃsāra. Therefore, the text says:
Because of this, one falsely undergoes the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). It is also said:

"Because there are various forms of affection, love, and craving, there is saṃsāra. This passage has three parts. First, from the words "that which initiates karma" (*karmotpādaka*) onwards, it reveals the faults to be eliminated.

The meaning of the section following "that which initiates and moistens" (*abhisyandaka*) shall be explained in full, as this applies to all teachings. Thus, the twelve links of dependent origination give rise to existence.

Continuation. Furthermore, regarding the single layer of cause and effect according to the Mahāyāna: first is ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance initiates karma; this karma is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*).

Once initiated, it becomes a seed. Next are the five branches [of the result]; then craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are able to moisten [the seed]. Once moistened, it is called existence (*bhava*).
"Because of existence, there is birth"—this refers to the latter two links. △ In the commentary, the section beginning with "If one does not recognize...

explains the reason why [ignorance] must be eliminated. Regarding the phrase "the thief is able to act," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one perceives the thief, the thief can do nothing. Here, the meaning is reversed:
if one does not recognize ignorance, then ignorance is able to act. "Able to act" means it is able to initiate karma. [End of] Commentary.

Regarding that which cannot be severed, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "If there were definitely attachment to permanence, then because it is permanent, it could not be severed—just like the essence of *tathatā*.
For this reason, one must first manifest its characteristics and subsequently manifest its fundamental emptiness, as detailed in the following text;

one should consult and explain it accordingly. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Buddha has two ways of teaching the Dharma: first, he discriminates all phenomena; afterwards, he speaks of their ultimate cessation."

"Thoroughly investigating emptiness" refers precisely to this meaning. △ [The commentary] states "Therefore, the answer below," which points to three passages concerning that which can eliminate [ignorance].

These should each be verified within their respective chapters and briefly recounted here. However, after revealing ignorance, one does not immediately proceed to sever craving and attachment because the severing of craving and attachment is a matter of the mind of cultivation;
the mental activities involved are difficult to bring into sudden accord, as they differ from the wisdom of realization.

One must rely on the principles of the three chapters beginning with Samantabhadra to achieve perfect penetration through contemplative observation; only then can one thoroughly penetrate to the root of subtle defilement and attachment.
Regarding the sixth [section] of the commentary, "searching" means seeking in detail and with thoroughness. "Obscuring the bodhi" means that it merely obstructs bodhi.
Because one does not give rise to delusion or create karma, "bodhi" (awakening) is cited here to designate its obstruction. This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the obscuration of bodhi.
Thus the text says: "Those who practice the path do not eliminate the mark of self; therefore, they cannot enter pure awakening. "Obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) carries the sense of covering and hindering.
"Obscuration" (*gūḍha*) is explained in the sub-commentary itself. This section of the text [is divided as follows]:
4. First, "I" and "person" (*pudgala*)—this directly points to the hidden obstacle. Second, "although the names are the same"—this explains the reason for its being hidden.
However, these four kinds take only the mark of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) as their object; this is the meaning of "sovereign. They merely have four names due to successive shifts in meaning.
Furthermore, these four names possess two aspects: first, delusion regarding the object of consciousness, which means grasping one's own substance as the mark of a self and reckoning it as "I."

The successive transition to other realms in the future constitutes the characteristic of a person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*). Calculating my various deaths and births from the beginningless past constitutes the characteristic of a sentient being (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*).
Calculating that my present life-force (*jīvitendriya*) remains uninterrupted as a single retribution constitutes the characteristic of a lifespan (*āyus-lakṣaṇa*).
The various teachings also speak of these four characteristics of "self" (*ātman*); all of them are this very thing. Therefore, it is said that their names are identical. (2)
The delusion regarding the realm of wisdom is precisely what this sutra elucidates. Based on the realization of principle through wisdom, the subject and object remain difficult to forget;

through subtle and successive transformations, these four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) are formed. The text states: "Taking one's own subtle realization as self-purification, one is still unable to exhaust the root of the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the four marks: first, identifying realization as the self; second, awakening to the self as forming a person; third, understanding the traces of the traces... [text fragment].
"Birth. The fourth [point], "continuing secretly like life," refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other such texts; the meaning lies in the original text.
▲ Regarding the section beginning with "It is like," the three metaphors can be clearly explained. ▲ Fourth, from "I too... onwards, the text is combined and its meaning indicated.

In the third section of the seventh [chapter] of the *Śāstra*, there are three parts. First, the treatise’s text lists the detailed and abbreviated versions in general. Regarding the phrase in the commentary, “As stated in the treatise”:
whenever a cited teaching is introduced with the word “said” (shuō), it is a citation of the general meaning rather than the full text.

When it says “such-and-such teaching states,” this refers to the literal transcription of the text in its proper sequence. Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with “Or there may be sentient beings...”: the treatise states in full: “The Tathāgata...”

For sentient beings living in this world who possess sharp faculties, and for those teachers whose physical, mental, and karmic activities are superior—such that a single utterance of the Perfect Sound is understood equally by all diverse classes of beings—then no treatise is required.
However, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, there may be sentient beings who, through their own power, attain understanding by hearing extensively;
or there may be sentient beings who, likewise through their own power, attain much understanding from hearing little; or...
There are sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding through extensive treatises.

Yet there are other sentient beings for whom the abundance of words in extensive treatises is a source of vexation; they delight in concise summaries (*dhāraṇī*) that encompass vast meanings in few words and are able to gain understanding thereby.
It is for this reason that this treatise is explained, in order to comprehensively summarize the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.

It is said: This is an intentional citation from within the *Sūtra* (the commentary). However, by reading this section in detail, one will naturally see for oneself what is complete and what is lacking.

Nevertheless, the original text consists of four categories—two *sūtras* and two *śāstras*. Now, for the sake of those with limited capacity, only three are briefly explained. (The passage in the *Sūtra* below, beginning with "These three categories...")

Second, regarding the correlation of various teachings through their extensive and abbreviated forms: to examine the meaning in detail, "extensive" refers to searching throughout all the sūtras and does not necessarily refer only to a single great collection.

However, because the present context concerns only the comparison between the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) and other sūtras within various collections, it takes the great collections as "extensive.
As for what is called "extensive in text," it refers to the six hundred fascicles.
Regarding "the brevity of meaning": this refers solely to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), which exclusively clarifies that all phenomena are empty.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Even if there were another dharma surpassing *nirvāṇa*, I would say it is like a dream or an illusion," and so forth; both the extensive and the concise versions can be understood accordingly. Regarding "the brevity of both text and meaning":
the text consists of only fourteen lines, and the meaning is solely the principle of emptiness. △ Below the phrase "the brevity of the three texts," the third section is the main body.

Clarifying the Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*). This briefly subsumes the extensive; the text has two parts. Now, first is the full manifestation. However, according to the analysis within the treatise (*Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*), the text is brief while the meaning is extensive.
While the treatise is judged [by this principle] but the sūtra is not, here we apply the same logic of inclusion.

Therefore, by means of this text, we judge the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*. Question: Why did Aśvaghoṣa originally compose this? It was because he saw that there is a class of sentient beings who detest complexity and delight in brevity. Thus, he composed it.

Regarding the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*: it is now determined that the *Awakening of Faith* is concise in its phrasing but expansive in its meaning; it is already suited to this specific capacity [of beings]. Why, then, would Aśvaghoṣa need to explain it again? Answer:

The sūtras spoken by the Buddha merely point to the essence of the Dharma; their intent is not to provide successive expositions on the meanings of *dharmatā* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics).

Consequently, sentient beings of middling and inferior capacities have no means by which to understand them. Therefore, it is necessary for Bodhisattvas to compose treatises (*śāstras*) to provide explanations. For this reason...
Aśvaghoṣa states his intention as follows: "There may be sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and rely upon extensive treatises;

or there may be those who understand through a brief text that condenses the extensive. Therefore, an ancient master said: 'The Sūtras are sought within their underlying intent (abhiprāya); the Śāstras are sought within their essential characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
Thus, when a Sūtra contains the extensive, it contains many extensive dharma-gates; when a Śāstra contains the extensive, it contains many..."

This refers to the meaning (*artha*). Question: If that is so, why does the present judgment of the sūtra state that "the phrasing is concise while the meaning is extensive," rather than saying "the phenomena (*dharma*) are extensive"?

Answer: "Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers collectively to the "meaning" (*artha*) when contrasted with the expressive phrasing (*vyañjana*). However, when contrasted with the meaning that is explained through successive interpretation, it is termed "phenomena.
Furthermore, this is because the commentary (*śāstra*) judges the sūtra by relying on its own original text; thus, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Below [this], one fascicle reveals..."

This is the characteristic of where the text is concise but the meaning is extensive. The mention of the number of pages demonstrates the conciseness of the text; all else constitutes the extensiveness of the meaning.

Thus, both the Four Teachings of Tiantai and the Five Teachings of Xianshou encompass all sutras; since the meaning of this present sutra is complete, it is "extensive. The Four and Five Teachings will be explained below as they appear.
What is here termed the "School of Emptiness" (Kongzong) and the "School of Characteristics" (Xiangzong) refers to the Initial Teaching (Shijiao). [The remainder of the passage is: "Solely..."
Taking the School of Emptiness (Kongzong) refers to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). The rest can be understood accordingly. Regarding the terms "comprehensive" (gai) and "inclusive" (han):

although they contain meanings pertaining to both the Hinayana and the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), these are not their primary tenets. △ The commentary states "Dragon Treasury" (Longzang) below; this is the second section, which serves as a summary.
When I first began to circulate the Tripitaka, I personally selected those that were complete in both realization and practice, yet concise in their volumes;
there are none equal to these.

In the second part of the eighth section of the commentary, there are two points. First, the correlation with the three faculties (*indriya*). The meaning of these three faculties is briefly outlined by examining the text. Second, from the words "A single dharma" (*yī fǎ*) downwards, the single dharma is explained.

In the ninth section of the commentary, from the words "Causing one to cultivate" (*lìng xiū*) downwards, the text has two parts. First, it cites the shallow level. Regarding the phrase "The meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of various schools," it refers to those that speak of exclusive tranquility.
The gateway of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) consists of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Within the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) likewise distinguishes its modes of practice solely in terms of the four dhyānas and so forth.

Furthermore, there are many passages throughout various sūtras that explain the principles and functions of sudden and gradual meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as the intent behind encouraging and praising its cultivation; yet, regarding the gate of contemplating the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*), [they do not...]
A separate essence of the school is established. Furthermore, there are no gates of expedient means regarding beginning or end.

Tiantai extensively elucidated profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet he likewise took the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis as the gateway for cultivation. [The commentary] states: "Only from the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* below," which is the second section, revealing its profundity.
Regarding the "Tathatā-samādhi," the treatise says: "If one practices *śamatha*, one should dwell in a quiet place and sit upright."
With right intention, do not rely on breath or physical form; do not rely on earth, water, fire, or wind, nor on what is seen, heard, sensed, or known.
By relying thus upon this samādhi, one then knows that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic:
namely, that the dharma-body of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings are equal and non-dual. This is called the One-Practice Samādhi. You should know that suchness is...
The Root of Samādhi. If a person practices, they will gradually be able to give rise to immeasurable samādhis.
The commentary states: This preceding section has both a beginning and an end; it distinguishes between demons and the false, and reveals both the capacity and the benefit.

Its doctrinal meaning and structural framework are entirely complete, and thus it differs from other teachings. While other teachings merely explain the doctrine, [this one]—despite having three roots—asks about the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

Each has its own specific title; why, then, is this further called the "Gate of Contemplation on Perfect Enlightenment"? Therefore, the answer states: "Although the three faculties are equal," and so forth.

In the commentary (*shu*) under the section "Ten Exhortations," the text is divided into three parts: first, clarifying that the various teachings do not necessarily depend upon [specific] persons; second, "In this sutra... and so forth.
To clarify this school, one must rely on a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Within this, there are two parts. First, the statement establishing the principle:

regarding the fact that delusion is fundamentally non-existent, the text says, "This ignorance has no real substance," and further states, "Nor does it possess a body or mind that undergoes birth and death."
Furthermore, it is said: "Birth in *nirvāṇa* is like a dream from yesterday. It is also said: "It is like seeing flowers due to an optical disorder (*taimira*). And it is said:
"In reality, there are no bodhisattvas nor any sentient beings, except for those who have severed [delusions]. The text states: "Only by permanently severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way.

It is also said: "First sever greed and desire, and eliminate craving and thirst. It is also said: "Relying on vows and practicing, gradually sever all hindrances. And it is said: "If one is able to sever..."
Regarding hatred, love, greed, anger, and delusion, it is further stated: "By the power of tranquility (*śamatha*), one eternally severs the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is also stated: "Without grasping at activity, one alone severs the afflictions. There are dozens of such passages. As for the Buddha being the primordial state (*ādi-bhūta*), the text says:
"One first realizes that sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning," and also: "All obstacles are themselves ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*)."
Furthermore, it says: "The Perfect Enlightenment is pure and fundamentally has neither cultivation nor a cultivator. There are many such examples in the text.
Regarding "diligent cultivation," the text states: "First, rely on the Tathāgata’s practice of śamatha, firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts, and so forth."
The verse says: "Those who wish to enter the Buddha-way should practice in this manner. To state the essentials:

the ten chapters from the section on Samantabhadra onwards all explain the cultivation of practice. Regarding "all ritual procedures": there is delusion and severance, as well as the absence of delusion and the absence of severance.

Fundamentally deluded, one is fundamentally the Buddha. There is cultivation and non-cultivation; there are the stages of cause and fruit, the realization of principle, and the saving of sentient beings, and so forth.
△ The commentary states "therefore he causes... and so on; this second section points to the text. It says in full:

"Sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who are about to give rise to the Great Mind, seeking a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and wishing to practice, should seek those with correct knowledge and vision whose minds do not dwell on appearances and who are not attached to sounds."
Hearing of the realm of the Pratyekabuddhas, though manifesting amidst the afflictions of the world, their minds remain ever pure.
They display the appearance of various transgressions yet praise the holy life (*brahmacarya*), ensuring that sentient beings do not enter into non-discipline.

One who seeks such a person shall immediately achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. When sentient beings in the final age see such a person, they should make offerings to them without begrudging anything.

Regarding body and life: that spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) constantly manifests purity throughout the four modes of conduct (*catur-īryāpatha*), even when manifesting various forms of suffering and affliction;
his mind is free from arrogance. How much more so when he surrenders wealth, wife, children, and kinsmen?

If a son of good family does not give rise to evil thoughts toward such a virtuous friend, he will be able to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment, the blossoming flower of his mind radiating light.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, it is further said: "One should, throughout one's entire life, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual benefactors (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When those spiritual benefactors wish to come near, one should sever arrogance; if they should depart, one should sever the root of anger.

Facing circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, one should regard them as being like space, realizing that body and mind are ultimately equal and that one shares the same essence as all sentient beings."
This is different. Only by practicing in this way does one enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vajra*).

The commentary below points to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as a parallel example, stating that in its "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" chapter, it is said that Mañjuśrī departed from the Buddha’s assembly to travel and transform beings in the human realm.
Upon reaching an ancient Buddha-stūpa to the east of Puṇyavatī City, he expounded the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharmadhātu*. There, the lay devotees (*upāsaka*) of the city...
Five hundred young men and five hundred young women went to the place where Mañjuśrī was;
having heard and received the teaching, they each returned to the city. Among the five hundred young men, there was one named Sudhana.
Having heard various teachings, he sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with single-minded diligence. He spoke a verse, praying for his observation, requesting instruction, and seeking protection.
[He] rescued [him]. Mañjuśrī said to Sudhana: "Excellent, excellent!

You have already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and further desire to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), inquire about the conduct of a bodhisattva, and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva.
Son of good family, drawing near to and making offerings to spiritual friends is the primary cause and condition for attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Therefore, regarding this, do not..."
One becomes weary and exhausted. ... Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who are able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this matter is difficult;
once they have given rise to that mind and seek the practices of a bodhisattva, it is even more difficult. If one wishes to accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), [it is most difficult].

One should resolutely seek true and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) without becoming weary or indolent. Upon seeing a virtuous spiritual friend, one should not be satisfied with merely meeting them.
One should comply with all the instructions of the virtuous spiritual friend and follow their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Do not look for faults. To the south of here, there is a land called Supratiṣṭhita. In that country, there is a mountain named Sumeru.
On that mountain dwells a bhikṣu named Meghaśrī. You should go and inquire of him.
Thus Sudhana inquired everywhere, traveling from one place to another until he had passed through one hundred and ten cities.

Therefore, the Commentary places the section beginning with "serving the teacher" below; since that [text] has already determined that the portion from "Sudhana seeking the Dharma" onwards until the end of the sutra constitutes the *Pravartana-vibhāga* (Section on Dissemination), its intent is to cause those of the final age to emulate this by practicing it perfectly so as to realize entry in a single lifetime. Thus, it says, "it serves as a model for posterity."

The Section on the Compendium of the Piṭakas. This section has two parts: first, the Piṭakas; second, the compendium. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the enumeration and general explanation; second, the inclusion.
Regarding the phrase "the commentary contains" (*shū kan-shō*): the first volume of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* and the fourth volume of the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* both ask:

"How are those three and those two called 'piṭakas'? They answer: "Because they comprise [them]. That is to say, they comprise all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Now, the term "contains" (*kan*) is added.
"Comprehensive" (han) means to include and encompass. It encompasses the Śāstras and the Piṭakas; because its meaning is clear and easy to understand, the character "han" is added.
Furthermore, it takes up the meaning of the treatises which speak of "comprehensive inclusion" (han-shè).

In the commentary, following the section on the Tripitaka, there are two parts: a restatement and a separate explanation. This section has two divisions: first, the Tripitaka; second, the Dvypitaka. Within the first [the Tripitaka], there are two parts:

first, the expressive words (śabdābhidhāna); second, the expressed meaning (abhidheya). Within the first of these, there are three: namely, Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Within the Sūtra, there are again two: first, the explanation of the name;

second, the manifestation of its characteristics. Within the first of these, there are again three. First, an explanation through a literal translation: the commentary states that *sūtra* is also called...
*Sūtra*. Regarding these two terms, Master Kumārajīva often used "er" (爾). The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty used "sūtrānta," which is the language of Central India.
However, the Tripiṭaka masters who came from the West may have been from Central India, or from the East, South, West, or North. Master Kumārajīva was from Kucha, which is close to Eastern India;
yet he also traveled through the Five Indies. Consequently, the versions he received at different times varied slightly in their phrasing, though they did not differ in their essential meaning.
In this way, although the spoken sounds differ across the regions of China, Wu, Chu, Yan, and Shu, that which is referred to is no different.

Regarding "conforming to principle" (*li*) and "conforming to capacity" (*ji*): "conforming" (*qi*) means to correspond with the principles of reality and to accord with the capacities of sentient beings. Within this context, there are four possible permutations:
first, conforming to principle but not conforming to capacity, such as when Bodhidharma encountered Emperor Wu of Liang; or [as in] the *Lotus Sūtra*...

Five thousand [people] cleared their mats; the *Avataṃsaka* [sūtra] mentions five hundred blind and deaf persons, and so forth. Whether these two cases accord with the capacity [of the audience] or accord with the principle can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the "pervasion" (*guànchuān*) mentioned in the Commentary: that which accords with the principle is "pervasion," while that which gathers and transforms [beings] is "inclusion" (*shèhuà*).

These two meanings of pervasion and inclusion are as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which will be interpreted below. ▲ The Commentary’s main translation follows. Second, the direct translation and paired explanation has two parts: first, the direct [explanation].
Explanation of the Translation: In the Western Regions (India), flowers are offered as worship by threading them with a string so that they are not scattered by the wind.

The sacred teaching (āgama) threads together the meanings it elucidates, just as a string threads flowers; thus, the name of the sacred teaching is established based on this metaphor, and it is called "the thread" (*sūtra*).
Regarding the phrase "maintaining the warp": the sacred teaching’s threading of meanings is not merely like a string threading flowers; it is also... [as follows].
"Like warp and woof in a cloth; the two meanings are not distinct. △ In the commentary, "In this land... and so forth, the second point clarifies the adoption and rejection [of terminology].

This means that although the two metaphors of thread and warp do not differ in meaning, because the customs of the Western Regions (India) commonly see "thread-flowers" (*sūtra-puṣpa*), they are designated by the name "thread" (*sūtra*).

In this land (China), however, the designation "classic" (*jing*) is highly esteemed, and thus it is called a "classic" (*jing*). △ In the commentary, "However, in India... and so forth, the third point...

An extensive translation and commentary follows, which consists of three parts. First, the direct translation of the four names. This is according to the custom of the Western Regions (India), as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
when referring to a horse, salt, a vessel, and water—these four things—all are called "siddhārtha" and so forth.
However, this region [China] also has similar cases, though the characters differ; for example, a servant is called a "slave" (*bi*), and that which can smell roots is called...
"Sniffing," "avoidance," and so forth—the meaning of *saindhava*—will be explained in detail below. [Commentary] "Therefore, beneath the beam...
Second, the establishment of a single name; this is fully explained in a separate fascicle. [Commentary] "The ancient masters... Third, the conclusion of the translation of the meaning.

The term "yi-fan" (meaning-translation) is added with the character "qi" (seal/contract). The text consists of two parts. First, the intent behind the meaning-translation: The Confucianists are the foremost among the Nine Schools.
During the late Zhou period, there was a Grand Master of Lu; his surname was Kong, his given name Qiu, and his courtesy name Zhongni. He was their leader. As for the Mohists...

Furthermore, Mozi served as a founding teacher; his primary tenet was the sacrifice of one's own person for the benefit of others, following the same intent as the diligent toil of Yu of the Xia dynasty.
Among the Confucians, there are the Nine Classics and the Five Classics, all of which are termed "Classics" (*jing*). A "Classic" refers to an eternal standard or canon.
Only the words of a sage may be designated as a *sūtra*. Thus, Laozi’s work is called the *Daode jing*, and Zhuangzi’s is called the *Nanhua zhenjing* (The True Scripture of Southern Florescence).
Since this land regards the words of sages as *sūtras*, the ancient masters translated the sacred teachings accordingly.
It is also called a *jing* (sūtra). Regarding the phrase "borrowing from that," it means that the arrangement of the text does not follow its original meaning.

△ As for the commentary’s statement "containing both," this is the essential method for applying the meaning and translating it. The two meanings referred to in the commentary are: first, the meaning of the sacred teachings; second, the meaning of the warp and woof (*jingwei*).

The two directions mentioned in the commentary refer to following the *jing* (warp) of Confucius and others, as well as following the *wei* (woof) of the sacred teachings of the Western Regions. The commentary states "borrowing."

Regarding the term "meaning-assistance" (*yìzhù*): "name" refers to the scripture itself. When it accords with the meaning of the characters and is supported by them, it becomes a scripture of the holy teaching;

it is not merely a scripture of held warp and woof [literary composition]. As for the claim that "characters accord with the meaning," this is because such a title does not exist in the Sanskrit original.
That is to say, in the Sanskrit language it is called *yukti*; this is translated here as "契" (*qiè*).

If the two characters for "Sūtra" were to fully represent the Sanskrit term, they should be rendered as *yukti-sūtra*. Since the Sanskrit title currently lacks the word *yukti*, it is clear that the character "契" is absent.

The character "qì" (契) signifies only its meaning. Since it is known that the substance [of the mind] has many names and that "citta" (心) has the sense of "arising together," the term is used to distinguish [the specific type of scripture].

By using the character "qì" to exclude the character "xí" (席), the sūtra becomes properly categorized. Furthermore, all *sūtras* (契經) are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (依士) compound; this is indeed appropriate.

Because the meanings of "containing both" (*ubhaya-saṃgraha*), "conforming to both" (*ubhaya-anukūla*), and "distinguishing from others" (*viśeṣaṇa*) are perfectly consistent [with the term *sūtra*], and because it is also called "non-loss" (*avipraṇāśa*), it is indeed appropriate.

"Yun" (允) means "to trust"; it carries the sense of being truthful and sincere. Question: Among the four names designated for the *Sūtras* of the Western Regions, since the character "jīng" (經, sūtra) is already present, then "jīng" should properly be its direct equivalent.
Why have the virtuous masters of old all said that it is a translation based on meaning (*yìfān*)? [They say it is] like a "thread" (*sūtra*).
Question: Since they are opposites, how can the word *jing* (sūtra) not be [the opposite]? Answer: If one were to take only the literal name, then it would indeed be as you have objected.

However, because it accords with the meaning, among the four [categories], the word *jing* belongs to the *xijing* (seated sūtras) and does not refer to the Buddha’s teachings. How, then, could it constitute an opposition?
If it were to oppose the Buddha’s words, it should be called *shengjiao* (holy teaching), for among the four [categories], there is the term "holy teaching" which constitutes the opposition.

Therefore, the statements in the sūtras are all translations of meaning. However, regarding these two characters [“sūtra” and “khyeh”], there are two types of identity and difference when contrasted with *sūtra*:

First, identity of name but difference of meaning; this refers to the character “jing” (經). They are different because the term “席經” (*xijing*) does not refer to the sacred teaching, yet they are the same because both are the character “jing.
Second, identity of meaning but difference of name; this refers to the character “qie” (契). This is because *sūtra* does not denote the character “qie.”

They are distinct; yet, because they truly accord with the principle and the capacity [of the audience], they are identical. ▲ In the commentary, from "However, its meaning" onwards, there are two parts that clarify the characteristics.
The text has two sections. The first concerns the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which is called the "first. This may encompass both what is taught and those who are to be converted.

This means that it penetrates the teachings that have been expounded, gathering them so they do not disperse; and it penetrates the mental activities of those to be converted, gathering and sustaining them without abandoning them.

Alternatively, each term may be restricted to a single meaning: "penetrating" refers to the characteristics of the phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) being elucidated, while "gathering" refers to the conversion and sustenance of sentient beings.

[From] the *Vyākhyā* on the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*: Second, regarding the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, the treatise says: "The *Sūtra*... [The text continues: "In general, the *Sūtra*..."
There are five meanings. First is "giving birth," because it gives birth to all meanings. Second is "a gushing spring," because its flavor of meaning is inexhaustible.
Third is "manifestation," because it manifests all meanings. Fourth is "the carpenter’s line," because it distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Fifth is "stringing together a garland," because it threads together all dharmas. These five meanings constitute the sense of *sūtra*. Now, the commentary cites them as follows:
Regarding the fact that the first two meanings are not in their sequential order: this follows the citation from the ancient commentary for the sake of convenience in grasping the meaning.

As for the detailed explanation of the five meanings in the commentary, the first two—“well” and “rope”—are displayed as the "cord" of the sacred teaching; they are the warp-thread that maintains the weft, equivalent to the "sutra" (scripture).

A flower garland (*mālā*) is identical to its string; it is because the string can thread the flowers together to form the garland. These five meanings, taken as a whole, do not go beyond "threading" and "gathering. Regarding the phrase "the two *vinaya*" at the bottom of the commentary:

"two" refers to the two codes of discipline (*vinaya*). There are two parts to the text: first, the primary meaning; second, the secondary meaning. As for the Sanskrit name and its significance, various schools differ on these points, as explained in a separate fascicle.

Regarding the phrase "karmas that are non-[virtuous]" in the commentary: these refer to [abstaining from] killing, stealing, and so forth; therefore, within the Vinaya, there are transgressions against the *pi* (precepts).

Regarding the *bhikṣuṇī* and the *adhikaraṇa-vinaya*, those afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root that gives rise to karma; thus, the Vinaya states that it is for the purpose of subduing greed and the like so that they may be exhausted.
For this reason, the World-Honored One established the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). As for the "extinction of the fruit," this refers to the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).
The Sūtra says: "With pure precepts and possessing wisdom, one shall attain the foremost path.

*Śīla* (尸羅), in its full form, is called *śītalā*. "Coolness" (*śītala*) is a name derived from both cause and effect. Regarding "Prātimokṣa" (別解脫), there are two meanings: first, as explained in the commentary;

second, it is termed "distinct" (*prātimokṣa*) because it distinguishes itself from the meditative (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the path (*mārga-saṃvara*) vows. That is to say, this is not the same as the two types of vows associated with meditative concentration or the path. This is...

To be far removed from the karmic conditions of bondage is called liberation (*vimukti*). "Conforming" (*anuloma*) refers to conforming with both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) liberation.
Therefore, the *Śāsanānuśāsana* states: "Precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation; thus they are named *pratimokṣa*.
Furthermore, there are many other aspects of the precepts and discipline, which are also found in separate fascicles. As for their manifest characteristics, the former is named... [text ends]
Within this, the aspects of cessation (*śamatha*) and application (*pravṛtti*) are already contained; this is precisely the characteristic of the Vinaya.

In the third section of the commentary (*śū*), there are two parts: first, the explanation of the name and meaning; second, the manifestation of the modes of practice. Within the explanation, there are two sub-sections: first, the explanation of the meaning.

Second, the explanation of the names. Within this, there are three parts. First, the object of reference. Regarding the statement, "There are two kinds of *dharma*," this is explained according to the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

That treatise states: "Because it can maintain its own nature (*svabhāva*), it is called *dharma*; this refers exclusively to *nirvāṇa*. If one speaks of *dharmas* in terms of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*), they encompass the four noble truths;
because these are wholesome and eternal, they are called 'supreme' (*viśeṣa*). This is the explanation of that treatise. [The commentary] notes the nature and the form.
The term "also" (*ye*) refers to both aspects. Within the Four Noble Truths, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the principle (*li*), yet it is also called an "aspect" (*xiang*);

this is because the aspect of the Truth of Cessation is its very essence-aspect (*ti-xiang*). The other three truths are treated in terms of "aspects," which refers to their phenomenal characteristics (*xiang-zhuang*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the 'counterpart' (*dui*) also has two meanings," these are the two: the subjective capacity (*neng*) and the objective referent (*suo*). This also adopts the intent of the treatise. That treatise states: "This is capable of counteracting and directing toward," or it is capable of... [text fragment].

Because it is a contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), this correspondence is established. △ Regarding the phrase "that which is capable of... below: this refers to the three types of capability for correspondence.

That which is capable of correspondence is precisely the *Abhidharma* (the Dharma of Correspondence). This refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) along with its associated mental factors (*caitta*).
As that verse states: "Pure wisdom and its attendants are called Abhidharma. The prose commentary explains: "Wisdom" means the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); "pure" means untainted.
Pure wisdom and its retinue are called "concomitants. Thus, the untainted five aggregates taken collectively are termed Abhidharma.
There is further question and answer regarding this in a separate fascicle. The commentary states: "Regarding 'Abhidharma' below," there are two explanations of the name.

If one were to rely on what it directly confronts, it should be called *Dharmakathā* (Discourse on Dharmas), because wisdom relies upon the dharmas. However, since wisdom is here treated as the primary subject, it is so named [Abhidharma].

This is the Treatise on Wisdom (*Prajñā-śāstra*). Therefore, among the subjects explained, it explains the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). Thus, the old translations render it as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*), because it explains the excellence of wisdom.

[Commentary] Regarding "Vasubandhu," etc., the second section clarifies the characteristics of practice. This text has two parts: first, the actual clarification; second, the numerical analysis. As for the number:

the character *shù* (number) applies to both the departing tone (*qùshēng*) and the entering tone (*rùshēng*); here it is marked with the departing tone when cited, but explained with the entering tone. As for the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*): form (*rūpa*) is characterized by transformation.

Obstruction (*āvaraṇa*). Feeling (*vedanā*) has the characteristic of experiencing (*anubhava*), and so forth. As for common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), they are shared [features] such as impermanence (*anityatā*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as explained in detail in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Regarding "subduing" (*vibhava*) in the commentary: because this [treatise] is complete in its locus of discussion (*sthāna*) and other factors, it is able to subdue the arguments of others.

This refers to the seven categories mentioned in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which the verse states: the essence of the treatise (*śarīra*), the locus of the treatise (*sthāna*), the basis of the treatise (*nidāna*), and the adornment of the treatise (*alaṃkāra*).

[The topics of] *vyūhana* (expansion), *parājitapraśna* (defeating arguments), *niḥsaraṇa* (emergence), and *bahukṛtyadharma* (dharmas of much activity) are explained as in other fascicles. Regarding the phrase "surpassing and subduing the arguments of others":

"surpassing" (*jaya*) refers to the capacity for establishment (*sādhana*), while "subduing" (*nigraha*) refers to the capacity for refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). Thus, the Liang commentary states: "Subduing means that this dharma can subdue all [opposing] doctrines;

it possesses both the capacities of establishment and refutation, due to the skillful means such as relying on correct exposition. "Pervasive" (*sāmānya*) is termed "understanding" (*prativedha*) in the Liang commentary.
Because the meaning is easily understood through the *Abhidharma-sūtra*, [the commentary] is also called *Upadeśa*.

Second, the specific explanation: "The *Mātṛkā*" is also translated as "basis" (*āśraya*). It is the basis upon which understanding arises; the Piṭaka is the mother-source for understanding, and thus it is the "Mother.
Furthermore, in Sanskrit it is called *mātr̥kā*, which here means "mother of practice. This is because one accomplishes practice by relying on the Piṭaka, and because it is the mother of practice.

However, within the Abhidharma Piṭaka, there are works spoken by the Buddha himself, and there are those composed by Bodhisattvas who have taken the meaning from the Sūtras and explained them extensively.
Because they take the fundamental [Sūtras] as the standard for the derivative [commentaries], these too are called the "Three Piṭakas Spoken by the Buddha. This is detailed in a separate fascicle.
The commentary states that from this point downward, there are two subjects to be explained. First, the first volume of Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* says:
"Furthermore, because it can expound the three trainings, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established; for it is capable of accomplishing the training in higher ethics and the training in higher mind."

The Vinaya Piṭaka is established because one who possesses ethical discipline (śīla) can gradually attain samādhi through repentance and so forth, and can thereby accomplish higher wisdom (adhiprajñā).
The Abhidharma Piṭaka is established because it is able to definitively discern the non-erroneous meaning.
The Liang commentary is likewise. Regarding the explanation of the three [piṭakas]: the scriptural texts on ethics and wisdom are not uniform; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* [states...]

The *Vinaya* also extensively explains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and it likewise speaks of both concentration and wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, the *Vinaya* increases [the trainings] by three. The text states: "What is the training in higher ethics?
It refers to the training in higher concentration and the training in higher wisdom; this is called the training in higher ethics," and so forth.
Within the commentary on the two Piṭakas, there are three sections. First, the formal exposition. The fourth chapter of the *Vyākhyāyukti* states:

"These three Piṭakas, due to the distinction between the higher and lower vehicles, further constitute the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also speaks in this same way.

As for "Śrāvaka," it means one who attains the Way by hearing the sound [of the Dharma]. This is as stated in the eighty-second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "The principle of the Śrāvaka..."

"Those" refers to the partial truth of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). "Practice" refers to the Four Noble Truths. "Fruit" refers to the two types of *nirvāṇa*: with remainder and without remainder.

The principle of the Bodhisattva is the twofold emptiness (*dvi-śūnyatā*). "Practice" refers to the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). "Fruit" refers to non-abiding *nirvāṇa* (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*). △ [The commentary] below "the three vehicles" [proceeds as follows].

The second [point] addresses potential objections. Regarding "the principles and fruits being identical": this means they equally realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and equally attain the two fruits of *nirvāṇa*, as explained in other fascicles.

△ In the commentary, the section beginning with "If one considers... adds further meanings. This includes the two aforementioned collections (*piṭaka*), yet since three collections are now separately expounded here, it is categorized as "adding meanings.
Regarding the difference in teaching, there are the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Regarding the difference in practice, there is...

Four points: first, cultivation and the mere severing of the active afflictions (*anuśaya*); second, general observation and specific observation; third, taking the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) as the gateway and taking the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as the gateway;

fourth, mastery over the fruit and lack of mastery over the fruit. The commentary states that below the section on the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance), the *Śatrujaya-rāja-sūtra* also explains this.
However, in the West there are further four, five, eight, nine, ten, and twelve piṭakas, as detailed in separate fascicles.
[The commentary] states: "Now, from 'this' onwards, there are two sections of subsumption. This text has two parts: first, how this sūtra is subsumed within the piṭakas;
second, from "if this" onwards, how this sūtra subsumes the piṭakas. These encompass both the three and the two piṭakas. First, "letting it be" and so forth, it is subsumed under the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Furthermore, "Gang-tsang" (剛藏) subsumes the *Śāstra-piṭaka* (Treatise Collection). "Khai-qian" (該淺) subsumes the *Hīnayāna-piṭaka* (Lesser Vehicle Collection).
This also serves as a response to an objection. The objection states: "The precepts, the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*), and the formal debates mentioned in this sutra are all Mahāyāna;

why then do you judge them to universally subsume the three collections (*tri-piṭaka*) and the two collections (*dvi-piṭaka*)? It is for this reason that the following answer is given: it subsumes the *Sūtra-piṭaka* and the *Bodhisattva-piṭaka*.
This is not to say that it is visible.

The text concerning the "Gates of the Vehicles and their Comprehension" has two parts: first, clarifying the vehicles; second, explaining the comprehension. Within the first part, there are six layers, each of which comprehensively subsumes all vehicles.
Regarding the "One Vehicle": this is the One to which the Three Vehicles ultimately return; it is not [merely] one among the three.

"First, regarding the number: as for the phrase 'the ten directions' and so forth, this is from the *Fahua wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra), as cited and explained below in the comparative analysis of the two schools.

Regarding the 'Two Vehicles' in the sub-commentary (*shu*): the definitive One Vehicle is contained within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, while the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle is contained within the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Regarding the 'Three Vehicles' in the sub-commentary: this distinguishes the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle but has not yet distinguished the Buddha Vehicle. Regarding the 'Four [Vehicles]':..."

The section below [the heading] consists of three parts within the fourth major division.
