First, the formal establishment: this means that within each of the two aforementioned vehicles, two are further distinguished, thus resulting in four. Second, the citation of evidence from the *Liang* [translation], specifically at the end of the eighth fascicle of the *Śāstra*, which states: "The Buddha has well-established the True Dharma. The commentary explains: "All Buddhas of the three periods of time together proclaim this Dharma. The passage continues: "What is it that all Buddhas of the three periods of time together proclaim? It refers to the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*. The commentary further explains: "Because the Mahāyāna is the ultimate truth, it is the teaching proclaimed by all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Third, the refutation of objections. This consists of two parts: first, the objection; second, the response. The objection states: "If the Mahāyāna is the teaching of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, why did the Buddha not preach it during his own lifetime? The response states: "It was because sentient beings were not yet mature. The objection continues: "If they were not yet mature, why did he not preach it after his passing? The response states: "It was because the assembly had dispersed. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not preach it to those who remained? The response states: "It was because they lacked the capacity. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not preach it to those who possessed the capacity? The response states: "It was because there was no one to receive it. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not preach it to those who could receive it? The response states: "It was because the time was not yet right. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not preach it when the time became right? The response states: "It was because the conditions were not yet complete. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not preach it when the conditions were complete? The response states: "It was because the Buddha’s lifespan was exhausted. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not prolong his life? The response states: "It was because he wished to demonstrate the impermanence of conditioned phenomena. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa earlier? The response states: "It was because he wished to establish the foundation for the future Mahāyāna. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa later? The response states: "It was because he wished to prevent the decline of the True Dharma. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa at a different time? The response states: "It was because he wished to conform to the karmic conditions of sentient beings. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa in a different place? The response states: "It was because he wished to conform to the karmic conditions of sentient beings. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa in a different manner? The response states: "It was because he wished to conform to the karmic conditions of sentient beings. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa with a different body? The response states: "It was because he wished to conform to the karmic conditions of sentient beings. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa with a different mind? The response states: "It was because he wished to conform to the karmic conditions of sentient beings. The objection continues: "If so, why did he not manifest parinirvāṇa with a different speech? The Buddha cultivates the perception of impermanence, or he may even say that the True Dharma is about to perish.

A wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of suffering for those who reckon things as pleasant, desiring to cause bhikṣus to cultivate the perception of suffering extensively.

Or again, it is said that what is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*); the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata’s teaching of right liberation as being free from the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
This is intended to cause the bhikṣus to practice and study the perception of emptiness (*śūnyatā-saṃjñā*). For this reason, this right liberation is so named.

They are [the metaphors for] emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Sentient beings, however, do not understand this; they indulge in sensory flavors as if they were real, laboring without ceasing. Though they expend great effort, what they obtain is extremely meager; they fail to earn even a day’s wage toward *nirvāṇa*.

However, Master Huayan Yuan refuted this, and Master Qingliang defended it, further establishing ten points of difference, all of which are contained in a separate fascicle (the "Discrimination of the Provisional and the Real" gate is extremely essential for this meaning).

Regarding the commentary’s reference to the Buddha’s transformative rituals: although the Buddha employs the Dharma of a single flavor, there are variations—both indirect and direct—in his methods of transforming sentient beings.
This intends to clarify that while the phenomena being explained do not differ, the teachings that explain them possess both indirect, winding paths and level, straightforward ones.
This merely concerns differences in the ritual procedures for transformation;
the commentary states that [the teaching] is complete in the "full" and deficient in the "crooked," while the seal is complete on level paths and deficient on winding ones.

Regarding what is deficient in the full [teaching], it refers to those who merely follow the general characteristics of the provisional and the real, yet do not understand the Buddha’s profound intent. The terms "half" and "full" clarify this.
Regarding the small and the great, there is a hidden intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) whereby the provisional (*upāya*) is taken as "half" and the ultimate (*tattva*) as "full.

Thus, within the Mahāyāna itself, there is also the distinction between half and full. This is just as with the *pratyekabuddhas* and *śrāvakas*: when differentiated, they constitute the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*);

Therefore, both are referred to as "full" (*pūrṇa*). Thus, the True Teaching (*saddharma*) is exclusively full; the Lesser Teaching (*hīnayāna*) is exclusively partial (*ardha*); and the Provisional Teaching of the Mahāyāna is both partial and full.
Consequently, in the tenth fascicle of the *Fahua Xuanshu* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra), Tiantai also refutes Bodhiruci, stating:

This is difficult to resolve. The *Lotus Sūtra* is a secret teaching entrusted to the bodhisattvas. If it were equally a "complete" (*pūrṇa*) teaching [as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*], how could one be secret and the other not?
Furthermore, if both were complete teachings, they should both equally bring about the convergence of the three vehicles.

Moreover, if both were equally complete, then the two types of clarified butter—raw and matured—should both be identical to the finest cream (*sarpis*), and the finest cream should likewise be identical to the raw and matured clarified butter. This results in many doctrines being conflated, leading people to fail to recognize the provisional and the real, or the definitive and the non-definitive meanings. [End of] Commentary.

Regarding "time": the sudden is taught all at once at the time of the initial attainment of Buddhahood; the gradual is taught over five periods, beginning with the Small Vehicle and subsequently the Great Vehicle. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says:

one school was that of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu, and the other was that of Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva. Thus, it is certain that there were two schools at the same time. "Nālandā" is translated here as "Unwearied Charity";
this monastery was located in Central India. Regarding the commentary’s mention of "two great virtuous ones existing at the same time," etc.:
According to the *Biographies of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang*, it appears that Jñānaprabha was a disciple of Śīlabhadra; yet, since the present account states they were contemporaries,

one suspects either that the names are identical but the individuals different, or that he first studied the school of Śīlabhadra and later changed his career to study the school of Bhāviveka and others—
just as the Venerable Heze first relied on this school under the Sixth Patriarch, Dàtōng Wǎngshàng, before subsequently going to Cáoqī.

I have received the teachings of the Southern School. According to this, Śīlabhadra was one hundred and twenty years old and had spent over eighty *varṣa* (rainy-season retreats) in the monastic life; he was titled the "Treasury of the True Dharma" (*Saddharmakośa*).
Because he remained in the world for such a long time, Jñānaprabha was able to study the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā* (the emptiness of emptiness) and achieve success in its widespread propagation.

It is not at all contradictory that Śīlabhadra was a contemporary [of Candrakīrti]. As for the "Five Seals," the Five Indias refers to the five regions of India. Regarding the "Six Teachers" mentioned in the commentary:

First are the non-Buddhists of the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), also called the non-Buddhists of the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). Second are the non-Buddhists of the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Third are the non-Buddhists of asceticism (*duḥkha-caryā*); they claim that the birth and death experienced by sentient beings all arise from attachment to pleasure, and that if one practices asceticism, one will attain liberation.
Fourth are the non-Buddhists of spontaneity (*svabhāva*); they claim that all phenomena arise spontaneously. Fifth...

These are the heterodox practitioners who worship fire and those who believe in the spontaneous arising of phenomena beyond the heavens. Sixth are the heterodox practitioners who hold that all dharmas are produced by past actions;

they assert that because all phenomena have their causes already established in previous lives, one need not create new causes, and thus by extinguishing present karma, one immediately attains liberation.

The names of these six masters are found in a separate fascicle. Regarding "kneeling with the forehead to the ground" (*jixiang*): Kong Yingda’s commentary on the *Shangshu* states that "to kneel with the head" refers to the head...
Regarding the phrase "touching the ground": some say that "sàng" (顙) refers to the forehead; thus, touching the forehead to the ground signifies the utmost degree of reverence.

Alternatively, "sàng" may refer to the throat; the interpretation that "sàng" is like the throat is currently the most essential, as seen in expressions such as "taking refuge" (*namas*). You may choose between these interpretations as you see fit.
Regarding "those of other schools who have returned to sincerity": the various schools of the Hīnayāna are different categories from the Mahāyāna;
many have taken refuge [in it] and reverently believe its teachings. Regarding "those who study the Mahāyāna": these mostly consist of the followers of our own school.
If even non-Buddhists and those of the Hīnayāna all respectfully submit, then there is no obstacle; furthermore, members of both one's own and other schools may all be honored.
Regarding the phrase "Looking up" (*yang*) and "Walking alone" (*dubu*) in the commentary: An objection is raised, "Since there are two people, why speak of 'walking alone'? The answer is:

"Because in each respective school there is only one person, it is called 'walking alone. Regarding the passage in the commentary, "However, the schools they inherit differ, and the teachings they establish are mutually contradictory":

The doctrinal principles of the Mahāyāna schools are as boundless as the teachings themselves; here, we shall briefly discuss the reasons for the distinctness of the two schools of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and Existence (*astitva*).
This refers to the Buddha’s gradual teaching of the Dharma for a certain class of disciples: first he taught existence; next, emptiness; then that objects are empty while the mind exists;
and finally, that both mind and objects are empty, such that only the Tathāgatagarbha and the eternally abiding Buddha-nature are truly existent.
After the Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, the noble disciples each compiled and propagated the teachings according to their inclinations, and further composed treatises to spread them.
Adapting to the times and responding to the capacities of beings, they addressed either the nature or the characteristics [of phenomena] to shatter attachments and give rise to understanding.

One thousand one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the two masters of the schools, Bhāviveka and Dharmapāla, engaged in polemical debate; each adhering to either emptiness or existence, they vied with one another as the teachings were transmitted.

When the transmission reached the dawn [of the new era], later students who did not understand the root source followed their own studies and formed factions; thus, differences and disagreements arose.
Therefore, the fourth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Regarding the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, it was divided into many schools one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
However, regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, for a thousand years prior [to that point], it remained pure and of a single flavor, without any discord or dispute. After a thousand years...
Subsequently, the two divergent doctrines of Śūnyatā (Emptiness) and Astitva (Existence) arose. Therefore, it is said that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata lasts for only a thousand years;
this meaning clarifies that by practicing the Eight Respectful Observances (*gurudharma*), the True Dharma is instead extended for another thousand years.

The *Śāstra* (the commentary) states that "Kuei-chien [Hui-xian] inherited [the lineage] from afar," and so forth. The second section explains each of the established positions, which is divided into two parts:

first, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and second, the nature (*svabhāva*). Each of these two sections contains four sub-divisions: first, the lineage of masters; second, the formal exposition of the established positions; third, the concluding judgment; and fourth, the authorities relied upon.
Now, regarding the first [of the two], the lineage within the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school: both Maitreya and Asaṅga were ancient masters; therefore...

"Yun-yuan says: Dharmapāla and Nanda were merely eminent scholars of their time; as they had not long since passed away from this world, it is said that [the author] followed closely upon their heels.

Regarding the reliance on the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other texts: these refer to the sūtras and śāstras relied upon, where 'others' includes sūtras such as the *Buddhabhūmi* and dharma-character (dharmalakṣaṇa) treatises such as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Vyākhyāyukti*.
The rest may be understood accordingly. The commentary takes the Mahāyāna of Dharma-character as definitive, thereby making it clear..."
The nature of dharmas is not understood [by them]. Regarding the school followed by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, according to the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions):

when the Tripitaka Master first encountered the master Nāgārjuna and wished to study the Dharma under him, the master commanded him to take medicine and seek longevity before he would be able to exhaustively investigate it.

The Tripitaka Master reflected to himself: "Originally, I intended to seek out the sūtras, yet I feared that my mastery of the arts of the immortals would not be perfected, thereby failing my long-cherished vow.

Consequently, I shall not study this school, but instead study the school of *dharmalakṣaṇa* (Dharma-characteristics). This is explained in detail in that record and in the biography of the Tripitaka Master.

Regarding the commentary (*shu*), it states that when the Buddha first descended [to earth], he was primarily manifesting what he had established. Furthermore, within each of these three teachings, there are three types of fixed natures (*niyata*).
First, certainty of time, meaning it refers to the initial period and so forth. Second, certainty of dharma, meaning it refers to [the truths of] emptiness, existence, and so forth.

Third, certainty of scripture, meaning it refers to the Āgamas and other such texts. Regarding "Deer Park": its significance has already been fully explained in the "Immortal Garden" section of the Preface to the *Śāstra*.

Regarding the "Dharma-wheel of the Four Noble Truths" in the Commentary: "wheel" (*cakra*) carries the sense of crushing and rolling over; it crushes the obstacles of afflictions. "Turning" (*pravartana*) means knowing suffering.

The abandonment of the origin [of suffering], the cultivation of the path, and the realization of cessation will be explained in the following text. Regarding the commentary’s mention of "reversing the externalist views on the self," the meaning of these views on the self is as explained in the "Chapter on the Universal Eye" (Puyan Zhang).
As for the sub-commentary’s detailed explanation of the three natures (trisvabhāva) and the three absences of nature (triniḥsvabhāvatā), there are two layers to this:

first, with respect to the three natures, at the initial stage, one speaks of existence based on the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva); second, with respect to the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), one speaks of emptiness; third, both are fully explained.

Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is empty, while the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures are existent; this constitutes the Middle Way.
Second, [the teachings] may be understood as being existent in terms of the three natures, yet empty in terms of the three absences of nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

When it was said in the first period that the three natures exist, and in the second period that all phenomena are entirely devoid of nature, these were spoken with a hidden intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding the three absences of nature. (This passage is found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.)

(As will be cited and explained below: This means that if one explains with full clarity, then elucidating both the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*) together constitutes the Middle Way;

thus, it is the most thorough exposition of the principle. [The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "First existence, then emptiness," etc., which is the final summary and judgment. However, the doctrines of the two schools differ.

Below, ten types [of views] are explained. Herein, for the time being, we shall discuss them in terms of the emptiness and existence of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). That is to say, regarding those three stages: the first conforms to the extreme of existence;

the second conforms to the extreme of emptiness; neither of these is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). At the final stage, it is fully explained that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty while the other two are existent;
this accords with the Middle Way and only then constitutes definitive meaning. [Note: "This relies on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*" refers to the fourth [chapter].
This forms the basis for reliance.
Regarding the passage "the light of the two wisdoms" (*shu*), the commentary also consists of four parts; this is the first.

As for the first master who took Mañjuśrī as his primary object of veneration, he studied that school's doctrine and lineage, which constitutes a formal succession of teachers. This is similar to how Master Huìwén followed Nāgārjuna from afar, and so forth. (Huìwén)
[He] was the teacher of the Great Master Sengzhao of Mount Nanyue. Now, Dharmapāla and Nanda commented on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; Qingmu commented on the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*;

and Bhāviveka also commented on the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, composing the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi-śāstra*. Regarding the phrase "the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras," the term "others" includes the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the *Madhyamaka* and other treatises," the term "others" includes the *Śata-śāstra* and the *Jñānasārasamuccaya*. He also established the three lower [levels]; this correctly indicates what has been established.
This can be understood. ▲ The commentary states that "the Buddha first descended" refers to the second [stage], the formal establishment [of the teaching]. Regarding "both mind and object exist":

"mind" refers to the sixth consciousness, the cognizing subject (which the Hinayana does not recognize as the seventh, eighth, or ninth); "object" refers to the perceived object. To contemplate the principle of the Four Noble Truths while each persisting in the view that they exist is the teaching of the initial period.
Regarding "objects are empty while mind exists": this refers to the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), which negates external false appearances.

The "objects" (viṣaya) consist of the four—name, meaning, and so forth—and these exist as mind alone; there is no object external to the mind. Regarding the statement that "both mind and objects are empty":
since the objects of perception, such as names and meanings, are already empty, the perceiving consciousness cannot be established.
Thus, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "Because the objects do not exist, the fundamental consciousness does not arise. The question "Why? [is answered] below by directly explaining the true equality.
Regarding the dharma of emptiness: does this mean that the dependent nature is a dharma that appears to exist? Therefore, the commentary answers: "Because they fear emptiness and so forth.

This means that when followers of the Hīnayāna hear of emptiness, they take it to mean the absence of things; thus, they conclude that everything is ultimately non-existent. Fearing that this would result in nihilism, they ask:
"If there were truly nothing, how could there be cause and effect? Birth and death, as well as nirvāṇa, would be rendered mere empty endeavors; what benefit would there be? For this reason...
The Sūtra says: "It is better to give rise to a view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness even as small as a mustard seed.
Therefore, [the teaching] causes [sentient beings] to feel alarm and fear, so as to maintain provisional names; it merely removes the illness without removing the phenomenon itself.

Thus, maintaining the provisional nature of the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is intended to accommodate those of inferior capacity with narrow minds. Only when one understands this through the commentary (*śāstra*) is it considered a definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This concludes the threefold judgment. Since...
By following the previous phrase, one realizes that when both mind and objects are empty and equal in their single flavor, this alone constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Thus, it is clarified by contrast that the prior positions—where both mind and objects are held to exist, or where objects are empty while the mind exists—are all non-definitive. Regarding the distinction between what is clear and what is not clear in terms of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and their emptiness or existence:
first, because the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of externalists and others is refuted, it is taught that dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) are definitively existent. Next...
Because it gradually refutes the Lesser Vehicle teaching that dependently originated phenomena are substantially real, it is said that the dependent nature is "semblance-reality.
This is because those [followers of the Lesser Vehicle] fear this true emptiness; therefore, they are guided by means of preserving conventional designations.

Only at a later stage does one proceed toward the ultimate, wherein it is taught that dependent origination is itself emptiness—that which is established through conditions is reality—and only then is this considered the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). [Commentary: Below this, the three stages are sequentially summarized and established.
The source relied upon is the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, which is essentially the five hundred verses of the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, titled *Vidyāmātrasamudgata-bodhisattva-vyākhyā*.

"Discrimination" (*vidya*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), and "clarity" (*mātra*) refers to light (*prabhā*); the difference lies only in the translators. Regarding the *Mahāyāna-sūkṣmajñāna-sūtra*, I have not seen the original text;
I rely only on the citation by Xianshou (Fazang). It is possible that the sūtra was in the Western Regions but has not yet arrived here, or it may simply be the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Prajñā is wisdom; mahā is great. Greatness is also wondrous.

This is the third, the "Extensive Discernment. The text has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. What follows is the question. Regarding the term "contradiction" (*máodùn*):

a *máo* (spear) belongs to the class of *gē* and *jì* (halberds), while a *dùn* (shield) is of the same category as *pái* and *jiǎ* (bucklers and armor). It is like a person selling both a spear and a shield who says: "The spear..."
Its sharpness is such that there is nothing it cannot penetrate without being obstructed; its shield is so solid that there is no spear or blade capable of piercing it.
These two statements regarding this person should not both be believed. Now, the two schools are likewise so. [The commentary] answers with three points below.

The answer is as follows. The text is arranged in three chapters, which are fully contained in the commentary (*śāstra*). Regarding the first: although the phrasing differs, the principle remains the same.

The Buddha originally taught the Dharma solely for the sake of one great matter; whether it results in benefit or harm depends upon those who propagate it. If the teaching accords with the capacities [of sentient beings], both the empty and the existent are beneficial;

if it misses their capacities, both principle and phenomena are detrimental. The essential point lies in observing the faculties and discerning the teachings according to the specific occasion. How could it depend on...?

How can one definitively judge the right or wrong of the teachings? Therefore, they should not be harmonized [into a single system]. It is like medicine: there is no distinction between noble and base; what matters first is the illness. Likewise, there is no depth or shallowness in the Dharma; what is wondrous is that which accords with the capacity of the recipient. An ancient worthy said: "To preach the Dharma by rolling up [the capacities of beings] is to be an enemy to sentient beings.

He also said: "If one understands [the teaching] through its penetration, every phrase is a wondrous medicine; if one clings to it, every word is a festering sore. [The Commentary on the Four *Siddhāntas* (Fourfold Purposes): 1. **The Worldly Purpose** (*laukika-siddhānta*): This refers to worldly dharmas such as wealth, status, and fame. By means of these, one causes sentient beings to abandon unwholesome deeds and cultivate wholesome ones. 2. **The Purpose of Individual Conversion** (*prātipauruṣika-siddhānta*): This refers to the various vehicles according to the individual capacities of sentient beings.

By means of these, one causes them to abandon the afflictions and attain liberation. 3. **The Purpose of Remedial Treatment** (*pratipakṣika-siddhānta*): This refers to the various teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. By means of these, one causes sentient beings to abandon all afflictions and attain the fruit of nirvana. 4. **The Ultimate Purpose** (*ātyantika-siddhānta*): This refers to the true nature of all phenomena. By means of this, one causes sentient beings to realize the ultimate truth of the Middle Way. △ [End of] the Commentary on the Four *Siddhāntas*.
Regarding the term *tan* (壇): *Sitan* (悉壇) is the Sanskrit term. Some say it is translated as "to gather here" (*jù cǐ shuō*), which refers to the fundamental tenets (*zōngyì*).

Others say it means "tenet-meaning" (*yìzōng*), because the names emphasize what is being prioritized. This refers to what are called the four categories of fundamental tenets in the preaching of the Dharma.
According to the Tiantai school, *si* (悉) means universal, spread, or pervasive; *tan* (壇) is translated here as "bestowal" (*shī*). To harmonize these meanings, it is said:
By means of the meanings of these four methods, one universally bestows upon sentient beings so that all may receive benefit.

If one does not obtain these four kinds of skillful means, then what is taught will be mismatched with the capacities of those to be trained; some will be benefited while others will not, and thus the gift of Dharma cannot be distributed everywhere.
As for the individual meanings of these four, they are as explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom): first, the world-encompassing method (*loka-saṃvṛti*). Or...

They may experience joy upon hearing the truth, or joy upon hearing the conventional, or joy upon hearing that which is intermediate; this is teaching according to their dispositions, as their degrees of delight differ.
Second, there is the *pratyekapudgalajñāna-saṃtuṣṭi* (knowledge of the specific person). Some, upon hearing the teaching of emptiness, find that their morality and wisdom increase;
others, upon hearing the teaching of existence, find that their morality and wisdom increase. This is teaching what is beneficial for sentient beings according to their individual dispositions.
Because they differ: third, the *sarvadharma-siddhānta* (the universal principle of remedial methods). Some hear that the existence of phenomena (*bhāva*) can destroy drowsiness and evil thoughts;

others hear that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can destroy drowsiness and evil thoughts. This is because [the Buddha] acts according to their inclinations to destroy evil for sentient beings in different ways.

Fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth). Some attain understanding upon hearing of emptiness; some give rise to awakening upon hearing of existence; and some develop [realization] upon hearing of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
"Thoroughly. This means that because there are differences in the way one enters awakening according to specific applications, the Tathāgata’s establishment of the Dharma does not exceed these four.

There are the four *sarvatobhadra* (all-sided) methods, the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma; all of these are genuine awakenings and do not contradict one another.

Now, if we refer to the suchness of phenomena (*tathatā*) and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), [the world] is non-existent because it is the *loka-sarvatobhadra*; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-sarvatobhadra*) is... [non-existent].
It exists according to the *saṃvṛti-satya* (conventional truth), but does not exist according to the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth).

This is because there is no separate person apart from the aggregation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Question: Why does the Buddha say, "I see sentient beings"? Answer: It is said according to the conventional truth; it is not so in the ultimate sense. Outsiders are deluded regarding this conventional reality, and therefore the Buddha speaks for their sake.
Third, regarding the *pratipakṣa-satya* (truth of remediation): it exists as a remedial method, but it does not exist as an actual nature. As for "remediation," it is as follows:
The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is called an effective antidote for the disease of craving (*rāga*), but it is not an antidote for the disease of hatred (*dveṣa*).

This is because when one contemplates a person with hatred, it further increases that hatred; thus, like the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*), it is an antidote for the disease of hatred but not for craving.
Likewise, the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*) serves as an antidote for the disease of delusion (*moha*).
It is an effective antidote; however, it is not an antidote for those possessed by hatred or greed. Regarding "delusion," this does not refer to beings such as oxen or sheep.
Such a person seeks the true path, yet because they contemplate with a distorted mind, various false views arise. Such a person should contemplate dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Fourth, in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all paths of verbal expression are cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Not seeking the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—which is without beginning, middle, or end—is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, in the first fascicle of Zhiyi’s *Fahua xuanyi shu* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), he explains the four *siddhāntas* as having ten layers: first, the explanation of names, up to the tenth, the comprehensive application of the sutra, as explained in detail therein.
To examine their meaning: causing [the teaching] to be distinguished so that it accords with the capacities [of beings] and brings them joy is the *loka-saṃvṛti-siddhānta*.

Causing the arising of wholesome thoughts is the "provisional" (for the sake of humans). Causing evil to be eliminated is the "antidote. Causing entry into the Noble Path is the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha).
Furthermore, speaking of both emptiness and existence together is the "worldly" (loka). Speaking of existence alone is the "provisional. Speaking of emptiness alone is the "antidote.
That which is neither emptiness nor existence is the "ultimate truth. The general meaning is as such; the specific text is found in another fascicle. △ Commentary 4.

Regarding the "intentions" (abhiprāya): first, the intention of equality; second, the intention of another time; third, the intention of another meaning; and fourth, the intention of the inclinations of individuals (*pudgala*).
One manuscript of the *Xinji xinyao* (信鈔) cites a separate commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, in which each of these is called an "intention.
However, upon personally examining the text of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* itself, it differs slightly from that [commentary]; this must be due to differences between earlier and later translations.
They are not the same; perhaps these are separate commentaries on the *Śāstra*. For now, I shall merely transcribe the text as it appears in my own examination.

As will be discussed later in the fifth section, there are four kinds of intended meanings (*abhiprāya*) into which all the Buddha’s words should be accorded and integrated: 1. **The intention of equality** (*samatābhiprāya*):
such as when he says, "In a former time, I was named Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*). 2. **The intention of another time** (*kālabhedābhiprāya*): such as when he says...
By reciting and upholding the name of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, one will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, as stated in a sutra, it is sufficient merely to make a vow to be born in the world of Sukhāvatī. Third, regarding the specific meaning: as stated in a sutra, one draws near to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in order to understand the meaning of the Mahāyāna teachings.
Fourth, according to the inclinations of people's minds: that is to say, for the sake of this person, [the Buddha] praises...
[He] praises giving, yet for this person he disparages giving. As it is with giving, so it is with morality and the other practices.
These are called the four kinds of intention (*cetanā*). [Commentary: Just as when someone, because they share the same qualities (*dharmas*), says "that is indeed me," the Blessed One is likewise;
because his mind abides in the *dharmakāya* of equality, he said, "At that time, I was..."
Names such as Vipaśyin and so forth do not mean that Vipaśyin is Śākyamuni; rather, it is because equality is intended here.

(Since the Buddha-body is named "equality," the two names Śākyamuni and Vipaśyin are said to be no different; thus, at times he says, "My name is Vipaśyin. Regarding the "intention regarding another time" (*paryāya-abhiprāya*):
this intention is not that merely by reciting the Buddha’s name one will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is like saying that by means of a single gold coin, one obtains a thousand.
"Money—how could it be obtained in a single day? This meaning refers to another time. (The intent is: by using one coin as capital for trade, one obtains a thousand coins;

it is not that the single coin remains stationary for a long time and naturally becomes a thousand on its own. The same applies to making vows: when there is a vow, there is practice; when practice is perfected, one is born in Sukhāvatī. It is not that one attains rebirth there through the vow alone.

Within the meaning of this "separate sense," "attaining understanding of the Mahāyāna teachings" means personally awakening to the characteristics of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). If the World-Honored One...

[The Buddha’s] intention is this: if one were to understand the meaning solely by relying on the literal words of the text, then even ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) would possess correct understanding.
However, such an understanding of the meaning must necessarily be attained through drawing near to immeasurable Buddhas; this is the Buddha’s intention.
[The phrase] "according to the mental dispositions of people" means that for one person he may praise generosity, while for another...

Having taken it, he returned home and boiled it to make a gruel, but it had no taste of milk at all. Although it lacked the taste of milk, among bitter flavors it was a thousandfold [superior].

It is twice as excellent. Good son, after my parinirvāṇa, when eighty years remain before the True Dharma has perished, there will be wicked bhikṣus who will abridge this sūtra and divide it into many parts, thereby destroying the color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor of the True Dharma.
These bhikṣus will associate with one another and accept and store impure things—such as impure wealth, gold, silver, ornaments, houses, and lands—yet they will claim, "The Tathāgata..."

They all permitted me to keep [the texts], mixing them like milk and water with worldly discourse and erroneously establishing them as this sutra, thereby causing many sentient beings to be unable to grasp it correctly.
The commentary states: The present intention is to say that those who study the characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa) value the treatises while disparaging the sutras;
they successively add names and categories, which results in those seeking the Dharma and seeking the Path being unable to hear each and every sutra when listening—how much less so this one?

Regarding the contemporary practice of "vulgar lectures" (sujiang) over the past century: for the most part, practitioners recite texts composed by later generations that merely conform to popular tastes.
They chant these as if they were the words of the Śrāvakas. Yet, in every lecture they deliver, not a single word can be said to accord with the sūtras or the Dharma.
Even when the instructors cite from the sūtras, they do so in a disordered and haphazard manner, failing to follow the authentic lineage of the original teachings.
The meaning is explained through a continuous discourse, precisely as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the characteristics of practice.

Furthermore, possessing many items such as saddles, horses, and stored wealth constitutes the eight kinds of impure assets (*aśuddha-vitta*). Now, when it says "milk with a surplus of water," it refers to milk that contains much water;

although its flavor is thin and bland, its color remains white. This is like a monk who seeks fame and profit preaching the Dharma: although he lacks [true realization], [his outward appearance remains pure].

The flavor of contemplation on principle, the gestures of bowing to the Buddha and reciting his name with reverence, and the various manifestations such as the striking of bells and chimes, the arrangement of seats, and the praise of the Buddha and the sutras, are all like the appearance of the Dharma teachings and their corresponding practices. Thus it is said:

"Though the color of milk remains, the medicinal decoction of the commentary has spread, yet the disease of delusion only increases. Now, the essential efficacy of prescriptions and medicines lies in their proven results.

Furthermore, as we instruct one another, the Great Flourishing [of the Dharma] has declined; those who cultivate and realize within the Sangha grow ever fewer, while those who seek fame and profit, display luxury, and indulge their greed and desire grow ever more numerous.
Someone has said: "The sutras and śāstras are the causes for the transcendence of sentient beings, yet upon understanding them, greed and anger only increase further.
My current view is this: since the situation is thus, it is clear that the commentaries and treatises currently transmitted do not capture the intent of the Buddhas.
This is the profound purport of the sutras and treatises expounded and composed by the Bodhisattvas.

If, upon taking medicine, one’s illness increases, one immediately knows that the medical manual contains errors, the compounding was out of proportion, or the dosage was improper; it stands to reason that one must seek out a skilled physician to obtain the deep and subtle principles.
How can one remain fixed like a stump waiting for a hare, or mark the spot on a boat to find a lost sword? Therefore, Master Zhigong said: "Non-action is great..."

The Way is joyful, yet sentient beings do not understand how to cultivate it correctly. Failing to encounter an enlightened teacher who has transcended the world, they have not yet taken the medicinal medicine of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
thus, despite their diligent efforts, their learning is no better than that of one who chooses a poor master.

Like a calf following another’s lead, the teacher is ignorant of the Three Vehicles, leaving the listener to his own devices. Such a teacher knows only how to amass wealth and silk; when he dies, he will suffer the miseries of the three evil realms.
It is said: "He truly resembles an old man with red eyes who hawks eye-medicine at the side-gate. Though he attempts to treat his own ailment, it remains unhealed;
thus one knows that the eye-medicine itself is the malady. The foolish do not understand how to reflect, but let the old man set the price as he pleases.

They buy the medicine and apply it to their eyes; yet the redness returns, and the sockets remain distorted. Since the nature of this teaching has been degraded for over a hundred and twenty years..."

Come. Since the teaching of the Dharma-nature has not been practiced in the two capitals, the stream of those who cultivate and seek realization within the schools of the sūtras and śāstras has become silent and is unheard of in this age.
This is likely because when a skilled physician has passed away, the sick no longer hear of his efficacy.
If this commentary were not composed, it would be like one wishing to travel to Chu asking for directions: one person directs them to drive south, while another...
Turning the carriage northward, the questioner was already in doubt and sought a resolution from me. If I were to say that both [positions] are correct, how could I point out where they lead?
Since those two views are diametrically opposed like north and south, one must necessarily be wrong and the other right;

logically, I ought to distinguish between right and wrong, as well as distance and proximity, benefit and harm, crookedness and straightness, and level and rugged terrain. [The commentary states: "However, regarding 'Mahāyāna' below," this is the second section, which opens [the discussion].

In the "Chapter on Distinguishing the Essentials" (Zhang liao jian), the initial opening of the chapter states as follows (in the *Shu*): Regarding the first two [points], the commentaries (*shu*) above and below repeatedly clarify the two schools of Emptiness and Existence.

However, those who have transmitted and studied [these teachings] in recent times have all recognized the doctrines adhered to [by the masters] as being solely those of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and so forth;
they have failed to realize that the purport of the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*) and the *Yogācāra* is fully realized through the evidence cited therein.
As for their doctrines, they both employ scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa*.

However, since the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras, as well as the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra* and other treatises, belong to the school that reveals the reality of *dharmatā*, they fundamentally lack any opposing or contentious sectarian tenets.
Because these two schools share such a common source, when one now examines and reconciles them based on this fundamental source, the former two [schools] become easy to understand.
This involves discerning what is contrary and harmonizing what is accordant. There are many points of distinction because if the source of the school is mistaken, everything becomes mistaken.

The Commentary [states]: "Furthermore, regarding the first two of the three [categories], there are two parts within the text concerning their mutual relationship: first, a general judgment; second, 'according to the characteristics of the dharmas' and below, a detailed explanation.

This latter part has two sections: first, clarifying the Three Vehicles; second, clarifying the Five Natures. This is the first [section]. Within it, there are three parts: first, stating the school’s tenet.
Second, 'Therefore, in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*' and below, citing texts to establish [the position]. This consists of two major segments: first, clarifying the Three..."

The *Yānāntaraviśeṣa* (Distinguishing the Vehicles) treats [the three vehicles] as definitive (*nītārtha*), while the *Ekayāna* (One Vehicle) treats them as non-definitive (*neyārtha*). Later, it clarifies that the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) are definitive, thereby establishing that the preceding three vehicles are definitive.

Within the former [section], two sūtras are cited; first, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*. Although it explains both those with the nature [of Buddhahood] and those without, its intent is to establish the three vehicles.

As for the statement that "initially none are established," this refers to what is taught in the Hīnayāna: that only the Buddha alone possesses the nature of great awakening (*mahābodhi-gotra*), while others do not.
Because they exist, none of them attain Buddhahood. Next, as for those who exclusively attain [Buddhahood]: this refers to the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) according to that school’s own tenet.

It asserts only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and can thus attain Buddhahood; this constitutes the teaching of the second period. This is not the actual text of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana* judges the second period to be merely the teaching of the School of Emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). Their intention is to say that it is entirely...
If [all] were established, it would be excessive; if none were established, it would be deficient. Therefore, both are expedient means and not definitive.

This is because, in the first period, since they were initially unable to hear the Great [Vehicle], there was a one-sided suppression. In the second period, they were encouraged to aspire toward Buddhahood, which was a one-sided exaltation. In the third period, the teaching was correctly expounded according to principle:
those with the nature [to attain Buddhahood] all achieve it, so it is not a case of deficiency; those without the nature do not achieve it, so it is not a case of excess.

This is an error. Therefore, the term "realization" (*yō*) is used to signify "perfection" (*ryō*). The preceding section clarifies that the Three Vehicles serve as evidence for this realization. The commentary further states: "Below," it again implicitly cites two passages;
the first is from the first and second fascicles of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, both of which state that the "One Vehicle" is taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Based on this, it is clear that this is a provisional teaching (*upāya*). Second, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states:

"If the Tathāgata, according to the inclinations of others, employs skillful means (*upāya*), this is the One Vehicle. That school points to this, saying that the One Vehicle is taught as a provisional teaching;

what is called a provisional teaching is precisely the provisional (*upāya*). Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* also says: "The three vehicles each have fixed distinctions. [The commentary] explains all of these.

Regarding the five [categories] established by nature: the third [section] concludes the preceding [discussion]. In the *Lengqie* (Laṅkāvatāra), the following clarifies the five natures (*pañca-gotra*).
This text has two parts: first, the formal establishment based on the sūtra, which extends up to "the fifth is the absence of nature" (*agotra*), which is exclusively the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
From "those of the natureless person" (*agotrastha*) onwards, it is supplemented by the *Śīla-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*. Those [texts] speak of only two types.
First, those with the lineage (gotra); second, those without the lineage—also called persons without the lineage. Because they lack the lineage, [the Buddha] brings them to maturity;
this is entirely identical to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. That treatise explains: "The nature-lineage (prakṛti-gotra) is the natural state (*dharmatā*) from beginningless time."
The six sense bases are preeminent; they continue in succession, and so forth. △ The commentary extensively cites sutras and treatises following the section on Prajñā;
these are all quoted in separate volumes.

In the commentary on the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-yāna*), the text is divided into two parts. First, the tenet to be established is indicated; second, from the passage beginning "The Lotus Sūtra" onwards, there are eight sections:

(1) establishing the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); (2) establishing the One Nature (*eka-dhātu*); (3) refuting those who seek quiescence (*śamaikāyana*); (4) refuting the absence of nature (*abhāva-dhātu*); (5) criticizing the extraction of [the essence].

Sixth, the citation from the commentary; seventh, the preceding [passage] is not definitive; eighth, the subsequent [passage] is the basis. Regarding the first [of these eight], there are two parts. First, the formal establishment based on the sūtra:
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions," and so forth, refers to the verse from the first chapter, the "Expedient Means" (Upāya). The first three lines constitute the formal establishment.
The fourth phrase resolves the doubt: "There are neither two nor three. There have been many ancient explanations. Ci'en (Xuanzang) states:
"Two" refers to the second [vehicle] and "three" refers to the third; because the Bodhisattva vehicle is superior, it is designated as the first.
This interpretation follows the intent of Master Daosheng but does not fully exhaust its significance. Master Daosheng says: "Two" is the second vehicle and "three" is the third vehicle.

Furthermore, there should be no "first" [vehicle] either. Since the "first" does not contradict the reason for being "great," it cannot be non-existent. Once the second and third are absent, the first also departs. The intent is this:
today, the One Vehicle possesses a profound and mysterious significance; this is why it is called "Great. That which is called "Great" is because its principles and meanings are deep.
Previously, within the context of the three vehicles, the Mahāyāna was based on what had not yet been fully integrated, while the other two were established as...
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): if one considers the myriad practices of compassion and wisdom, they do not contradict this single [truth] of today;

thus it is said that because they do not contradict it, the "Great" (*mahat*) is not non-existent. As for the statement, "Since there are neither two nor three, even 'one' departs," it refers to the past teaching where there were three vehicles.

Since "two" are no longer established, how could the "Great" alone remain? Because it does not include the two vehicles and is merely an expedient indication, it is likewise like the sheep and deer [carriages], both of which are absent.

Because they are attained; as explained in Guangzhai’s *Four Vehicles*. According to the views of Tiantai and others, "no two" means there are no two vehicles of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and "no three" means that the former three vehicles are entirely non-existent, clarifying that none are real.

Thus, their doctrinal assertions differ, and one may choose between them according to one's own inclination. However, from the perspective of the intent of the sutras, only the establishment of the One Reality is taken as the true goal; thus, citing this one...
[The three] sections all reject [this view]. It does not matter whether [the person] is great or small; as it is said, "In this world, this person stands alone, and there is no other like him.

This does not necessarily refer specifically to two individuals, such as Zhang and Wang. The following sentence resolves a doubt: [The doubt is] that if there were only one, [how could there be others?]
Previously, why did [the Buddha] speak of three? Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In some lands, one vehicle is taught; in others, two, three, four, or five;
and so on, even to an immeasurable number. Why, then, do you say there is only one? Therefore, the sūtra addresses this doubt by stating:
"Except for the Buddha’s skillful means. The meaning of this explanation is that if it is through the Tathāgata’s skillful means, then whether many or few are appropriate.
This clarifies that the previous teaching of the three vehicles was merely a skillful means and not the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, it follows that "he uses only provisional names to guide sentient beings. Based on this, it is clarified that the three vehicles are expedient while the one vehicle is real.
Second, it further states: "First he guides sentient beings with the three vehicles, and subsequently he delivers them by means of the Great Vehicle alone."
The commentary states: "Even if one were to synthesize the two [vehicles] into one, it is still said that the three are the provisional means (upāya), while the single [vehicle] alone is the reality.

The passage in the sub-commentary beginning with "以性" (by means of nature) uses the latter single nature to consolidate the preceding One Vehicle; this also serves as a heading for the subsequent text.

This means that if there were multiple natures (*aneka-dharmatā*), the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) would be possible; since there is but a single nature (*eka-dharmatā*), all shall equally become Buddhas, and thus there is but a single vehicle (*eka-yāna*).
In the *Fahua Xu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), it says: "Knowing that dharmas are eternally of the nature of non-existence," etc.

This establishes the second point, the single nature. The sutra text contains three verses whose meaning flows continuously: "The Buddhas of future ages / Will find it difficult to speak [of this] for hundreds of thousands of billions..."

The countless Dharma-gates are in reality but a single vehicle. The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature and that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions;
for this reason, they speak of the One Vehicle. This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.

Having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher spoke through skillful means. Now, I shall cite but a single verse to reveal that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, thereby establishing the meaning of the "single nature.
However, regarding the three preceding verses, various interpretations differ; here, I will directly explain the scriptural text.

The first verse clarifies that the Buddha, having opened the provisional gates, ultimately returns to the single reality; thus it says, "In truth, there is but one vehicle. As for the following two verses:
The commentary explains the reason for teaching the One Vehicle: it is because there is only a single nature. If there were two natures, there would be room for two vehicles;
since there is only a single nature, it is therefore called the One Vehicle. "Knowing that phenomena are eternally without nature" means knowing through direct realization.
"Dharma" refers to all phenomena, such as form and mind. "Eternally lacking intrinsic nature" refers to the principle that is realized;

it is because one awakens to all phenomena through the principle of lack of intrinsic nature. Why is there no intrinsic nature? It means that from the very beginning, the nature and characteristics of form, mind, and so forth, are empty and quiescent.
They are neither self nor other, neither identical nor separate, and are profoundly and eternally tranquil; therefore, they are said to be without intrinsic nature. And yet...

Regarding the term "permanent": it means that these dharmas and so forth exist when they arise and cease to exist when they pass away; it is not that they become non-existent through external investigation. Therefore, it is said that their nature is eternally non-existent.

As for the statement "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions," there are two meanings. First, in terms of its various manifestations, it refers to the direct cause of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
This Buddha-nature of *nirvāṇa* is precisely the seed of the Middle Way within unsurpassed *bodhi*. This seed is...

Because there is no prior nature (svabhāva), the Buddha-nature of nirvāṇa is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā); that is, the meaning of being without nature is itself emptiness.

Conditions refer to the six perfections and the myriad practices; these myriad practices are the conditional cause (pratyaya-hetu) of the Buddha-nature, which gives rise to the direct cause (hetu-hetu).

It causes them to attain Buddhahood. For this reason, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is taught: it arises solely from the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) by means of the Buddha-nature, and there is no other nature.

Therefore, it is called the One Vehicle; this is an exposition in accordance with the principle. "Nature" (*dhātu*) refers to identity of essence, while "seed" (*gotra*) denotes similarity. Thus, it is said in Guanzhong:
"Just as rice naturally produces rice and does not produce other grains—this is what is meant by 'nature. As for the sprouts, stalks, flowers, and grains..."

There is no difference in their categories; this refers to the "seed" (gotra). Second, regarding the "seed-nature of the fruit" (*phala-gotra*): Guāngzhōng says, "The Buddha’s retribution is only the Buddha;

its principle is without deviation. This is the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*). As for teaching the Dharma to deliver humanity, all [beings] are similar; this is the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*). The seed-nature of the fruit arises from the True Principle;
therefore, it is said to "arise from conditions. Thus, the commentary on this verse states: "The Buddha arises from conditions based on the Principle; the Principle..."
Since there are not two, it is therefore called the One Vehicle. The underlying intent is this: attaining Buddhahood by realizing the principle is termed "oneness of principle.
Herein, knowing that phenomena are eternally without self-nature is entirely identical to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Chapter on the Manifestation [of the Tathāgata]. It says therein:

"When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, within his own body he universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment," and so forth, until "he universally perceives all..."
Sentient beings enter nirvana; all are of one and the same nature, namely, the nature of non-nature (*abhāva*).

Even to the point of knowing that all phenomena are of the nature of non-nature, one thereby attains omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and continues in great compassion to rescue and deliver sentient beings. This is because one knows that the Buddha-nature is identical in its lack of intrinsic nature.
By this principle, it should be understood: if even through non-nature one attains perfection and all things are perfected, how much more so when [non-nature] is not explicitly taught?

One delivers them by means of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The subsequent scripture states: "Only then does one know that sentient beings have fundamentally accomplished the Buddha-way. This is also this same meaning.

Regarding the later verse which says, "This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma," etc., it is a re-explanation of the preceding verse. As for "this Dharma," it refers to the Dharma previously known.
The reason it is eternally without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is because it abides in the true state of suchness (*tathatā-samyaṅgavasthā*). Because it is conditioned by the non-existent...

Nature (*dharmatā*). Dependent origination is itself reality (*tattva*). Because it is itself reality, it was previously described as being "without nature. As for the term "dharma-position" (*dharmasthiti*), it refers to the true state of suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that dharma-nature, dharma-position, and so forth, are all synonyms for suchness. Worldly phenomena are themselves suchness.
Therefore, all things are eternally abiding. This means that by deviating from the principle of permanence, the three realms become impermanent;
yet if one realizes the reality of impermanence, then through impermanence itself, they become permanent. Thus, the two aspects of permanence and impermanence are not partial or biased.

Now, within the *dōjō*, one realizes and knows that the impermanence of all worlds is precisely the principle of true permanence—just as when a mirror is suspended in a lofty hall, the myriad images are all reflected therein.
"Two yet not two; it cannot be expressed in words. By the power of skillful means, one resorts to provisional verbal expression.

Since even 'one' is but a provisional designation, how much more so 'two' or 'three'? Therefore, we know that the preceding verse is a passage concerning the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*); the commentary briefly summarizes this by citing only a single phrase.
Thus, we know there is only the single nature. Furthermore, the third [verse] says: 'The single characteristic, the single flavor, ultimate nirvana.'"

The mark of eternal quiescence ultimately returns to emptiness. In the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) beneath the term *nirvāṇa*, he cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to clarify that the establishment of the vehicle’s nature and characteristics is not based on the single nature alone;
therefore, it is called the One Vehicle. The sutra clarifies that the single nature is itself the One Vehicle.
Thus, the twenty-seventh fascicle of the sutra states: "Good son, there are two kinds of ultimate: first, the ultimate of adornment; second, the ultimate of exhaustion."
...are ultimate and final. There are two kinds: first, the worldly ultimate; second, the supramundane ultimate.
The ultimate of adornment refers to the six *pāramitās*. The ultimate of the final goal refers to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) attained by all sentient beings.
The One Vehicle is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). For this reason, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. All...

Sentient beings truly possess the One Vehicle (ekayāna), yet because they are shrouded by ignorance, they are unable to perceive it. The commentary states: Because all possess Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu), there is only the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, Buddha-nature is the principle of the ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā).

Since this principle is capable of conveying [beings] across, it carries the very meaning of "vehicle" (yāna). [The section] beginning with "The Lion’s Roar" below consists of twenty-seven sūtras. The Lion’s Roar...
The sequence of chapters states: "If one does not proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, then such a person is a jackal;

even if they remain within the Buddha-dharma for ten million years, they will be unable to produce the lion’s roar. This is true not only of their cause being the same, but also of their fruit being the same.
Thus, the thirty-third chapter says: "All sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; they are all identical in the One Vehicle."
One liberation, one cause, one fruit, and the same nectar (*amṛta*); all shall attain the eternal bliss of the self that is permanent.
This is called "one taste" (*ekarasa*). The commentary states: This is from the "Lion’s Roar" chapter, clarifying the eight virtues of the ocean and applying them to the following.
This corresponds to the third meaning, "one taste. Regarding the phrase "one nectar," it specifically reveals the nectar of one taste, using it as a metaphor.
*Nirvāṇa*.

In the sub-commentary (*śū*) on the *Lotus Sūtra*, section three, it refutes the tendency toward quiescence (*śamaikāyana*). Since there is no such tendency toward quiescence, there are no śrāvakas of fixed nature.
Since śrāvakas do not exist, the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is thereby revealed. This section has two parts: first, citing the text; second, concluding the refutation. Now...

This first citation refers to the passage on the four stations (*catvāri sthānāni*). It is the very first [of these], namely the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter (*Tathāgatapratibhāsa-parivarta*).
In concluding the assembly of the disciples transformed by the World-Honored One, it says:

"Those immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time—these are you, monks, and the śrāvaka disciples in future ages after my parinirvāṇa. My parinirvāṇa...
Later, there will again be disciples who have not heard this sutra; they do not know and are not aware of the conduct of bodhisattvas.

Regarding the merits they have attained, they give rise to the thought of having reached extinction and believe they have entered nirvana. I shall become a buddha in another land under a different name.
Although these people give rise to the thought of extinction and enter into nirvana, they shall seek the Buddha-wisdom in that land.
"Wisdom. Having heard this sutra, they attain extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle," and so forth. The commentary explains:
Regarding the phrase "other lands," some say it refers to any land other than Sahā. However, according to Tiantai, "other lands" refers to the Land of Provisional Remainder (*upapattiśeṣa*).

He establishes four lands: first, the land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, which corresponds to the *pariṇāmika* (transformation) land within the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) system.

The Land of Transformation (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). Second, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-kṣetra*). Third, the Land of True Reward without Obstruction (*vipāka-nirāvaraṇa-kṣetra*), which is the *vipāka-kṣetra* within the Dharma-characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) school;
it encompasses both self-enjoyment and other-enjoyment. Fourth, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-praśānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*), which is the Land of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).

This "Land of Skillful Means" does not exist in the Dharma-characteristics school; it was established by Tiantai based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, as cited below. An external opponent objects: "The Dharma..."
Those who, after the parinirvāṇa of Mahākāśyapa, have faith and enter the One Vehicle in other lands are transformation śrāvakas of expedient means;

they are not those who have entered the state of quiescence. How can you cite them to refute the meaning of entering quiescence? Now, I shall refute this, saying that there are two errors in your position.

The provisional must transform the real; if there were no reality, whom could it transform? Thus, you fall into the error of attempting to transform that which exists while failing to utilize that which does not.

If there were śrāvakas of indeterminate nature, then a bodhisattva would manifest as a śrāvaka to entice them to turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]; this would be a transformation that brings benefit.

However, in your school, those of determinate nature are decided never to turn their minds. What use is there for manifestation? Since there is nothing to be transformed, [your position is untenable].
If this opportunity were lost, it would become useless. Would these two [teachings] not lead to the error of a certain class of timid beings who favor extinction?

That is to say, there are those who loathe the suffering of birth and death, yet upon hearing that the Buddha-way is long and distant, their hearts become timid and weak, and they constantly desire to hasten toward quiescent extinction.
If they knew that once extinguished they would sink forever, they would not dare to seek extinction.
Now, seeing those who undergo transformation arise from cessation, these timid individuals claim that there is a true path where one arises from cessation;

they then immediately enter into quiescence, hoping to arise later. Your school maintains that once extinguished, one definitely does not arise, which consequently misleads them and causes them to sink forever.
This is precisely what is meant by those words. Regarding the statement "the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is also the same," this is the second point. That is to say:
The ninety-fifth passage. The Treatise says: "The body received by an Arhat due to causes and conditions from previous lives must necessarily perish.
Abiding in what place does he fulfill the Buddha-way? Answer: Having attained Arhatship, one is no longer reborn within the three realms.
There are pure buddha-fields outside the triple world, where even the name of affliction does not exist.

In those lands, at the abode of the Buddha, one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and fulfills the path of the Buddha, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "There are arhats; I [taught them] in other lands," and so forth.
The full citation is identical to what was stated previously. The treatise further states: "If that is so, then arhats receive the dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*)."
"One ought to attain Bodhi; why then do you delay? He replied, "Because by abandoning sentient beings, one abandons the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, though one speaks of attaining the Way with empty words, even if one does not undergo birth and death, one's faculties regarding Bodhi are dull and one cannot attain it quickly.

It is better to proceed directly toward Bodhi. The commentary states: The text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is self-evident and accords perfectly with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. One knows for certain that although [the practitioner] has emerged...
The three realms do not lead to tranquility. Regarding the *Fahua lun shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), there are three [types]. The full text of the treatise states:
"As for the statement regarding the bestowal of prediction upon śrāvakas, there are four kinds of śrāvakas: first, the śrāvaka of fixed destiny; second, the śrāvaka of overweening pride;

third, the śrāvaka who has regressed from the bodhicitta; and fourth, the śrāvaka who is a manifestation of transformation. Of these, two kinds of śrāvakas [receive predictions] from the Tathāgata..."
Regarding the granting of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*): this refers to those śrāvakas who are subject to transformation and who, having regressed, again resolve their minds toward bodhicitta.
As for those with fixed, superior pride (*abhimāna*), the Tathāgata does not grant them predictions because the faculties (*indriya*) of these two types of śrāvakas have not yet matured.

When a bodhisattva grants a prediction of awakening, it is as a skillful means (*upāya*) to cause them to resolve their minds [toward enlightenment]. This is a brief citation from the commentary; the treatise further provides a question-and-answer regarding the granting of predictions.
The meaning is found in another fascicle. Regarding the statement that one may fall back from the mind of bodhi yet still be able to attain realization:

this refers, for instance, to Śāriputra, who had already been taught by twenty thousand Buddhas. Furthermore, as it says below: "Now, I cause you all to recollect the path practiced according to your original vows.
This indicates that it is not only Śāriputra; it also clarifies that the four great śrāvakas themselves confessed to having abandoned their fathers and run away.

First, regarding conversion: within the third week [of the Buddha's enlightenment], he led them to the presence of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, where they had previously been extensively converted;

all of these were those who possessed the bodhicitta. As for those who are "transformed" (nirmāṇa), such as Pūrṇa, they secretly maintain the practices of a bodhisattva while outwardly appearing as śrāvakas.
Furthermore, it is said: "For this reason, various bodhisattvas manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Also, Ānanda himself recalled his original vow in verse, saying:
"I employ skillful means to serve as an attendant. Regarding Rāhula, the verse says: "Rāhula’s secret practice—only I can know it;
he now appears as my eldest son. These are all manifested śrāvakas. Therefore, Master Sengsheng said: "One who is able to respond and proclaim [the Dharma]..."

In the Holy Teachings, every manifestation of his traces is without exception a provisional means (*upāya*). To claim that only Pūrṇa was a manifested incarnation (*nirmāṇakāya*) is likewise to disparage the various arhats of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that bodhisattvas were given predictions, the Master [Zhiyi] previously cited from the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" (*Anihīna-pūrva-yoga-parivarta*), showing that one should know how to manifest by prostrating to, praising, and speaking thus: "I do not disparage..."
"O you, all of you shall become Buddhas," because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. All of the above has been discussed;
however, Master Lishi does not accept this interpretation. How could there be a prediction given in a former time to Bodhisattvas who were present at today's assembly of Śrāvakas?
This refers to those Bodhisattvas who propagate the Dharma, such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and others, who are to receive their predictions now. Now...
The commentary states: The Master of the Treatise cites past events as examples for the present and future, because the Way of the past and the present are identical.
Suppose there were someone today who says to sentient beings: "Your own mind is itself the Buddha-nature; awaken to the mind and cultivate the mind, and you will certainly become a Buddha."
This is identical to that case; it does not mean that the former Constantly Not-Light (Sadāparibhūta) was given a prediction of enlightenment by the present-day person [Maitreya].
This is truly because they cling to their own sectarian tenets, which prevents them from understanding the intent of the treatise, leading them to reject and disbelieve it.

Thus we know that even for those who follow the Five-Nature school, it is impossible to attain transformation through Maitreya’s teaching, let alone others. Since it is said that "the faculties are not yet mature," one knows that on another day...
They will certainly ripen; they will definitely turn their minds [toward enlightenment]. This is not because they belong to a fixed nature (niyata-gotra).
If it were certain that they would not become Buddhas, the treatise should have stated that the Buddha did not grant them a prediction because the other two types of śrāvaka root-natures were absent.

If a Mahāyāna Dharma Master says, "It should have said 'not yet ripened' (*a-pakva*), and the translator erroneously wrote 'unripened' (*apakva*)," he then annotates his refutation by saying: "The character 'un' (*wei*) is unacceptable, as it does not accord with one's own [interpretation]."
The Master [Xuanzang] maintained that there is a definitive teaching on the transition to quiescence (*nirvāṇa*). He then judged the treatise [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] to be erroneous.

Even if one were to say it was due to immaturity, this would not imply a lack of innate capacity (*gotra*); rather, it is simply because the capacity has not yet matured. In the fourth section of the lower fascicle of the *Lengqie shu*, three sūtras are cited by way of illustration;
the present passage is the first of these, namely the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* (the ten-fascicle version translated by Bodhiruci of the Wei dynasty), chapter two, section four.

All seven [scriptures] state the same: the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is not ultimate; rather, it is due to the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that they will inevitably attain unsurpassed *bodhi* later on.
The commentary explains: If this is so, why speak of "attaining *nirvāṇa*"? From the perspective of their own respective stages, this is called "nirvāṇa without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

However, viewed from the standpoint of the Mahāyāna, it is merely a state of meditative absorption. Because they have entered deeply into *samādhi*, they become submerged in emptiness for a long time.
At that time, "nirvāṇa" was used merely as a provisional term to attract those of inferior capacity. The intent of the *Fa-hua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) is likewise the same:
there is no actual nirvāṇa. In the commentary on the parables, the fourth [parable] is the metaphor of the conjured city spoken for those with fixed natures. The treatise says:

Fourth, that which does not exist in reality yet appears to exist: those with overweening pride (adhimāna) perceive worldly, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) as being nirvāṇa, even though nirvāṇa is not actually present there.
Such is this perverted grasping; it is for the sake of counteracting this that [the teaching is given].

The parable of the conjured city is taught for this purpose; one should understand it thus. The commentary states: Since it is said that *nirvāṇa* does not truly exist, it is clear that such [teachings] are merely provisional expressions.
Therefore, they are the same as what was stated previously. Regarding the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, that sutra also says: "To say that the two vehicles attain *nirvāṇa* is the Buddha’s skillful means.
