the commentary contains both teaching (*kyō*) and practice (*gyō*). As for those who do not adhere to these yet extinguish consciousness, this is the third school. This school also originally branched out from under the Fifth Patriarch;
it was founded by Rōbo Anwashō. He left home at the age of sixty and received the precepts. It was only after sixty summer retreats that—
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he was one hundred and twenty years old; thus, he was known as "Old An" (*Lǎo Ān*), "An" being his name. He was revered by Empress Wu Zetian as her teacher.
His virtue and conduct were profound, and his integrity and character were solitary and lofty; among all those of renowned merit, none could be compared to him.
He had four disciples, all of whom were eminent for their high realization and fame. Among them was one lay disciple named Chen Chuzhang (the other three...).
He was known as Chen Qige. There was a monk named Wuzhu who, upon meeting Chen and receiving his instruction, attained realization.
He too was solitary and firm in his practice. Later, while traveling through Shu, he encountered Master Jin and entered his assembly to study Chan.
However, he consulted further; seeing that his previous realization was not erroneous, he intended to transmit it to those who had not yet heard it.

Yet, thinking it might be inappropriate to confer it upon a layperson, he instead took the Venerable Jin as his teacher. The essential meaning of the Dharma they pointed out was largely the same, but the ritual for its transmission was entirely different from that under the Golden Gate (the secular tradition).
The point of difference was that all the formal procedures of the Śramaṇa gate were absent.
As for their practice: once they have shaved their heads, they wear the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) and do not receive the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*).

Regarding rituals of worship and repentance, the recitation of scriptures, the painting of Buddha images, and the copying of sutras—they disparage all of these as mere delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*). Consequently, no Buddhist rites are established in the monasteries where they reside;

thus it is said that their teachings and practices are unrestricted. What is called "extinguishing consciousness" (*vijñāna-nirodha*) refers to the path they cultivate. Their intention is that [this path leads beyond] the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
To turn [the mind] is entirely to give rise to thought; to give rise to thought is delusion. Whether good or evil, non-arising is the truth. It is also not like the practice of phenomenal forms.

Taking discrimination as one's enemy and non-discrimination as the wondrous path—this is also the oral teaching of the Three Phrases transmitted by Preceptor Jin, with only the character "forgetting" (*wàng*) changed to the character "delusion" (*wàng*). He said to his fellow students: "You have mistakenly followed your former master."

The purport of these words is that non-recollection and non-thought are the truth, while recollection and thought are delusion. Since he does not permit recollection and thought, he says, "Do not be deluded.
As for his disparagement of various doctrinal forms, his intent lies in extinguishing discrimination to realize the absolute truth.

Therefore, regarding what he maintains, he does not deliberate over clothing or food; he leaves it to others to provide or not. "Providing" refers to warm clothing and ample food; "not providing" means leaving it as it is.
One endures hunger and cold, seeking neither transformation nor alms. When someone enters the monastery, one does not distinguish between noble and humble;
one neither greets them nor rises to meet them. Whether they offer praise and offerings or inflict blame and harm, one leaves everything to them.
This is because the fundamental tenet teaches non-discrimination; thus, in the practice of the Way, there is neither wrong nor right—only the value of being without mind.

This is the ultimate excellence; therefore, it is called "extinguishing consciousness. The three schools mentioned above all share the same teacher as the Sixth Patriarch as their root, differing only in their respective secondary and primary emphases.

The commentary states that those who consider every contact to be the Way and act according to their own minds belong to the fourth school. This lineage originally branched out from the Sixth Patriarch;
it refers to the Venerable Rang of Nanyue Guanyintai, who was a disciple of the Sixth Patriarch. Originally, he did not transmit the Dharma.
He dwelt only in the mountains to cultivate the Way. There was a śramaṇa named Daoyi from Jianyang whose secular surname was Ma; he was a disciple of the Venerable Jin.
Possessing lofty integrity and a resolute commitment to the Way, he practiced seated meditation wherever he went and resided for a long time at Mount Mingyue in Jingnan.

Later, while on a pilgrimage to visit sacred sites, he arrived at the place of the Venerable Rang. There they discussed the course of the school’s destiny and debated the ultimate principles; however, Daoyi’s reasoning could not surpass that of Rang.
Furthermore, knowing that Caoxi was the legitimate successor in the transmission of the robe and the entrustment of the Dharma, he practiced accordingly.
He resided in Gansu, Hongzhou, and Huzhou, whether in mountains or monasteries, extensively opening up offerings and guiding practitioners. He propagated this Dharma widely;
every movement of thought, the snapping of fingers, the ringing of a bell, the clearing of the throat, or the waving of a fan—all actions and deeds were the total functioning of the Buddha-nature.
There is no second sovereign; just as when flour is made into various kinds of food and drink, each and every one is flour, so too is Buddha-nature.
Since the entire body—through greed, hatred, and delusion—creates good and evil and experiences suffering and pleasure, each and every part is that very nature.
If one investigates with the mind, one finds that the four elements, the flesh, bones, tongue, teeth, eyes, ears, hands, and feet cannot themselves speak, see, or hear.
As for movement: suppose at this very moment, at the end of a single thought, the entire body has not yet undergone decay or disintegration;

yet immediately, one is unable to speak with the mouth, unable to see with the eyes, unable to hear with the ears, unable to walk with the feet, and unable to act with the hands. Thus we know that the agent of speech must be the Buddha-nature.
If one carefully examines each of the four elements, bones, and flesh, none of them can be found to understand greed or anger. Therefore, it is greed... [and so forth].
Both hatred and afflictions are the Buddha-nature. While the Buddha-nature is not itself any particular variety of differentiation, it is able to produce all varieties of differentiation.
This meaning accords with the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which states: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;

it is able to universally provide for the creation of everything. It gives rise to and produces [beings] who experience suffering and pleasure, existing together with their causes. It further says, "The Heart of the Buddha’s Words," and also says:
In some Buddha-fields, raising an eyebrow, moving the eyes, smiling, yawning, clearing the throat, coughing, or even making physical gestures—all these are acts of the Buddha.

Thus it is said that "everything encountered is the Way. As for the phrase "following the mind," this refers to the practice of ceasing worldly activities to nourish the spirit (or, as some say, ceasing the spirit to nourish the Way).
It means not giving rise to the thought of creating evil or cultivating goodness, nor practicing the Way; for the Way is itself the mind. It is not...
One may take the mind and cultivate it back within the mind. Evil, too, is the mind; one cannot use the mind to sever the mind.
By neither severing nor creating, one becomes spontaneously free and sovereign—this is called a person of liberation, and also a person who has transcended all measures.

There is no dharma that can bind them, and there is no Buddha to be made. Why is this? Because outside the nature of the mind, not a single dharma can be found. Therefore, it is said: simply let the mind be as it is.
This constitutes cultivation itself. This stands in direct opposition to the third school; whereas the former asserts that all is false, this [school] maintains that all is true.

The commentary states that there were those who forgot worldly attachments without having any underlying motive; this refers to the fifth school. This school branched out from under the Fourth Patriarch.
Its predecessor was the Great Master Wutou Huirong, who was a fellow student of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Huineng.

It was only after the Fourth Patriarch had entrusted Master Huineng with the succession of the Dharma that he met Huirong. Huirong’s nature was lofty and simple, and his spiritual wisdom was profound.
He was of keen faculties. Having long refined himself in the Prajñā school of emptiness, he had already become free from all conceptual attachments regarding dharmas.

Later, he encountered the Fourth Patriarch, who revealed the absolute, numinous mind of original enlightenment within the essence of the void and signless. Consequently, without waiting for prolonged study, he attained awakening and became profoundly clear in understanding.
The Fourth Patriarch said: "From the time of our predecessor, this Dharma has been entrusted to only one person at a time. I have now [entrusted it to you]."

There was a successor who could establish his own lineage. Rong subsequently retired to Mount Wutou, where he ceased worldly attachments and forgot his emotions to cultivate the principle of formlessness (*animitta*).
He was the first patriarch; Zhiyan was the second; Huifang the third; Facheng the fourth; Zhiwei the fifth; and Huizhong the sixth.
Zhiwei’s disciple was Venerable Masuo of Heilin Monastery in Runzhou; Masuo’s younger brother...
The Venerable Daoqin of Mount Jinshan succeeded him and transmitted this fundamental teaching. To say that "fundamentally there is no affair" refers to the principle realized:
that the mind and its objects are originally empty, not merely becoming quiescent now. When one is deluded, one says they exist; thus, emotions such as hatred and love arise.

Once these emotions arise, one is bound by all manner of sufferings, for one dreams and experiences within a dream. Therefore, to thoroughly realize that from the beginning there is no such thing as equality [between self and other] is—
One must lose oneself and forget emotions; for when emotions are forgotten, one transcends suffering and calamity. Thus, the forgetting of emotions is taken as the practice.

Previously, "contacting all things" was considered awakening while "following the mind" was considered practice; here, however, "the original absence of affairs" is taken as awakening and "forgetting emotions" as practice.
Furthermore, what distinguishes this from the two previous schools—speaking specifically in terms of the principle of awakening—is as follows: first, [the former]...
In all three cases, everything is false; in the fourth, everything is true. According to the principle of Suchness (tathatā), everything is non-existent.

As for those who speak in terms of practice: in the third stage, the mind is subdued and delusions are extinguished; in the fourth, the nature of the mind is allowed to function freely, whereby the mind comes to rest and does not arise.
Furthermore, the third is the illness of cessation; the fourth is the illness of indulgence; and the fifth is the illness of stasis, as explained in the following text.
Regarding those who rely on the transmission of incense to preserve the Buddha, this refers to the sixth school, namely the Chan lineage of the Nanshan Nianfo Gate.
Its predecessor also branched out from under the Fifth Patriarch; his Dharma name was Xuanshi, and he was the Preceptor Wei of Guozhou in Langzhou.
In Zhōuzhūn, Yù, and Xiāng rú County, Ní Yīchéng propagated [this practice]. I do not know for certain the lineage of his teachers and disciples or how their illumination was harmonious;
however, regarding the transmission of the incense, its initial assembly of the ritual of repentance and other ceremonies was like that under the gate of Master Jìn.

When he wished to confer the Dharma, he used the transmission of the incense as the token of the disciple’s reliance upon the teacher. The Master would hand it over with his own hands, and the disciple would receive it back.

The preceptor bestows [the transmission] upon the disciple; the disciple then bestows it back upon the preceptor. This is done three times. All persons are like the earth. Regarding those who maintain mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*):

at the time of the formal transmission of the Dharma, one first explains the principles of the Dharma-gate and the intent of the practice, and then causes them to recite the Buddha’s name with a single syllable.
Initially, the sound is drawn out through mindfulness; subsequently, the sound gradually fades away—from a faint sound to no sound at all—thereby escorting the Buddha.

"Regarding 'the utmost intention': the mental intention is still coarse. Furthermore, one should extend this to the ultimate mind, maintaining the visualization in every thought-moment that the Buddha is constantly present within the heart.
This continues until, even in the state of non-conceptualization, one attains the Way."
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "quiescent awareness" takes "the essence being free from thought" as its tenet:

this refers to the seventh school. It was transmitted by the Seventh Patriarch of the Southern School, the Great Master Heze. He maintained that since all phenomena are empty, the essence of the mind is fundamentally quiescent;
this quiescence is the *dharmakāya*. To know within this quiescence is true wisdom (*jñāna*), which is also termed *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. This is explained in detail in the "Introductory Discourse."
This is elucidated within the five pairs of meanings in the *Faxing jiao* (Teaching on the Nature of Dharmas) as a critique of the *Poxiang jiao* (Teaching on the Refutation of Characteristics).

This is the intrinsically pure mind that is the source of all sentient beings; it is a dharma that exists naturally and primordially. Regarding the statement that "non-thought" (*wunian*) is the fundamental principle:

once one has realized that this dharma is fundamentally quiescent and fundamentally knowing, one must, in accordance with this principle, employ the mind in accord with its original state. One must not give rise to deluded thoughts; rather, simply be without [delusion].

Deluded thought is itself cultivation; therefore, this one gate takes non-thought as its primary principle. Regarding the commentary’s statement that it "universally leaves behind the former errors while comprehensively gathering all that is correct," there are two meanings.
First, by means of the first house, it distinguishes and gathers the preceding six. That is to say, the upper phrase distinguishes and the lower phrase gathers.
"Distinguishing" refers to the "former errors," namely the first, second, and sixth houses, which stagnate in the conditioning marks of defilement and purity, thereby losing [the true nature].
The original nature and inherent virtue of primordial purity lack the practice of expedient means in the fourth and the three [sections] above it;

consequently, they exhaust themselves within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). (This contradicts the teachings of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*. Among these, the third further incurs the fault of repudiating the teaching.

Moreover, none of the six schools point directly to the numinous mind. Now, the seventh [section] penetrates the essence and points directly to quiescent awareness, without relying on various phenomenal forms.
This is the measure of the Dharma. Furthermore, it is said thus because one practices in accordance with the nature through non-recollection.
The phrase "the latter sentence subsumes this as correct" means that taking quiescent wisdom as the foundation, one cultivates the preliminary expedient practices in accordance with conditions;
these refer to the aforementioned six schools, all of which are wondrous gateways for treating specific ailments. This is what they penetrate, yet it is free from their respective ailments. (2)
In summary, the seven schools are all subject to inclusion and exclusion.

Specifically, within the seventh school, if one were to exclusively exclude the deluded mind of discursive thought, the characteristics of form, the objects of the sensory realms, and the inert, solid void, establishing only quiescent awareness as the ultimate, then [the other methods] would mutually come to be the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*).
For those who perceive through Perfect Penetration, they must necessarily integrate the aforementioned various dharmas of acceptance and rejection into a single whole.
The nature of quiescent awareness—this nature of quiescent awareness—manifests as various gateways throughout its entire substance in accordance with conditions; only then is it true seeing.
Quiescent awareness is like the pure brightness of a mirror, while all conditions are like that which can manifest images. The profound intent of Heze was originally such as this.
However, because at that time the gradual teachings flourished greatly while the Sudden school declined and fell into neglect, he focused on providing a remedy for them.

Thus it is said: "Therefore, the school maintains only non-thought (*amanyana*) and does not establish various conditions (*pratyaya*). It is like addressing someone who does not yet recognize the nature of a mirror;
one simply says, 'This pure clarity is the mirror,' rather than saying, 'The blue or yellow is the mirror. Now, regarding the seventh school, there is also a point of distinction;
however, this merely distinguishes the limited views of later followers, not the original masters (*ācārya*). Based on this principle, one should know that among the seven schools, if...

When one synthesizes them into a single, perfectly interfused whole, then all seven are correct. However, if one clings to each school as being exclusively its own and refuses to acknowledge the others, then all seven are incorrect.

This is as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: there were people who felt an elephant; although each claimed their perception was the truth while the others were wrong, none of them failed to touch the body of the elephant itself.
It is simply that they grasped it in part, yet that part is the entirety of the elephant. Therefore, the commentary refers to it as "the body of the elephant."

Below the various schools mentioned above in the Commentary, the third section synthesizes these schools according to their teachings. This is done solely by reconciling the methods of sudden and gradual awakening and cultivation with the principle of spontaneity (*ziran*).

Once this is understood, all schools are harmonized, for none of them deviates from this principle. Now, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are precisely the path that is to be cultivated;
suddenness and gradualism are merely the formal procedures for awakening and cultivation. Regarding the path to be cultivated, there is both the primary and the auxiliary. Concentration...
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the true path; the myriad other practices are the auxiliary paths. Because they assist concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"It is like a powerful king whom all the land reveres and looks up to; concentration and wisdom are likewise that upon which Bodhisattvas rely. Such teachings are not limited to one.

Awakening and cultivation are mostly comprised of understanding and practice. Both sudden and gradual approaches apply to awakening and cultivation; there is no fixed distinction between them, as they are clarified through their mutual interrelation.
The deficiency of concentration refers to wisdom that lacks stability; such wisdom is "wild wisdom," like a lamp in the wind or water being stirred.
Concentration without wisdom is "foolish concentration," like a person in a swoon without consciousness, or like a withered stump devoid of sentience.

Furthermore, practicing concentration exclusively increases ignorance, while practicing wisdom exclusively increases false views. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of the concentration of the śrāvakas.

Because the power of strength (*bala*) is predominant, one does not see the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Because the Bodhisattva’s power of wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant, one sees the nature but not clearly.

Below this, the two are practiced in tandem to clarify the benefits of equal training, as also explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. The Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings is perfected in merit and wisdom;

meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the essence of merit, and wisdom (*prajñā*) is the root of knowledge (*jñāna*). Regarding cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), [this is as stated in] the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Ten).
In the preface to the *Two Fascicles of Minor Calming and Contemplation*, it says: "Calming (*śamatha*) is the initial gateway for subduing the fetters;

contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is the essential method for severing delusions. Calming is the excellent provision for nourishing the mind-consciousness; contemplation is the wondrous art for illuminating and examining spiritual understanding."

Calm abiding (*śamatha*) is the supreme cause of meditative concentration (for through the cessation of all conditions, one attains calm abiding), while insight (*vipaśyanā*) is the basis for wisdom (for through the observation of all phenomena, the power of wisdom is perfected).
This is explained in detail as cited in the introductory section on the fundamental gates at the beginning of the "Chapter on Majestic Virtue" concerning the three contemplations.

Regarding the section "Its Sudden and Gradual Aspects" below: Fourth, the general explanation of the Dharma-gates. Now, both awakening (*bodhi*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) encompass both the sudden and the gradual. Furthermore, awakening includes intellectual understanding (*parijñāna*) and realization (*sākṣātkāra*);

cultivation includes that which accords with appearances (*nimitta-anusārin*) and that which is free from appearances (*nimitta-vinirmukta*). This means that one first relies on intellectual understanding as the cause; based on this awakening, one practices.

When the practice is fulfilled and merit perfected, one immediately attains realization. This constitutes the true and correct [path]. If, however, each follows their own faculty and nature... and so forth.
Good friend, the provisional arrangements of skillful means have no fixed order of priority. In the present text, there are nine pairs: first, five [cases] of awakening through understanding;

second, third, fourth, sixth, and ninth, awakening through realization; seventh and eighth, both types of awakening. Regarding "sudden awakening" in the commentary: the sun of wisdom rises all at once (the perfectly luminous nature of enlightenment), and the delusions of frost and dew gradually dissolve.
It is also like a newborn child, whose six sense organs, four limbs, and hundreds of joints are all complete instantaneously.

(The myriad virtues within the nature) are nurtured by milk and food, gradually growing until they emerge from the household and enter official service; the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*) serve as adornments, bringing the *nirmāṇa-kāya* and *saṃbhoga-kāya* to perfection.

To cite two metaphors: the severing of delusions and the realization of principle represent two distinct aspects. The latter follows this same pattern. This awakening occurs at the beginning, and thus belongs to "awakening through understanding" (*parijñāna-bodhi*).

The cultivation subsequent to awakening possesses both conformity with phenomena and detachment from phenomena; because one cultivates both principle and phenomena simultaneously, one's meritorious practice becomes perfected, necessarily following upon realization.

"Awakening" (*wu*) belongs to the subsequent pair. In the commentary (*shu*), following the section on "gradual cultivation and sudden awakening," the next three pairs concern the realization of awakening (*zhengwu*).

Regarding the first point, "gradual cultivation and sudden awakening," there are two meanings: first, it refers to the gradual cultivation of the aforementioned intellectual understanding (*jie-wu*); because this cultivation reaches its culmination, realization occurs.
Second, it refers to those who proceed gradually from the very beginning, such as the various *śrāvakas* who, through forty years of gradual prior cultivation, [attain] the Three Vehicles.
Because of practicing the teachings, within the assembly on Vulture Peak, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the net of doubts was suddenly severed and the mind became as calm as the ocean;

they were granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. This is like a person felling a tree: though struck by a thousand or ten thousand blows of the axe, it gradually cuts until the tree finally falls all at once (this metaphorizes the severing of delusions).
It is also like traveling from a remote borderland to the capital: after walking step by step for several months, on the day one enters the great city gate, [the destination is finally reached].

To arrive all at once (this is a metaphor for realizing the principle). For instance, Tiantai spent several years in cultivation and training, then for one hundred days applied himself with diligent effort and practice;
suddenly he realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and the *Svadhāraṇī-mukha*, attaining complete penetration into all dharmas.

This is precisely that matter. Such is the view regarding the teachings of the Northern School’s gradual approach; however, they mostly enter the realm of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

It is difficult to attain the realization of perfect penetration. Therefore, those who awaken gradually are so called because, although they hear the Perfect Teaching and believe in the Perfect Dharma, their faculties and natures are dull and they cannot achieve sudden awakening.
Even though they do not achieve sudden awakening, their longing and aspiration for the profound essence and the principle of suddenness are intense.
Suddenly one arouses the Great Mind, suddenly severs all conditions, and suddenly subdues the afflictions. Through these preparatory practices (*prayoga*), one gradually attains awakening.
Awakening is itself realization; it is not merely intellectual understanding. It is like a person polishing a mirror:
they polish one face all at once, never applying effort to a single fraction or inch at a time. As the dust and grime vanish bit by bit, the radiance gradually emerges.

[The text] says: (Gradual Illumination) Furthermore, it is like one learning archery who, upon first grasping the bow and arrow, immediately fixes their attention on the target (this is a metaphor for giving rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta).

From the beginning, they do not intentionally create distinctions of intimacy or distance, nor do they establish a sequence of stages (meaning they do not first cultivate the ten faiths before selecting the ten abodes and so forth). Yet, over a thousand or a hundred days, they shoot hundreds of millions of arrows.

Gradually drawing closer, one eventually reaches the point where one hits the mark a hundred times in a hundred attempts. (The preceding metaphor already addressed both severance and realization; the subsequent metaphor concerns realization alone. The Commentary states:

"Those of gradual enlightenment believe that the fundamental nature is perfect and complete, yet they still reckon that there are karmic afflictions and delusions acting as obstructions and coverings. Therefore, they diligently wipe away the dust from the mirror."

Gradual awakening to the nature of mind is as illustrated by the metaphors cited in the commentary. The metaphor of treading with one’s feet represents cultivation (*śikṣā*), while that which is reflected upon represents realization (*bodhi*).

(If contrasted with the subsequent metaphor of suddenly severing afflictions like cutting through bamboo joints, this is different. The commentary’s phrase “and [this] constitutes realization” summarizes the three preceding pairs.

In the commentary’s statement “if one speaks of sudden awakening and sudden cultivation,” the following three pairs indicate that both awakening and cultivation are sudden; however, they differ only in terms of their respective delusions.

Because they occur either sequentially or simultaneously, there arises the distinction between "understanding" (*jie*) and "realization" (*zheng*). First, the sudden awakening and sudden cultivation are established;
the analogy of cutting dyed silk is used to illustrate this: "cutting" represents sudden awakening. To realize that afflictions are fundamentally non-existent is what is called "severance.
This is like a single strand of dyed silk that cannot withstand even a single stroke of a blade but is severed all at once. (This is the analogy cited by Heze. "Dyeing" represents sudden cultivation.
One suddenly invokes the *saṃkhyeya* merits that accord with the nature of reality, cultivating them in every thought-moment without interruption. It is like dyeing a single skein of silk:
thousands and tens of thousands of strands all take on the color at once. Thus, the Great Master Qingliang’s *Xinyao* says: "In every mind, one becomes a Buddha."
There is not a single thought that is not the Buddha-mind; the Way is realized everywhere. There is not a single speck of dust that is not the Buddha-land.

Furthermore, the *Xingyuan su* (Commentary on the Vows) states: "Practice is sudden cultivation, while the stages are distinguished by cause and effect—all of which pertain to the meaning of sudden cultivation.

As for the statement in the commentary regarding "first awakening and then practicing," this refers to the initial stage. As explained in the sub-commentary (*zhù*), it means that through the sudden realization of body, mind, and the sensory environment...
Because all things are empty, one does not cling to various marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and does not realize a "mind-nature" (*cittatā*), for the mind-nature is fundamentally unmoving.

Furthermore, because one suddenly realizes that the merit as vast as the sands of the Ganges is fully present, one accords with it in every thought-moment; this is called "conforming to the Way" (*mārga*).

Since this awakening comes first, it should be understood [as such]. Regarding the commentary’s statement "first practice, then awakening," this refers to the subsequent correspondence. That is to say, suddenness arises from the severance of...

Regarding the various conditions and so forth (as cited above), the ground of the mind thus opens wide. Because both the faculties (*indriya*) and the aspiration (*chanda*) are superior, this differs from the "sudden cultivation and gradual awakening" mentioned previously.
The commentary states that cultivation is like taking medicine: a single dose brings immediate realization. Awakening is like the removal of illness:
when a feverish disease breaks into a sweat, the four limbs and all joints become simultaneously light and clear. This does not involve a gradual process.

The sense of gradual restoration is such that since awakening occurs subsequent to cultivation, it must pertain to realization (*sākṣātkāra*). However, this realization and its preceding understanding are not two distinct phenomena.

The commentary’s statement that "cultivation and awakening are simultaneous" refers to their posterior correspondence. That is to say, taking non-characteristic (*animitta*) as cultivation and clarity as awakening:
awakening is wisdom (*prajñā*), which is function; cultivation is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is essence. Heze said: "Function is precisely the essence."

"Self-awareness," etc. This is an abridgment of the essential meaning drawn from the commentary. The full text states: "When the mind is free from both forgetting and illumination, all myriad burdens are cast off;
when one proceeds spontaneously with tranquil awareness, all practices arise. Here, we have taken only the first phrase of each pair.
One metaphor is for awakening, and one metaphor is for cultivation. If one employs the latter two lines in their entirety, they inherently contain both cultivation and awakening;

that is, the upper line refers to awakening and the lower line refers to cultivation. The *Xinyao* further states: "If not a single thought arises, the past and future limits are severed" (this is sudden cultivation);
"The luminous essence stands alone, and both self and others are as such" (this is sudden awakening). Heze said: "Do not deliberate at all upon any good or evil. Thus it is said.
Below is the cessation of the marks of thought (the stage of cultivation). When there is truly no conceptualization, the mind knows itself (the stage of awakening).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "realization and understanding are both pervasive," there are two meanings. First, as explained above, realization and understanding likewise lack dual characteristics; therefore, both are pervasive.
This means that realization is itself understanding, and understanding is itself realization. Second, it may refer to either realization or understanding, meaning they occur simultaneously.

The phrase "comprehending and suddenly ceasing" and so forth constitutes awakening through understanding (*jiewu*). "Suddenly exhausting and suddenly awakening" constitutes awakening through realization (*zhengwu*).

It is like waking from a great dream; upon waking, there is sudden awakening, because the dream must necessarily end all at once. (As stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which shall be explained in detail below.

The commentary states that the section beginning with "if originally possessed" constitutes the eighth pair. It concludes by saying this encompasses both understanding and realization. This also contains two meanings, as explained sequentially above; this is the first meaning.

This can be understood. The latter meaning should now be explained. Regarding the explanation by way of interpretation (*vyākhyāna*): one takes only the untainted fundamental awakening (*anāsrava-mūla-bodhi*) as enlightenment, without adding a mind of conscious awareness;
one takes only the virtues inherent in the nature (*dharmatā-guṇa*) as practice, without depending on the cessation of the mind for practice.

In the commentary, both the characters "to drink" and "to obtain" are metaphors that correspond to this. Regarding the explanation by way of realization (*adhigama*): it is the union of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) with the fundamental [awakening].

At that time, there is no distinction between an initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* states: "The newly accomplished is the ancient Buddha; the ancient Buddha is the newly accomplished.

It is called a "sutra" (*sūtra*) because it is the path traversed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and because it is the vehicle that carries sentient beings across the ocean of suffering.

Furthermore, it is called a "sutra" because it is the teaching that flows forth from the mouth of the Buddha. Thus, the title of this sutra is established based on these meanings. Regarding the second part, the specific correlation: as for the term "Great" (*Mahā*), it refers to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). As for "Correct" (*Saddharma*), it refers to the True Dharma (*saddharma*). As for "Lotus" (*Padma*), it refers to the Lotus of the Tathāgata. As for "Sutra" (*Sūtra*), it refers to the teaching that is the source of all dharmas. As for "Expounded by the Buddha" (*Bhagavat-bhāṣita*), it indicates that this is not a teaching of a disciple or a Bodhisattva, but is the direct teaching of the World-Honored One. By correlating these terms individually, one understands that this sutra is the ultimate teaching of the Buddha. Regarding the third part, the conclusion: "This is then" means that by observing the title of this sutra, one knows that it universally encompasses all the teachings of the Buddha, including the three vehicles and the one vehicle, as well as the provisional and the real. Therefore, it is named the *Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma*. This concludes the first section. "How shall we practice the Path? Who shall serve as our teacher? How shall we dwell together with Channa, who speaks such harsh words?

[This section] explains [the body] by way of five aspects. Regarding the "seed" (bīja) in the commentary: it refers to the seeds of consciousness, defilements, karma, and the vital essence of the father and mother, which are gathered together to form the physical body.

though one provisionally sustains it with bathing, clothing, and food, it inevitably returns to destruction. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Examine this body with discernment: it must return to the place of death;

Now, as for "swallowing and chewing" in the mouth: on each of the two corners there is one character; these are *ā-ū*. It is also called *ā-ō*;

they differ only in the lightness or heaviness of the Sanskrit pronunciation. In the sub-commentary (*shu*), the phrase "furthermore, like... refers generally to both the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*), encompassing both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*). "Principle" here refers to the underlying logic, not merely *tathatā* (suchness).
This is exactly what Master Sheng explained in his commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The note states that this is the same as Master Yuan’s [view].
This is a supplementary explanation by Master Yuan, based on the Dharma, regarding the commentary of Master Sheng. It clarifies that Master Yuan’s intention is identical to Master Sheng’s.
However, he states in full: "The understanding of all dharmas is the path of the Tathāgata.
Because it accords with all dharmas, it is called 'Tathatā' (Suchness). It explains principles as they truly are; it explains phenomena as they truly are; it explains causes as they truly are."
The fruit is like the fruit. Since words that accord with the Dharma are consistent with principle, they are called "thus" (evam).

For it is precisely because words that deviate from the Dharma are termed "not so" (naivam), that words in accordance with the Dharma can be termed "so. Although such words are many, they are merely words that accord with principle; thus, they do not differ from Master Sheng.
Furthermore, the phrase "there is no 'below'" (wú xià) generally synthesizes the previous explanations regarding breadth and narrowness. △

Commentary: If we consider only the subsequent section, these two [terms] are explained solely in relation to the present sutra. That is to say, "not different" (*na-anyathā*) has the meaning of "resemblance," and thus it is called *tathā* (thus).
To exclude what is not [the case] is to reveal by contrast the meaning of "it is" (*asti*), and thus it is called *iti*.

Although this is based on the present sutra, it is largely consistent with the principle that existence and non-existence are non-dual as *tathatā* (suchness), and that which is neither existent nor non-existent is *iti*. This is the sole cause.

Regarding the "fruit" (*phala*): The *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source) states: "Without conduct that flows from the True, one cannot accord with the True. How could there be conduct that adorns the True if it does not arise from the True?

Thus we know that only that which is not different from Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is the cause for departing from transgressions. The fruit should be understood by analogy with this.

As for the principle that "the Dharma should follow the gates of teaching," this is explained in the *Huayan chao* (Notes on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) by correlating it with the five teachings; that is to say, once one knows...
These are words of principle. To clarify the two truths: for those of the Hīnayāna, the person and phenomena are the conventional, while the emptiness of birth is the ultimate.

Within the Initial Teaching, there are four layers of the conventional and ultimate; within the Final Teaching, there are the conventional and ultimate of phenomena and principle, with these two mutually penetrating one another.
According to the Sudden Teaching, both the ultimate and the conventional are extinguished; words cease and thought is cut off. This is called "conformity to reality" (*yathābhūta*).

Statements such as those in the *Anityatā-sūtra*, which definitively declare that birth, aging, sickness, and death are to be loathed, are termed "words conforming to reality. Any teaching other than what is clarified here [is not so].
One must not refer to these matters and so forth. Other teachings may be considered accordingly.

In the commentary, from "Thus have I heard" onwards, there are two parts. Within this, there are again two: first, the direct explanation; second, the resolution of objections. In the first of these, there are three further sections.

First, an explanation according to the teachings on the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; second, an explanation according to the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatāvāda*); third, an explanation according to the Final Teaching (*paryantayāna*). Regarding the first [of these three], there are two parts:
first, an explanation of "I" (*ātman*); second, an explanation of "heard" (*śruta*). Regarding the first of these, there are further four sections. Now, for the first:

it is explained by directly pointing to the provisional name, because this refers to the sūtras spoken in the Pure Land. Furthermore, the compilation includes both Bodhisattvas; however, this is a general indication.
[This concerns] the teaching that contains the ultimate truth. The *Śāstra* asks: "Why is it called 'I'? This is posed as an objection to raise a challenge. The intention is this:
All Buddhist teachings expound non-self (*anātman*). Ānanda was a sage who had entered into the principle; why then does he speak like an ordinary person, saying "I heard"?
The Commentary states: "I have four kinds. This first point generally lists the heterodox and the orthodox. Among these, the first two are as distinguished below.

The third encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles (Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna) as well as the sages and saints. The fourth clarifies only the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, speaking in terms of the fundamental [nature], Ānanda also penetrates the *dharmakāya*-self, as will be explained below.
The Commentary continues from "Now, this is... with the fourth point, which uses the orthodox to distinguish it from the heterodox; that is, although the Dharma...
There is none. This is because [the term "self"] is a conventional designation used in accordance with worldly convention. Nor is it because there is a true self within the dharmas that lack a self.

As for the phrase "not [due to] false pride," etc., this first section explains what was excluded; the true self will be clarified further below. Herein, the general intent of this treatise is as follows:

in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the first chapter contains three successive expositions explaining how the "self" is spoken of despite the teaching of "no-self. The first states: "The 'self' is spoken of within the context of worldly dharmas, not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*)."

It is explained within the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra*: "For this reason, all phenomena are empty and selfless. Because they are worldly conventions (the term 'world' refers to the mundane world), there is no fault in speaking of a 'self.
Second, it says: Furthermore, worldly speech has three roots: first, falsehood; second, pride; and third, conventional designation (*nāman*).
The former two are impure, while the latter one is pure. All ordinary persons possess these three types of speech. Thus it is seen.
Practitioners of the Way possess two kinds of speech: namely, arrogance and conventional designations. The various sages possess only one kind of speech: namely, conventional designations.

Because their minds do not conceptualize phenomena as real, they follow worldly people in transmitting these expressions. Thus, when a disciple of the Buddha speaks of a "self" in accordance with worldly convention, there is no fault.
Thirdly: furthermore, if a person clings to the mark of non-self and asserts that all phenomena are real...

All else is false speech. This person should raise an objection: "If the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is selflessness (*anātman*), why do you say, 'Thus have I heard' (*evam mayā śrutam*)?
Now, for the disciples of the Buddhas, all phenomena are empty and non-existent; therein, the mind does not cling."
Furthermore, one does not even cling to the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, much less cling to a self within a state of non-self.

For this reason, one should not raise the objection: "Why do you speak of a self? The commentary states: The three preceding repetitions were for three purposes: first, to conform to worldly convention; second, to refute false views;

and third, to avoid clinging to [the notion of] non-self. Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that there are four meanings [for speaking of a self]: first, the wisdom of compassion (*maitrī-anugata-jñāna*).
The intent of this treatise is to establish three types of "self," none of which carry distinct meanings; these are all reconciled as explained in other fascicles.

All that has preceded serves to eliminate false pride and to reveal the third type—the "self" that conforms to worldly convention. As for the fourth, the "self" of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), this is the Perfect Teaching of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

It is the true self of the Dharma-body revealed by the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other scriptures, which reconcile provisional teachings with the ultimate reality. This is not the same [as the preceding types].
The Dharma-characteristics and the refutation of characteristics merely speak of what resembles a self and what is non-self. As for these compilers, since they are Mañjuśrī and Ānanda—
Ānanda being the third "self" because he is equal to the various sages, and Mañjuśrī being the fourth "self" because he is a Mahāsattva of the Dharmakāya—
and furthermore, because Ānanda’s provisional essence also constitutes the fourth, Mañjuśrī, who does not destroy the semblance of characteristics, likewise constitutes [the fourth].
Third: Either by way of superior correspondence, or by the mutual interpenetration of the root and its branches—both interpretations are acceptable.

△ Regarding the phrase "As for 'hearing'... below, there are two explanations of "hearing. Within this, there are further two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the resolution of objections. In the first part, there are again two sections: first, explaining the meaning of the "one who hears";

second, explaining the meaning of "arousing consciousness. In the first of these, there are again two sections: first, a direct indication; second, [the section beginning with] "In the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna... and so forth.
Explanation of the meaning. Regarding the three explanations for each: as for the three [explanations] of the Hīnayāna, within the Sarvāstivāda school itself there are three positions.

First, the master Dharmatrāta holds that hearing is not consciousness (*vijñāna*). He maintains that although one's own constituent consciousness depends upon the sense organ (*indriya*) to hear, the essence of hearing is the organ itself and not the consciousness.
As it is with hearing, so it is with seeing and the other [faculties]. Thus, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* says: "One's own..."
The eye sees forms; it is not the visual consciousness that sees, nor is it wisdom, nor is it their conjunction. This is because obstructed forms are not seen.

Second, the teacher Subhūti holds that it is consciousness that hears, not the ear, because the sense organ lacks sentience. Third, the teacher Saṃghabhadra holds that it is the conjunction [of the three] that is able to hear.

These three views are all as explained in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter on Elements (Dhātunirdeśa), verse 10, and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, regarding the teaching on sensation (*vedanā*). [Commentary: However, some...

The first part below provides two explanations for the arising of consciousness. The previous section spoke of "conjunction," which refers merely to the conjunction of the sense organ and consciousness enabling hearing.

Regarding the three factors in the Mahāyāna: first, the ear hears, not consciousness. As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Compendium of Abhidharma), fascicle 1, states: "What is the characteristic of the auditory element (*śrotra-dhātu*)? It is that which is capable of hearing sound."

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Trisatikāyāḥ Prajñāpāramitāyāḥ Kārikā), chapter thirty-five, states: "Because the ear can hear by repeatedly attending to sounds, it is the two consciousnesses that hear, not the ear.

The *Liang Translation of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "There are three meanings of 'hearing': first, the essence of hearing, which is the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*); second, the provisions for hearing, which are sounds;

and third, the fruit of hearing, which is the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). Only this auditory consciousness is considered the primary act of hearing through the conjunction of the three [factors]."
"One is able to hear. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing refers to the ear-faculty giving rise to consciousness and manifesting sensation.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* states: "Hearing refers to listening; that is, the ear-faculty produces sound and the ear-consciousness hears. This clarifies that the ear, possessing conditions, gives rise to consciousness;

hence it is called 'four and eight. The four conditions refer to the Hīnayāna: first, emptiness (space); second, the faculty; third, the object; and fourth, attention (*manasikāra*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*..."

It is said: At that time, the faculty of hearing is unimpaired (the *indriya*); the sound is within the range of audibility (space); there is the mental application of the desire to hear (mental application);
the sentient faculty (the sense organ joined with consciousness); the object (the environment); and the mental faculty (the *manas-indriya*).
With these five factors combined, auditory consciousness arises (the fruit of the combination of conditions). As soon as auditory consciousness arises, mental consciousness arises simultaneously.
To discriminate names and phrases is not itself the condition (*pratyaya*). It is through the ability to discriminate various causes and conditions that one is able to hear sounds. (Summary:

However, since the mental faculty (*manas*) is merely the root of attention (*manaskāra*), there are only four [conditions]. The meaning explained in the ninth chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* encompasses both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;

furthermore, these four conditions are common to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. As for the "eight conditions" mentioned in the commentary, these belong to the Mahāyāna and are based upon those same four.

Furthermore, four [factors] are added: first, emptiness; second, the faculties (*indriya*); third, the objects (*viṣaya*); fourth, mental attention (*manasikāra*). Fifth is the fundamental basis (*mūlāśraya*);
sixth is the basis for defilement and purification (*saṃkleśavyavadānāśraya*); seventh is the basis for discrimination (*vikalpāśraya*); and eighth is the seed (*bīja*).

The seed serves as the causal condition basis (*hetupratyayāśraya*), and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are said to have this as their basis, because they necessarily do not arise apart from their own causal conditions. The basis for discrimination is the sixth consciousness. [Defilement...]

The pure support (*viśuddha-āśraya*) is the seventh consciousness; the fundamental support (*mūla-āśraya*) is the eighth consciousness. This is because the "root" is identical to the support of the same object (*sabhāga-ālambana*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 4, states:

"For this reason, the simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the five consciousnesses are necessarily of four kinds: namely, the five material faculties and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.

If any one of these is missing, [the five consciousnesses] will certainly not arise. [These four] are the support of the same object, the support of discernment (*vikalpa*), and the support of defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*)."
This is because their fundamental bases (*āśraya*) differ. As a verse says: "Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions;

ear-consciousness only from eight; nose, tongue, and body from seven, three, and two respectively; the latter three from five, three, and four. These are explained in detail within the sections on the eight consciousnesses below.

Although the commentary (*ṭīkā*) addresses two objections following the section on the ear-sense base (*śrotra-āyatana*), it states: Suppose someone asks, "If it is the ear that hears, why do you say 'I hear'?"

Therefore, this general explanation is made to clarify that "I" is the totality, as it encompasses all the sense organs, such as the eye and so forth. This is from the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. Regarding the passage "If there is no characteristic... and below:

secondly, this is an explanation according to the Emptiness school (*śūnyatā-vāda*), which includes the three teachings—namely, the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), the Sudden Teaching (*tadaṅga-yāna*), and the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*).
Thus, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used. Although it includes these three teachings, the doctrinal principles of the No-characteristic school (*alakṣaṇa-nikāya*) are predominant; hence the statement.

Regarding the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*): if one merely says, "Since there is no self, there is likewise no hearing," this constitutes the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna and represents the intent of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

If, however, one says that both subject and object are simultaneously quiescent—such that there is neither hearing nor non-hearing, and neither self nor non-self, manifesting through the transcendence of conceptual thought—this represents the intent of the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*).
Because emptiness arises from conditions, it is twofold: first, [the aspect of] ascending to perfect the former two.

This explains the reason for teaching non-self. Second, looking downward, it does not destroy conventional designations; this is "hearing that which is not heard," which constitutes the intent of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*).
This is because phenomena and principle are unimpeded, and because there is no duality between hearing and not hearing. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

How does one who hears hear? Is it by means of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) that one hears? Is it by means of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) that one hears? Or is it by means of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) that one hears?
If it were the ear-faculty that hears, the ear-faculty lacks sentience and cognition; therefore, it should not be able to hear.

If it were the ear-consciousness that hears, the ear-consciousness cannot perform discrimination for even a single moment. The mental consciousness cannot [hear] the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) in the present; rather, the five consciousnesses arise first, and once they have cognized the five sense-objects, only then does the mental consciousness cognize them. Thus, [the mental consciousness] does not [hear] in the immediate present.
[Question: Since [the five objects] such as past and future forms and so forth are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), they should all not be heard. [Answer:

It is not the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), or the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) alone that performs the act of hearing sound. Rather, sound is heard through the convergence of many causes and conditions;

one cannot say that a single dharma can hear sound. (The above clarifies that hearing is impossible apart from these conditions. At that time, when the ear-faculty is unimpaired and various other causes and conditions are met, one is able to hear.

Sound. (The preceding has already been fully cited within the section on the four conditions. The commentary states: Since it is heard through their conjunction, hearing is itself non-hearing; this is entirely the purport of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*).

If Master Liu’s commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are not the subject; it is the 'self' that hears and receives. That which is non-sentient is called 'hearing.

One deeply illuminates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and awakens to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Regarding such a person, one considers the causes of their final instructions, and only then transmits [the teaching] without attachment.

Sentient beings and self reach the same realization. [The author] explains: This initial portion also follows the intent of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*). From the phrase "deeply illuminating dependent origination" onwards...
This is precisely the intent of the True Teaching (*shijiao*). Nevertheless, all [these teachings] are subsumed within the School of Non-Characteristics (*wuxiang zong*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement "not hearing what is heard," this refers to what is taught in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter 19. Therein, there are four propositions: namely, not hearing what is heard; not hearing what is not heard;

hearing what is not heard; and hearing what is heard. Here, we employ only one of these phrases and cannot fully cite the intended meaning of the scripture. Tiantai employs these four propositions to correlate them with...
The four teachings refer to the "hearing of hearing" and so forth of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao), as cited in a separate fascicle.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "If one relies on the dharma-nature," the following three points explain according to the Real Teaching (Shijiao)—which combines the Final and Sudden Teachings under the general name of Real Teaching—and yet also clarifies the intent within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). This is because [the text speaks of] "self and non-self."
This encompasses the intent of two sutras. First, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Self and non-self are non-dual; this is the meaning of non-self.

Second, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Within the dharma of non-self, there is a true self; therefore, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One. This precisely accords with the present meaning:
the mouth conforms to worldly convention, while the mind creates the realm of truth. This is the true, sovereign self. [The commentary on] the sense bases and objects is not [the case here].

Regarding "identity and difference": because the sense organs and their objects arise together as conditions, one speaks of the object by means of the organ, and speaks of the organ by means of the object;
they are mutually fused and identical, hence it is said they are not different. Yet, as the two characteristics remain distinct, it is said they are not one. This is truly subtle!
What could there be that is not heard?
Below the section on Ānanda, the second major heading addresses and resolves potential objections.

This refers to those who have heard it said that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment, whereas the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says he was born twenty years after the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment.
Ānanda was serving as an attendant; yet, for twenty years prior to this, he had not heard what the Tathāgata taught.
When the Tathāgata was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, Ānanda was obscured by Māra and likewise did not hear [the final teachings]. Why, then, do the sūtras all begin with "Thus have I heard"?
It is for this reason that this explanation is provided. This explanation has two meanings; here, first, it is an explanation that incorporates the provisional (*upāya*). Therefore, first—
Furthermore, to raise an objection, it is said: "That which Ānanda did not hear," and so forth.

Regarding the "repeated explanation" in the commentary, the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), fascicle six, clarifies that when the Buddha appointed Ānanda as his attendant, Ānanda followed the Buddha and requested three vows:
first, not to accept the Buddha’s old robes; second, not to follow the Buddha in accepting separate invitations; and third, to request further instruction on any teachings he had not yet heard.
Because it was for the sake of explaining this, the Tathāgata, prior to entering *nirvāṇa*, spoke it once more for Ānanda.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also explains this meaning, as found in another fascicle. Regarding the phrase "one who attains the profound *samādhi* and achieves self-communication," the *Vajrapuṣpa-ṛṣi-sūtra* states:

Because Ānanda had attained the Samādhi of Sovereign Enlightenment in the Nature of Dharmas (*dharmatā-avabodha-vaśitā-rāja-samādhi*), he was able to remember and maintain all the sūtras previously preached by the Tathāgata, no differently than if he had heard them directly.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states: "Whether the learned Ānanda is present or absent, he can naturally understand the meaning of permanence and impermanence.
Furthermore, after receiving his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it says: "World-Honored One..."
How truly rare! It has caused me to recollect the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, just as I have heard them today.
I now have no further doubts and am firmly established in the Buddha-way. Acting as an attendant through skillful means (*upāya*), I shall protect and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas.

Since it is said that he has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), his mind remains attached to the provisional; yet, acting as an attendant through skillful means is precisely the secret revelation of the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, there are several other points of significance.

And it is also in another fascicle. Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with "If one traces back to the source," there are two parts that clarify the reality through its universal application, which further consists of three sections:

first, a direct indication; second, "As for 'not below,'" which refers to the sutra. The sutra says: "At that time, there were again ten trillion bodhisattvas who manifested in the forms of śrāvakas and also came to sit in the assembly.
Their names were Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and so forth, up to Ānanda and Deva."
With Pūrṇa, Upananda, and others as their leaders, they have all long cultivated the six pāramitās and are close to the bodhi of the Buddha;
for the sake of other sentient beings, they manifest in the form of śrāvakas within births free from defilement. The commentary states: these are great bodhisattvas.
This is precisely to reveal the fundamental [nature]; therefore, it is spoken as the truth. As stated in the "Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"O Bhikṣus, listen attentively! The path traversed by the sons of the Buddha involves skillfully training in the power of expedient means, which is inconceivable.
Just as some delight in minor dharmas and fear great wisdom, for this reason the Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."—The Chapter of Ānanda.
The middle passage states: "Using skillful means as an attendant, he protects and upholds all Buddha-dharmas. This clearly demonstrates his great transformative power (*mahopāya*).

The commentary’s comparison is the same as below. This is the third section, the conclusion and response. As for Mañjuśrī, he is as cited previously from the *Zuǎnlíng jì* (Record of the Collated Spirits). Why would one be hindered by his physical traces?
This refers to the teachings of a single lifetime, which were intended for a multitude of capacities. Since these capacities and their responses differ, what is seen and heard varies accordingly;

thus, the various teachings present many perspectives on the provisional and real aspects of the noble assembly. One must skillfully grasp the underlying intent rather than becoming mired in the literal traces.

Moreover, as previously cited from the *Mahāyāna-saṃghāṭa-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, it speaks of three Ānandas, making the manifestation of the provisional and real clearly evident. This is also the case in the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* and the works of Paramārtha.
The *Prajñā-piṭaka-śāstra* (Commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom) cites the *Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru’s Repentance* and other texts, all of which provide this same explanation.

Below the section "At one time," this constitutes the third major division of the text. This section has three parts: first, an explanation according to conventional characteristics; second, an explanation based on ultimate reality.

Third, the general exposition of the essence. This section has three parts. The first is the formal explanation. Regarding "time" (*samaya*): in Sanskrit it is *samaya*, which here means "time. Regarding "the meeting of teacher and disciple":

Master Daosheng said, "The capacity of the recipient and the teaching coincide at one time. This means that although the aforementioned words "Thus have I heard" are consistent with the truth, if they do not coincide with the proper time, they would still be a hollow proclamation.
Here, it is clarified that when the capacity of sentient beings moves the Sage, the Sage is able to manifest a responsive appearance. As for ordinary people...

The Noble Path intersects; one does not miss the opportune moment, hence it is called "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*). Master Zhaolun stated: "This refers to the time when the Dharma King inaugurates his auspicious reign.
The meaning of this can likewise be understood. "Inaugurate" (*qi*) means to open; "auspicious" (*jia*) means good. The *Yijing* says: "The Prime (*yuan*) is the beginning of goodness;

Prosperity (*heng*) is the assembly of the auspicious. This means that by opening the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), he expounds the True Vehicle (*saddharmayāna*), which is precisely what is meant by "the auspicious assembly."

Regarding the phrase "the assembly of the good": as for the commentary’s explanation that the teaching and listening reach their conclusion [in a single moment], one should first raise this objection:

since a single assembly involves many words and phrases, and each word and phrase consists of many *kṣaṇas*, how can it be said to be "one"? The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "This refers to the uninterrupted continuity of *kṣaṇas*;

because the teaching and listening reach their conclusion [within this flow], it is generally termed 'one time' (*ekakāla*). (There are two further interpretations of 'time,' which are found in a separate volume. This is not the case here.
It is not fixedly defined by a single *kṣaṇa*, nor is it fixedly defined by a continuity [of moments], nor is it fixedly defined by four periods, eight periods, or twelve periods.
Nor is it fixedly defined as a "single period" (*eka-kāla*) consisting of the number of years and seasons following the completion of the attainment of enlightenment.

Rather, it is simply that when the faculties of the listener have matured, they evoke the Buddha to speak for them; and the speaker, out of compassion, expounds in accordance with their capacity. Thus, the matter of speaking and listening is concluded.

Third is the treasury of the *dharmakāya*, because at the stage of fruition it is the locus upon which the qualities of the Dharma depend.

Fourth is the supreme-transmundane treasury, because it has emerged from the entanglements and transcends both the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas. Regarding the commentary on the *Candraprabha-paripṛcchā-sūtra*: the first two phrases testify to the commonality with the sages, while the last phrase testifies to the commonality with ordinary beings.

Therefore, it is named "Suchness" (Tathatā). Outside of Suchness, there are no phenomena; even that which comes is itself Suchness. One who comes in this manner is the True Tathāgata.
Regarding the phrase "the ground of original enlightenment": the ground is that which can generate and sustain all things; all things depend upon it for their arising.
Based upon this, all teachings employ the analogy of the earth for ignorance (*avidyā*), wisdom, and the source of the fundamental mind. Regarding the analogy for ignorance:

it refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is capable of successively generating various views, afflictions, karmic actions, and their retributive fruits (as stated at length in the treatise).
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that fundamental ignorance is the "ground-abiding from beginningless time" (*anādikālika-sthiti-bhūmi*). As for the analogy for wisdom:
Regarding "wisdom," the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Actions) explains the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Each stage is called a "support" (*dhāraṇī*), for it supports millions of asaṃkhyeya merits;

"Because they generate and sustain the Buddha-wisdom. To provide an analogy for the fundamental mind: it is the Tathāgatagarbha mind. Although it is not defiled...

It is pure, for it can give rise to all that is defiled and pure. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, *Awakening of Faith*, and *Ratnagotravibhāga* all state that the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
that is to say, the essence of the mind is pure and unchanging. When one is deluded regarding it, one follows defiled conditions and gives rise to all causes, karma, and outflows;
when one awakens to it, one follows pure conditions and is able to give rise to all that is stainless.
The causes and effects of the outflows (*āsrava*) are like the earth, which produces sweet or bitter medicinal herbs and grasses according to their respective seeds.

The hall of flowers is a metaphor for the Great Treasury of Radiance (*Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*); those who have first awakened are a metaphor for all Tathāgatas. One sees only this...

All such things are entirely impermanent. For this reason, there is no distinction between the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "Originally existent, now non-existent; originally non-existent, now existent.

There is no distinction. This is the seventeenth [section]. Because Kāśyapa questioned the Buddha regarding the meaning of "having nothing to attain," he cited a verse previously spoken by the Buddha concerning "original existence" (*pūrvam asti*) and asked about it.

Pāramitā. Because there is no prajñāpāramitā, all afflictions and fetters exist in the present. (This explains the first half [of the verse].
If there were any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, brahmās, or humans who claimed that the Tathāgata has afflictions in the past, future, or present, such a thing is impossible.
(This explains the second half. Up to the twenty-seventh, it is spoken because of all...
Because sentient beings will certainly attain bodhi, it is said that they definitely possess buddha-nature; yet, in reality, they do not yet possess the thirty-two marks and so forth.
Therefore, I spoke this verse, and so on, up to the twenty-eighth. This was spoken because it clarifies that food is the cause of life, whereas food itself is not life.
The commentary states: Although the four points are largely the same, their underlying intent differs slightly. That treatise provides a definitive response.

The *Kāśyapaparivarta* states: "To speak for the sake of the two vehicles is not to slander the Mahāyāna (because, according to their perspective, phenomena exist throughout the three periods of time);

however, to speak for the sake of the Mahāyāna is to slander the Mahāyāna (because the true nature of *nirvāṇa* is not a phenomenon that exists within the present). Next, the verse is judged as having two meanings. First, it refutes erroneous views—namely those of the non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna.
The first three lines refer to the doctrines established by these erroneous and inferior schools; the fourth line universally negates them, stating: [text omitted].
This is impossible. Second, establishing the correct principle: that which exists originally and exists now, transcending the three periods of time—this is called the correct principle.

From the initial generation of the mind until the attainment of the single fruit of nirvāṇa, there is no difference. It does not depend on the cause of arising, nor does it depend on the cause of cessation;
its existence is pure, undefiled by the ordinary and unpurified by the holy. (The above is from the *Śāstra* commentary. Master Qingliang.

First, I shall distinguish how the various schools’ interpretations deviate from reason; subsequently, I will resolve these doubts based on the *Śāstra*. (The commentary states: "Cunda perceives the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) but does not perceive the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);

Mañjuśrī perceives the specific characteristic but does not perceive the common characteristic; therefore, he harbors doubt. Regarding the initial meeting through conditions, it appears as if something originally non-existent has now come into being.

However, the nature of *nirvāṇa* does not belong to the three periods of time. When wisdom accords with this nature, that which shares this nature is eternal. How can you raise the objection that "that which has a beginning must necessarily have an end"?
"Is it impermanent? Thus was Cunda’s doubt dispelled. As for Mañjuśrī dispelling [the doubt] through his own perspective: Mañjuśrī sees this because he does not see the same.

That is to say, he sees the distinctions between the three vehicles regarding delusion and awakening; now, since they are the same as the two vehicles in being impermanent and subject to extinction, there is no distinction.

This is called "seeing the difference," which gives rise to the doubt: "Why do you not see them as the same? Not seeing them as the same means not seeing them as existing across the three periods of time.

Therefore, the present answer states that [the Dharma] accords with the absence of the three periods of time; once attained, it is eternally constant. How could it be the same as the impermanence and the lack of the nature of the three periods found in the Two Vehicles?
If there were no nature across the three periods, there would be no distinction; however, there is a distinction between those who have realized this and those who have not.

When those of superior faculties hear this once, their two doubts are instantly dispelled; those of middling and inferior capacities have not yet awakened. Thus, Kāśyapa gives rise to compassion. In the "Chapter on Brahma-Conduct," it is because of non-attainment [that he speaks].

He questioned the Buddha. The Buddha cited eight sections; in each section, he concluded by stating that it is impossible for there to be any phenomenon existing throughout the three periods of time—this is unattainable.

There is no principle that is not fully exhausted. Next, the explanation shall follow. The intent of the present commentary, based on the *Seventeen Sutras*, is as follows:

both "originally existing" and "now existing" may be applied to the delusory [aspect], while both "originally non-existent" and "now non-existent" are applied to the True [aspect]. Therefore, it is said: "I originally possessed afflictions" (referring to a previous life);

"now there is no nirvāṇa" (the conduct manifested in the past is referred to as "now"); "originally there was no prajñā" (also referring to a previous life); and "now there are afflictions" (also referring to what is currently manifesting in the past).

Regarding the phrase "Because of this": it refers to the Buddha’s past causes. Up to the twenty-seventh sūtra, it is stated that sentient beings, by means of the causes and conditions for severing afflictions in the past, now perceive the Buddha-nature;
this is the True Dharma because it was originally non-existent and is now present.

Consequently, Cunda gave rise to doubt, specifically challenging the World-Honored One on the grounds that the Buddha-nature was originally non-existent and is now present. Thus we know that whether [it be] true or...
[The term] "false" (*mṛṣā*) applies universally because it encompasses both that which was originally existent but is now non-existent, and that which was originally non-existent but is now existent.

The *Śū* (Commentary) alone follows the meaning of the *Duan jing* (Sutra on Severance) and the intent of that treatise; thus, regarding the relationship between the arising Buddha and [the original state], it speaks of both the True and the False.

Furthermore, since the various Buddhas spoke [of this] in the past according to the *Shiqi jing* (Seventeen Sūtras), the time of the Buddha's past is taken as the "original. It is also said that the past time is the "present," and this is applied by analogy to sentient beings.
Thus, the present time is taken as the fundamental basis, and the present time is also taken as "now. This is no different from the Buddha having possessed afflictions (*kleśa*) in the past;
all such statements are merely abbreviated expressions. In this commentary, taking the intent of severance as the standard, the past is taken as the fundamental basis and the present as "now.

When it is said that "afflictions existed for the Buddha in the past but are now absent," it means that when the Buddha was formerly an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), he possessed afflictions. (From the past...)

Because one has now attained perfect enlightenment, there are no afflictions (*kleśa*). (Here, "now" refers to the present moment. To say that sentient beings are "originally non-existent but now existent" is with respect to their intrinsically pure nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*):

originally, they have no afflictions. (Here, "origin" refers to the source. With respect to adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-mala*), they "now have" afflictions. (Here, "now" refers to the manifestation of delusion.

Since there has been no realization of *bodhi*, it is said that "it does not exist now. As for the statement that "for all Buddhas, it is originally non-existent and now existent," this refers to the perfectly pure *bodhi*:
