(The "original" and "now" of sentient beings and Buddhas are both to be assigned accordingly as above. Thus far, he has already revealed that.

however, according to the intent of the treatise, all three phrases are sublated within the fourth phrase; only then does it constitute true nature (*dharmatā*). Now, in this commentary, the third phrase summarizes the three periods of time, and the fourth phrase negates them;
therefore, it says that the second half of the verse concerns "nature. This is a minor textual variation in the phrasing. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is...

The purport of the treatise is as follows: How can one speak of the difference between delusion and awakening? It means that when one is deluded, there is delusion, yet it is not that the Truth is absent.

When one awakens, one perceives the nature; yet this nature was not something that came into being at that moment. Therefore, Master Sengsheng said: "It is simply that I have now for the first time understood it; it is not that I am perceiving something newly existent."
The illumination does not reside in the present; this is precisely what is meant by "non-action is great. Since it is called "great," it is therefore termed "constant.

Thus we know that although delusion and awakening differ, the nature of *nirvāṇa* does not shift throughout the three periods of time; it is profoundly and eternally abiding. When one realizes this, it accords with and is identical to that constant nature of suchness (*tathatā*).
Initial awakening becomes identical to the fundamental [nature], and the distinction between the beginning and the source no longer exists. How can you raise the objection that it "exists"?

If there is a beginning, there must be an end; thus, Cunda’s objection is resolved. Although this preceding point seems to have come as a digression, the profound purport of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is revealed therein.

"Pure below. Third, this refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which is simultaneous equality. The text has two parts. First, the heading: "The thirty-first is also different.

Regarding "permanence" (*nitya*): the *Śāstra* states that if something exists inherently from the beginning and continues to exist now, this constitutes the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Thus, there are two interpretations regarding the provisional and the real. First, the essence is high while the traces are low; this refers to Mañjuśrī himself. Third, the essence is low while the traces are high.

This refers to a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) who, having fulfilled the ten stages of faith (shixin), attains Buddhahood through the eight phases (baxiang) in a world where no Buddha exists, thereby teaching and transforming sentient beings.

Within each of those ten billion Jambudvīpas, there is a World-Honored One sitting upon a lion throne within a Lotus Treasury.

Seated, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, in each of the eastern directions there was a great bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, came to where the Buddha was. (The same occurred in each of the nine directions, though the names of the bodhisattvas were different.
At that time, the Mañjuśrī Bodhisattvas in every location simultaneously uttered these verses at their respective Buddhas’ abodes:

There are ten verses in this hymn. (In these verses, only Mañjuśrī is mentioned; the other nine bodhisattvas are not. This applies throughout the subsequent sections. This radiance transcends this world-system.
Each one illuminates ten Buddha-lands in the eastern direction (and likewise in the other nine directions). In each world, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas.

Thus it is said, "All see [him]. Regarding the exhortation to Sudhana, this refers to what is taught in the sixty-second chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where Mañjuśrī, at the site of an ancient Buddha’s stupa to the east of Puṇḍravardhana City, expounds the *Samantāvabhāsa-dharmadhātu-sūtra*.
In the city of Rāḍhā, five hundred upāsakas, upāsikās, boys, and girls each gathered together.
Among the boys, Mañjuśrī specifically gazed upon Sudhana; having known the events of his previous lives, he expounded for him all the Buddha-dharmas.
He earnestly exhorted and instructed him, increasing his spiritual power and causing him to rejoice and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he preached the Dharma as was appropriate for them, and then departed. Having heard this, Sudhana single-mindedly and diligently sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He spoke verses to repent for his past and rejoice in the future, praying for compassionate instruction. Mañjuśrī was like an elephant.
The King turned to look at Sudhana and said: "Excellent, excellent, noble son! You have already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, you wish to attend upon various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to inquire about the conduct of Bodhisattvas and cultivate the Bodhisattva path.
To attend upon and make offerings to spiritual friends is the primary cause and condition for attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Therefore, do not [be negligent] in this regard."
"Experiencing weariness" refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, as explained in detail in the section on the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*) within the Five Teachings;

one may consult that account for a full description. Regarding the commentary’s response concerning "the light," it is taught in the twenty-first chapter (chapter nineteen in the Southern edition), the "Chapter on the Noble Virtuous King" (*Gao-gui-de-wang-pin*), of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
It describes how, because the Bodhisattva Lapis Lazuli Light (*Vaiḍūryaprabha*) was about to arrive, the Buddha first emitted a radiance and questioned Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī...
When he first entered the primary truth (*paramārtha*), he replied: "World-Honored One, such radiance is called wisdom;
it is the eternally abiding dharma and is without causes or conditions. Why, then, does the Buddha ask by what causes and conditions this radiance exists?"
Having extensively clarified that there are no causes or conditions, the Buddha’s seal of approval was reached. At the end, it says: "The World-Honored One also has causes and conditions;
namely, by extinguishing ignorance, one attains the blazing radiance of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it states that within the various Mahāyāna sūtras, the Buddha frequently expounds profound and wondrous principles with Mañjuśrī.
In the dialogues, Mañjuśrī frequently employs the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to cross-examine the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One invariably affirms this as being so.
This occurs throughout the Mahāyāna sūtras in great abundance. Furthermore, in the places where Mañjuśrī expounds the Dharma, he most often relies upon the profound purport of the *prajñā*.
There is also a separate *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*. Therefore, the Contemplation of the Three Sages is correlated with the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the primary text.

Regarding the section on "Provisional and Real" (*shu quan-shi*) below, the *Ratnakūṭa*, fascicles 26 and 27, contains the "Contemplation of the Perfect Interfusion of the Three Sages" (*san-sheng yuan-rong guan*), which was composed by Qingliang (Chengguan).

It first clarifies the two sages and their three pairs of represented dharmas: first, Samantabhadra, who is the Tathāgatagarbha that is the object of faith (the *Líqù bōrě* states: "All sentient beings are the Tathāgata...").

The "Treasury" (garbha) refers to the fact that the essential body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is all-pervasive; thus, in the first assembly, he immediately enters the Tathāgata-garbha-kāya-samādhi. Mañjuśrī is the mind capable of faith, as stated in the *Buddhāvatamsaka-nāma-mahāvaipulya-sūtra*.

First, Mañjuśrī represents the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, for all Buddhas arouse their minds because of Mañjuśrī, and Sudhana first beholds him when he first resolves upon the Great Mind. Second, Samantabhadra represents the myriad practices that arise [from that resolve], for the scriptural texts throughout both the beginning and end speak of "the conduct of Samantabhadra.

Third, Mañjuśrī represents the wisdom capable of giving rise to those practices, as Maitreya says: "That you were previously able to see the various spiritual friends, hear of the Bodhisattva practices, and enter the gates of liberation—all this is due to the power of Mañjuśrī.
Third, Samantabhadra represents the dharmadhātu free from entanglement which is realized, for the sutra states: "His physical form is like space," and Sudhana enters into his body.

When Sudhana sees him, he immediately attains the *prajñāpāramitā* (because the function arises based on the essence). Mañjuśrī represents the great wisdom that is capable of realization (for the Buddha whom he originally served was named Acala-jñāna [Immovable Wisdom], and because he is eternally the mother of all Buddhas).

That one must see Samantabhadra only after seeing Mañjuśrī again reveals that it is only when one possesses wisdom that one realizes the principle; thus, ancient masters name the latter Mañjuśrī as "the illumination of wisdom" (*jñāna-āloka*), signifying that they are non-dual in aspect.

Nevertheless, these two sages each mutually encompass the other: this means that while practice arises based on the essence, practice is also able to manifest the principle. Thus, there are three Samantabhadras.
They are of one essence. If faith lacks understanding, that faith is ignorance; if understanding lacks faith, that understanding is false view.

Only when faith and understanding are authentic does one realize the original source and achieve ultimate wisdom. Because this ultimate wisdom reflects back upon itself and is not different from the initial mind, Mañjuśrī is likewise of one essence with them;
thus, he was previously designated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode) in the aggregate. Furthermore, these two sages are also mutually interfused.

"Contemplate this according to the principle. Regarding the phrase "investigating the true and the false in the commentary," this refers to the wisdom of understanding (*adhimukti-jñāna*) that arises from faith; it is the wisdom that exhaustively investigates through understanding.

These three—faith, understanding, and wisdom—are unified as the single entity of Mañjuśrī. Regarding the phrase "the commentary interrogates the illusory phenomena and so forth," this refers to the arising of practice from the essence (*tattva*).
The practice that accords with principle, the fused essence, the practice, and the principle—these three are one as Samantabhadra.

Regarding the commentary’s passage from "the universal eye" to "the virtuous and good," simply examine the preceding and following scriptural texts; the meaning of the commentary will become clear of itself. Each dharma-gate serves as a distinct point of illumination and focus.

The Commentary (Sū), Part Three: General Praise of the Following. This section of the commentary consists of three parts: first, a general explanation of the main intent. Within this, the first two phrases provide the heading; from "Because of honoring virtue" (*chóngdé gù*) onwards, the text provides the exegesis.
This refers to what is said in the *Zhou Yī* (Book of Changes), in the *Shàng xì* (Upper Sequence): "Is not the *Yī* the ultimate [of all things]? (*yì qí zhì yú hū*).

Now, the *Yi* (Book of Changes) is that by which the sages exalt their virtue and broaden their enterprise. (The commentary states: "To exhaust principle and enter the divine, their virtue is exalted; to universally benefit all things, their enterprise is broad.

Here, borrowing these words, "exhausting principle and entering the divine" is equivalent to the Bodhisattva’s illumination of true reality, wherein initial awakening merges with the fundamental; this is the meaning of achieving perfect awakening, and thus it is said that one "advances to equal the Buddha-fruit. "Universally benefiting all things" is equivalent to the Bodhisattva’s great compassion for beneficial transformation.

As the *Sūtra of Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices* says: "The Bodhisattva takes great compassion as the root"; thus, benefiting others is the Bodhisattva’s practice. Because sentient beings are boundless, the Bodhisattva’s practices are inexhaustible; thus it is said that "practice accords with the Dharma-realm.")

Wisdom is lofty and ritual is humble; loftiness emulates Heaven, while humility follows the pattern of Earth. (The commentary states: Wisdom takes loftiness as its achievement, while ritual takes humility as its function. These constitute abundant virtue and expansive enterprise.
How great it is! To possess abundance is called a "great enterprise"; to renew oneself daily is called "excellent virtue.
Regarding the statement on emptying the mind and casting aside the body, the *Laozi* says: "The sage governs" (this refers to the sage governing the state and governing the self).

He empties his mind (removing desires and discarding confusion and vexation), fills his belly (embracing the Dao and holding to the One, guarding the vital breath and nourishing the spirit), weakens his will (harmonizing his actions with humility and yielding), and strengthens his bones (cherishing the essence and valuing its application, so that the marrow is full and the bones are firm). It further says: "He puts his person last..."

[The Master] himself [placed others before himself]. By placing himself first, he led the way for the world and taught it; by taking precedence, he served as its leader. He disregarded his own person [putting himself last while honoring others], yet his person survived.

The common people loved him as parents, and the spirits and deities protected him as an infant; thus his person constantly endured. (All of the above is the commentary of He Shang Gong. Now, borrowing these words, it means that the Bodhisattva makes his mind vast and empty, transcending the duality of subject and object through wisdom, and forgetting his own body for the sake of sentient beings to single-mindedly benefit others.

*Commentary:* From "Now this" onwards, the second section correctly explains this passage. Regarding the phrase "merely praising the principal and the retinue," etc.: merely... The title has two intended meanings. First, it is a general and brief praise of his qualities rather than a detailed enumeration of each individual practice and virtue;

yet, though not listed individually, they are already contained within this summary. Second, it serves to manifest the loftiness and profundity of his wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*), which is suddenly equal to the fruit of Buddhahood;

Abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, one must necessarily possess the profound and vast virtues of the two benefits.

Therefore, by merely stating that they "dwell together in the Buddha’s assembly of equality," the myriad virtues are already extolled. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "elucidating the primary teaching," this refers to the meaning of the principal and attendant bodhisattvas dwelling together with the Buddha;
it does not adopt the sense of the word "merely" (but). Because the text of this sūtra is so concise and brief, [the commentary] addresses the location...

Within the two accomplishments of the assembly, this is the sequence for initiating [the teaching]. Therefore, from the previous point that the ordinary and the sage share the same essence, up to this point where cause and effect converge in a single harmony, they are interfused without duality;
only then is Perfect Enlightenment (Vajraśekhara) revealed. Hence, it is called "initiation. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "each according to what is appropriate":

this refers to the praise of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī in all these sutras compared with the praise found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; the difference lies entirely in their scope—whether universal or limited.

The distinction between superior and inferior is as vast as the distance between heaven and earth; this is because each [commentary] manifests according to the specific tenet of its respective scripture.

For example, suppose there is a person who possesses many arts: one might praise him among a circle of literary scholars, or praise him within a community of athletes. Even in such cases of praise, the tone varies according to the context.
As for the statement that a commentary must necessarily include both the primary subject and its associates, this refers to the *Huayan*...
Within the sublime midst, whenever a single dharma is raised, it necessarily encompasses all dharmas. This is like when Samantabhadra enters the Vairocana-garbha-kāya-samādhi:
within every single atom of all the lands throughout the ten directions of the entire dharma-realm, before each and every Buddha, [the same occurs].

There were as many Samantabhadras as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, all of whom likewise entered this Samādhi of the Tathāgata Vairocana’s Treasury-Body of All Buddhas, which is the body of Samantabhadra. Furthermore, it says:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra arose from this samādhi; upon arising, he immediately [entered] as many samādhis as there are atoms in an ocean of all worlds."
Arising from the gateway of the ocean, it may emit a single ray of light, which is immediately accompanied by a retinue of rays as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field.
Or it may expound a single sūtra, which is immediately accompanied by all sūtras as its retinue; every such instance is like this.
This is because their nature is without limitation and each is mutually interfused. Regarding the inclusion of external followers, as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*, it may manifest...
There may be many people—perhaps ten, five, or even three, two, or just a single individual—who practice the internal Dharma.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas; skillful means is their father; a mind of goodness and sincerity is the son;

a heart of compassion is the daughter; and the joy of the Dharma is the wife. Regarding the commentary on the assembly of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), each and every one of them is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

This is the assembly of dependent origination. ▲ Commentary: Following this preface, there are three sections that collectively re-explain the introductory portion (*nidāna*), which is manifested according to the specific school (*zong*).

Within the section on the "Correct Teaching" (Zhengzongfen), there are three parts: first, the opening chapter; second, the establishment of the thesis; third, the explanation of the textual meaning. The first part has two sections:

first, the classification based on sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation; second, the classification based on faith, understanding, practice, and realization. Regarding the phrase "the first is faith":

although one possesses the understanding that thoroughly penetrates ignorance and so forth, this constitutes only the understanding belonging to the category of faith, and thus it is entirely subsumed under faith.

Therefore, it is as explained in the "Chapter on the Clarification of Questions" (*Prajñāpariccheda*). Next, regarding the five types of understanding: one must fully clarify the expedient means for cultivating true cultivation to sever delusions—namely, [the practice of] Samantabhadra’s illusory nature and the universal realization of the two emptinesses and the dharmadhātu;

the definitive resolution of the three doubts by Vajragarbha; the removal of craving and attachment by Maitreya, which is the very root of cutting off saṃsāra; and the mode of entry into realization (as described in the "Chapter on Pure Wisdom")—only then can it be called genuine understanding.
This is like the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, from the twentieth "Assembly on Faith" up until the seventh, where the causes are perfected and the fruit is realized.
When the assembly is complete, this is called the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Giving Rise to Understanding. Next, regarding the four practices:

the three contemplations of the various wheels constitute the very essence of the practice of cultivation, which is the practice that realizes truth. The four marks and four illnesses constitute the practice of removing hindrances. Regarding the final realization, the text states:
"When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, awareness pervades the hundreds of thousands of worlds; when sentient beings give rise to a single thought..."

One is able to know this. Furthermore, it is said that one may even come to know a single drop of rain throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds as clearly as if one were looking at an object being used before one's eyes;
this extends even to the realm of the Buddhas, which then manifests before one. Below, at the conclusion of each section, there will be further specific assignments.
For now, we shall rely on the former approach, employing the previous sections alone to explain the sutra according to its intended meaning.
The profound and far-reaching chain of the bloodline [of the teaching] is detailed and distinct from beginning to end.

Regarding the commentary: first, the intent for the application of the mind; second, the establishment of the thesis. This section has four parts: first, the formal establishment of the thesis; second, the refutation of provisional doctrines (beginning with "As for the provisional doctrines");

third, the citation of examples (beginning with "As for the *Avataṃsaka*..."); and fourth, the specific explanation. As for the mention of that sutra, it refers to the text of the "Brahmacarya" chapter. The note says:
To resolve this objection: one might raise the following challenge: "If one has already attained Buddhahood, why must one still progress through the stages of practice?

This is resolved by means of the analogies of a nobleman’s descendant who, after falling into a lowly state for many years, is later declared to have suddenly become a nobleman again through the gradual study of rites, music, and virtuous conduct;
and the principle that while a child is born with the six sense faculties all at once, they develop gradually thereafter. These serve as the resolution.
[The commentary] comments on this. From "The Commentary here below" onwards, four points are indicated by the text.

From "The Commentary now, first" onwards, there are three parts explaining the meaning. The text has two sections: first, explaining the topical outline; second, explaining the scriptural text. Within the first section, there are two parts:

first, the actual explanation; second, the summary of the intent. Within the first of these two, there is first the explanation of the genuineness of faith and understanding. Within that, there are two parts; first, the citation... [and so forth].

According to the *Zhengshi* (Correct Explanation): "Later, now" and below refers to the text. The sub-commentary (*shu*) further states "below," which consists of two parts: first, establishing the origin of the cause;

second, within that, there are four sections: (1) a direct indication; (2) "Now, this... and below, which establishes the intent; (3) "Rooted in seeking the source... and below, which provides the headings and enumeration.

Below "the nature of thorough awakening" (*bodhicitta*), there is the citation and explanation. This section has two parts: first, the explanation including the practices that arise; second, the explanation including the results that are accomplished.

Regarding the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, the nature of thorough awakening; second, the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*); third, the practice. Regarding the first of these [three], there are three further points: first, the formal explanation.
Second, citing scriptural evidence; third, concluding the determination. Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts. First, the exegesis in accordance with the text.

Within this, the first phrase cites the subject, while the second phrase dispels the deluded attachments of ordinary beings—that they have not yet transcended the vehicles of humans and devas. Although only the four great elements are mentioned, the intent includes the four aggregates (*skandha*), as all are likewise non-self.

Fearing that the text would become redundant with two mentions of "aggregates," the term "aggregates" is not explicitly stated. The subsequent phrase dispels the attachments of the Śrāvakas (the Lesser Vehicle).

This clarifies that each and every constituent of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is empty in its very essence. It is not merely that the aggregates are called "empty" because there is no self within them;
this already transcends the teachings of the Hīnayāna. The next two phrases transcend the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

Within the Initial Teaching, both the Dharma-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and Dharma-phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) schools have yet to reveal the originally existent true awakening. Now, it is revealed that the Dharmakāya is the self-awakened sacred knowledge (as in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*).

Because it is so stated in the *Gā-sūtra*, all [attributes] are transcended. Nevertheless, the term "emptiness" (śūnyatā) carries three meanings: first, it merely dispels the affliction of clinging to emptiness and does not indicate anything else that is revealed;
second, because emptiness is itself form, it is not merely empty; third, its essence is suchness (*tathatā*) and original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

There is nothing that is not empty. Now, the intent lies in the third [teaching], and thus it transcends the Initial Teaching (*śāstra*). Next, the four lines beginning with "sages and ordinary beings" transcend the Final Teaching.
Although within each of these teachings the true nature (*tathatā*) is revealed, there still remains the distinction between being entangled in afflictions and being free from them;

being entangled constitutes the ordinary person, while being free constitutes the sage. However, through this Sudden Teaching, it is revealed that the entanglement of afflictions is fundamentally empty; what, then, is there to be entangled in, and what is there to be freed from?

To perceive that there are sentient beings who can be saved is not the state of a Bodhisattva. If one perceives by means of marks (lakṣaṇa), one does not see the Tathāgata; therefore it is said that what is different is not true.
Only suchness (tathatā) and the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna) remain alone; therefore it is said that the essence of sentient beings and Buddhas is identical.
The above has clearly revealed the characteristics of sudden awakening to the emptiness of delusion and the reality of truth. Next, from "relying on this" onwards, awakening is elucidated.

Subsequently touching upon objects and acting in accordance with principle is what is called practicing in accord with the nature (*dharmatā*). Within this, the first four lines briefly subsume the preceding two lines to establish the latter two.
Regarding "no difference between beginning and end": the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) and the ultimate state (*niṣṭhā*) are not distinct.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that at the very moment of the initial arousal of the mind, one attains perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*). [This refers to] the reunion at the Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabha*) in the stage of fruition, as seen in the case of Sudhana.

"Once again we see the Great Sage"—all such instances are of this nature. The four lines following "seeing and hearing" correctly clarify that at all times, one encounters phenomena in union with the Way.

Regarding the terms "images and echoes": seeing all forms as being like reflections, hearing all sounds as being like echoes in a valley, and perceiving all phenomena as being like illusions—all these do not destroy their appearances while being immediately empty. Why?
"Reality" (shi) is so called because it is unborn and quiescent. Why is it "not empty" (he xu)? Because it responds to forms and sounds, and because the nature of awakening follows conditions.

The commentary states that this does not rely on what follows; these two points are a reductio ad absurdum (reversive demonstration). As the text below says: "Even if one practices diligently and with hardship for many kalpas, it is merely called 'conditioned' (saṃskṛta);
in the end, one cannot achieve the holy fruit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). It further says: "Because all [conditioned things] are in saṃsāra, they do not constitute the holy."
The Way. Since it is said that all [of these] do not achieve sainthood, they do not escape karmic retribution. The commentary (*shū*) therefore cites two proofs from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The text has two parts: first, citing the sūtra to prove only the realization of nature; second, citing the śāstra to prove the three stages in their entirety. Within the first part, there are again two sections:

first, proving by way of negative implication that [realization] exists inherently. This section has two parts: first, proving that failing to realize [nature] entails harm, which clarifies that one must first realize it for oneself.
Only when one understands the mind does one know the true path; thus, the realization is revealed by its opposite. As for those with inverted wisdom:

if they do not understand the mind, all their views and interpretations are entirely inverted wisdom. Even if they speak of dependent origination and non-arising, or the six perfections and the two kinds of emptiness, they cannot avoid being inverted as long as they fail to understand their own mind.
Because understanding phenomena outside the mind is entirely erroneous, it obstructs the sudden awakening to the ground of the mind.

This is the core principle. Therefore, it leads to the prolongation of evil. The preceding section clarifies that there is harm in a lack of understanding. The commentary further states: "The following section clarifies that deluded cultivation is of no benefit.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Manifestation" (*Prasphuṭapadā*), states in full:

"Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, fully cultivated the six pāramitās and practiced various factors of enlightenment; yet, if they have not heard..."
This Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majesty:

if, upon hearing it at some time, one does not believe, does not understand, does not comply with, and does not enter into it, one cannot be called a true Bodhisattva, because such a person is unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

(The commentary on that passage explains: "If one does not rely on this Dharma-gate, even if one practices for many kalpas, one is still not 'true'; how much less could one swiftly attain Bodhi? The phrase "even if" (*shê-yǒu*) here seems to function as a concessive hypothetical. Furthermore, when the Holy Maitreya praised Sudhana, he said: "Other [Bodhisattvas]...")

A Bodhisattva can only fulfill the vows and practices of a Bodhisattva after hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* kalpas; yet now, Sudhana is able to purify Buddha-fields and so forth in a single lifetime. This is an instance of using the provisional to reveal the real, not a mere arbitrary fabrication.

Alternatively, even that which lacks a locus of abiding is included in analytical cessation, because it is attained by extinguishing obstacles through the power of true analysis. There are two types of analytical cessation:

*Commentary:* Regarding the passage "However, these three... and below, the three are interfused and unimpeded. This section has two parts: first, establishing the point through a metaphor; second, summarizing according to the sutra. First, establishing the point through a metaphor:

I, too, constantly dwell within this, even as I enter into nirvāṇa. What is called the "Secret Treasury"?
It is like the three dots of the letter *i*; if they are placed side-by-side, they do not form the letter *i*, nor do they form it if they are placed vertically. Just so...
The three eyes on the face of Maheśvara must come together to form the letter *i*; if the three dots were separate, they could not form it either.
I am likewise: the dharma of liberation is not itself nirvāṇa, nor is the body of the Tathāgata itself nirvāṇa.
The *Mahāprajñā* is not *nirvāṇa*. The three dharmas being distinct from one another is also not *nirvāṇa*.
It is because I now abide in these three dharmas for the sake of sentient beings that it is called "entering *nirvāṇa*. The Commentary on the Jianfu [Temple] explains:

"If one employs analogies to illustrate the dharma, the text of the analogy is insufficient. Regarding the statement in the [main] text, 'The dharma of liberation is also not *nirvāṇa*, etc.,' within the analogy..."
It is said that not even a single point constitutes "it" (the state of Nirvana). This is because each of the three factors—liberation and so forth—is individually insufficient.
To realize Nirvana, there must be a body capable of realizing it, there must be wisdom to sever the afflictions, and so on;

these three factors combined are termed the realization of Nirvana. If there were only the body, it would not be Nirvana; if there were only *prajñā* (wisdom), it would likewise not be Nirvana. Only...
Liberation is also not nirvana; these three are distinct from one another. As long as there has been no severance [of afflictions] or realization [of the path], it is also not nirvana.

Merely using metaphors for their distinctions is also insufficient. According to the intention of Tiantai, worldly meanings differ: east and west are called "horizontal," while north and south are called "vertical."

"Vertical" (*zòng*) means "upright. This refers to the sense of verticality where the *dharmakāya* is originally present, followed by the cultivation of *prajñā*, and finally the attainment of liberation;
for it spans across lifetimes and worlds, pervading both the pure and the defiled—just as three dots arranged vertically (as shown here).

"Horizontal" (*héng*) refers to the three dharmas being distinct entities yet simultaneous, like three blazing fires—just as three dots arranged horizontally (as shown here). When combined, they form [the character for "one"].

They are one essence; their differentiation is merely that they each reside in a separate location. Thus, one simply takes up a single dharma. Now, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is likewise not distinct from Nirvāṇa and the other two.
This is a combined exposition: to clarify these three vertically is called "vertical" (zòng); to cite one while encompassing the other two is called "simultaneous" (bìng).
Therefore, it says "Prajñā is not [distinct]," because within Prajñā the other two are already subsumed. If the Three Virtues were different, then even Nirvāṇa would not be [identical to them].

This forms four [aspects]. The general explanation states: "Now, when the three are simultaneously inconceivable, how can they be arranged vertically? When the three are simultaneously inconceivable, how can they be arranged horizontally?

In the present, it likewise does not give rise to the characteristics of duality or non-duality. The commentary states: This is the "Chapter on Manifestation.

This passage from the *Fojia riyi xia* (The Sun of the Buddha’s Meaning Descends) cites the fourth chapter of that sutra, "The Door of Non-transmigration in the Waning and Waxing," which states in full:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising sun that shines universally upon the world; its reflection appears in every vessel of pure water, pervading all locations."
There is no coming or going. If even one vessel is broken, the reflection no longer appears. Son of the Buddha, what do you think?
Is the sun at fault for that reflection not appearing? He replied, "No. It is simply because the vessel is broken; it is not the fault of the sun. Son of the Buddha.
The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: it manifests universally throughout the entire dharma-realm without priority or sequence.

Within the vessel of the pure minds of all sentient beings, there is no one before whom the Buddha does not appear. If the vessel of the mind is constantly pure, one constantly beholds the Buddha-body;

if the mind is turbid or the vessel is broken, then one cannot see him. Commentary: It is not that the image itself exists or does not exist; rather, it depends on the deficiency or fullness of those vessels. It is not that the mind itself [is the cause].

How could this manifestation not precede or follow the Universal Manifestation? If the vessel of the precepts is broken, upon what can the water of meditative concentration rely? If the vessel of Bodhi is broken, how can the water of wisdom remain?
Although this section clarifies the manifestation of the body, it is in fact the great function of the Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues, and is thus subsumed within Nirvāṇa.
If that is so, how does it differ from the Body of Universal Manifestation? The Body of Universal Manifestation takes the Dharma-body as its gateway, yet it discusses the Truth.
It is so. It is not that the two virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and liberation are absent.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that each possesses four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), there are three types of four permutations. First, each individual item is categorized into four permutations in relation to its own kind.

Regarding the four permutations within the category of giving (*dāna*): the first is "giving that is not a perfection" (*pāramitā*), because it is a gift that does not correspond with the seven excellences.

The second is "deliverance without giving," because one rejoices in the giving of others and possesses the seven excellences. The third is "both giving and deliverance," because one possesses the seven excellences while practicing giving.
The fourth is "neither giving nor deliverance," because one rejoices in the giving of others and does not possess the seven excellences in conjunction with it.

Second, regarding those who do not practice according to the sequence of the categories, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are clarified as follows: the single category of giving (*dāna*) possesses only two permutations, because the other perfections (*pāramitā*) have not yet arisen;
thus, it lacks two permutations, namely: "that which is a perfection but not giving" and "that which is neither giving nor a perfection.

As for the remaining five, such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth, they possess all four permutations. This is because, since the perfection of giving has already occurred, there can be that which is a perfection but not ethical discipline, and so on. That is to say:

First, there is that which is morality but not a perfection (*pāramitā*): this refers to cases where it is not associated with the seven excellences. Second, there is that which is a perfection but not morality:

this refers to the aforementioned perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) when it is endowed with the seven excellences. Third, there is that which is both morality and a perfection: this refers to the observance of morality when it is endowed with the seven supreme excellences.

Regarding patience (*kṣānti*) in relation to morality, and vigor (*vīrya*) in relation to patience, the sequence is the same as that of morality. Regarding the third [category], those that are not cultivated in sequential order: each perfection can individually possess all four logical possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*).

As for the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), from the first generation of the bodhicitta until sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, one establishes all bodhipakṣadharma-corresponding wholesome karmas of body, speech, and mind; this is called vigor.

It is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Furthermore, it is called the perfection of vigor because it is a vigor not shared with ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
There are three types of vigor, namely: of body, speech, and mind; among these, mental vigor serves as the precursor, and so forth.

Moreover, there are thirty-two kinds of bodhisattva vigor (such as the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels). When a bodhisattva practices these various forms of vigor, they arise from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Because they are detached from body, speech, and mind, there are four kinds of *dhyāna*, namely the four *dhyānas* such as "perception of equanimity," and so forth.

Within these four, there are sixteen kinds of *dhyāna* for Bodhisattvas who, having distanced themselves from realizing the stages of the Two Vehicles, dedicate [their merit] toward the stage of Buddhahood.
These are not possessed by those of the two vehicles; that is to say, they do not grasp at reality, they do not cling to flavors, and they take great compassion as their object, and so forth.
[In the] commentary, following these five, there are four remaining *pāramitās*: namely, skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).
These four are all subsumed within the *prajñā-pāramitā*. When the Buddha, beneath the Bodhi tree, through wisdom associated with mindfulness...
To fully awaken to all phenomena is the *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, it is characterized by non-obstruction; because it is without self, and so forth.
Such wisdoms comprise eighty-four thousand modes of activity (*ākāra*); this is the *jñānapāramitā* known by the bodhisattva.
Were one to wish to expound them in full detail, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, could do so. These six *pāramitās* collectively constitute the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisaṃbhāra*).

Just as empty space completely encompasses all things, so too should it be understood that the remaining provisions, such as the provision of hearing and so forth, are subsumed within the six perfections;

This refers to what is called the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal. Regarding the term "not yet" (*wei*) used in the commentary:

Chapter on Ignorance (Avidyā). The commentary on the sūtra asks: "What is ignorance? This section has two parts: first, the explanation of the text; second, from "Now, this" onwards, the clarification of the underlying meaning.

Regarding the eighty thousand afflictions and the twelve links of dependent origination, these shall be explained below. As for the phrase in the commentary, "the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," etc.:
The *Buddhanāmasūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying, "Your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Once the power of his concentration was exhausted, he immediately received this retribution. [Please consult the original sūtra text for a detailed explanation.]
As for the commentary stating that there are no pits of non-action (*wuwei*), it refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Chapter on the Manifestation (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), which says:
