When its roots take root, they cause all the roots of the trees in Jambudvīpa to grow; [the same applies to] their trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Yet, there are only two places where it cannot provide the benefit of growth."
This refers to the deep pits of hell and within the water-wheel; yet even there, from the very beginning, there is no weariness or abandonment.
It is likewise with the Great Medicine King Tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and so forth.

When its roots first sprout, they cause all bodhisattvas to give rise to the root of great compassion that does not abandon sentient beings (the trunk of profound resolve, the branches of the pāramitās, the leaves of pure śīla and dhūta, the flowers adorned by the marks and signs, and the fruit of the Buddha’s consecration and patience).
Only in two instances is it unable to bring about growth and benefit:

namely, when the followers of the Two Vehicles have fallen into the vast and deep pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and when sentient beings who lack the capacity due to their destruction of roots of goodness are submerged in the waters of great false views and craving.

"Yet, even therein, there has never been any wearying abandonment. The commentary states: This passage from the *Wuwei* (Unconditioned) section is used by the Subcommentary (*Shuyong*) to demonstrate that although those of the Two Vehicles have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), they have not yet severed fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Regarding the "illness of the practitioner," this refers to the chapter on Ignorance in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Within the explanation of its name, there are two parts: first, explaining the primary name; second, explaining the specific [distinctions]. In the first part, there are two further sections.
First, regarding the Dharma-character school (Xiangzong), it is said that "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is explained as the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*).

This means that because this ignorance is not subsumed under the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*), it must be analyzed through a combination of *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) and *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds. The non-co-referential analysis clarifies that it is the "discernment of dharmas," and discernment of dharmas is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*).

The prefix "a-" carries the sense of non-existence. Subsequently, these are combined: because this [wisdom] is the essential nature [of ignorance], it is said that "it lacks that clarity" (*avidyā*). (In the Dharma-character school, ignorance and sentient beings are taken as the fundamental basis.)

Therefore, it is by means of the wisdom that apprehends phenomena (*dharma*) that [ignorance] is characterized; this is either an *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), meaning that what is absent is itself the illumination, and thus it is called "non-illumination" (*avidyā*). There is also a tradition which states:
"It lacks another designation. Here, "another" (*para*) refers to that very thing [the absence].
The Commentary further states, "Although there is the fundamental [nature]," and so forth. These two points are explained according to the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong).

Herein, sentient beings are considered the derivative (the "branch"), while the awakened nature is the fundamental (the "root"). Because one is deluded regarding this awakened nature, it is termed "ignorance" (avidyā). Therefore, it is said that there is no beginning to the illumination of awakening.

Just as the substance of a mirror is inherently luminous and reflects only when free from dust—as the Chan school speaks of "reflective observation" (*pratyavekṣā*)—it is the awakening of the primordial source. The preceding and following sections are explained in a similar manner.

Regarding the note on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*: these two treatises refer to one of the six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), all of which are mental factors (*caitta*).

Regarding "delusion," the *Buddhāvatamsaka* (or *Śrī-mahādevī-bodhisattva-sūtra*) states: "In the past, there was fundamentally no delusion; it is as if there were a perception of delusion. When one awakens to delusion, delusion is extinguished;

once awakening has arisen, delusion is not produced. There are many such passages concerning delusion in both preceding and succeeding texts, as well as in various other sūtras. As for "inversion," it will be explained below.

Regarding the two [sections] on the essential nature [of the members], the first concerns the Sūtras and the second concerns the Śāstras; this is the first. As for the passage beginning "The Avataṃsaka says," etc.:

although all twelve members arise based upon the Truth (tathatā) and possess no intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva)—as that verse states, "When one contemplates the true meaning of all causes and conditions, they are empty"—ignorance (avidyā) is the primary factor that directly deludes one regarding the principle of the Truths (the reality of the Four Noble Truths).
As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states, "The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) among all truths," it gives rise to formative action (saṃskāra). Since these [members] are transverse...

Arising from emptiness, it cannot return to its source; therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) is specifically designated by the term "delusion. The present commentary states, "delusion regarding the self," meaning delusion regarding the true mind.
Thus, that verse says: "One understands that the three realms exist based on the mind; the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so.
That treatise judges this by means of the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Furthermore, that verse says: "Not knowing..."
Because the True Meaning (Paramārtha) school names it "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Regarding the passage in the *Commentary* beginning with "Lack of awakening," there are two parts based on the treatise.

This section has four parts: first, the treatise from the perspective of the Nature School; second, the treatise from the perspective of the Characteristics School; third, an analysis of depth and shallowness; and fourth, a general examination of what is complete or missing.

Now, for the first part, there are two sections: first, citing the text to clarify the point directly. Examining the metaphorical text, it also contains the two meanings previously mentioned: delusion regarding the truth and grasping at the false. That is to say:
To mistake east (east being true) for west (west being false) is to be deluded based on direction. Regarding this, there are two further phrases which state:
"If one were apart from direction, then there would be no delusion. These are omitted in the Commentary. Below, the Commentary explains by using the treatise as an illustration for this sutra.
As for the "two sections of text," the first is the passage beginning with "falsely recognizing... up to "...thereby there is cyclic existence."
"Birth and death are called ignorance (*avidyā*). This identifies its essential nature (*tattva*). Next, it says, "This ignorance does not have a real substantiality;
it is like people in a dream. This reveals that its nature is empty. [The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*] states below: "The second is the treatise of the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇavāda*)."

The text has two parts: first, defining the essence [of ignorance] in contrast to reality; second, defining the essence in contrast to its function. Regarding the first part, there are two sections. The first concerns the *Abhidharmakośa*.
To clarify that which is to be remedied, the *Kośa* asks: "What is the meaning of 'ignorance' (*avidyā*)? It means "that which is not knowledge" (*ajñāna*). [Objection]:

If that were so, then the eye and other [faculties] would be ignorance, for the five faculties such as sight are also not "knowledge-illumination" (*jñāna-prakāśa*), and thus they too would be ignorance. [Response]: If this were the case, then the meaning [of ignorance] would simply be the absence of knowledge (*vidyā-abhāva*). This is a further, distinct explanation.
"The absence of knowledge (*vidyā*) is called ignorance (*avidyā*). [Objection: If this were so, the essence of ignorance would not exist. [Response:

To clarify that it does possess an essence (distinguishing it from the second interpretation), and to ensure its meaning does not overlap with other categories (distinguishing it from the first interpretation), the verse says: "Ignorance is that which is the opposite of knowledge. This indicates that ignorance has a real entity;

it refers to the failure to comprehend the Four Noble Truths. That which is the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) to knowledge is named ignorance. Only that which is diametrically opposed to knowledge is ignorance; it is not the case that everything outside of knowledge is ignorance.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not the absence of knowledge; it is not named "ignorance" simply because knowledge is absent. This is explained by means of an analogy, such as "non-friend," "unreal," and so forth. The prose commentary explains:

Just as those who are enemies of one's friends are called "non-friends" because they are contrary to friends, yet this does not mean they are something other than friends—it refers to the enemies themselves being called "non-friends"—and it does not mean that everyone outside of friends is called a non-friend; this is the analogy for ignorance.

This clarifies that [ignorance] does not overlap with the eye-faculty and so forth. "Non-friend" (apriya) means one who is not a friend; this metaphor indicates that ignorance possesses a substantial entity (*dravya*).

"Truthful speech" is called "real" (*satya*); this explains what is "unreal" (*asatya*). That which is the object of opposition—the discourse of falsehood—is termed "unreal. It is not something other than the real, nor is it the mere absence of the real; all such things are termed "unreal. Furthermore, it is not the case that the non-existence of the real is itself termed "unreal.
This discourse of delusion, which is the object of opposition, is termed "unreal"; it is not distinct from the real, nor is it the simple non-existence of the real.

The word "etcetera" (ādi) serves to indicate that which is non-dharma (unwholesome phenomena), non-meaning (unwholesome meanings), and non-activity (unwholesome activities)—all of which are contrary to wholesome phenomena and are thus termed "non-dharma," etc.
Their nature is neither different [from the wholesome] nor non-existent. Likewise, ignorance (*avidyā*) exists as a distinct substantial entity;

it is the antithesis of knowledge (*vidyā*), being neither different [from it]—which would exclude the eyes and so forth—nor non-existent—which would exclude the absence of knowledge. The rest is as explained in other volumes. [This concludes] the second section of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vṛtti* (Commentary on the Proof of Consciousness-Only): "Obscuration."
"Reality" (tattva) here refers to the ever-active ignorance within the seventh consciousness. In that treatise, among the seven mental factors, it mentions "self-delusion" (ātma-moha).
However, its detailed explanation—in the passage citing scriptures to prove the existence of the seventh consciousness—states: [text follows].
As stated in the Sūtra (the commentary also does not provide its name): "Non-common ignorance" (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*). (The meaning of "non-common" will be explained immediately below.

It is subtle and constantly active, obscuring reality. (That is to say, this subtle and constant activity is difficult to perceive in its mode of operation; it conceals the principle of selflessness and obstructs untainted wisdom. Therefore, it is called "obscuring reality. If this consciousness did not exist, that [ignorance] would not exist either.

That is to say, for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)—and for other noble ones (*ārya*) on the Path of Seeing—in all states (which refers to minds of the three natures, explaining the Sūtra’s term "constantly active"), it is always present.
It gives rise to the uncommon ignorance that deludes one regarding the nature of reality (*tattva*), obscuring the true meaning and obstructing the noble eye of wisdom.

(As stated in the *Gāthā*s... Therefore, the Sūtras say: "All classes of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwell perpetually in the long night. (Night is darkness; it is "long" because it is constant. Otherwise, there would have to be light in the interim.

They are blinded by ignorance—meaning that this uncommon [ignorance] is constantly active, thus blinding their eye of wisdom—and their minds are entangled in stupor (*styāna*, lack of awareness) and intoxication (*mada*, lack of sobriety), never attaining awakening. (That is, *styāna*...)

[The phrase] "He is intoxicated" means that if one were to become enlightened midway, there would be awakening. This [explanation], based on the six consciousnesses, cannot be established in all cases; it serves as proof that [the subject] is the seventh consciousness.

Regarding the commentary's statement, "Those who are deluded regarding phenomena and principle," this intends to refer to the ignorance (*moha*) among the six root afflictions within the sixth consciousness.
That text asks: "What is ignorance? Its nature is to be deluded and dark regarding all phenomena and principles. The commentary explains: "This refers to independent ignorance (*svatantra-avidyā*)."

"Delusion regarding principles" (this refers primarily to the dominant [affliction]; if referring to non-dominant [afflictions], it also extends to delusion regarding phenomena; the distinction between dominant and non-dominant will be listed below). "Associated [delusions]" and so forth also refer to delusion regarding phenomena. Regarding the commentary’s mention of "common" and "uncommon":
"common" means that they extend to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as well as their association with greed and other [afflictions].
The "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) is the opposite of this. Thus, regarding the proof of the seventh consciousness (*manas*), the subsequent passage states:

"There are two types of unshared ignorance (*avidyā*): first, the ever-active unshared, which does not exist in other consciousnesses (it exists only in the seventh; just as the 'unshared qualities' of a Buddha are designated 'unshared' in the sense of being preeminent, rather than everything that is not mutually present being called 'unshared.

This means the ignorance associated with the seventh consciousness has been ever-active since beginningless time, obstructing the wisdom of true reality. Because it exists only in this consciousness, it is called 'unshared. This entire section is from the treatise itself.

[Text]: (2) There is no such thing as a "solitary" [ignorance] that does not coexist [with other afflictions]. This consciousness does not exist [in such a state]. (It is called "solitary" because it does not arise in association with anger and so forth;

or, it refers to ignorance that arises alone, deluded regarding the principles of the truths, without being accompanied by others. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "There are two kinds of ignorance. If it is associated with craving and so forth, it is called 'associated ignorance' (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*)."

(That is, it is as described above regarding its association. That which is not associated with greed and so forth is called "solitary" (*kevala*) ignorance. (By stating simply that it is not associated with greed, it is understood to be associated with the sixth consciousness;

this does not mean that the seventh consciousness is not obstructed from arising simultaneously with anger and other afflictions. Thus, one knows that it exists only in the sixth consciousness. This is the primary solitary [ignorance], which is abandoned only by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*). (Within these solitary types, there are further two kinds.)

The primary [affliction] that is deluded regarding the principles of the truths arises solely from conceptual construction and is abandoned only by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). It does not associate with the ten [secondary afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth. If it exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it co-arises with five of the subsequent [secondary afflictions], namely those excluding shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), making seven; or with eight; or with twelve.

Or [ten]. As stated previously in the fourfold explanation, all secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are associated with universal defilements. How is this known? Without citing a scriptural proof, it is as the Sūtra says: "The noble ones who are still in training (*śaikṣa*)."

Because the non-associated ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) has been eternally severed, one does not create new karma. (This is stated in the second chapter of the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtra*.

It should be understood that this discussion is based solely on this specific type of ignorance and does not refer to all forms of it. It is not the "independent" [ignorance] that acts alone, nor is it abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

This is because anger (*krodha*) and the other [afflictions] all pertain to what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*). (The word "also" (*api*) is used because they pertain to both insight and cultivation; since the ten afflictions beginning with anger all pertain to what is abandoned by insight, the text mentions their connection to insight. It is clear that they also pertain to cultivation because this is universally established, which is why it is not explicitly stated. This is because the ten afflictions such as anger each function individually.)

Because it arises first, it shares its name with those [afflictions] associated with it; it does not act alone as a primary factor. These ten [secondary afflictions] are also predominant because they are primary. When these ten are absent, only ignorance increases; thus, according to the Hīnayāna, this is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).

However, since these [secondary afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) have no separate substantial entity other than the root [afflictions], they are termed "unshared" from the perspective of their minor characteristics. Although these two types differ, both are nonetheless non-pervasive regarding the three natures (*tridhātu*) and are subsumed under the ignorance that arises in the mind.

The "constantly active unshared" (*nitya-pravṛtti-asādhāraṇa*) is absent in other schools; the "acting-alone unshared" (*kevala-pravṛtti-asādhāraṇa*) exists in both [Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna]. This distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles lies therein. Only the Mahāyāna possesses [the latter]. Now, by means of the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*), one is compelled to believe in the "acting-alone" [unshared].

[The phrase] "the activity not shared [with others], which exists in both the Great and Small [vehicles]" (疏). If one takes "initiating" as the primary meaning, these two are distinguished by their function to establish the essential nature [of karma].

Regarding the term "initiating karma" (*karmasamutthāpaka*): this is explained in terms of the fundamental [structure of the] links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Therefore, in his commentary on the link of ignorance (*avidyā*), Cien states: "It takes ignorance within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as its essence.

Since karma is itself a formation, "initiating karma" refers specifically to [ignorance] within the aggregate of formations and does not include other dharmas. Furthermore, he cites various treatises, all of which state that it is precisely [ignorance] that initiates karma.
This refers solely to ignorance (*avidyā*); the others are merely its auxiliaries, and thus they are not included. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:

"The seven types of non-knowledge—(1) regarding time, (2) regarding phenomena, (3) regarding transmigration, (4) regarding supremacy, (5) regarding reality, (6) regarding defilement and purification, and (7) regarding overweening pride—each containing the character 'delusion' (*mūḍha*)—constitute the limb of ignorance."

Thus, we know that no other dharmas are included. Furthermore, it says: "There are these nineteen types of ignorance, such as the six ignorances, the five ignorances, and so forth," as explained in the *Mahāśāstra*, fascicle nine, and elsewhere.
△ [In the commentary] from "These etc. onwards, there are three sections that distinguish the depth and shallowness of the treatises.
Among these, only the Mahāyāna treatises are analyzed. As for the statement "they are the sixth and seventh mental factors (*caitta*)," this is the doctrine of that school.
The eighth consciousness is unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). It is only in the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that ignorance (*avidyā*) exists.

In the seventh, there is the non-common [ignorance] that is constantly active; in the sixth, there is the non-common [ignorance] that acts independently. As for the common [ignorance], it is pervasive, as explained above. △ The commentary states:

"Furthermore, regarding 'delusion concerning the self' and below, these four lines generally distinguish between what is complete and what is lacking. This means that according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, [the position of those who deny the ālayavijñāna] lacks the meaning of delusion concerning the self and the meaning of being identical with emptiness. It lacks...

Regarding "delusion regarding self": the previous statements that one is deluded about the principle of non-self (*anātman*) and deluded about the principle and phenomena (*dharmas*) both refer to the objects of delusion.

It does not mean that there is a self-existent *dharmakāya* or true self; rather, because of delusion, one falsely clings to non-self as a false prideful self. Regarding the absence of "immediate emptiness" (*jìkōng*):
in the fifty-fifth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, among the explanation of the provisional and real nature of the various afflictions, it says: "Five..."

Seeing is provisional, whereas ignorance is substantial; therefore, both the *Pañcaṣaṣṭika-śāstra* and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* extensively provide question-and-answer expositions that distinguish it from all other dharmas, and thus it is called "ignorance.
(This "distinguishing" means that while other dharmas may themselves possess ignorance, this [specific] ignorance is the very essence and is not empty.)
The "root" in the commentary refers to fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodha*) as cited in the main treatise. The "branches and tips" refer to the three subtleties and six coarsenesses.
Regarding "common" and "uncommon," it is also as explained above. Regarding "associated" and "non-associated," it is as previously cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

As for "delusion regarding principle," both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess it; as for "delusion regarding phenomena," it belongs solely to the sixth consciousness. As for "independent [mental consciousness],"...
There are two meanings. First, the *Buddhanāmasūtra* states that "independent ignorance" (*mukhyāvidyā*) serves as the seed of afflictions;
here, it is simply termed the "root. It is called "independent" because it arises without a cause, which accords with the explanation of the "root" in the *Awakening of Faith*.

Second, it refers to the two types of "solitary" [ignorance] previously cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: that which has a master and that which lacks a master. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ṭīkā* explains delusion...

Regarding the passage on principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), it says: "That is to say, independent ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) is deluded regarding principle, while associated [ignorance] and the like are also deluded regarding phenomena.
As for the commentary stating they "occur together": when performing the three types of wholesome karma, they must necessarily be accompanied by ignorance. Therefore, the *Abhidharmapitaka* states:

"By means of the delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*), one initiates non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karma*); because that is invariably of a defiled nature, when it is conjoined with ignorance, it certainly..."

Because they consist of the certainty of experience (*niyatavedanīya*), the liberation [from suffering], and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Regarding "concealing karma" (*āvṛtakarman*): it causes untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) to not arise.
Regarding "initiating karma" (*pravartakarman*): it is the root of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Its nature is both unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Nevertheless, it initiates the three types of karma—meritorious (*puṇya*), non-meritorious (*apuṇya*), and immovable (*āniñjya*). (There are three [kinds of] initiated [karma], but the initiators are only two. The *Abhidharma* states: "By delusion regarding maturation (*vipākasaṃmoha*), one initiates non-meritorious karma; because that is invariably defiled in nature. By delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārthasaṃmoha*), one initiates meritorious and immovable [karma]. )

[The phrase] "practice" refers to the true meaning, which is the Four Noble Truths. Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of producing and moistening [karmic seeds], at the stage of initiating karma (*karma-pravartaka*), the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) is predominant.

Regarding the distinction between seeds and manifest activity (*bīja-vartamāna*): the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that there are four types of ignorance: first, the manifest (*vartamāna*, i.e., active); second, the seed (*bīja*); third, the associated (*saṃprayukta*);

and fourth, the non-associated (*asaṃprayukta*). (This also serves as proof for the aforementioned categories of associated and non-associated. This explains that the limb of ignorance (*avidyā-aṅga*) encompasses both manifest activity and seeds.
This constitutes the essence. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* also states: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is twofold: namely, the time of the seed (the causal state) and the time of the fruit (the manifest state).

Regarding "past afflictions," the verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The stage of past afflictions is ignorance; past various karmas are called formations (*saṃskāra*). The prose commentary explains: [Past afflictions are ignorance; past various karmas are called formations.]
Regarding the state of the various afflictions during previous lives that continue until the ripening of their fruit in the present life, these are collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
This is because they function simultaneously with ignorance and manifest through the power of ignorance;

just as it is said that when a king travels, he does not do so without attendants, yet because the king is preeminent, the journey is collectively called "the king’s journey. (Next, the following phrase is explained: Regarding the state of meritorious and other types of karma during previous lives...

Upon reaching the ripening of the fruit, it collectively receives the designation "formative action" (*saṃskāra*), and so forth (up to old age and death). The treatise subsequently states: "The term 'stage' in the first phrase flows through until old age."
Regarding the second section, the detailed explanation of the four karmic functions, the commentary states: "As for the phrase 'capable of producing the three subtle [states],' the treatise says:

'Based on non-awakening (a-vijñapti), three kinds of marks arise; they correspond with and are not separate from that non-awakening' (because the mark is not separate from the substance, and the derivative is not separate from the root;

because the deluded mind arises based on ignorance, and ignorance arises based on the deluded mind). What are these three? First, the mark of the activity of ignorance (avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa), and so forth. [End of] Commentary Two.

Regarding the "seeds": the first is the aforementioned independent [seeds], which are the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); the second is that which gives rise to karma, which are the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Alternatively, they may correspond respectively to the aforementioned "concealing karma" and "arousing karma. In the commentary, it is stated in summary that the following two points provide a general explanation.

As for the term "sustaining" (*sthiti-dhara*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings are sustained by their collective perceptions. In the section of the commentary that poses a question, it is as follows:
Regarding the "eighty thousand roots of affliction (*kleśa*) and so forth" mentioned above, the Commentary determines that these do not refer to the middle two [categories].
First, it explains the structural outline of the text; second, within that outline, the lower section explains the scriptural passage.

As for the phrase "all-encompassing various inversions," even the followers of the Two Vehicles possess the four inversions, such as the inversion of selflessness and so on, within the provisional teachings. Accumulated...
In practicing the bodhisattva path, there is likewise the inversion of taking the characteristics of defilement and purity as existent and the true nature as empty;

therefore, it is said that [the teaching] "comprehensively encompasses" all. The commentary on this single dharma has two parts: first, following the preceding section to state the intent; second, from "Now then," below, the explanation of the topical outline.

Third, the explanation of the scriptural text. Within the second [section], there are two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, from "Therefore, Zhaò... onwards, citing evidence. "Form" (xing) and "body" (ti) serve as evidence for the recognition of the body;

"conditions" (yuan) and "objects of thought" (lü) serve as evidence for the recognition of the mind. Therefore, it is said that this precisely corresponds to this section. In the commentary (*shu*), the explanation of the scriptural text is divided into two parts:
first, the direct explanation of this text; second, establishing the various [preceding points]. Within the first part, there are two: first, the body; second, the mind. Mind...
Regarding the two explanations for the middle [section]: first, explaining "reflection" by means of the mind; second, explaining "reflection" by means of the object.

As for the phrase "In reality, there exist... and so forth, the intermediate text states: "It is in order to dispel the attachment to the existence of objects external to the mind and mental factors that it is said 'there is only consciousness.

If one were to grasp at this 'consciousness-only' as being truly existent, that too would constitute attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* says: "If one discriminates, etc."
In that sutra, Ānanda was first questioned by the Buddha regarding whether the nature of the mind resides within or without; in both cases, faults were established. Finally, it says:
"World-Honored One, you now question me about my mind. I wish to investigate and seek out this mind. Is this very act of investigation itself the mind?
The Buddha said: "Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind; this is merely a portion of the external objects."

Regarding the perception of distinct characteristics: "Or perhaps your true nature [is it]? ... up to: "If there were a nature of discrimination apart from the objective fields, that would indeed be your true mind.
As for the statement, "If the discriminating mind is devoid of substance when separated from the fields," the meaning is this:

since it has no substance when separated from the fields, one knows it to be a reflected image of the discrimination of those objective fields. Since it is a reflection of the objective fields, when the fields undergo transformation and cease, the mind likewise transforms.
[It is] extinguished. At the time of extinction, there is no mind, like the hair of a tortoise and so forth. Who could realize the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*)?

Based on these numerous faults, it is sufficient to clarify that what Ānanda recognized was not the true mind. Therefore, what is cited here serves to prove that he erroneously recognized discriminative thought as the mind.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “the rest is the same as the previous explanation,” this refers to citations such as those from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
The meaning of the emptiness of the conceptual mind that realizes [these truths] is entirely the same as before. ▲ In the Commentary (*Sū*), the heading "Inverting the Prior" is placed below;
second, it establishes the various [preceding points]. The text has two parts: first, a general summary based on the various teachings.

Regarding the note stating that "the initial contemplation of the two empties should be fully recounted," I shall now state it briefly. "Self" (*ātman*) refers to a sovereign, like a ruler of a nation, because it possesses autonomy.
Furthermore, because it is like a sovereign and a minister: the sovereign is my essence, while the minister is my function.

The sovereign is non-conceptual and co-emergent, whereas the minister is conceptual and possesses the capacity for decisive severance. Within this context, there are further worldly and scriptural teachings.

In the world, what I call a "sentient being," a "mind-born," a "manava," a "nourisher," a "person who goes from birth to birth," a "life-principle," a "spiritual person," an "agent," an "experiencer," a "knower," or a "seer"— and what I, as a Noble One,
teach as a "stream-enterer," a "once-returner," a "non-returner," an "one who does not arise," a "Mahāyāna practitioner," a "faith-resolver," or an "attainer," and so forth.
"Dharma" refers to the principle of "guiding and maintaining. Worldly dharmas refer to the nature of the grasped sense organs, bodies, objects, and environments.

The dharmas of the Noble Teaching refer to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the [four] truths, the [three] vehicles, and so forth. Regarding the commentary stating that there are three types of inversion:

these are the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary* by Zezhou states: "The seven consciousnesses, along with their associated mental factors..."

The substance is this: the substance of that mind is inverted and falsely grasps at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). (The seventh [consciousness] falsely clings to the seeing-part of the eighth [consciousness] as the self; the sixth [consciousness] universally clings to both internal and external objects of perception as the self.)

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of dharmas," this is called the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*). To establish the characteristics of that which is grasped is the seventh [category]; these five are definitively called the perversions of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*) (which is to say, they are conceptual discriminations).

They may also be considered false imaginings (*parikalpita*), meaning that various dharmas exist as the perversions of perception. When one repeatedly gives rise to mental engagement (*manasikāra*) by taking what was previously perceived as an object, it is called the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*).
To grasp that which is the object of the mind with fixed clarity is called the perversion of view. Both of these two explanations are the marginal notes of Zeshou.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states that "having the same" refers to the three inversions being the same. "Having them separately" means that the two sets of four inversions are distinct. Regarding the three inversions of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*):

they likewise do not know the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, and because they falsely grasp at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they are in every respect the same as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The texts and commentaries of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* all concern these inverted characteristics of the Two Vehicles. The four inversions are fully detailed as in the first [section].

The *Chao* (Commentary) explains this in the section on "Permanence, Bliss, Self, and Purity. It is also as indicated by the *Zhu* (Annotation) regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). Question:
What is the distinction between the three inversions (*viparyāsa*) and the two kinds of four inversions? Answer: The two sets of four inversions arise based upon the three inversions. Zezhou says:
The three inversions are delusions regarding principle; they involve establishing the characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa while being deluded about the suchness of all phenomena.

This differs from the three inversions taught in the Hīnayāna (since it distinguishes itself from the Hīnayāna, one knows that these are not what they have realized). As for the eight inversions, these are delusions regarding phenomena, namely:

the inversion of perception, which is delusion regarding the defiled phenomena of prior saṃsāra and establishes them as permanent; and [the inversion of perception] which is delusion regarding the pure phenomena of prior nirvāṇa [which one establishes as impermanent].
Regarding the arising of impermanence and so forth: within those three inverted establishments, eight inversions arise (that is, two sets of four).
Therefore, it is said that the eight inversions arise based on the three inversions. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, following its discussion of the eight inversions, states:
"Why is this? Because of the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view—due to these three inversions—people in the world perceive suffering within what is pleasant."

[The phrase] "etc. (referring to the calculation of suffering and so forth) indicates that these are the delusions of the two vehicles. △ Regarding the commentary’s statement "If one specifically addresses... and below: this second section distinguishes [the teaching] according to this specific sutra.
The logic and phrasing are extremely clear; only those whose eye of wisdom is opened can perceive it with vivid clarity.
If one's eyes are blind, even further explanation will provide no benefit whatsoever.
Regarding the initial section of the Commentary which directly illustrates the preceding text, there are two parts: first, a direct manifestation of the characteristics of the analogy;

second, the application of this to the Dharma from the phrase "empty flowers and illusory moonlight" onwards. This [second part] has two sections: general and specific. Within the general section, there are again two parts.

The first follows the analogy in accordance with the flow of the textual structure; thus, it should state: "In reality, the Dharmakāya is devoid of the four great elements; the true mind is truly devoid of discursive thought. It is only the deluded who falsely..."

[The word] "Grasping" [concludes the previous section]. △ Second, from "If one awakens to the True... onwards, it is the synthesis of awakening. "The opposite" refers to the fact that the phrasing of the analogy is inverted.

Regarding "hearing the return," that sutra says: "Returning the hearing to hear one's own nature. ▲ In the commentary, "It may also be... and so forth, there are two distinct parts. The text has two sections: first, the synthesis of body and mind;
second, the synthesis of appearance and seeing. Within the first, there are two sub-sections: first, the formal synthesis; second, from "However, beneath the moon... onwards, which is a supplement.
[Omission]. △ The commentary (*śūtra*) further [proceeds] below. Second, the combined view (*saṃyukta-darśana*). The text has two parts: first, the actual combination;

second, from "Worldly Relatives" (*loka-sambandha*) onwards, the resolution of objections. An objection is raised: The concluding verses of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* translated during the Wei dynasty state:

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are like stars, a cataract, a lamp, a phantom, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud; one should contemplate them in this way. The treatise (*śāstra*) provides a heading and an explanation, stating: "The star is a metaphor for seeing (*darśana*)."

The cataract is a metaphor for the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect), and the lamp is a metaphor for the essence of consciousness (*vijñānatattva*). Now, using the cataract as a metaphor for the *darśanabhāga* (perceiving aspect), does this not contradict that treatise?
Therefore, it is explained here by reference to the commentary on the passage, which means:

the treatise cites and explains [the analogy] by saying, "Just as when the eyes have a cataract one sees colors such as floating hairs, so too is the observation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), because of seeing them erroneously. The *Mahāmegha-ṭīkā* states:

This metaphor [of the cataract] refers to the grasping that occurs if there is a mind that perceives a real self and dharmas; this cataract is assigned to the seventh consciousness because it functions constantly. The critique states:
Since it resides in the seventh consciousness, it is known to be the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect). The metaphor of the "hair-tuft" represents the self and dharmas;

the "self" is the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) belonging to the seventh consciousness, which is the eighth consciousness. The "hair-tuft" is precisely these "empty flowers" (*śūnya-puṣpa*). Therefore, one knows that what is grasped is that which is seen.

It is like flowers [seen in the air]. Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing composed a verse on this metaphor, saying: "It is solely due to the power of eyes afflicted by cataracts that one comes to see flowers in the empty sky.
From this, one should know that the "flowers" represent the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect), while the "cataracts" represent the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect).
Regarding the subsequent instances of successive citations seen in the *Śāstra* (Commentary), there are three parts. First, the explanation of the metaphor.

As for the statement, "It does not mean a real flower," this refers to the erroneous interpretation by Anxi (闇席). He claimed there was a commentary stating that "real flowers" refers to flowers on trees. Such an interpretation is truly lamentable.
For now, I shall preserve the general principle and refrain from naming him specifically; furthermore, this person actually possesses virtue within himself.
[He] practices. As for his other profound and heavy virtues, they are not mentioned here for that reason. ▲ Second, "If one possesses... and below explains the correspondence with the Dharma.
▲ Third, "This is indeed... and below clarifies the underlying intention.
The commentary states: "By this" refers to this false attachment to body and mind. "As numerous as motes of dust" refers to the faults and calamities arising from this false attachment.

"Hell-beings, ghosts, and animals" refers to the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*). "The eight sufferings" refers to the human realm; namely: birth, old age, sickness, [death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair].

Death; separation from the beloved; encounter with the hated; failure to obtain what one seeks; and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). As for the five signs of decay, these pertain to the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*):

first, the fading of their flower crowns; second, the breaking out of sweat; third, the extinction of their bodily radiance; fourth, separation from their retinues; and fifth, a lack of pleasure in their own seats.

Regarding the initial heading of the commentary, there are three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of evidence starting from "Therefore, the treatise says," which establishes that since nothing has its own characteristic apart from fundamental awakening (*mūlajñāna*), it is empty and non-existent;
third, the analogical explanation of other meanings starting from "Having understood this," which contains two sub-sections.
First, a brief exposition of the Mahāyāna *Nirvāṇa*, namely the verses spoken by a yakṣa to the youth of the Snowy Mountains in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Second, "knowing the lower," which briefly explains the *nirvāṇa* of the various vehicles; that is, following the deluded perception of the twelve links [of dependent origination].

The "place of cessation" refers to the *nirvāṇa* of the *pratyekabuddha*. Master Sengzhao stated: "The *pratyekabuddha* awakens to conditions; by departing from them, they immediately realize the truth.

The *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvaka* is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). This Truth of Cessation likewise carries the same meaning as the total extinction of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Therefore, this section speaks of "all vehicles" (*yāna*).
Below the section on the "Vajra Samādhi," the commentary cites a sūtra as proof that all sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent.

This also serves to resolve a potential objection. The objection states: "If there is neither a phenomenon of saṃsāra nor a person who undergoes saṃsāra, for what reason do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear in the world?
For whom do they appear to teach, and for whose sake do they preach the Dharma? It is for this reason that the following passage is cited.

The *Jing* (Sūtra) states generally: "Transformation has nothing that is transformed. Master Xiao’s commentary on the *Śāstra* explains: The first phrase cites the subject and object of transformation;
the final phrase praises the greatness of transformation; the middle two phrases correctly clarify the characteristics of contemplation. Regarding "no arising of transformation":

when first practicing contemplation, those various marks [of existence]—within the nature of illusory transformation—cause the mind of arising to cease, and thus they do not arise. Regarding "no transformation": furthermore...
It is sent into emptiness; because it does not arise even within the unconditioned emptiness, as stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"All four modes of birth and the nine classes of beings are led to nirvana, yet in reality there are no sentient beings who attain extinction.

It is also like the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, which views sentient beings as being like the sixth aggregate (*skandha*). To preach such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings is called true compassion.
Regarding the four stages of "sweeping away" (*śu-fu*): first, "sweeping away the wisdom that perceives delusion," which refers to the first two lines.
"That" (*pi*) points back to the preceding text; it means that the aforementioned wisdom which knows there is no cyclic existence is also like empty space, having nothing at all.
Second, "obliterating the mind that performs the sweeping away," which refers to the next two lines. This means that the mind of the aforementioned perceiving wisdom is also...
It is like a flower in the sky, having no existence at all. Third, the negation of annihilation refers to the following two phrases.

Fourth, the conclusion regarding the departure from faults refers to the final phrase. Not speaking of existence or non-existence is precisely non-thought (*amanasikāra*). Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the paths of mind and speech are cut off”:
the characteristics of what is contemplated are the very pathways of the mind, for it is there that the mind travels. The names by which things are spoken are speech.

Regarding the phrase "the path of speech": it refers to what has been traversed; thus, when it is said to be "cut off," it means that as the mind is about to engage with objects, deliberation vanishes, and as the mouth is about to speak, words are lost.
This is precisely what is meant by "the path of language is severed and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.

As for the passage "Master Kumārajīva says," this refers to the *Preface on Awakening to the Profound* (*Wù xuán xù*) composed by Master Kumārajīva himself. Its opening states: "Now, a fortunate era is difficult to encounter again," and so forth, up to: "As for the profound Way..."
It cannot be attained by setting up merit; sagely wisdom cannot be known with a mind possessed of intentional thought; the True Truth cannot be realized through the persistence of the "I";
and sagely achievement cannot be performed through active affairs. Only those who forget merit can harmonize with the Dao; only those with empty minds can merge with principle;
only those with true hearts can attain oneness with the Real; and only those who have cast off wisdom can be equal to the Sages. Although...
It is said that the Way is united, yet there is no intention to unite; where there is union, it is simply union. Though it is said that the sages are identical, they do not seek identity;

where there is identity, it is simply identity. Regarding the passage about "gathering sand" and so forth, this refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*, which brings provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality, clarifying that all practices are none other than the Buddha-way.
It states, for example, that the countless Buddhas of the past all preached the One Vehicle Dharma, and so on. Furthermore, by means of various...

Skillful means assist in manifesting the ultimate truth. If there are any classes of sentient beings who encountered the Buddhas of the past and, having heard the Dharma, practiced giving, or observed the precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom—such persons as these have all already attained the Way of the Buddha.
(The phrase "all have already" cites past examples, etc., up to: If, in the midst of a wilderness, one piles up earth to form a Buddhist temple, or even...
As children at play, they made stūpas out of piles of sand, and so forth; or with their fingernails, they drew images of the Buddha, and so forth;

or there were those who prostrated, or again, merely joined their palms, or even raised a single hand, or slightly lowered their heads, and so forth—[all] have already attained the path to Buddhahood, and so forth. [And so it shall be for] the future World-Honored Ones, whose number...

There is no measure. These Tathāgatas likewise employ skillful means to teach the Dharma, and so forth, in order to deliver all sentient beings and cause them to enter the untainted wisdom of the Buddha, and so forth (up to) innumerable dharma-gates; yet in reality, they constitute the One Vehicle. The commentary states:

Examine this in detail. Although these Buddhas of the three periods have preached various teachings, they all constitute the One Vehicle; this is the ultimate intention to cause all beings to attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the subsequent analysis of the "wiping away" (*vighāta*) and so forth, the text has two parts: first, the explanation of the three characters "kě yǐ gù" (can [be] because); second, the explanation following the word "yì" (intention).

This passage on the nature of emptiness (*ākāśatva*) consists of two parts: first, a general explanation of the overall meaning; second, a detailed explanation of the text itself, beginning with the words "In this...

What are these four? First, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); second, śrāvakas; third, pratyekabuddhas;
and fourth, bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to attain awakening (*bodhicitta*). As it is said in the noble *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*: "World-Honored One, as for the *tathāgatagarbha*..."

“World-Honored One, the *tathāgatagarbha* is not within the sphere of those sentient beings who hold to the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). World-Honored One, the *tathāgatagarbha* is not within the sphere of those sentient beings who grasp at the four inversions.
World-Honored One, the *tathāgatagarbha* is not within the sphere of those sentient beings whose minds are distracted and who have lost [the realization of] emptiness.

What is the meaning clarified by this? ‘Sentient beings who hold to the view of a self’ refers to all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); it is because of those ordinary worldlings [that this is said].”
In reality, there are no such phenomena as the five aggregates, including form; yet one grasps them, thinking "this is me" or "this is mine. One falsely clings to the conceit of "I" and "mine.

Consequently, one lacks even the faith to believe in the nectar-like Dharma of the untainted nature—the Truth of Cessation—which is free from the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and other [defilements].
How much less could one realize or understand the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the realm of all-transcending worldly omniscience? It is impossible.

There is such a possibility. Furthermore, regarding those sentient beings who grasp at the four inversions—namely, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—they ought to cultivate the Tathāgatagarbha as permanent, yet they do not cultivate the Tathāgatagarbha as permanent.
Because they grasp at all phenomena as impermanent through inversion, they cultivate the Tathāgatagarbha as impermanent.
One should constantly cultivate the bliss of the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet one does not cultivate the *tathāgatagarbha* as bliss.
Because of inverted grasping, one perceives all phenomena as suffering and thus cultivates the suffering of the *tathāgatagarbha*. One should cultivate the self of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

They do not cultivate the practice of taking the *tathāgatagarbha* as the self, yet they grasp at all phenomena as being without self through inversion, practicing instead the non-self of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
They should cultivate the purity of the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet they do not cultivate the practice of taking the *tathāgatagarbha* as pure;
their minds grasp at all phenomena as impure through inversion, practicing instead the impurity of the *tathāgatagarbha*. By means of this...
Because they do not know and do not perceive [it], like the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, none of them are able to practice in accordance with the dharmakāya as it truly is.

For this reason, the supreme dharma of the other shore—eternal, blissful, self, and pure—is not within the cognitive domain of those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Such is the meaning of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.

In the middle [section], the analogy of the pond water extensively clarifies this meaning (the text of the preface has already cited it). Furthermore, regarding sentient beings who lose emptiness due to a distracted mind:

this refers to bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, who depart from the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as emptiness and practice by means of things that are subject to loss and transformation.
Each constitutes a gate of liberation through emptiness. In what sense? A bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening conceives such a thought:
"There truly exist dharmas that are annihilated, and later one attains nirvāṇa. Such a bodhisattva loses the practice of the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness.
Furthermore, there are some who regard emptiness as a substantial entity and think, "I should attain emptiness. They also give rise to this thought:

"Apart from dharmas such as form (*rūpa*), there is a separate emptiness; I should practice so as to attain that emptiness. Such people do not know that emptiness is the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is the unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas.
As the verse says: "The non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* refers to the unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas. It is not...

Mutually abandoning [them], they neither increase nor decrease [the dharmas of merit (guṇadharma), nor the afflictions (kleśa)]. This single dharma is the Tathāgata’s unconditioned body (*asaṃskṛtakāya*);

its self-nature (*svabhāva*) is originally pure, yet it is defiled by adventitious, false dust. Its original self-nature is empty. The subsequent text explains this verse and extensively cites the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*;
both are found in separate volumes. △ Regarding the "three types of vessels" in the Commentary: the second part explains being a vessel. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "There are three kinds of sons of good family who, regarding the profound meaning, avoid self-injury (this implies that lacking these three knowledges leads one to not believe in the *tathāgatagarbha*, which constitutes self-injury), and who give rise to great merit and enter the path of the Mahāyāna. What are these three?"

This refers to "having personally accomplished the profound," and so forth, as explained in the commentary. Following this, it concludes: "This is called 'looking up to and relying upon the Tathāgata.
Aside from these three kinds of noble sons, all other sentient beings are firmly attached to false teachings regarding the profound dharmas;
they oppose the True Dharma, practice the ways of external paths, and possess rotten seeds. Regarding such individuals, one should employ the power of the king and..."
"By the power of devas, nāgas, and spirits, they shall be subdued. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
Śrīmālā, you have skillfully guarded the profound Dharma and subdued what is not the Dharma; you have attained the proper measure. The commentary states:

According to the Tiantai school, based on the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties, there are those who practice according to the Dharma (dharmānusārin) and those who practice according to faith (śraddhānusārin); these correspond to the first and second types of knowledge mentioned herein.
Following the Dharma involves the predominance of one's own power (*svabalavaipulya*); following through faith involves the predominance of external conditions (*parabalavaipulya*).

This refers to encountering the Buddha’s teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and true, sublime spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and being able to accord with them. Regarding the loss of the third type of wisdom:

this refers to when one reads and studies the definitive, supreme, and sudden teachings, or encounters the principles of the perfect and sudden taught by a virtuous friend, yet the principle contradicts one's habitual emotions, making it difficult to accept.
I accept this. I shall not give rise to doubt or confusion because it contradicts my own inclinations. Rather, I must look up to and infer the Dharma known by the World-Honored One.

Although the principle is equal and no different, there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority between ordinary beings and sages regarding intellectual understanding. This profoundly deep Dharma is not within the scope of what I can know;
I shall simply apply myself with diligence to correct contemplation. For now, I offer this explanation and do not yet dare [to proceed further].

*Guide*. I shall await the examination of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* and will subsequently provide a detailed account. △ Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* that "furthermore, reversing the three non-vessels," this means that by reversing the three [conditions of] being non-vessels, one becomes a vessel in all three respects.
"Reversing" refers to being free from the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), free from the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), and not losing the empty Tathāgatagarbha, and so forth.
As for the principle that being a vessel in these three [conditions] is equivalent to not being a vessel in those three, it may be understood by analogy. (This refers to the first...)
[Regarding the phrase] "There is no profound knowledge of dharmas," etc., and so forth.

The commentary explains the meaning of the sūtra in three parts: first, pointing to the essence as contrasted with what preceded; second, from the words "The Tathāgata... onwards, the formal explanation of the sūtra text;

and third, a summary that establishes the preceding meaning. Within the second part, there are again two sections: first, the analytical inquiry; second, from the words "Without arising or ceasing... onwards.

Explanation. Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the "Empty Treasury"; second, the explanation of the "Non-empty. Within the section on the Empty, there are again two parts. First, the analysis of the text.
Regarding the phrase "that which is known as birth-and-death, etc.": the Sūtra says, "Within non-arising, one falsely perceives arising and ceasing;

therefore, it is called transmigrating through birth-and-death," up to, "Furthermore, there is neither body nor mind that undergoes such birth-and-death. It is not because of a lack of action that they do not exist; rather, their original nature is non-existent."
Therefore, the intent of the current explanation is as follows: because within the *tathāgatagarbha* there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing, the preceding text made such a statement.
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "that which perceives" (*taj-jñāna*) and so forth in the upper section, the text says: "That which perceives is like empty space;

that which perceives empty space is like the relative existence of flowers in the sky. That which was previously known as birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is here called the "wisdom that knows" (*jñāna*). Now...

Regarding the meaning of the commentary: because within the *tathāgatagarbha* there is fundamentally no cognition that confronts conditions as an object of knowledge, the preceding text makes this statement.
The sub-commentary states: "The 'grasper' and the 'knower' are so called because one reckons that birth and death exist; [to] realize that birth and death do not exist [is the true state]."
[This is] called "capable of knowing. △ In the commentary, the section beginning with "This is not merely... serves to manifest its virtues.

Within this, first, the passage from "taking the directions as its own substance" onwards follows the momentum of the preceding text on the *Ākāśagarbha* (Space-Treasury). The phrase "truly cognizing and knowing," etc., is a passage from the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "Capable of seeing [the same as this 'non-knowing and non-seeing'] and that which is seen [the same as this... (as above, that "cognition and awareness" is like space).

There is neither arising nor ceasing. Those who see [this]—that is, those who, as stated above, know it to be like flowers in the sky—completely eliminate [all misconceptions]. (This concludes the preceding section. Not destroying the true Dharma is what is called being a "true seer.

(This corresponds to the three phrases beginning with "like the dharma-realm" and so forth). In the commentary (*shū*), the passage beginning with "like the dharma-realm" provides a second explanation of the "Non-empty Treasury.

Regarding "Buddha-nature" and "Dharma-nature," that treatise states: within the category of sentient beings, it is called Buddha-nature; within the category of non-sentient things, it is called Dharma-nature.

This is termed "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). This has already been cited and explained previously. Regarding the phrase "that which can create," etc., this text appears in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Ratnagotravibhāga*;

they are largely the same with minor differences. As for the distinction between the two meanings in the commentary: [the former] refers to the Tathāgatagarbha as the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

[the latter] refers to their identity as one essence, as the sūtra says: "knowing that this is the nature of the dharma-realm. Here, "as" (*ru*) carries the sense of "identity. How could the commentary...?

Regarding "must be equal" (*samatā*): the phrase "extinguishing old delusions" concludes the preceding section on sweeping away the emptiness of the *jñeya* (the object of knowledge), namely birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

The phrase "adding newly arisen ones" concludes the preceding section on sweeping away the knower and so forth. As for the commentary’s statement "repeating the meaning": this refers to repeating the sense while the phrasing is not repeated. This should be distinguished by means of four permutations:
namely, cases where the phrasing is repeated but the sense is not, and so forth.

The commentary explains: "Broadly speaking" and below, the general discussion is divided into two parts: first, a general clarification of the various teachings; second, a specific analysis of this sutra. Within the first part, there are four sections.
The first establishes four types [of verse]. Regarding the first name, Cien (Ci'en) says:

a *śloka* consists of thirty-two syllables and is a medium-length stanza. (In the West, there are five types of lines: first, short lines, which have five syllables in the first half and three in the second; four such lines constitute a verse. Second, preceding lines, which consist of only six or seven syllables; these also form a verse of four lines.)

1. Three-character phrases; 2. Eight-character phrases; 3. Four-character phrases, with subsequent lines ranging from nine characters up to twenty-six characters; 4. Five-character long lines (and beyond, there is no fixed limit). When various treatises refer to Mahāyāna sūtras, stating that they consist of "so many gāthās," this refers precisely to these [verses].
For example, when it is said that the *Avataṃsaka* consists of one hundred thousand gāthās and so forth, the places where verses are actually concluded are extremely few;
the remainder is entirely in prose (*gadya*). Thus, we know that the number "one hundred thousand" does not refer to *gāthā*s.
The *geya*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, and so forth, refer to verses consisting of the initial three or twelve syllables. Regarding the phrase "the *gāthā* of the *uddāna*" in the commentary:
in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, whenever a verse text is cited, it is invariably referred to as an *uddāna*. Question: What constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of a verse? Answer:
It has names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) as its essence; this differs from the Hīnayāna view that a verse depends upon syllables (*akṣara*) and phonemes.

The term "shi" (士) refers to the *śloka* (verse). [As cited above in the commentary: "The 'shi' is that which constructs the verse; it is a provisional entity (*prajñapti*). This text and the term 'shi' are both the basis for the verse. Question:

Why is "number" (*saṃkhyā*) not included among the one hundred dharmas? Companion-Grace (*Cien*) answers: Because its function in expressing the meaning of the essence is inferior to that of names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*).
Because it is a sound that serves as a basis for regression and is inferior [to others], it is not established separately among the one hundred dharmas. △ Regarding the phrase "Why is this...
below, there are two parts: first, the formal exposition; second, from "Now, in this... onwards, the correlation with the sutra.

As for the statement "The actual [recitation] consists only of three times seven," this refers to the repeated teaching for those of dull faculties (at that time, all in the assembly of the Pure Land had entered samādhi, so although there were no dull-facultied ones present, it is not precluded that they might exist during the degenerate age). The intention is to cause them to... [totalize].

Only after examining the prose and its corresponding verses will one understand the meaning and principle. Thereafter, according to one's capacity, one should merely recite and uphold the text of the verses; by doing so, one will naturally remember the meaning of the prose and further clarify what was previously explained (the textual characteristics being self-evident).

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "one, five, and six": this refers to the fact that these three [types of texts] all apply to the direct verses (*śloka*), as they may each contain a few additional words. This is intended to allow for ease of reception according to one's preference;

the intent is to ensure that at least one person maintains the textual transmission. "Textual maintenance" (*wen-chi*) means that those who possess it practice the prose (*gadya*), while those who do not practice the verse (*śloka*).
Second, those who delight in comprehensive study practice the *prose* (gadya), while those who delight in chanting practice the *verse* (gāthā).

Third, those with strong mental faculties practice the prose, whereas those with weaker mental faculties find it easier to receive and uphold [the teaching], and thus practice the verse. Regarding the commentary’s statement that it is "neither two, four, nor eight":
"not two" means this is not a solitary praise; "not four" means that the Dharma assembly of the Pure Land dwells together in the equanimity of the Tathāgata.
...the assembly of the Dharma. Because there were no followers who arrived later, as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The Buddha said in the past... [and so forth]. This explains the intent of the sūtra:
at that time, there were again sentient beings of sharp faculties who arrived later for the sake of hearing the Dharma, and so on. This was already cited among the preceding twelve divisions.

It is not "eight" because it has already been explained in the prose commentary (*gadya*). △ In the sub-commentary (*śū*), from "Furthermore, Ci'en" onwards, three citations from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* are provided.
The meanings are also twofold. Following the above, although it is said there are ten meanings, these constitute ten pairs.

In each pair, the upper term refers to the prose (e.g., *li* [sharp], *qian* [benefiting others], *qu* [crooked], *nan* [difficult], *zhen* [true], *qu* [grasping], etc.), while the lower term refers to the verse (e.g., *duan* [dull], *hou* [subsequent], *zhi* [straight], *yi* [easy], *su* [worldly], *she* [abandoning], etc.). First, regarding the two faculties of sharpness and dullness: *li* (sharp).

1. For the two assemblies of former and later [disciples]. 2. For the two preferences of the crooked (referring to indirect or elaborate explanations) and the direct (referring to speaking the matter plainly); that is, the preference for the crooked and the preference for the direct. 3. For the two modes of explanation:

the difficult (wherein those hard to understand are explained at length and with detail) and the easy (wherein those easy to understand are explained concisely in verse). 4. For the two types of compliance: the ultimate (true words according to principle) and the conventional (ornamented according to worldly custom);

that is, compliance with the ultimate and the reversal of the conventional. 5. For the two divisions of taking up (taking what is good) and abandoning (abandoning what is evil). 6. For the two functions of indicating (listing principles and phenomena) and explaining (expounding upon them).

The two distinctions of "meaning" (*artha*) are subtle; the two differences of "wisdom" (*jñāna*) are discerned through eight [aspects]; the two variations of "understanding" (*avabodha*) and "retention" (*dhāraṇā*) are ninefold; and the two distinctions of "exposition" (*deśanā*) and "practice" (*pratipatti*) are tenfold.
Regarding the points in the commentary that can be understood by comparison: these are assigned to correspond with the preceding eight meanings.

That is to say, "sharp and dull" faculties corresponds to the third [point] above (it simply states it is for those of dull faculties, but one should know that for sharp faculties, it refers primarily to prose [*gadya*]. All subsequent instances follow this pattern; understand it thus). "Before and after" corresponds to the fourth. "Crooked and straight" [corresponds to the fifth].

The fifth [topic] is "Difficulty and Ease. The sixth is "The Real and the Conventional. The second is "The Statement and the Explanation" (since it is not mentioned in the prose commentary, we know it refers only to the statement).

The seventh is "Wisdom and Eloquence" (because there is beneficial eloquence, which increases clarity and manifestation). The first is "Understanding and Retention": when one must seek the meaning in detail through the prose commentary, that is understanding;

once understood, one needs only to retain a few words to encompass many meanings, which requires verse. Regarding the taking up and discarding, these are mentioned only in the latter part and do not exist in the former or the middle.
Because suffering is not the ultimate truth (*satya*), both prose and verse may interchangeably occur. The remaining eight [categories] are all present in relation to the former.
By means of these eight dharmas, these sixteen dharmas are subsumed; furthermore, they are listed according to their meaning so that one may understand them upon reading.
Let the wise examine this in detail. △ In the commentary, from "However, in the prose... onwards, the fourth section, "Discerning the Five Examples," also has two parts. First, the main [text].
To illustrate this point: the Ci'en school added the pair of "ornate" (*wen*) and "plain" (*zhi*). We do not adopt this because prose and verse translations differ;

whether a style is ornate or plain depends on the translator. How could it be that one [translation] must be exclusively ornate and another exclusively plain? There are indeed those who translate the scriptures [in various ways].

The prose is also stylistically refined; furthermore, there is someone who translates it as such. Within the verses, too, there is a plain style. In the commentary (*śāstra*) below the current sutra, [the text] is divided into two parts and assigned to this sutra.
In the commentary below this section, the second part specifically analyzes this sutra. Regarding the slight differences in nomenclature:

only the fourth section, which serves as the concluding summary, is identical in its entirety; the remaining first three sections all have minor variations in their expansion and contraction, which will be demonstrated further below.

Regarding the statement that "the prose [commentary] and the verses are both 'separated' and 'combined'": in the first section of the prose, it first designates the fundamentally existing awakened mind and subsequently clarifies that awakening constitutes Buddhahood;
thus, it is called "separated. In the verses, however, it simply states that "all are awakened by means of wisdom"; thus, it is called "combined.
Because the structural divisions of the text do not entirely coincide with the preceding [section], it is said that "the names differ slightly. The second section consists of the prose.
First, the characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*) are shown; subsequently, its fundamental emptiness is revealed. Now, one directly realizes that emptiness;

therefore, the two phrases "long" (*cháng*) and "separation" (*lí*) are combined. As for this combination: the two characters "realization" (*liǎodá*) encompass both the characteristic of realization (*xiàng*) and the nature of realization (*xìng*). (To realize true emptiness is precisely the nature. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "first, long," etc.:
the main text states, "Only by permanently severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way"; it then proceeds to interrogate and explain ignorance.
The nature and characteristics [of the deluded mind] are now presented following the detailed explanation and resolution. Furthermore, the long passage states:
"Just as various empty flowers vanish into space," and subsequently says: "That which perceives is like space. This current passage refers precisely to the dissolution of the illusion.
Regarding the phrase "after wiping away the traces, [the commentary by] Chang Yin and others..."—whereas the prose version merely says "arouse a pure mind," this text directly states "bodhicitta.
This concludes the Chapter on Mañjuśrī.
