Fascicle Five (Part Two) / *Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Sub-commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Fascicle Six (Part One).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Temple on Mount Zhōngnán.

From here begins the second major section: causing [the practitioner] to rely on understanding for cultivation and realization. This section has three parts. First, the presentation of the general meaning.

"The initial cause" refers to first hearing the preceding chapter, which suddenly points to the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*). "The Dharma-mirror illuminates the mind": "Dharma" refers to the teachings; "mirror" is a metaphor.
It is like a person who possesses eyes and ears but has no means to see for themselves; if they use a mirror to reflect upon it, they then see.

The nature of the minds of sentient beings is likewise. There is no means by which one can see it oneself; only by hearing the holy teachings and relying upon them to reflect inwardly does one finally perceive it.
Furthermore, Master Sengzhao said: "When an ancient mirror reflects the essence, that essence manifests its own form;

when the ancient teaching reflects the mind, that mind becomes self-illuminating. Thus, Qingliang said: "Use the holy teachings as a bright mirror to illuminate and perceive one's own mind; take one's own mind as wisdom."

The lamp illuminates the profound purport of the sutras; Heze also spoke thus. As for "obstructions," this primarily refers to karma and afflictions, while also including the obstruction of retribution (since practices such as repentance within the *daochang* remove the obstruction of retribution).
Regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties, this refers to the depth or shallowness of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): this treatise refers to the habitual tendencies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), not to the subtle residual habitual tendencies remaining after the seeds and manifestations of the two obstructions have been severed.

As for the habitual tendencies of ordinary beings, they are explained in the section of this treatise concerning the mutual reinforcement of defiled and pure perfuming, as well as in the sections concerning the habitual tendencies of the various karmas and the dual grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) within Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*); these shall be explained below. Regarding "reliance and opposition": reliance...

This teaching contradicts other teachings. For example, in the "Chapter on the Questions of Samantabhadra" (*Prajñāparipṛcchā-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, it says: "The poor count the treasures of others," and so forth.

Therefore, the commentary must proceed below to correctly clarify the intent of the sūtra. The phrase "in every place" and so on employs the literary style of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; that text states: "Sentient beings are attached everywhere; [the Buddha] leads them out [of attachment]."

The commentary then explains the structure of the text below [the preceding section]. This consists of three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the general judgment beginning with "The former... (*qian ze*); and third, the citation of examples beginning with "Therefore, in the *Avataṃsaka*... (*huayan*).
Regarding the statement "it is also only four," these are faith (*śraddhā*), understanding (*adhimukti*), practice (*caryā*), and realization (*adhigama*). As for "faith":

it refers to the six chapters and eleven fascicles of the first assembly, which present the two fruits—the environment and its inhabitants—and exhort the great assembly to have faith and joy. As for "understanding": it refers to the second [assembly], the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-nirdeśa*.

Based on the cause, one accords with the fruit, thereby giving rise to wisdom and understanding. This refers to: the second assembly, the ten stages of faith; the third assembly, the ten abodes; the fourth assembly, the ten practices;
the ninth assembly, the ten dedications; the sixth assembly, the ten grounds; and the seventh assembly, the two awakenings of Equality and Wondrous Enlightenment.

The "Practitioner" (xingzhe) relies upon the aforementioned methods of faith and understanding to advance in cultivation so as to perfect right practice; this corresponds to the eighth assembly. The "Realizer" (zhengzhe) corresponds to the ninth assembly.

This is the assembly. At the beginning, when the Buddha entered the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*), the entire ocean-like assembly suddenly realized the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Sudhana, on the other hand, personally visited his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and gradually realized the stages through successive positions. Regarding the "threads of the beginning and end": from the initial revelation of the original mind (*mūlacitta*), one successively generates practice and understanding until the sequence of entry into realization;
thus, the gateways are distinct and the vital currents are interconnected. Regarding the "continuous flow of the lifeblood": [it refers to the seamless continuity of the teaching].

Only the Avataṃsaka and the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra [provide such instruction]; although the Benevolent Kings and the Garland Sūtras list the stages of realization, they merely explain their doctrinal meaning and do not point to the gateway for directing the mind toward entry.

In the lower part of the commentary, the third section explains the scriptural text. This section is further divided into two parts: first, the opening of the chapters; second, beginning with "Now, first," the citation and explanation of the text.
Regarding the phrase "this therefore": "this" refers to the essence of Samantabhadra’s practice. Regarding "according to the faculties":

the Sūtra says, "Those who cultivate the Mahāyāna and hear of Perfect Enlightenment," which distinguishes the intended audience. Those who do not cultivate the Mahāyāna are clearly not included among those who receive and practice it.
Regarding the vessels of the Dharma-gate: if there are those who cultivate the Mahāyāna but have not yet heard of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), they are shown not to be vessels.

This is as previously cited from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which states that practicing the six perfections for many kalpas does not constitute being a Bodhisattva and so forth. Now, to summarize: those who possess these two types [of qualities] are "those who penetrate the natural truth.
As stated in the preceding chapter, the nature of enlightenment is naturally and fundamentally pure; birth, death, and other such phenomena are not [inherently existent].
"Because it is created, it does not exist.

Regarding the commentary on "How can one cultivate the illusory and the illusory?", the text has two parts. First, a general explanation of this section. As for the question "This question follows from the preceding," it refers to what was stated previously:

[Section on] the Explanation of the Meaning of "Illusion" (māyā). This section has two parts: first, stating the general meaning; second, opening up the categories for detailed explanation. First, stating the general meaning: it is said that this is difficult to understand because such things do not exist here [in this land].

Second, from "Now, following the ancient masters" onwards, there is the opening of the categories and their explanation. This means that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is like a piece of cloth; the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) is like a magician;
and the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) is like the magical arts. As for the magical arts, they have various distinctions; likewise, the discriminating consciousness is also one.

Although there are various distinctions, the true mind is but one. In the analogy, since it is simply that the horse is non-existent, this does not preclude the fact that the cloth was originally present and the illusionist’s technique was effective.
Correspondingly, in the application of the teaching, although the self and dharmas are non-existent, this does not preclude the fact that the mind exists;
it is merely consciousness that discriminates these various [appearances]. However, those who are deluded and cling to the horse as real are bystanders, not the illusionist himself.

Regarding "clinging": among the mental factors (caitta) within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), those that cling to a self and dharmas are the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. These correspond to the "characteristic of wisdom" and the "characteristic of continuity" within the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith).

They are not the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*) nor the three subtle states of the ālayavijñāna. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also describes the ālaya as unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
If one wishes to take the true and the false as being of one mind without any separate external clinging, it may be like a magician who has practiced for a long time.

Regarding the practice of illusionary arts (*māyā-dharma*): once the technique has been mastered and the ritual procedures completed, one may suddenly become deranged and deluded, regarding the illusory objects as real.
Although this sudden madness occurs, because the mastery of the illusionary art is so profound, one involuntarily maintains it;
thus, the illusory objects do not cease (just as a dog barking at its own reflection in a well might even leap into the well and die).

It is like the water of the great ocean, which is stirred by the wind; the characteristics of the water and the characteristics of the wind do not separate from one another, yet the water does not have motion as its intrinsic nature (it is not inherently mobile, but moves only in accordance with other conditions).

Regarding the phrase "layer upon layer" (*chongchong*) in the commentary: wishing to demonstrate the meaning of layered inclusion, we shall first explain it by way of the first layer.

The *Yì* is easy to explain and easy to see. If one wishes to encompass all things within this single matter, one must first see that this single matter fully encompasses the true mind (*zhēn xīn*).
Because it fully encompasses the true mind, it is then able to encompass all things. What is the meaning of this?
That is to say, if this single phenomenon did not fully encompass the true mind, then the mind would exist outside of that phenomenon; how then could it be said that "it is only the true mind"?
If it were to encompass it incompletely, then the mind would have limitations; how could it possibly be the true mind?

Therefore, one knows that this single phenomenon must fully contain and encompass the true mind. When this single phenomenon fully encompasses the true mind, it causes this [phenomenon] to be non-different from the mind.

Many phenomena follow their dependent mind and all manifest within this single phenomenon. If those many phenomena did not manifest in accordance with the mind, then the phenomena would exist outside the mind.
Since this single phenomenon now fully encompasses the true mind, how could those numerous phenomena not manifest within it?
As it is with one phenomenon, so it is with all; therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "Within each and every atom, one sees the Dharma-realm; the jewel-light manifests Buddhas."
They gather like clouds. This [sovereignty over the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata] and so forth all arise because each and every thing is entirely the true mind, and so on.
Because everything is entirely mind, it can contain all things. As for the commentary’s statement that what is contained is also only mind, and thus contains all things again:
this refers to what was previously explained—that within a single phenomenon, all phenomena are likewise each and every one only mind.
Because it is the true mind, it further encompasses all phenomenal dharmas; that which was previously encompassed now becomes the encompasser.
(The former is like many jars within a single house; the latter is like every jar containing numerous bottles and so forth. Regarding the "inexhaustible within the inexhaustible" in the Commentary:
this refers to the second level of what is encompassed, which is also entirely the true mind, and thus is likewise able to encompass the third level of all things.
All phenomena are contained within the third layer, which likewise consists solely of the true mind; thus, it is further able to encompass the fourth layer.

In this way, as the capacities of the "able" (the container) are inexhaustible, the objects of the "contained" are likewise infinite. This is entirely because [the preceding layers] are not yet solely the true mind.
The subsequent summary, "all due to," etc., refers to this. However, these three meanings above are identical to the Ten Mysterious Gates of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
These are the three gates: first, the gate of the mutual inclusion of the one and the many without confusion; second, the gate of the mutual identity and sovereign freedom of all phenomena;
third, the gate of the realm of Indra’s net.

The sub-commentary (*śū*) below these five teachings concludes the third section, which summarizes all the teachings. Regarding the "eight gates": there are three in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), two in the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), and one each for the remaining three;
thus, they constitute eight. Although there are three meanings within the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), it constitutes only a single gate.

As for "beans and barley" (*mudga-yava*): "beans" (*mudga*) refers to legumes. This is because [the author] feared that the meaning and intent of the eight gates would not be clearly distinguished, as if one were as ignorant as a fool.
The foolish person cannot distinguish between beans and wheat.
[The commentary] below generally explains this. Fourth, it explains the reason for adhering to the specific tenet. One should first ask:

Based on what has been stated above, only the Sudden Teaching and the Perfect Teaching are the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) that accords with reality; how then can there be other such [teachings] in various sutras and treatises?

This differs from the previous explanation; therefore, this commentary states: "It is because the sūtra teaches according to the capacities of beings," and so forth. Regarding "according to capacity":

as in the section on the inverse and sudden [teachings], it refers to the expressive medium (*vyañjana*). It follows the order of the text while reversing the sequence of the Dharma, proceeding from one to seven in successive stages.

The meaning of the *Shu* (Commentary) and the *Chao* (Excerpts) may be understood by taking the intent and applying it to this explanation. Question: Since the sūtra text was already delivered by the Buddha at that time to address specific differences...

Regarding the explanation of the skillful means for distinguishing [the teachings]: why is it that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various bodhisattvas composed treatises to establish fundamental tenets or to comment upon the scriptural texts, and yet there are differences among them?
Therefore, it is said next that "treatises follow the sūtras to provide comprehensive understanding.

This means that it is not only during the time when the Buddha was present that there were distinctions among those with differing capacities; even after the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, up to the present day, it remains the same.

When Bodhisattvas compose treatises, they likewise follow the fundamental tenets of the sūtras to provide a comprehensive explanation of the Buddha’s intent. They compose *mūla-śāstras* (root treatises) that each accord with a specific class of sūtra and respond to a specific class of spiritual capacity.

They compose *vyākhyāna-śāstras* (explanatory treatises) that each comment upon a single sūtra, further elucidating its specific tenets according to whichever sūtra’s fundamental principle it follows.
For example, when the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed Abhidharma treatises of the Hīnayāna, he followed sūtras such as the Āgamas regarding the themes of defilement and purification.

The distinctions are fixed. In works such as the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, the characteristics and categories are strictly defined. In his commentary on the *Śata-śāstra* and his exegesis of the *Vajracchedikā*, he clarifies that emptiness sweeps away all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
In his treatise on Buddha-nature, he asserts that sentient beings are the Dharmakāya Tathāgatagarbha.

In his commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s Ten Stages, he explains the perfect fusion of the six aspects (*ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, one should know that each work follows the specific tenet of its respective sūtra; how could there be any stagnation in clinging to a single fixed position?

Regarding the phrase "the commentators follow the tenets of the treatises," the fault lies with later generations who merely transmit these traditions. This is truly due to their narrow-mindedness and lack of learning;

unable to study extensively, they encounter a single teaching and immediately claim it to be the perfect and all-encompassing truth. When they encounter an expositor whose explanation contradicts their own understanding, [they reject it].
He immediately rejected it and would not accept it, instead claiming it was erroneous; thus it is said that they both adhere to shallow provisional teachings.
Regarding "shallow provisional teachings," each preceding stage is shallower than each succeeding one. Now, I shall provide a detailed analysis, for the essential meaning lies herein.

In the commentary below the section on "beginning and end," the fifth part provides a comprehensive reconciliation of the forward and reverse sequences. This section has two parts: first, stating the intention;

These three [categories] are largely the same, yet because each treatise has its own preferred tenet, they consequently result in various enumerations of the divisions of the seen and the seeing.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because the faculties [of beings] vary," there are two points of intent. As for the terms "superior and inferior" and "shallow and profound":

The former refers to the meaning within the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*), while this refers to the meaning within the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*). However, the essence of the one true awakened mind is neither defiled nor pure.
When there is delusion, all is defiled; when there is awakening, all is pure. Because purity accords with the essence of awakening, it is called "fulfillment of awakening" (*jue-man*);

because defilement opposes awakening, it is the principle of concealment and thus not called "fulfillment of awakening. The arising of delusion constitutes the meaning of defilement, as explained previously.
This is explained in sections. The meaning of awakening as purity is as stated in the *Zhengzong* (The Main Doctrine): it refers to the threefold causes and the resulting fruits. Question:

The Sub-commentary (*Śāstra*) states below: "Second, the *Śāstra* presents both [aspects] together, namely, the dharmas of defilement and purity.

just as a worldly garment has no fragrance in itself, yet through being perfumed by someone with incense, it comes to possess a fragrant scent. Thus the sutra says: "Because the *tathāgatagarbha* exists, one grows weary of birth and death and seeks nirvāṇa. [This refers to the stage] prior to delusion.

Within the first part [defilement], there are two sections: first, the explanation; second, the proof. Now, for the first: the explanation consists of citations drawn from the essential meaning of the treatise. The treatise states in full:
"How does the perfuming (*vāsanā*) give rise to the uninterrupted continuity of defiled dharmas? It is because, by relying upon the dharma of True Suchness, there exists ignorance (*avidyā*)."
(This passage sets forth the essential natures of the perfuming agent and the perfumed object. Alternatively, one might mention only the perfuming agent, ignorance (*avidyā*), here;

however, because it necessarily relies upon the True [Suchness], it is presented by reference to its root. Because there is the cause of defiled phenomena, namely ignorance, it perfumes True Suchness. (This is the meaning of the perfuming of fundamental ignorance. Because of this perfuming, there arises the deluded mind.

(Based on the perfuming of ignorance, the True [Suchness] is moved, giving rise to the mind of karmic consciousness. Although the deluded mind also extends to the phenomenal consciousness, it is called "karmic consciousness" here because we are referring to its root. Because there is the deluded mind, it in turn perfumes ignorance.
Because they do not clearly understand the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), they fail to perceive it, and thoughts arise, manifesting as delusive objects.

By means of this deluded mind, they in turn nourish and permeate ignorance (avidyā), increasing their lack of understanding and causing it to transform into the evolving consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna) and the manifesting consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna). Because there are the conditions of these defiled dharmas—the delusive objects—they then permeate and habituate the deluded mind.
This causes them to become attached through mindfulness, whereby they create various kinds of karma and undergo all manner of suffering of body and mind.

(By means of these objects, they further perfume and stir the ocean of the mind, giving rise to the waves of the various consciousnesses; by taking those objects as conditions for mindfulness, the *vastu-vijñāna* (empirical consciousness) arises. Among the six "coarse" factors mentioned above, the first two are called "mindfulness" (*smṛti*), the middle two are called "attachment" (*abhiniveśa*), and the latter two are the same as this [present case]. Furthermore, the meaning of the three types of perfuming—delusive objects, delusive mind, and ignorance—each has two aspects, as explained extensively in the treatise). △ The commentary states "Śrīmālā-sūtra," etc., which is the second part: citing scriptural evidence.

"They are able to paint all worlds; the five aggregates arise entirely from them; there is no phenomenon that they do not create. In the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) on the Pure Dependent Origination (*viśuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*), the text is divided into two parts.

It is severed. This is because there exists the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is able to permeate ignorance (*avidyā*).
By the power of the causes and conditions of this permeation, it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to earnestly seek *nirvāṇa*.

[This refers to] the power [of cultivation]. The former is original perfuming (*mūla-vāsanā*), while the latter is newly perfumed (*nava-vāsanā*). Below, this explains the stage of the path of cultivation within the ten stages, wherein one extensively cultivates the myriad practices. By means of...
Manifesting True Suchness through various skillful means, one initiates practices that accord with it.

Not grasping at the grasped (the signless), and not recollecting the recollector (the non-arising of the subject), and so on until, by the power of long-term cultivation (cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*), ignorance is extinguished.

Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind has no arising (the deluded mind is exhausted). Because there is no arising, objects are accordingly extinguished (deluded objects cease). [The above all concern the extinction of delusions; this reverses the three preceding types of defilement. Below...]

[Regarding the statement, "The realization of the principle and the perfection of virtue are clarified": Because both the cause (*avidyā*) and the condition (*viṣaya*) have ceased, the manifestations of the mind (*citta-lakṣaṇa*, i.e., the defiled mind) are entirely exhausted;

this is called attaining *nirvāṇa*. (Because both of these are extinguished, the fundamental nature of the mind undergoes a transformation of the basis, which is called attaining *nirvāṇa*. Second...

because it possesses power, it enables sentient beings to loathe the suffering of birth and death, to joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*, and to gain self-confidence that they themselves possess the *tathatā*-dharma, thereby generating the resolve to practice. They give rise to the three minds—disgust for the conditioned, aspiration for bodhi, and the desire to benefit sentient beings—and the four great vows. They cultivate the six perfections, sever the two obstacles, and realize the two kinds of emptiness. Nevertheless, although they rely on...

He teaches that one should practice in this manner. If one has not yet heard the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) which accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there will ultimately be no real fruit;

therefore, it is called "partial purity" (*bhāga-śuddha*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* cited previously states that there are bodhisattvas who have practiced the six perfections for many kalpas, yet ultimately fail to be born into the family of the Tathāgata, and so forth.
As for the phrase "vertically exhausting the past," it is truly because they rely on the practices of those [lesser] teachings.

Explanation: To say that there are afflictions (*kleśa*) to be severed implies that the noble ones (*ārya*) of the Three Vehicles have been definitively possessed of outflows (*sāsrava*) since beginningless eons, and only become pure after severing their obstructions.
Regarding ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), it is stated crosswise that while the noble ones are pure, all ordinary beings do not attain purity.
As for "Sahā" (the Endurance World), it refers merely to [the contrast with] "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*) and so forth, as well as the Enjoyment Bodies for oneself and others. And...
The Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*) is pure; all other transformation lands (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*), such as this Sahā world, are said to be impure.

Since there are both pure and impure aspects within the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the bodies and lands of ordinary beings and sages alike, it is said that they are "divided. It is by virtue of forming this understanding that [the distinction is made].
Though one may diligently practice for many kalpas, no real fruit will ultimately be attained. Regarding the commentary’s statement on "perfect purity," there are two gates within it:
first, sudden enlightenment; second, gradual cultivation. To realize that one's own body and mind are not to be identified as a self through the five aggregates is sudden enlightenment.

This means that because one heard the Perfect Teaching in past lives, the seeds of the Perfect [Teaching] were perfumed; thus, upon hearing it again, the latent seeds from the past are awakened, and one suddenly comes to know.
All sentient beings possess the wisdom-tathāgatagarbha and have no seeds of the eight consciousnesses characterized by arising and ceasing.
Afflictions and birth-and-death are themselves bodhi and nirvāṇa. All lands—their defiled appearances are fundamentally empty; there is nothing that is not a pure land.

At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Seeing all sentient beings, one likewise sees them as such. Therefore, [the Buddha] emerged.
The *Xianpin* (Chapter on Manifestation) states: "A Bodhisattva should know that within every thought-moment of their own mind, a Buddha is always attaining perfect enlightenment.
As it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings. Based on this, at the moment of sudden awakening, one penetrates the *dharmadhātu*;

whether regarding oneself or others, one perceives only purity. The commentary notes: "Greed and anger gradually subside" refers to gradual cultivation; that is to say, although [the realization is] perfect...

Although one may attain sudden awakening and understanding, because of the inverted and deluded attachments accumulated over many kalpas, these have become habitual and ingrained in one's nature; thus, they cannot be exhausted all at once.

Therefore, it is necessary to practice and cultivate until one accords with the fundamental nature. This cultivation further has two aspects: first, the elimination of faults; second, the fulfillment of virtues.
Regarding the phrase "free from faults": this reverses the aforementioned successive branches and secondary hindrances.

Once one personally realizes the true, pure *dharmakāya* and the numinous mirror of the true mind, one will no longer falsely identify with the body of the four elements and discursive thought, which is fundamentally caused by afflictions (*kleśa*) for the sake of this very body.
Since one no longer identifies with this body, greed and anger naturally subside. When greed and anger have subsided, one ceases to create karma.
The absence of karma means there is no retribution of suffering or pleasure within the six realms; thus, it is said that one is "free from faults. Regarding the phrase "accomplishing virtue":

when one suddenly awakens to the fact that there is fundamentally no obstruction or affliction, one then practices exclusively in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), manifesting the wondrous functions of the countless virtues inherent within that nature.
However, this does not mean that one first abandons faults and only thereafter accomplishes virtue; rather, it is within the very state of mind and its objects that one is free from faults.

At that time, one accords with the nature of reality; in every thought-moment, one perfectly cultivates the myriad practices, and in every thought-moment, one perfectly accomplishes the myriad virtues.

Thus, although from the very first arousal of the mind one is identical to perfect enlightenment, this does not obstruct the distinct unfolding of the stages of practice. Nevertheless, each practice interpenetrates the others, and each stage is harmoniously subsumed within the rest.
The cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause. The severing of hindrances is immediately identical to the same essence as all sentient beings.
It is universally severed. Upon attaining Buddhahood, one immediately realizes the same essence as all sentient beings and achieves universal perfection. Thus, the "Appearance Chapter" states:
"When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment; he universally perceives all sentient beings entering parinirvāṇa.
This refers to the forty-two stages within this Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), whether they pertain to the wise or the sages, the mind or the objective realm, or the basis.
Whether it be persons or dharmas, if they are correct, they are all perfectly pure (*pariśuddha*). As for "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*):

it is because one originally hears the perfect teaching, believes in the perfect dharma, gives rise to the perfect understanding, initiates the perfect practice, perfectly eliminates all obstacles, and perfectly realizes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Since this cultivation and realization of dependent origination relies upon various conditions, at the moment of realization, one sees that both the ordinary and the holy are likewise so; therefore, it is called "perfect purity. Thus, the Great Sūtra says:
All dharmas have causes and conditions as their basis. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions;

for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught. The previously cited treatise states: "True Suchness perfumes ignorance, and so forth. Regarding the passage in the commentary stating "there is no exhaustion or cessation," the treatise says:
"Furthermore, defiled dharmas have been perfuming [the mind] uninterruptedly since beginningless time, continuing until the attainment of Buddhahood; thereafter, they cease to exist."
[The former] is severed; however, the perfuming of pure dharmas has no severance and continues until the end of the future. What is the meaning of this?

Because the True Suchness (*tathatā*) constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) manifests. Since it gives rise to the perfuming of functional activity (*vṛtti-prabhāva*), there is no severance.
The commentary states: This is truly because, by overturning the deluded defilements, the original pure nature is revealed. Because it is originally pure, it is ultimately clear.

Purity is without interruption or exhaustion. If there were originally no pure dharmas and they were only attained through cultivation, then what was originally non-existent would now exist, and what already existed would return to non-existence;
how then could it not be subject to interruption? Thus, perfect purity is uninterrupted—this is where the wondrous principle lies.
In the *Commentary on the Cheng weishi lun*, Part Four, there is a reconciliation with the provisional teachings (*prādeśika-śāsana*).

Because the True Suchness (*tathatā*) taught in those schools is described as being exclusively quiescent and immutable, entirely lacking the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*), the [text] distinguishes it from True Suchness. Thus, that treatise asks:

"Based on what meaning is 'perfuming' established? It states that if both the perfumer (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*) each possess four conditions, they cause seeds to grow; therefore, it is called "perfuming."
Regarding perfuming (*vāsanā*): what are the four characteristics of that which is perfumable? First, the quality of stable endurance (*sthira*).

If a phenomenon persists as a single, continuous stream from beginning to end and is capable of sustaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is perfumable. This excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) as well as sound, wind, and so forth, because their nature is not stably enduring;
therefore, they are not perfumable. Second, the quality of being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If a phenomenon is neutral and free from contradiction, it can accommodate habitual tendencies.
The vital energy (*vāyu*) is that which is perfumed; this excludes the wholesome and the defiled, as their power is so intense that they leave no room for [new] reception.

Therefore, they are not what is perfumed. Consequently, the Tathāgata’s eighth pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) carries only pre-existing seeds and does not newly receive perfuming. Regarding the third characteristic of being perfumable:
if a dharma is sovereign, its nature is neither solid nor dense, and it can receive perfuming, then it is that which is perfumed. This excludes the mind...
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not perfumable because they depend on others and are stable and dense.

Fourth, that which possesses the nature of being in common conjunction with the perfuming agent—meaning it exists simultaneously and in the same location as the perfuming agent, being neither identical to nor separate from it—is the perfumable.

This excludes other bodies and moments before or after, as they lack the sense of being in conjunction; therefore, they are not perfumable. Only the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) possesses these four characteristics.

However, that which is perfumed is not [limited to] mental factors (*caitta*) and the like. What are the four characteristics of that which is capable of perfuming? First, it must possess arising and ceasing.
If a phenomenon is impermanent and possesses functional activity capable of producing and increasing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is then capable of perfuming.

This excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they do not change before or after and lack the function of production and growth; thus, they are not capable of perfuming. Second, it must possess superior efficacy. If there is arising...
Cessation: that which possesses powerful intensity and is capable of inducing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is a perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*).
This excludes the mind and mental factors of maturation (*vipākaja*), because their power is weak and inferior, and thus they are not perfuming agents. Regarding increase and decrease:

that which possesses superior function and is subject to increase or decrease, thereby gathering and planting habitual tendencies, is a perfuming agent. This excludes the perfected wholesome dharmas of the Buddha-fruit, as they neither increase nor decrease.

Because it is diminished, it is not a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*). If it were a perfuming agent, it would not be complete, and there would consequently be superiority or inferiority between the preceding and succeeding fruits of Buddhahood.

Fourth, it must evolve in conjunction with the perfumable (*vāsyatva*); if it exists simultaneously and in the same location as the perfumable, yet is neither identical nor separate from it, only then is it a perfuming agent.
This excludes the possibility of conjunction with another person’s body or across successive moments, and therefore it is not a perfuming agent.

"Infusion" (*vāsanā*). Only the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) possess the dominant power and function to increase or decrease [the seeds];
being endowed with these four meanings, they are capable of infusion. Such an infusing agent arises and ceases simultaneously with the consciousness that is the infused object;

thus the meaning of infusion is established, causing the seeds within the infused object to grow and develop. Because it is like infusing sesame seeds (*tila*), it is called "infusion. This refers to the infusing consciousness.

...and so forth. At the moment they arise from the seeds, they are immediately able to act as causes and further perfume new seeds. These three factors revolve in a cycle where cause and effect are simultaneous.
This is like a wick producing a flame while the flame produces the charred wick; it is also like bundles of reeds leaning against one another.

The principle that cause and effect exist simultaneously is unshakeable. The commentary states: the third characteristic among the "perfumable" [dharmas] and the first characteristic among the "perfuming" [dharmas] are both...
This excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as they cannot permeate that [consciousness] and do not receive its permeation;

furthermore, because True Suchness (*tathatā*) lacks the principle of permeation, the commentary states "all" to exclude True Suchness. Regarding the phrase "according to one class of teachings," this refers to the Initial Vehicle of the Mahāyāna within the Five Teachings.

Furthermore, regarding one aspect of the conceivable meaning: True Suchness (tathatā) possesses two meanings—immutable nature and conforming to conditions (as explained at length in the third section of the *Xuantan*).
Because it does not cling to its own nature, it can conform to conditions to become all phenomena;

because it does not lose its own nature, while acting as the substance of myriad things, its essence remains eternally immutable. If one were to speak exclusively of the meaning of immutability, then...

It is inconceivable (*acintya*) and ineffable (*anirvacanīya*). This teaching has two meanings so that they do not obstruct one another; thus it is both inconceivable and ineffable. As previously cited from the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"O Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming (*vāsana*) and the inconceivable transformation (*pariṇāma*) are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*)," and so forth.

(As explained previously: the ignorance perfuming the True Suchness (*tathatā*)—perfuming where there is no place for perfuming—is called "inconceivable perfuming. The True Suchness remaining immutable while being able to transform is called "inconceivable transformation. It is not a case of emphasizing the act of perfuming itself; this perfuming of that which is not perfumed is what is meant.)

The transformation through inconceivable perfuming is precisely the transformation of that which is unchanging within the unchanging; this is the inconceivable transformation. Therefore, when the Buddha addresses those of shallow capacity and initial stage within the Mahāyāna, he speaks only of the aspect of non-change;
thus it is called the Initial Teaching (*Ādikarmika-yāna*). When he fully explains both aspects, it is called the Final Teaching (*Niṣṭhā-yāna*). The commentary states: "This treatise, etc.
refers to the Final Teaching, because it is an exposition of the ultimate definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). For this reason, it is further named "Reality" (*Tattva*).

"Teaching" (also used to refer comprehensively to the Sudden Teaching). "Generally termed 'Reality' (shí)"—Reality refers to the Final and Sudden [teachings]. The phrase "and so forth" includes teachings of this same category.

However, within the single collection of the Mahāyāna, such types are numerous. As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without arising; it manifests as having arising," and so on.
The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "It is like gold and a finger-ring," and so forth. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Being unstained, yet stained," and so forth.
The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta* states: "The Dharma-body flows through the five realms of existence," and so forth. These cannot be cited in full; they are as previously cited.
Regarding "inconceivable perfuming," this was already explained above with detailed annotations.

The commentary below the section on "Pure Dependent Origination" summarizes this gate (which is precisely the gate of "the exhaustion of illusion and the fulfillment of awakening" from this sutra). It also serves to explain the meaning of the non-interruption of pure dharmas within the *Śāstra*.
That is to say: because of delusion and inverted false defilement, there is the Buddha’s teaching; by relying on the teaching to awaken and practice, one attains pure dharmas.

Since these exist in mutual opposition and arise from conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As for the statement that "both are fused," it refers to the arising [of delusion] from the obscuration of the Truth.

Delusion. Awakening to the real overturns delusion. Apart from one’s own true nature, there is no separate defilement or purity; therefore, defilement and purity are identical in essence with the True.
Thus it is said that they accord with the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. Hence, the treatise states that there is no distinction between an "initial awakening" (*ādikṣayabodhi*).

As for "arising is solely the arising of nature," this refers to the "Gate of the Arising of Nature" within the Huayan school. It means that the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmatā* arise as the totality of their very substance.

This pertains to all dharmas. Since the Dharma-character school (Faxiang zong) asserts that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is exclusively quiescent and unchanging, it maintains that there is no meaning of arising from non-substantiality (*amūla*).
In contrast, what this [present] school teaches is that the true nature is profoundly illuminating and spiritually luminous; its entire substance is itself its function.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) constitutes all phenomena. This nature is eternally quiescent by itself, for this quiescence is the quiescence that encompasses all phenomena in their entirety.
It is not like empty space, which is a mere void of insentient stagnation. All phenomena are the phenomena of total quiescence;

thus, they do not consist of fixed characteristics or substantial obstructions as conceived by the inverted views of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Since this applies to both the mundane and supramundane realms...
All dharmas are entirely the manifestation of nature (*xingqi*), for there is no dharma existing apart from this nature. That sutra states:
"The Buddhas and sentient beings interpenetrate; pure lands and defiled lands are mutually integrated; every dharma encompasses and includes every other."
Every atom contains all worlds; they are mutually identical and mutually inclusive, unimpeded and perfectly interfused, possessing the ten gates of mystery, infinitely layered and inexhaustible.

This is truly because everything is the manifestation of the nature (xingqi). Thus, in the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source), within the section on the five gates of cessation (*pañca-sthiti*), it says:
Regarding the third point, "The Arising of Nature (Shōki): The Natural Course of Profuse Manifestation," it is said: "Arising function from the essence is called the arising of nature;

because these manifestations respond to the myriad differences, they are termed 'profuse manifestation'; that this has been so throughout past and present is termed the 'natural course' (hōni). Since it is stated that this has been so throughout past and present, [it is understood as such].
One thus knows that it does not depend on encountering external conditions to draw it forth; rather, it arises eternally as the fundamental nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Even if one speaks of various conditions mutually supporting and stimulating one another, within this gate, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) also constitutes the arising of the nature (*svabhāvodaya*).
Based on this meaning, the Buddhas eternally and universally expound the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm within every single atom without ever ceasing. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka*.
"Opening the Key": There is the "Gate of the Arising of Nature. The *Huayan jing* translated during the Jin dynasty contains the "Chapter on the Arising of the Tathāgata-nature.
Based on this, the name "the Illusion Exhausted and Enlightenment Full" (*huàn jìn jué mǎn*) is established; this precisely constitutes the conclusion of this section.

Regarding the annotation that "the characteristics of awakening and cultivation are like those in the 'Universal Eye' Chapter," this merely explains the principle that when illusory delusions are exhausted, the nature of enlightenment is perfect and full, being neither interrupted nor terminated.

This serves as the answer to Samantabhadra’s question regarding annihilationism. It correctly explains the characteristics of awakening and cultivation; the textual passages for these appear both earlier and later.

The characteristic of awakening is found in the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter, while the characteristics of the initial cultivation of expedient means in practice are found in the subsequent Samantacakṣus chapter, including the analysis of the four great elements, the contemplation of body and mind, up to the manifestation of clarity once defilements are exhausted, as well as the various subsequent chapters.

In the lower part of the commentary, there are three sections based on the text for detailed explanation. Regarding the term "comprehensive" (*gai*): this primarily illustrates that when illusion is exhausted, awakening is fulfilled;
it is also comprehensive in that it includes the preceding various illusory flowers arising from the awakened mind. Therefore, it is called "comprehensive. Regarding the term "exclusive" (*wei*):

this refers only to the subsequent point that although the illusory flowers perish, the nature of emptiness is not destroyed; it does not refer to the flowers arising from emptiness. Therefore, it is called "exclusive."
That "the flower arises from the void" is identical to the previous passage concerning the illusory arising within awareness; therefore, it is not redundant.
This is because the compiler of the sutra skillfully employs brevity (brevity meaning that a single metaphor suffices to encompass both preceding and succeeding sections).
Regarding the three stages of severing tendencies: the first stage severs the duality of opposites, while the latter two stages sever existence and non-existence;

thus, one naturally cuts off the gateway for the arising of thoughts. Those of superior wisdom attain accord with the awakened mind from this point onward, whereas those of middling and inferior capacities—

Even if one does not attain accord, one will nonetheless remain in a state of bewildered ignorance; from beginning to end, one will be filled with trepidation, losing what one maintains and having no trace upon which to rely.
Therefore, it is said that there are three ultimate layers.

In the commentary on "successively departing from illusions," there are two parts: first, the specific explanation of "successive departure"; second, the general explanation of "distancing oneself. Within the first part, there are two stages.
Regarding the first stage, the phrase "departing from all illusory objects" means that all phenomena produced by illusion—whether mind or environment—are collectively termed "illusory objects.
This is because it is not only external objects that are so called; rather, they are all that which is perceived. Therefore, within the second stage...
Regarding the first phrase, it simply states "departing from delusion. The Commentary (*Sūtra-śāstra*) distinguishes this by specifying "that which is not the illusory mind.

Since the Sūtra says, "That which is like the illusory mind is also far removed," this clarifies that that which is not illusory cannot be abandoned. Thus, Qingliang said: "To discard it yet not depart from it. The subsequent Sūtra text states:
"Because illusion is extinguished, [illusion] is extinguished; that which is not illusory is not extinguished. Question: Since the non-illusory mind has already been distinguished...
[The interlocutor] asks: What is this "illusory mind" that is to be abandoned? How does this illusory mind differ from what was stated in the first line?
In the previous explanation of the first line, it was said: "Whether mind or object, all are termed illusory phenomena. Why, then, is the illusory mind mentioned separately here? [The response:

The preceding statement explained that from time immemorial, both internal sentient beings and external sensory objects are entirely illusory transformations. Therefore, it is said below: "the defilements of body and mind."

This phrase refers precisely to illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna*). It is the mind that is capable of both transcending and cultivating. Therefore, it is the second layer. The subsequent phrase says "transcending awareness.
Furthermore, it was stated above that "one may employ illusion to cultivate illusion. The commentary’s third point concerns "the transcendence that transcends illusion."
The first phrase refers to being able to leave behind only illusory delusion. The second phrase refers to being able to leave behind only illusory wisdom.

In both cases, one has not yet left behind the "leaving" itself—the subject that performs the leaving. Therefore, this [text] leaves it behind. As the Sūtra says: "That which distances itself is itself an illusion" (the word *wei* means "is").
It is not only the two types—illusory delusion and illusory wisdom—that are illusions; even this very capacity to distance itself from those two illusions is itself an illusion. Hence, it is said:
It is likewise removed. Therefore, it is explained again below. The third phrase says, "removing the removal. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the four remove the removals" and so forth:
the first two phrases merely remove what is to be removed; only with the third phrase is the remover itself removed.

Although both the subject (the remover) and object (that which is removed) are extinguished, this still belongs to the category of "brushing away and extinguishing," as one has not yet attained the state where both existence and extinction leave no trace. Thus, this concludes the whole: there is no trace of removing or leaving behind.

This is because it cuts off the arising of the mind and the movement of thought. (The *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* says: "To say 'it is not permissible' is also not permissible. This very statement is not accepted. It is utterly transcendent and without dependence [beyond the reach of words and the arrival of intellectual understanding]; this is the sphere of practice.

If one gives rise to the mind or moves in thought, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma, for one has lost right mindfulness. This serves to prevent the fault of infinite regress. As the Sūtra says: "That which departs from even the departure from illusion.

The meaning is that the "departure" by which one departs from "departure" is itself also an illusion. Regarding the commentary's phrase "it may also be," it is a further explanation of the four [aspects].
This is a phrase. It merely consists of concise wording with clear meaning and does not differ from what preceded it;
however, because one must thoroughly and minutely analyze the aspects of the practice (*ākāra*) based on the preceding text, the phrasing appears somewhat redundant.

Although each sentence can be understood individually according to its own context, if one surveys all four sentences simultaneously, one perceives the distinctions between their respective stages. This, moreover, summarizes...

This is a brief indication; it refers to the manifestation of the visualization through complete contemplation. ▲ In the commentary (*shū*), the phrase "all say 'far below'" provides a general explanation of "distancing" (*yōri*).
This passage consists of four parts: first, it clarifies the characteristics of distancing by way of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

Second, the text states "as the following passage says," citing the second sentence from the latter part of the root text and the first two sentences of the *Buddhagocarāvatāra-sūtra*; both serve as proof for the distancing of contemplation. The subsequent sentence says, "distant from all illusory phenomena."
Therefore, it is proven that [this] is cessation (*śamatha*). Because there is one final additional phrase, "I pay homage to the objectless," its meaning is as follows:

because one desires to become detached from all illusory phenomena, one pays homage to the objectless. The sub-commentary briefly explains the last three points regarding the characteristics of the practice of cessation and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
That is to say, not allowing the mind to remain attached or stagnant is precisely the resting of the mind and the calming of mental activity; therefore, this is cessation.

Furthermore, not engaging in conceptualization or discrimination while giving rise to clinging views is precisely what is meant by "contemplation" (*guan*). From the passage beginning with "The commentary [states] 'but below...
onward, the four points establish the perfection of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), which is the benefit of being far removed from delusion.

Because the equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom leads to the clear vision of the Buddha-nature, the text—from the subtle revelation of true awakening up until the end of the verse—is clearly evident throughout.

The commentary on the second fascicle of the *Śāstra* extensively clarifies the characteristics of practice. The text is divided into three parts:

first, regarding the assignment of the Dharma-gates according to the three-part structural analysis, it is not as in the teachings of the Three Vehicles, where each is applied to a specific faculty of the Three Vehicles; rather, this is a single-flavored Dharma that is skillfully applied.
These are the three roots. ▲ Commentary: Regarding the section below, it follows the topical outline (*ko*) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. First is the primary outline; second, "Although there is...
and so forth, which addresses potential objections. The objection states: Puxian asks, "How does one practice? The "Puyan" chapter says:

"First, relying on the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, sits in quietude in a still chamber," and so on, up to "cultivating this mind until it is perfected."

Regarding "etcetera": In the chapter on Maitreya, it concerns severing the root and branches of saṃsāra and cultivating the practices of compassion and wisdom; in the chapter on Pure Wisdom, it asks how the stages and grounds of cultivation are established.
The judgment states that these are all encompassed within the categories of understanding (*adhimukti*), for it is said generally that they are merely for the sake of [understanding].
This is subsequently identical to the examples cited below, namely that the entire *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is categorized into four divisions: faith, understanding, practice, and realization.

In the second division, from the second assembly to the seventh assembly, the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the two types of sublime awakening are explained in sequence;

these collectively constitute "understanding. This means that one must understand the dharmas of the ten faiths up to the dharma of the fruit of Buddhahood in its perfected form before it can truly be called understanding.
(The commentary states: "However, for the time being..."—the third point returns to using what was previously discussed.

Regarding the commentary on the text: as for the phrase "the equality of body and mind, etc.," it may be assigned to the corresponding sections of the sūtra in sequence. This demonstrates that for the listeners, there is a profound flavor [to this teaching].

In the first section of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), under the heading "Requesting the Dharma," the text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the introductory request; second, from the words "How so... onwards, the explanation of the specific enumeration. Furthermore...

Second: One section. Second: Explanation by way of beginning, middle, and end. Within this explanation, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the question regarding wisdom; second, from "Sentient beings have not yet awakened" onwards, the explanation of the question regarding compassion.

"Yao-yao (夭如也). (The commentary on that passage states: "Shen-shen and yao-yao are the appearances of harmony, relaxation, and ease. My current interpretation is as follows: one must clearly contemplate and penetrate both principle and phenomena (*li* and *shi*).

"Because it is a commentary, it establishes Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*)," and so forth. This is the second section, which cites scriptural evidence. Only the essential meaning is extracted and summarized for use;

the full text is not provided. Within this, there are three parts. First, "Awakening to the Principle": regarding the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*), some refer to them as person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*), while others refer to them as sentient beings and phenomena (*sattva-dharma*).
Cien (Ci'en) says: "Because it speaks only of humans and does not discuss other realms of existence, it was changed to 'emptiness of persons' (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, the *Yanshi yanmi* (演秘) states: "Phenomena (*dharma*) also possess a self; the term 'self' is broad and pervasive, as it applies to both persons and phenomena.

The Path is like Śakra, the Lord of Devas; he is the one who can ask, or the one who can explain. Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma that is asked about, or the Dharma that is explained, and so forth.
How could Śakra then belong to the human realm? Furthermore, "I" (ātman) signifies a sovereign master, carrying the sense of one who exercises control.

[Is it] the same regarding the creation of karma and the receiving of its retribution? Therefore, one should know that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) are vastly different and should not be said to be identical.

Furthermore, the term "arising phenomenon" (*utpādadharmaka*) established by them also fails to avoid the fault of being overly broad (*ativyāpti*), because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), whether sentient or insentient, possess the meaning of arising.
In response, Yanmi (Yanmi) offers this defense: "The world also reckons [some things] as non-existent..."

Those who hold that "sentience is the self" distinguish it from insentient matter, thereby avoiding the fault of over-extension; for instance, if one reckons physical form as the self, then hair, body hair, and so forth would also be included among what is grasped as the self.
Is this not then reckoning the insentient as the self? Now, we further refute this by saying: we only take that which is actually reckoned [as the self].
If one grants that [the opponent’s] rebuttal is valid, then for those who do not grant it, all phenomena would still possess the sense of arising;

how could they avoid the fault of being overly broad? If you claim it is not overly broad, why did the earlier translators use the term "sentient beings" (sattva)? Furthermore, that school refutes this by saying:

Is this not an overextension to insentient things? Therefore, one should know that when discussing the self (*ātman*), phenomena (*dharma*), arising phenomena, or produced phenomena, it suffices to distinguish clearly between two types of aspects;

according to the terminology used, both are applicable. Specifically, when referring to what is identified as oneself, one should say "self" (*ātman*); when pointing indirectly to what is identified by others, one should say "person" (*pudgala*).

When referring collectively to the various realms of the six paths of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and the other destinies (*gati*), where there is death here and birth there, [the term "person" is used].
If arising and ceasing were uninterrupted, one should simply say "arising"; "arising" refers to sentient beings (*sattva*) and does not concern the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

Now, because the term "self" (*ātman*) is most intimate [to us], it is said that both self and phenomena are empty (*dharma-ātma-śūnyatā*). "Empty" means that what others grasp as existent is here described as empty; emptiness is simply the absence of that [grasped object], having no separate essence.
Wisdom arises taking emptiness as its object, serving as the gateway through which one traverses, and it reveals the two kinds of *tathatā* (suchness); thus they are named the two [emptinesses].

Regarding the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): although its essence is existent, it is neither existence nor emptiness; it is not a marvel that it is empty. It is designated as the "two kinds of emptiness" based on what is manifested.

This refers to the actual nature manifested by these two kinds of emptiness. As for the term "emptiness," it is spoken of from the perspective of its predominant capacity; thus, the nature of the two kinds of emptiness is named "the two kinds of emptiness."
"Nature" (*svabhāva*) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. To say that "True Suchness is empty" does not exhaust the full meaning of the principle.

This is because ordinary beings and non-Buddhists do not understand it at all; they are thus called "deluded. As for the followers of the Two Vehicles and those with erroneous interpretations among the various schools, they possess a partial understanding;

Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*) and "without outflows" (*anāsrava*): this means that those who are deluded give rise to understanding, while those who are mistaken attain correct understanding. In the commentary, "giving rise to understanding" is treated as the lower [stage]. Second is the severing of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*).
Since there are two hindrances because of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), one should know that when one realizes both types of grasping are empty, the two hindrances are then severed.

Regarding the term "heavy obstacles": these are words of censure. Because of the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one is obstructed from Great Nirvāṇa and wanders through birth and death.

Because of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one is obstructed from Great Bodhi and fails to realize the nature and characteristics of all phenomena; for they are as difficult to sever as a diamond.
Because one falls into this stream of birth and death that is difficult to cross; because sentient beings are oppressed and submerged by the four dharmas;

and because sentient beings fall and sink into the three realms—it is therefore called "heavy. There is an interpretation which holds that only the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are explained as heavy obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), while all other secondary obstacles are light.

This interpretation correctly reveals that these are the obstacles severed by the realization of the two emptinesses (*dvi-śūnyatā*). As for "obstacle" (*āvaraṇa*): it means to cover and obstruct. It covers the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and obstructs great *nirvāṇa*. [Question: ...

For what reason was this treatise composed? To this, it is said: [The purpose] is to generate understanding regarding the two attachments (*dvigraha*), rather than the two obstructions (*dvibandhana*);

and to state that they are for the sake of severing the two obstructions, rather than merely refuting the attachments. The treatise answers: Because of attachment to self and phenomena (*ātmadharman-graha*), the two obstructions arise together.

If one realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaividhya-śūnyatā*), those obstructions are severed accordingly. (This explains the reason why only the two attachments are mentioned. Regarding the answer to the first question: Furthermore, the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consist of many categories; attachment to self is their root, giving rise to all afflictions. One does not cling to a self because there are no afflictions (*kleśa*). Having realized the principle of non-self (*anātman*), the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is eliminated; since the root has been severed, the branches are also exhausted. This is said in reference to the severance of afflictions during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the stage of finality (*niṣṭhābhūmi*);

it is not so for other stages, because one first abandons eight grades of affliction, and only at the time of the ninth grade does one then sever the view of a self. The same applies to the view of a self in the fourth ground (*bhūmi*). As stated in the ninth fascicle of that treatise regarding the Stage of Provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*), there are two interpretations. Within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the types are likewise not uniform.

Taking attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) as the root, the remaining hindrances arise. When the emptiness of phenomena is realized, attachment to phenomena is severed; because the root is cut, the trunk and leaves are also removed. These two attachments—to self and to phenomena—are the direct hindrances to the two types of emptiness; the other hindrances and secondary afflictions are seen as their outflows. Therefore, regarding ultimate truth, only the two emptinesses are taught.

Furthermore, to explain this comprehensively, there is no need for separate explanations: since other afflictions and so forth arise with these attachments as their root, the two attachments fully give rise to the two hindrances. There is not even the slightest hindrance that does not arise in dependence upon attachment. This is what is meant by the term "arising."

The meaning lies herein: since the root has already been exhausted, the branches follow in its cessation. If one realizes the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), all remaining obstacles are severed. Regarding these obstacles, although they are fundamentally explained as the two emptinesses, the arising of understanding and the severing of obstacles simultaneously eliminate the afflictions (*kleśa*). This does not refer to non-afflictive [obstacles], nor to other obstacles or other delusions. Realizing emptiness does not mean that grasping (*abhiniveśa*) is not severed;

rather, it refers to the universal apprehension of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). [This] answers the two questions posed above according to their respective meanings. (From the *Śū*, "Severing Obstacles" serves as the basis for the third [section], "Attaining the Fruits").
Regarding *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*: the treatise first states that they are "the severing of hindrances" for the sake of attaining these two supreme fruits.

It subsequently explains: "Because one severs the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that cause rebirth, [one attains] true liberation. (True liberation is precisely *nirvāṇa*; thus, its commentary states: "The essence of true liberation is perfect quiescence [*parinirvāṇa*].

The fifty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says that all afflictions are capable of causing rebirth; these are the afflictions that project karma and moisten rebirth. In this present treatise, these are all termed "causing rebirth"; it is specifically the afflictive hindrance that projects karma and moistens rebirth, as its essence is...)

This is the nature of bondage. It is not the case that the meaning of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is likewise [the cause of bondage]. Therefore, it is stated that rebirth occurs solely through afflictions (*kleśa*). Sentient beings constantly dwell in birth and death; once they have realized parinirvāṇa, they are able to abandon those bonds. What is established as "liberation" is precisely the afflictions; thus, it is called the "affliction-hindrance" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

It covers and obstructs nirvāṇa, preventing one from attaining its realization. The various practices cultivated by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are merely temporarily extinguished. Even when non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) practice asceticism and calculate that they have realized nirvāṇa—up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—where all delusions are temporarily severed, they still cling to the *tathatā* (suchness) revealed therein.

Because the seeds [of existence] are not severed, it is not true liberation. Furthermore, although the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) attain the two types of cessation, by abiding within these two, they do not abide [in non-abiding]; thus their liberation is not true, as it is merely provisional. Thus, all the above cases are liberations that are not true.

While the ten stages (*bhūmi*) accord with principle, they are not true liberation. To distinguish them from those, it is called "true liberation. The provisional substance is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), while the reality is suchness (*tathatā*). Now, for those who fully explain the root treatise, let it be complete according to the root text. Since the commentary (*śāstra*) mentions only "nirvāṇa," one need only explain the characters *nie* and *pan*;

there is no need to fully recount the meaning of "true" (*zhen*) or the meaning of "liberation" (*jie tuo*). The subsequent explanation of *bodhi* is likewise. Because the obstacles to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed through understanding, one attains the Great... [text ends].

*Bodhi*. (Regarding "that which is known": this refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*), whether existent or non-existent, for they are all objects of knowledge. The wisdom that thoroughly understands these objects of knowledge is called "understanding" (*vidyā*). "Obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) has the meaning of hindering. Because the category of clinging to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) covers the objects of knowledge, it obstructs the understanding of the mind, preventing it from arising.

As for "right understanding" (*samyag-vidyā*): "right" (*samyak*) means distinct from what is erroneous; in Sanskrit, *bodhi* is translated as "awakening," because one awakens to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). *Mārga* means "path," in the sense of a course to be traversed. The ancient translation of "Bodhi-path" is incorrect.)

Because the category of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) obscures the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) such that wisdom does not arise, it is called the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This name for the obstruction is established based on that which is obstructed; it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "an obstruction to what is to be known.

The essence of that which is obstructed consists of the four types of gnosis (*jñāna*) and the four nirvāṇas, which will be explained in detail below in the section on the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). Although ordinary beings may practice the contemplation of the two kinds of selflessness and suchlike, their [realization] is not "Great" (*mahat*). The wisdom of the Two Vehicles is not Great Bodhi. Furthermore, although ordinary beings and non-Buddhists possess some slight wisdom, it is not Great Bodhi.

The Bodhi of the Two Vehicles possesses untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), yet their Bodhi is not Great. Here, by excluding those cases, it is termed "Great Bodhi. Moreover, this excludes only the wisdom-Bodhi of the Two Vehicles from being Great; as for the wisdom of a Bodhisattva—

The Great is not bodhi. The wisdom of ordinary beings is neither of the two types. Question: These are called the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*); each obstructs one fruit. Are they fixed as distinct obstacles, or do they also interpenetrate? Answer: This is not fixed; they may be either distinct or common.

This refers to the benefit of the fruit (*phala-anuśaṃsa*). It is that which accords with and benefits the cause, because it is the benefit obtained through cultivating the causes for three *kalpas*.

In the lower part of the commentary, there are three sections that open the chapters and provide explanations. Regarding the phrase "clinging is precisely the self-dharmas, etc.":

however, based on the refutation of clinging to reveal the truth, there are two agents and two objects, which together constitute four factors of conditions. The agent that refutes and the agent that reveals are both its wisdom; therefore, there are only three factors.

The refuter and the refuted. Previously, these were the deluder and the deluded; now, they are the revealer and the revealed. Regarding the first part of the commentary, "I" (*ātman*), etc., there are two sections:

first, the refuted; second, the refuter. Within the first section, there are two: first, the self (*ātman*); second, phenomena (*dharma*). Within the [section on] the self, there are again two: first, the essence of the self as it is grasped;

One merely gives rise to conceptual discrimination, yet the meaning can be understood. As for the statement that the *ātman* is a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 40, states:
Question: Are [the categories] from the *ātman* up to the "seer" one and the same thing, or are they each distinct? Answer: They are all one and the same *ātman*; it is only by means of...

The distinctions are made according to specific instances. Within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), because there is the mind of "self" and "what belongs to self," it is called "self. The *Yogācārabhūmi* also states:

"Self" refers to the fact that the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self" manifest and proceed with respect to the five aggregates. [The commentary] says: "As for what is called... and so forth; this second section sets forth the essential nature and characteristics.
This is the specific characteristic of the self. To summarize, it is simply the various aggregates. "Designated entity" (*prajñapti-pudgala*) means that within the aggregates—

Because it is established as a designation, it is called "self. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "In both worldly convention and the noble teachings (*ārya-śāsana*), the existence of self and phenomena is spoken of;

however, this is merely by way of designation (*prajñapti*) and not by way of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). second, designation of that which has substance (*sārthavat-prajñapti*), which is a forced designation applied according to various stages and conditions, as taught in the noble scriptures. Regarding "the noble [ones] and the self" in this context: "the noble ones" refers to the noble beings of the three vehicles, such as the stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*).

The "self" (*ātman*) in the world is precisely what is being analyzed here. However, since its alternative names vary according to specific contexts, the accounts provided in various teachings differ in their number—whether increasing or decreasing—and sometimes even change the terminology.
The names listed here are taken from the fourteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which contains seventeen aspects;
this version is the most extensive. Nevertheless, these have been further condensed, resulting in only ten.

1. Regarding the seventeenth [set], there are ten: (1) the self (*ātman*; this is the general term mentioned above); (2) sentient being (*sattva*; the *Avataṃsaka* calls them "living beings"); (3) life-force (*jīva*); (4) born-being (*jantu*; the *Avataṃsaka* calls them "existence");
