This "dust" (object) is explained in the section on "All Phenomena are Mind-Only" within the Chapter on Samantabhadra; one may consult that for further details.

Regarding the third point, the breadth or narrowness of the objects of the three [types of] conditions: the objects of the five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness can be understood [therein]. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:

"However, because the bases and objects of the six evolving consciousnesses are coarse, manifest, and universally established, they are not discussed here" (this refers to their non-discussion in the *Kārikā*, though they are discussed below under the section on "the commonality of the basis and object"). For now...

Regarding what is not mentioned in the verse that reveals the uncommon basis: first, because it is coarse and manifest; second, because it is universally established (*prasiddha*) as all treatises contain it, the root verse does not state it separately.

That is to say, in the root verse, the first transformation consciousness explains only the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and not the basis (*āśraya*); the second transformation consciousness explains both kinds. These six consciousnesses are excluded from having no basis because their basis is not explained [separately], due to being coarse, manifest, and universally established.

As for the seventh [consciousness] taking the *ālayavijñāna* as its object, the treatise verse says: "Depending on that, it transforms; taking that as its object. "That" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*. This consciousness takes only the *ālayavijñāna* as its object.

The seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) is nothing other than this; for since beginningless time, it has continued as a single stream, appearing as if permanent and unitary, and is grasped solely as one's internal self.

Once the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) has been attained, it likewise takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) and all other phenomena as its objects. Regarding the "eight conditions" and so forth:

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, within the section on the objects of the first transformation of consciousness (*prathama-pariṇāma-vijñāna*), a verse states: "The appropriating (*upādāna*) and the locus (*sthāna*) are the objects;

'appropriating' has the sense of grasping (*parigraha*) and the sense of maintaining (*dhāraṇa*). "Appropriating" means to take [something] as one's own essence (*svabhāva*) and maintain it so that it does not perish. It refers to experiencing [the body] through a commonality of welfare and security, and it is called "appropriating" because it gives rise to sensory experience (*vedanā*).

Taking the "appropriated" as the object has two aspects. First is the seed, which refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the various marks, names, and conceptual discriminations (that is, the provisional nature of the three natures of contaminated phenomena).

Although the seeds of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) rely upon this [basis], they are not subsumed within its nature; therefore, it is not their object-condition (*ālambana*). Nevertheless, they are not separate from it, just as the nature of suchness (*tathatā*) does not contradict the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Second is the "body with sense organs" (*sendriya-kāya*). The aggregation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth is called "body," or it is called "body" because it serves as a support. This refers to the ultimate designation for a single physical form. The term "sense organs" (*indriya*) is used specifically because the organs produce subtle [consciousness]; thus, the emphasis is placed on the organs.

This refers to the five material sense organs (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) and their respective bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*). One speaks of "taking the body as an object" (*kāyālambana*) fearing that the material forms devoid of organs might be included; therefore, by prioritizing the specific organs, one distinguishes them from the body as a whole. This reveals that the objects of perception include both the five organs and the material supports of those organs. Since these specific organs exist within the totality of the body, it is termed the "body with sense organs."

Furthermore, that which constitutes the body takes the faculties (*indriya*) as its primary basis. "Body" (*kāya*) is a general term; it is designated by its principal component and thus called "body. Regarding the "body with faculties" (*sendriyakāya*), the faculties are common to all five types of faculties. As for "only one's own body," this refers to the physical locations (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the various faculties across the five sense bases.

These do not grasp sound, because the *Abhidharma-kośa*, chapter five, states that they are not appropriated (*anupātta*). Nevertheless, they actually serve as internal conditions and also take the five external objects as their conditions (i.e., they are not appropriated).

Both of these [the faculties and their locations] are subsumed under the appropriation by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its own substance, because they share the same security and peril (*ekayogakṣema*). [The commentary] explains the meaning of "appropriation" (*upādāna*), stating: "Because they share the same security and peril. "Location" (*sthāna*) refers to...

The "location" (*sthāna*) refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), as it is the locus upon which all sentient beings depend. Both the appropriated [body] and the location are objects of perception (*ālambana*).

By the power of the causal conditions of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, at the moment its own substance arises, it internally transforms into seeds and the body with sense organs, and externally transforms into the receptacle world.

(This reveals that the internal and external appearances arise through transformation from the seeds of direct causes and the seeds of karmic conditions. All of these are the objective images (*nimitta*) perceived by consciousness.

Within this objective division (*nimitta-bhāga*), there are two types of active manifestation (*pravṛtti*). First, the transformation of the external vessel-world: this refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

By the power of the ripening of common seeds, it transforms into the appearance of the vessel-world, such as form and so forth—namely, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Although the transformations of each sentient being are distinct, they are similar in aspect and occupy the same location, like many lamps [illuminating the same space].
[The opponent] says: "It is clear that each [transformation] appears as if it were one and the same, namely that which belongs to the present and that which will arise in the future.

This is the transformation of the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness). [Objection: It is difficult to maintain that what belongs to a future birth can [perceive]. For example, sentient beings within the territory of Tang cannot perceive those in foreign lands. Furthermore, regarding the initial formation of a world-system: when sentient beings from the upper realms—the first *dhyāna*—have not yet descended to the established states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), who is it that transforms [the world]? Even if one claims it is the sentient beings of the first *dhyāna* in the upper realms who transform it, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* does not permit transformation across different realms.

Moreover, at the time the world is destroyed, during the twenty *saṃvarta-kalpas* (aeons of destruction), the first nineteen aeons involve the destruction of sentient beings, while the twentieth aeon involves the destruction of the physical world (*bhājanaloka*). Second is the body with sense organs (*sendriya-kāya*). This refers to the transformation of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) through the power of the ripening of its non-common seeds (*asādhāraṇa-bīja*), appearing as the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) and their physical bases (*āśraya*).

These consist of the internal primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derivative matter (*upādāyarūpa*) they produce. Regarding the distinction between common and non-common [seeds], this follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

An analysis in four propositions: reflect upon this according to the principle. (1) Common within the common [are mountains and rivers]; (2) uncommon within the common [are fields and houses]; (3) common within the uncommon [is the supporting sense-faculty]; (4) uncommon within the uncommon [is the pure sense-faculty].

As for their being unknowable, it is because the atoms of the appropriated objects are extremely subtle, and because the dimensions of external worldly objects are vast and difficult to fathom. The commentary states that "direct perception" and so forth are mentioned because of this explanation.

Regarding the objects of perception (*ālambana*), I shall now elaborate upon the meanings of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the distinction between the real (*dravya*) and the conventional (*prajñapti*), which will be appended to the subsequent text.

That is to say: the fifth and eighth consciousnesses perceive only objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); the seventh consciousness perceives only that which is not valid cognition (because its objective self-substance is entirely non-existent); and the sixth consciousness universally perceives all three types of valid cognition.

Furthermore, the objects perceived by the fifth and eighth consciousnesses are real dharmas; the seventh perceives conventional dharmas; and the sixth universally perceives both the conventional and the real.

Regarding the opening and closing of the four aspects (*ākāra*), "opening and closing" refers to the fact that each of the various consciousnesses consists of either four parts, three parts, or two parts.
This is because the various masters of India established these varying numbers of parts, each according to its own principle.
Regarding this, to explain it specifically in terms of the eighth [consciousness]: this refers to the character *liao* (了) in the verse of the treatise. "Liao" means "to discern" (*vijñapti*).

This refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which possesses the function of discernment with respect to its own objects of cognition—namely, the reflected images it itself has transformed, which are subsumed under the aspect of the direct object of cognition (*sākṣātālambananimitta*)—and is comprised within the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).

However, when the substance of any contaminated consciousness (referring generally to all eight consciousnesses; Dharmapāla, following Asaṅga, established this as a single part) arises, it always appears as...

The aspects of the object-cause (ālambana) and the subject-cause (ālambaka) appear; [these are the two parts of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), appearing as the two parts of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva)]. It should be understood that the associated mental factors (saṃprayukta-dharma) are likewise.

The aspect that resembles the object of cognition is called the *nimittabhāga* (image division). The aspect that resembles the subject of cognition is called the *darśanabhāga* (seeing division). [This teaching holds that the capacity to resemble is subsumed within the seeing and image divisions.
If the mind and mental factors lacked the aspect resembling the object, they would be unable to cognize their respective objects;

alternatively, each one would have to be able to cognize all things [because its own object would be like others, and others would be like it]. If they lacked the aspect of being a cognizer, they would be like space. Therefore, both [divisions] must necessarily exist.

The self-substance upon which the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) depend is called the "matter" (*vastu*); this is precisely the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). (That is to say, apart from the image and the seeing, there is no separate, distinct, and independent self-substance for these two.

If these two lacked a single common basis, then the image and the seeing would each have to be a separate entity, like the mind and its objects; however, they do not have separate substances, but are merely two functional capacities. Therefore, there must be a separate substantial basis that gives rise to these two functions.

Because this substance exists, it is said that the self-substance of the image and the seeing is called "matter," which is none other than the self-verifying part). This is because the image and the seeing must necessarily have a basis; if this were non-existent, [the following would ensue].

One cannot recollect mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) as one recalls objects previously experienced; for it is impossible to recollect what has never been experienced. Therefore, there must necessarily be three parts:

the object of cognition (the *nimitta-bhāga*, such as a piece of silk cloth), the means of cognition (the *darśana-bhāga*, as explained in the commentary), and the fruit of cognition (the result that fulfills the internal purpose, namely the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga*, like the wisdom that understands a number).

Since the means of cognition would otherwise have no fruit, what benefit would there be in cognizing an object? This distinction applies equally to the categories of mind and its objects. If one analyzes this further...

There is a fourth [aspect], the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). If this did not exist, what would cognize the third [aspect]? Since the mental portions are identical in nature, they should all be capable of cognition. (The formal argument is as follows:

The third aspect must have a cognizer, because it is subsumed under the category of mental aspects, just like the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*); yet, while the seeing aspect and its object are incapable of self-illumination, this [third aspect] lacks such a capacity).

Furthermore, the self-cognizing portion would lack a result (*phala*), for every means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily have a result. (The seeing aspect is the means of cognition, and the third aspect is the result; the third aspect serves as the cognizer...)

[Question: Whom do you establish as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*)? [Response: The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is sometimes not valid cognition; it cannot be the third fruit. (Fearing that one might attempt to rescue the position by claiming the seeing-part is the third fruit, this is refuted as follows. That which realizes its own essence must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

(This concludes that the essence of consciousness, when self-reflexively perceiving, always realizes its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as the fruit, and this too is exclusively direct perception. Since the seeing-part perceives the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it may be either valid or non-valid;

therefore, one should not say that the seeing-part is the fruit. A factor that is not a valid cognition cannot be the fruit of direct perception. Furthermore, it is impossible for the seeing-part to perceive the object-part such that it would be an inference (*anumāna*) or non-valid cognition, while conversely perceiving the self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) and being admitted as direct perception.)

Objection: If the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its condition to constitute either valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), and if self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is invariably taken as the fruit of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), what prevents [the claim that] self-cognition, as direct perception, can also be the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that inference (*anumāna*) or non-valid cognition may likewise be the fruit?

Response: Direct perception cognizes its own essence; inference and non-valid cognition may be the fruits, but only direct perception and inference [can be the means], not the two together. Since [inference and non-valid cognition] do not cognize the essence, how could they serve as the fruit of direct perception? If the fruit of direct perception were the fruit of inference, then inference would not be the fruit of direct perception. The same applies to the question and answer regarding inference. Now, as for the cognition of one's own essence:

Since it must be subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one cannot say that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object, nor can it be said that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) serves as the fruit of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*). This is because the seeing-part cannot be perceived [by itself], and because within a single moment it would be contradictory for it to be both valid and non-valid cognition simultaneously.

Even if one were to grant that the seeing-part is either inference (*anumāna*) or non-valid cognition as a third fruit, this too is indeterminate; therefore, the meaning of direct perception as the fruit is established as definitive. Within a single mind, because they are contradictory, it is impossible for it to be established as either valid or non-valid cognition.

Thus, the fourth position is established, just as before. Among these four parts, the first two are external and the latter two are internal. (This explains the seeing-part: if at times it is direct perception, it should face the difficulty of being the second fruit. However...)

Because the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) appears as if it were external and manifests as external, it is called "external"; however, its essence is not external. Therefore, this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not take the latter three [aspects] as its object; these latter three are called "internal" because their essence is internal and they take the internal as their object. Among these, the first [aspect] is exclusively the object (*ālambana*), while the latter three are both [subject and object].
That is to say, the second takes the first as its object, the third takes the second and fourth as its objects, and the fourth takes the third as its object.

Thus, the four aspects of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) together constitute a complete structure of both subject and object, without the fault of infinite regress. They are neither identical nor separate; this is the nature of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

The principle is established. Question: According to the meaning of the preceding text, all [Vinaya schools] possess four divisions (*caturvarga*). How is it that the current commentary contains references to "three" or "two"?

The Master [Zhi] does not establish four divisions. The various masters of India each have their own reasoning; furthermore, all conditioned mental factors (*caitta*) are merely false conceptualizations (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
When one traces them back to their ultimate source, they are but the single *tathāgatagarbha*-mind. For this reason, the present commentary does not definitively fix upon a specific number.

Furthermore, since they are not mutually exclusive, it is said that "four, three, or two. Thus, that treatise follows this by stating: "Alternatively, they may be subsumed into three, because the four are included within the three;
