or they may be subsumed into one, because their essence is non-distinct. The present [text] abbreviates this by means of the principle of their single essence.
This is precisely the true mind. If one discusses the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), there must necessarily be the subject and the object; therefore, it cannot be a single unity.

Master Sthiramati belonged to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, which takes the eight consciousnesses as the foundation of all phenomena; thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality, he speaks of only one portion.

Because it is taught that apart from the eight consciousnesses there is no separate true mind (*tathatā-citta*), five types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) are briefly categorized into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding their existence or non-existence: 1. Pervasive but not conceptualizing: This refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). It pervasively takes the three objects as its domain, yet does not engage in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). It also includes the untainted (*anāsrava*) aspect of the eight types of conceptualization. 2. Conceptualizing but not pervasive: This refers to... [the second permutation]... which is the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). It constantly conceptualizes the eighth consciousness as a self and its possessions, yet its objective range is not all-encompassing. It also includes the tainted (*sāsrava*) aspect of the eight types of conceptualization.

3. Both pervasive and conceptualizing: This refers to the first six consciousnesses. They take all objects as their domain and are characterized by conceptual construction. They also include the eight types of conceptualization. 4. Neither pervasive nor conceptualizing: This refers to the five sense-consciousnesses when they are in a state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), such as during the initial moments of perception or in the absence of mental engagement. It also includes the untainted aspect of the eight types of conceptualization. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the second permutation.)
1. The seven consciousnesses arise by taking only the ālayavijñāna as their object and generating conceptualization. 2. That which is both pervasive and conceptualizing is the sixth consciousness;

it takes all things as its object and gives rise to discursive calculation. 3. That which is neither pervasive nor conceptualizing consists of the five evolving consciousnesses; they take only the five sensory objects as their objects.
Because there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the presence or absence of the six root afflictions among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): within the root afflictions, all six are both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).

Those that are conceptually constructed are abandoned at the initial stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); as for those that are innate, they are removed only by the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). As for the secondary...
The twenty delusions also pertain to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*) types, as they arise through the power of the fundamental delusions.

For this reason, they also pertain to both what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). As for the statement that "the entirety of the eighth [consciousness] is absent," it refers to the section on the nature and concomitants of the first transformative consciousness in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Most of it is non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because it obscures defiled phenomena and obstructs the Noble Path; since this consciousness is not defiled, [it is not included].
"Without afflictions. Regarding the phrase "all are present" in the sixth [section] of the Commentary: this is the broadest interpretation.

It is because its objects of perception are universal, because it pervades all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and because it fully possesses the six categories of mental factors (*caitta*). This will be explained in detail below. Regarding the "four innate afflictions" mentioned in the Commentary:

since this is the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), [it is as previously noted]—in Sanskrit, *kliṣṭam manaḥ*, which is translated here as "defiled mind. The verse states: "The four afflictions are always present together."
The *Śāstra* states: "In this context, the word 'together' (*saha*) signifies the meaning of association (*samprayoga*).

That is to say, from beginningless time until the transformation of the basis has not yet occurred, this manas functions spontaneously and constantly takes the *ālayavijñāna* as its object, being associated with the four fundamental afflictions—namely, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*) (these four are explained below in the section on mental factors).
Regarding the 'co-emergent three poisons' mentioned in the *Vyākhyā*, they are divided into six when combined."

Because all [consciousnesses] possess spontaneous (*anābhoga*) greed, hatred, and delusion. The *Śāstra* states: "With which consciousnesses are these ten afflictions associated? They are entirely absent in the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The manas-consciousness possesses four; the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses all ten; the five sensory consciousnesses possess only three—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion—because they lack conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*).

Pride and the others arise from weighing and so forth" (the meaning of this will be explained below). The commentary notes that the number and function of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are the same.

As for their distinctions: the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) have, in general, the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) as their essence, while the afflictions (*kleśa*) have, in general, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) as their essence.

Furthermore, the objects of knowledge only obstruct the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) but do not produce birth and death (*saṃsāra*); the afflictions, however, both obstruct the noble path and produce birth and death.

Moreover, the objects of knowledge only obstruct the noble path of the Mahāyāna, whereas the afflictions universally obstruct the noble paths of all three vehicles (*triyāna*). Regarding their numerical equality:

Although the number of innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) [afflictions] is the same, their names differ slightly. Regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), one should say "attachment to phenomena" (*dharmarāga*), "aversion to phenomena" (*dharma-dveṣa*), and so forth, up to "view-grasping of phenomena" (*dharma-dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and "precept-and-vow grasping of phenomena" (*dharma-śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The twenty [secondary afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth should be called "anger toward phenomena" (*dharmakrodha*) and so on.
This can be understood from among the seven types of karma. Regarding the eight types of retribution, as for what is meant by "general and specific," the treatise states:

"The ripening habitual tendencies act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to induce the eighth consciousness; conversely, the power of projective karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) induces the first six consciousnesses, because they recompense the power of completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*)."
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "A single karma draws forth one birth; multiple karmas can bring it to completion. The commentary explains:

Among the six [consciousnesses], only the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) minds and mental factors of the six consciousnesses are termed "distinct retribution" (*vipāka*), because they follow the specific faculties drawn forth by prior karma.
Consequently, the wholesome and unwholesome states of these six consciousnesses arise according to present conditions and are therefore not termed "retribution."

Regarding the phrase "among the nine mental factors, the dharma-factor always arises in dependence upon the mind," this is from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Briefly, the general name "mental factor" (*caitta*) is explained through three meanings.

The first sentence generally reveals that mental factors arise in dependence upon the mind; if the mind were absent, they would certainly not arise, as they require the mind as their basis to be produced.
This thus excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for the unconditioned does not arise in dependence upon the mind.

It is not a mental factor (*caitta*). Question: If mental factors are defined as those that arise depending solely upon the mind, then matter (*rūpa*) and the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) would also have to be called mental factors, since they too arise depending upon the mind.
The answer in the following phrase is: "Because they are associated with the mind" (*cittasaṃprayuktatvāt*). Now, as for the meaning of "mental factor":
They are associated with the mind, but matter (rūpa) is not. Although it arises in dependence upon the mind, because it is not associated with the mind, it is not a mental factor (caitta).
Question: If they are called mental factors by virtue of being associated [with the mind], then since the mind is also associated with those factors, the mind itself should be called a mental factor.
Answer: Because they are bound to the mind. That is to say, although the mind-king (citta-rāja) is associated with mental factors, it is not...
Because they are bound to the mind (*citta*), they are not called "mental factors" (*caitta*). It is said that because these mental factors are bound to the mind, [they are so named].

(This clarifies that the name "mental factor" arises from these three meanings; thus, the other four groups are not called mental factors. Just as things belonging to a self are designated as "mine" (*ātmīya*), [so too are these]. (The above explains the meaning of "mental factor"; this explains the etymology of the term:

the six categories, such as the universal (*sarvatraga*) and so forth, are the possessions of the mind, hence they are called "mental concomitants" [*cittasamprayukta*]). Regarding the note "the mind apprehends the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)": it means that the mind merely grasps the general aspect of the object.

It merely grasps the whole and does not engage in further discrimination. For example, when one says "perceiving blue," it simply grasps the blue as a whole without further differentiation (because this is the primary function;

if it were to grasp particulars, it would then be a mental factor). As for the perception of the whole, it is like a magistrate, whereas mental factors are like subordinate officials such as district magistrates and the like, because they grasp both general and specific characteristics within that [primary cognition].
Question: Why does the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) take only the general [object], while the mental factors (*caitta*) take both the general and the particular?

The treatise answers next: "Because they assist in accomplishing the work of the mind, they receive the name 'mental factors'. This is followed by the commentary cited therein: "It is like a master painter and his apprentice making a draft and filling it with colors.

The explanation says: Because they assist in accomplishing the work of the mind, they are also mental factors; just as the master makes the draft to delineate the form, so too does the disciple fill it in.

Color. Color is applied according to a mold; because it does not depart from the mold, it is like grasping the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). When applying color, one causes it to appear beautiful; this is like grasping the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The same applies to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) grasping their objects. The treatise says: "Apart from the mental factors, names and meanings have no correspondence;
yet there are six categories of distinctions. Namely, the universal [factors] (five) are present in all minds. It is fixed.

Because they can be obtained. (That is to say, regardless of what the mind is, as long as it arises, [the five] specific objects necessarily arise. They are called "specific objects" because they obtain their arising by taking distinct and individual objects as conditions. ("Specific" refers to the object;

alternatively, "specific" means that the five [mental factors] are mutually regarded as objects, which are thus the objective supports). The wholesome [eleven] can only arise within a wholesome state of mind.

(These possess a nature of benefit both in this world and the next, are free from defilement and corruption, and surpass unwholesome dharmas; therefore, they are named "wholesome"). The afflictions [six] are by nature subsumed under the root afflictions. (They are able to give rise to the secondary afflictions).

The twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are exclusively of the nature of outflows from the primary afflictions (*kleśa-niṣyanda*), because they arise following the substance [of the primary afflictions]. (Regarding "following the substance," this means they are the outflows of the root [afflictions]. "Outflow" (*niṣyanda*) has the meaning of being induced by a similar type; it does not refer to sequential outflows.

The four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) are so called because they are all indeterminate with respect to the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth (that is, they are indeterminate within the minds of the three natures).

This distinguishes them from those mental factors that are exclusively defiled. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes those that do not arise in all minds and do not exist in all stages. These two categories respectively distinguish the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors. These six mental factors take as their essence the concomitance (*samprayoga*) with the mental king (*citta-rāja*) at the same time.

Regarding their nature (*svabhāva*), yoga consists of six factors which are condensed into five, because both the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are equally defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

Furthermore, distinctions are established by means of four "all-inclusives" (*sarvatraga*): namely, nature (*svabhāva*), stage (*bhūmi*), time (*kāla*), and association (*samprayoga*). As for nature, they arise in all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). As for stage, they may pertain to the three realms (*tridhātu*) and nine stages (*navabhūmi*), or to the three stages such as those with discursive thought (*savitarka*, etc.). The latter interpretation is superior, because pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is not universal across all stages.

As for time, they exist whenever there is a mind—whether it be uninterrupted (*anivṛta*) or otherwise—or when they take all objects as their domain; thus, they are collectively termed "time. According to the *Bai-fa-shu* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas), "time" refers to the fact that all mental factors (*caitasika*) share the same temporal locus.

They arise at the same moment; that is, they all coexist, because they are necessarily co-arising. According to the *Bai fa shu* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas), those that coexist with the three [mental factors] pervade the eight consciousnesses; among the five categories, the universal factors possess the four object-specific factors.

The first two [types of non-informative matter] (due to not being continuous, etc., they lack "time"; because they do not necessarily arise simultaneously, they lack "co-existence") are wholesome factors belonging solely to their respective stages (*bhūmi*)—[namely, *vitarka* and so forth belong to three stages]. Defiled factors are entirely absent [from them].

This is stated according to the majority of cases, such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*rāga*), which pervade the nine stages across the three realms. The indeterminate [factors] consist solely of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The eighth section of the *Śāstra* (Commentary) concerns the five so-called "universal" (*sarvatraga*) mental factors. The verse of the *Treatise* states: "Always associated with touch, attention, feeling, perception, and volition.
(Regarding the *Dharmadharmatāvibhaṅga*, it says that among the one hundred dharmas, attention is primary; this is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. This refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

From beginningless time until the stage where karma and its results have not yet been transformed, it is always associated with these five mental factors. Because they are universal mental factors, they are present at all times.

Because it is inclusive. "Contact" (*sparśa*) refers to the conjunction of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness. (The distinct entities of faculty, object, and consciousness are termed "conjunction" when they do not oppose one another but rather interact.

For instance, if consciousness does not arise while the faculty and object are present, this is called opposition. Furthermore, the triad of the ear-faculty, eye-consciousness, and the object of odor are opposed; they do not conjoin or harmonize. If they are mutually compatible, these three necessarily arise together.

Since they are not contradictory, it is called "conjunction. The faculty can serve as a support and the object can serve as an apprehended [object]. That which is produced by these two depends upon the faculty to apprehend the object. This interaction constitutes the nature of the three entities. It causes the mind and mental factors to contact their objects.

Its nature is [the state of] being a basis. Its function is to serve as the support for sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth. Contact (*sparśa*) arises depending upon them (those three); it causes them to be in conjunction, and is therefore called their "basis.

For two reasons, it is simply termed the "conjunction of the three": first, contact arises based on the conjunction of the three; second, it contains the three harmonies and is thus the singular fruit of their union. Question: Since the object resides in the future, the sense faculty abides in the past, and consciousness dwells in the present, how can there be a conjunction?

Answer: Each acts in mutual accordance with the others—serving as the basis, serving as the object of apprehension, and being produced by both. This is precisely what is called the "conjunction of the three. How could it be that the three must actually meet and abide in a single location to be termed a "conjunction"? [The term] *saṃnipāta* (conjunction) means one.
That which causes all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to encounter their respective objects is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of contact (*sparśa*).

Since it functions as the basis for the arising of mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*), its activity (*karma*) consists in serving as the support for them. Mental attention (*manasikāra*) is defined as that which can awaken the seeds of the mind that are due to arise, drawing them toward their objects;

therefore, it is called "mental attention. (That is to say, regarding [the phrase] "mental attention and so forth" [referring to the state before they have arisen]: the meaning of the seed of mental attention is that it awakens the seeds of the mind that are about to arise, enabling them to proceed toward their objects. It does not awaken [seeds that are already active].)

It is the seed of all minds. Because it does not necessarily arise when its conditions are not favorable, attention (*manasikāra*) has two functions for awakening the mind: first, to cause the mind that has not yet arisen to arise; second, to cause the mind that has already arisen to engage with its object.

Therefore, it is said that it awakens the seeds of the mind that ought to arise and leads them to engage with their objects. Thus, the masters of the *Nyāya* school state that the function of attention lies in its arising in the future; this is also true in terms of the meaning and force regarding the seed. It is called "attention" because it moves the mind. Feeling (*vedanā*) means experiencing.

Its nature consists of the aspects of objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neither (i.e., neither disagreeable nor agreeable). Its function is to give rise to craving. It is capable of producing attachment or aversion.

It is because there is no desire for duality. (That is to say, regarding pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), there is the desire to obtain what has not yet been obtained and the desire that what has already been obtained shall not be separated from; regarding painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*), there is the desire not to encounter what has not yet been obtained and the desire to be separated from what has already been obtained.

"Desire" (*tṛṣṇā*) refers to longing and seeking, which thus pervades all three moral natures (*tri-śīla*). This karma can pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); here, however, it is explained solely in terms of the feeling produced by contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*), and this is strictly love (*tṛṣṇā*) based on its defiled aspect.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) has the nature of grasping the image of an object. Its function is to establish various conventional designations (*nāma-paññatti*). That is to say, one must first establish the distinctions of the object.

Only when this limit is established can various conventional designations subsequently arise. (In this context, "establishing" and "apprehending an image" are synonymous; that is to say, "this is blue, not non-blue," and so forth. It is based upon this limit [that such designations occur].)

Grasping at the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is called "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*). Because one grasps these characteristics, verbal designations (*nāma-pada*) arise. Since these categories such as "blue" and so forth are manifold, they are termed "various" (*vicitra*). When various treatises state that "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is its name, this is said from the perspective of the cause;

conversely, saying "perception" is the name is said from the perspective of the effect. This is like what people in the world say: "What is your perception? or "What is your name? This karma is exclusively the perception associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because perceptions associated with the other consciousnesses do not give rise to verbal designations.

There is no fault in using the term "arising" even for those [perceptions] that are remote. How then can the eighth consciousness give rise to names? For this reason, this karma is not pervasive. "Volition" (*cetanā*) has the nature of causing the mind to engage in activity regarding what is wholesome or unwholesome.

Taking the mental factors (*caitta*) as their objects is their function. (This may be understood. Since these five are subsumed under the category of universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), they do not necessarily correspond with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

This is because when the [storehouse] mind does not arise, not even one of these five occurs. Although these five differ from the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), they are simultaneous—being fixed, complete, and occurring in a single moment—and thus share the same basis (*āśraya*).

(The "basis" refers to the sense faculty; that is, they are co-existent and immediate bases, which will be explained below. They do not take seeds as their basis, because those are distinct. They are called "same" because they rely on a single, fixed basis at the same time.)

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by" (*pratyaya*): here, the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is designated as the mode of activity (*ākāra*), while the aspect of the image (*nimitta-bhāga*) is designated as the object-condition (*ālambana*). The term "entity" (*vastu*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The word "etc. (*ādi*) signifies similarity; since the individual entities of the various aspects are each restricted to a single objective sphere and are similar in their characteristics, the objects of these entities are all termed "equal" (*sama*).

This is because the five [mental factors] such as contact (*sparśa*) arise based on the production of a substantial form; since their objects of cognition are thus similar, they are called "equal. In the context of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), the term "object-condition" is not applied to the primary substance (*bimba*). This is also like how the image itself is termed the "mode of activity."

Based on these four meanings, it is said that [the mind] is associated (*saṃprayukta*). Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because of the fourfold equality, it is called 'associated. Furthermore, each of these has its own specific exclusion: "time" excludes what precedes or follows; "basis" excludes distinct consciousnesses;

"object" excludes distinct aspects (*ākāra*); and "matter" excludes the discerning [mental factors]. How could this consciousness not be associated with mental factors such as those of the "distinct sphere" (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*)? (The following explains why it is not associated with others. Because they are mutually contradictory.

(This is the general answer. The following is the specific answer: That is to say, desire (*chanda*) functions by aspiring toward a desired object; whenever there is an object in any world that is pleasant, desire arises. This consciousness, however, is... [text ends]

*Manasikāra* (attention) functions by being free from expectation regarding objects (i.e., not viewing the object with longing). *Adhimokṣa* (resolute determination) functions by determining and holding a specific object (i.e., it holds an object previously subject to doubt, now attaining the seal of certainty).
This consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is obscure and lacks such holding [of certainty]. (It is not that it was previously indeterminate and must now be determined.

*Smṛti* (mindfulness) functions solely by clearly recollecting things previously experienced. This consciousness is dull and inferior, unable to recollect clearly. (It constantly takes as its object spontaneously present phenomena; it cannot clearly recollect objects previously experienced. Therefore, it possesses no mindfulness. *Samādhi* (concentration)...

It merely causes the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object. (Although the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of meditative concentration arises anew at every moment, when one applies the preparatory effort (*prayoga*), the fundamental reality (*maulika-svabhāva*) being contemplated continues as a prior-and-subsequent succession;

one constantly focuses the attention upon it. This consciousness spontaneously (*svarasena*) perceives different objects from moment to moment. (Spontaneously, without applying preparatory effort, it focuses on the fundamental reality and constantly takes the present as its object. The perceived image (*pratibimba-ālambana*) arises only anew at each moment.)

Furthermore, regarding the aspect of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): in each and every moment, it deeply grasps and focuses upon its object (*ālambana*). This consciousness is superficial and unstable; its aspect of activity (*ākāra*) is not so [as that of concentration]. Therefore, the term "concomitant with concentration" refers to what occurs spontaneously—that is, that which follows the bonds of karma.

Wisdom (*prajñā*), by contrast, functions solely as the virtue of discernment (and so forth, including its faults and neutral states). This consciousness is subtle and obscure, incapable of such discernment; thus, it is not associated with the specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).

(This is the summary. Below, it distinguishes it from the wholesome and so forth: Because this consciousness is exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), [it is] necessarily not [wholesome or unwholesome].

Because it pervades both the wholesome and the defiled: the eleven wholesome [factors], the six defiled [factors], and the twenty [others]. (The term "etc. includes the remaining wholesome and other factors, namely the four indeterminate ones; since it pervades all three natures, they are also included therein. It is also dissociated. (This concludes the summary. Question:

Why are the neutral factors among the indeterminate not associated with this consciousness? Therefore, the following answer is given: As for the four neutral factors such as regret (*kaukṛtya*), because they are intermittent, they are certainly not maturation (*vipāka*).

(It is not that they are not directly maturation, nor does it exclude the "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*); however, even those born of maturation include regret and so forth, as they do not persist in constant continuity at all times.)
Upon reaching the stage of untaintedness (*anāsrava*), it is associated with twenty-one mental factors. As the treatise states below:

"However, the eighth consciousness has two general stages: first, the tainted stage, which is subsumed under the neutral nature (*avyākṛta*) and is associated only with five factors—contact (*sparśa*) and so forth—and takes as its objects only the previously mentioned realms of appropriation and the environment.

(This refers to the stage of neutral maturation (*vipāka*) prior to the ten stages of the Bodhisattvas and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the Two Vehicles. Although this is the case in the stage of no-more-learning..."

All karma has already been severed because it was summoned by prior karma; thus, the momentum of past karma is also termed "maturation" (*vipāka*). It is associated only with the five [mental factors] such as contact (*sparśa*), and takes as its object only the aforementioned appropriated root-body (*indriya-śarīra*) and the seeds within their locations.

Second, the untainted state (*anāsrava-avasthā*) is comprised exclusively of Bodhisattvas. (This pertains only to the stage of the Tathāgata, not to Bodhisattvas or the two vehicles, because their fruits are not yet perfected and their qualities are inferior, and because they have not yet attained the four wisdoms.

This untainted state belongs only to the Tathāgata, for the Tathāgata possesses no maturation-dharma, as his body is not summoned by karma or afflictions. It is associated with twenty-one mental concomitants (*caitta). (This is stated by combining both the provisional and the real. If...)

In reality, there are only eighteen [mental factors], because the three—equanimity (*upekṣā*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)—are all nominal (*prajñapti*). That is to say: five universal factors, five object-specific factors, and eleven wholesome factors.
Because it is always associated with all minds (the universal mental factors); because it constantly delights in realizing and knowing the objects of observation (therefore there is desire);
because it constantly maintains the objects of observation (therefore there is resolve); because it constantly and clearly remembers previously experienced objects (mindfulness);
because the Blessed One has no unconcentrated mind (concentration); because he constantly discriminates all phenomena (wisdom); and because of his supreme pure faith.

Because they are always associated [with the mind] (the eleven wholesome factors); because they are non-defiled (there are no roots or secondary afflictions); and because they are free from distraction (there are no four unconcentrated states).

The Commentary on the Seven [Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī] states that there are eighteen [mental factors]. Regarding the phrase "the five universal, etc.," the final correct doctrine of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:

(That treatise first recounts the various masters’ views—some saying that these mental factors associated with the manas number nine, some fifteen, some nineteen, or some twenty-four—and refutes all of them as irrational; they are not recounted here. Only the final correct doctrine is recounted: However, the mental factors associated with this manas are eighteen.

That is to say, the aforementioned nine dharmas (namely, the five universal and the four afflictions; these are referred to as "the aforementioned" because they were last recounted in that treatise), plus eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

The afflictions (*kleśa*), along with the discernment (*prajñā*) among the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*), and the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*) have already been explained above.

Regarding the absence of the first four among the object-specific factors, it will be discussed below in the section explaining the term "discernment" (*prajñā*). Regarding the absence of the eleven wholesome factors, because the wholesome is pure (*śubha*), it does not coexist with this consciousness (as this consciousness is exclusively defiled).
As for the "four afflictions," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: "Namely, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and self-pride (*ātma-māna*)."

The *ātmasneha* (self-love). From beginningless time until the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) has not yet occurred, this *manas* spontaneously and constantly takes the *ālayavijñāna* as its object.
It is associated with the four fundamental afflictions. *Ātmamoha* (self-delusion) refers to ignorance that is deluded regarding the characteristics of a self;

it is confused about the principle of non-self (*anātman*). [The treatises cited here are all abbreviated from their original texts. *Ātmadṛṣṭi* (self-view) refers to the false conceptualization of a self within phenomena that are not the self (also termed *ātma-grāha*, self-clinging). *Ātmamāna* (self-pride) refers to... [dwelling]...
Relying upon and being arrogant toward the self that one clings to causes the mind to become uplifted; as for "self-love," it arises as an attachment toward that very self one clings to.

The "one who is defiled" (also called the self)—as explained in detail regarding the meaning of these names in the sixth fundamental section—these four arise constantly, agitating and turbidifying the internal mind and causing the external evolving consciousnesses to perpetually become defiled;
therefore, they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*). There are ten types of them; why are there only four here?

Because when the view of a self exists, other views do not arise, as two forms of wisdom cannot coexist within a single moment of mind. (This is the general answer. The two graspings (the grasping at views and the grasping at precepts and observances) are false.

The view [of self] arises solely from discrimination; it is abandoned only by vision (*darśana-heya*). The afflictions associated with this [view] are exclusively innate (*sahaja*), as they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The view of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) arise dependent upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); however, the views associated with this [consciousness] do not arise dependent upon them, because [this consciousness] constantly clings to an internal self.

There must first be the view of self [for the others to follow]. The view of "mine" and the view of extremes arise subsequent to the view of self; these views associated with this consciousness do not arise dependent upon that [view of self], as they spontaneously take the internal continuum as their object.

[It] arises [without depending on others]. Because doubt cannot arise when there is decisive certainty through vision, and because hatred cannot arise when there is a sense of "I" regarding craving, only four afflictions are associated with this consciousness.
(This concludes the summary. Question: The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that greed causes the mind to sink, while pride causes the mind to be uplifted.

How can they arise simultaneously? The answer is that there are four reasons why they do not coexist: 1. If they were distinct entities (*bhāga*), they could not coexist; however, since they are co-arisen (*sahaja*), their simultaneous arising is possible.
2. When directed toward external objects, they do not coexist; when directed toward the self, they arise together. 3. Because the object of disparagement and the object of reliance differ:
if pride arises by disparaging another, craving certainly does not arise [toward them]. If pride arises from relying on oneself, the mind is necessarily uplifted. 4. Craving is coarse and violent.
Pride does not coexist with subtlety; it can arise together with what is obtainable.
Regarding the "eight concomitants" mentioned in the commentary, I have recorded them as a private note, though their names were not yet complete. The complete list consists of:

torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and lack of correct awareness (*asamprajanya*). These eight are universally associated with all defiled minds.

Because it is so. When afflictions arise, the mind is already defiled; therefore, in the state of a defiled mind, it necessarily arises in association with the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

(The above is a summary of the treatise, presented out of order; these points were clarified section by section to refute the doctrines of various masters rather than being taught in a single location.

The meanings of the names of these eight are all explained below. "No other secondary afflictions" refers to those whose modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse, such as the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*).

"Moving. Because this consciousness is subtle and discerning, it does not coexist with those [afflictions]. Shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), whereas this consciousness is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

therefore, it is not associated with them. Regarding the phrase "including wisdom (*prajñā*)": this refers to wisdom among the "object-specific" (*viṣaya-viniyata*) mental factors. Question: Is wisdom identical to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*)?

Why is it explained separately? Answer: Although the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is subsumed under the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) as a specifically determined object, it is distinguished as two separate factors because there is a difference in their meaning among the fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*). Question: Why are the other four [mental factors] not included? Answer:

"Desire" (*chanda*) is the longing for an object that has not yet been attained (that which is desired is called an "unattained object"). This consciousness, however, functions spontaneously (*svarasena*) by taking as its object that which is already attained (since it is always "I"), and thus it has nothing to long for.

*Āśā* (aspiration). Resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) maintains an object that has never been previously determined; (it arises precisely from the aforementioned state of doubt and non-comprehension).

This consciousness, however, from beginningless time, takes only determined objects as its domain and possesses nothing to maintain through resolute conviction. (This is because it is always determinately conceiving "this is the self and not another," and it only establishes its conviction after first having experienced doubt and non-comprehension.

*Smṛti* (mindfulness). It is solely the recollection of things previously experienced. (The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Mindfulness arises only with respect to things with which one is familiar. This consciousness, however, takes only present, perceived objects as its domain and lacks [recollection].

That which is remembered is focused exclusively on a single object (a distinct mental application binds the mind to a single object; by means of the preparatory mind, one seeks a single object, taking only the essential nature of a single phenomenon as the focal point).

It does not involve the conceptualization of distinct objects across preceding and succeeding moments, nor is it a permanent cognition. This consciousness functions spontaneously; because it takes distinct objects moment by moment and is not focused on a single thing, it lacks concentration (*samādhi*).

[This is so] unless one pursues a goal deeply, focusing exclusively on a single phenomenon, which constitutes momentary distinctness. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Concentration arises only with respect to the object under investigation; that which functions spontaneously lacks this concentration. Question: Why are the four factors of non-concentration (*asamāhitabhūmika-dharma*) absent here?
Answer: Regarding remorse (*kaukṛtya*), it is the regret for actions previously committed. This consciousness, however, functions spontaneously and constantly takes these as its object.

Manifest objects do not arise from remorse for past karma, nor from sleep. Sleep necessarily depends on the heavy dullness of body and mind and the power of external conditions; it may occasionally arise briefly.

This consciousness, however, has been of a single class of internal grasping since beginningless time and does not depend on external conditions. (If sleep arises, it must depend on the body and mind; how much more so in the case of heavy, profound slumber.)

This is the internal condition. As for the power of external conditions, such as the onset of illness or a cool breeze, these may arise momentarily and then immediately cease; they do not possess the quality of continuity.

Vitarka (initial inquiry) and vicāra (sustained investigation) both operate through the external gate, involving shallow or deep deliberation and coarse or subtle verbal expression. This consciousness, however, relies solely on the internal gate, being of a single type that clings to a self.

(The two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra both arise based on external objects; because these two primarily function through the gates of body and speech, vitarka involves shallow investigation while vicāra involves deep investigation. Vitarka produces coarse speech, whereas vicāra produces subtle speech.

This consciousness, however, relies solely on the internal gate and arises based on an internal self; thus, one class [of beings] clings to a self. Because it lacks shallow or deep investigation and the production of coarse or subtle speech, it does not coexist with those [two]. Therefore, all [these] are without self (conclusion).

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Commentary), "All six possess [them]," this means they possess all fifty-one [mental factors]. The universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) mental factors have their modes of activity (*ākāra*) as explained above.

Next are the wholesome (*kuśala*) factors, which number eleven (because they are conducive to benefit in both this life and future lives). The verse says: Wholesome refers to faith (*śraddhā*)—[which is] because of deep conviction (*kṣānti*), desire (*chanda*), and aspiration toward the principles of the Truths (*satya*), the true virtues of the Three Jewels (*ratna*), and the mundane and supramundane efficacies;

it is the purification of the mind. Shame (*hrī*)—[which is] revering and honoring the noble and good. Remorse (*apatrāpya*)—[which is] slighting and rejecting the violent and evil. Non-attachment (*alobha*)—[which is] being without clinging toward existence (*bhava*) and the requisites of existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*).

[The three roots: equanimity (which includes non-aversion and non-delusion; "non-aversion" refers to the absence of resentment toward suffering and the causes of suffering; "non-delusion" refers to clear understanding regarding all principles and phenomena). [Summary: The three roots. Diligence (*vīrya*; vigor; courageous perseverance in the tasks of cultivating the wholesome and abandoning the unwholesome).

Tranquility (*praśrabdhi*; pliancy; freedom from heaviness and rigidity; the body and mind become harmonious, supple, and capable). [The eight factors above are distinct functions of the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*); the following three are conventional (*prajñapti*), as they lack a separate substantial entity. Non-negligence (*apramāda*; this consists of diligence and the three roots;

it is able to guard against and cultivate what is to be abandoned and cultivated). Equanimity (*upekṣā*; this consists of the four aforementioned factors; it causes the mind to abide in a state of evenness, rectitude, and effortlessness). And non-harming (*avihiṃsā*; toward all sentient beings...).

[It] does not cause harm or affliction, and its nature is non-hatred (*adveṣa*). There are six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*); because their nature is subsumed under the roots, they receive the name "afflictions. The verse says: Afflictions are: greed (*rāga*) [which is attachment to existence and the means of existence];

hatred (*dveṣa*) [which is resentment toward suffering and the means of suffering]; delusion (*moha*) [which is confusion and darkness regarding all principles and phenomena]; pride (*māna*) [which is relying on oneself and being haughty, overbearing, and contemptuous toward others]; doubt (*vicikitsā*) [which is hesitation regarding the principles of the truths];

and wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) [which is inverted speculation regarding the principles of the truths]. This view has five distinctions: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which grasps at a self or what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). Second...

Extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consist of adhering to either annihilationism or eternalism regarding those same objects. The three types of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) involve the denial of cause, effect, function, and substantial reality, as well as other erroneous attachments. The four types of dogmatic attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consist of grasping at various views and their underlying aggregates (*skandha*) as being supreme and capable of bringing about purification.

The fifth, attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), consists of grasping at various views, precepts, and ascetic observances as being supreme. The twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are merely specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), because they are of the nature of their outflow (*niṣyanda*).

(These too are afflictions, but they are so called only because they follow upon the primary ones. The verse says: Secondary afflictions are said to be anger (*krodha*)—[which is] the outburst of indignation toward a presently manifest object that is disadvantageous.

*Upāyāsa* (resentment): harboring a grudge due to anger. *Nivaraṇa* (concealment): hiding one's own committed misdeeds out of fear that they will damage one’s reputation. *Pradāśa* (malice): pursuing one's own fame and profit, unable to endure the success of others.

*Mātsarya* (miserliness): being attached to wealth and the Dharma, unable to practice generosity. *Māyā* (deception): feigning the possession of virtues in order to gain profit and reputation. *Śāṭhya* (sycophancy): falsely assuming an unusual demeanor in order to deceive others. (*Dā*) [particle used as a grammatical auxiliary]. *Vihiṃsā* (harmfulness): a mind devoid of compassion.

*Āghāta* (malice toward sentient beings), *mada* (intoxication with one’s own prosperity, characterized by deep attachment to it)—these ten arise individually and are therefore called the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

*Ahrī* (lack of shame, disregarding one’s own Dharma and failing to respect the virtuous) and *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread, disregarding the world’s esteem for evil and violence)—these two are universal among the unwholesome and are therefore called the intermediate secondary afflictions. *Auddhatya* (restlessness, causing the mind to be uneven toward its objects) and *styāna* (torpor).

(Lack of mental fitness regarding objects) lack of faith (in reality, virtue, and capability; characterized by a lack of forbearance, delight, and desire, with a defiled mind as its nature), along with laziness (indolence in the cultivation and abandonment of the categories of the wholesome and unwholesome), heedlessness (inability to guard or cultivate the defiled and pure categories;

characterized by dissipation), and loss of mindfulness (inability to clearly remember various objects of focus), distraction (causing the mind to wander among various objects of focus), and lack of correct awareness (misunderstanding the object under observation).

These eight [mental factors] are pervasive throughout all defiled minds and are termed the "great secondary afflictions. The four indeterminate factors are [present] in both the wholesome and the defiled.

Because these are all indeterminate, they are not like contact (*sparśa*) and other factors which are necessarily pervasive of the mind, nor like desire (*chanda*) and other factors which are necessarily pervasive of the ground.

The verse says: "The indeterminate are remorse (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra. (Remorse refers to *kaukṛtya*, meaning that which was previously done badly and is subsequently regretted. Sleep (*middha*; i.e., drowsiness) means the body lacks self-mastery because the mind becomes extremely dull and weak, functioning in a single door [of consciousness].

Vitarka (*vitarka*; seeking) causes the mind and its objects to be hurried; it functions coarsely toward the objects of mental discourse. Vicāra (*vicāra*; examining) is the observation of those same objects; while the former is coarse, this is subtle. The rest is the same. [There are two types: first, remorse and sleep; second...
*Vitarka* and *vicāra* each have two [types] (the latter two types each having both defiled and non-defiled; this is not like the wholesome and defiled [states], which each have only one).
[Commentary, Vol. 5, Section 34b]: This refers to the number of mental factors (*caitta*) within the first five consciousnesses.

"The pervasive, the specific, and the wholesome in their entirety" means that the five pervasive factors, the five specific-object factors, and the eleven wholesome factors are all fully present. [Regarding] the three fundamental afflictions...

These are greed, hatred, and delusion. Regarding the "intermediate" and "great" universal [afflictions] and so forth: there are two intermediate universal afflictions and eight great universal afflictions;
these are all complete. The characteristics and meanings of these thirty-four factors have already been explained above.

However, although the five consciousnesses lack superior aspiration (*chanda*), discerning determination (*adhimokṣa*), clear recollection (*smṛti*), focused concentration (*samādhi*), and selective discrimination (*prajñā*), they nonetheless possess a subtle...

Regarding the five factors such as subtle desire (*parīttakāma*) and so forth: they may be absent when one has not yet attained mastery; however, once the state of mastery is attained, these five are necessarily present.

It should be understood that [the mind] is endowed with the eleven wholesome factors. Among the six fundamental [afflictions], pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*) are absent because they are non-conceptual (*avikalpa*).

Because pride and other such afflictions arise from weighing an object, these ten minor derivative afflictions do not exist [in the five sensory consciousnesses]. This is because these ten are coarse and violent; thus, the characteristics of the medium and great [degrees of affliction] apply to them.
Regarding the statement that the five sensory consciousnesses may or may not possess [these mental factors], making them "indeterminate," the meaning is likewise understandable.

However, the number of mental factors associated with these eight consciousnesses is explained based on the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). If the basis has been transformed, each [consciousness] is associated with twenty-one mental factors.
They are associated [with the categories] as previously explained (i.e., the universal, object-specific, virtuous, and so forth).

Among the ten [mental factors], those that are determinate (*vijñapti*)—meaning they are wholesome or unwholesome and thus can be specifically defined by their results—are eight; those that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are seven, because their basis is subtle.
Therefore, the verse on the ālayavijñāna states that it is "unobscured-neutral" (anivṛtāvyākṛta), while the verse on the manas states that it is "obscured-neutral" (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
As for the six [consciousnesses] being of the three natures, this includes both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Regarding the eleven categories of the provisional and the real: as for why it is said that the eight [consciousnesses] are all substantially existent, it is because each arises from its own seed.

As for the annotation stating that they are all conventionally existent in terms of their nature (*dharmatā*), this is according to the Dharma-nature school (*Faxiang zong*). In this school, the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses are integrated and all return to the *tathāgatagarbha* nature;
since the *garbha*-nature alone is real, the eight [consciousnesses] are all conventional.
Regarding the analysis of the twelve *dhātus* (realms) and *bhūmis* (planes): "realm" (*dhātu*) carries the meanings of cause, support, and division. Here, we take the sense of "division.

This refers to the distinct realms and planes of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). These consist of the desire realm and the eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Specifically:

first, the plane of the five destinies where beings dwell in mixture within the desire realm; second, the plane of joy and bliss born of seclusion; third, the plane of joy and bliss born of concentration; fourth, the plane of the absence of joy... [and so forth].
The Stage of Wondrous Joy; the fifth, the Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness; the sixth, the Stage of the Sphere of Infinite Space;

the seventh, the Stage of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; the eighth, the Stage of the Sphere of Nothingness; and the ninth, the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. "Stage" (bhūmi) carries the meaning of growth and development.

Regarding the meaning of "reliance" (*niśraya*): here we take it in the sense of reliance, not in the sense of growth. The commentary states that the three—eye, ear, and body—pertain to two realms and two stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding these two stages, they comprise two realms: namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) together with a portion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

This is because the form realm contains the term "stage," and these three consciousnesses only pervade the first dhyāna. Therefore, the note says: "The stages are complete, but the realms are incomplete. Question 2:
Question: Do the three consciousnesses arise from the dhyānas upward? Answer: They do arise. Since it is said they arise, how can one say they do not exist? It is simply that they borrow power;

because the causal factors for their own level are absent, they borrow the *vitarka* and *vicāra* of the first dhyāna to induce the three consciousnesses of the second dhyāna, taking the three objects of the higher levels as their cognitive domain.
Question: The six [consciousnesses] of the higher levels are not associated with *vitarka* and *vicāra*. How, then, can they be induced? Answer: Although...
They are not associated [with the mind], but merely borrow its power; thus there is no contradiction. Furthermore, at the initial moment of borrowing, they depend upon vitarka and vicāra;

however, once they have arisen for a long duration, they do not depend on vitarka and vicāra due to the force of habitual cultivation. Question: Upon which bases (āśraya) and faculties (indriya) do these three consciousnesses arise?

Answer: From the second dhyāna upward, the eighth consciousness possesses seeds of the [respective] stages (*bhūmi*). It relies upon the faculties (*indriya*) of the higher stages; thus, there is no fault in the consciousness arising to perceive objects.
This, however, is merely a matter of borrowing power for its function. Regarding the commentary’s statement that the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue belong to one realm and one stage:

because in the higher stages there is no solid food (*kavadīkārāhāra*), there are no objects of smell and taste. Since there are no objects to be perceived, these two [consciousnesses] do not exist there. Question: Since they are absent...
Regarding the five consciousnesses: why are there five sense organs? The answer is that through the power of superior karmic retribution, one brings forth this adorned physical form.
As for the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses, they pervade all three realms and nine stages; this is clearly evident.
Regarding the thirteenth [section], the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*): "taint" (*āsrava*) refers to the active manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because they cause the mind to flow and wander incessantly, and because they extensively damage and defile the locus [of the mind], they are established under the name "taint. A brief explanation is as provided previously.

As for the essence of the three taints, the meaning of the four taints, and the meanings such as "flowing out," "flowing in," and "defiling," these are fully contained within the topical headings in the *Supplemental Volume* (*Pūchüe juàn*). Now...

Furthermore, I shall briefly clarify the meaning that all eight consciousnesses are permeated by both [cognition and wisdom]. This means that for ordinary beings, consciousness is predominant and wisdom is inferior; thus, all eight are with-outflow (*sāsrava*). When the Buddhas transform them, they become the four wisdoms;

the consciousnesses associated with these wisdoms are exclusively without-outflow (*anāsrava*). As for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), when they realize the principle or are in meditative observation, their consciousness is without-outflow;

however, when they emerge from observation and are in a distracted state of mind, it is with-outflow. Regarding the term "transformed consciousness," this refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

The transformation occurs at the stage of the cause; five and eight transform at the stage of the fruit. Regarding transformation at the cause: prior to the [first] bhūmi, all are with outflows (*sāsrava*).

Upon reaching the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the first bhūmi, one is able to sever the two obstacles of conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and realize the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness.

The sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform simultaneously to become the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), both of which are without outflows (*anāsrava*). However, when emerging from meditative observation (*vyutthāna*), they are still with outflows. The second...
From the sixth to the eighth stage, the two types of grasping are forever suppressed; one forever attains the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The seventh stage’s grasping at a self is likewise forever suppressed and extinguished, and the name *ālaya* is relinquished, being called the "maturation-consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*). Regarding the transformation of the fruits of the fifth and eighth:

the eighth is the sovereign of total retribution, for it is able to maintain the seeds of the three realms, the untainted, and the three natures, as well as the tainted faculties and body. At the final moment of the heart of the fulfillment of the tenth stage—

Within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one finally and permanently abandons [the outflows], attaining the wisdom of prajñā, the dharma-body of liberation, and the realm of absolute purity (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
As for the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), it persists until the end of the future. Regarding the first five [consciousnesses]:

because their sense organs (*indriya*) are the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, and because the eighth consciousness is with-outflow (*sāsrava*) during the causal stage, the outflowing sense organs cannot give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) five consciousnesses. Upon reaching the stage of fruition, they [coexist] with the eighth.
At one time, this was transformed into the Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done;
all other meanings, as well as the questions, answers, and resolutions of difficulties, are likewise contained within the supplementary volume.
Regarding the fourteenth [section], the analysis of the bases (*āśraya-vibhaṅga*):

it refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which, by relying upon three bases and depending on nine, eight, or other such conditions, are then able to discern and perform their various functions. This section analyzes the bases; what follows analyzes the conditions (*pratyaya*).
Now, as for the bases upon which they rely, there are generally three types, which are three of the four conditions. To be a condition is broader in scope than to be a base. As for being a base...

Narrow. The inferior conditions depend upon the superior. Briefly stated, there are four conditions: first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

third, the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); and fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Among these four, the object condition corresponds to the "object" among the [subsequent] nine conditions; it is exclusively an object-condition and nothing else.

Regarding the three types of supports (*āśraya*), the commentary explains that as for the support of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*): all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) rely upon this support, because the mind does not arise apart from its own causes and conditions.
However, while causes and conditions encompass both seeds (*bīja*) and active manifestations (*pravṛtti*), this support consists only of seeds and not manifestations;
it may also be called the "seed-support" (*bījāśraya*), because all minds that serve as conditions arise individually from their respective seeds. Some say that the seed perishes.
The production of the manifest result is like that of the seed at the end [of the process]. It should be understood as being like the flame and the wick. Regarding the "predominant" (adhipati):
however, the predominant condition is broad in scope, encompassing both the powerful and the powerless, as well as the favorable and the adverse, because all of these are predominant conditions.

If one says that the basis of the predominant condition consists solely of the internal six sense bases (ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana), then it is only the powerful and the favorable; yet even these may be said to be co-existent (sahabhū).

Regarding the support (*āśraya*): it is said that if consciousness does not arise, that is one thing; but once it arises, the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the consciousness (*vijñāna*) are necessarily simultaneous. There are two types of predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*).
As for the statement "five based on the five faculties, and six, seven, and eight," this refers to the co-existent support (*sahabhv-āśraya*). The number of the eight consciousnesses is not fixed.
The simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the five consciousnesses are invariably fourfold: namely, the five material sense-faculties, and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.

This is because if any one of these is missing, [the five consciousnesses] will certainly not arise. These are assigned respectively as: the objective field (the material sense-faculties), the discerning [consciousness] (the sixth), the defiled and pure [consciousness] (the seventh), and the fundamental [consciousness] (the eighth).
Regarding the note that the sixth depends on the seventh and eighth: the simultaneous supports of the sixth mental consciousness consist of only two types.
This refers to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses; if either one is missing, the other necessarily does not function. Regarding the note on their mutual dependence:
the seventh depends on the eighth, and the eighth depends on the seventh; if either one is missing, neither can function. (The *Manas* verse says: "It depends on that and takes that as its object.
To summarize in verse: "Five, four, six have two [supports]; seven and eight both depend on one. Regarding the commentary on "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*):

This refers to the equal, non-hearing condition (*asamanvāgata-pratyaya*). This condition applies universally to both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). If it is taken as a support (*āśraya*), it is exclusively the sovereign (*rāja*) and not its objects.

It is also called the "opening-and-guiding support" (*unmeṣa-nimitta-āśraya*); that is to say, the cessation of the preceding moment’s mind and mental factors opens the way and guides the arising of the succeeding moment’s mind and mental factors.

(The cessation of the preceding moment’s mind has two meanings: first, the meaning of opening; second, the meaning of guiding. Thus, these eight consciousnesses cease in the former and arise in the latter.
Regardless of the duration of time, when the primary mind itself is separated [from its subsequent state] by its own kind, it is termed an "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*).
All minds and mental factors are equal in their functional efficacy and possess five kinds of superior capacities; they are equal in their association (*samprayoga*).

Although minds and mental factors of different classes arise simultaneously, they correspond with one another, merging in harmony as if they were one. They necessarily arise and perish together, and their activities must be identical.
Because when one [consciousness] opens the way, the others also open the way, they act as *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately antecedent condition) for one another in succession.

Now, when it is said that the "opening and guiding support" (*āśraya*) belongs only to the "kings" (*rāja*) and not to the "retainers," this is stated from the perspective of what is predominant; therefore, one should not harbor doubts. The modes of activity (*ākāra*) of all eight kings are identical.
There is no further meaning [to be derived].

Regarding the fifteen types of consciousness and the number of superior conditions they require, these are assigned according to the verses. Specifically, the single type of visual consciousness arises from nine conditions, as cited in the commentary (*ṭīkā*).
I shall now explain them in sequence; this will make them easier to distinguish and easier to memorize for those who follow. Hereafter...

The factors excluded [from the conditions for visual consciousness] are: first, darkness (because it obstructs seeing); second, light; third, the sense organ (the material faculty); fourth, the object (the material dust);

fifth, attention (a mental factor that alerts and causes the seeds of the mind to arise); sixth, the fundamental [consciousness] (the eighth); seventh, defilement or purity (the seventh); eighth, discrimination (the sixth); ninth, the seeds (the seeds within the eighth).
Among these nine, if even one is lacking, [visual consciousness] will not arise. Regarding the note "excluding light": this refers to auditory consciousness.

Both light and darkness are perceived; therefore, illumination is not required, but rather the eight remaining [elements] within the nine. Regarding the "three sevens": the three types of consciousness—those of the nose, tongue, and body—each have only seven conditions. This excludes space, as these three consciousnesses are all internal cognitive perceptions. Regarding the "three after" and the "five, three, and four": these refer, in order, to the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses. [The text continues: ...the five, three, and four... Next, the six consciousnesses are all called "consciousnesses of the sense bases. The seventh is called the "mind-consciousness," and the eighth is called the "storehouse consciousness. The first five are called "sense-consciousnesses" because they are based on the five physical sense organs. The sixth is called "mind-consciousness" because it takes the mind-organ as its basis. The seventh is called "mind-consciousness" because it is the primary mind. The eighth is called the "storehouse consciousness" because it stores all seeds. It is also called the "root consciousness" because it is the root of all phenomena. It is also called the "appropriating consciousness" because it appropriates the body. It is also called the "defiled mind" because it is always associated with the four afflictions. It is also called the "unmanifested consciousness" because its mode of activity is subtle and difficult to perceive. It is also called the "greatly pervasive consciousness" because it pervades all states of existence. It is also called the "seal of the Dharma" because it is the source of all dharmas. It is also called the "wonderful observation" because it observes the nature of all things. It is also called the "true suchness" because it is the ultimate reality. It is also called the "Buddha-nature" because it is the potential for enlightenment. It is also called the "Tathāgata-garbha" because it contains the essence of the Tathāgata. It is also called the "Dharmakāya" because it is the body of the absolute truth. It is also called the "Vajra-body" because it is indestructible. It is also called the "Body of Wisdom" because it is endowed with perfect wisdom. It is also called the "Body of Bliss" because it is free from all suffering. It is also called the "Body of Eternity" because it is unchanging. It is also called the "Body of Purity" because it is free from all defilements. It is also called the "Body of Self" because it is the true self. It is also called the "Body of Peace" because it is tranquil and serene. It is also called the "Body of Liberation" because it is liberated from all bonds. It is also called the "Body of Omniscience" because it knows all things. It is also called the "Body of All-pervading Light" because its light shines everywhere. It is also called the "Body of Infinite Life" because its life is inexhaustible. It is also called the "Body of Unobstructed Vision" because its vision is unhindered. It is also called the "Body of Unimpeded Hearing" because its hearing is unimpeded. It is also called the "Body of Unobstructed Smell" because its smelling is unobstructed. It is also called the "Body of Unobstructed Taste" because its tasting is unobstructed. It is also called the "Body of Unobstructed Touch" because its touching is unobstructed. It is also called the "Body of Unobstructed Cognition" because its cognition is unobstructed. It is also called the "Body of Non-duality" because it transcends all dualities. It is also called the "Body of Non-conceptualization" because it is free from conceptual thought. It is also called the "Body of Non-attachment" because it is free from attachment. It is also called the "Body of Non-obstruction" because it is unobstructed by anything.
