This gives rise to the wisdom that observes and shatters attachments. The present citation, for its part, exclusively cites the characteristics of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Under the section on the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) in the commentary, it is cited by way of its essential meaning. The full text states: "Great King, the earth element is of two kinds:
internal and external. What is the internal earth element? It refers to whatever is internal to one's own body, possessed, and grasped within each respective body."
Because each respective [body] is distinct from others and not one, they are called "respective. Whatever there is that is acquired or grasped—(grasping means clinging; acquiring means receiving;

it is so called because one clings to and receives it as one's own self, sharing its safety and peril)—that which is solid and firm—(firmness here takes the sense of resistance, for the earth element has solidity and resistance as its intrinsic nature)—namely, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, feces, membranes, placenta, armpits, and so forth: these are called the body.
The internal earth element. What is the external earth element of the body? It refers to all that exists outside the body which is not appropriated (i.e., not grasped or sustained by consciousness).
That which is solid and firm is called the external earth element of the body. [The commentary] mentions "sparse soil, stones, and so forth";

this is added to clarify its characteristics, as it was omitted in that sutra. [The commentary] mentions "tears, sweat, and so forth"; the term "and so forth" includes the subsequent items: mucus, saliva, pus, and so on.

Blood, sores, lymph, fat, marrow, milk, bile, urine—(according to the *Yuánjué jīng*, both feces and urine belong to the water element; however, according to the *Bǎojí jīng*, feces belong to the earth element)—such substances as these are called the internal water element (*ābdhātu*) of the body.
"Dew, rain, and so forth" is an addition by the commentator (*shū*), as it is missing from that sutra.
"Digesting food and drink, etc. refers to the subsequent passage which states: "All the warmth and heat within the body that enters into the heating [process]..."
Regarding the "enumeration" [of the elements]: as for the passage in the commentary concerning "heat outside the body" and so forth, the text states:

"That which exists outside the body, which is neither grasped nor appropriated, is namely fire—the substance of fire, the characteristic of fire, its warmth and steaming heat," and so on. Regarding the passage in the commentary concerning "the four limbs" and so forth, the text states:
"That which dwells in the four limbs of the body is wind; that which dwells in the stomach; that which moves through the five limbs; and that which moves through the various minor extremities."

Regarding those who practice both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: as for inhalation and exhalation (which each phrase states is also wind), to speak briefly, that which circulates throughout the entire body is entirely wind.

Regarding "the external body and so forth," the full text says: "Wind, the substance of wind, the name 'wind,' swift, the substance of swiftness, and the name 'swiftness'—this is the external wind element.
Regarding the section "and these four great elements" (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) below, this is the commentary’s own subsumption.

The passage concerning the prior emptiness of each of the four great elements is a comprehensive summary and judgment. From the section beginning with "From the time of arising and the time of abiding" onwards, each part is entirely the text of the sutra itself;

as for the commentaries stating they share "but one meaning," although it is said to be one meaning, that sutra merely clarifies that arising and ceasing have no substance due to the conjunction and separation of conditions, whereas this sutra [clarifies] that because it is the perfectly luminous nature of awakening, all things are pure.

The commentary states: "Furthermore, 'internal and external' below clarifies that there are no dharmas external to the mind, thereby establishing the tenet that all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

This also serves to resolve potential objections. Fearing that an opponent might object: 'Since you speak of the pearls of the four great elements as being both internal and external, is this not evidence that objects truly exist outside the mind?

Therefore, the commentary resolves this by stating: 'They must necessarily arise through internal transformation. 'Internal' refers to the sense organs and consciousness; the meaning of 'transformation' is as explained previously."
Commentary: Among all worldly phenomena, there are seven textual sections; the first explains the "basis" (*āyatana*). Regarding the meaning of "gate of birth":

the six consciousnesses depend upon the six internal sense organs and take the six external objects as conditions, thereby attaining growth and development. Thus, the preceding phrase says, "this is the place where consciousness is born.

The "gates" refer to the six gates. Regarding the number six and so forth: many sutras also frequently speak of the "six bases" (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). As for "relative," it refers to the sense organs (*indriya*).
Because consciousness arises only when the sense object and the faculty encounter one another, it is simply called the "six bases" (ṣaḍāyatana).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "within each gate of the faculties," this is a second explanation of the *dhātus*. That is to say, since each of the three [categories] has six gates, they constitute eighteen;

this means that six times three equals eighteen, rather than three times six equaling eighteen. The note states, "The eye and consciousness constitute a *dhātu*," etc., which serves to distinguish [the meaning].

It is not that the eye and ear constitute the *dhātus* (elements) and so forth. Regarding the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) in the commentary: the six consciousnesses arise depending upon the six sense organs (*indriya*) and are drawn forth by the six objects (*viṣaya*).
Furthermore, those organs and objects exist because they are transformed by consciousness. Since there is no phenomenon among the myriad dharmas that does not depend on these, it is called a "cause.
Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*) in the commentary: it is like the various species of tigers, deer, and other beasts found in the mountains, each of which has its own distinct category.
The various species of fish and turtles in the ocean each have their own distinct lineages, and within each lineage there are many individuals.

These eighteen dharmas are likewise so; each dharma itself contains many sub-varieties. For instance, a single *rūpa-dharma* (form-phenomenon) is divided into eleven types, or a single visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is divided into four parts along with its associated mental factors (*caitta*).
[Commentary: The preceding section [deals with] the six pairs; below, thirdly, is the analysis of contemplation.

This is for the benefit [of the reader]. It is the general intent of the Buddha’s teachings throughout all his discourses regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), not merely a localized praise.
As for the statement "six pairs," within each category, the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) enter into one another;

because they are deluded regarding the nature of the realms (*dhātu*), consciousness merges with them so inseparably that they are reduced to only two. Thus, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also speaks of "six pairs."

This is the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "ceasing karma": it means awakening to and understanding that this Dharma consists of the distinct roots and objects, as well as the mental factors, which are separate from the consciousness;
being clearly aware that they do not merge with one another, and that there is neither self nor master, one does not give rise to karma and thereby attains liberation.

Regarding the phrase "remedying the grasping at a self": the five contemplations for settling the mind each remedy a specific affliction. Among these, the text states: "For the sake of sentient beings who are attached to a self."

This explains the contemplation of the analysis of the *dhātus*. It means that by awakening to the fact that the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) each have their own respective domains, one realizes for oneself that there is no sovereign master at all;
thus, there is no "self" (*ātman*) to be grasped. [The commentary] below the phrase "furthermore" points to the four aggregates (*skandhas*) to indicate the three categories [of the *dhātus*].

Regarding the statement "the fourfold two truths," the meaning is discussed in the preliminary discourse. As for the term "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*), that text states regarding the first level: "An army... [is merely a designation].
Forests, vases, and basins constitute conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) constitute ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the phrase "as previously stated," etc., this distinguishes the various phenomena of this world; it does not list the reasons for the five aggregates within the text. [Commentary:

Below the section on these three categories, there are five explanations of the meaning of the three categories. As for the terms "superior, middling, and inferior": the superior [explanation] provides a brief exposition of the five aggregates. That is to say—
Those who understand the characteristics of phenomena such as form and mind, and who personally comprehend the meaning of the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), are of middle capacity;

for them, the twelve bases are taught so that they may understand all phenomena, at which point they also master the remaining two [categories]. For those of inferior capacity, it is necessary to explain all eighteen [elements] before they can understand all phenomena.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of "inferior, middle, and superior," this refers to three grades of individuals, which is the reverse of the preceding order; that is to say, the superior...

Because those with superior faculties and sharp wisdom are able to survey extensively in advance, eighteen [dhātus] are fully explained for them. Among these, those of middling faculties can somewhat receive and retain [the teaching] in advance;

therefore, twelve [āyatanas] are taught for them. As for persons of inferior grade, whose faculties and natures are dull and obtuse, they cannot memorize and maintain such a multitude of dharma categories;
therefore, only the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are taught for them. Question: Why do these two explanations contradict each other so fundamentally? Answer: Although...

Each has its own basis, and their meanings do not contradict one another. That is to say, those of superior faculties understand the three categories (triskandha) immediately upon hearing about the aggregates (skandha), whereas those of inferior faculties only comprehend the three categories after hearing about the elements (dhātu).
All of these are intended to provide a thorough understanding of all phenomena, both material and mental.

The subsequent statement—that the elements are taught for those of superior faculties and the aggregates for those of inferior faculties—is merely a way of describing how they understand the teachings they have heard; it does not [imply that the teaching itself is partial].
Because it is said that through this one attains full mastery, the two explanations do not contradict each other. Regarding the "three grades of joy" (*sukha*) in the commentary:

the brief [joy] is explained briefly, and the medium and extensive [joys] are likewise. Regarding the "three types of delusion" in the commentary: this refers to being deluded regarding the three mental factors (*caitta*).

The Buddha, in order to clarify them, established three designations: "this is feeling" (*vedanā*), "this is perception" (*saṃjñā*), and "this is formations" (*saṃskāra*); he did not [delude] the mind (*citta*).
Because of [delusion regarding] form (*rūpa*) alone, and because only one form and one consciousness were taught, they are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Furthermore, because there is delusion regarding form, the Buddha opened this up and taught it as eleven types, namely the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the six objects (*viṣaya*);

since there is no delusion regarding the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), he taught only the single term "basis" (*āyatana*), and thus they are called the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). Furthermore, because there is delusion regarding both form and mind, the Buddha opened up the category of form...

[The eighteen elements] are formed by dividing ten into two halves (referring to the fact that within the *dharmadhātu*, one takes only the "matter included [within it]"). By expanding the mind into seven—namely, the six consciousnesses and the mental faculty (*manas*)—because the mental factors (*caitta*) are not confused with the mind, they are contained within these seven minds.
Alternatively, within the *dharmadhātu*, their names and meanings are not explicitly distinguished; thus, they are called the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).
*Commentary:* Now, below this section on the three categories, the six are correlated with the hundred dharmas (*śatadharma*). The aggregates (*skandha*) encompass only ninety [of those hundred].

4. (The *skandhas* have the meaning of "accumulation. Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not an accumulation, it is not included within the category of *skandhas*. The other two [categories] both include everything completely. Regarding the statement "included in form" (*rūpa-saṃgraha*), etc.:
This refers to the eleven types of form included within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) among the one hundred dharmas;

the single primary name for each from among the universal (*sarvatraga*) factors included within the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); and the seventy-three dharmas included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), namely:

the three universal factors (the first two have been explained above), the five object-specific (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*) factors, the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) factors, the six root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the four indeterminate (*aniyata*) factors, and the [factors of] non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Twenty-four; thus, they total seventy-three. That "consciousness has eight" refers to the eight consciousnesses. The following two [categories] are to be understood accordingly.
When it says "the mental faculty (*manas*) corresponds to the eight consciousnesses," it refers to the sense-base of mind (*mana-āyatana*). Regarding "the dharmas are eighty-two":

within the previous seventy-three, one adds the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as the two factors of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), along with the matter included within the base of dharmas (*dharma-āyatana*). Thus it is said.
Regarding "the mind subsumes two consciousnesses," these are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses; the principle is the same as above.

[In the] commentary, under the section "The twenty-five states of existence" (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), the seventh part explains the various existences. This text has two sections. First is the formal explanation. As for the "four continents," they are Pūrvavideha and so forth.
The four destinies are hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras. The four dhyānas and the three [realms] such as the non-conceptual beings (asaṃjñin) are all the form realm (rūpadhātu).
The four emptinesses are the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). The six heavens of desire consist of the two heavens dwelling on the earth and the four heavens dwelling in the clouds.
These enumerations are all contained within the chapter on Maitreya, where they are explained in detail; here, only twenty-five categories are indicated. All of these...
There are. To speak briefly, there are only three realms of existence (*bhava*): namely, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

[Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "However, as for the Brahmā King," this addresses two general objections. The objection states: "The four dhyānas listed above already include the Heaven of Non-conception, the Pure Abodes, and the Great Brahmā Heaven;
how can they be listed again? Therefore, the commentary cites the words of the objection, saying, "However, as for the Brahmā King, etc."
Regarding those who hold the view of Brahmā: they reckon that at the beginning of the kalpa there were no sentient beings at all, but only the deity Brahmā himself.

Later, seeing that sentient beings gradually appeared below the realm of desire, they reckoned, "It was I who was able to produce them. Thus, they possess this view. As for the non-Buddhists who maintain the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*):
while the six heavens of desire and the four dhyānas all possess mental perception, this class alone is distinct; therefore, it is listed separately.

The Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes) are inhabited exclusively by noble ones (*ārya*). Within the fourth dhyāna, the third stage, the Devanikāya of the Śakras, is divided into two paths: first, the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and second, the noble ones.
The ordinary beings are those in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); the noble ones are the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.

These are mostly inhabited by Anāgāmins, though there are also other noble ones present. The subsequent statement, "because they differ from the other heavens," precisely establishes the principle for this separate enumeration.

Chapter on the Ten Powers; Chapter on the Four Fearlessnesses; Chapter on the Four Unimpeded Analytical Knowledges; Chapter on the Eighteen Unique Qualities of a Buddha;
Chapter on the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment; Chapter on the Attainment of Buddhahood by Sentient Beings.
In the fifth section of the commentary on the supramundane dharmas, there are two parts. First, the general resolution of objections; the intent of these objections can be understood.
However, regarding the statement "it is also said to be empty," the Sūtra states that "purity" is the meaning of "emptiness.

As explained at the beginning of this major section by citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, emptiness and purity are taught as having the same meaning. Regarding the phrase "like a mirror" and so forth, it refers to objects within a mirror.
However, to perceive them as truly existent is called defilement; to perceive that each and every one is entirely empty and is merely the essence of luminosity is called purity.
Therefore, this is used as an analogy: both mundane and supramundane phenomena are entirely pure and without distinction.
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-realm is like flowers in the sky," this means it is equal to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, being like a dream from yesterday.

Furthermore, in the subsequent passages, specifically the chapter on the Ten Powers (*daśabala*), where this is explained in detail at the opening of the section, various sūtras repeatedly clarify these ten powers; these are the powers of all Buddhas.
The virtue shared [with others] is possessed by the Buddhas and others. Bodhisattvas resolve their minds upon this. The *Brahmacarya-parivarta* states: "Furthermore, one should practice;
within each and every power (*bala*), there are immeasurable meanings, all of which should be inquired about, for they must not remain unknown.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 27, intends to show that the Great Beings, the Buddhas, possess true power, thereby causing the minds of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) to be subdued.
One should aspire toward this. Bodhisattvas who emulate it are able to accomplish great deeds and ultimately attain their fruit; therefore, it must be discerned.
However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (53), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (4), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (14), and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (27–28) all discuss this extensively.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there is a sevenfold classification: first, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, its differentiation (*vibhāga*); third, its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇa*); fourth, its equality (*samatā*)...

[The categories are: 1. Name, 2. Substance, 3. Characteristics, 4. Synonyms, 5. Activity, 6. Sequence, and 7. Distinctions. Now, the commentary uses the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Zhilun) to explain these;

however, it also harmonizes them with the seven gates of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Where there are omissions, they are supplemented within the "Supplementing Omissions" section, which the lecturer must examine.
Within the text there are three parts. From "The Tathāgata... onwards, the first part generally reveals the essence and function [of wisdom], which is able to know all...
The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the essence of the ten powers (*daśabala*). The function of these powers is the thorough and correct knowledge regarding the ten objects.
[In the commentary] below the general term "powers," the second part explains this general term; it can be seen in the respective passages.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (49) states: "Because it is endowed with the capacity to benefit all sentient beings in every way, it is ultimately supreme."

Because it possesses great power that subdues all Māras and adversaries, it is called "power" (*bala*). The *Abhidharma* states: "Because it skillfully subdues all Māras and skillfully answers questions and debates, these ten are called powers.
The term "ten" is a numerical designation used in an appositional compound (*saṃkhyeya-saṃkhyā-vigraha*). [The commentary] begins with "First, knowing all in general," and so forth;
this third section explains the individual names to clarify their functional applications. This clarification of the functional applications corresponds to the fifth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
This is the section on the gates of activity. The ten powers (*daśabala*) are divided into ten parts;

here, the first is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). The text has two sections: first, the explanation of the name, which is the discernment of its characteristics.
In various sūtras and śāstras, the object known is always presented first, and only then is the name established based on the power of the knowledge that realizes it.
Sometimes it is simply called "wisdom" (*jñāna*), sometimes just "power" (*bala*), and sometimes both are mentioned as "the power of wisdom," as is the case with the title given here.

In this present commentary, I have used the term "that which knows" (*jñāna*) to refer to the means by which one knows, following this sequence for two reasons: first, because the wording is clear and easy to understand;
second, because the wording is concise and eliminates redundancy. Let the wise examine this carefully. When the text speaks of "general wisdom," this refers to this single power.
Because this is the totality of the others; thus it is said that "one knows all things in their totality," and so forth. The Treatise further states:
"Next follows the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*). One definitively knows that from these causes and conditions, this retribution emerges.
Within this, the nine powers are subsumed in their entirety. For the sake of delivering sentient beings, nine types are distinguished within the first power. Why is this? Because of this world...

Sentient beings see before their eyes that grain emerges from seeds, yet they cannot understand it; how much less could they understand the causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions of the mind and mental factors?
The Buddha understands the causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions of both the internal and external realms with complete clarity and universality;

therefore, this is called a "power" (*bala*). As for the term "basis" (*sthāna*), it carries the meanings of establishing, relying upon, and arising. It is able to establish the fruit and serves as the basis for the fruit.

"Dependent upon [the cause], it is able to produce the fruit; therefore, the name 'basis' (*sthāna*) is established. The *Śāstra* states: "To know as they truly are what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*) is one of the powers.
Regarding the note on "female universal monarchs" (*cakravartinī*), etc., this is a private record; all serve to demonstrate the meaning of the "impossible."
The treatise says: It is impossible for a woman’s body to become that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
Why? Because all women are subject to men and lack self-mastery. If even a woman cannot become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, how much less can she become a Buddha?
Even if a woman attains liberation and *nirvāṇa*, it is likewise attained through a man; there is no such thing as spontaneity.
Regarding the attainment of the Dharma of the Path: as for the "two kings," the *Śāstra* states that it is impossible for two *cakravartin* universal monarchs to appear in the world simultaneously.
Why? Because there is no such accomplishment of karma involving enmity. Since even two *cakravartin* universal monarchs do not exist in the same world, how much less so two Buddhas?
Regarding the note on "evil karma yielding pleasant retribution," the *Śāstra* states: it is impossible for evil karma to result in the experience of pleasant retribution. Evil karma...
One cannot even attain worldly happiness, let alone supramundane happiness. If one who engages in unwholesome conduct were to be reborn in heaven, such a thing is impossible;

if unwholesome conduct cannot even lead to rebirth in heaven, how much less could it lead to nirvana. This refers to the commentary on the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment by one who has abandoned the five hindrances.
The five hindrances shroud the mind and cause distraction; it is impossible to attain nirvana while remaining apart from the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment.

When the five hindrances shroud the mind, one cannot even attain the path of a śrāvaka while apart from the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment, let alone the path of a Buddha. Only when the mind is free from such coverings [can this be achieved].
The path of the Buddha can be attained; how much more so the path of the śrāvaka. Such is the meaning of "what is possible" and "what is impossible.

In the sūtras of the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā*), the Buddha himself spoke these words from his own mouth. Various masters of discourse rely upon this speech of the Buddha to further elaborate upon what is possible and what is impossible.

As for those who attribute faults to the Buddha, saying "this is a fault of the Buddha" and so forth—this refers to the section following "from the fault of the Buddha," which enumerates numerous other [faults].
Regarding the matters concerning their status, the conclusion states as follows. The *Śāstra* says: "If it is said that a Buddha hears of his own transgressions;
or if noble ones (ārya) seek out the places of non-Buddhists; or if noble ones claim for themselves, 'I am a Buddha'; or if noble ones fall into the evil destinies (durgati);
or if the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-heya) arise again; or if noble ones conceal their offenses."
The twenty-five [categories] of the *srotāpanna*—none of these are possible. Below this, there are ten further matters;
all those above are essential to know and are fully contained within the *Bùquē* (Supplement). In the commentary (*shū*), the phrase "subduing those below" refers to the second function.

Regarding the phrase "those who may be saved," the *Lùn* (Treatise) says: "Having attained universal knowledge, one saves those who may be saved, and for those who cannot be saved, one creates the conditions [for their future salvation]."
Just as a physician knows whether a disease is curable or incurable, the Buddha has no such limitations.
He cannot be defeated, nor can he be surpassed, because he possesses universal knowledge. This is called the first power.

The commentary [states] "knowing the past and present" and so forth; this is the power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma across the three periods of time. The text has three parts: first, the explanation of the name; second, the performance of the action;
third, the distinction from what precedes, which also serves to resolve potential objections. These three parts appear frequently below as well and can be distinguished within the text itself;

I shall not further subdivide each one here. The treatise immediately preceding this states: "The Buddha knows that these sentient beings have afflictions and delusions as the causes and conditions [of their state]."

[Referring to this section] It is explained as liberation due to the causes and conditions of the fetters, pure meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), samādhis, and liberations. [Referring to the third section] These are all sentient beings.
The Buddha universally knows the three types of karma and afflictions of the three periods of time—whether light or heavy, deep or shallow, coarse or subtle;

therefore, they are called "powers" (*bala*). [Returning to this section] Regarding the knowledge of the past, present, and so forth, the *Śāstra* states: "He knows the past and future of sentient beings."

Regarding present karma: one knows the locus where karma is created, knows its causes and conditions, and knows its retribution; this is the second power. As for the phrase "knowing past karma, retribution, and so forth," the *Śāstra* states:

"The power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma" means knowing the actions performed by body and speech, as well as the karmic merit of precepts received during this life even when no action is currently being performed.
It also means knowing how evil karma follows and functions day and night, and how karma that produces sin or merit arises.
The Buddha briefly explains that these karmas are subsumed within three categories; this is called all karmic activity.
The Buddha knows that among all sentient beings, there are karmas whose past retribution has also passed; there are karmas whose past retribution is in the present;

and there are karmas whose past retribution is in the future (the above are all single cases). There are karmas whose past retribution is in both the past and the present; [and there are karmas whose past retribution...]

Regarding the past and future: there are actions that are past while their retribution is present or future; there are actions that are past while their retribution is in the past, future, or present.

(The above are all "repeated" [cases], being either two or three [time-periods]). The same applies to present actions. (Taking the present as the starting point, the two examples above are applied accordingly;
hence they are called "single" and "repeated. [Commentary on] "Wholesome, etc.": "etc. refers to unwholesome and immovable karma. [Note: the three natures.]
Regarding "the mind and so forth," the treatise states next: "Furthermore, within a wholesome mind, one experiences the retribution of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate karma.

It is the same for an unwholesome mind and an indeterminate mind [one should say: within an unwholesome mind, one experiences the retribution of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [karma]; within an indeterminate mind, one experiences the retribution of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [karma]].

Furthermore, due to the causal conditions of pleasant karma, one experiences a pleasant retribution... [Suffering and neither-painful-nor-pleasant [retributions] are each experienced as their respective outflows (niṣyanda), following this same principle]. — *Śū* (Commentary).

Regarding "karma to be experienced in the present life" and so forth, the treatise states: Due to the causal conditions of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*), one experiences retribution in the present life.

Due to the causal conditions of karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*), one experiences retribution in the next life. Due to the causal conditions of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karman*), one experiences retribution in subsequent lives.

Due to the causal conditions of impure karma, one experiences afflictive retribution. Due to the causal conditions of pure karma, one experiences retribution free from affliction. Due to the causal conditions of mixed karma, one experiences mixed retribution. (Note)

Regarding "retribution is equal [to the cause]," the *Śāstra* states: Furthermore, there are two kinds of karma: karma that must be experienced as retribution (*niyatavedanīya-karma*) and karma that need not be experienced as retribution (*aniyatavedanīya-karma*).
Karma that must be experienced as retribution cannot be avoided; it is experienced by depending on time, depending on persons, or depending on places.

For example, if a person is destined to receive blessings together with a Cakravartin King, they will only experience them when a Cakravartin appears in a favorable age. This is what is meant by "depending."
Regarding "at that time" and "the person": the person is the Cakravartin (Wheel-Turning Sage King). Regarding "the place where he awaits": it is the place from which the Cakravartin emerges.
Furthermore, this is karma that must necessarily be experienced; it does not depend upon his skills or meritorious achievements.

Whether good or bad, [retribution] comes of its own accord without being sought, just as for those born in the heavens, blessings and joy arrive spontaneously, while for those in the hells, the suffering of their transgressions follows them of its own accord. It is not...
It awaits causes and conditions, for this karma is profound and grave. Furthermore, there is karma that must necessarily yield its retribution.

For example, when the army of Virūḍhaka slaughtered seventy-two thousand practitioners who had attained the Way, as well as immeasurable upāsakas who observed the five precepts—even great masters of supernormal powers such as Maudgalyāyana were unable to save them.
It is also like Bakula, whose stepmother threw him into fire, boiling water, and cold water.

In the interim, one does not die. Just as when the Buddha traveled through various countries, although he went forth from home to practice begging and required no formal meal offerings, five hundred chariots followed him carrying the king’s own raw non-glutinous rice and a hundred flavors of soup for his meals. In this way, one must necessarily experience the results of wholesome and unwholesome karma;

other [neutral] karmas need not be experienced. In the Desire Realm, there are three places where the retributions of karma are received: the karma that results in pleasant feeling, the karma that results in painful feeling, and [the karma that results in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling].

The karma of feeling pleasant sensation; the karma of feeling neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation. In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are two types of places where the retribution of karma is experienced:

the karma of feeling pleasant sensation and the karma of feeling neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is one type of place where the retribution of karma is experienced: the karma of feeling neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
Or there are those who await their karma; depending upon these matters, they receive the retribution of their actions.

For example, when King Pukkasāti had a thousand lotuses grow in his pond—golden lotuses as large as chariot wheels—it was because of this great assembly that many people experienced happiness, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha knows the places where all sentient beings create various karmas, whether in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
In which realm does the desire realm reside? If it is in the heavenly realm, in which heaven?
If it is among humans, in which continent? If it is in Jambudvīpa, in which country? If it is that country, in which city, which village, which monastery, or which territory?
If it is that city, in which street, which lane, or which house? In what specific location? One knows what kind of karma this is.
He knows whether [the karma] was committed in one past life, two lives, or even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of lives;
he knows how much of this karmic retribution has already been experienced, how much remains unexperienced, how much is certain to be experienced, and how much is not certain to be experienced.

He also knows the materials employed for wholesome and unwholesome deeds—namely, weapons such as swords and staves used for killing, orders to kill, and so forth—as well as killing by oneself or dispatching others to kill. He likewise understands all other evil karmas in this same way.
One should understand wholesome karma in this same way. For instance, regarding giving, ethical discipline, and the cultivation of virtue: within the act of giving, what are the objects given?
They may be lands, houses, clothing, food and drink, medicine, bedding, the seven treasures, or material wealth;

or they may be various wholesome and unwholesome deeds—indeed, the many causes and conditions of all such karmas are fully detailed in the *Bupue* (Supplement). Furthermore, as stated in the *Karma-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "When one acts..."
Evil people are born in good realms; those who practice goodness are born in evil realms. Ānanda asked, "How can this be?
The Buddha said, "For an evil person, the karmic retribution for their sins in this life has not yet matured, whereas the wholesome karma from past lives has already matured.

Due to these causes and conditions, although they commit evil now, they are born in a good realm. Or, at the time of death, wholesome states of mind and mental factors arise; it is because of these causes and conditions [that they are born in a good realm]."
Therefore, one is also born in a good place. As for those who practice virtue yet are born in an evil place:

their wholesome karma of this life has not yet matured, while the unwholesome karma of their past lives has already matured. For this reason, although they perform wholesome deeds now, they are born in an evil place.
Or, at the time of death, unwholesome states of mind and mental factors arise; for this reason as well, they are born in an evil place. Question: What is the meaning of "matured" and "unmatured"?
It may be so. At the time of death, how can a mind lasting for only a brief moment overcome the power of a lifetime of conduct? The answer is:
although this mind lasts for only a short duration, the power of the mind is fierce and sharp; like fire or poison, though small in quantity, it can accomplish great things.
This is the mind at the time of death belonging to those who ride this vehicle; because it is resolute and courageous, it surpasses the power of a hundred years of practice.
This final mind is called the "Great Mind" (*mahācitta*), for the matter of relinquishing the body and the sense faculties is urgent.

It is like a person entering battle who does not spare their own body or life, and is thus termed "valiant. It is like an Arhat who, by relinquishing attachment to this body, attains the path of Arhatship. As...
These various karmic retributions of sins and merits, as well as their transformations, should likewise be understood by śrāvakas;

however, they only know the retribution for the sins of evil karma and the rewards for the merit of good karma, and cannot make such subtle distinctions. The Buddha fully and universally knows these karmas and their retributions;
because the power of his wisdom is unimpeded, inexhaustible, and indestructible, this is called the second [mark].

[The section on] Power. ▲ Regarding the commentary’s phrase "knowing what is possible" (*sthāna*) and so forth: this is second, the functional application (*karmayoga*). ▲ Regarding the sub-commentary’s phrase "the preceding clarifies," etc.:

this is third, the differentiation from the power of knowledge regarding the possible and impossible (*sthānāsthānajñānabala*). (One should first raise an objection, etc. This means that in the previous general discussion, it was established that karma already created must necessarily result in the experience of suffering or pleasure according to whether it is wholesome or unwholesome;
for there is no principle whereby an unwholesome cause could yield a wholesome retribution. Therefore, it says "what is created is contrasted with the impossible. Now, directly...
The analysis of karma is complete with the discussion of killing and so forth. This karma necessarily brings about its fruit, and is thus termed "the created" (*kṛta*).

If this person performs acts such as killing, they will necessarily fall into hell, or must necessarily experience the results in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives; therefore, it is called "the creator" (*kartṛ*).

Furthermore, it is said that this clarifies how each [action], according to its being wholesome or unwholesome, brings about its respective fruit. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the former was general while this is specific," the treatise says:

"The first power is general, while the remaining nine are all specific. The general power [of karma] knows all causes and conditions, whereas this [specific power] demonstrates that there is only the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma. Thus, it applies to all nine powers.
The Commentary (Sūtra) states: "Knowing all dhyānas," and so forth. This refers to the power of knowledge regarding all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis. The Treatise (Śāstra) says:
"To know the characteristics of all dhyāna-concentrations, liberations, and samādhis—whether pure or defiled—and to know them as they truly are;

this is the third power. Regarding the phrase "all dhyānas" and so forth, the Treatise says: "Dhyāna refers to the four dhyānas. The Buddha knows these dhyānas as that which assists the factors of the Path, according to their names, characteristics, meanings, and divisions. Next...

Furthermore, regarding cultivation: there are distinctions such as those between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and pure and defiled *samādhis*, as well as the degrees of depth and shallowness.

The eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*)—as their characteristics are distinguished within the section on dhyāna—encompass all meditative absorptions of the form realm when one speaks of dhyāna; they encompass all concentrations when one speaks of the liberations.
The perfection of dhyāna (*dhyānapāramitā*) is precisely these various liberations, dhyānas, concentrations, and samādhis; all are so named.

This is for the sake of concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration is defined as cessation (*śamatha*); it is the absence of distraction. Regarding the phrase "attachment, views, and so forth," the treatise states subsequently:

"Defilement refers to the various afflictions such as attachment, views, and pride; purity refers to true meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), which is not intermingled with the afflictions of attachment, views, pride, and so forth."
Just as with the analysis of refined gold, among the various meditative concentrations (samādhi), there are those that involve a single mental application and those that do not;

those that are constant and those that are not; those that are difficult to enter and easy to enter, or easy to enter and difficult to enter; those that are difficult to emerge from and easy to emerge from, or easy to emerge from and difficult to emerge from; those that grasp specific characteristics and those that grasp general characteristics; and those that undergo transformation through cultivation and those that do not.
One should apply remedial countermeasures as follows: for one who harbors lust, cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; for one who harbors anger, practice the meditation on impurity;
for one who is deluded, contemplate the finite and infinite limits of existence; for a mind that is agitated by restlessness, use wisdom to discern all phenomena;

and for a sunken mind, one should seek to uplift it. If one does not do so, it is called "failing to apply remedial countermeasures. Within this meditative concentration, one must distinguish between the appropriate time and the state of abiding. If the body is weak...

Emaciation is not the time for practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, when a bodhisattva practices asceticism, he reflects: "I am currently unable to give rise to meditative concentration.
Furthermore, a place where many people reside is also not a place for practicing concentration. Moreover, the Buddha knows that this meditative concentration leads to loss;
this meditative concentration leads to stability; this meditative concentration leads to the increase of wisdom; and this meditative concentration leads to the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.

Because of this turning back. Furthermore, the Buddha knows that such a person finds it difficult to enter meditative absorption (samādhi) and difficult to emerge from it; easy to enter and easy to emerge; easy to enter and difficult to emerge;
or difficult to enter and easy to emerge. The Buddha knows that such a person should attain such dhyānas;

he knows that such a person shares in the five desires while in meditative concentration; and he knows that such a person, having experienced the five desires, returns to attain dhyāna. Relying upon these various dhyānas, they attain Arhatship.
Han: All such meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis are precisely samādhi.
This meditative concentration the Buddha knows exhaustively through his profound wisdom; it cannot be destroyed and cannot be surpassed. This is called the third power.

[The commentary] states that he also knows the fruits produced in the lower realms, as well as the form and formless realms, and the supramundane fruits of the three vehicles of the noble ones. [The note] refers back to the preceding section on penetration.

The term "etc. (*ādi*) serves to distinguish this from what preceded. Question: Previously, the retribution of wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable karma was explained; "immovable" refers to the various dhyānas. Why is this stated again? Answer:

This is said to distinguish it, because the previous discussion applied to both concentration (*samādhi*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*). Although concentration was mentioned there, the focus was solely on karmic retribution.

Now, although defilement and purity are known, the emphasis is solely on the essence and function of purity. The textual structure is thus clearly illuminated, which is why the treatise makes this distinction.
It is said: "One knows that sentient beings are bound due to the causes and conditions of karma and afflictions" (this is the second gate).

"They are liberated due to the causes and conditions of pure dhyāna, samādhi, and liberation" (this is the present gate). The various schools distinguish these two gates, yet none are as clear as this treatise.

That is to say, the first gate distinguishes between the possible (*sthāna*) and the impossible (*asthāna*); the second abandons the false views regarding the impossible and discusses only the possibility of good and evil.

1. The correct view regarding the karmic retribution of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*). 2. Third, further abandoning distraction and speaking exclusively of the defilement and purity of meditative concentration, clarifying only the essence and function of purity, and manifesting supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.

3. Fourth, within the pure dharmas that are free from outflows (*anāsrava*), there are furthermore the five faculties (*indriya*)—faith and the others—in their superior, middling, and inferior grades.
4. Fifth, preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations and desires in order to increase the power of these faculties. 5. Sixth, it is necessary to cultivate past... [text ends].
The nature of the seeds of birth and so forth, as well as the skillful means for delivering sentient beings—how could these not be manifest?

In the commentary on the passage beginning "the four wisdoms, faith, and so forth," it refers to the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of all beings. The *Śāstra* says (citing the treatise along with annotations to provide a comprehensive explanation):
"The Buddha employs this power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties" means that the Buddha knows whether sentient beings possess sharp, dull, or middling faculties. Sharp...

Sharp wisdom is called superior; dull wisdom is called inferior. By means of this power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties, the Buddha discerns that among all sentient beings, some have sharp faculties, some have middling faculties, and some have dull faculties.

He knows that such a person, with such faculties, can only attain the first fruit in this present life, but cannot further attain the second, third, or fourth fruits; and that such a person can only attain the first dhyāna.

This person is able to attain only the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, up to and including the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*); it is likewise so for all [levels].
This person can be foremost among the śrāvakas and foremost among the pratyekabuddhas. This person is fully endowed with the six pāramitās and is able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(The commentary notes: "Brief and extensive" refers to the following section on functional activity. The treatise continues: "Thus..."
Having known this, he brings about liberation for some through a brief teaching, for others through an extensive teaching, and for others through both brief and extensive teachings.
He may instruct with gentle and kind words, or with harsh words, or with words that are both gentle and harsh.

The Buddha also discerns which person possesses remaining potential for correspondence [with the Dharma], causing them to increase their faculty of faith, or determining which person should be made to generate the faculty of diligence.

The faculty of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom refers to those who enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of the faculty of faith; those who enter the state of right determination by means of the faculty of wisdom;
those of sharp faculties who are obstructed by the fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), such as Aṅgulimāla and others;

and those of sharp faculties who are not obstructed by the fetters and proclivities, such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others. Regarding the faculty of knowledge: although it may be dull, it is nonetheless free from [obstruction].
[This is] a prohibition. For example, in the case of Cūḍapanthaka: there are those whose faculties are dull who are [nevertheless] prohibited [from higher realization].

This person is known to have dull faculties regarding what is abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*), but sharp faculties regarding what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); or dull faculties regarding what is abandoned by cultivation, but sharp faculties regarding what is abandoned by seeing the truths.
In this person, all faculties are equally dull or equally sharp; in this person, all faculties are neither equally dull nor equally sharp. This person...
In some cases, the power of past causes is great; in others, the power of present conditions is great.

Thus, there are those who seek bondage but obtain liberation, and those who seek liberation but obtain bondage. For example, Aṅgulimāla intended to kill his mother and harm the Buddha, yet he attained liberation.
For example, there was a bhikṣu who attained the four dhyānas; yet, due to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), he fell back into hell.

Knowing that such a person will certainly fall into the evil realms, one knows whether this person will find it difficult to emerge, whether they will emerge easily, whether they will emerge quickly, or whether they will emerge only after a long time.
In this way, he thoroughly knows the characteristics of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings; it is indestructible and unsurpassed.
This is called the fourth power.

The commentary states that "knowing the various desires and inclinations" refers precisely to this power of knowledge (*jñānabala*). The *Śāstra* says: "Knowing the various desires of other sentient beings is the fifth power.

It means knowing the two kinds of desire in sentient beings—namely, the causes and conditions for superior or inferior faculties—and the two kinds of desire regarding wholesome or unwholesome [actions], as well as the various distinctions among desires such as faith, preference, and inclination. Because the Buddha knows these all-pervasively, it is called a "power."
Regarding the mention of Nanda and others, the *Śāstra* states: those who delight in the five objects of desire, such as Sundarananda; those who delight in fame, such as Devadatta;
those who delight in worldly wealth and profit, such as Sumatiśreṣṭhin; those who delight in leaving the household life, such as Yaśas;
those who delight in the dhūta practices, such as Kātyāyana; and those who delight in extensive learning, such as Ānanda. Thus it is said.

[The text says: "Thus, the disciples of the Buddha each have their own preferences; ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) likewise each have their own preferences—some delight in sensual desire, others in anger, and so forth.
The Buddha knows them all. [Commentary: "Causing them to abandon" [refers to] the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*).
[Note: "Knowing what precedes" [refers to] distinguishing it from what was mentioned before.

Commentary: "Sixth, knowing one of three" (refers to) the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñāna-bala*). "Element" (*dhātu*) refers to nature (*prakṛti*). The *Śāstra* says:

(also providing a rough commentary) "Knowing the various and innumerable natures of the world" is the sixth power. ▲ The note "nature is below" [refers to] the second note, which is a selection (*viniścaya*).
This section first performs a selection, and only later clarifies the functional activity; this follows the convenience of the text. The text has two parts: first, the selection.

The Fifth Gate. The Treatise states: "Nature (*xing*) refers to accumulated habituation. From nature arises desire; one acts according to nature. At times, desire functions as nature; by habituating to desire, it becomes nature.
'Nature' refers to the defiled mind taking an object; 'desire' refers to arising in accordance with conditions.

The commentary notes that "nature" extends downward [to the subsequent sections], distinguishing it from the Fourth Gate. This is because one might raise the objection that the Fourth Gate already addresses knowing whether the faculties (*indriya*) are sharp or dull. Furthermore—
This refers to past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). How does it differ from this present gate? Therefore, it is distinguished:

whereas [the previous section] spoke exclusively of the sharpness or dullness of the five faculties—faith and so forth—for those entering the Path, the present passage universally clarifies the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three levels of lineage (*gotra*) regarding both wholesome and unwholesome, defiled and pure states;

it does not speak of faith, diligence, and so on. Because they are thus distinguished, they are not the same. [In the *Śāstra* (Treatise),] the commentary states: "Knowing" refers to the function of the three karmas. The *Śāstra* says: "Knowing..."

Sentient beings have such natures and such inclinations; they come from such places; they are those who can be delivered or cannot be delivered, those who are fixed or unfixed, those who are certain or uncertain, and those who are not necessarily so.
They practice such conduct, are born in such places, and abide in such stages.
[The Buddha knows] that some may be delivered in this life, some in a future life, some immediately, and some at another time. This person the Buddha can deliver; this person a *śrāvaka* can deliver.

"Can be delivered. This person can certainly be delivered; this person cannot certainly be delivered. Regarding "brief, extensive, etc.": briefly explaining those who can be delivered; extensively explaining those who can be delivered;

praising those who can be delivered; subduing those who can be delivered; welcoming those who can be delivered; abandoning those who can be delivered. Regarding "and so forth (*ādi*)," it further says:
through subtle teachings, coarse teachings, or piercing words, they can be delivered; through gentle speech, they can be delivered.
The commentary states that from "knowing the seven" onwards refers to the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminīpratipad-jñānabala*).

The treatise says: "All wholesome paths, all unwholesome paths, and all noble paths—each and every path is known. (A note clarifies: these are wholesome, unwholesome, and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) actions.

"Destinations" (a note clarifies: these are the five destinies and *nirvāṇa*; outflow-tainted actions lead to the five destinies, while outflow-free actions lead to *nirvāṇa*). The Buddha knows them all completely; this is called the seventh power.

The commentary states: "Knowing the past without obstruction" refers to the power of knowledge (*jñānabala*). The note regarding "the past," etc., explains the meaning of the term *pūrvanivāsa* (past lives).

Regarding the phrase "in general," the treatise says: "There are three types of knowledge of past lives: those that are supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), those that are clear visions (*vidyā*), and those that are powers (*bala*).
Ordinary persons possess only supernormal powers; Śrāvakas possess both supernormal powers and clear visions; Buddhas possess supernormal powers, clear visions, and powers. Why is this so?
Ordinary persons (who have attained the five supernormal powers) know only the past lives they have experienced, but do not know the continuity of the causal conditions of karma.
For this reason, ordinary persons possess only the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) but lack clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

Śrāvakas, because they understand the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), clearly know the continuity of the arising of karmic causes and conditions. For this reason, Śrāvakas possess both the supernormal powers and clear knowledge. As for the Buddha...

Disciple: When one was formerly an ordinary person, one attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). Upon entering the Path of Seeing the Truths (*darśanamārga*), one understands the causes and conditions of origination (*samudaya-pratyaya*).

With the eighth untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), because one has attained the abandonment of views, this [knowledge] transforms into clear vision (*vidyā*). Why is this? "Clear vision" is the name for the root of seeing.
If a disciple of the Buddha first attains the Noble Path and subsequently the knowledge of past lives arises, they likewise understand the causes and conditions of origination.

By virtue of this power, it transforms and becomes "clarity" (*vidyā*). The Buddha employs this clarity to know the causes and conditions of his own past lives and those of sentient beings throughout immeasurable and boundless eons;
he fully and universally knows all the various experiences undergone therein. This constitutes a "power" (*bala*). [Note:

The preceding "knowing" is distinguished from other similar terms. The *Śāstra* states: "He knows up to hundreds of thousands of eons, from the beginning of the kalpa until its end: 'I was among that assembly...'"
Regarding birth: such-and-such a name and surname, food and drink, suffering and pleasure, and the length of one's lifespan;

dying there and being born here (this "here" refers to this world); dying here and being born again here; and the name, surname, food and drink, suffering and pleasure, and length of lifespan in this world—these are called the eight powers.

The commentary states: "The nine knowledges below" refer to the power of knowledge regarding the unimpeded divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The Buddha’s divine eye is pure and surpasses the eyes of all devas and humans.

He sees sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—whether they are handsome or ugly, great or small, following the path of merit or the path of evil—and how they receive retribution according to such karmic causes and conditions, and so forth. The *Śāstra* says: "The Buddha uses his divine eye to see..."
Regarding the places where sentient beings die: ordinary persons, using this divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), see at most the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*).
Śrāvakas, at most, see sideways the small thousandfold world system (*sāhasracūḍikalokadhātu*), and they also see it pervasively above and below.
Question: The Great Brahmā King is also able to see a thousand worlds; what is the difference between them? Answer: The Great Brahmā King stands within his own thousandfold world system.
[If one] looks all around, if standing at the edge, one does not see other places.
It is not so for the Śrāvaka; wherever they dwell, they constantly see a thousand worlds. The Pratyekabuddha sees a hundred thousand worlds. The Buddhas see immeasurable and boundless worlds.
The divine eye-knowledge of ordinary persons is a supernormal power (*abhijñā*) but not a clear vision (*vidyā*); it is likewise [limited], seeing only...
Regarding all matters, one cannot see how beings take birth according to the causes and conditions of their karma, as explained in the *Pūrvanivāsa* (Recollection of Past Lives).
Furthermore, when a Śrāvaka enters another samādhi from the state of mind in which he dwells [with the divine eye], his divine eye ceases;
the Buddha is not so, for even though his mind enters another samādhi, his divine eye does not cease. Furthermore, among those who have attained the divine eye, he is the foremost.
First, regarding Aniruddha: the matter derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) at the crown of his head is pure; this is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
The Buddha’s divine eye is distinguished by the fact that the matter derived from the four great elements is pure throughout his entire head.

As for the commentary stating "only these," it means that because one can know birth and death through the divine eye, it is called the power of knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-jñānabala*); the others are all obtained based on what is known.
Regarding the phrase "The commentary states that it encompasses clear insight (*vidyā*) and so forth," this has already been cited above.
In the *Śāstra*, following the section on the ten knowledges, it refers to the power of the knowledge of the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The treatise says:

"Because the Buddha’s outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, he possesses the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and the liberation of wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*). Within the present, he personally cognizes through his own awareness: 'Birth for me has been exhausted,' and so forth. It further says: "The Buddha..."

Knowing the two kinds of causes and conditions within the three periods of time, he discerns and evaluates the faculties and inclinations of sentient beings, preaching the Dharma for the sake of exhausting their outflows (*āsrava*).
This is the power of the exhaustion of outflows. Furthermore, with his wisdom, the Buddha severs the afflictions of all sentient beings;
that wisdom is neither dull nor diminished. It is, for example, like a red-hot iron ball placed upon a small amount of cotton: although it burns this cotton, [it does not burn the earth].

(The power of speech according to one’s own intent, another’s intent, and the intent of both; the ten powers that crush [adversaries]; the fearlessnesses that subdue non-Buddhists; the unique Buddha-qualities that distinguish [the Buddha] from the two vehicles;

[Commentary: The two instances below are the same as this. Second, judging the eloquence of speech (*pratibhāna*) has two parts. Regarding "all [types of] speech are the teaching of both the words and the meaning":

At the time of planting [the seeds], one establishes various principles and delights in expounding them without interruption or exhaustion.

Regarding the statement that "the words are poured forth like clouds, without error or mistake, and the exposition is without end," this is the first of the ten characteristics, specifically the section on the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): the note states that while the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) possess a portion of [the first] two, such as power (*bala*) and so forth, they do not possess this [full set]. The treatise says: Question:

For example, Śāriputra was well-versed in all dharmas, and Aniruddha was foremost in the divine eye. Furthermore, the Buddha spoke of those among his disciples who possess the lion’s roar and so forth.
Regarding the "first, second, third, etc. mentioned in the commentary: this refers to (1) no failure in body, (2) no failure in speech, and (3) no failure in mindfulness.
Since the intent here is to be concise regarding the text, these are collectively concluded with the term "no failure" (*amogha*). Thus, the marginal note states that "no failure" refers to "karma.
Regarding the note on "many eons" and so forth, the treatise states in full: "For immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddha has maintained pure precepts."

Therefore, his physical and verbal karma are without fault. Other Arhats, such as Śāriputra and others, have many faults because they have practiced the precepts for no more than sixty kalpas and for not long.
The Buddha, however, has accumulated the pure precepts of all dharmas for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
he constantly practices profound meditative concentration and has attained all subtle and wondrous wisdom. Thus, he is virtuous.

Because he cultivates the mind of great compassion, there is no fault. Regarding the phrase "infusing all sins and so forth," the *Śāstra* says: Furthermore, because the Buddha has uprooted the causes and conditions of all roots of sin, there is no fault.
There are four kinds of causes and conditions for the roots of sin: namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and fear (as well as habitual tendencies).
Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have uprooted the causes and conditions of sin, their habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted; or...

At that time, there was an omission. Because the Buddha’s wisdom is all-pervasive regarding all phenomena and is always perfected, if one were to fail due to ignorance, it would be like when Śāriputra was traveling with five hundred bhikṣus and stayed for the night at an empty dwelling.

At that time, during the recitation of the precepts, he did not know the matters concerning internal or external boundaries. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "We have been staying at this residence for as long as a single night."
If one abandons [them], there are no boundaries. Furthermore, at another time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana returned with five hundred bhikṣus.
Because they were making loud and boisterous noises, the Buddha drove them out; this constitutes a fault of speech.

Moreover, since all the physical and vocal actions of the Buddha proceed in accordance with wisdom, his body is without fault and his speech is without fault. Regarding the mention of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, there are four...

Regarding the mind of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): because it has been well-cultivated throughout the long night, one has thoroughly cultivated profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by severing attachment to sensual desires as well as attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
As for "focusing the mind without gain or loss," the *Śāstra* states: if the mind relies on haste, there will be forgetfulness and loss;

The Commentary states: "There is no difference" and below (this includes the commentary). The Buddha has no discrimination toward any sentient being;
he has no thoughts of distinction regarding distance or proximity, such as thinking, "This one is noble and may be taught," or "That one is base and cannot be taught.

Just as the rising sun shines universally upon all things, so too does the light of his great compassion pity all equally, delivering with impartiality those who are respectful and those who are disrespectful, as well as enemies, kin, the noble, and the lowly.
All are entirely equal. For example, the Buddha transformed and delivered the dung-remover named Nanda, who attained the state of a Great Arhat;
likewise, there was no difference in the householder Kṣemadatta’s attitude toward the fire-pit.

Furthermore, regarding those who practice in accordance with the Buddha-dharma, such as Śāriputra and Maitreya Bodhisattva, the Buddha felt no partiality, nor did he feel any distinction toward Devadatta, Pūraṇa, or non-Buddhist teachers.
He does not even harbor resentment toward the six heterodox teachers and those with false views; this is because the Buddha has cultivated and perfumed his mind for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

The four noble lineages, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the samādhi of non-contention,
the knowledge resulting from aspiration, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge— possessing such sublime qualities as these, the Buddha enters meditative concentration within the desire realm.
It is called "having no unsettled mind.
(The commentary on the sixth [point], "no realms," follows below; subsequent notes are to be understood accordingly. Sentient beings have three kinds of feeling:

painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Painful feeling gives rise to aversion; pleasant feeling gives rise to craving; and within neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, delusion arises.

Delusion (*moha*). These are the three kinds of feeling (*vedanā*): painful feeling is suffering when it arises, suffering while it persists, and pleasant when it ceases; pleasant feeling is pleasant when it arises, pleasant while it persists, and suffering when it ceases;

Within this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they remain without perception or knowledge, yet possess a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This is being driven by the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). The Buddha, within the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), knows when awareness arises, when it abides, and when it ceases.
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha has no state of mind that is not known and then relinquished. Question:

"Equanimity in the middle is called 'equanimity' (upekṣā). The answer states: "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] is equanimity; equanimity in the two [other] states is also equanimity.

For this reason, the Buddha entered meditative absorption with a single-minded focus. Furthermore, after the Buddha had preached the Dharma, he constantly instructed the bhikṣus: "Always..."

Practice seated meditation; do not allow yourself to regret it later. Let what you speak with your mouth be what you also practice with your body; therefore, enter into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

Regarding the note on "the Buddha’s knowledge of wholesome dharmas" and so forth, the treatise states in full: "Because the Buddha knows the kindness of wholesome dharmas, he constantly desires to gather them."
Because of all wholesome dharmas, his desire does not diminish. Because he cultivates all wholesome dharmas with a mind that knows no satiety, his desire does not diminish.
For example, there was once an elder bhikṣu whose eyesight had grown dim; while sewing his saṃghāṭī robe, the needle’s eye came loose, and he said to the people, "Who among you delights in merit?
Please stitch this needle for me. At that moment, the Buddha appeared before him and spoke.
"I am one who delights in merit and is never satiated. Bring me a needle.
This bhikṣu, who was not merely familiar with the patterns of seeing the Buddha’s radiance or recognizing the Buddha’s voice, addressed the Buddha, saying:

The devas and people of the world are startled and awakened to realize that even the Buddha has no satiety regarding merit, let alone others.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for the bhikṣus. At that time, his physical eye was immediately clarified and his wisdom-eye was perfected.

In the eighth section of the Commentary, regarding the note "as explained in the section on desire (*chanda*) and so forth," the Treatise states:

This serves as the initial practice for those who wish to increase their diligence. As the Buddha taught, desire is the root of all phenomena.
Desire is like a person’s thirst for a drink; diligence is like the skillful means and conditions used to seek out food and drink. Desire is the mind’s longing to obtain.
Diligence is for the accomplishment of those tasks. Aspiration belongs to the mental action (*manas-karman*), while diligence belongs to all three actions.
Aspiration is internal; diligence is external. Such are their distinctions. Furthermore, this diligence is what all Buddhas delight in.
For example, by the power of his diligence, Śākyamuni Buddha transcended nine *kalpas* and swiftly attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Upāli] said: Furthermore, as it has been told, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus; my back is aching and I wish to rest for a moment.

For this reason, the Buddha’s diligence does not diminish.

Regarding the commentary’s note on "loss of mindfulness," "error," and so forth: the treatise states: Question: It was previously stated that there is no loss of mindfulness (*smṛti-akṣaya*), yet now it is further stated that there is no diminution of mindfulness (*smṛti-aparihāṇi*).

"Abiding in meditative concentration and supernormal powers" means that one remembers the past and present worlds, penetrating them without obstruction. Question:

For what reason is the non-decline of mindfulness unique to the Buddha-dharma? Answer: Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have skillfully cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, their mindfulness [is likewise non-declining].

It is firm. Although mindfulness is firm, it may still diminish and be obstructed such that it does not achieve full penetration, as explained in the section on the power of knowledge regarding past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*).
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, when recollecting past lives, can at most reach eighty thousand *kalpas*;

In the Buddha’s mind, there is not a single dharma that exceeds it. For this reason, the Buddha alone possesses mindfulness that never diminishes.

Regarding the tenth section of the commentary, under the note on "all [dharmas] of the three periods of time," the treatise states: Because the Buddha has attained all-encompassing wisdom, his wisdom does not diminish;

Because he has accomplished unimpeded wisdom, his insight does not diminish. Furthermore, it is like a lamp that is abundant with oil and ghee, whose wick is pure and whose radiance is intense;

the Buddha is likewise. With the oils of various samādhis and meditative concentrations, such as the King of Samādhis, being undiminished and his pure wick intact, for these reasons, the radiance of his insight is immeasurable and never diminishes.
Regarding the commentary on the eleventh fascicle: The treatise states, "There are two kinds of liberation: conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation.
Conditioned liberation is defined as liberation associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Unconditioned liberation is defined as the total exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*) without remainder. The Buddha does not diminish in these two liberations. Why is this? [Because] the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas..."
Because the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddhas is not extremely sharp, their afflictions are not entirely exhausted, and thus their wisdom undergoes diminution.
Because the Buddha’s wisdom is supremely sharp and his afflictions along with their habitual tendencies are forever exhausted without remainder, his liberation does not diminish.

Furthermore, as stated in the section on the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*), there is a distinction between the liberation of the Buddha and that of the Śrāvakas; this is because the Buddha has attained the power of the destruction of the outflows.
Liberation does not diminish; it is because the Two Vehicles lack power that there is diminution.
In the twelfth section of the *Śāstra*, the commentary notes: regarding the phrase "knowledge and vision," the treatise asks:
