When combined as one, it is firm and stable. Furthermore, to recite, analyze, and deliberate upon [the teaching] from another person is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
to personally attain realization is called "vision" (*darśana*). For example, to hear of a matter with one's ears yet still harbor doubt is called "knowledge."
To see with one’s own eyes, clearly and without obstruction, is called "seeing. This distinction also applies to knowledge and vision within liberation.

The rest is as explained in the *Bùquēshū* (Supplementary Commentary); there is nothing lacking. (With annotation) The Treatise says: Question: It is said that the Buddha has no deficiency among all dharmas.
Why is it that he is said to have no deficiency only in six matters? Answer: Among all matters of self-benefit and benefit for others, [he is complete] in four...

When one is able to fulfill the task, seeks the root of all wholesome dharmas, practices with diligence, and guards with mindfulness—like a gatekeeper who admits the good and bars the evil—and illuminates all phenomena with wisdom to sever all afflictions, through these four dharmas the task is accomplished.
There are two kinds of fruits of these four dharmas. The first is...
Liberation. Second is the knowledge and vision of liberation. The meaning of liberation is as previously explained. Regarding the knowledge and vision of liberation:

by means of this knowledge and vision of liberation, one knows the characteristics of these two kinds of liberation—the conditioned and the unconditioned—and knows the various characteristics of liberation, namely:
liberation at times, liberation not at times, liberation through wisdom, twofold liberation, and liberation through destruction.
Liberation, non-declining liberation, the eight liberations, inconceivable liberation, unimpeded liberation, and so forth.
(Commentary, Vol. 13, Fascicle 45, with annotations) The treatise states: "The Buddha first knows all actions of body, speech, and mind, and subsequently acts in accordance with wisdom.

This is called "first attaining knowledge and subsequently acting in accordance with wisdom. As it is said in the sutras: "The Buddhas benefit sentient beings even through their exhalations and inhalations;
how much more so through the actions of body, speech, and mind? Therefore, they never act in a way that is not beneficial.
Even hostile and wicked sentient beings, upon smelling the fragrance of the Buddha’s breath as he exhales and inhales, all attain pure faith and come to love and revere the Buddha. All...
When the devas smell the fragrance of the Buddha’s breath, they too all renounce the five desires and resolve to cultivate wholesome deeds.
For this reason, their actions of body, speech, and mind proceed in accordance with wisdom. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess such a quality;

they intentionally perform wholesome acts so that the actions of their body and speech subsequently become wholesome, yet their mental action may at times be neutral (*avyākṛta*), arising spontaneously rather than following wisdom. How much more so for others?
There are people such as the bhikṣu Gavāmpati, who, although he had attained arhatship, would eat his own vomit and then eat again;
such karma does not follow wisdom. Furthermore, there was the bhikṣu Madhuvāsistha, who, having attained arhatship, would leap onto beams, rafters, or climb upon walls and trees.
Also, there was Pilindavatsa, who reviled the deity of the Ganges, calling her "little girl."
"O slave! Such bodily and verbal actions as these were previously devoid of wisdom and did not proceed in accordance with wisdom.

The Buddha does not possess such things. [The interlocutor] asks: "If that is so, then at times the Buddha’s bodily and verbal actions also appear not to proceed in accordance with wisdom. Why is this?
Because when he enters among the beings of non-Buddhist paths to preach the Dharma, there are none at all who believe and accept it. Furthermore, on one occasion, while [he was]..."
While preaching the Dharma amidst the great assembly, he manifested the maṇi-jewel upon his chest.

Furthermore, because people doubted that he did not possess the two marks, he manifested the mark of the tongue and the mark of the concealed organ within the great assembly. Moreover, there were disciples who were deranged and foolish.
He reviled Devadatta, saying: "You are a madman, a dead man, a consumer of spittle. The Buddha established a precept that eight kinds of bowls should not be kept;
he permitted monks to use two kinds of bowls—either earthenware or iron—yet he himself used a stone bowl.

On occasions when non-Buddhists posed difficult questions, the Buddha remained silent and did not answer. Furthermore, in some places the Buddha spoke of a self (*ātman*), while in other places he spoke of its non-existence.
In various places I have taught that all phenomena exist, and in various places I have taught that all phenomena do not exist.

In such cases, [it may seem that] my body and speech do not follow the movement of wisdom. Since bodily and vocal karma are not separate from mental karma, it would follow that mental karma also sometimes does not follow wisdom.
How then can you say that [the Buddha's actions] always follow wisdom? The answer is: This is not so. Regarding these matters:
All [beings] first possess wisdom; subsequently, all karmic actions follow the movement of that wisdom. Why is this?

When the Buddha enters among the assemblies of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), although he knows they will neither believe nor accept him in this present life, he does so for various great causes and conditions pertaining to future lives.
Furthermore, it is to stop the slander of the non-Buddhists who claim that the Buddha is self-exalting and arrogant; for this reason, he personally goes to enter their assemblies.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhists said: "The Buddha himself claims to possess great compassion and to universally save all beings; yet he preaches the Dharma only for his own fourfold assembly.

We too have left the household life to seek the Way, yet he does not preach for us. Moreover, as in this sutra, when the Buddha preached the Dharma among the assembly of non-Buddhists regarding the Buddha-nature, they did not say that they believed and accepted it.
Then the Buddha, seeing from afar that the great assembly of non-Buddhists was making a loud clamor, [spoke].

While they were engaged in debate, wishing to go elsewhere, they turned their course toward him. When the masters of debate saw the Buddha approaching from afar, they said to their assembly, "All of you remain silent;
the Buddha is one who delights in tranquility. He may come here if he sees that you are all silent."
The assembly remained silent. The Buddha entered among them and taught the three truths for brahmins; the group of non-Buddhists all remained silent.
The Buddha thought to himself: "These madmen are all possessed by Māra.
This Dharma is subtle and profound, yet not a single person has accepted the precepts to become a disciple. Having had this thought, he rose from his seat and departed. This man was Māra.
Having attained liberation from their obscurations, they thought to themselves, "We have heard the sublime Dharma; why should we not benefit ourselves?
Thereupon, they all went to the Buddha’s presence and became his disciples, attaining the Path and being freed from suffering.

Furthermore, because the disciples of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) dared not go to the Buddha’s presence for fear of challenging their own teachers, the Buddha himself entered among their assembly. Thus, the multitude heard the Dharma and developed faith.
He received [the teachings] with firm resolve and no longer found fault with his teacher; he became a disciple and attained the fruit of the Path.
In this way, there were various causes and conditions for wisdom. For these reasons, he went among the followers of external paths. Furthermore, there was Satyaka Nirgrantha-putra.
With copper rings encircling his belly, he made this vow: "There is no one who, upon hearing my roar, shall not break out in sweat and be destroyed.
Even great elephants, down to trees, tiles, and stones, shall all break out in sweat upon hearing the sound of my roar. Having made this vow, [he roared].
He came to where the Buddha was and engaged him in debate. The Buddha questioned him, but he was unable to answer any of them.
His sweat flowed down and soaked the ground, drenching his entire body. The Buddha said to the Nirgrantha, "You previously made this vow:

'There is no one who, upon hearing my challenges, will not break into a sweat. Now you are sweating and soaking the ground. Do you truly observe the Buddha and see any sign of perspiration? At that time, the Buddha...
The Buddha removed his *uttarāsaṅga* and showed him, saying, "Where is the sweat? Furthermore, there are some people who have sweat on their heads but not on their bodies;
although the Buddha had no sweat on his head, he certainly had sweat on his body. For this reason, the Buddha removed his *uttarāsaṅga* and revealed his body.
Because of this, the non-Buddhists gained great faith and turned toward the teaching, all entering into the Buddha-dharma. This is wisdom.

Regarding the causal conditions for wisdom and the conduct of bodily karma: when the Buddha manifests the mark of the tongue and the mark of the concealed organ (*kośagatavastiguhya*), there are those who doubt these two marks of the Buddha’s body.
Such a person ought to attain the Way, yet because of their doubt, they do not. For this reason, he manifests these two marks. He extends his tongue until it covers his face;
though the tongue is vast, it returns into his mouth without any hindrance. Those who see this have their doubts severed. There are those who see...
He extended his tongue. If someone were to give rise to a mind of contempt, his tongue would appear like that of a small child;

upon seeing it return into his mouth, they would realize there is no hindrance to his preaching the Dharma, and would immediately give rise to reverence, exclaiming, "How marvelous! Some people doubted whether the Buddha’s male organ was concealed and not visible.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a precious elephant and a precious horse, pointing them out and saying, "The non-manifestation of the male organ is exactly like this."
Some say that the Buddha reveals the mark of the concealed organ (*kośagatavastiguhya*) only to a single person in order to sever their doubts.

The masters of debate (*vādin*) say that because the Buddha possesses a heart of great compassion, if there is anyone who, upon seeing the Buddha’s mark of the concealed organ, is able to accumulate roots of goodness,
generate the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and give rise to a heart of great joy, faith, and reverence, he causes them all [to do so].
Those who are able to see him have their doubts severed; others cannot see him at all.

Out of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), for the sake of delivering sentient beings, the Buddha emerges from three kinds of concealment and appears for a moment like a flash of lightning. Once these sentient beings have seen this illusory manifestation, they believe that the Buddha possesses a heart of great compassion.
Thus, regarding my Dharma, they neither grasp nor cling. For such reasons as these, he manifests two forms.
It is not jesting; it is not shamelessness. When the Buddha spoke harsh words to the bhikṣus, saying, "You are mad and foolish men," there are two kinds of such harsh speech:
first, reviling with a defiled mind and anger; second, speaking out of compassion for sentient beings, desiring to transform them.
One who is free from desire has no reviling with a defiled mind or anger, let alone the Buddha. Because the Buddha speaks out of compassion and a desire to transform others, his harsh words exist.

Regarding speech: there are sentient beings who do not enter the discipline of the Path through gentle words or skillful instruction; they must receive harsh and severe teaching before they can enter the Dharma.
It is like a fine horse that gallops at the mere sight of the shadow of a whip, whereas a dull donkey only moves when struck by a painful hand.
It is also like a wound that heals when treated with a mild ointment and sucked with saliva, yet requires a sharp blade to cut open and extract the harmful pus if it is treated with a harsh medicine.
This leads to recovery. Furthermore, if the Buddha speaks of "mad" or "foolish" people, these are gentle words and words of truth.

Why is this? Because they are called "mad and foolish" due to the arousal of the three poisons, and so forth. Some people, upon hearing harsh and cutting words, respond with joy, saying, "He loves me," and so forth.
[Note: See the third section below. The *Śāstra* states: Question: It was previously said that his body is without fault and his speech is without fault. What does this mean?
Regarding "mindfulness is without loss": what is the difference in meaning between this and the statement that now one’s bodily, verbal, and mental actions follow wisdom?
The answer is: previously, the three kinds of non-loss were stated without explaining their causes and conditions; here, it is explained that because they follow wisdom, there is no loss.
If one gives rise to bodily, verbal, or mental actions without prior deliberation, then there is loss. The Buddha first [employs] wisdom...

There is no fault, because he initiates the actions of body, speech, and mind [with prior awareness]. Furthermore, he has accomplished the three kinds of pure actions, the three kinds of tranquil actions, and the three kinds of unguarded actions.
Someone may doubt, saying: "For what cause and condition does the Buddha accomplish such actions?
For this reason, the Buddha said: "All my actions of body, speech, and mind are first preceded by wisdom, and subsequently proceed in accordance with wisdom."

In the commentary on sections sixteen, seventeen, and eighteen (including the sub-commentary), the *Śāstra* states: "Because these three kinds of wisdom penetrate the three periods of time without obstruction, the three types of action follow the movement of wisdom.
(This meaning is used to explain the preceding text. Question: Past phenomena have already ceased and been exhausted;
they no longer exist. Future phenomena do not come now nor are they born; they have not yet come together. As for present [phenomena]...
"Even within a single thought-moment, there is no time that abides. How, then, can one know the three periods of time with unhindered penetration? The answer is:
"The Buddha has taught that he possesses unhindered penetration regarding the past, future, and present. How could these words be false?
Furthermore, if the past and future did not exist and only the present moment of a single thought existed, the Buddha would likewise be unable to accomplish immeasurable merit."
Virtue is like the ten kinds of knowledge (daśajñāna) which possess the ten powers (daśabala). For this reason, it is also impossible for a single mind to possess ten knowledges simultaneously.
If that were the case, the Buddha would likewise not be able to fully encompass the ten directions. By these causes and conditions, one knows that the past and future exist.
Question: If [dharmas] exist in the past, future, and present, what is it that is non-existent? The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths;
regarding the Truth of Suffering, one contemplates its characteristics such as impermanence. "Impermanence" means arising, ceasing, and disintegration, which are unobtainable.

If past dharmas truly exist now, they would not be called "non-existent," nor could they be characterized by disintegration and unobtainability. [Commentary on the question]: Regarding the passage beginning with "If the three... the treatise states:
Furthermore, if the past, future, and present all exist simultaneously, one falls into the error of eternalism (*śāśvata*). Why?

Because these phenomena, while existing in the future, would certainly transition into the present, and from the present, transition into the past—just as when a person moves from one room into another, they are not said to have "lost" their identity.
The reply is: If there is no loss [of identity], what fault is there? The questioner asks: What fault is there?
If there were no impermanence, there would be no sin, no merit, no birth, no death, no bondage, and no liberation. "Sin" refers to the ten unwholesome paths of action, such as killing and so forth;
if there were no impermanence, there would be no sins such as killing, as explained in the section on the analysis of false views.

"Power" refers to that which exceeds the seven constituents of the body, being incapable of causing affliction or harm. "Merit" refers to the ten wholesome paths of action, such as non-killing and so forth. [All these] depend upon impermanence.
This is called the conceptual differentiation of birth and death. If there were no impermanence, there would be neither birth and death, nor bondage, nor liberation.
Such are the immeasurable faults [of such a view]. The reply is: All phenomena of the three periods of time each possess their own characteristics.
Past phenomena have the characteristic of the past; future phenomena have the characteristic of the future; present phenomena have the characteristic of the present. If the past...
If the future possessed the characteristics of the present, such an objection would indeed apply. However, the past, future, and present each abide in their own respective characteristics.
Furthermore, if there were no past [or future], there would also be no monastic discipline (*pravrajyā-śīla*).
Why is this? If one were abiding in a present state of unwholesome mind, and the past did not exist...

I am not a bhikṣu. Furthermore, when a noble person’s mind dwells within the mundane world, at that time they should be considered an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because there is no path [realized] in the past, future, or present.
Likewise, they would also be without the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and other such offenses.
These ordinary beings have no past karmic offenses. Why is this? Because these five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) have already passed;
at the time of death, one enters hell. As for the future, since there is no karma, there is no retribution.
The present body does not commit the heinous crimes. If there is no past, then there are no heinous crimes. If there are no heinous crimes, how could there be anything else?
Sin and merit are also like this. If there were no sin or merit, that would constitute wrong view; one would be no different from birds and beasts. [Commentary:
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Moreover, I do not say that the past and future exist with the same characteristics as the present.

I say that although the past has ceased, it can give rise to recollection and can produce the mind and mental factors, just as the fire of yesterday, though extinguished, [remains as a cause for memory]."
Today one may give rise to thoughts and recollections; however, fire does not exist simply because of those thoughts and recollections.
If one sees a pile of firewood, one knows that it will naturally burn. When sentient beings think of tomorrow’s fire, it is like the fire of the past;
fire does not exist simply because of the present thought of fire. The affairs of the future are also like this; though the present mind lasts but a single moment.
At that time, it does not abide, because it arises in a continuous succession. It is able to know all phenomena (*dharma*). Internally, it takes the present mind as its cause;

externally, it takes all phenomena as its conditions. From within these causes and conditions, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises. Operating with mastery through this mental consciousness, it knows the phenomena of the past, future, and present;
however, it alone cannot know its own present mind and mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), while knowing everything else. Question:
In the "Chapter on the Suchness of the Perfection of Wisdom," it is stated that the three periods of time share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
How then can it be said that the Buddha’s wisdom knows the three periods of time with unimpeded penetration? The answer is: Buddhas employ two modes of teaching the Dharma.

First, they differentiate all phenomena; subsequently, they teach ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). When it is said that [the Buddha] penetrates the phenomena of the three periods of time without obstruction, this refers to...
It is explained through analysis. To say that the three periods of time have a single characteristic—that of being without characteristics—is to speak of ultimate emptiness.
Furthermore, it is not the case that for an omniscient one, regarding another omniscient one, their wisdom is obstructed within the three periods of time;
this extends even to such noble sages as Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and Śāriputra, whose wisdom [is likewise unobstructed] within the three periods of time.
All things possess obstruction. For this reason, it is said that the Buddha’s wisdom penetrates the three periods of time without obstruction;
it is not spoken of as being for the sake of an empty matter.

The Commentary asks: "Regarding 'the invisible crown of the head' and below. This is an exposition based on the functional application of the meaning, rather than the literal text of the treatise itself.

Within the treatise, while refuting the tenets of the Hīnayāna schools, it separately explains the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), stating that the mark of the invisible crown of the head exists;

that the soles of the feet are soft and supple, such that whenever sentient beings encounter them, they immediately obtain happiness; and furthermore, it states that he attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to transform the minds of sentient beings, as when he manifests [his form] upon entering a city.

Regarding the power of supernormal transformations and so forth, the treatise refutes this by stating: "These eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) are not taught within the Tripiṭaka" (the Tripiṭaka refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna;
the meaning is that when the Buddha taught the Hīnayāna, he did not speak in this way). Furthermore, they are not mentioned in any other sūtras.
Because there were those who sought after these dharmas, various Śrāvaka masters of debate compiled them here and there to praise the Buddha's virtues.

Regarding the absence of error in speech, the absence of decline in wisdom, and the non-loss of mindfulness—these are all included among the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Mahāyāna;

this is why they are discussed in the treatises. Although there are many other such qualities, such as the invisible crown of the head and the softness of the soles of the feet, these should not be included among the eighteen unique qualities.
This is because the unique qualities are defined by their nature as wisdom, whereas the physical strength of the Buddha’s body is not.
The strength of a hundred thousand white fragrant elephants, as well as powers such as those of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), are not mentioned at all.

For this reason, one should know that among the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), only the virtues of wisdom and so forth are spoken of, while the dharmas that are the natural fruition of retribution are not.
Furthermore, these eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are categorized within the five aggregates (*skandha*) according to the Abhidharma.

The absence of error in body and speech, and the fact that body and speech follow wisdom, are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). The absence of manifold perceptions is subsumed under the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The absence of non-concentrated mind is subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
The remaining qualities are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). All of them exist within the four dhyānas; for the Buddha, they exist within the four dhyānas.

Because attaining the Path enables one to enter nirvāṇa. Some say that the four material non-common dharmas (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) are subsumed within the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and desire (*kāmadhātu*), while the remaining nine stages are also subsumed therein;
all are wholesome and all are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. The four material dharmas arise from two conditions:

the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The remaining [non-material] dharmas arise from four conditions. Four are without objects (*anālambana*), and fourteen have objects (*sālambana*). Four follow the movement of the mind (*cittānuvartin*).
Some are not associated with the mind; thirteen are both associated with the mind and follow the mind;
one is neither associated nor does it follow the mind. Such various categories are analyzed and explained in the Abhidharma.

When first analyzed in this way, upon entering the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena within the Prajñāpāramitā, they are all of a single characteristic—that is to say, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Entering the Buddha’s mind, all are the single mark of quiescent extinction.
*Great Commentary on the Meaning of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Fascicle Eight (Part One);
*Great Commentary on the Meaning of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Fascicle Eight (Part Two).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Caotang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
In the first section, "Explaining the Names," regarding the category of the "Correct Cause" (*zhengyin*), it says: "This cause that aids the Path is a branch of the cause of the Correct Path."

It is a category (*jāti*). Furthermore, it is also a cause that serves as a category for its fruit; thus, it is of the same class as *bodhi*. Therefore, it is next called the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*).

"Factors of enlightenment" also carries the sense of being a cause, meaning they serve as the common causes for all three vehicles. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Awakening (*buddhi*) refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising;
because they accord with this, they are called 'factors' (*pakṣa*). The commentary explains: "Awakening means that the sleep of ignorance has been forever severed."

Therefore, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) constitute the essence of this awakening. These thirty-seven [factors] cultivated as the path leading to awakening are called the "limbs of awakening" (*bodhipakṣa*).
Thus, it is said that "limb" (*pakṣa*) also carries the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
The commentary [states] "In general" and so forth. The text has two parts: first, it clarifies the differences regarding the scope and limitations of the Great and Small Vehicles.

Regarding the statement that "the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) in the Mahāyāna are immeasurable," this means they are not limited to merely the thirty-seven. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The thirty-seven factors are the cause for *nirvāṇa*."

The immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*) are not the causes of Great Nirvāṇa; rather, it is the immeasurable factors of the path that serve as the cause for Great Nirvāṇa.

In the fifth stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the immeasurable factors of the path are likewise taught. Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), both the path and the auxiliary paths (*pakṣya-dharma*) are each said to be immeasurable.
[Commentary: If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are only thirty-seven [factors]. Second, the clarification of the identity of the Dharma and the diversity of the mind.

Regarding the statement that the thirty-seven factors are not excluded from anything: the immeasurable *bodhipākṣika-dharmas* (factors conducive to enlightenment) previously mentioned are also included therein;

it is merely that the scope of their mental application differs in magnitude. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The *bodhipākṣika-dharmas* are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because they abandon conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, when Vimalakīrti manifested illness and the great assembly came to inquire after him, he used his physical ailment as a cause to extensively explain the nature of the body.

Regarding impermanence and so forth, the conclusion states: "This is to be regarded with weariness and aversion; one should instead delight in the Buddha-body. The Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body.
It arises from immeasurable merit and wisdom, and even arises from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).

Thus, these factors of enlightenment are the causes of the Dharma-body. Furthermore, in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, it says that if a bodhisattva possesses the *Ratnolkā Dhāraṇī*—[it is called a "jewel" because it possesses all virtues, and a "torch" because...]
That which can destroy darkness and encompass all phenomena is called a *dhāraṇī*. How could it be something minor? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The equality of all Buddhas is like empty space."
All sentient beings share this in common. If one can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, then one will attain clear vision.
According to the various passages cited above, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment encompass immeasurable categories of the path.

As for the note stating that "the Four Truths have immeasurable aspects," this is an indirect citation of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as an example. It refers to when Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha..."
Once, at one time, while staying on the banks of the Ganges in the Śīśumāra forest, the Tathāgata took up a few leaves from a tree and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Are the leaves in my hand now more numerous, or are the leaves of all the grasses and trees upon the entire earth more numerous?
The bhikṣus replied, "World-Honored One, the leaves of all the grasses and trees upon the entire earth are more numerous; they cannot be measured or calculated. The Tathāgata said—
"To grasp but a small portion is not worth mentioning, O Bhiksus.

Of all the dharmas I have fully realized, those that I have proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings are like the leaves in my hand; whereas those not so proclaimed are like the grasses and trees upon the great earth.
"World-Honored One," [the monks asked], "at that time, when you spoke of these immeasurable dharmas thus realized, were they already included within the Four Truths, or were they not?"
[If that were so,] there would have to be five truths. The Buddha praised Kāśyapa: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
The question you have now asked will bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
Son of good family, all such dharmas are entirely subsumed within the Four Noble Truths. Below it says: "Wisdom is of two kinds: first, middling wisdom; second, superior [wisdom]."
"Wisdom. Good son, knowing that the aggregates (skandhas) are suffering is called middle wisdom.

To discern the immeasurable characteristics of the aggregates as being entirely suffering—something not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—is called superior wisdom. Thus it is explained at length, and so forth.

Regarding the seven categories in the commentary: first, the path that counteracts perversions (the four foundations of mindfulness); second, the path that abandons all laziness (the four right efforts);

third, the path that brings forth supernormal powers (the four bases of power); fourth, the path of the means for clear realization (the five faculties); fifth, the path of approaching clear realization (the five powers);

sixth, the path of the essence of clear realization (the seven factors of enlightenment); and seventh, the path of the subsequent arising of clear realization (the eightfold noble path). Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "Seven..."

The awakening to the eight factors of the path is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). As for the three, four, five faculties (*indriya*), and powers (*bala*), they pertain to both types [tainted and untainted];
thus, there is no separate cultivation prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Regarding the sequence of these seven: once one has heard the Dharma, one should first recollect and maintain it;
next, one should diligently practice. Through diligent practice, the mind is gathered and made pliant; consequently, faith and the other qualities become faculties and increase into powers.

Next, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are distinguished from the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). At times there are eight [factors], yet when the former [seven] have not yet been distinguished as the "path-enlightenment" (*mārgabodhyaṅga*), it is said in the *Triśarīra-vibhāga* (The Exposition of the Three Bodies):
"It takes ten dharmas as its essence. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, in the chapter on the Noble Ones (*āryapudgala*), states: "This is indeed..."

The entities consist of only ten; that is to say, their substance is wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), concentration (*samādhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and investigation (*vitarka*).

The commentary states: "Investigation" (*vitarka*) refers here to discursive thought (*manasikāra*). Regarding the mention of "two types of faith," these are: first, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), and second, the power of faith (*śraddhābala*).

Regarding the mention of "eight types of diligence," these are: first, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); fifth, the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*); sixth, the power of diligence (*vīryabala*); seventh, the factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīryasaṃbodhyaṅga*); and eighth, right [effort] (*samyag-vyāyāma*).

This refers to diligence (*vīrya*). Regarding the four things to be kept in mind: first, mindfulness of the faculties (*indriya*); second, mindfulness of the powers (*bala*); third, mindfulness of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); and fourth, right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Regarding the three types of precepts:
these are the three [factors] among the eightfold path, namely right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).

Regarding the eight factors each for concentration and wisdom: concentration consists of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) as four; fifth, the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*); sixth, the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*); seventh, the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-bodhyaṅga*); and eighth, [right concentration].

This refers to right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*), it is fourfold, namely the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*). The four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom as their essence, because "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is so named due to its proximity [to wisdom].

There are five faculties of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), six powers of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*), the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*); since view is itself wisdom, these constitute one category.

First, the essence of the wisdom of vows is empty; its characteristic is called "illusion. Second, all things produced by that wisdom—such as the manifestation of Buddhas and so forth—are also illusions. This is the gate of liberation.

This occurs due to the karma of sentient beings; since karma involves good and evil, defilement and purity, the lands consequently involve suffering and bliss, and purity and impurity. Because of power. (Among the ten great vows, the vow for establishing purity is for the sake of the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of practice. Because of the Bodhisattva’s non-retrogression in practice—(the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* contains a section on the Pure Land; this is due to the non-retrogression of practice.

The remaining six phrases. (In the sutra there are ten conditions; four are used in the commentary. That is to say, because sentient beings resolve to attain bodhicitta and abide [in it], the world becomes purely pure, and so on up to the tenth.

Regarding the three phases of formation, abiding, and destruction in the commentary: however, the world’s formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness each consist of twenty periods of increase and decrease.
When the period of abiding is full for twenty kalpas, it reaches destruction. When the kalpa is about to be destroyed, the destruction occurs within nineteen kalpas.

next, those in the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, the four continents, and the six heavens of the desire realm—all are terrified by the great calamities and cease to create any karma, whether wholesome or unwholesome, pertaining to the desire realm.
All practice the second dhyāna; upon death, they are reborn above in the heavens. They are no longer born among ghosts, in the hells, as humans, or as devas.
After nineteen kalpas, sentient beings therein have been exhausted. Next, the receptacle world is destroyed. First, the sunlight becomes four times hotter;

then it increases to two, three, and even four or five suns; finally, seven suns appear simultaneously. A great conflagration erupts, its heat surging up to the first dhyāna heaven, where fire breaks out all at once.
It arises. Among those sentient beings, some have already been reborn there previously. Once the world has become empty and twenty kalpas have passed, the subsequent kalpa begins to form.
First, a great wind sustains the realm; from the second dhyāna heaven, clouds spread across the three thousandfold world-system, raining down like chariot axles.
The wind holds back the flow, and the water solidifies into a golden wheel. Thus, the water wheel is formed first; subsequently, the realm of Brahmā gradually descends.
It is accomplished. The wind stirs the clear water, forming Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, and so forth; as these are formed, sentient beings dwell within the turbid sediment.

This constitutes the four continents up to the hells and the surrounding salt ocean, which is then designated as the establishment of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). When the merit of the second dhyāna is exhausted...
Descending to be born in Jambudvīpa, there was initially the radiance of the body, the earth-cake, forest creepers, and wild rice that appeared spontaneously.

Later, as things gradually deteriorated, the radiance, the earth-cakes, and so forth vanished. Thereupon, the sun, moon, agriculture, and sowing appeared. Because of this gradual degeneration, beings were born into the three miserable realms;

fearing their transgressions, they cultivated goodness and were born into the four continents, the six heavens of the desire realm, and even up to the Brahma world—this is called the kalpa of formation.
Regarding the increase and decrease [of lifespan]: when the human lifespan is at its maximum of eighty thousand years, it decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years.
Furthermore, during the period when the lifespan increases, with each birth of a son or daughter, the lifespan doubles. In this manner, it gradually increases back to eighty thousand years.
Therefore, it is called "increase and decrease. "Bifēn" (繽紛) refers to a state of being disordered and chaotic.

Following the passage "The commentary says that sentient beings [become] Buddhas," the second section provides a specific explanation of sentient beings attaining Buddhahood. This section has four parts: first, stating the intent;

second, the specific explanation; third, the analytical discussion (*lìjiǎn*); and fourth, the citation of the sutra. Within the first part, regarding the phrase "adorned by the *Sūtra*": its meaning is as in the *Nītārtha-saṃgraha*.
This has already been explained in the preceding verse. Regarding the phrase "also causing the subsequent text," etc.:

below, Vajragarbha takes up the meaning of sentient beings attaining Buddhahood within this passage and raises an inquiry through three gates; the Tathāgata clearly demonstrates it, which leads to the following section where it is summarized for easy understanding.
The commentary states: "First," and so forth, which is the specific explanation. Within the first [section], the term "Sautrāntika" refers to the Sarvāstivāda school.

This is the tenet [of our school]. The Sautrāntika school does not hold this view that only Siddhārtha possesses buddha-nature while other sentient beings lack it and will never have the capacity to attain buddhahood.
As for the "thirty-four minds," these consist of eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*), totaling sixteen minds.

Entering the Path of Seeing and proceeding to the stage of the Path of Cultivation, one finally abandons the nine grades of subtle afflictions of the single stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

For each grade, there is one path of uninterrupted realization and one path of liberation, thus forming eighteen moments. When these are added to the preceding sixteen, they constitute thirty-four moments of mind.

The meanings concerning the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), as well as the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in each of the lower eight stages, are all fully explained below in the "Vajragarbha" chapter.

Regarding the fivefold *dharmakāya*—namely, ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*)—these are established simply by reversing the order of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
[Commentary: As for the phrase "possessing only the Mahāyāna," this refers to the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) school.
The Thesis: Among the five portions of sentient beings, only one portion and a half possess the Mahāyāna nature;
they thus give rise to the bodhicitta, cultivate the six perfections, and attain Buddhahood after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. The remaining three portions and a half fundamentally lack Buddha-nature;

even if they were to practice, they would not achieve it, as they consist only of those of the two vehicles and those without nature (as explained previously in the "Introductory Discussion"). As for the stages of suppression and abandonment across the five positions, these are all contained within the "Pure Wisdom" section of the lower [division].

This clarifies the explanation within the section on the stages (*bhūmi*). △ Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* from "The true mind of original enlightenment" down to "not departing from original enlightenment," the meaning has been frequently recounted previously according to the *Awakening of Faith*.
As for "internal and external perfuming": original enlightenment acts as the internal perfuming, while hearing the Mahāyāna True Teaching from virtuous friends acts as the external perfuming;
this is also as explained in the commentaries on the treatise. Regarding the phrase "initially severing the marks of extinction and so forth," the treatise states:
It says: "Just as an ordinary person, because they perceive that an evil thought has arisen in the preceding moment, is able to arrest the succeeding thought so that it does not arise.
Although this subsequent state is called 'awakening,' it is in fact non-awakening," and so forth, as explained in detail in the section on the stages (*bhūmi*) in the *Qingjinghui* chapter.

To briefly clarify the general meaning: the treatise states that there are three subtle and six coarse [delusions], which are subsumed into four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) is...

The first is the phase of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). The phase of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) consists of the latter two subtle phases and the former two coarse ones. The phase of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) consists of the third and fourth coarse phases.

The phase of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is the fifth coarse phase, the phase of initiating karma (*karmotpāda-lakṣaṇa*). (Regarding "cessation caused by karma": beginning from the single thought-moment of the phase of karma, it proceeds successively until the initiation of karma.

Once the initiation of karma is complete, this mind immediately ceases, thereby forming the seed of karma. The sixth coarse phase is the body of retributive suffering; as it is not a dharma that can be severed, it is not explained here. By severing one phase, one establishes one stage.
This establishes four stages, which are the four types of awakening mentioned in the text: (1) awakening to karma, (2) awakening to similarity, (3) awakening by degrees, and (4) ultimate awakening.
The remaining points should be understood in detail by consulting the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) below. Regarding the note on "the lack of fixed duration for extension or contraction":

A question arises as to whether the statement in the treatise that there is no fixed duration is a provisional teaching (*upāya*), while the fixed period of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is the definitive meaning. Why, then, does the present text say that this [period] is subject to extension and contraction?
There is no fixed [limit]. The answer is given in Sanskrit: *kalpa*. This is translated here as "time-period" (*shifen*).

Whether it be a great eon (*mahākalpa*) or a small eon (*antarakalpa*), whether long or short, down to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), all are termed "time-periods. *Asaṃkhyeya* means "innumerable"; the intended sense is "many.
When people of the world wish to speak of a long duration of time, they all say things such as "time of immeasurable number" or "unlimited time," which generally refers to years.

On certain days, or even within a single day, people may grow impatient with the passage of time and say things such as, "I have waited for countless ages and still have not seen [the Buddha]," and so forth.

Now, it is simply said that one attains Buddhahood after three immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Within this framework, there is no contradiction in some accounts describing the period as extended or others as abbreviated.

While the treatises state that it is fixed, they merely intend to establish the duration as three [immeasurable eons] and do not specifically point to "countless" (*asaṃkhya*) as the limit. Since it is already called "countless," how can this be?

It is capable of stabilization. Regarding these three capacities for stabilization: from the time one fulfills the aspiration of an ordinary person to generate the bodhicitta and practices through the cultivation of hearing, by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), after an immeasurable period of time, one attains direct realization of *tathatā* (suchness); this is called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). This constitutes one incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*).

After the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the two innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*) still remain and arise spontaneously and frequently. By the power of the noble path (*āryamārga*), one gradually abandons and cultivates them.

It is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that after an immeasurable period of time has passed, one attains a state where, without relying on effort, one naturally and moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*) proceeds toward cessation and enters the stream of the Dharma.
This is called the two incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). Following this spontaneous progression, it is by the very nature of things...

After an immeasurable period of time, one finally attains the relinquishing of inferior goodness and the abandonment of the indeterminate. This is the Buddha’s majestic deportment and transformative practice;

it is free from cultivation and free from realization, entering the ultimate while having nothing to enter. It is vast and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, taking the Dharma-realm as its body, transcending the measures of cause and effect, and continuing without interruption until the end of the future.
This is called the "three incalculable eons. However, these three are merely established for the sake of definition; they are not fixed.

There are no fixed numbers. Within these countless [eons], the lengthening or shortening of time depends respectively on the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties. Furthermore, time has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for it is seen only by the mind.
Thus, the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), in explaining the scriptural references to the number of eons, states that they may be expressed in terms of years, months, or days;

however, the Characteristics School (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*) establishes fixed durations, while the Nature School (*dharmatā-yāna*) holds that all is mind. (As it is said: "In a dream one thinks many years have passed, yet upon awakening it is but a brief moment. Therefore, those [fixed measures] are taught [only from the perspective of conventional truth].
This is not fixed. Therefore, the commentary explicitly states that this depends solely upon the extension or contraction of one's own mind.

△ The first section of the sub-commentary (Sū), "The initial dwelling is accomplished," has two parts: first, it is revealed by means of the Sūtra; second, from "That sub-commentary" onwards, it is explained by means of the sub-commentary. This can be seen by setting aside conceptual thought.

△ The fifth section of the sub-commentary (Sū), "In a single thought," has four parts: first, the direct demonstration; second, from "At the beginning of the dream" onwards, the illustration by means of a metaphor.

Third, the *Treatise* below cites scriptural evidence (citing one treatise and four sūtras to prove that awakening is itself Buddhahood). Furthermore, there is no distinction between initial awakening and fundamental awakening;

being in profound accord with fundamental awakening is precisely ultimate awakening. The *Treatise* states in full: "If one attains non-thought, one immediately knows the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of mental characteristics.

Because of non-thought, the four marks of sentient beings move and turn within a single thought-moment. Because [non-thought] is equal to [the state of] non-thought, it is the original nature of the thoughts of sentient beings."

When one comes to see that there is nothing [to be grasped], non-thought is equal to the Buddha; thus one is able to know it. Yet, in reality, there is no distinction between original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). As for initial enlightenment, it is the awakening to the four marks [of existence]; these four marks do not exist apart from original enlightenment.

This emptiness is without dependence; how, then, can one speak of a beginning? Therefore, it is followed by the statement: "All lack self-establishment," and so forth. Because the four characteristics exist simultaneously, they all lack self-establishment; they are fundamentally equal and identical with awakening.
As for the phrase "if one is free from deluded thoughts" and so on, this precisely refers to the moment of awakening in the preceding thought-moment.
It is realized that the originally existing awakening manifests upon the departure from thought; it is not something newly acquired. (From the *Sūtra of Vast, Sublime, and Pure [Adornment]*)

"We are now able to believe and understand this Dharma, and we give rise to no doubt or uncertainty. Why is this?

"If one were to say, 'I am the World-Honored One,' these words would indeed be a correct statement. Why is that? Because I [have given rise to no doubt or perplexity] regarding this Dharma."
Because they do not give rise to doubt or confusion. At that time, a third son of good family, who sought the Bodhisattva vehicle, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if one were to say, 'I am the Buddha,' this statement would indeed be a correct one. Why is this so?"
"Because I have no doubt regarding this Dharma. At that time, the minds of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the assembly were all agitated;
they could not remain settled in their seats and thought: "There are never two Buddhas appearing simultaneously in the world.

[The assembly] remained silent. The World-Honored One sat upon his seat and would himself explain the meaning of these words spoken by these bodhisattvas.

Abiding rightly within birth and death, he transforms and delivers all sentient beings; therefore he is called the World-Honored One.

One who has never given rise to fear is called the World-Honored One.
Having realized that all phenomena are non-existent, and having awakened to the fact that no phenomenon exists, he is therefore named Buddha.

Having awakened to the fact that ignorance and lack of knowledge are by nature non-existent, and having attained clear wisdom, therefore he is called a Buddha.
Knowledge, conduct, and the body are like the plantain tree; one who can realize this according to reality is therefore called a Buddha.

Fundamentally, there is no world to be eliminated, nor is there a dharma-realm to be realized. Originally it was not defiled, and now it is not pure.
Therefore, the sutra below says: "Originally there is neither bodhi nor nirvana; there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the failure to attain it; there is neither false saṃsāra nor..."
It is not saṃsāra. Based on this principle, how could there be a beginning of initial transformation or an end of ultimate realization?

Therefore, within the school of the True Teaching (Shōgyō-shū), it refers to the Provisional Teachings (Gonkyō) as having only the scriptural texts but lacking actual fruition. This is what the commentaries (*sho*) and expositions (*hyō*) indicate.
These two sentences in the commentary both employ the text of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. That text states: "Arising indicates that this dharma previously did not exist;

ceasing indicates that this dharma subsequently does not exist. Regarding the present abiding kalpa and so forth, the meaning of the four phases—abiding, formation, destruction, and emptiness—is as explained previously.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*) and so forth, this is spoken in terms of sentient experience. "Active manifestation" refers to the time when the perceiving mind and the perceived object correspond.
"Subduing" (*vinaya*) means to pacify and suppress the mind so that thoughts do not arise. When thoughts do not arise, objects do not exist independently;

therefore, all are brought to cessation. This is like the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), or the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

However, among the preceding six pairs, the first two apply to both sentient beings (*sattva*) and the physical world (*bhājana*). The next three pairs refer exclusively to the physical world, while this final pair refers exclusively to sentient beings.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of "self and what belongs to self" (*ātma-ātmīya*): "self" refers to sentient beings.
"What belongs to me" refers to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). "That which is the basis of suffering" refers to the body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Regarding the commentary’s mention of seeing real objects in a dream: suppose there is a person who, while dreaming beneath a window where books are kept, still sees himself lying beneath that same window.
Although the physical location is entirely real, that which is currently being perceived does not exist; this is a dream. △ Commentary: Four pairs of analogies.
In the first analogy, it is like when a person moves their eyeballs or rubs the corners of their eyes with their hands;
what is seen then becomes tilted, rotated, or a single object appears as two, and all such various distortions occur.
Now, the reason for mentioning only "water" is that water sometimes wavers due to causes other than the movement of the eyes, arising from its own distinct conditions.

As for "wave," one who blinks their eyes might suspect it occurs spontaneously and fail to recognize that it is caused by the eye; other things are not like this, which is why only the metaphor of water is used.

Next, regarding the phrase "the visual consciousness is dull," this explains the fixed nature of the eye. It implies that because the consciousness is sluggish and obstructed, it cannot swiftly catch up with the whirling firebrand;
thus it is called "fixed. This does not mean that only something utterly motionless, solid, and eternally unmoving can be termed "fixed."

Regarding meditative concentration: suppose a person takes a branch from a staff and holds it near the head; when it has been scorched by fire for about half an inch and becomes glowing red, they quickly rub and rotate it with their hand.
Immediately, the appearance of a red wheel manifests. If the branch of the staff is long and slightly curved, the appearance of the wheel will likewise be so.
It immediately expands and widens further. According to what is seen, it may appear to be three or two feet in circumference.
How could a fire that is only half an inch wide suddenly expand? Therefore, we know that it is merely the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that is dull and sluggish;

because it is not swift, it cannot keep pace with the turning of the fire, and thus it appears as if the entire perimeter were ablaze. When the Sūtra simply says "the eye," it speaks in accordance with worldly convention.

Regarding the general statement in the Commentary that it "also includes consciousness," this is an explanation of the meaning; however, one must specifically identify that which is directly capable of seeing.

Thus, the waves upon water and the fire-wheel [illusion] are merely the movement and stillness of the eye, serving as metaphors for how, within Perfect Enlightenment, seeing ordinary beings or seeing sages is nothing but the流转 (zhuanliu) of the deluded mind.
The shifting of the bank and the movement of the moon are merely like the rushing of clouds or the sailing of a boat; this is the same principle. "Rushing" (sì) means a swift current.
"Running hastily" refers to the manner [of the author]. Regarding the statement "The commentary (*śūtra*) is not yet a response to the difficulties," etc.:

someone composed a commentary stating that from the section on the arising and ceasing of the world up to this point is the response to the first difficulty; the metaphor of flowers in the sky responds to the second difficulty;

The Commentary states that this is to prevent a regressus ad infinitum. When the ultimate mystery is reached, names and words fall short; yet when divergent views arise, they lead to an endless succession.
