(In the four truths of the two higher realms, one instance of hatred is excluded from each, leaving twenty-eight afflictions per realm; totaling fifty-six. When combined with the thirty-two of the preceding desire realm, they constitute eighty-eight. All of these are abandoned by the Path of Seeing. The commentary states:

"Excluding the three views" refers to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Regarding the view of a self-body...

This is the root of suffering. When the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) is contemplated, it is already severed; since the view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi) relies upon the body, it is also severed accordingly.
Regarding the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya), one does not misapprehend what is not the path as being the path. Furthermore, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) is not a stage of practice.

Therefore, in these two truths, there is originally no grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) to be severed; hence it is said that one is "free from three views. As for the exclusion of two views regarding the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya), these are also the view of self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes.

The meaning is as explained above. Regarding "clinging to precepts and prohibitions" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it refers specifically to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), wherein one reckons what is not the path to be the path.

According to the intent of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, this refers solely to reckoning the mere observance of precepts as the cause for attaining the fruit, while failing to realize that the attainment of the fruit depends upon penetrating the principle and practicing meditative cultivation;
this constitutes clinging to precepts. It does not mean that only the precepts of chickens, dogs, and so forth constitute such clinging to precepts.

[The stage of] "Taking" (*ādāna*). In the higher realms, there is no anger; rather, there are stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Fundamentally, these afflictions do not exist there. Regarding the "sixteen moments of mind" mentioned in the commentary:

this refers to contemplating the Four Noble Truths of the desire realm, with one Patience (*kṣānti*) and one Knowledge (*jñāna*) for each, totaling eight. These are then combined with the corresponding categories of the Four Noble Truths of the two higher realms.

Observing the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one respectively achieves one category of patience (*kṣānti*) and one category of knowledge (*jñāna*); thus, there are sixteen. (Patience is the acceptance [of the truth]; knowledge is the decisive determination.

That is to say, when observing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), if it is truly as the Noble Teaching has taught—that it is indeed a dharma of suffering—and this is accepted within the mind, it is called "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*). When this acceptance is certain and the decisive determination is free from doubt, it is called "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*).

Likewise, observing that the Truth of Suffering of the two upper realms is also thus, it is called "subsequent patience regarding the knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*). With two each for the upper and lower realms, and the same being true for the remaining three Truths, there are eight patiences and eight knowledges in total; hence they are called the "sixteen moments of mind. [The *Śāstra* states: "Immediately upon entering cultivation..."

Regarding the "Path" (*mārga*): some say that all sixteen moments of mind constitute the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), while others say that the sixteenth moment already belongs to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Here, we adopt the latter interpretation. This is because, when following the analogy of the Mahāyāna, it is established by principle that at the time the Path of Seeing eliminates the two obstacles of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-āvaraṇa*), it also actually eliminates a small portion of the innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*).
Regarding the term *srotāpanna*: this is a Sanskrit word; here it is translated as "Stream-enterer. It means to enter into...

Because they belong to the class of the noble ones (*ārya*), they are also called "those who have entered the stream" (*srotāpanna*). Because they do not enter into form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects (*dharmas*), they enter the stream of the noble ones;

this refers to the eight stages of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), which constitute the essence of this fruit (taking only the eight knowledges [*jñānas*] and not the eight patiences [*kṣāntis*]). Regarding the phrase "the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm" (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) in the commentary:

those that obstruct the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are called "afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation. These are the four delusions—greed, hatred, ignorance, and pride—which arise from being deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*).

As for the statement that they are divided into nine grades: although there are four afflictions in total, when these are divided into light, medium, and heavy categories—nine grades in all—then each grade contains all four afflictions, and each individual affliction likewise possesses the nine grades.
It is like combining four flavors and forming them into a single mass of fragrance.
They are divided into great and small. As for the nine times nine, each set of nine possesses four flavors, and each flavor contains its own nine times nine.

Regarding the nine grades of lightness and heaviness, these refer to the upper-upper, upper-middle, and so on, down to the lower-middle and lower-lower. The commentary states that this extends up to the fifth grade;
this refers to the upper-upper, upper-middle, upper-lower, middle-upper, and middle-middle grades. "One-returner candidate" (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) is the Sanskrit term.
*Sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) is here translated as "one who returns once. This will be explained in the text below.

As for the term "candidate" (*pratipannaka*), it refers to a person in this stage who, if one were to designate them by their first fruit, has already abandoned five grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation;

yet, if one were to designate them by their second fruit, they have not yet abandoned the sixth grade. Because such a person is one who is progressing toward the second fruit, they are termed a "candidate. [Having abandoned] the six lower...

The two phrases can be understood [as follows]. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Having abandoned up to five [categories], one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six, one attains the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

The commentary explains the name "Once-returner" by referring to the nine grades [of defilements] starting from the lower. Regarding the statement that "afflictions moisten rebirth," it means that because these afflictions moisten karma, one takes birth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This refers to a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*); although they have abandoned the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), if they do not abandon the nine grades [of the path of cultivation], [they remain a Once-returner].
Regarding the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*): one must still come to birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) seven more times. It is like a venomous snake;
if it bites a person, even if that person exerts great strength, they cannot travel beyond seven paces and will inevitably die. The afflictions are likewise:

if they are severed by the wisdom of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga-jñāna*), the remaining afflictions of cultivation that moisten karma may strongly impel rebirth in the desire realm, yet they will be exhausted after no more than seven births.

Now that six grades [of afflictions] have been severed, one is exempt from moistening [the seeds of] six births; yet because one birth still remains, one must go once to the heavens and return once more to be born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), and is therefore called the "Once-Returner" (sakṛdāgāmin).

This fruit takes as its essence the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) state resulting from the abandonment of the six grades of afflictions through cultivation in the desire realm, combined with the unconditioned state resulting from the eight grades abandoned through the vision of the truths (darśana-mārga). Each successive grade [of abandonment] moistens two [births].

Regarding "one who is born" (*upapadya*): because their afflictions (*kleśa*) and heavy latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) are coarse, their afflictions gradually become lighter next, and the moisture for rebirth (*janman*) gradually diminishes;

the meaning of this can be understood. As for the commentary’s mention of "severing seven or eight [grades of] afflictions": this refers to a specific category in the *Abhidharmakośa* text, meaning that whether one has severed and attained the seventh grade or the eighth grade, both are termed "candidates" (*pratipannaka*).

(Following the previous example, it should be stated: severing one, two, three, four, or five grades is termed a "candidate for the Once-returner" [*sakṛdāgāmī-pratipannaka*]). This is because, having severed two grades, one is not yet [able to... *(Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end. The provided fragment discusses the classification of practitioners based on the number of affliction-grades severed, specifically citing the *Abhidharmakośa* regarding those who have severed up to the eighth grade as candidates for higher fruits.)*
One’s entire [future] life is forfeited; therefore, it is not called a "fruit. Only when the ninth grade is completely severed does one further forfeit the attainment of one more birth.
Since the afflictions of the lower grades have been exhausted, there is no longer any defilement to moisten [rebirth]; thus, one does not return again to the desire realm.

Therefore, they are called *anāgāmin* (Non-returner), also known as "one who does not come. In Sanskrit, this is precisely *anāgāmin*. This term generally encompasses the eight grades of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)...

The nine grades of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and constitute the essence of this fruit. Regarding the commentary’s statement that the upper two realms (*dhātu*) are abandoned sequentially:

because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the upper realms are subtle, they are categorized according to the nine stages (*bhūmi*), with nine grades for each stage; thus, they are abandoned in opposition to eighty-one grades.

(Now, a doubt arises: If one were to abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) all at once from the first fruit and immediately attain arhatship, there would be eighty-one categories. However, if one first attains the realization of the two higher realms and subsequently abandons them, there should be seventy-two categories in total, as each category consists of one path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Thus, it is said that "the afflictions of the two upper realms are abandoned," etc.

When the paths of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation are combined, there are eighty-nine categories of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas which constitute the essence of this fruit. [Specifically,] there are eight [categories] of seeing and eighty-one of cultivation. This is based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.)

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that the *anāgāmin* (non-returner) abandons the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), while the *arhat* abandons the five upper fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
This has been explained in detail in another fascicle. Regarding the term "Arhat," it is a Sanskrit word that has three translations in Chinese:

first, "one who is without thieves," because the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms—both those to be abandoned through vision and those to be abandoned through cultivation—have already been exhausted; second, "one who is not born," because they do not undergo further existence; and third, "one who is worthy."
"Offerings. Because one receives vast offerings from humans and devas, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Making offerings to an Arhat brings about retribution in the present life.

Regarding the commentary on "the accomplishment of my births," etc.: this refers to "my births are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further existence.
The first three phrases constitute the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), while the final phrase constitutes the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). If...

Discussed from beginning to end, there are in total ten knowledges (*jñāna*). Furthermore, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) entities that constitute the substance of these four fruits are all treated in separate fascicles.
The phrase "that which is perfected" and so forth concludes by returning to the scriptural text; "that which is personally realized" refers to the two types of *nirvāṇa*.

This is the Dharma realized and attained by those śrāvakas. Therefore, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one takes the intent [of the teaching] as the primary meaning, though the text itself states:
"Even if the entire world were filled with beings like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom," and so forth.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved [to attain enlightenment], who have made offerings to countless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. One...
The mind deliberates together [with its objects], yet it likewise cannot know them, and so forth.

Regarding the commentary’s first point, “lacking a substantial entity,” there are two parts: first, the explanation of the text; second, from “In this context, beginning and end” onwards, the elimination of confusion.

To say it “lacks an entity” means that this mind is originally empty by nature; because it has no name, it is said to lack an entity. This does not merely refer to an entity as contrasted with its function.
Yet it is said that they have no substance.

Regarding the four conclusions in the commentary (*shu*), there are two parts: first, distinguishing against confusion; second, posing questions regarding the preceding praise and subsequently resolving objections.

As for the phrase "mutually having and mutually lacking" in the commentary: in the prose (*changxing*) version, there is no mention of relying on understanding to give rise to practice, yet there are concluding questions; this does not accord with reason.
In the verse there is no concluding question, yet there is practice arising from reliance on the explanation.
This concludes the chapter on Thoroughly Investigating Saṃsāra (The Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva).
Regarding the commentary on the five eyes: first is the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). This refers to the pure form within the physical mass of flesh, which is able to see forms obstructed by barriers.

Second, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): based upon the fleshly eye, it induces the pure divine eye to see forms beyond obstructions. Third, the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*): by means of fundamental gnosis (*mūlaprajñā*), it illuminates and perceives ultimate truth.
Fourth, the dharma eye (*dharmacakṣus*): by means of subsequently attained gnosis (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it expounds the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. Fifth, the Buddha eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
The first four [eyes] reside in the Buddha and are all termed the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*). Furthermore, because the nature of seeing is perfectly fulfilled, it is called the Buddha-eye.

Thus, an ancient master said: "The celestial eye (*divyacakṣus*) penetrates without obstruction; the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is obstructed and lacks penetration. The dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) observes only the conventional;

the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) directly takes emptiness as its object. The Buddha-eye is like a thousand suns: while they illuminate different forms, their essence remains the same. Other meanings are found in a separate fascicle. Regarding the "wondrous faith" (*adhimukti*) in the commentary:
According to the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, not believing in anything is called "wondrous faith" (*miao-xin*).
Wondrous faith is the wisdom that is capable of believing, while the eternally abiding [nature] is the dharma that is believed.

Since this sutra states, "One gives rise to decisive faith in Great Nirvana," it cites wondrous faith and eternal abiding as proof (because eternal abiding is Great Nirvana). Furthermore, this mind of wondrous faith can simply be constant...

Abiding, without falling back and without losing [the state], one’s deluded imaginings are utterly extinguished; thus both intentions are encompassed. Regarding the commentary’s statement, “not clinging to the movement of the moon and so forth”:
although this employs a metaphor, the intent lies in the Dharma itself. The Dharma refers to the beginning and end, arising and ceasing, and so forth of all worlds.
Nevertheless, even though those present at the assembly have attained realization of the Buddha’s teaching, they do not cease to still perceive the arising and ceasing of the world.

As for these marks: simply understand that they arise from the transformations of the mind, and that these transforming marks are themselves empty. Do not grasp at them or recognize them as real. Therefore, the Sūtra says, "no longer following after them.
This does not mean that one does not see them at all before one's eyes. Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, "desiring to roam in cessation," it means not abiding in Nirvāṇa;
thus, it is called "roaming. As for "the single root," it is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). How many kinds of distinctions are there? [The answer follows: etc.

Below. The Sūtra says: "Various forms of affection, craving, and desire. Furthermore, because one craves the commission of transgressions, craves the places of rebirth, and craves superior, pure, wondrous, and beneficial things;
and because one craves five kinds of dharmas, these form the five natures through perfuming.
Regarding the phrase "the dharma-gates are boundless" and so forth: this corresponds to two of the Four Great Vows.

When a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind on enlightenment, they must necessarily possess these four. Now, as one cultivates the path in accordance with these vows, how could one possibly be separated from them?

The previous question regarding the severing of saṃsāra corresponds to the vow to sever all boundless afflictions; the present question regarding the cultivation of bodhi is precisely the vow to attain unsurpassed Buddha-way.

May it be fulfilled. Desiring to achieve the wisdom of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), one must extensively study the Dharma gates; thus, within this interval, this vow is further subsumed: entering the dust [of the world] to save sentient beings.
The text makes this clear of itself. The four great vows are complete. Regarding the phrase "adding ice to a small amount of hot water":

the "hot water" is like wisdom, and the "ice" is like afflictions (*kleśa*). When one with little wisdom enters the dust to transform and save sentient beings, they do not realize that they themselves have spontaneously produced worldly thoughts. It is as if taking...
A little hot water melts ice; yet the hot water itself may freeze. In the past, when I was in the capital and preparing to enter the mountains, I once spoke this verse:

"When hot water is poured to melt the ice in the pond, the ice remains firm and the water likewise freezes. If one holds water and pours it into the cauldron, the needle and the eye will naturally meet.

Having spoken this verse, I entered the mountains, where I remain to this day. Regarding the phrase "the great compassion of detachment from attachment and views," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
That sick bodhisattva should further reflect: "Just as this illness of mine is neither real nor existent, so too the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent.
When making this contemplation, if one gives rise to a great compassion based on affectionate attachment toward sentient beings, [one must recognize it as such].
One should immediately abandon them. Why is this? A bodhisattva eliminates adventitious afflictions and gives rise to great compassion;
however, one whose compassion is based on attachment and views will experience weariness and aversion toward birth and death. If one can remain free from these, there will be no weariness.

In every place of rebirth, one is not obscured by craving or views. Even to the point where there is no bondage of wisdom through lack of skillful means, there is liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
As for the phrase "a mind as clear as a bright mirror": the original nature of the minds of all sentient beings is like a bright, clear mirror; it is not... [obscured].
It is like a mirror stained by dust; only the Venerable Master Huineng, with his wisdom-eye cleared and purified, can illuminate it.

Fools, being deluded and inverted, cannot illuminate it. Therefore, the Sixth Patriarch was able to transmit the seal of the mind. It is not that the Sixth Patriarch’s mind alone was as pure as a mirror.
If we speak according to the gate of dependent origination, gradually severing habitual tendencies and following worldly convention, there is no contradiction in saying it is so.

Only when the dust is wiped away does the mirror of the mind become clear. The origin of this verse has already been explained in detail within the eighth section of the *Xuantan*, the "Gate of the Stages of Cultivation and Realization.
Regarding the statement that the commentary (*shu*) is identical to the *Lotus Sūtra*, that sūtra states:

"I wish to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Vasubandhu’s commentary (*lun*) judges this by stating: "'Opening' signifies the sense of being unsurpassed; it is the simultaneous opening of both."
Bodhi and Nirvana are both supreme; that is to say, apart from the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna), there is nothing else, and thus they are called "supreme.
The present sutra speaks of "unsurpassed knowledge and vision," which precisely accords with this meaning; therefore, it is said to be identical.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary [describes them as] profound and abstruse," etc.: if one were to speak of saṃsāra within the context of defiled objects, or discuss categories within the context of distinctions, that would be considered superficial;
such is merely a matter of common worldly understanding. Now, however, the textual passages of these three chapters have already revealed that ignorance has no real substantiality;
fundamentally, there is no body or mind, nor birth and death. From the faculties and objects to the internal and external, nothing is not pure.
Perfect enlightenment shines universally; it is quiescent and non-dual. Even down to all sentient beings, they have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning.

Layer upon layer, this is revealed and made manifest, such that principle and wisdom are clearly apparent. Now, within this purity, you inquire about the dharma of saṃsāra through a cycle of question and answer.
Furthermore, within the state of non-duality, there are various distinctions in the categories of questions and answers; therefore, it is profound, secret, and subtle.

Regarding the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) in the commentary, there are five sections. First is the formal explanation of non-arising. As for the statement "realizing that the mind is non-arising," it refers to the deluded mind...

1. Fundamentally, there is nothing that can arise; the true mind is inherently present and does not depend on new production. 2. Since these two dharmas have already been explained by analogy as being without cessation, 3. "Therefore, in the *Avataṃsaka*...
and so forth, this section provides a general proof for the absence of both arising and cessation. 4. "Therefore, in the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā*...

and so forth, this section provides a specific proof for the absence of cessation. 5. "However, there is no arising... and so forth, this section provides a detailed explanation of the absence of arising and cessation, which consists of two parts: first, stating the intention and providing a general heading.
Next, the opening chapter is first explained in detail. Regarding the initial section:

as for what is called "the essence of the Buddha-dharma," it is because all ordinary beings who resolve their minds to seek the Buddha-way do so solely because they are distressed by the suffering of birth and death; once they realize non-arising, they are immediately liberated from this distress.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. Hence, it is called the essence of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding "the beginning of the Eight Negations" in the Commentary (*Shu*): this refers to the first verse of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, which sets forth the tenets of the treatise, stating:

"Neither arising nor ceasing; neither permanent nor annihilated; neither identical nor different; neither coming nor going. This immediately employs the gateway of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) to explain the meaning of non-arising;
hence it is called "the beginning of the Eight Negations. Regarding "the object" (*viṣaya*) in the Commentary: it refers to the principle (*tattva*) that is the focal object (*ālambana*).

Regarding the objects of reality, falsity, and delusion: the practitioner’s capacity to take as objects the mental states and the meanings traversed by the mind and intellect—whether these thoughts be defiled or pure.

As for the commentary’s reference to the "imputed nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and so forth: each of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) possesses two pairs of meanings concerning arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing.

In all cases, the former pair provides a general indication, while the latter pair provides a specific correlation. Now, within the context of the *parikalpita* (the imagined nature), each pair possesses two meanings:

first, in terms of subjective emotion (*qing*), and second, in terms of principle (*li*). Regarding the first pair, which provides a general indication: "erroneous attachment" refers to emotion, while "non-existence of phenomena" refers to principle.

Here, however, because one relies on principle itself, one contemplates that such emotion is non-existent; therefore, it is called a "general indication. The subsequent pair states: "Furthermore, [it is] non-existent in principle," and so forth.

This refers to the meaning of the one side of non-arising as explained from the perspective of principle (li), and the meaning of the one side of non-extinction as explained from the perspective of emotional cognition (qing);

this constitutes a specific correlation. Furthermore, regarding the person who has attained awakening, they contemplate the dharmas imagined by the deluded person; this is the "correlation through contrast" for the sake of the awakened one.

One may personally observe that all phenomena also possess the meaning of being neither arising nor ceasing. However, non-arising is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), whereas non-ceasing is not the ultimate reality.

It is simply because, when one correctly penetrates the principle that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature through wisdom, the mind still perceives the characteristics of substantiality and obstruction within the realm of consciousness;
thus, from the perspective of such mental consciousness, it is said that they do not cease. This is like the case of a person with worldly knowledge.

When the mind reaches the state where empty flowers are entirely non-existent, yet the chaotic appearances of flowers are still manifest before one's eyes, this is precisely what is called "non-extinction.
Regarding the phrase "a single dharma": that which the mind perceives as present does not arise; that which the eye perceives as not arising is the present.

This correspondence between phenomena can be understood. Therefore, it is called "a single dharma. In the second section of the commentary, concerning the *paratantra* (dependent nature), there are also two meanings: first, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the second [of the two] absences of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*): in the first [section], which addresses the middle [truth], it says, "That which arises through the convergence of conditions is itself non-arising," and so forth.
All phenomena are like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water. This means that above there is the moon in the sky and below there is clear water;

this is the convergence of causes and conditions. Then, within the water, a lunar disc suddenly appears. That which was originally non-existent and now exists is a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions (the meaning of dependent origination).
To realize this is that it does not descend from the heavens, nor does it emerge from the bottom of the water; this is non-arising (the meaning of being without intrinsic nature).
Whether the water dries up or the moon sets in the sky, these are the severance of conditions; thus, the moon in the water is no longer seen—this is cessation.

(Regarding the meaning of dependent origination: To realize that what was previously existing is not coming from a path and has only now ceased to be is "non-extinction" (the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature).
Non-arising also employs two meanings, and non-extinction likewise employs two meanings; therefore, it is said that these are collectively revealed as a single pair.

In the subsequent pair, the absence of intrinsic nature is assigned to non-arising, and dependent origination is assigned to non-extinction; thus, it is called a "distinctive assignment. The text states: "Dependent origination is non-existent..."
Regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*): although the term "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is raised, the intended meaning is "the absence of nature.

This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the absence of nature in dependent origination," rather than a statement of two simultaneous meanings. As for "dependent origination of the absence of nature," this refers to explaining dependent origination by means of the absence of nature.

The meaning is as explained above. Regarding the citation of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, it serves to prove that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) exists as a phenomenal phenomenon precisely because of the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

The meaning of [the phrase] "being a single entity" is thus understandable. However, the meaning that the phenomena of dependent origination are definitively without intrinsic nature is explained in detail in the "Dharma-Emptiness Gate" chapter of the *Puyan* (Universal Eye) section;
if one wishes to state it again, one should consult the relevant passage in that commentary. — From the *Śu* (Commentary).
Third, regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there are also two meanings: namely, the essential nature (*tattva*) and the relative (*pratītya*).
However, while in the previous two sections both meanings were applied collectively to each pair, here one meaning is applied to each of the two pairs respectively.

In the first pair, the essential nature reveals the true nature of the perfected reality as being free from birth and cessation. As the text says, "that which is non-arising" refers to this very nature.
"There is no dharma of arising for that" means that this nature is not the non-arising of that;

"saying there is no cessation" means that this nature lacks the dharma of cessation for that, rather than meaning this nature is the non-cessation of that. As for the subsequent "mutual correspondence," this refers to the two minds of delusion and awakening.

It speaks only of the three periods (*trikāṇḍa*): namely, dependent origination from the first period to the middle period, and from the middle period to the last period.
It does not mean three times, two times, two pasts, five presents, three presents, or two futures.
The commentary on that sūtra was composed by Vasubandhu; Vasubandhu’s *Pratītyasamutpādavyākhyā* also speaks of the three periods, as in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

...and so forth. (The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 9, states: "By obtaining the preceding seven [links], there is craving, grasping, and becoming; by obtaining these three, there is birth, aging, and death.
As for the "three periods" mentioned here, this is a mistranslation intended to conform to human expectations. Now, we refute this: the treatise and the sūtra permit such a [correct] translation.

Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* translated during the Jin dynasty and the reign of Empress Wu also agrees with the treatise in speaking of the three periods. As for the original Sanskrit text, it was translated as follows: [text omitted].
Regarding the term "those who speak": [the texts] were compiled, refined, and verified by various individuals who lived at different times and were separated by vast intervals of years.

If this were a mistranslation, how could so many have made the same error? Even granting that they might have coincidentally erred together, why would the error occur precisely in this specific section?

Therefore, we know that these masters merely claimed it was a scriptural error whenever they encountered passages they did not understand or where the doctrinal tenets differed from their own. Such instances abound.
Furthermore, it is likely that you have been naturally indulgent and self-indulgent by nature; I also fear you may not be able to seek out the Sanskrit manuscripts from the previous dynasty.

Even if the Sanskrit manuscript says "the three limits" (*trikāla*), it intends to mean the "three periods" (*tryadhvan*), because the other two versions of the sutra likewise refer to the three periods.
Regarding the phrase "from this point onward" in the commentary, it refers to the second section. This means that if one does not obtain the remedy, there will still be future lives.
From one future life to another, and from one subsequent life to the next, it continues infinitely; therefore, it is called "saṃsāra" (flowing on).
It is like the flow of water that never ceases, revolving without end.

In the commentary on the section concerning the separation and combination of the seven causes and effects, there are two parts: first, the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) school; second, the *dhātu* (nature) school. Within the first part, there are six sections. The first explains according to a single cycle:

that is, because ignorance (*avidyā*) has no source from which it arises, it is solely a cause; because old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) have nothing from which they arise, they are solely an effect. As for those that are both cause and effect:

taking the link of formations (*saṃskāra*) as a reference, it is an effect in relation to ignorance and a cause in relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*); this continues up to birth (*jāti*), which is an effect in relation to existence (*bhava*).
It serves as the fruit; with respect to old age and death, it serves as the cause. △ The commentary states: "If one reveals [the following]...

This refers to the second section, which explains according to the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), specifically the concluding passage of the third section, the "Gate of Karmic Function," previously explained. Furthermore, this is found within the ten topical meanings in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā*.
The eighth section is the "Gate of Explaining Various Objections through the Analysis of Abolishing, Establishing, Increasing, and Decreasing.

It states that ignorance has improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as its cause, and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) has sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction as its fruit. This is cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*’s *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.

However, this is intended to show that [the sequence] is not strictly mandatory, as explained in another fascicle. Furthermore, in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there is also a question: "If [it is asked] regarding the object..."

Regarding the statement that there are "only twelve members of arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this is because the fruit of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is not mentioned; otherwise, birth and death would have an end. Nor is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*) mentioned;

otherwise, birth and death would have a beginning. Alternatively, one would have to establish further members of dependent origination, and those further members would require yet more, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
The treatise answers this itself: "There is no need to establish further [members], yet the aforementioned fault does not apply. In this context, by way of meaning, the Blessed One [taught thus].

It has already been explained. How has it been explained? The verse says: "From afflictions arise further afflictions and karma" (this has two meanings). [Now, I shall provide an explanatory commentary on this verse. From afflictions arise further afflictions and karma. (This has two meanings.)

1. Because grasping (*upādāna*) arises from craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is said that "affliction gives rise to affliction. 2. Because existence (*bhava*) arises from grasping, it is said that "affliction gives rise to karma" (where karma refers to *saṃskāra*). From karma, the actual entity (*vastu*) arises (this refers to consciousness, *vijñāna*; furthermore, birth arises from existence).

From the actual entity, the actual entity and affliction arise (this also has two meanings: First, the actual entity arises from the actual entity: this means that consciousness gives rise to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so on, up to contact giving rise to feeling (*vedanā*), and birth giving rise to old age and death;

hence it is called "actual entity to actual entity. Second, affliction arises from the actual entity: this means that feeling gives rise to craving. There should also be the term "birth" arising from old age and death, and [the cycle] above. The first instance of the word "entity" (*vastu*) refers to that which produces, while the second instance of the word "entity-affliction" (*vastu-kleśa*) refers to that which is produced. The two instances of the phrase "from birth" are used twice over. Existence (*bhava*).

The underlying principle follows this (the commentary explains and addresses the objection). △ Regarding the passage "Furthermore, ignorance... and below: the third [section] explains by way of the root and the branches. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi shu) states:
"Ignorance, craving, and grasping—these three are afflictions (*kleśa*) by nature; because they are the root of karma and suffering, they are exclusively causes.

Birth and old age/death—these two are by nature exclusively suffering, as they are the fruits of delusion and karma. Those that pertain to both the root and the branches are the five [factors] beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

It refers to the seeds (*bīja*), the formations (*saṃskāra*), and existence (*bhava*). Furthermore, as for "also being causes": these are the causes of birth, old age, and death. As for "also being fruits": these are the fruits of the afflictions (*kleśa*). [Commentary]:

Regarding the section "Furthermore, the causes of delusion," etc., this fourth point explains it in terms of the three paths (*trivartman*). (The previous explanation consisted of three causes and two fruits, with seven factors common to both cause and fruit; this, however, consists of three causes and seven fruits, with two factors common to both cause and fruit.

Therefore, it differs from the former. The causes of delusion are ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*). They are that which can initiate karma (*karma-pravartaka*) and moisten karma (*karma-paripuṣṭaka*); thus, they are the [causes] of karma.
The proximate cause is the conditional cause of suffering. As for "suffering," it refers to the five links beginning with consciousness, as well as birth, aging, and death.
These are the immediate effects of karma and the remote effects of afflictions. Regarding karma as pervading both cause and effect: it is the effect of afflictions and the cause of suffering.

△ In the commentary, from "Furthermore, regarding afflictions and karma" onwards, the fifth section explains five causes and seven effects in relation to the Four Noble Truths. Viewing them in reverse order refers to the two truths of Cessation and the Path.
△ In the commentary, from "Moreover, all ten" onwards, the sixth section explains this in terms of the two time periods.

Since all ten belong to the same single present life, they are collectively considered causes; only the [results] such as birth and so forth, which pertain to future lives, are therefore finally designated as effects. However, there is [a discussion] in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識疏).
There are five layers of cause and effect: first, the cause and effect of simultaneous arising (*samutthāna*), which refers to the entirety of the first cycle mentioned above;
that is to say, among the twelve links, each preceding factor corresponds to each succeeding one, and because many factors arise simultaneously as effects, it is called "simultaneous arising.

Second, the cause and effect of root and branch (*mūla-śākhā*), also as explained above. Third, the cause and effect of maturation (*vipāka*) and non-maturation. Fourth, the cause and effect of the matured and the immature. Fifth...
Regarding "proper maturation" and "improper maturation," both are as described in other fascicles. In the commentary (*shu*), the section beginning with "Furthermore, the True Mind...

pertains to the second school, the Nature School (*xingzong*). It is like a sleeping person; [the mind] is the cause of dream-thoughts, the dream-body, and dream-objects, etc. The citations from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and others are as previously explained.
However, regarding Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*), there are subsequent explanations through various gates, namely: the nine real and three provisional [dharmas] (including existence and...).

Birth, aging, and death have already moistened the six links; because they combine to constitute existence (*bhava*), once these six links are combined to form the link of aging, the link of existence has no separate substance.

Thus, the five [links] beginning with consciousness are distinguished by three phases, which are designated as birth and so forth. Since these two links (birth/aging-death) are identical in substance to consciousness and the others, one knows that they lack an intrinsic nature of their own and are therefore merely provisional designations.

Among the five results, four are single entities (ignorance, consciousness, contact, and feeling), while the others are not single entities. Three are exclusively defiled (the afflictions), and seven are exclusively non-defiled (suffering).

The others pertain to both types (of karma). Three are unique characteristics (because ignorance, craving, and grasping do not intersect with all other factors). The rest are characterized by separation. Six are exclusively non-material (ignorance, consciousness, contact, feeling, craving, and grasping);
the others pertain to both types. All are contaminated (*sāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Following this, there are further [categories]:

the three natures, the three realms, the moistening agent and the moistened, the learned (*śaikṣa*), the non-learned (*aśaikṣa*), the abandoned, the three feelings, the three sufferings, and the four truths.
The analysis of the three paths and so forth is as explained in a separate fascicle.

In the commentary (*śāstra*), section eight, "The Manifestation of Both the Provisional and the Real," there are two parts: first, the question and answer that state the intent; second, the detailed exposition based on the sutra. Within the first part, the question and answer are further divided into two.

Regarding the phrase "categories of nature" (*prakṛti-jāti*) in the question: "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the nature of the faculties (*indriya-prakṛti*) and the lineage of the seeds (*gotra-prakṛti*), meaning the inclination toward the wholesome.

"Those" refers to the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, which also constitute "lineage" (*gotra*), namely the lineages of the three vehicles (*triyāna-gotra*), as well as the natures of being dominated by greed, hatred, or delusion, along with their various inclinations (*ruci*), each of which is likewise distinct.
"Category" (*jāti*) refers to types, such as physical characteristics, forms, and substances.

The forms of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) and the appearances of the six realms of existence (*ṣad-gati*) differ according to their respective types; yet, as for those that possess no distinction of superiority or inferiority, they all fully possess the twelve [links of dependent origination].

*Commentary:* Regarding the section "Answering the Ten Thousand Dharmas" below, there are three parts within the answer: first, overturning the intent of the question; second, explaining the purpose for establishing this gate.
The third section correctly establishes this gate. Regarding the first part: the initial four lines clarify the root of the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).

Although they generally speak of "all phenomena" (*dharmas*), the intent is specifically directed toward the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the twelve links. That they exist due to delusion is precisely the meaning of emptiness. The subsequent four lines directly address the question posed:
the first line restates the question, while the [remaining] three lines respond to it. The statement that "awakening arises from the faculty" clarifies...
He establishes the teachings and commands them to observe; because the faculties of those to be converted differ, the teachings consequently vary.

The commentary cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to provide proof for these levels of depth. This principle—that the fundamental and derivative teachings correspond to varying depths—has been stated repeatedly throughout the preceding and following sections.

△ The sub-commentary (*shu*) intends to point toward what follows below. Second, it articulates the purpose for establishing this section. The first two phrases exclude the possibility of questioning based on what preceded.
This means one should ask in succession: "Since the teachings are each distinct, which teaching speaks that accords with the ultimate reality?

Please provide a guide. (This is like seeing a guide-cart that definitively distinguishes north from south. Therefore, it says here, "desiring to cause," and so forth. This means that according to the ultimate reality, there is only Buddha-nature;
the twelve [links of dependent origination] do not exist at all. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The twelve links of dependent origination are themselves Buddha-nature. (Commentary)

The second section, "Wishing to Understand," also consists of two lines that respond to questions in succession. The question asks: "Up to this point, you have asked about the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the twelve links of dependent origination;

why is it said that these constitute 'understanding'? Who has asked about the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), and why is it subsumed within true nature (*tathatā*)? Therefore, the next response follows:
"If one wishes to understand the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination, one must thoroughly investigate the teachings of the Sage from beginning to end. Thus it is said:
The teaching extends to many gates; each and every one must be fully understood and integrated. The first two phrases of the commentary clarify the error of partial study.
The latter two phrases clarify that only through complete learning can one achieve true understanding. "The staffs are all gold" is a metaphor borrowed from the five schools of the Hīnayāna.
As it is said there: "It is like analyzing a golden staff; the substance of the gold is no different. The commentary continues: "However, regarding..."

The four lines also follow from what precedes. This means that someone might ask: "Since each teaching is expounded according to the capacity [of the listener], it would be appropriate for one to practice according to one's own inclination;
why must one master both the provisional and the ultimate? Therefore, the answer is given: "For one who practices for their own sake, it is indeed as you say;

those at shallow and deep levels each attain the essential meaning" (the note citing the intent of the four types is also as previously explained; the meaning of 'merely specializing' and so forth can be understood). However, if one wishes to...
One who serves as a master revered by others must first master both the provisional (upāya) and the ultimate (tattva); only then may they employ these to deliver beings according to their capacities.

In the commentary following the term "Pure Name" (viśuddhanāman), it is proven that there is a profound dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). By "profound," one understands the exclusion of the shallow. Within the sub-commentary: the dependent origination of the six consciousnesses is what is explained in the Hīnayāna;
the dependent origination of the eight consciousnesses is what is explained in the Mahāyāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa school. [The dependent origination of] the dharma-nature (dharmatā)...

Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) belongs to the Hīnayāna. Regarding the phrase "severing all false views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): false views also differ in their coarseness and subtlety; therefore, the text says "all.

This refers to [the analysis of] dependent origination within the six consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and so forth. When these are compared with one another in sequence, the preceding is considered false.
The subsequent stages serve to sever [the afflictions]. However, regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the earlier stages are shallow and the later stages are deep;

regarding false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the earlier stages are coarse and the later stages are subtle. [Commentary: Regarding the seven sections mentioned above, this third part correctly establishes the present section.

The first four lines connect the preceding with the following. As for the "seven sections," they refer to the previous seven gates. "The meaning is already complete" refers to the existence of both the Hīnayāna meaning and the Sarvāstivāda (Phenomenal) school.
"Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the meaning of the Nature School (*xingzong*). The phrase "for this reason, below" introduces the subsequent two sentences;

it anticipates the doubt that one might exclusively adopt the meaning of the Nature School while discarding the *dharma-lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The *Sūtra Commentary* states, "Now, [I] merely rely upon... and so forth.

Since a single teaching inherently possesses both the shallow and the profound, we know that to claim it is either exclusively shallow or exclusively profound is itself a provisional (*upāya*) teaching. Only when the profound and the shallow mutually illuminate one another can it be considered a definitive (*nītārtha*) teaching.
That which penetrates the preceding explanations refers to the first and seventh of the ten successive layers below.
The second layer penetrates the second gate; the third layer is identical to the third gate; the fifth layer penetrates the seventh gate;
and the sixth layer penetrates the fourth and sixth gates. As for the first gate, it serves merely as a general overview.

The *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) sets forth the essential substance. As for the reason why the *Shu* (Commentary) adds numerical categories where there is no distinction of depth or shallowness, it refers to the three layers consisting of the seventh, ninth, and tenth [chapters].
Regarding the "提綱" (*Tigang*, Outline), it does not list the explanations in full, leaving it to those who examine the text to verify them.

One should carefully investigate within each subsequent section how the three contemplations (*sanguan*) observe their objects, what they know, and how they counteract [afflictions], thereby discerning the depth or shallowness, partiality or completeness, of the various phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. This is according to the same treatise.

The Master [Xuanzang] stated: "The meaning of dependent origination according to the Hīnayāna is explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*. The meaning of dependent origination according to the Dharma-characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) is subsumed within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, among others.
Now, this meaning of dependent origination according to the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

All these treatises were composed by Vasubandhu; therefore, it is said that they are the same. (Although the prose commentary of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* was not composed by Vasubandhu, since it is the *Vijñaptimātratā*..."
(The root verses are the basis of this meaning. "Those who fortunately practice them together" refers to those who consult with masters of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Since these are both the teachings of a single Bodhisattva, how can one cling to the former while doubting the latter?

The commentary states: "As for 'the Sūtra says below,' the second section fully elucidates this based on the Sūtra. It consists of seven parts: first, a general indication of the text and its meaning; second, an explanation of the meaning following the text;
third, a preliminary judgment of its meaning; fourth, a detailed pointing-out of its meaning; fifth, the harmonious integration of nature (svabhāva) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa);

sixth, the correlation with the four causal natures; and seventh, a summary of its essentials. Now, regarding the first: 'it is said that there are ten levels' clarifies that these are arranged vertically."

This is not an arbitrary interpretation. It refers to the ten types of observation, which are all identical to the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), as there is no separate dharma apart from them.
Regarding the commentary, I have previously provided annotations by citing and explaining the scriptural passages; these were concluded at the end of the preceding exposition.

Since those original scriptures were not included here, I have now extracted and recorded the essential notes beneath each concluding phrase. This is because it was previously stated that the explanation was finished, and thus...

It is annotated again; thus it is said, "it is reversed. Regarding the fact that the annotations follow the text in its forward order: the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*) is that observing the meaning of the text in reverse is largely the same [as the forward order].

Furthermore, because the faults of the seven preceding sections are coarse and the faculties of the persons being addressed are inferior, they are treated as faults by way of the forward order, while observing them in reverse serves as the antidote.
The latter three are the opposite of this; therefore, one is instructed to observe both the forward and reverse orders.
Regarding the illness, it shall be understood below. As for the notes on the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), they are found below; here they are also briefly correlated.

The first corresponds to the second, the contemplation of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) that accords with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). The remaining two contemplations will be correlated later. However, in the intervening sections where the scriptural text is analyzed, [the correlations are provided].
Furthermore, interspersed throughout, there is the meaning of the first "correlative contemplation" (*pratyavekṣā*).
What the commentary refers to as "below" constitutes the second part: the word-by-word explanation of the meaning. Each instance of the character *gu* (hence) represents one layer;

what is now called "the continuity of the links of existence" (*bhavāṅga-saṃtati*) is the first. The note stating "from 'World-Knower' (*lokavid*)" onwards marks the commencement of the scriptural text. This...
Within a single layer, there are inherently two layers of dependent origination; therefore, the cited sutra contains two instances of the word "etc.

Regarding the phrase "the manner of the arising of its meaning has been briefly explained," this was already concluded in the first section of the second gate, which provides a detailed explanation of the distinctions between the characteristics of the perfected answer within the contemplation of the distinctions of the marks of truth (*lakṣaṇasatyavibhāga*).
As for the treatise’s judgment that it is "ignorance" (*moha*) and so forth, this refers to the second [section].
Within the contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā-vipaśyanā*), there are four types of contemplation: first, contemplating how sentient beings are deluded and inverted;

second, seeking liberation elsewhere; third, seeking liberation through heterodox paths; and fourth, seeking a different kind of liberation. This [first point] refers to those who, though [the world is] without self by way of causes and conditions, nevertheless cling to a self.
This is precisely what was indicated above in the sūtra concerning "the taking of birth in the world," etc. The full text states: "The world..."
All intermediate births arise from attachment to a self. If one is free from this attachment, there is no place for birth. Furthermore, he reflects:

"Ordinary beings, lacking wisdom, cling to a self; they constantly seek existence and non-existence (the former is ignorance), engage in improper reflection, give rise to deluded formations, and proceed upon deviant paths—namely, unwholesome actions, meritorious actions, and immovable actions (these are the 'formations' limb, etc.). This constitutes the first layer of dependent origination. (Note)

Regarding the phrase "the causal conditions [arise] from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)": this refers to the aforementioned sūtra passage beginning with "in the ultimate sense," and so forth.

To state it in full: "Furthermore, one reflects: because of the lack of understanding regarding the ultimate sense, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). The karmic fruit produced thereby is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)."
The practice based on the initial mind is consciousness; continuing until the destruction of the aggregates is death (this constitutes the latter cycle of dependent origination).

As for those who are deluded regarding the truths, this refers to what was stated above: "not understanding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Because [the sūtra] is subsumed within a single mind, the commentary states:
"The text and meaning are both as explained above. This refers to the preceding fifth section. "Both" means both the text and the meaning. Sūtra.

Regarding "due to the differentiation of one's own karma," this is the third section. Within the text, there are two parts: first, a direct explanation referring back to the previous [section], which is the third gate;
second, the treatise’s judgment below, which further employs the treatise for explanation. This latter part also has two sections: first, the coarse [explanation];

second, the general presentation of the three gates, followed by the specific explanation of this gate alone. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, the formal presentation and explanation; second, this...
"Toppling downward" reveals that which is to be refuted below. The initial statement, "The treatise judges these four gates below," refers to the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth gates.
"For the sake of those on heterodox paths and so forth" refers to the third of the four contemplations within the previously listed Great Compassion Contemplation.
Regarding the phrase "but a single thought-moment," etc.: when not a single thought arises, that is the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because ignorance is absent, the formations (*saṃskāra*) and subsequent links are all non-existent. This is the fundamental path for seeking liberation; to seek it elsewhere is to follow a divergent path.
Thus, it says next, "yet one seeks separately," which is why it is called "divergent. Regarding the commentary on "this inversion," etc., the second [point] clarifies what is to be eliminated.
Furthermore, because there are four objects to be refuted, the Sūtra presents these four levels of dependent origination. The Śāstra states: "There are three kinds of causes for inversion:

the cause of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the cause of a sovereign lord (*īśvara*), the cause of ascetic practices, and the cause of no-cause (*ahetu*). (Including this view of no-cause, which is a single misconception, they constitute the four objects to be refuted.

These are refuted respectively by the four gates. This note explains that the present gate refutes [the first], while the second gate exclusively explains this very section. That is to say, the Saṃgha...
The Kaṇādas and others posit twenty-five principles (*tattva*), the first of which is primordial nature (*prakṛti*). From this, the remaining twenty-four [principles] arise.
Regarding the statement that "each has two functions," both the text and its meaning are explained as previously.

As for the matters of the causes and conditions for their arising, each preceding principle acts as the producer and each succeeding one as the produced. Since one who seeks liberation must sever these, it is the preceding [principles] that must be abandoned.
"Clouds are severed" refers to the aforementioned [factors] and so forth. This is because it is the skillful means for liberation. Third, what connection is there with the nature of darkness?
Regarding the scriptural passage "they are not separated from one another," this is the fourth section. The commentary contains two parts. First, a brief citation of the sutra:

it states in full, "In this context, ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), up to birth conditions aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This means that by virtue of ignorance, up to birth, acting as conditions, they cause volitional formations...

This continues until old age and death, because they do not cease and assist one another in their formation. This commentary follows the refutation of Īśvara below; it provides two interpretations of the sutra.
Regarding Īśvara, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* records that the minister Kṣemadatta said:
"All sentient beings are created by Īśvara. When Īśvara is pleased, sentient beings experience peace and happiness; when Īśvara is angry, sentient beings suffer."
[He] afflicts all sentient beings; whether it be sin or merit, it is that which is produced by Īśvara, and so forth.
The commentary from "Now, below" onwards is the direct refutation; its meaning is understandable. Regarding the phrase "the three paths are not severed" in the sutra, this is the fifth section.

It corresponds to the "Classification of Delusion, Karma, and Suffering" chapter in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. The text has two parts: first, the citation of the sutra, which is evident; second, [the explanation].

"Delusion and karma below" is entirely an explanation of the sutra. It further consists of two parts: first, an explanation based on the first aspect, the contemplation of the truths; second, an explanation based on the second, the contemplation of great compassion.
Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, a general heading which is easily understood; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "The three periods of time below.

This text has two divisions, namely: the three periods of time and the two periods of time. Within the section on the three periods of time, "the three [beings] of the past who were deluded regarding the original limit" refers to—

This is because if one were to list the scriptural passages while enumerating the topical headings (*ko-dan*), the sections would become overly numerous, thereby interrupting the flow and momentum of the commentary (*śū*).

Therefore, it is only here, at the conclusion of this section, that the meaning is summarized and the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are enumerated before their names are finally annotated.
"Seeking awakening" (*xúnjué*) means not becoming weary.
The Commentary states: From "If one follows from defilement and purity" downwards is the fifth section, which integrates and subsumes nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*).

This means that defilement is the defilement of the entire nature; thus, when defilement is raised, there is no purity, yet it is not defilement. Purity is the purity of the entire nature; when purity is raised, there is no defilement, yet it is not purity.
Therefore, it is said that they are unimpeded and mutually penetrating. Since defilement and purity are thus mutually inclusive, so too are all things within purity each mutually [inclusive].

They mutually encompass one another. Within the defiled, all things likewise mutually encompass one another. Taking up any single phenomenon, it immediately contains all defiled phenomena and all pure phenomena;
they are thus mutually related. Therefore, it is said that they "interpenetrate in layers. This is as explained previously in the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "if based on the defiled and pure, etc.," this means that as for the defilement of the entire nature, there is nothing outside of that defilement.
"Non-purity" refers to the fusion of purity. When purity is the totality of the nature, there is no defilement outside of that purity; this is the fusion of defilement.
When both are simultaneously fused, it is neither defiled nor pure; this is the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which transcends speech and thought, and is thus called "profound stillness.
The section on "Dharmatā" below concludes by establishing the ultimate limit.

The sub-commentary (*śūtra*) states that from the section "these very causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) below, six items are correlated with the fourfold nature of causes. That is to say, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

"Buddha-nature has a cause (the twelve links of dependent origination), it has a cause-cause (the wisdom that realizes the conditions of dependent origination), it has a fruit (bodhi), and it has a fruit-fruit (nirvāṇa).
This has already been established in the section on the threefold and fourfold sequences of cause and effect at the beginning of the Main Doctrine (*zhengzong*).
The "Great Meaning of Dependent Origination," Part Two: This seventh section summarizes the essential points. It serves as a general eulogy for the principle of dependent origination as a whole;
it is not restricted solely to the eighth chapter, which fully elucidates the gate of the provisional and the real. Therefore, it is called a "general summary.

However, for the sake of convenience in following the sequence of the text, this section is categorized at the end of this current chapter. Within it, the first two phrases constitute the summary eulogy, while the latter two...

The "Discernment of the Essential Points" clarifies that this single chapter by Maitreya solely elucidates the principle that one must thoroughly investigate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) regarding saṃsāra.

In the sub-commentary (*śūtra*), following the explanation of the text, there are three parts: first, the opening of the chapters and the categorization of the scripture; second, the section beginning with "This is the same as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*," which provides a comparative reference.
[It is] complete in its constituent factors. As that treatise states: "Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*).

Here, the term "afflictions" refers to the defilements that initiate karma (*avidyā*) and those that moisten rebirth (*tṛṣṇā* and *upādāna*). "Karma" refers to the various actions capable of inducing future existence (*saṃskāra* and *bhava*). "Suffering" refers to the manifold sufferings produced and drawn forth by that karma.
One should understand that these afflictions, karma, and suffering collectively encompass the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). That is to say, from...

From ignorance up to old age and death, as explained extensively in the treatises (referring to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* chapters 9, 10, and 13; the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* chapter 40; the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* chapter 82; the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, etc.).
Nevertheless, these twelve links are briefly subsumed into four categories: first, the projecting links (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), and so forth. As that treatise explains the root verse:

"Due to the habitual tendencies of karma, together with the habitual tendencies of the two graspings (*upādāna*), once the previous maturation (*vipāka*) has been exhausted, another maturation arises again. When these maturations are assigned to the three paths [of existence], they unfold into the twelve links. How much more so now, when this sutra fully clarifies the cycle of samsara from its beginning to its end, making the three paths clearly manifest.

Is it not necessary to provide a complete explanation of the twelve [points]? Let the wise examine this in detail). ▲ Regarding the section "Also below": there are three distinct sections for detailed explanation.

The first of these refers to the scriptural passage from among the four [sections] that identifies craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as the root. The remaining three refer to the second [section], "The Desires and Aids," and so forth.

Regarding the section "Its five natures" and below: the structural divisions are shifted and rearranged; that is, the preceding division of the scriptural passage on the five natures answers the question regarding the types of spiritual capacities (*gotra*).

Regarding the question concerning "nature" (*gotra*): the current explanation—beginning with the assistance of desire and so forth, proceeding through successive stages up to the arising of karma and the receiving of retribution—is entirely a response to the question regarding *gotra*.

Consequently, the scriptural passage on the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) would have no place to be subsumed; it must therefore be understood as a response to the question concerning the cultivation of the Buddha’s bodhi.
The commentary begins by focusing on greed and desire as its central theme, which consists of three parts: first, the assignment of the factors [of dependent origination] to explain craving;
second, from "Śūraṅgama" onwards, citing the sūtra to prove that craving is the root and using analogies to urge its abandonment; third, from "As for desire," explaining the remaining text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "it corresponds to the afflictions of the previous life," there are two interpretations. The first is that taking the state of beginningless [affliction] as the branch of ignorance (*avidyā*):

the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states, "Ignorance is the state of past afflictions; past karmas are called formations (*saṃskāra*). Since the present text speaks of the "initial limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*), it refers to the stage of the previous life;
therefore, it is said to include the branch of ignorance. Furthermore, the previous interpretation stated that ignorance is delusion.
This is because it refers to the meaning of the "original limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*). Regarding the commentary’s mention of "ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth," this is the second interpretation;

it points to ignorance as discussed in the preceding section on Mañjuśrī. This "beginningless craving" (*anādikālikatṛṣṇā*) is simply the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*). Regarding the commentary’s description of "the characteristic of the increase of craving," the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"The increase of craving constitutes grasping (*upādāna*)," as explained in the previous citation. The present intention is that various forms of greed and desire are themselves craving.

Because it increases, it is assigned as the link of grasping (*upādāna*). The commentary now refers to craving (*rāga*); while craving is subtle, greed (*lobha*) is coarse, and thus it is manifested by means of greed.

"Flowing craving" refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless craving, which flow spontaneously and continue in an uninterrupted succession. Regarding the phrase "acting as the seed":
it is like when a woman is about to conceive, she must rely upon the male seed. "Apprehending through ideation" refers to the former [state].
There is innate craving (*sahaja-tṛṣṇā*) and there is conceptual craving (*vikalpita-tṛṣṇā*). It is only through conceptual craving that karma is moistened and rebirth is experienced;

as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, a male fetus views the mother as a wife and feels aversion toward the father, while a female fetus perceives the father as a husband and feels aversion toward the mother.
"Encounter" (*gou*) means meeting; this sexual union is the manifestation of the seeds.
The meaning of mutual support, perfuming, and harmonious integration. "Attraction" refers to being drawn along by causes and conditions, like a magnet attracting iron.
"Common karma" refers to the ripening of karma created in previous lives, which now manifests as either a human or an animal and so forth.

Therefore, it is said that "by these causes and conditions, there is birth and death. The rest—the text concerning the names of Nirvana and the Buddhas—is all visible [in the source]. The commentary intends to respond...
Regarding the phrase "this mind and so forth": however, the term *kāma* (desire) as indicated in various teachings does not have a fixed, singular meaning.
Sometimes it is taken to mean the mind, and sometimes it is taken to mean the object. As the verse of Śāriputra says: "The wondrous objects of the world are not true desire;

true desire refers to the specific greed of human beings"—this takes it to mean the mind. In other passages, the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are all treated as the five desires (*pañca-kāma*), which refers to the objects themselves.
Therefore, these are combined here for explanation. Regarding the phrase in the *Sūtra* (or *Śāstra*), "due to the objects of desire" (*yuan-jing*): An objection is raised:
What prevents the interpretation that "desire" (*yu*) refers to the desiring mind and "objects of desire" (*yuan-jing*) refers to the objects desired?

Why is it definitively determined that both characters [in the compound] refer exclusively to the objects? Answer: If they were exclusively objects of desire, they would not be contrary to one's feelings (*qing*). Now, [the context implies]...
The next sentence states: "Giving rise to various things favorable and unfavorable. This clearly indicates the five sense objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
it is only within these that there can be the favorable and the unfavorable, which is why one might doubt this. Furthermore, it was already stated above that one should not take [the object] alone;

who says there is a fixed determination? Moreover, the *Anityatā-sūtra* says: "Constantly seeking the realm of desires, one does not practice wholesome deeds. From this, it is known that this refers generally to both favorable and unfavorable objects.

One gives rise to unwholesome karma; it is not permissible to perform actions solely for the sake of what accords with one's desires. Thus, we know that the two characters "desire" (*yù*) and "objects" (*jìng*) collectively refer to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Regarding the phrase "the passage from that sutra says 'and so forth' (*děng*)," the term "and so forth" (*děng*) refers to the subsequent clause. The commentary states that "various kinds" (*zhǒngzhǒng*) consists of two parts.
First, the general explanation; second, the sequential explanation. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the analytical selection (*vibhaṅga*).

In the formal explanation, regarding "natural affinity" (*svabhāva-bandhu*): the way of father and son is natural. This means it is produced by Heaven as a matter of course, a bond of mutual affection that does not arise from the attachment of clan ties or emotional passion.
Liu Shang says: "Below this, one obtains natural kinship through dependent origination; even between flesh-and-blood relatives who are enemies, the bond is only formed when..."
A few characters remain; the rest of the text can be understood by oneself. Regarding the "six relations" (*ṣaṭ-kula*): they are parents, children, and spouses.
However, there are those among humanity who possess these six relations yet cannot love one another spontaneously; here, the explanation follows the majority case. Regarding "veneration as a cause":

this refers to those with deep faith in the Buddha-dharma who, upon seeing the Triple Gem, their preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), and various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), [feel reverence].
Originally, it was out of reverence for the Dharma; gradually, it developed into a deep affection of the heart.

Although all needs were fully met, one could not bear to part. The rest of the text is understandable. Regarding the phrase "gratitude is not love," etc., this is one of the four lines: "gratitude is not love.

For example, suppose a person has previously received various forms of profound kindness from another, yet the former person’s initial motive for forming the connection and bestowing that kindness was merely strategic. Originally, [the benefactor] did not...

Because of affectionate attachment, one may encounter such a person who has received one's kindness; yet, should that person later lose their rank and position or gradually fall into poverty, the benefactor might further impoverish them.
