He said, "I am currently under the earth as a servant of Mount Tai. For five hundred years, my suffering has been extreme. He said that south of the Yudan Prefecture there is one named Sun A;
the Lord of Mount Tai wishes to summon him to serve as a provincial clerk. I pray that my parents will entrust me to his care."
"I have attained a place of peace and happiness. His wife woke up in alarm and wept as she told Ji. Ji was a man of stern character and at first did not believe her.
When the following night came, his wife again saw her deceased son in a dream, and it was exactly as she had said in her previous dream.
Consequently, Jiang Ji went south to the Lingdan Commandery and found Sun A; he then entrusted him with the words of the deceased son from within the dream.
"Ā. Ā said, "If you know this, you should go underground and provide a means for the young master. After two months, Sun Ā fell ill and died overnight.
Ten days later, his wife saw her deceased son return and told her: "While I was underground, I obtained an exemption from labor through the Records Office of Mount Tai.
This was recorded in a separate biography of a person from the Wei period. As for the term "petty concubine" (*bìqiè*), it refers to a minor [wife].

The History records: Wei Wuzi, the Grand Historian of the Jin state, had a favorite concubine. While he was ill, he instructed his son, saying: "When I die, you must marry this concubine; do not disobey my word.
When his illness became critical, he again commanded Kui (the son) to say: "You must kill this concubine and follow me [in death]. Kui reflected on this, saying:
"I shall follow my father’s words when he was clear-headed and conscious, and not his speech when he was delirious and confused. Thereafter...
She was given in marriage to him. Qin appointed Du Hui as general to punish Jin, while Jin appointed Zeng Ke as general to resist them.
At dawn, they engaged in battle. That night, Ke dreamed of a man who said to him, "General, you shall fight early tomorrow morning;
I will lead my forces to assist you and ensure your victory. Ke asked him, "Who are you that can provide such assistance? He replied, "I am your General."
He was the father of my late father’s concubine. Moved by the General’s sparing of my daughter and his subsequent remarriage of her, he led ghostly troops to assist you.
Du Hui, delighted, mobilized his forces at dawn to strike the Qin army. Du Hui bound him with grass to surround him;
with no way to advance or retreat, he was defeated by the Jin forces. As the saying goes, "ghosts employ bound grass"—this is what that refers to.
Regarding the commentary on Su Shao: the *Book of Jin* states that Su Shao served as the Magistrate of Zhongmou during the Jin dynasty and died there.
His nephew, Shi Jie, frequently saw Shao appear and converse with him, no different from when he was alive. He appeared on some forty occasions in total.
Jie asked, "How is death compared to life? Shao replied, "It is no different. Jie said, "It must surely be inferior.
Shao smiled and said, "You shall know this for yourself later. Jie asked, "Why do the dead not return to their former bodies? Shao said, "It is like this:
suppose one of your arms were severed and cast to the ground, and you were then flayed and carved; would that cause you any distress? [The corpse...]
The remains are like this. Su Shao’s statement that they are no different from those of the living indicates that one knows the spiritual consciousness of a person does not perish after death.
Furthermore, her statement that the corpse after death is like a discarded severed arm shows that when a person dies, the spirit departs from the human form.

It can also be understood that they further receive the forms of ghosts. Regarding the commentary on the words of Confucius: Zi Gong asked Confucius, "Do those who have died possess consciousness, or do they not?

The Master said, "If I were to say that the dead possess consciousness, I fear that filial sons and obedient grandsons would neglect their own lives to attend to the funeral rites for the deceased. If I were to say that the dead possess no consciousness, I fear that the unfilial..."
The son abandons his parents and fails to bury them. Yanzi’s desire to know whether the dead possess consciousness or not is not an urgent matter of the present;

he will come to know it for himself later—it is not too late. [Commentary: The section below "Therefore, as for sacrifices" provides three proofs that establish that [the ancestral rites] are not discontinued.
Now, those who debated in antiquity all held that the dead possess no consciousness; yet they nevertheless performed sacrifices and offered prayers.

To act upon every impulse—how can this not be a contradiction between word and deed? If one were to claim that because the present age is desolate, devoid of intervals [of time] and lacking vision, death must therefore be a state of unconsciousness, such a view might be examined.
Yet from antiquity until now, there have been instances of both calamity and fortune, all of which are matters of direct perception and report;
thus, they are certainly not absent from our time. Nevertheless, those who debate the matter still treat ghosts and spirits as slaves, asserting them to be unconscious. Such is their speech.
This is because they are strong proponents of the theory that consciousness exists [only in the living], and thus they fail to illuminate its fundamental nature and fail to reach its source;
this is what causes such a situation. Furthermore, as for the common view that ghosts and spirits are without consciousness, it is based on the fact that they are not seen.
My own reasoning for providing proof is likewise based on one particular aspect. If one were to conclude that something does not exist simply because it is neither heard nor seen, then—
Within the realm of heaven and earth, those things that are neither heard nor seen are exceedingly numerous. How can one simply take what is not heard or seen to be non-existent?
Nevertheless, the deluded all share this same attachment; how could I possibly provide a comprehensive explanation for it? I shall merely cite examples to clarify the point.
To illustrate the accounts of those who returned from death and spoke of matters in the dark passages: Liu Chong, during the Linjia era...
In the second year, the *guihai* (year of the Water Pig), it was the Prince of Dongping, Yuao, who was [the subject]. After Lü Cóng died, his body remained warm for one night;
consequently, he was not yet coffined or buried. He then revived and said that he had seen Yuan Hai at Mount Buzhou.

After five days, he followed him to Mount Kunlun, and after three days, he returned to Mount Buzhou, where he saw all the deceased kings, dukes, high ministers, generals, and officials, all present in the palace.
The palace was most magnificent. It was called the Kingdom of Mengzhuli. Yuanhai said to Yue: "To the northeast lies Chaxuyi, which has been without a ruler for a long time and awaits one.
Your father shall be its ruler; he will come in two years. After his arrival, there will be great chaos in the kingdom and widespread slaughter.
Families will perish, and the population will be almost entirely wiped out, with only about ten people remaining, such as Yongming and others. You should return for now."
"I shall come again in a year; it will not be too long before I see you. Having made this appointment, he departed and passed through a country named Yiniquyu.
He led Zhuo into the palace and gave him a leather bag, saying, "Present this as my gift to the Han Emperor.
Zhuo took his leave and returned home. He placed the leather bag upon a side-table and soon regained consciousness. He then ordered his attendants to take the bag from the table and open it.
There was a piece of white jade inscribed with the following text: "The Heavenly King of the country of Yiniqiu respectfully believes in the Heavenly King of the country of Chaxuyi.
In the year of Sheti (Caitra), he shall dispatch a messenger to present this to Cong.

Cong said, "If you are indeed as you say, I do not fear death. Subsequently, as his death drew near, [the spirit] appeared to him repeatedly during the day. Disgusted by these words, he spoke to Crown Prince Can, saying:
"I was lying ill in bed, exhausted and emaciated, when strange and extraordinary phenomena became particularly intense. Previously, I took my restrained speech to be a sign of demonic interference;
however, having seen this for several days now, it must be that this child has come to welcome me. Who would have thought that upon the certainty of death, there is such spiritual efficacy?
Da Yu died in the first year of Taiyu, and he was buried together with this king. From this we may conclude that those who die possess consciousness; how could this not be so?"
How empty it all is! Furthermore, there are those who die and then revive one after another without ceasing;

they all see the places where the officials and subordinates of the netherworld undergo suffering, which corresponds exactly with the *Nanjing* (Inner Scripture). If this were merely awaiting a karmic trigger for revival, how could such visions be anything other than empty?
Regarding the matter of spirits appearing after death to partake of food and drink: this occurs most frequently, being found throughout both ancient and modern times.
During my forty years, I have seen and heard of approximately twenty or more instances. Among these, there are only three or five cases that I have personally investigated and verified as authentic;
these were not obtained through the study of historical records, and thus I do not dare to commit them to writing. Furthermore, the span of time between the ancient and the modern is vast.
How much more so when many people see and hear it? It is left to the lecturer to speak according to their own observations and hearing;

however, one must not speak of "connecting the sprouts" (superficialities) or of those who falsely claim transmission while lacking a fundamental basis. Regarding the "repaying of kindness and resentment" in the commentary: repaying kindness is as previously established in the chapter.

As for repaying resentment, there have also been many such cases in antiquity; this refers to instances where the soul of a person killed through injustice comes to seek vengeance. Only those in official robes (*yìguān*)...
Officials often speak of this matter. Formerly, there was Yan Zhitui, who compiled accounts of enmity and resentment following death from ancient times based on books and histories.
His work consists of three fascicles and is titled *Yuanhun ji* (Record of Vengeful Spirits). The events narrated therein total seventy entries.
Now, selecting those instances that are clear and easy to understand, I have compiled seven entries below. Dou Ying, styled Wangsun, was the nephew of Empress Dou of the Han Emperor Xiaowen.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wei’i and served as Chancellor; later, he was relieved of his post.
Following the death of Empress Dou, Ying became increasingly marginalized and lacked influence. Feeling frustrated and dissatisfied, he associated with Grand Carriage Officer Guan Fu.
The two men were like deer in a herd; they became fast friends and rejoiced greatly, lamenting that they had known each other so late.

At that time, Emperor Xiaojing’s consort, Empress Wang, and her uterine younger brother, Tian Fen, served as Chancellor. With imperial favor and influence at their disposal, they sent an agent to Yin to request several *qǐng* of farmland south of the city.
Yin did not grant it, saying, "Though I am but an old servant cast aside, and though you, Chancellor, are noble, how could I allow my property to be seized by your power?"

Guan Fu also joined in his indignation, and Wei Qianfen harbored resentment toward both of them. Later, when Qianfen married a wife, Empress Dowager Wang issued a decree for the marquises and members of the imperial clan to go and offer congratulations to him.
Guan Fu was a man of wild drinking habits; having previously offended Qianfen while intoxicated, he refused to go and congratulate him. Dou Ying forced him to accompany him.
When they had reached a state of drunken revelry, Guan Fu served the wine until it reached Qianfen. Qianfen said, "I cannot [drink this]."
He filled his cup. Because of these insolent words, Gao Fen became enraged and said, "This is the crime of my overbearing toward Guan Fu.
He then bound Fu and addressed the Chief Secretary, saying, "Despite the imperial decree regarding the imperial clan, Guan Fu has insulted the assembly and shown disrespect;

furthermore, he has acted with arrogance and tyranny in his home village. He subsequently petitioned for Fu’s execution by public stoning. Dou Ying returned and said to his wife, "I shall never again issue such a command."
Guan Fu alone died while Yin alone lived. Yin then submitted a memorial detailing that Guan Fu’s drunken excesses were not grounds for execution.

The Emperor summoned him for an audience. Yin and Wang Rong spoke of each other’s faults and virtues. The Emperor asked the court officials which of the two was right; most of the officials said Yin was right.
When Empress Dowager Wang heard this, she became enraged and refused to eat, saying: "While I am still alive..."
"Everyone is bullying my younger brother. After I am dead at a hundred years old, will they treat him like fish or meat?
When he went out, Huo Fen again acted as Ying’s agent, fabricating malicious words to report upward to the Emperor. The Son of Heaven also considered Fen to be untrustworthy;

however, solely for the sake of the Empress Dowager, he sentenced Ying and his husband to execution by exposure in the marketplace. As Ying was about to die, he cursed, saying: "If you believe that death brings no consciousness, then let it be so."
There was one who knew that he would not die alone. After more than a month had passed, Duan Fen’s entire body was afflicted with pain as if struck by blows;
he could do nothing but cry out and prostrate himself, confessing his crimes. The Emperor sent a spirit-seer to observe him, who saw Dou Ying and Guan Fu together guarding and flogging him.
Fen subsequently died, and the Emperor also saw Ying in a dream, who apologized to him. During the Han dynasty, He Chang served as...
The Imperial Protector of Jiaozhi was on an inspection tour when he arrived at Shangyao County in Cangwu Commandery. That evening, he stayed overnight at Queben Pavilion.
When the night was not yet half over, a woman emerged from beneath the pavilion and said, "I am a servant girl; my surname is Su, my given name is E, and my courtesy name is Shizhu."
She was originally a native of Xiuli in Guangxin County. She lost her parents at an early age and had no brothers. Her husband also passed away.
She possessed one hundred and twenty bolts of various silks and a single maidservant named Zhifu. Being a widow, orphaned, destitute, and frail, she was unable to support herself.
Desiring to go to a neighboring county to sell the silk, she hired a carriage and oxen from Wang Bo, a man of the same county, for a price of [money].

Twelve thousand *zai* of concubines and silks were bestowed, enabling Fu Zhipei to achieve great wealth. Then, on the tenth day of the fourth month of the previous year, he arrived outside this pavilion.
At that time, as evening fell and all travelers had ceased their journey, he did not dare proceed further and consequently remained there.
Having become wealthy through sudden gains, she fell ill with a stomach ailment. Her concubine went to the residence of the *ting-chang* (village head) to beg for some gruel and to borrow fire.

The *ting-chang*, Gong Shou, took up a blade and held a halberd as he approached the side of the carriage and asked the concubine: "From where does the lady come? What is being carried on this carriage?

Because the concubine’s death was so cruel and she had no one to whom to appeal, she has come to seek refuge with you, the enlightened Magistrate. Chang said, "I now wish to exhume your remains."
"What is the proof of this? the woman asked. She said, "I am wearing white garments from head to foot and blue silk sandals; they have not yet decayed. When she was dug up, it was indeed so.

Liu Chang then dispatched an official to arrest Shou for interrogation, and he fully confessed. The case was sent down to Guangxin County for examination, and the findings matched what the girl had said.
Shou’s parents and brothers were all arrested and imprisoned. Liu Chang memorialized that Shou had committed murder. If...

such cases are rare even in a thousand years. I request that you execute them all to assist the secret killing of the retribution of their own deeds.

During the Yongkang era of the Song dynasty, there was a man named Lü Qingzu from Yongkang. His family was very wealthy and prosperous. He once employed a stone statue to instruct his son in the observance of [moral] conduct.
While inspecting the country villa, Qinzǔ went there in person during the Yuánjiā era. Suddenly, he was murdered by someone.
His cousin Wúqī had previously gambled away Qinzǔ’s money at the Great Dance festival; everyone suspected that Wúqī had committed the murder.

Wúqī then took wine and arrived at the site of the madness at the hour of *bū*, where he swore an oath, saying: "If this is indeed a case of bitter cruelty, even if my soul has no spirit, let it be known [to the authorities]."
When her master returned at the third watch, he saw Qingzu approaching. He said, "I recently went out and saw that your fields and plots were not being tended;
I shall punish you severely for this. The slave then struck my back with an axe and stuffed a cap into my mouth. Because I bit the slave's finger, it was completely crushed.
He then took a knife and stabbed me in the head, dragging me to the rear gate. When I first saw him about to kill me, I rose up as if I were a traveler.
"He was also among them. This slave now wishes to rebel; I have already driven his head into the wall. Having finished speaking, he vanished. At dawn, [the son] informed his parents.
They secretly inspected the wall where the slave had stayed and indeed found a handful of hair fastened there with a bamboo pin.
Upon examining his fingers, they were all split open. They immediately arrested the slave for interrogation, and his confession matched the account. "Since you are so wicked..."

[He] rebelled. Why did he not defect? It was said that his head felt as if it were bound, and though he wished to escape, he could not. Those who shared his views found their circumstances and affairs to coincide;
they immediately burned the teachings and his two sons, Lang and Langzhugefu. This occurred during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
He served as the Governor of Jiuzhen. His family and dependents were all in Yangdu, and he had brought only his eldest son, Yuanchong, with him to fulfill his official duties.
While en route, Yuanchong fell ill and died in the commandery. He was only nineteen years old when his funeral party prepared to return home.

Yuanchong’s disciple, He Zeng, coveted the deceased's wealth and, conspiring with his companions, pushed Yuanchong into the river so that he would die. They then divided the property among themselves. That very night, Yuanchong— (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.)

His mother was Lady Chen. She dreamed that Yuanchong returned and related in detail the circumstances of Wen’s death and her own execution, how his remains had drifted away, and how the cruelty of the execution was peerless.
She had been held in custody for many years; now, on this single day, he has departed forever. Her grief is intensified by this bitterness—how can it be described?
She sobbed, unable to restrain herself. She further said that because he had traveled so swiftly and his steps were exhausted, he had consequently lain down upon the bed beneath the window.
He used his head as a pillow against the window. When his mother looked at where her son had slept the next day, she knew for certain that it was no illusion.

Lady Chen, overcome with grief and alarm, sprang up and took a torch to illuminate the place where her son had lain; the dampened traces still formed the shape of a human body. Thereupon the entire family wailed and wept.
Then, as if prompted by a divine inquiry, it so happened that Xu Senzhi had just been appointed Governor of Jiaozhou, and Xu Daoli served as his Chief Secretary (Changshi). At that time, Daoli...
This was the daughter of the elder sister of the Chen family. She detailed her dream in a written report and entrusted it to the two Xu to investigate.

Xu Daoli encountered Zhuge, who provided the evidence for the removal of the funerary tablets. The dates on which the father and son died all matched the words of the ghost. Consequently, the two villains were arrested;

they immediately confessed their crimes and were executed according to the law. Furthermore, another person was dispatched to escort the funeral procession to Donghai Prefecture. This was the case of Xu Sijia.
His wife was surnamed Xu. They had one son named Tiejiu. When Xu died, he remarried a woman surnamed Chen.
Chen was cruel and tyrannical, intent on exterminating the son of her predecessor. She gave birth to a son and, as soon as he was born, cursed him, saying:
"If you do not eliminate Tiejiu, you shall not be my son. For this reason, she named him Tiechu, intending for him to strike down Tiejiu. Thus, [Tiechu] began to shake...
He worked at a blacksmith’s forge. He was subjected to all manner of bitter suffering; when hungry, he was not given food, and in the cold, he received no padded clothing.
This man, so-and-so, was dull-witted and weak, and was frequently absent. His stepmother acted as she pleased, inflicting violence and cruelty upon him.

Iron-jew (Tiejiu) eventually died of cold, hunger, and exhaustion. At that time, he was sixteen years old. More than ten days after his death, a ghost suddenly returned home. He climbed onto Chen’s bed and said, "I am..."

The iron mortar: "In truth, I have committed not even a fraction of a sin, yet I have been subjected to this cruel slaughter. My mother appealed her grievance to Heaven, and now the Office of the Cao has come to fetch the iron pestle.
I shall cause the pestle to suffer quickly the same agony as I did when I encountered it. It is said that there will be a specific date for this;
I shall remain here and wait for it, appearing just as I did in life, so that my family and guests may not see my form. All [were thus moved].
Upon hearing these words, he remained constantly perched upon the roof beam. Chen bowed in gratitude and, with a heavy heart, prepared offerings and sacrifices for him.
The ghost said, "Do not trouble yourself so; my current pain of death is something that cannot be recompensed by a single meal.
Chen then spoke of this in secret during the night. The ghost said in a stern voice, "How dare you speak thus? I shall now destroy this house!"
As the saw sounded, the shavings fell away with it, and a loud *la-raṇ* noise arose, as if the ridgepole of a house were collapsing.
The entire family rushed out; when they looked back with torches, there was no difference at all. The ghost again cursed the iron pestle, saying:

"You have just killed me, yet you sit comfortably upon my house—do you take such pleasure in this? I shall burn your house! Immediately, fire broke out, and the smoke and flames became fierce and violent, both inside and out.
In a state of utter distress, he suddenly perished. Yet the thatched cottage remained solemnly intact, showing no sign of damage. Day after day he cursed and reviled; at times he would sing:
"The peach and plum flowers—how can they endure the severe frost? O peach and plum fruits, the severe frost has fallen too early. His voice was filled with profound sorrow and lamentation.
He lamented within his heart that he would not be allowed to grow up. At that time, when the child was six years old, a ghost arrived;

he immediately fell ill with an epidemic, his belly swelled, he suffered from labored breathing, and his appetite was ruined. Wherever the ghost struck him, there were dark bruises. Within a month he died, and the ghost then vanished into silence.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty wished to build a monastery atop the tomb of Emperor Wen, but had not yet obtained suitable timber. He announced his intention to the relevant authorities.
He was commissioned to search further. Previously, there had been a man from Qu’a (Qū’ā) surnamed Hóng (Hóng), whose personal name has been forgotten; his family was extremely wealthy.
He had gone with his kinsmen, carrying a great deal of goods, to reside in Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu) to conduct business. After several years, he managed to acquire a forest of timber for a raft.
The raft was a thousand paces long, and its wood was so magnificent that it was rarely seen in the world. Upon returning to Nánjīn (Nánjīn), he was seized by the Magistrate Mèng Shǎoqīng.
The Emperor then issued an edict to impose strict regulations. Regarding the garments, silks, and colored fabrics that Master Hong had brought with him, there were still remnants remaining;

these were falsely accused of being obtained through extortion and robbery, and it was further claimed that their initial manufacture exceeded the prescribed limits and was unsuitable for a merchant. Thus, they were subjected to legal penalties.
He was about to be executed when his raft was confiscated and used for the monastery’s needs; the imperial decree was subsequently carried out.
On the day Hongshi was to be executed, he instructed his wife and children: "Take one hundred sheets of yellow paper along with brushes and ink and place them inside the coffin.
If there is consciousness after death, you must surely present this petition. He also wrote the names of several dozen minor officials and swallowed them, saying, "It may take some time..."

After one month, while the Vice Minister sat upright, he saw Hong arrive. At first, [the minister] still resisted and tried to ward him off, but later he gradually became submissive and humble, merely pleading for his life.

Drinking blood and burrowing into holes, all the prison officials and masters—those who had participated in the affairs of this prison and those who had drafted the petitions—perished entirely within less than a year after Hong’s death. The construction of Huangji Temple was then undertaken.

From beginning to end, it was consumed by a celestial fire until not even a single speck remained. Even the pillars and timber that supported the structure were reduced to ash, sinking into the earth.
When Jiangling fell, there was a man from Guannei named Liang Yuanhui who captured a gentleman surnamed Liu. Weeping, he said, "I have lost the name of Xincheng.
This man had previously suffered through the chaos of Hou Jing’s rebellion and lost his entire family, leaving behind only his young son.
The child was only a few years old; [Liu] carried him on his own back and also used a flail. When they encountered snow and muddy ground, he was unable to move forward.
Yuan Hui forced him to abandon the child. Out of affection for his son, Liu pleaded with him to death.
Yuan Hui then forcibly seized him, threw him into the snow, struck him with a branch, and drove him away. As Liu went step by step, he turned his head back, wailing until his voice failed.
Exhausted by toil and further afflicted by grief, Yuan Hui died after several days.

Following his death, Yuan Hui saw Liu Shen daily calling out for and demanding his son. Consequently, he fell ill; though he offered repentance and apologies in his presence, the persecutions did not cease.
Yuan Hui died at home while still burdened by illness. These seven cases have been briefly recounted; the others are all similar. Some harbor accumulated grievances and deep-seated resentment.

In the end, they were afflicted by venereal diseases. When they discussed their circumstances and appealed their grievances, entrusting themselves to the spirits for assistance in seeking redress, the divine responses were indeed numerous;
thus, there is no falsehood in this. How could it be that the dead falsely manifest such anomalies?

Furthermore, there are shamans and sorcerers who see the ancestors and parents of the living, describing their physical appearances and recounting their words and deeds throughout life without a single discrepancy. How could these shamans be capable of deception and fabricate such accounts? [Commentary]

As for those who are cured of demonic illnesses through incantations and prohibitions: there are indeed demonic illnesses where, by means of talismans, written spells, beating, and exorcising, one immediately attains recovery.
Such instances are extremely numerous in the human world; since they have been so frequently seen and heard, there is no need for a detailed account.

Furthermore, because these matters vary according to the different customs of the states of Chu, Xia, Wu, and Yue, it is impossible to provide a comprehensive description of the world’s various customs regarding the propitiation and warding off of ghosts and spirits.

This is a worldly convention; each speaks according to their own perspective. How much more so regarding the great principles that follow—can they not be sought and can right and wrong not be distinguished?
Regarding the word "ye" (or "yes") in the phrase "shu deng ye" (the commentary etc., yes): it serves as a general conclusion. The word "deng" (etc. includes other things not mentioned.

The single character "ye" runs through the four subsequent lines beginning with "kuang si er su" (even if one dies and revives). It should be applied to the word "kuang" (even if). There ought to be four instances of the character "ye," but now, because... [text ends].

Unify this [into a single unit]. Those who read the commentary should treat everything from the character "況" (kuàng) up to the character "耶" (yé) as one sentence, reading it with a continuous cadence, and only then divide it into four sections for explanation. Regarding the note "Wang Si died, etc.":
during the Han dynasty, there was a Wang Si who composed the *Wu gui lun* (Treatise on the Non-existence of Ghosts). Here, we take his words and refute them. Wang Si said: "As for Tian Fen..."
The mind harbors resentment and indignation. In the confusion of illness, one has delusory perceptions. When ordinary people fall ill, they become fearful;

fear gives rise to delusive thoughts, and these delusive thoughts produce false visions. Now, the answer is this: if Tian Fen had experienced a false vision, he would not have been summoned, nor would he have confessed his guilt.

How could one experience physical pain through a false vision? It must be that the mind corresponds to the delusive perception, and through that delusion, the pain is felt. If it were merely a false [vision]...
As for the "one who saw": Emperor Wu ordered a spirit-medium to observe him. The medium saw Dou Ying and Guan Fu both guarding [the patient] and beating him.

Could it be that the medium was also afflicted by delusion and had a false vision? If one were to claim that the medium also had a false vision, then it would not be right for the perceived forms to be identical in every detail to those of the patient.
It must be that the patient can cause a non-existent thing to appear as having form, thereby inducing the medium to see it as well.
Does one see them? If one cannot, then the shaman should have nothing to see.

From this it may be said that to cling to empty visions and thereby claim there are no ghosts—has not yet been found to be correct. There are several further instances, as explained in another fascicle.
Even if the matter of Tian Fen lacks a basis, it is as stated in the first section of the five-part "Record of the Wronged Spirits" cited previously.
▲ Regarding the section "If a person dies" in the *Śāstra*, four questions and answers resolve potential objections. This also serves as a response to the inquiry concerning the death of King [Wang].
The *Śū* (Commentary) adopts the essential meaning for its use and does not include the full text; therefore, it directly states "question and answer" to mark the heading of this section.
The objection states: "Now, since heaven and earth were first opened, if every person who dies immediately becomes a ghost, then there must be a ghost at every step upon the roads.

One would expect to see hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of ghosts filling the halls, overflowing the courtyards, and clogging the streets; it is not fitting that we should see only one or two.
The response is: "When a human dies, they become a ghost; when a ghost dies, they become an ox; when an ox dies, they become a fish; when a fish [dies, they become...]"
The dead become gods; gods die and become ghosts; ghosts die and return to being humans. They undergo transformations according to their karma, not restricted to a single category.
This cycle through the six realms of existence has never had a beginning nor will it have an end. How could it be that only humans die while ghosts do not?
If ghosts were to live forever without dying, then your argument would indeed be like that of the Tathāgata.
The commentary states: Furthermore, as for the descent of the qi of Heaven and Earth—this is the third major section, which refutes the error of [claiming] there is no nature [of consciousness].
It means that if sentient beings possess cognition, they receive the qi of Yin and Yang; whereas insentient objects do not receive this qi. Thus, cognition and its absence would each be distinct.

Now, since both [sentient and insentient things] equally receive the qi of Yin and Yang, there is no need to posit them as different. For what reason, then, are plants and trees insentient while humans [are not]?
Animals possess consciousness. Based on this, we know that this spirit-mind is not dependent upon vital energy (*qi*).

If it were claimed that humans and animals receive a greater amount of yin and yang *qi* while plants and trees receive less, and therefore the latter lack consciousness, then it would follow that plants and trees have little consciousness while humans and animals have much.

Since this is not the case, how can one say that consciousness arises from *qi*? Furthermore, the spirit possesses a thousandfold distinctions such as the wise and the foolish, or the good and the evil; yet the [amount of] yin...

How could such a thousandfold variety exist within the yang-qi? For consciousness and qi are distinct: that which exists in qi is without cognition, while that which exists in consciousness possesses cognition.
How could they be conflated into a single qi? The Sūtra says: "The aggregation and dispersal of the four great elements have the mind alone as their basis."
Within the three realms, one comes alone and departs alone, with not a single follower. From this, it is known that the vital breath (*qi*) is not the fundamental basis.

If [the mind] were produced from the vital breath, then each instance of consciousness would not distinguish between good and evil. If good and evil were also merely the vital breath, they would not depend upon cultivation and study.
Since they do not depend on cultivation, what need would there be for Confucius and Laozi to establish teachings to encourage the study of benevolence and righteousness and the reforming of evil?
"Is it for the sake of goodness?

From this point downward, the commentary [shows] the third section: the reconciliation of the two teachings, internal and external, so that they do not contradict one another (for each adheres to its own single perspective, and thus perceives them as contradictory).

Regarding the phrase "to attach to the vital breath": when the mind-consciousness possesses the karma of humans, animals, and so forth, it then takes refuge in and attaches itself to the vital breaths of yin and yang.

Regarding the formation of the body: consciousness is said to be the primary cause, while the vital energy (*prāṇa*) is the auxiliary condition. Consciousness is able to cognize all objects and perform various functions;
the yin-yang vital energy is able to form the physical substance of bones and flesh. As stated in the *Zhù* (Commentary), the treatise says:
"There has never been a single dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions. As for the phrase "transmitted and continued from lifetime to lifetime," it is as follows:
In the *Guang hongming ji*, Shen Yue states: "That these sentient beings possess Buddha-nature truly resides in the fact that their cognitive nature is constantly transmitted.
This refers to the mind-spirit (*xinshen*). Since it was first free from defilement, it has undergone thousands of millions of births and has discarded thousands of millions of bodies.
In each instance of receiving a body, it invariably receives vital breath (*qi*); therefore, it is said to be 'transmitted and continued. Thus, whether benevolent or violent..."
From the reigns of Yao and Jie downward, this has resulted in the establishment of the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism as profound principles for beneficial cultivation and training.
If one does not interpret it according to this [explanation], then there will be various faults as previously refuted; the benefit of the teaching will not be realized.
Thus we know that all three teachings were established by sages; their expressions differ, but their principles accord. It is only later generations who cling to the literal text.
Those who are deluded regarding the principle merely cause disputes over praise and blame to arise.

Regarding the second section of the commentary, which clarifies what is correct: this is the second major division of the text. Previously, in response to external criticisms, we briefly harmonized the teachings of the Dharma-character (Hossō) school with our own;

thus, there was already no contradiction. Now, we shall directly rely upon the definitive, ultimate teachings concerning both the origin and the culmination, while also incorporating the [Dharma-character]...

The provisional teachings and others are all harmonized and integrated to establish the correct principle; therefore, this is established as the explicit teaching. The text consists of two parts: first, the explicit exposition itself.

This meaning is fully contained within the "Profound Depth of the Scope" section of the fourth chapter of the *Xuántán* (Introductory Discourse), as well as in the "Five Teachings of Mind-Only" section of the *Púxián Zhāng* (Chapter on Samantabhadra).
One should consult these for a summary account, or simply refer to the specific passages therein.
It is also acceptable to provide a narrative [introduction]. Alternatively, one may briefly explain this passage by taking its essential meaning; the text itself is clearly evident.

Regarding the section of the *Sūtra* beginning with "Thus, Master Huiyuan," the second part provides scriptural evidence. As for the phrase "by means of that path" (*dao*), "path" refers to a track or gateway, not the Ultimate Path (*zhidao*).
The intended meaning is: how could the body produced through the influence of causes and conditions not follow a track, yet [the text says] it is without cause?

"How has this body suddenly come to be? Regarding "the net of delusion": delusion refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). Afflictions are like a net that entangles and binds sentient beings, such that they cannot find a way out.
Regarding "the abyss": it is water of extreme depth. Regarding "all accumulated burdens": these are all karmic retributions (*vipāka*). There are two kinds of karmic retribution;
they are great calamities and burdens that cause all sentient beings to undergo manifold sufferings. "Palace" (*fu*) refers to the accumulation of various things.

Regarding the phrase "the place of accumulation," the *Commentary on the Analects* states: "To store wealth and goods is called a 'storehouse' (*fu*). Therefore, a populous capital city is referred to as a 'storehouse'.
As for the equality of these two principles: ignorance initiates karma, and craving moistens it; both of these principles operate secretly as functions of the mind and spirit.
Because deluded beings do not perceive them, they are said to be "dark" (*ming*). Matters of good fortune and misfortune do not transcend these.

Second: "Ignorance obscures illumination" refers to fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodha*), which is delusion regarding original awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*). "Sentient feelings and perceptions, etc.

refers to the phase of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), the phase of evolution (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), and the two coarse phases (*dausthulya-lakṣaṇa*). "External objects" refers to the phase of objective realms (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*). Initially, one is deluded regarding the True and gives rise to the semblance;

this constitutes ignorance, which acts as the cause to produce the three subtle phases. Subsequently, one is deluded regarding the semblance and clings to it as real; this constitutes wisdom and its manifestations.

Continuing with the grasping at the aspect of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*): the grasping at a self takes the objective sphere as its object. Regarding "craving and so forth": "flow" (*srotas*) refers to that which moistens; "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the seeds of karma;
"forming a shape" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to receiving a body of maturation (*vipāka*). Regarding "those selves and so forth":

since this very body of mine is the body, all other things are therefore "that," leading to stubborn attachment and clinging. The remainder of the text is easy to understand. (The explanation of the meaning is hereby concluded.)
Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Sub-commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Nine (Part Two); Scroll Ten (Part One).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.
This is the second major section within the "Chapter on Karmic Retribution," which provides an explanation of the text.

Within the detailed exposition, the three types of karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable—are precisely the three types of conduct, such as "sinful" and so forth, mentioned in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. That sutra states: "Ordinary beings cling to attachments, constantly seeking existence or non-existence;
through improper reflection, they give rise to deluded actions, namely, sinful action, meritorious action, and immovable action. The commentary explains:
The two types of conduct, sin and merit, are precisely these two karmas of evil and good.

They share the same name, "immovable," because through delusion regarding the cause and effect of maturation (*vipāka*), one opposes right faith and understanding, thereby giving rise to the evil karma that brings about the general retribution of the three miserable realms, as well as the karma of suffering that brings about the specific retributions of humans and devas.
All are termed "meritorious actions" (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*). Because they are deluded regarding the true meaning [of reality], they do not know that the three realms are entirely suffering;

instead, they falsely claim them to be happiness and give rise to wholesome karma of the desire realm pertaining to humans and devas—this is termed "meritorious action. The tranquil karma of the four dhyānas and eight meditative absorptions is termed "immovable action" (*āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*).

Regarding the first point, the suffering retribution of evil karma: it is called "suffering" because the three evil fruits are not to be desired; it is called "retribution" because it compensates for prior evil karma.
This encompasses both the primary (the body) and secondary (the environment) retributions, which will be pointed out below according to their specific categories.

The text consists of two parts: first, a brief commentary on the scriptural passage; second, an opening of the chapters to explain the meaning. Within the first part, the phrase "the object is contrary," etc., is like failing to pass an examination when one has already been nominated.
For instance, one may be selected for promotion only to be dismissed, or harbor resentment toward a subordinate; furthermore, one’s desires may be obstructed by others, leading to ruin and failure.
Instances of this kind among humans number in the hundreds of thousands of millions, and cannot be recorded in full.
Since these various forms of killing, harming, and oppression result in mutual retribution of enmity with no end in sight, they all arise from the evil karma of hatred.
Furthermore, it may also be that one proceeds downward from greed to initiate unwholesome karma; this text is easy to understand.

In the former case, three unwholesome karmas—killing, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech—are predominant. In the latter case, three unwholesome karmas—sexual misconduct, stealing, and frivolous speech—are predominant.
False speech applies to both cases, thus completing the sevenfold karma. All of these are what is initiated; greed, hatred, and delusion are that which initiates them.

Therefore, they are collectively termed the "ten evil deeds. Furthermore, acts such as inflicting distress, humiliation, and devouring are all subsumed under the minor offenses and do not fall within the count of the ten evils.
If one were to categorize them according to the violation of the ten heavy precepts, then selling alcohol, stinginess, and self-praise should be added to the category of greed;
malice and slandering the Buddha by speaking of his faults should be included in the category of hatred; and delusion, as it permeates both poisons, is not mentioned separately. Moreover, due to...
Those who break the precepts out of greed or hatred are all called *rākṣasas* of craving. Those who break the precepts out of delusion (*moha*) are called *rākṣasas* of views.
As for the deluded person, they give rise to divergent views, such as claiming that there are no transgressions; yet these are not like the case of cattle or sheep.

The characteristics of the transgressions upon which they rely do not differ from those of killing, stealing, and so forth; therefore, they are not mentioned separately. Furthermore, even among deluded people, there are those who are merely indifferent and incapable of performing wholesome deeds.

Committing evil is equivalent to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, it is not mentioned here. The reason for not mentioning the retribution of the indeterminate, but speaking only of the retribution of the wholesome and the unwholesome, is also based on this principle.
Even when investigated minutely, these [indeterminate] characteristics are subtle and inferior; thus, they are not mentioned.
In the commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is proven that there are indeed three types of evil rebirths, not merely those of hell-beings and hungry ghosts.

The commentary states: "Below the three evil realms" refers to the second section, which opens the chapter and provides its explanation. This section contains two parts: first, the presentation of the headings;

second, the subsequent explanation. Within the first part, there are again two sub-sections: first, the general presentation of the headings; second, the detailed opening of the items according to those headings.
Regarding the phrase "In the beginning of the commentary," this follows the sequence of the chapters and consists of five segments; the present passage is the first. As for "Hell": *naraka*.
*Naraka*. This raises the name for the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution). The etymology has already been explained;

since the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is precisely the *niśraya*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "In *naraka* (which means hell), one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of the five aggregates.

Once this maturation has arisen, it is called *nāraka* (here translated as 'the evil one,' referring to the sentient being who commits evil). Although the *niśraya* and the *sattva-vipāka* (the primary retribution of the sentient being) differ, they both constitute extreme suffering."

This is a name for *vipāka* (maturation). Its location is not fixed; it is not found exclusively beneath the earth. If one were to translate it according to its literal meaning, there would be no such term as "hell" (*naraka*).
Therefore, the Commentary states that it accords with the *Vaipulya* (Mahāyāna) scriptures. Regarding *preta* (hungry ghosts), the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says: "Furthermore, they have many cravings."
Regarding the phrase "sustaining oneself," etc., as for the name "animal" (*tiryag-yoni*): the *Nyāyānusāra* states that it is because beings in that realm mostly dwell with their bodies horizontal;
or because within that realm there may be some who move horizontally.
Below the section on the six destinies (*ṣaḍgati*), the second [point] clarifies the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding "all [are] by means of the eighth":

the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that "herein, the eighth consciousness is the basis for the designation of realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). It further states: "This consciousness definitely arises as the [basis for] the realms."

There is no need for the essence of birth to undergo further exertion, nor is there any point in separately maintaining that it possesses substantial reality. Since the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) remains uninterrupted, it is truly a matured result (*vipāka*).
Because it is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), these three evil realms likewise all take the eighth consciousness as their essence.
Regarding the commentary on the hells, the text is divided into two parts. First, a detailed explanation of the dimensions, names, and characteristics of suffering for three types of locations.
Second, following the phrase "above this" and so forth, an incidental clarification that the hell-wardens are both sentient and insentient.
Within the first part, the commentary relies upon the *Yogācārabhūmi*. The phrase "below this" refers to beneath this Jambudvīpa; as the *Abhidharmakośa* also states: "This Jambudvīpa..."
Two thousand [yojanas] below Jambudvīpa lies the Avīci hell, called the Mahānaraka. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (172) states:
"The Venerable One (*Bhadanta*) has declared that beneath Jambudvīpa there is the Great Hell, as well as the Neighboring Hells (*utsada-naraka*) and the Solitary Hells (*pratyeka-naraka*).
In the other three continents, there are only the Neighboring and Solitary Hells, but no Great Hell. This is because..."
However, it is only the people of this continent who create both good and evil with such intensity, as is not the case for those in other continents.

Some say that even the Northern Continent lacks the neighboring hells and so forth, because it is a place where the fruits of purely wholesome karma are experienced. Regarding the Reviving Hell (*saṃjīva*):
it is said that many sentient beings gather there together, produced by the sovereign power of their karma, and various instruments of suffering [arise] in succession.
They rise up and again slaughter one another, falling to the ground in a swoon. Then, from the midst of the sky, a great voice proclaims: "These sentient beings may be revived! They may be revived!
Suddenly, those sentient beings rise up once more and are subjected to the instruments of torture as before, slaughtering one another again.

By reason of this, they undergo suffering for a long time, until [the karma] created in previous lives—[one... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a description of the Saṃjīva hell, likely from a sūtra or śāstra. The final portion of the sentence is incomplete.)
Because all evil and unwholesome karma has not yet been exhausted, one does not depart; thus it is named accordingly. Regarding the "Four Thousand Below Saṃjīva":
this means that after passing four thousand [yojanas], one reaches the Black Rope Hell and the other seven hells; it is not within those four thousand. As for the Black Rope Hell:

It means that for the most part, those sentient beings are seized by them; the hell-wardens bind them with black ropes, or divide them into various sections, drawing patterns and images upon them and joining them together.
Then, along the paths thus marked, they are either gouged or severed, or hacked and carved.

By reason of these causes and conditions, they remain there until their karma is exhausted before they finally emerge. As for the "Mass Crushing" (Saṃghāta) hell, it refers to those who... [have] those... sentient beings.
Due to their karma, they may at times gather and assemble together.
At that time, there appear wardens who drive and compel them between two great mountains with the heads of rams. Once they have entered, the two mountains press upon them.
Having been pressed, blood flows forth from all the apertures. Thus it is with the two mountains having the heads of rams, horses, elephants, lions, and tigers.
The same applies to the others. Second, they are further combined and placed in a great iron vat, where they are pressed like sugarcane.

Once they have been pressed, blood flows forth. Third, after being combined again, a great iron mountain descends from above, causing those sentient beings to fall upon the iron ground, where they are hacked, pierced, pounded, or torn apart; thus their blood—

The flow returns and continues until their karma is exhausted, at which point they finally emerge. As for those who "wail," it refers to those sentient beings who, seeking shelter, enter a great iron chamber;
as soon as they have entered, fire breaks out, blazing, fiercely blazing, intensely blazing, and all-pervasively blazing.
Once they have been burned, they are oppressed by excruciating pain and let out wails, continuing thus until their karma is exhausted.
As they emerge, those who cry out loudly differ from those previously described in their manifestation of suffering. That is to say, their dwellings are like wombs;
since their suffering exceeds that of the former, they let out great cries. Regarding "being burned," there are three types:
first, the hell-wardens place sentient beings upon iron skewers three *yojana* in length and rotate them back and forth. This signifies—
First, they are roasted from within. Second, it is like roasting a fish: with a large iron skewer, they are pierced through the feet and emerge from the crown of the head;
they are turned over and roasted until flames erupt from all the pores of their sense organs and from their mouths.
Third, they place the sentient beings upon the aforementioned great hot iron ground, either face up or face down, with three [iron] spikes...
An iron club. Whether striking or prodding, they strike and prod them everywhere until they become like lumps of flesh.
They suffer for a long time, only emerging once their karma is exhausted. As for "extreme burning," this also has three types:

first, they are pierced from below with a large three-pronged iron skewer that passes through both shoulders and emerges at the crown of the head; consequently, from their eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and pores, a fierce [flame]...
2. Furthermore, their bodies are completely wrapped in three-fold sheets of hot, large copper and iron.
3. Moreover, they are cast upside down into great iron cauldrons filled with the ash-water of the Samiṃpha river and boiled therein.
The broth surges and boils, causing these sentient beings to drift and swirl about, emerging and submerging, until their flesh, blood, skin, and sinews are all entirely...

It is dissolved and rotted away, leaving only a skeleton. Then, they are again filtered out and placed upon a floor of glowing red-hot iron, where their skin, flesh, blood, and veins are made to grow back as before.
They are then returned to the cauldron; the rest is as described in the section on the "Great Heat" (Mahāraurava).

Only when their karma is exhausted do they emerge. As for the Unrelenting Hell (Avīci), there are six types. The first is that within it, in the eastern direction, there are many hundreds of *yojanas*... three.
Upon a vast ground of glowing iron, there are fiercely blazing fire-spikes. Leaping with flames from the east, they pierce those sentient beings;
they penetrate the skin and enter the flesh, severing tendons and breaking bones, further piercing through to the marrow and burning them like fat candles.

Thus, their own bodies become entirely composed of fierce flames. It is likewise in the other directions as well. Consequently, those sentient beings are intermingled with these fierce flames, and [there is nothing but]...
They see masses of fire approaching from the four directions; the flames intermingle without any interval, and the suffering they endure likewise has no interval.
They hear nothing but the sounds of their cries of agony. Because of this, these sentient beings are named "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted).
Second, furthermore, an iron winnowing basket filled with the fierce flames and iron ashes of the three hot hells is used to sift them. Third, again...
They place them upon the ground of glowing red iron. They make them climb a great mountain of glowing red iron and then descend; having descended, they make them climb again.
Furthermore, they pull their tongues from their mouths and, using a hundred iron nails, nail them down and stretch them so that there are no wrinkles.
It is like stretching a cowhide. Furthermore, they lie face up on hot iron ground;
with iron tongs, their mouths are pried open, and large, glowing-hot iron balls are placed within them, immediately burning their mouths and throats and penetrating deep into their internal organs.
It exits from below. Sixth, molten copper is poured into his mouth; it burns the throat and the tongue, penetrating through to the internal organs, and exits from below.
The remaining torments are like a fierce conflagration. Only when the karma is exhausted does one emerge. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Within this [hell], one undergoes uninterrupted suffering; it is not like the other seven great *naraka*s, where the suffering is not constant. Therefore...

It is called "Avīci" (Uninterrupted). For instance, in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) hell, although the bodies of the sentient beings there are repeatedly cut, pierced, ground, and crushed, they are restored to their original state as soon as they encounter a cool breeze;
it is for this reason that the name Saṃjīva is established.
In the Avīci hell, such a thing does not occur. Furthermore, it is said to be "uninterrupted" because there is no interval of pleasure between the sufferings. This is not the case in the other hells.
There is the intermittent arising of pleasure; although there is no pleasure of maturation (*vipāka*), there is the pleasure of outflow (*niṣyanda*).

According to the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the critical school (*viniścaya-vādin*), it should be stated as follows: because they are born from the performance of predominant unwholesome karma, the physical forms they obtain are vast and expansive.
Since the bodies of these sentient beings occupy many locations with no intervening gaps between them, they are called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*). Question: If one...

Question: Since the body is all-pervasive, how can other sentient beings be accommodated? Answer: Because their karmic power is identical, although one [body] fills [the space], there is no hindrance to accommodating others;
they occupy adjacent positions. As for the statement that "all are separated by two thousand *yojanas*," this is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
For it merely states that thirty-two thousand *yojanas* below here lies the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*), and four thousand *yojanas* below the Reviving Hell lies [the Black Line Hell].
Regarding the other hells: according to this calculation, descending thirty-two thousand [yojanas] from the ground, one reaches the summit of the Saṃjīva (Reviving) hell.
The Saṃjīva is ten thousand [yojanas] in length and breadth. Descending another four thousand [yojanas] from there, one reaches the Kālasūtra (Black String) and the seven [hells] that follow.
Each of these seven is ten thousand [yojanas] in length and breadth; based on this, they should be situated as if arrayed side by side.

It is not that they are stacked one above the other. Since Mount Sumeru enters eighty thousand *yojanas* into the water and rests upon the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*) below, if they were stacked vertically, the distance from the level ground to the bottom of the Avīci Hell would be approximately one hundred twenty-eight thousand *yojanas*.

This would mean it would penetrate more than halfway through the Golden Wheel. For this reason, the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* offers two interpretations, taking the side-by-side arrangement as the correct one. All [of these]...
"Separated by two thousand [yojanas]" means that seven [hells] are arranged side-by-side; the distance between each one is two thousand yojanas, not the vertical distance. [Commentary:
Regarding "The Eight Cold [Hells]" below, the second section clarifies the arrangement of the eight cold hells.
First, the Arbuda (Blister) Hell: it refers to those sentient beings who, being extremely heavy and vast, are oppressed by the touch of intense cold. All...
The limbs all contract and shrivel, appearing like festering sores. Regarding the descent of two thousand *yojanas*: this refers to the first cold hell being level with the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell;
that is, it is situated alongside the Saṃjīva. From the base of the Saṃjīva, descending two thousand [yojanas], there are the remaining seven [cold hells] as well.
These seven are also arranged by spreading out horizontally, not vertically. According to this, they should all be situated adjacent to the Saṃjīva.
The Reviving Hell lies beneath the Black Rope Hell and exactly between them. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, descending from this level by twenty thousand *yojanas* one reaches the Avīci Hell;
its depth and breadth are each also twenty thousand *yojanas*, making its bottom forty thousand *yojanas* below this point.
The other seven hells, beginning with the Black Rope, are situated above the Avīci Hell, stacked one upon another. This is one explanation.
They all lie adjacent to the Avīci Hell. Those eight cold hells likewise lie on the periphery of that great primary hell.
Question: This Jambudvīpa is quite small in size; how can it possibly accommodate the Avīci and other such hells beneath it? Answer: The continent is like a heap of grain.
It is pointed at the top and narrow at the bottom; therefore, the great ocean becomes gradually deeper and narrower, enabling it to contain [the beings].

As for "Bubbling and Bursting" (Phalgu-bhedana), the suffering of the cold is even more extreme than before; it is like a blister that bursts, with pus and blood flowing out and the wound contracting and shriveling.
The first two names are derived from what they resemble on the body, and thus they are so called. Regarding "Khaḍatāla" (pronounced *khā-ta-la*): the *Abhidharmakośa* states that it is *Arbuda*.

*Ṭha.* (The *sha* is pronounced with a retroflex; it is the sound of enduring cold. Because the cold increases further, the mouth cannot open, but one can only move the tongue to produce sounds such as *he*, *zha*, and *tie*.
Regarding *hao hao fan*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* calls this *ho-ho-pa*;

this refers to when the cold becomes even more intense, so that the tongue can no longer move, but one can only produce the sound *ho ho*. Regarding *hu hu fan*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* calls this... [text continues].
"Hu-hu-po. This [sound] cannot even be articulated; one merely makes the sound "hu-hu.

These three names are established based on the distinct sounds produced as they endure the suffering of the cold. As for the Blue Lotus Hell, it is so named because of the sensation of being touched by that cold.
All parts of the body become entirely livid and bruised; the skin cracks, either five or six times.
As for the "red lotus," the lividity exceeds the previous color and turns a reddish hue; the skin splits, either ten times or more.
As for the "great red lotus," it means those parts of the body become extremely large and reddish; the skin splits, either a hundred times or more. The latter three [stages] follow from...
The name is established based on the color it resembles. The above constitutes the explanation of the fundamental [hells]. Regarding the "adjacent" [hells] below:
this is the second section, the detailed explanation of the adjacent [hells]. These are situated immediately outside the gates on the four sides of the eight hot hells;

as each gate has four such locations, they are called "adjacent" because they border the vicinity of the fundamental [hells], much like the gardens and groves surrounding a city wall. They are where those sinners wander.

In these locations, the [suffering] increases day by day. As that verse states: "The eight increases are all sixteen," namely: the Pit of Embers (*Kukūla*), the Quagmire of Corpses and Excrement (*Kuṇapa*), the Forest of Sharp Blades (*Asidharā*), and the River of Boiling Water (*Vaitaraṇī*).
Regarding these, the prose commentary explains them as "increases" (*utsada*) because they are sites of additional torturous harm; therefore, they are called "increases."
In the primary hells, having already been afflicted, they suffer further affliction; thus, because the suffering is intensified, it is called "Increasing" (*ūṣmaghāta*).
First, as for the "Hot Ashes" (*Kukūla*): this refers to hot ashes that reach up to the knees. When the sentient beings of the eight hot hells seek to escape their dwelling, [they fall into it].
When they arrive here while wandering about, at the moment their feet touch the ground, their skin, flesh, sinews, and bones all immediately dissolve and rot away;
yet when they lift their feet, these regenerate, restoring them to their original state. Regarding the second [hell], the Excrement of Corpses: the excrement of corpses forms a mire.
These sentient beings, seeking shelter, emerge from the previous [hell] and wander forward until they sink into it, with both head and feet submerged. Furthermore, in...
Within the mud, there are many *narkuṭa* worms, each one foot in length, with white beaks and black heads.
They pierce the skin and enter the flesh, severing tendons and breaking bones to extract and eat the marrow. Among the three types of sharp-edged weapons, the third is a sword with a keen edge;
its blade is turned upward to form a path. When those sentient beings, having emerged from the previous [hell], wander here and set foot upon it, their skin—
The flesh, sinews, and bones all rot and dissolve away; yet as soon as they lift their feet, it regrows, restored exactly as before. Second is the Forest of Swords.

When those sentient beings have emerged from the former [forest], they go toward its shade. As soon as they sit beneath it, a gentle breeze arises, causing the blade-leaves to fall and sever their bodies.
All their limbs and joints immediately fall to the ground. There are black *tarakṣu* dogs and *śālāvṛka* wolves.
They tear away the fat from their spines and devour it. There is also the Iron Śālmalī Forest, which is like a tree of soapberry thorns.
Once those sentient beings have emerged from the former [place], they rush toward it; pursued by dogs and other creatures, they consequently climb upon it.
When they ascend, all the thorns point downward and pierce them; when they wish to descend from the tree, the thorns turn back upward and pierce their bodies, penetrating all their limbs and joints.
At that time, there appear great iron-beaked birds that alight upon their heads.
Or they are placed upon their shoulders; their eyes are pecked out and they are devoured. As for the Four Fierce Rivers:
there is a vast river filled with boiling, scalding ash-water. Those sentient beings, seeking shelter, emerge from the previous [hell].
They fall into this place, just as if beans were placed in a great cauldron and boiled over a fiercely blazing fire.
They surge and tumble along with the boiling water, rising and sinking all around. On both banks of the *āpa* river stand rows of hell-wardens, holding clubs, ropes, and large nets;
they block those sentient beings, preventing them from escaping, or else they ensnare them with ropes.
Or they may be fished out with a net and placed upon a vast expanse of glowing red-hot iron. With the sentient beings lying face up, the wardens ask them:
"What do you now require? They reply: "I am currently devoid of all perception; however, I am oppressed by various sufferings of hunger.
Then the wardens immediately use iron tongs to pry open their mouths and pour in [molten metal] that is intensely hot and burning.
A red-hot iron ball is placed in his mouth; the rest is as previously described.

If he answers, "I am suffering from thirst," they immediately pour molten copper into his mouth, where he undergoes suffering for a long time until his karma is exhausted and he finally emerges. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"This river is like a moat, while the [first] three are like enclosures, because there are four *utsada* (additional hells) on each of the four sides; thus, it is said that there are sixteen in total. It further cites a sutra, saying:
These eight *naraka*s, I declare, are difficult to transcend. Their ground is made of glowing iron, surrounded by iron walls, with four gates on the four sides;
these are opened and closed with iron bolts. Their dimensions are skillfully arranged, and each has sixteen secondary hells (*utsada*).
[It extends] for many hundreds of *yojanas*. Filled with those who have committed evil deeds, it is surrounded by intersecting flames, and fierce fires burn constantly within it.
Regarding the phrase "descending to the solitary ones," this is the third specific explanation of the solitary [hells].

Furthermore, while the fundamental hells have sixteen subsidiary hells (*utsada*) as their retinue, and although the cold hells lack such a retinue because their locations are primary, only this [hot hell] is not like that; therefore, it is said:
The solitary [hells]. The *Abhidharmakośa* also states that the other solitary hells are produced by the individual karma of sentient beings;
they are of many varieties, their locations are indefinite, and they may even exist beneath the earth, in the air, or in other places.
The receptacles of the various hells are arranged in this manner: while the primary location is below, the branches are indefinite. This concludes the general section above.
The initial section, which separately explained the names, locations, and characteristics of the three categories of hells, is now concluded.

The commentary on the passage "above" and "below" constitutes the second section, which incidentally discusses whether the hell-wardens (*yamarāja*) are sentient or non-sentient beings. Question: Are there hell-wardens present in all the aforementioned hells? Answer:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is without error to say that they exist in all of them. However, if one follows the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (the *Xianzong lun*), it is said that in the Great Avīci Hell...
The three hells of Heat, Intense Heat, and Great Heat have no hell-wardens (*yamaraka*) to guard them. The three hells of Great Wailing, Crushing, and so forth have few hell-wardens;
there are only the messengers of King Yama who inspect them from time to time. All others consist entirely of non-sentient beings (*asattva*).

If one follows the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they are exclusively non-sentient; however, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, both interpretations apply. That text states: "Some say they are non-sentient."
[Question: How does this action [occur]? [Answer: The karmic force of sentient beings is like the wind at the time of the formation of a kalpa (*vivartakalpa*).
[Question: If that is so, how do you reconcile this with what the Great Virtuous Subhūti said? As his verse states:

"Those whose minds are constantly corrupted by the poison of anger, who delight in various evil deeds, and who rejoice at the suffering of others—upon death, they become the henchmen of Yama. [Question: The King Yama dispatches the *kṣetrapāla* spirits to hurl the sinners...
[Question: Those who cast sentient beings into hell are actual sentient beings; it is not that those within hell are called "sentient beings.

Therefore, the hell-wardens are not actual sentient beings. [Answer: Some say they are sentient beings. [Question: If that is so, since this is an evil karma, where would its maturation (*vipāka*) be experienced? [Answer:
Since even within hell there is room for the maturation that is produced, what principle is there to exclude this?

(Question: If that is so, for what reason is it not burned by fire? (Answer: This is certainly because it is obstructed by the power of karma, or because it brings about different primary elements (*mahābhūta*);
therefore, it is not burned. The *Vibhāṣā* is the same. The Commentary follows the former method and the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The above concludes the section on the hells within the detailed explanation. The Commentary states: "Animals also have three [types]," etc. Second.
This is a separate explanation of the categories of animals. Regarding the commentary on "mutually harming one another" and so forth:

for instance, those who are weak and frail are harmed by those with great strength and undergo various sufferings; being devoid of autonomy, they are driven by others and frequently subjected to whipping and flogging.
Serving as the means of subsistence for humans and devas, they experience all manner of extreme [suffering] due to these causes and conditions.
"Severe suffering. The commentary also states that there are three types of hungry ghosts (*preta*). This third section provides a detailed explanation of the ghosts.
Regarding the phrase "passing from here to other places," the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The primary abode of all ghosts is the realm of King Yama.
Five hundred *yojana*s beneath this Jambudvīpa lies the kingdom of King Yama; its length and breadth are likewise. From there, they disperse further and further..."
Dwelling in other places, some are handsome and possess great majesty, enjoying various riches and pleasures with sovereignty like that of the gods;
others are emaciated by hunger and have ugly countenances. Such categories are explained at length as in the sutras.
*Yama* (here translated as "Quiescence") means that until all sentient beings reach that realm, they all say, "I have committed no sin"; yet as soon as they arrive there...
Thus, through the mirror of karma and other such means, their transgressions are revealed of themselves, and they dare not speak further; hence it is said that [the suffering] is stilled.
In the eastern and western continents, there are the first two classes of hungry ghosts. In the northern continent, there are only those of great majesty and power.

Some say that hungry ghosts do not exist there because they are produced by stinginess and greed, and because the northern continent is a place where sentient beings are free from possessiveness. [In the realm of] the Four Great Kings, there are thirty...
For three days, there are spirits of great majesty and power who, together with hosts of devas, guard against their return. The remaining meanings are as explained in other fascicles.

Regarding the first point, "obstruction from without": because of the habitual practice of extreme stinginess, one is born into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), constantly beset by hunger and thirst.
Their skin, flesh, veins, and blood are all withered and parched, like dregs or charcoal; their hair is disheveled and matted, and their faces...
Dark and lusterless, with lips and mouth parched and withered, they constantly lick their faces and mouths with their tongues. Hungry, thirsty, and terrified, they run hither and thither;
yet whenever they reach a spring or pool, other sentient beings—holding swords, staves, and nooses—stand in rows to guard them, preventing them from drawing near.
Or, even if they are forced to take some, the spring immediately transforms into pus and blood before their very eyes. They themselves...
They wish to drink. Such cases as these are called being obstructed from food and drink by external factors.

Second, those obstructed by internal factors refers to those sentient beings whose throats are like needles, whose mouths are like torches, or who have goiters on their heads and distended bellies; due to these causes and conditions, [they are unable to eat or drink].
Even if they obtain food and drink, although there are no external obstacles, they naturally cannot consume them; this is called being hindered by internal obstacles.
As the Sūtra says, "Their throats are like needles"—this refers to such beings. Third, those who have no obstacles at all refers to hungry ghosts named *Jvālāmāla* (Flame-Wreath).
Whatever they drink or eat is entirely consumed by fire; because of this, they constantly undergo the great suffering of hunger and thirst. Furthermore...
The hungry ghosts (preta) are called "those who eat excrement and filth. Some eat a portion of excrement, rice, and urine;

others are able only to drink and consume things that are utterly loathsome, raw or cooked, smelling of stench. Even if they happen to obtain something fragrant and delicious, they are unable to eat it.
Or some cut off their own flesh to devour it; even if they happen to obtain other food, they ultimately cannot eat it. Such as these are called those who subsist on food and drink.
There are no obstructions.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the body are sparse" below, this is the fourth textual passage. As for "having the same dimensions as the hells," this refers only to the vast physical bodies obtained in this Avīci Hell;
each such body pervades the entire space therein without any small gaps remaining. In other hells, however, the dimensions are fixed.

The animals (*tiryagyoni*) range from small to large, and the forms of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) are ten thousandfold. Some say that for the most part they resemble humans, yet they also resemble animals;

generally, their manifestations are unstable. At the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), all spoke the noble language (*āryabhāṣā*), but later, as they followed their various locations, they produced all kinds of speech.
Thus, the commentary collectively states that "the rest are all indeterminate."
Regarding the commentary on the lifespan [of the gods] below, this is the fifth section of the text.

As for the lifespan of the Four Great Kings and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that five hundred years of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings constitute one day and night in the Reviving (Saṃjīva) hell.

Thirty such days and nights form a month, and twelve such months form a year. By such years, their lifespan is five hundred; this continues up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
