Sixteen thousand years constitutes one day and night in the [Heats] Hell. Calculating months and years by accumulating these [days], their lifespan is likewise sixteen thousand years.

As for an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*): it is the period from when the human lifespan increases from ten years to eighty thousand, and then decreases again from eighty thousand back to ten years;
this is called one intermediate kalpa. Regarding "in sequence" (*yathākrama*) in this context, it refers to these eight hot hells respectively.
It is nearly half [of that]. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: Suppose one were to place *kṛsarā* seeds (Sanskrit: *tila*; "one *vāha*" means ten *shí* in this context) to fill a *vāha*.

Even if someone were able to remove a single seed every hundred years, those *kṛsarā* seeds would be exhausted more easily than the lifespan of one born in the Arbuda hell, which is difficult to bring to an end.
Twenty times this [lifespan] is the lifespan in the Nirarbuda hell. In this manner, each subsequent [hell] is twenty times the preceding.

[The lifespan] increases to become the life-span of the eight cold hells. Regarding the fact that animals have a maximum life-span of one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The life-span of animals (*tiryag-yoni*) is for the most part without fixed limit; if it is extremely long, it is also one intermediate kalpa—referring to the great nāga kings such as Nanda and others.

Therefore, the World-Honored One said: 'There are eight great nāgas, all of whom abide for one kalpa and are able to support the great earth. As for the life-span of hungry ghosts being five hundred [years], the *Abhidharmakośa*..."
Śāṅguān says: For ghosts, one human month constitutes one day. Calculated by this standard, they form months and years; their lifespan is five hundred years.

In the commentary on the "rewards of joy from wholesome karma," there are two parts: first, a brief explanation of the text; second, the section beginning with "The two paths of humans and devas," which specifically clarifies the joys.
This is the retribution. The text has two parts: first, an explanation via five gates; second, a judgment on the following section which clarifies and resolves potential objections.

Regarding the phrase "because of much thinking" (*sū-muò-sī-gù*), the two characters *suō* (多) and *mò* (思) are not consistent across various editions. Consequently, ancient masters have each provided a distinct interpretation based on these characters.

If one reads it as *sī* (思), it means that [the being] is well able to contemplate various kinds of good and evil, thereby distinguishing itself from other realms of existence. If one reads it as *sī*...

This refers to those who possess the virtue of intentional compassion (*cetanā-maitrī*), as they also differ from other realms of existence. Regarding "those whose minds are tranquil" (*śānta-citta*): most people lack the intense sufferings and disturbances of others;
unlike hungry ghosts (*preta*) and the like, who experience much seeking and excessive craving, fear and dread, and extreme great suffering and affliction, these are called "tranquil.
As for the categories in the commentary, there are two: first, humans; second, devas. Regarding "humans have four continents," this is based on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Upon the Golden Wheel, there are nine mountains in total. Sumeru stands in the center, while the other eight surround it.

Between each mountain, there is further a sea. Within the salt ocean, inside the ninth Iron Ring (Cakravāḍa), there are great continents on the four sides—namely, those of the east, south, west, and north—each directly facing its corresponding side of Mount Sumeru.

It is where humans dwell; that is to say, Jambudvīpa and so forth. Therefore, the commentary states: "The land within the ocean refers to the soil of the shores and islands. There is a tree named after this continent.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, in the center of this continent, facing north, there are nine Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇaparvata*).

North of the Black Mountains is the Great Snowy Mountain (*Himavat*); north of the Snowy Mountain is the Fragrant Intoxication Mountain (*Gandhamādana*). North of the Snowy Mountain is the Fragrant... [text ends]
To the south there is a great lake called Anavatapta (The Untroubled). Beside this lake is the Jambū forest; because it relies upon this forest, it is named Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, this continent is broad in the north and narrow in the south, with its three sides being equal in measure, its shape resembling a chariot.
The southern side is only three and a half *yojanas* wide; each of the other three sides is two thousand [yojanas] long.

Regarding Pūrvavideha (Eastern Victory Body): it is called "Victory Body" because its inhabitants excel. It is narrow in the east and broad in the west; its three sides are equal in measure, and its shape is like a half-moon.

The eastern side is three hundred and fifty-three [yojanas], while each of the other three sides is two thousand [yojanas]. Regarding Aparagoyānīya (Western Ox-Product): it is circular like the full moon, with a diameter of two thousand [yojanas].
It is five hundred [yojanas] in height and seven thousand and a half [yojanas] in circumference. As for Uttarakuru, it is also called Kuru;

its shape is like a square seat, with equal dimensions on all four sides, each measuring two thousand [yojanas]. Because the characteristics of each continent differ, the facial features, lineage, physical form, lifespan, and so forth of the inhabitants are each distinct.
Therefore, we now distinguish the types of humans according to their respective continents. Furthermore, there are eight intermediate [continents].
The continents (*dvīpa*) are the satellites of this great continent; there are two at each side of every continent, as explained in another fascicle.

Regarding those with a fixed lifespan of one thousand years, it is because they do not suffer premature death (*antarāmaraṇa*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In all other places, there is premature death, except for the northern continent of Uttarakuru.

The commentary on the heavens refers to the six lower heavens; subsequently, it clarifies the categories of celestial beings, meaning the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the two upper realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), all of which are collectively termed "heavens" (*deva*).

Because [the term] "destinies" (gati) is used loosely in that context, it is specifically distinguished here. The meaning of this scriptural passage refers exclusively to the six desire realms (*kāmadhātu*).

As the sutra says: "Abandoning evil and delighting in good, they again appear as humans or devas. Since this is clearly explained in conjunction with humans, it is the retribution induced by dispersed goodness (*vicitra-kuśala*).
Therefore, the higher realms are excluded. Furthermore, the structure of the scriptural passage from beginning to end naturally consists of three sections; by this, one knows for certain.
These are exclusively the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding the "six classes of desire," the first is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
This refers to the lower half of Mount Sumeru, which has four terraces. The lowest terrace is ten thousand *yojanas* above the surface of the water;

likewise, each of the three upper terraces is separated from the one below it by ten thousand *yojanas*. Residing on these, in order from the bottom, are three assemblies of yakṣa deities. Specifically:
The Four Great Kings—Dṛḍha-hasta, Mālādhara, Nitya-pramudita, and Vaiśravaṇa—dwell together with their retinues.

Furthermore, the yakṣas of the lower three [heavens], the inhabitants of the palaces of the sun and moon, and the celestial hosts dwelling upon the seven golden mountains, all belong to the jurisdiction of the Four Kings.
Since the first heaven governs these four kings as its masters and the multitudes as its subjects, they are called the "Four."
The second [heaven] among the assembly of the great kings of gods is the Heaven of the Thirty-three, also called Trāyastriṃśa.

This means that from these Four Great Kings, ascending forty thousand yojanas, one reaches the summit of Mount Sumeru. On each of the four sides of this summit, there are eight heavens, totaling thirty-two;
with the abode of Śakra added to these, they constitute the thirty-three, forming the second heaven in total. The third...
Furthermore, eighty thousand yojanas above this, in the sky, there is a heaven called *Ratnaprabhāsa* (Time-Portion), where the inhabitants enjoy the objects of the five desires;

they are so named because they know the divisions of time. Fourth, sixteen thousand [yojanas] above this, there is a heaven called *Tuṣita* (Joy-Sufficient), also known as *Saṃtuṣita* (Contentment-Sufficient);
its inhabitants enjoy the objects of the five desires and are so named because they give rise to joy and contentment. Fifth...

Thirty-two hundred thousand [yojanas] above this, there is a heaven called Nirmāṇarati (Delighting in Emanations). Because they emanate objects of desire themselves for their own enjoyment, it is so named.
Sixty-four hundred thousand [yojanas] above this Nirmāṇarati, there is a heaven called Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Mastery over the Emanations of Others).
This means that those devas exercise mastery over the objects of desire manifested by others and enjoy them.

The first two [heavens] reside on the earth, while the latter four are located in the empty space; in their respective abodes, there are also palaces, yet they dwell merely upon wind and clouds. These six above are collectively termed the "Desire Heavens" (*kāmadeva*).
That which is characterized by the mind's longing and seeking is precisely the essence of desire; this refers to the two types of craving: sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and... [the second type].
Dharma corresponds with the mind, causing the mind to have that which it desires; therefore, it is called "desire-mind. Thus, Śāriputra spoke in verse:
"The wondrous objects of the world are not true desire; true desire refers to the greed of human conceptualization.

That which combines with the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) is precisely the object desired. As for what is termed "sexual desire" and so forth, this refers to the substance of the aforementioned sense-objects, as well as their general application.

This addresses the external objection regarding the reason why the six heavens are designated as "desire realms" (*kāmadhātu*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes food, drink, sound, and the like;
for instance, the four kinds of *sodāsa* flavors and exquisite music constitute objects of sublime desire. This also resolves the general objection.
An external objection states: "The higher realms also possess desire; why then are they specifically designated as 'heavenly beings who experience desire'? Therefore, the answer is given:
it is based on their coarse nature and their union with the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), which constitutes the reason for their designation.

Regarding the phrase "the six types of experiencing desire up to smiling and gazing," this clarifies the characteristics of experiencing desire. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, in the first two [heavens], there is sexual intercourse, identical to that of humans.
However, as soon as the wind-energy is released, the feverish affliction is immediately removed; it is not like humans, who possess residual impurities.

In the Yāma heaven, sexual union is accomplished merely by embracing, and so forth, including even holding hands, laughing, or looking at one another—all are likewise [efficacious]. Furthermore, some say that all six heavens involve physical union;
the descriptions of embracing and so forth are intended only to demonstrate the differences in the duration of those acts. As for the higher heavens, the objects of desire become increasingly subtle.
"Excellent. It is because the mind of craving becomes increasingly heavy that it causes such a thing. Question: Do the various devas have males and females? Answer:
Upon the laps of those devas, male and female children suddenly manifest through transformation; these are what are called the sons and daughters born of those devas. Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "the others in the east, west, and north increase successively by double," this means that in the eastern continent [Pūrvavideha], the height is eight *hasta*. And so forth.
Regarding the measurement of thirty-two *zhǔ* (cubits) for the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) and so forth:

as for the description that their shapes follow one another like the form of a chariot and so on—namely, the Southern Continent is like a chariot, the Eastern like a half-moon, the Western continent is circular, and the Northern continent is square—the dimensions of the land of each continent are likewise identical to the shape of its face.
Regarding the celestial realms, the Four Heavenly Kings' realm is slightly more than half a *lǐ*, and each subsequent level increases fivefold.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In the desire-realm heavens, [the height] increases by one-quarter of a *krośa* at each successive level.
Thus, one-quarter of a *krośa* is added incrementally at each subsequent stage until, on the sixth heaven, the body length reaches one and a half *krośas*.
A *krośa* is translated here as "calling out" (*ming-huan*); it refers to the distance covered during the duration of a single call. This applies to both near and far distances.
Two *li* is approximately one-quarter of a *li*, which constitutes half a *li*; therefore, the height of the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*) is half a *li*.
The height of the gods of the sixth heaven is three *li*. Regarding the statement that the lifespan in this continent is indefinite:

at the end of the kalpa of decrease, the maximum lifespan is ten years; whereas at the beginning of the kalpa, the lifespan is immeasurable, numbering hundreds of thousands and more, beyond calculation. Thus, they are both [included].
The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "In this continent, the lifespan is indefinite; at the end it is ten years, and at the beginning it is immeasurable.

As for the heavens, [the calculation] begins from below that of humans. This is a verse from the *Abhidharmakośa*. One must first establish the day and night of the heavens before one can calculate the length of their lifespans.
To establish this: for instance, fifty human years constitute a single day and night for the lowest heaven. Based on these days and nights...

Thirty days constitute a month; twelve months constitute a year. Their lifespan is five hundred years. In the higher heavens of the five sense-desire realms (*kāmadhātu*), the duration of life increases progressively by doubling.
Specifically, one hundred human years constitutes a single day and night in the second heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three). Based on this day and night, months and years are calculated;

their lifespan there is one thousand years. For the four heavens beginning with Yāma, the calculation follows the same sequence, doubling respectively to two thousand, four thousand, eight thousand, sixteen thousand, thirty-two thousand, and sixty-four thousand years.
One year constitutes one day and night. By multiplying this day and night, months and years are formed in succession.

Their lifespan is thus two hundred thousand, four hundred thousand, eight hundred thousand, and six hundred thousand years respectively. The above concludes the explanation via five gates. The commentary states: "Regarding 'joy' and below," this is the second section, which resolves objections.
First, it reconciles the contradiction between suffering and joy; subsequently, it addresses the differences between the five and six realms of existence. As for the first objection: Now...

As long as one has not yet transcended the triple world, there is nothing that is not a fruit of suffering; how much more so when this realm possesses the eight sufferings, the five signs of decay, and various forms of mutilation and injury?
Yet you rashly judge it to be happiness—what is the reason for this? Answer: This is indeed suffering.

For now, we shall provisionally judge it to be happiness based on the retribution of the "suffering of suffering" found within the three lower realms of existence. Therefore, the commentary states: "Speaking in terms of coarse characteristics, [we refer to] the five signs of decay."
As it is said in the sūtras: there are certain devaputras who, when they are about to pass away, first manifest five signs:
first, their garments become soiled; second, their flower garlands wither; third, sweat flows from both armpits; fourth, their bodies emit a foul odor;
fifth, the devas and the devaputra no longer take pleasure in their own seats. At that time, that devaputra lies prostrate among the trees, and all his female attendants [join him] with others...
The deva-sons sport together. Having seen this, they give rise to great sorrow and suffering; furthermore, they undergo the pain of being reviled, despised, and struck with terror.

Because of the accomplishment of a vast accumulation of merit and the birth of a deva-son endowed with the five great sensual pleasures, the remaining former deva-sons of meager merit, upon seeing this, become terrified and undergo great sorrow and suffering. What has been described above applies generally to all.
The gods of the six heavens of the desire realm—the two lower classes of devas among them—also undergo the sufferings of being cut, severed, destroyed, driven away, and harmed.
This occurs when they engage in battle and conflict with the asuras;

as the gods and asuras oppose one another, they take up the four types of weaponry—namely gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli—and fight together. At that time, both the various devas and the asuras...
Some have their limbs severed; some have their bodies shattered; others are even brought to death. Yet, if their limbs are severed, they are restored to their former state;
if their heads are cut off, they immediately perish. Thus, between the devas and the asuras, there is mutual victory and defeat.
However, because the devas generally possess superior strength, power, and lineage, when either of these two is defeated by the other, they retreat into their own palaces.
They do not even offer consolation to their own kin; for this reason, they harbor grief and sorrow.
If the gods are victorious, they enter the palace of the asuras to seize their daughters, thereby giving rise to conflict and contention.
If the asuras are victorious, they enter the celestial palace to seek the four kinds of *sodā* nectar, and thus they wage war against one another. Furthermore, there are powerful devaputras.
As soon as he became incensed, that inferior deva was driven out from his own palace. For this reason, the various devas undergo three kinds of suffering:
namely, the suffering of death and its attendants, the suffering of being despised and slighted, and the suffering of being cut, broken, harmed, and expelled. [Commentary:
"Regarding devas, ghosts, and so forth" refers to the second contradiction; it refers to the *asuras*, for in various sūtras there are some [passages] which state...

If one opens them up separately as distinct paths, there are then six realms. Alternatively, if those who are subsumed within the realms of devas, hungry ghosts, or animals are included, there are only five realms.
The explanation of the five realms is complete.
The commentary on the third section, the retribution of immovable karma, has four parts: first, the formal explanation of the original text; second, a summary of the three types of karma;

third, the clarification of the timing of receiving retribution; and fourth, the reconciliation of the provisional and the ultimate. Regarding the first part, "immovable" refers to the four dhyānas, the eight samādhis, and so forth.

It refers to the retributions of the form and formless realms and so forth, because both cause and effect possess the quality of immovability (*āniñjya*). The text contains two parts, as listed in the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the initial explanation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) in the commentary: furthermore, speaking of this in terms of its general characteristics, it is called the "eight attainments" (*aṣṭa-samāpatti*), all of which are equally wholesome.

It is *samādhi* by nature. To speak of the distinctions: that which belongs to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is called "dhyāna" (meditative absorption), while that of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is simply called "samādhi.

This is because there are differences regarding the presence or absence of the constituent factors (*aṅga*), and whether calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are balanced or unbalanced, as will be explained below in the section defining their characteristics.

Furthermore, the practices cultivated by the noble ones and ordinary beings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are largely the same with minor differences; ordinary beings merely seek higher states out of a sense of expediency.
It is sublime. It is practiced out of weariness with the suffering of the lower realms and so forth.

Furthermore, those of the Two Vehicles practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) out of a desire to weary themselves of birth and death, a longing for higher and higher stages, and the severance of lower and lower stages, or seeking to escape the triple world.

If it is Bodhisattvas, they enter meditative concentration by practicing solely to accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), to transform sentient beings, to subdue externalists, to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle, and as a manifestation; this is explained in detail in other volumes.

Therefore, all cultivation of causes and their resulting retributions does not exceed the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). When the followers of the Two Vehicles cultivate this, they transcend the Triple World forever.

Bodhisattvas, however, manifest entry [into these realms] with mastery over supernormal powers to bring about vast benefit; furthermore, regarding the essence, characteristics, names, aspirations, and realizations of what they cultivate— *Note: The original text contains a typographical error "忻趣" (xīnqù) which should be "欣趣" (xīnqù), meaning "to aspire to and enter. The translation reflects this correction.*
These are essentially the same, with only minor differences. The present sutra concerns exclusively that which is cultivated by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Nevertheless, the explanations regarding the definition of the names, the extraction of their essence, and the demonstration of their characteristics in the commentary (*śāstra*) are largely identical to the main sections. Within the text, there are first the four dhyānas and subsequently the four concentrations (*samādhi*).

Regarding "dhyāna" within the section on the dhyānas: in the new terminology, there is both a general and a specific sense. Generally, it is called *dhāta*. The three phrases following "in a single object of focus" are as follows:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* contains twenty-three sections. The first phrase, "causing the mind to be one-pointed," explains the meaning of the term *samādhi*.
The following two phrases explain the term *dhyāna*. As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks: "By what definition is the name 'dhyāna' established? it replies:

"Because by means of this tranquility (*śamatha*), one is able to deliberate (*pravicinoti*) with precision. This is the same here as well, because the essence of deliberation is wisdom (*prajñā*). The subsequent text states: "Deliberation is precisely..."

It truly understands the meaning; that is, it certainly possesses the function of tranquility (*śamatha*), because it can produce wisdom (*prajñā*). It is called "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) based on this function and its fruit.

[The sub-commentary] below the section on the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) addresses an objection. The objection states: "If this is so, then the formless attainments and the mental concentration (*samādhi*) of the desire realm [would also be called meditative absorptions]."

This name should be established; therefore, this general explanation is provided. The *Abhidharmakośa* also poses this question, and its response offers four meanings, as explained in a separate fascicle.
The present commentary briefly addresses only the single meaning of "superior observation" (*adhyālambana*) being equal.

Regarding the four [meanings] in the commentary, they follow the sequence below, and subsequently distinguish the specific names. These first four—[one, two, three, and four]—are taken as the distinct names. First, *vitarka* (applied thought).
Regarding "vicāra and so forth": The *Abhidharmakośa* asks: "If one-pointedness of mind is the essence of dhyāna, on what basis are the first, second, third, and fourth established?

The verse answers: "The first has vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha; the subsequent ones gradually abandon the preceding factors. This means that the first is established by having vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha.
As one gradually abandons the preceding factors, the second, third, and fourth are established. [The second] is established as having abandoned vicāra while still possessing prīti and sukha.
Regarding the second dhyāna: if one is free from *vicāra* and *prīti*, and possesses only *sukha*, it is established as the third dhyāna.

If one is further free from the preceding three [factors], it is established as the fourth dhyāna. Thus, while they share the same objective support (*ālambana*), they are divided into four types. Question:
If this is so, why not simply name them *vitarka-vicāra-prīti-sukha-dhyāna*, rather than using "first," "second," and so forth, as their distinct names? Answer: If one were to name them...
Vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha are each non-pervasive within their respective stages. For instance, regarding the first dhyāna:

if one speaks of vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha, these do not pervade the intermediate dhyāna, because that stage has vicāra but lacks vitarka, and furthermore lacks both prīti and sukha, possessing only the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā).
Moreover, most defiled dhyānas do not possess all the factors (aṅga), and neither the preparatory stage (anāgamya) nor the access concentrations (sāmantaka) possess prīti.

Because they are also exclusively associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), they are designated only as the first, second, third, and fourth [dhyānas]. Thus, within their respective stages, there is nothing to which they do not pervade.

The rest is as explained in other volumes; this applies equally to all eight concentrations (*samādhi*). Below the section on the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) in the commentary, the four dhyānas are explained. These also have both general and specific aspects.

Within the general aspect, the first two lines merely receive the name "concentration" (*samādhi*) and are not identical to the "meditative absorptions" (*dhyāna*); they possess distinct superior names.
It may be followed. Regarding "surpassing and violating that which is harmful," the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (141) states:

"Within these four stages, one transcends all that possesses form (*rūpa*), violates all dharmas possessing form, and because form-dharmas have no possibility of arising therein, one eliminates and abandons all perceptions of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The formless (*ārūpya*) refers to..."

The formless [attainments] involve the cessation of the three types of perception of obstructive form (*sapratigha-rūpa-saṃjñā*). One contemplates "boundless space" and so forth; this carries the meaning of opposition, harm, and transcendence.
Because one cultivates entry into these meditative absorptions while remaining within the desire and form realms, physical form still persists.

One simultaneously forms a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) to suppress the perception of form, taking emptiness, consciousness, and so forth as one's objective domain, thereby entering these absorptions. According to the commentary, the first three [formless attainments] proceed from preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Proceeding downward, the second [section] explains the specific names. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The three names beginning with 'Infinite Space' are established based on their preparatory stages (*prayoga*).

That is to say, during the stage of preparatory application prior to cultivating meditative concentration, because one detests and destroys form (*rūpa*), one forms a conceptual resolve (*adhimokṣa-saṃjñā*).

When this preparatory stage is perfected, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Furthermore, within that preparatory stage, by detesting infinite space and forming a conceptual resolve toward it, one contemplates infinite consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
When the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) is perfected, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Furthermore, during that preparatory practice, one becomes weary of infinite consciousness and gives rise to a perception of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-saṃjñā*), relinquishing all that exists and abiding in tranquility. When this preparatory practice is perfected, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Therefore, it is said that the first three stages are named according to their preparatory practices. As for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), its time is inferior; when a name is applied based on the essential nature of the stage itself, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "No..."

"Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā) is a designation established on account of its dullness and inferiority. Because it lacks the clear, superior perception of the lower stages, it is called "non-perception" (asaṃjñā);

because it possesses a dull and inferior perception, it is called "not non-perception" (na-asaṃjñā). Thus, the name is applied to that state based directly upon the dullness and inferiority of its perception.

Question: At the time of this preparatory application (*prayoga*), what kind of mental aspect (*ākāra*) is cultivated? Answer: According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, at the time of this preparatory application, one also reflects thus:
"All perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are like a disease, like an arrow, like an abscess; if perception were entirely absent, it would be like a state of deluded darkness.

Only that which is neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is contrary to the aforementioned [states], being tranquil and sublime. Thus, one knows that at the time of the preparatory application, one contemplates [in this manner].

The fundamental [state] is characterized by dull perception; it must necessarily be preceded by preparatory application (*prayoga*). For this reason, it is designated by its essential nature as "dull and inferior perception.

Why is this not the same as when, during the three preceding preparatory minds, one contemplates infinite space and so forth? In reality, the fundamental state does not take space as its object in a permanent manner.
It is from this that the name is established, following its preparatory application; for the preparatory application does not take the root [element] as its object.

Because this treatise forms its conceptualization based on the [fundamental] practice, here in the fourth stage of application (*prayoga*), one takes the dull and inferior conceptualization of the fundamental [state] as the object and reflects thus:
"There is no superior, clear conceptualization; at times there is an inferior conceptualization, which necessarily arises depending upon the fundamental.
This is precisely the reason for establishing the name. Furthermore, this establishment of the name refers only to the fundamental state, differing from the previous three.
The "explication of the preparatory means" (*upāya*) refers to the preparatory means for entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*). However, the preparatory means and the intent for entry differ;

as previously stated in brief, the intent for entry varies among ordinary beings, followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), and Bodhisattvas. When one is about to enter through cultivation, they all share the same preparatory means:

namely, revulsion toward the lower realms and aspiration for the higher. These "preparatory means" refer specifically to the means employed immediately prior to entry. [This concludes] the six practices.

As for these, there are three types each of delight (*abhinandana*) and aversion (*vidveṣa*), as listed by name in the commentary; their number is fixed and not otherwise. However, as for the actual entities (*bhāva*) that are delighted in or averse to, they differ according to each respective stage (*bhūmi*).
For example, sensual desire and unwholesome states are what is averse to the first dhyāna; applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are what is averse to the second dhyāna;
and so on, up to the state of dwelling in the tranquility of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which is what is averse to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and so forth.
This may be understood by analogy with the desire for the higher [realms].

Furthermore, the first dhyāna is regarded as "calm, sublime, and detached" by the mind of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) below it, whereas it is regarded as "suffering, coarse," and so forth, by the minds of the neighboring stages (*sāmantaka*) of the other two dhyānas; thus, the phenomena of the desire realm [are so regarded].
Only those [dharmas] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are objects of aversion and not of aspiration; the dharmas of the intermediate stage are objects of both aspiration and aversion.
Regarding "subduing the afflictions of lower stages": this is like subduing the afflictions of the Desire Realm and attaining the concentration of the First Dhyāna.

Because one subdues the afflictions of the first dhyāna and attains the concentration of the second dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is said that one progressively attains the concentrations of the higher stages.

Regarding the definition of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are two types: first, the essential nature as intrinsic substance (*svabhāva-svabhāva*), which is precisely meditative equipoise (*samādhi*); second, [the essential nature as associated factors].
The essence of its retinue (parivāra) comprises all five aggregates (skandha). That which is matter (rūpa) that functions in accordance with the mind is the aggregate of matter;

the remaining four aggregates are likewise understood. Thus, a verse states: "Together with its associates, it has the nature of the five aggregates; the formless (arūpin) retinue consists of only four aggregates, because they likewise function in accordance with the mind.

Another verse states: "The four aggregates are separated from the lower stages. For now, this commentary relies upon its essential nature (svabhāva), which is subsumed under the category of the wholesome (kuśala).
"One-pointedness of mind" indicates concentration (*samādhi*). The phrase "by means of wholesome meditative absorption" (*kuśala-samādhi*) and so forth constitutes the actual definition (*svabhāva*).

Because it defines the essence of concentration, one first specifies the category and subsequently provides the definition. According to various sacred teachings, the nature of concentration is established solely upon the wholesome minds and mental factors within the twelve bases (*dhātu*);
when these mental factors focus intently upon a single object, there arises pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and adaptability.
It is pervasive because it is defined by the excellence of being free from those [states of] sinking and agitation.

Thus, although states such as the defiled and the neutral, as well as the minds of the desire realm, also possess one-pointedness of mind, they do not receive the designation "concentration" (samādhi) because they are not excellent. Furthermore, this concentrated mind is not capable of such a state by itself.
Nor is it caused by other mental factors concomitant with the mind;

rather, it is solely through the power of the single factor of samādhi that the associated mental states are able to abide in tranquility upon a single object. Therefore, it is said to have "wholesome samādhi as its intrinsic nature."

Regarding its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): by "excluding its attendants," it is distinguished from its associated factors; by "wholesome" (*kuśala*), it is distinguished from the defiled; and by "neither-defined-nor-undefined" (*avyākṛta*), it is distinguished from that which is not the essence of mind.

This is *samādhi* among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) and *samādhi* among the specific objects of the Mahāyāna. It may be translated as "equipoise" (*samādhāna*), which applies to both concentrated and distracted states, and is restricted to states with mind.

Alternatively, it is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*), which applies to both states with and without mind, and is restricted to concentration. Or it is called "equipoised induction" (*samāhita*), which applies only to...
There is the concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*). According to the Sautrāntika masters, this is simply the mind itself when it functions by awaiting [the presence of] a single objective aspect;
thus they establish the name "concentration" for this state, as it has no separate substantial entity. Within the Mahāyāna system, there is no further divergent explanation regarding its essence.
The commentary distinguishes their characteristics. The text has two parts: first, the four dhyānas; second, the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). The four dhyānas are divided into four sections.

These branches of the four dhyānas—“branches” (*aṅga*) having the meanings of cause and constituent part, as these constituent parts serve the purpose of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*)—total eighteen in all. In the first [dhyāna], there are five: vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and samādhi (concentration).

In the second, there are four: adhyātmasaṃprasāda (internal clarity), prīti, sukha, and samādhi. In the third, there are also five: upekṣā (equanimity), smṛti (mindfulness), saṃprajanya (clear comprehension), sukha, and samādhi. In the fourth...

The middle [dhyāna] also has four [factors]: equanimity, mindfulness, feeling, and concentration. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, in terms of actual entities (*dravya*), there are only eleven.
That is to say, the first five are all actual entities; in the second, only internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is added, while the rest are as before, thus making six.

In the third, four are added to the preceding, making ten; the factors of concentration are also as before. In the fourth, only equanimity and feeling are added; therefore, the total number of actual entities is...
There are only eleven [factors]. If one considers only the Mahāyāna, there may be cases where *praśrabdhi* (tranquility) and *sukha* (pleasure) are not distinguished;

if they are shown separately, there are ten items. If *adhyātmasaṃprasāda* (internal clarity) has no separate substance, then there are only nine. According to the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*, however, each dhyāna has four factors:
first, the factor of abandoning hindrances (*vairāgyāṅga*); second, the factor of counteraction (*pratipakṣāṅga*); third, the factor of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*); and fourth, the basis for those two.

Commentary: Now, based on this scriptural passage, other meanings shall be examined as they appear extensively in separate volumes. Regarding the phrase "detached from desires, evils, and unwholesome states":
according to the *Abhidharma*, being detached from the five desires is called "detachment from desire" (*vītarāga*); severing the ten unwholesome paths of action is called "detachment from evil";

and eliminating the five hindrances is called "detachment from unwholesome states. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Volume 88), it says that "detachment from desire" is the same as in the *Abhidharma*. "Desire" refers to...
The five desires and evil, unwholesome dharmas are precisely the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Because they lead people into the evil realms, they are called "evil" (*akuśala*);
because they obstruct wholesome dharmas, they are called "unwholesome dharmas. As stated in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, fascicle 8:

"To sever desire, ill-will, and harmfulness—these are 'evil' and 'harmfulness,' which are themselves unwholesome dharmas. Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these should also be subsumed under "evil and unwholesome dharmas. (30)

Third, regarding "detachment from desire": there are two kinds of desire. First, the desire of affliction (*kleśa-kāma*); second, the desire for objects (*vastu-kāma*). Detachment also has two aspects.

First, detachment through dissociation (*saṃprayoga-viveka*), because the internal mind is no longer associated with the craving for seeking. Second, detachment from objective spheres (*viṣaya-viveka*), because one is not defiled by external objects.
As for the phrase "detached from evil and unwholesome states," this refers to the various evils and unwholesome states produced by the causes of the desire of affliction.
The Dharma refers to the unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind. This [passage on] the mind generally abandons all evil and unwholesome states of the desire realm;
this is consistent with both the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Nyāyānusāra*. Regarding "with vitarka and vicāra," the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Vitarka and vicāra are the coarseness and subtlety of the mind. Vitarka means searching; vicāra means examining. The coarse nature of the mind is called vitarka; the subtle nature of the mind is called..."

They are *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought). Because these two dharmas possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are able to cause a single moment of mind to be simultaneously neither coarse nor subtle;
that is to say, they cause a single moment of mind to achieve the state of being neither coarse nor subtle. Therefore, they are called *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

Their essence is not the mind itself, but are mental factors (*caitta*) subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*aniyata*). In the Mahāyāna, their essence is taken to be volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), which are likewise mental factors.
These are subsumed within the indeterminate [factors]. In the ancient sūtras and śāstras, they are termed *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).

The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "With *vitarka* and with *vicāra*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "For example, it is like ringing a bell; the coarse sound is a metaphor for *vitarka*, and the subtle sound is a metaphor for *vicāra*. These all clarify the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these two dharmas.

Regarding the commentary on their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Book 11) states: "By means of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*) and examining (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), one contemplates impurity, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and compassion (*karuṇā*)."

This treats the obstacles of sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), there are sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness, as well as thoughts of immortality, relatives, and homeland;
these are now countered by giving rise to wholesome thoughts. Moreover, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Knowledge), fascicle 44, states:

"In the Hīnayāna, thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and affliction are considered coarse, while thoughts of relatives, homeland, and so forth are considered subtle, as are other wholesome thoughts."
That which is subtle [in one context] is coarse in the Mahāyāna; thus, one realizes that emptiness is brief. In all these cases, each subsequent subtler stage serves as the remedy for the preceding.

For this reason, the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* classifies them as "limbs of remediation" (*pratipakṣa-aṅga*). The *Abhidharmakośa*, however, speaks only in terms of their general characteristics, stating they are merely the obstacles of revulsion toward suffering and so forth.
The underlying intent is no different. Question: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, are the meditations on impurity, loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth also considered [remedies]?

[Question: They are capable of acting as antidotes; why then are they not established [as such]? [Answer: [The answer is that] the "impurity" (*aśubhā*) and so forth are specifically discussed from the perspective of one portion of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, these are precisely the same as the aforementioned "vitarka" (applied thought) and "vicāra" (sustained thought), which perform the observation of those [objects] such as impurity.

Now, speaking generally of all noble ones and ordinary beings across both the Great and Lesser Vehicles, we simply designate "vitarka" and so forth as the factors of the antidote for the sake of producing seclusion.
Regarding "joy and bliss" (*prīti-sukha*): the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that joy is the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*).

Because one experiences a sense of exhilaration within the path of liberation resulting from detachment from desire and evil, and because the mind becomes tranquil and at ease, it is called "joy and bliss born of detachment. Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* classifies this as the "factor of benefit.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 33, states: "Detachment" refers to the attainment of the "attention of the culmination of application" (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manasikāra*).

This refers to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), which has already abandoned desire, evil, and so forth. Regarding "arising": it arises immediately after this [path] by virtue of being its cause and condition;

that is, with this immediate succession as the cause, joy and bliss arise. This is because one attains the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that constitutes the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Thus, joy and bliss are the fruit. As for "joy and bliss," it means that one has already attained the object desired.

Therefore, one attains great pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Because body and mind are harmonious and supple, they possess functional capacity. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "joy arises because body and mind are pliant":

the meaning of pliancy is as explained in the section on the Three Contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*); it refers to the state where heaviness is abandoned for lightness. "Pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) means that body and mind are harmonious and supple.
It fully sustains the physical basis, and this lightness, serenity, and adaptability serve as the cause of joy; thus, it is given this provisional designation.

It is pleasure (*sukha*), not the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In the first two [dhyānas], pleasure consists of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). This means that within the first two dhyānas, there is no faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).

It is not that there is bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) in the first two dhyānas, because in the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are absent.

Furthermore, there is no pleasure derived from feeling, as it is also said that joy (*prīti*) exists; and joy is itself the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*). Two feelings do not coexist within a single moment of mind.

Therefore, there is no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*). The rest is as explained in other fascicles. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "abiding in the first dhyāna": this refers to the fourth phrase, where the basis is itself the concentration (*samādhi*).

Because its power is most preeminent, it serves as the basis for the two factors (*aṅga*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that this is both the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and a factor of meditative absorption;
the remaining supported factors are factors of meditative absorption, but not the meditative absorption itself. "Abiding" (*sthiti*) has the meaning of being securely established.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Abiding" means that at a later time, because of the extensive accomplishment of what has been practiced, one attains whatever is desired and achieves it without difficulty, such that one can remain correctly established for as long as seven days and seven nights.
The subsequent fourth phrases are all to be explained according to this principle. The commentary notes: "As the basis for the two factors of benefit and remedy. Regarding this:

Regarding the obstacles abandoned: because they lack the substance of active application (*cāra*) and are not constituent factors (*aṅga*), it cannot be said that they serve as the basis for those [factors].

Among the four alternatives, it is stated only that they serve as the basis for two; namely, by means of the counteractive investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*), one is able to transcend sensual desires and evil, thereby entering the first *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, upon entering the state of benefit, physical and mental pliancy does not exceed joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*). They are identical.

The "time-dependent basis" (*kāla-niśraya*) is precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*); therefore, it is established as a factor (*aṅga*) based on its predominance. Among these five, the first [dhyāna] is specifically designated by the name of its factors.
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of applied and sustained thought" (*vitarka-vicāra-śamatha*): this is the factor of abandoning obstacles. These two are coarse and mobile;

they serve as the preliminary application for speech and give rise to bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), thereby obstructing the second dhyāna. Since they must now be abandoned, they are said to be "ceased. This [cessation] constitutes the first dhyāna.
Regarding "the ability to cure" and "further cultivation": the third dhyāna is precisely the remedy for the diseases that were previously treated.

As for the note stating that "three consciousnesses arise," the fundamental nature of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is that it lacks the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue, because the objects of smell and taste do not exist there; this has already been explained previously. Now, regarding the second dhyāna:

It is simply said that there are no three consciousnesses [in the higher realms], because the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses are initially absent there, as is the case from the second dhyāna upward.
To produce bodily and vocal intimation (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti*), as well as seeing, hearing, smelling, and touching, one must borrow the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna.

This is because when there are objects of form, sound, and touch, or when moving the body and speaking words, from the second dhyāna upward, these functions still rely on those three consciousnesses; furthermore, this is established according to the *dharmas* of the respective stages.

It is not possible for [vitarka and vicāra] to exist [there], because they are absent. Therefore, it is explained in meaning as being "borrowed. The analogy of water and waves can be understood from this.

Regarding "inner serenity and one-pointedness of mind," these are the two factors of antidote; this is a passage from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. The treatise (*śāstra*) states that the sūtra says, "the mental formations abide in a single place.

The commentary notes that "its essence consists of equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension," which refers to the texts of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*), the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and others.

Furthermore, because these three factors are still overshadowed by extreme joy (*prīti*), their functional power is not yet predominant; they can only serve to eliminate external vitarka and vicāra, and are therefore termed "internal clarity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).

Because they continue in a single object, they are further called "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*), as they function solely through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) with respect to mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).
For this reason, since these three factors are relatively weak within this dhyāna, they are combined into a single branch. Regarding the three...
Within dhyāna, the functional power is sovereign and established distinctly. If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, it takes faith (*śraddhā*) as its essence. As the verse states:

"Inner purity is the faculty of faith," etc., as cited in detail in another fascicle. Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "joy and bliss born of concentration" (*samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha*), this refers to the third member [of the second dhyāna].

Thus, the function of joy and bliss is first explained as either pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) or the experience of bliss (*sukha-vedanā*). The note clarifies that one rejoices in the applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

"Cessation of the mind" (*cittasyopaśama*) explains the meaning of "born of concentration" (*samādhija*). Because the first dhyāna stage turns its back on sensual desires and evil, it is called "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*).

Because it causes the mind to rejoice in applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and brings tranquility and pleasure to both body and mind, it is called "born of concentration. This explanation is made from the perspective of being born from the concentration of that very stage.
The treatise categorizes this as the "benefit of cultivation," because joy and bliss arise due to the cultivation of this concentration; thus, it is a benefit.

This is so. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, [joy] arises precisely from the concentration (*samādhi*) of the first dhyāna. Since the desire realm lacks concentration, the first stage is merely described as "separation.

Now, by relinquishing the initial investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*), one rejoices in the arising of joy and bliss; thus, it is said that concentration arises on that very day. The commentary states: "As for the metaphor of clear, still water:
the evils of desire are like mud, while the concentration of the first dhyāna is like clear, moving water. Now, with the absence of desire and evil, [the movement] is further stilled."

Vitarka and vicāra are like clear, still water; this is the first celebration of what has been abandoned. This is the celebration of what has been attained, because one has attained the illumination of non-conceptualization.
For one who dwells in the second dhyāna, the fourth phrase may be understood accordingly.

Regarding "detaching from joy": this refers to the detachment from obstacles. In the second dhyāna, the mind of joy arises as a conceptualization; because it causes agitation, it must be eliminated when transitioning to the tranquility of the third dhyāna.
Regarding "dwelling in equanimity with mindfulness and clear comprehension": these are the two antidotes and the three factors [of the third dhyāna].

As for "equanimity" (*upekṣā*), it is the equanimity of mental formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), not the feeling of equanimity (*vedanā-upekṣā*). It is the mental formation that balances the mind by relinquishing the fault of that joy. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "the equanimity of mental formation."

This is the equanimity (*upekṣā*) within the great wholesome ground (*mahābhūmika*). It is said that the third [dhyāna] possesses "equanimity of extreme joy" (*prīti-sukha-upekṣā*), while the fourth [dhyāna] possesses "equanimity of extreme bliss" (*sukha-upekṣā*);

therefore, in these two [stages], equanimity as an application (*prayoga-upekṣā*) is established as a factor (*aṅga*). In the first two [dhyānas], this is absent, so pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is established [as the factor].

In the Mahāyāna, it is the equanimity among the eleven wholesome factors; its meaning is as explained previously. Regarding the phrase "attending to the joy and bliss already arisen," this refers to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*).
The word "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) means that one does not tolerate or accept joy (*prīti*) that has already arisen; because one does not tolerate it, there is the sense of relinquishing.
It also carries the sense of being an antidote (*pratipakṣa*). From "equality" (*samatā*) onwards, the characteristics of the three grades of equanimity are presented:

first, equality, which is identical to *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only), as it is the initial state free from sinking (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*); second, rectitude (*ṛjutā*), because one is not timid toward defilements; and third, unwavering stability (*aniñjyasthiti*).

Subsequently, because one dwells in tranquility, that which possesses mindfulness (*smṛti*) is simply mindfulness itself. In the Hīnayāna, it is categorized among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*);

in the Mahāyāna, it is subsumed within the object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣya-viṣaya*). Regarding the commentary on "not forgetting," this refers to clear recollection; since clear recollection constitutes mindfulness, Master Huiyuan stated:

"Mindfulness follows after joy and transcends [distraction], maintaining the mind upon a single object. The *Abhidharmakośa* states that although mindfulness is present throughout all stages (*bhūmi*), the third and fourth dhyānas establish it as independent.
Regarding the "limbs" (*aṅga*): the third [limb] is the second, as it is overwhelmed by superior joy; the fourth is the third, as it is obstructed by superior pleasure.
Because one is hindered and obstructed by the lower stages, one is unable to transcend the defilements of one's own stage. Therefore, the Blessed One exhorted them to abide in right mindfulness.

As for the term "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*), this is wisdom (*prajñā*). In the *Abhidharmakośa*, this is categorized among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*); in the Mahāyāna, it is distinct.

It is subsumed within the objective sphere (*viṣaya*). Now, following the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it is called "correct knowledge" (*saṃprajanya*). Master Huiyuan says: "To distinguish the faults of joy is what is meant by 'correct wisdom' (*samyag-jñāna*).

The *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* instead uses the term "tranquil wisdom" (*samprajanya*). Master Huiyuan says: "The purity of wisdom is termed 'tranquility' (*sam*); this tranquility is precisely the meaning of 'correct' (*samyak*)."

Because it calmly reflects upon the two flows, it is called "right" (*samyak*). Being right, one attains peace. According to the intention of the *Abhidharmakośa*, this refers to the superior bliss of that particular stage;
fearing attachment to this, one might not take delight in the higher stages. To counteract this, the factor of "right wisdom" (*samyak-prajñā*) is established.

In the Mahāyāna, these three—equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and clear comprehension (*samprajanya*)—are precisely the aforementioned internal purity (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*) gradually cultivated to its most excellent state, wherein sinking and subtlety are separately opened up and stilled.

Because it is tranquil, it can counteract the lower state of joyful exultation and restlessness. Regarding the phrase "the body experiences bliss," this is the third limb of benefit (*anuśaṃsā-aṅga*).

Its essence is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), not the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*). "Body" here refers generally to both the physical form and the mind; that which arises simultaneously with the six consciousnesses is collectively termed "bodily experience.

This means that this superior pleasure, conjoined with equanimity (*upekṣā*), universally benefits both body and mind, remaining detached from joy and profoundly serene. Even if it were only associated with...

It is associated with the mental faculty (*manas*) and is also called "bodily sensation" (*kāyika-vedanā*). In the lower stages, there is pleasure (*sukha*) but no equanimity (*upekṣā*); in the higher stages, there is equanimity but no pleasure.
Because this specific equanimity and pleasure are exceptionally superior to those maintained [in other stages], they are termed "bodily sensation. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:

"That which the noble ones describe as 'the experience of pleasure through equanimity and mindfulness' refers precisely to this pleasure. This means that within this stage, both equanimity and right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) are present.
Knowing this, one experiences joy; it is not like the joys of the lower or higher stages. Thus, the Buddha and his disciples declare that this experience alone is supreme.

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "By means of equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, through repeated cultivation, [this] clarifies the antidote, causing the mind to leap with joy."

The concomitant feeling of joy is then extinguished. (This explains the capacity [of the mind] by way of its freedom from hindrances. Free from [the agitation of] joy, there arises a mental feeling that is supremely tranquil and diametrically opposed to joy.
(This precisely clarifies the essence of bliss. At that time, his physical body and mental body experience the pleasure of sensation and the pleasure of pliancy.

(This correctly explains the meaning of "bodily sensation of pleasure. Therefore, it is said: "He experiences pleasure with the body. (This is the conclusion. This clarifies the state of being free [from joy].

[The Master] rejoices. Furthermore, he states that mental feeling arises; this clearly shows that while one experiences pleasure associated with the mind (*manas*), it is also called "bodily experience of pleasure" (*kāyikī vedanā*).

The commentary notes: "Even if this is mental pleasure, it is still called 'bodily experience. Thus, this feeling associated with the mind is distinct from the former [physical sensation]; the word 'body' (*kāya*) is added [to distinguish it]. Master Huiyuan [explains]:

"That which is associated with the five [sensory consciousnesses] is called bodily experience; that which is associated with the mind is called mental experience. This is an explanation based on their respective supports (*āśraya*).
The text states: "Inferior-grade feeling of pleasure pervades and fills the mind; this is called mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*). Superior-grade feeling thoroughly moistens both body and mind;
because it is named after its secondary aspect, it is called bodily feeling (*kāya-vedanā*). This is an explanation based on what is benefited. Now, we follow the latter definition.

The mental factor of the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*) is predominant in this stage; because it pervades both body and mind, it is called "bodily" (*kāyika*). Master Huiyuan’s two interpretations take the latter explanation as primary.
This present commentary employs both. From the note beginning with "corresponding correctly to the second dhyāna" up to "also called bodily feeling," this refers to the former interpretation.
However, when the mental consciousness is accompanied by a state of detachment from joy and is concentrated and tranquil, although it is a mental feeling, it is also called "bodily."

It is "feeling" (*vedanā*). The commentary below the section on the First Dhyāna explains this according to the meaning of "conforming to what follows. It is spoken in terms of the benefits received, as there are distinct categories [of experience]. The earth is a metaphor for the mind; the stones are a metaphor for the body;
and the water is a general metaphor for bliss, because the mind in the First Dhyāna experiences bliss. Thus, it is like water not entering into the midst of stone: this refers to the Second Dhyāna.

[In the Second Dhyāna, bliss] pervades both body and mind, just as water pervades [everything]; yet, because the mountain's original stones are obstructive, it is nevertheless covered by joy (*prīti*), just as...

Earth covers water, yet it remains moist within; so too, in the third dhyāna, bodily pleasure increases to its utmost extent. It is as if there were a pool of water outside, with the water pervading the interior of the mountain—this can be clearly understood.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is also stated that this is mental pleasure (*citta-sukha*). The verse says: "That which does not gladden the body is called suffering (*duḥkha*);
that which gladdens it is called pleasure (*sukha*), as well as the mental gladness of the third dhyāna. In other stages, this is called joy (*prīti*). This refers to the first and second [dhyānas].
Regarding "the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*)," as previously cited from the sūtra, the third dhyāna is understood through the fourth phrase [of the verse]. The commentary states:

"First abandoning suffering, and with the cessation of joy and sorrow" refers to the obstacles abandoned at the outset. The superior bliss of the third dhyāna is harmful to this [state of equanimity];
it is like a seriously ill person for whom the bliss of a sublime purpose is perceived as an obstacle. Because there are four such obstacles, they must be eliminated. Thus it is said.

Regarding "previously abandoned": this refers to the three—sorrow (*daurmanasya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and joy (*saumanasya*)—which have already been relinquished, in order, in the first, second, and third dhyānas.
Now, one merely abandons pleasure (*sukha*) to attain this concentration (*samādhi*). However, at that very moment, all [the remaining] suffering, pleasure, and so forth, are transcended;

therefore, they are spoken of collectively. The intent of speaking of them collectively is to manifest their superior excellence. Thus, the term "previously abandoned" extends through the subsequent mention of "suffering."

Regarding the note stating that [the faculty of suffering] is excluded in the second dhyāna: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 11, asks: "For what reason is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) not yet abandoned in the first dhyāna?
It answers: "Because the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of that category have not yet been abandoned. If this is so, why does it not manifest? It answers:

"Because its associated factors (*sahāya*), which are comprised within the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), have already been abandoned. If the faculty of suffering has already been abandoned in the first meditative absorption (*prathama-dhyāna*), then...

In that case, when a practitioner enters the first dhyāna and the second, there would be no distinction in their abiding in what has been accomplished, because both possess joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).
This point clarifies that [the first dhyāna] does not abandon the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*), and thus it differs from the second dhyāna;

yet, while [the heaviness] does not manifest [in the second], they are alike in establishing bliss as a factor (*aṅga*). If one follows the Hīnayāna, suffering (*duḥkha*) is identical to the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) in the first dhyāna.
They are collectively excluded. The first two [types of] pleasure are pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), while the third is the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*); this is why they differ.

The commentary states that the phrase "first removing suffering" (*duḥkha-prahāṇa*) is used in contrast to the preceding [mention of] pleasure; this serves to address an objection. The objection asks: "If one follows the sequential order [of the four feelings], one ought to mention sorrow (*daurmanasya*) first and joy (*saumanasya*) later.

Why is it not done so here? The intended meaning of the answer is as follows: By virtue of the preceding statement regarding the abandonment of pleasure, the discussion proceeds immediately with suffering. Thus, the sequence is maintained by following the logic already established.

...and so forth. This is the sequence for this [section]. Regarding the phrase "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" in the commentary (*śāstra*): this is a clause concerning the branch of benefit (*anuśaṃsa*) for this stage.
While in other dhyānas the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is presented first and the benefit follows later, here the benefit is explained first because the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, since there is generally an absence of the four types of sensation (*vedanā*) in the preceding [stage], 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant' is mentioned for the sake of textual convenience; it is not [the primary] meaning."
This follows in sequence; it now constitutes the second statement. It clarifies that within the five sensations (*pañca-vedanā*), there is only equanimity (*upekṣā*), because it is immovable.

Question: Since both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*) are extinguished, why does it not say "neither sorrow nor joy"? Answer: Within the five sensations, there is no separate category of "neither sorrow nor joy.

This is explained through the meaning of the three sensations, because suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*) are subsumed within sorrow and joy. In this context, regarding sensation, it simply says:
It is neither painful nor pleasant. If that is so, since it is subsumed under a single characteristic, why not say it is "neither sorrowful nor joyful"?

Answer: First, because within the five feelings there is no distinct name [for it]. Second, the pleasure it opposes is proximate, whereas sorrow and joy are remote; thus, it is appropriately described in contrast to them as "neither painful nor pleasant.
Regarding the phrase "equanimity and mindfulness are purified": this refers to the names and essential natures of the two factors of the antidote, which are identical to [the preceding stages].
Regarding the third dhyāna: it is divided into two solely because of differences in its basis (the meditative level) and the joy and bliss that are its specific antidotes.

The commentary states that "the equanimity, mindfulness, and so forth differ from those of the third dhyāna" to explain how it acquires the designation "pure. The *Yogācārabhūmi* further clarifies this purity, stating: [text].
In all stages from the first dhyāna upward, calamities have been severed—namely, vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and inhalation and exhalation.
Therefore, within this state, equanimity and mindfulness are pure and pristine. Consequently, the mind dwells in this dhyāna without fluctuation.

According to this treatise, although it briefly mentions six factors as being complete, it also includes the absence of both grief and suffering. The *Abhidharmakośa* states that one is free from the eight calamities; however, this...

Although it is said to be "unmoving," there is still the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*); one has not yet attained the state of being without sensation. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 11, states:

"Furthermore, as for 'non-perception' (*asaṃjñin*), the sūtras describe it as the 'attainment of non-perception' (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Within this attainment, the faculty of equanimity is eternally extinguished.

From the state of non-perception up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all possess the sensation of equanimity. Question: Why is there no correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*)? Answer: Because the mind of joy is buoyant and restless. (3)

One must maintain correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*). The bliss is profound and subtle; there is merely the mindfulness of equanimity at the crown. For those who dwell loosely in the four dhyānas, the fourth line refers to their basis.

However, when entering the higher formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*), the physical appearance of the body is as if dwelling within a chamber; when entering the lower four formless realms, it is as if dwelling in empty space.
Regarding the passage "The four formless [attainments] below," in the section analyzing their characteristics, the second part clarifies the four formless attainments.

Although they all consist of one-pointedness of mind, they are established as four distinct names because they involve detachment from the defilements of the lower stages. That is to say, by departing from the fourth dhyāna, the four concentrations beginning with the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana) are established;
these constitute four sections. Only the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* classifies each of these four formless states as having its own...

Fourth, [the factors] such as "separation from hindrances" (*viveka*). Now, according to the text of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, each section contains only three phrases, yet their meaning encompasses four.

This is because within the first phrase, "separation from hindrances," the sense of "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*) is implicitly contained. Question: If there are meanings such as "antidote," do they constitute [independent] factors (*aṅga*)? Answer:
According to treatises such as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Abhidharmakośa*, they do not. However, according to the *Ratnakaranda-śrīkūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo benye jing), they do.

Each has five factors: namely, perception (*saṃjñā*), protection (*saṃvara*), tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). If these were combined, they would contradict [the established categories], for the treatises do not consider them identical due to their distinct characteristics.

Furthermore, the four dhyānas differ in having applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and so forth; moreover, because the function of wisdom (*prajñā*) is inferior [in the lower stages], it is not established as a constituent factor (*aṅga*).

The Sūtra, however, treats them as similar and identical in all cases, each possessing five factors. For example, in the first dhyāna, one becomes weary of the perceptions of the lower realm of form and gives rise to the perception of emptiness (*ākāśasaṃjñā*).
Resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) constitutes perception (*saṃjñā*), which serves as the antidote; it prevents the perception of form from arising and thus acts as protection.

Being able to transcend the perception of form is termed "stopping" (*śamatha*), which corresponds to the present "separation from hindrances. The practice of the sphere of infinite space, characterized by clear and distinct illumination, carries the meaning of "insight" (*vipaśyanā*), which constitutes the present "benefit.
One-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) is the basis for both of these. Thus, the four meanings are established.
The five factors are thus complete. The commentary states that "transcending all [perceptions] up to the non-attention to various perceptions" consists of three types of phrases;
specifically, this is solely the phrase regarding the initial abandonment of obstacles. Within it, the term "non-attention" further contains the sense of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Regarding "transcending all perceptions of form," the sub-commentary cites the root treatise’s explanation as "surpassing visual consciousness."

Regarding the characteristics: in the Hīnayāna, [the formless attainments] arise through cultivation while remaining within the realm of form and desire, because the physical form has not yet been abandoned; thus, it is not said that "form is extinguished. In the Mahāyāna, it is determined that only perception (*saṃjñā*) is extinguished.

If there were no form, then when space and consciousness are subsequently extinguished, space and consciousness should likewise not exist. However, in the *Dhātunirdeśa* chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*...
Having distinguished the three types of color—fine, coarse, and the three kinds of obstructive color—one explains, in sequence, the colors excluded by these three phrases.
Now, in order to provide a detailed commentary, one should first briefly state the meaning of their respective categories.

Within that chapter, among the various analytical gates of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), there are twenty-two gates in total. The first is the gate of "visible" and "invisible"; the second...

There is the category of "having an object" (*sapratigha*) and "not having an object" (*apratigha*). Regarding this, it was previously asked: "Among these eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and how many are invisible (*anidarśana*)?

How many have an object (*sapratigha*) and how many do not have an object (*apratigha*)? The verse answers: "One is visible, namely form (*rūpa*). (This means that among the eighteen elements, only the element of form is called "visible," because it is that which is observed by the visual faculty;

the remaining seventeen are invisible. "Ten material elements have an object. (That is, the five faculties and the five objects. These ten elements are called "material and having an object. It should be understood that "having an object" [refers to the general definition of *sapratigha*].)

There are three kinds [of obstruction]: first, physical obstruction (*āvaraṇa*); second, objective obstruction (*viṣaya*); and third, cognitive-object obstruction (*ālambana*). Here, the meaning is that of physical obstruction. Furthermore, the meaning of obstruction is twofold: first, the obstruction of physical resistance; second, the obstruction of confinement. These ten material elements (*dhātu*) constitute the obstruction of physical resistance;

that is to say, their substance is composed of the accumulation of matter, which mutually obstructs one another—such as a hand obstructing a hand, a stone obstructing a stone, or a hand and a stone obstructing each other. Since the substance of these ten elements is said to be matter, and since matter possesses obstruction, they are called "possessing form" (*rūpin*). Because they possess the quality of obstruction, they are called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*), and they also act as obstructions.

Furthermore, that which is obstructed by resistance is called "obstructive resistance" (*āvaraṇa-pratighata*). This is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). Second, "resistance regarding the object-field" (*viṣaya-pratighata*) refers to the twelve elements (*dhātu*), namely the six sense faculties (*indriya*) and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), as well as a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) consisting exclusively of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).

These thirteen dharmas have the six types of objects, such as visible form, as their objective fields; because they are thereby constrained and obstructed by those forms and so forth, they are termed "with resistance.
