Thus, it means there is a constraint regarding those objective fields, and is called "resistance regarding the object-field. This is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Third, "the object-condition" (*ālambana*)...

This refers to the seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*) in their entirety, as well as a portion of the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*) that consists exclusively of mental factors (*caitta*). Since these minds and mental factors are capable of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*), they must rely upon the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) as their objective supports (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, because they are immediately obstructed by those forms and other objects once they have apprehended them, these minds and mental factors are also termed "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*). Thus, regarding the "resistance of the object," this is also a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. As for the latter two types of resistance, "resistance" here refers to physical obstruction. Now, setting aside the threefold classification of form (*rūpa*), we explain the latter two types of resistance solely in terms of the aforementioned "resistance through obstruction";

the others are not required here. Alternatively, one might raise the following doubt: "Based on this definition, form is merely an object of obstruction; its essence is not that of a mind or mental factor. How can it be said that there are 'three kinds of resistant form'? The answer is given by means of form itself.

Because one element (the visible form-element) is both visible and obstructive, it is called "visible and resistant matter" (*sanidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*). The other nine, such as sound and so forth, lack the quality of being visible; they possess only substantial resistance and are thus called "invisible and resistant matter" (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*).

As for non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), it lacks both of these two meanings and is therefore called "invisible and non-resistant matter" (*anidarśana-apratigha-rūpa*). Thus, the first two [categories] among those three types of resistant matter are what are termed "threefold resistant matter. It is not that this category of matter itself pervades all three types of resistance and is therefore named "threefold resistant matter.
Now, this first phrase refers to the transcendence of all coarse matter that is visible and resistant; that is to say, this [pure] form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Within the gate of "seeing" versus "not seeing," this is "with seeing. Within the gate of "resistant" versus "non-resistant," it is "with resistance.

Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that it transcends the characteristics of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* calls it "transcending visible form" (*varṇa*). That treatise states:
"Next, because one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) toward space, all perceptions of visible forms associated with blue, yellow, red, and white [are transcended]."

Because they are not manifest and because of weary detachment, one is able to transcend them all. Regarding "the cessation of the perception of resistance" (*sapratigha-saṃjñā-vyupaśama*), the *Mūla-śāstra* explains:
it is because the composite perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness have ceased.

This refers to that which is "invisible and resistant," namely the coarse form of the five sense organs (eye, etc. and the four objects (sound, etc.). That which is not seen by the eye is called "invisible. Regarding "resistance" (*pratigha*)...
Within the section on "non-obstructive" (*apratigha*), that which is "obstructive" (*sapratigha*) is precisely what was previously identified as the first of the three types of obstructive form:

the obstructive form of physical resistance (*āvaraṇa-sapratigha*). This means that consciousness only arises when these sense organs and objects serve as its support (*āśraya*) and objective condition (*ālambana*), thereby forming a conception of conjunction.
Now, to give rise to this conception is called "the cessation of the conception of conjunction. Since the eye-faculty is both invisible and obstructive, it is likewise...
In this phrase, "cessation" serves as the objective color-form (*rūpa*) for the preceding phrase; because it already lacks the meaning of combination, it is simply called "cessation.
Regarding the perception of the combination of the four consciousnesses, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"Because they do not manifest, and by taking the transcendence of those perceptions as the cause, all various aggregates of many categories arise from the combination of various manifest colors (*varṇa-rūpa*)."

The accumulated [notions] and the notions of obstruction are all eliminated. Regarding "not attending to various notions," the *Mūla-śāstra* commentary explains that this is because one does not attend to the notion of the conjunction of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Since the mental consciousness discriminates all phenomena (*dharma*), it is termed "various."
This refers precisely to subtle matter that is invisible and non-obstructive; it is the unmanifest (avijñapti). Furthermore, this unmanifest has many types, namely:

that associated with the prātimokṣa, that associated with meditative concentration (dhyāna), that which follows the path, and that which conforms to the mind (cittānuparivartin), all of which are subsumed within the dharma-dhātu.

This is because they are objects of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) alone. The commentary explains: "Because the mental consciousness discriminates all phenomena, it is called 'various' (vicitra). Although its intention—

It is also capable of taking non-material (arūpa) objects as its cognitive domain; however, for now, we take only those that take material (rūpa) objects as their domain, because material objects themselves possess various kinds [of characteristics].
Therefore, the commentary states: "This is said solely with reference to the cognition of material objects. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it further states:
"Because the cause consists in being far removed from those perceptions, the various distinct characteristics within that collection of manifold things arise—namely, food and drink."
The characteristics of jars, clothing, vehicles, ornaments, cities, houses, armies, forests, and so forth—all these proceed without mental engagement (*amanasikāra*).
This is a general statement regarding the departure from all form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, regarding the term "perception" (*saṃjñā*) being applied universally:

the intention of the Hīnayāna is that since this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is cultivated while remaining within the realm of form and desire, it is not possible for the physical body to be absent; rather, it is only the perception of form that is extinguished, because perception grasps form.

Therefore, they are extinguished individually. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Collectively, they are called the 'removal of the perception of form' (*rūpa-saṃjñā-vyupaśama*). However, in the Mahāyāna alone, it is truly only the extinction of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*).

If one speaks of the "formless" (*ārūpya*) because one has transcended the perception of form, then when the perceptions of space (*ākāśa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are later extinguished, there should likewise be no perception of consciousness or space.

[Regarding] the perceptions of odor and taste: in the first dhyāna, one has already abandoned the perceptions of form, sound, and touch; in the second dhyāna, two [of these] are removed; and although in the third and fourth dhyānas...

There are [cognitions] such as seeing, hearing, and perceiving, which furthermore borrow the consciousnesses of lower stages. How, then, can it now be said that these are the consciousnesses of the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?

Master Yuan replies: There are four kinds of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). First, the antidote to obstructive matter (*rūpa-pratigha*), which refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) observing the impermanence and other [aspects] of the contaminated phenomena of the lower stages.

Second, the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) correctly severing the afflictions. Third, the antidote of time... [text fragmentary].

Remedy (*pratipakṣa*) refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) as the primary factor, along with all subsequent paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation that maintain that unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) so that it is not lost or destroyed.
The remedy of distant separation (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*) likewise refers to all subsequent paths of uninterrupted transition and paths of liberation following the path of liberation;
because the former obstacles will never arise again, this present concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is stated in general terms according to the fourth type of remedy.
"Extinction of all perceptions of form. The above clarifies the teaching on being free from hindrances.

Regarding the phrase "not bringing to mind" (*amanasikāra*) used previously, which contains the meaning of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), it means not discriminating between objects such as form and so forth. The root treatise explains: "Why does one not bring them to mind?

Because one perceives non-self (*anātman*). This means that form lacks intrinsic reality; its very substance is emptiness, and thus it is called "non-self. This refers to the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Furthermore, according to the statement regarding "transcending and extinguishing" mentioned above, this too is an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

However, because the meaning of "antidote" is not explicitly stated in the phrase "not recollecting," the Master [Vasubandhu] interpreted the underlying intent and categorized it as an antidote. This is based on the actual antidotes of a Bodhisattva; hence he says "non-self.

If one follows the intent of the present sutra, when speaking of the outflows (*āsrava*), one merely employs the six modes of aspiration and aversion as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for subduing them, or as an antidote.

Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* explains the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) as follows: "If there is a phenomenon (namely, space) which, although coexisting with form, does not depend upon or belong to form (because space pervades all places, whether material or immaterial;

this clarifies the essence of space above, while the following clarifies the contemplative practice), then those who seek liberation from form must first contemplate that phenomenon—namely, the essence of space—even though it coexists with form."

When both [the presence and absence of form] are present, form can be clearly discerned without restriction. (The manifestation of the characteristic of emptiness has two meanings: first, the negation of form to clarify emptiness, meaning that previously there was form, but now it is no longer here;

second, the clarification of emptiness in contrast to form, meaning that where there is form, there is no emptiness, and where there is no form, there is emptiness. It is subsumed under external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*), and its characteristics are boundless. When one contemplates them, one is able to become detached from form;

this is also the characteristic of preparatory application (*prayoga*). Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 86, states: "It is merely by means of preparatory application that it is so named."
The Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). This refers to the practitioner at the initial stage who first contemplates the characteristics of space above walls, on ground, or within houses.

Having grasped these characteristics, they cultivate the preparatory application (*prayoga*) by means of imaginative resolve (*adhimukti*), observing and clearly discerning the characteristic of infinite space.
Thus, they successively induce the first formless absorption (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); for this reason, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space.
I have heard that after a bhikṣu has emerged from this meditative absorption, he raises both hands and feels about the empty space.
Someone seeing this asks him, "What are you searching for? He replies, "I do not see my own body. The other says, "Your body is right here on the bed;

why are you searching for your body elsewhere? Thus, one knows that even after entering this absorption, one does not see the body; yet upon emerging from the absorption, [one perceives it as before].
"Thus, 'entering the boundless empty space' is the third sentence concerning the benefits of practice;

it means that when the three perceptions of form are extinguished, one enters the principle of emptiness, which is vast and boundless. 'Abiding in the station of boundless empty space' is the [fourth...]"
The fourth is the emptiness that serves as the basis for those two supports. Only the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Abiding in the sphere of infinite space.

Now, saying "infinite space" does not lose its essential meaning. As for the term "sphere" (*āyatana*), it refers to contemplating space with the mental aspect of infinity, thereby being able to extinguish the perception of form and settling the mind in the meditative concentration on space;
this is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). The *Nyāya* states:
Regarding the four formless bases (*ārūpyāyatana*): they are so called because they are the places where sentient beings grow and develop. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Because one has already transcended the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and attained the meditative absorption that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭha-phala-manasikāra*), it is therefore called the 'base of infinite space' (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), wherein one dwells in full possession.

According to the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, among the four meanings [of the term], "transcending obstacles" refers to surpassing the lower stages, while "antidote" refers to the preparatory application.

The *niṣṭhā-manasikāra* (mental attention of culmination) is so called because it is explained as "the mind attaining liberation from fetters. The *adhimukti-manasikāra* (mental attention of resolute belief) is so called because it is explained as "being precisely the practice.
These two are based upon the *prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manasikāra* (mental attention of the fruit of the culmination of application), which is explained as "attaining immediate realization.
Of these, the first three are the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), while the last one is the fundamental stage (*maula*). Subsequently...

The three stages are likewise the same as this. Furthermore, regarding these four meanings: first, what is it that is transcended? It is form (*rūpa*). Second, how is it transcended? It is by means of non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*).
Third, what object does the transcendence take as its condition? It is the boundless space (*ākāśa*). Fourth, what is realized through the transcendence?

It is the one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) in the sphere of infinite space. The commentary states that "transcending space and entering the sphere of infinite consciousness" clarifies the first consciousness.
This is the stage. "Transcending space" is the first phrase regarding the departure from obstacles. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Transcending all infinite space.
The commentary (*shu*) now says simply "transcending space," following its abbreviated style. What obstacle does that space present that it must be transcended and left behind?
Because external thoughts are coarse, one perceives the faults and afflictions of those coarse external conceptualizations; thus, the meaning implicitly contains the second [stage].
This is the text concerning the antidote. "Entering the infinite consciousness" is the third phrase regarding the benefits of practice.

Whereas previously the relinquishing of the external was clarified, here the internal object of focus is distinguished. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "That is to say, within the pure sixfold body of consciousness capable of cognition, having joyfully grasped its signs, one dwells in resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
By the power of mental construction (*parikalpa*), one contemplates and examines the signs of infinite consciousness."
This preparatory practice (*prayoga*) precedes the entry into the fundamental state (*maula*). This explains the characteristics of the preparatory practice;

hence the commentary states: "The mind takes internal consciousness as its object. As for "abiding in the place," this refers to the abode. It is the fourth of those two sentences concerning the basis.

According to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, this sentence says: "Abiding in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Now, the present commentary establishes the preceding phrase as "infinite consciousness," and so forth.
I shall first state the general principle here; my intention is to follow brevity without losing the essential meaning, and all subsequent sections shall be based on this.

In the commentary, regarding the phrase "surpassing consciousness" (*vijñāna-samatikrama*) under the third concentration: "surpassing all consciousness" refers to the first clause concerning the abandonment of obstacles. As the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:

"Surpassing the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one perceives the objects abandoned [therein]. This refers to the meaning of reflecting upon the faults of coarse conceptualization (*vitarka-vicāra*). This constitutes the second pair.
This is the treatment. "Entering into non-existence" is the third phrase concerning the benefits of cultivation. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Entering into non-existence.
Previously, one had already abandoned external conditions and internal [objects], which were considered coarse thoughts; now that there is nothing to be grasped, the grasper also ceases to exist.

When both internal and external are absent, this constitutes the benefit. The *Junzhengli lun* (Treatise on Accordance with Correct Principle) states: "One perceives the boundless aspects of the preceding [states]."
This application is coarse and agitated; therefore, this stage is called "supreme equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Because one no longer delights in producing infinite mental aspects within it, the mind relinquishes all that it possesses regarding its object and abides in tranquility. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
when proceeding upward from the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one seeks further objects beyond that consciousness but finds nothing at all. This...
This clarifies that since consciousness is coarse and agitated, and there is nothing external to consciousness, it is "nothing whatsoever.
To abide in the sphere of nothing whatsoever is the fourth basis of reliance. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Abiding in the sphere of nothing whatsoever. [The commentary] skips below this point.
This is the fourth station. This means that having already transcended the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"Transcending all spheres of nothingness" is the first phrase regarding the departure from obstacles.
Seeing those abandoned spheres of nothingness as the fault of coarse conceptualization and discrimination is the second antidote. According to the treatise and the sūtra, next...
There is one further phrase here: "Knowing that the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful.
This phrase constitutes the third benefit of practice. Because this passage from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* was missing [in the manuscript], the present commentary also follows it for now.
"Dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" is the fourth basis of reliance (*niśraya-pada*). The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Neither with perception nor without perception.
Here, however, it is simply said to be "neither," meaning neither existent nor non-existent. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"First one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), thereby transcending all perceptions of existence; now, one further transcends the perception of nothingness itself."

Therefore, it is called "neither-perception" (explaining *na-saṃjñā*). Furthermore, it is called "not non-perception" because, unlike the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), where all perceptions are entirely extinguished, here there remains only the most subtle perception, which functions by taking the object of non-perception as its focal point.

By generating resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding this very state, one transcends the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and enters the fundamental concentration (*maula*). (Explaining *na-asaṃjñā*) — Master Qingliang.

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), these four emptinesses are clarified as follows: contemplating that form (*rūpa*) is itself emptiness and resting the mind in emptiness is the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Next, knowing that both emptiness and form do not transcend the mind is the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Next, when both mind and object are said to be non-existent, it is the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Finally, this too is called dwelling in the absence of conceptualization; it is named the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Regarding the sphere of perception (*saṃjñā-vihāra*): if one does not take this "non-perception" as an object, then all outflows (*āsrava*) are eternally stilled and one transcends the three realms.

The commentary states, "In this context, there is no emergence," which clarifies whether this concentration is definitive or non-definitive. Within this, there are three parts: first, the non-Buddhists; second, "If one knows...

and below, referring to those of the Lesser Vehicle who extinguish sensation and perception, which is the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); third, "If one has not yet attained... and below, referring to the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).
These are the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) among the gods of the fourth dhyāna; they are also followers of external paths (*tīrthika*).

*The Great Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra, Fascicle Ten (Part One)* *The Great Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra, Fascicle Ten (Part Two)*
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Caotang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.

Regarding the section "Those Who Receive Retribution Later," this is the second part, which specifically clarifies the retributions induced by the preceding meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). The text is divided into two sections.

The first part is general; the subsequent section, "All those above and below," provides the specific explanation. Regarding the "five gates," these are the same five gates as those for humans, devas, and so forth:
namely, the explanation of names, the determination of essence (*svabhāva*), types, physical characteristics (*vigraha*), and lifespan.
Although there are five chapters, the actual commentary consists of four, because within the explanation of names, the meaning of "types" is already included. Now, the first [gate] is explained.

This is the name. Furthermore, there are two parts to this: first, the explanation of the general name. The general name is "the Formless Realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding the presence or absence of form:
the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the formless realm do not have form as their essence; therefore, they are called "formless. It is not merely that form is absent that constitutes being "formless."

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In that realm, because form (*rūpa*) does not exist, it is called 'formless' (*ārūpya*). What is called 'form' has the meaning of being subject to change and resistance, or the meaning of manifestation.
Since its essence is not form, it is designated as 'formless. It is not the case that it merely takes form as its substance and thus lacks any distinct entity;
nor is it space, for it consists of the four aggregates (*skandha*), not [space]. It further states: "The formless is entirely without [form]."

There is a point [to be made]: because it is logically certain that formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*) have no spatial location, they are designated as the "formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*) solely by virtue of the four distinctions arising from their maturation (*vipāka*).
These four are not distinguished by spatial height or depth, but rather by the superiority or inferiority of their rebirth (*upapatti*).
The treatise further asks: "How, moreover, is it known that they have no spatial location? It answers: "Because in this regard..."
Regarding those who have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*): because they are reborn in that very same place immediately upon the end of their life;

and because when they pass away from there and are reborn in the desire or form realms, an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises in that very same place—it is therefore known that those in the formless realm do not depart from the desire and form realms to receive those four places.

The four aggregates are born of maturation (*vipākaja*). However, because there are four distinct types of results induced by the respective meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of space, consciousness, and so forth, there are four distinctions.
Just as in a single location one may attain four types of absorption and subsequently experience four kinds of fruits within that same location, there is no difference in the place itself.

Furthermore, when cultivating these absorptions, nine locations in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are involved—excluding the northern continent (*uttarakuru*), animals, hungry ghosts, and the hells—and eleven locations in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the abodes: excluding the five Pure Abodes and the station of Mahābrahmā, one is born as if newly seated in dhyāna.

Having attained the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), at the end of life, one immediately receives the retribution of the four aggregates for twenty thousand *kalpas* within that first dhyāna. Thereafter, one passes away from that state.

Those born by combination arise in the desire realm; immediately in that very place, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests. Other instances of consciousness arising in different locations should be understood by this analogy.

Regarding the term "realm" (*dhātu*), it is an explanation of the meaning of "limit" or "demarcation. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because they can maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are called realms.

The realm to which form belongs is called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); the realm to which the formless belongs is called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Thus, one should know that it is not merely the absence of form [that defines the formless].

This is precisely what is meant by "formless" (*ārūpya*). As for the statement that "the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) possesses form and so forth," this serves as a general rebuttal to objections. Regarding the establishment of names based on "coarseness and heaviness" (*dausthulya*), this refers to what was previously mentioned:
the conjunction of the five sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "As for the separate explanations of the names, they correspond to their respective categories," this is because their meanings are consistent; thus, they are not treated separately.

The text has two parts, as it distinguishes between the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*). Within the realm of form, there are two sections: first, a general presentation of the realms and dhyānas to indicate the number of heavens;

second, a detailed explanation according to the sequence of the dhyānas, which constitutes four segments. This is the first [segment]. Furthermore, within each of the first three [segments], there are two parts each, namely:

There are both general and specific [designations]. Regarding the initial general designation as "the Brahmakāyika gods" and so forth, this refers to their specific characteristics. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Because they are produced by extensive virtue (*bṛhat-kuśala*), they are called 'Brahma' (*brahman*). This Brahma is also 'Great,' hence he is called Mahābrahmā.

This is because he has attained the intermediate dhyāna (which possesses vicāra but lacks vitarka), because he was the first to be born [at the beginning of the kalpa], because he is the last to perish [at the end of the kalpa], and because his majesty and power are superior."

Therefore, they are called "Great" (*Mahā*). (Because their bodies, lifespans, and so forth differ in measure, and because there is further distinction between ministers and sovereigns. Because they are those who are emanated and governed by Mahābrahmā, they are called the "Assembly of Brahmās" (*Brahmapārṣadya*).
Because they stand in rows before Mahābrahmā to attend and protect him, they are called the "Ministers of Brahmā" (*Brahmapurohita*). The full term *Brahmā* and so forth is the general name.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "they lack vitarka and vicāra," this is as explained previously in the section on dhyāna-concentration. The third [category] refers to the lower [level]; this is the specific name.
Regarding the phrase "according to the smallness, greatness, and superiority of light," the following provides the explanation. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Within the heavens of its own stage, the radiance is the smallest, and is thus called 'Limited Light' (*Parīttābha*). Because the radiance becomes increasingly superior and its measure is difficult to fathom, it is called 'Immeasurable Light' (*Apramāṇābha*)."

Because it purifies and illuminates the spheres of both self and others, it is called *Abhāsvara* (Utmost Radiance). Regarding the commentary’s statement that this deva-realm is free from joy (*prīti*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) of the mental level (*manobhūmi*) is designated as 'pure' (*śubha*).

As for the specific explanation that it is named after its light, one should say that the names *Parīttaśubha* (Limited Purity) and so forth are established according to the degree and excellence of that purity, respectively. The *Nyāyānusāra* further states: "Within its own level..."

Among these, this purity is the most inferior; therefore, it is called "Limited Purity" (Parītta-śubha). Because its purity increases further until its measure becomes difficult to fathom, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇa-śubha).

Because this purity is all-pervasive, it is called "Universal Purity" (Śubha-kṛtsna). This indicates that no pleasure can surpass this. [The commentary states: "Regarding the eight levels of the fourth dhyāna:
among these, the first three are exclusively distinct [realms], while the latter five have both common and distinct aspects. As for "Cloudless" (Anabhraka) and so forth, they follow...
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Below this is the ground where the gods dwell in the sky, like dense clouds joined together. Above these various heavens, there is no further ground of clouds;

because it is at the head of the 'Cloudless' (Anabhraka), it is called 'Cloudless. Because there is another place for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of superior merit to be reborn, it is called 'Merit-Born' (Puṇyaprasava).
This is the most excellent, and is thus called 'Vast Fruit' (Bṛhatphala). As for the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*):"

These are precisely the latter five [heavens] which are named the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa). The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The noble ones who have abandoned desire wash away the stains of affliction with the water of the Noble Path;
therefore, they are called 'Pure' (śuddha). Because these are the dwellings of those with pure bodies, they are called 'Pure Abodes.

Alternatively, because those who dwell here reach the very limit of saṃsāra—like having fully repaid a debt—they are called 'Pure. Since these are the abodes of the pure, they are called 'Pure Abodes.'"

They dwell there. Because in this celestial realm there is no mixture with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and it is inhabited solely by noble ones (*ārya*), it is called the "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Regarding the note "without proliferation," etc., these are the five distinct names listed. The *Nyāyānusāra* explains: "Proliferation" (*prapañca*) means either "confusion and mixture" or "vastness and expansion."
Because it is the first among those that are not "proliferated" (apramāṇa), and because it is the most inferior among the "vast" (vipula) heavens, it is called "the Unproliferated.

(In the former interpretation, defilements are taken as "proliferation"; in the latter, qualities are taken as "vastness. Alternatively, it is called "the Unseeking," because there is no seeking to enter the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).

(These individuals who have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* proceed as far as the Bṛhatphala heaven, where they then diverge into two paths. Those who delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are not reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, but proceed directly to the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) to attain extinction. Those who delight in wisdom (*prajñā*) are reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and then proceed to extinction.

As for the "Heatless" (*Atapa*), because they have already skillfully subdued and eliminated the obstacles to concentration, their mental dispositions are harmonious and supple, and they are free from all burning afflictions (*paridāha*), they are thus called "Heatless."

In other places, there are separate fascicles. Alternatively, the afflictions that arise below [the first dhyāna] are called "heat" (*paridāha*); because one has now distanced oneself from these for the first time, it receives the name "freedom from heat" (*atapā*).
Or again, "heat" signifies being "blazing" (*tīvra*), referring to the superior cultivation of dhyāna and its fruit; this has not yet been realized.

Therefore, it is named "Without Heat" (*Atapa*). (In this context, "heat" refers to the blazing intensity of meritorious qualities. Having already attained the superior grade of the meditative absorption of detachment, its resultant virtues are easily manifested;

therefore, it is named "Well-Appeared" (*Sudṛśa*). As for the obstacles to mixed cultivation, their remaining grades have become extremely subtle, and vision is utterly clear and penetrating; therefore, it is named "Good Vision" (*Sudarśana*).
There is no other place within the realm of form that can surpass this; it is called the "Ultimate of Form and Name" (*rūpa-nāma-akaniṣṭha*).

Alternatively, because one has reached the final limit of the body which is the basis for all suffering, it is called the "Ultimate of Form and Name. (This refers to those born there who are necessarily noble ones (*ārya*) dwelling in the third dhyāna realm;

having now reached that state, they are certain to attain parinirvāṇa, and it is impossible for them to receive a second birth-body. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Above this Desire Realm, there are seventeen places, namely:"

Each of the three dhyāna stages has three levels, while the fourth dhyāna stage alone has eight. The environment (*bhājana*) and the sentient beings (*sattva*) together are collectively termed the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Following the above, this refers to the "retribution" (*vipāka*) consisting of both the environment and the sentient beings—the two types of retribution based on the primary and secondary supports.
Furthermore, according to the exposition in this treatise, all form (*rūpa*) existing from the Yāma heaven of the Desire Realm upward, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and so forth, [is included].
All the devas dwell entirely within palaces suspended in space; these palaces and such constitute the external vessel-world.
Because they dwell in space, there are no longer mountains, rivers, forests, or trees. However, from below the Cloudless Heaven (Anabhraka) downward, clouds still serve as the ground;
from this point upward, there are no longer even clouds, and the palaces are scattered throughout space like stars and the moon.
Furthermore, if one wishes to discuss the respective distances from the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) for each of those heavens, one must first know how many distinct locations they possess.

It should be understood that there are only sixteen distinct heavenly abodes; thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (Brahmapāriṣadya) and so forth comprise sixteen locations.
As for those who claim there are seventeen or eighteen, this refers to a separate enumeration within the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita).

From among the Mahābrahmā and Bṛhatphala heavens, the Āsaṃjñika (Unconscious) Heaven is separately distinguished. Its meaning as the "highest" is that its lifespan, measured in kalpas, is most profound.

From the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) upward, these qualities double and increase in excellence, culminating in the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana (Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception) Heaven, which is the most supreme.
Nevertheless, it is not free from form and desire; since it lacks physical form, it has no distinct location.

Regarding the term *yojana*: sixteen *li* constitute one *yojana*, which is the height of the Brahmakāyika gods; half of that is eight *li*. Regarding the subsequent three [levels], each increases by half a *yojana*:
the Brahmapurohita gods are one *yojana* (sixteen *li*) in height, and the Mahābrahmā gods are one and a half *yojanas* in height.

(24 *li*) The Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) is two *yojana*s in height. (32 *li*) Regarding the subsequent five [heavens] where the measure doubles successively: the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*) is four *yojana*s;

the Heaven of Pure Light (*Śubhakṛtsna*) is eight; the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*) is sixteen; the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*) is thirty-two; and the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*) is sixty-four.

Delusions and the like have no distinct substantial entities of their own; rather, when one is in a state of confusion and fails to comprehend the principle and its phenomena, this is termed "ignorance" (avidyā).

The sub-commentary (*śū*) next provides a detailed explanation of the following passage, which consists of two parts: first, the establishment of the principle; second, the citation of scriptural authority. Regarding the first, it says, "designating the name," and so forth.

This refers to establishing a name based on the essence (the fact that only when there is a moist essence is the name "water" established). The "essence" is the essence underlying the name, and it is merely a single dharma.

In this school, that which is known and seen is taken as the ultimate truth; this is precisely what was stated previously: "The primary tenet of this sutra is that its principle is wisdom. As explained previously:

"Principle (*li*) is original enlightenment (*benjue*); wisdom (*zhi*) is initial enlightenment (*shijue*)," and so forth. This shows that although one speaks of "principle and wisdom," both are in fact wisdom.
A brief explanation is as provided previously; a detailed account is fully set forth in the *Xinji er zhizhi ju chao* (Excerpts on the Phrase "The Mind is Quiescent yet Knowing").

Furthermore, the *Huayan wenming pin* (Chapter on Questions and Clarifications) and Chengguan’s commentary on the phrase "the Buddha’s realm of knowledge" also convey this same meaning, as cited previously in the *Shu* (Commentary).
Regarding the phrase "each time one brushes away illness and so forth," the Sūtra says: "When all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoved.

It further states: "Neither bound by dharmas, nor seeking liberation from dharmas; even regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the observance of precepts and the harboring of doubts—all these are brushed away, whether by those who have long practiced or those who are beginners.
It then concludes: "Why is this? Because everything is awakening. Furthermore, it says: "Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are identical..."
Arising and ceasing; the wondrous awakening shines perfectly, free from the cataracts of conceptual flowers. It is further said:
"The wondrous, perfect, awakened mind originally has neither *bodhi* nor *nirvāṇa*, nor does it have the attainment or non-attainment of Buddhahood, nor the delusory cycle of saṃsāra.

This first establishes the awakened mind, yet within it, these phenomena are dissolved to reveal that the awakened mind is beyond all relative dependence—not that the awakened mind itself is dissolved. Such is the meaning of the text from beginning to end.
All examples are thus. The Treatise states: "All dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression," and so on, up to "they are but the single mind.
Even this is subsumed; only the mind remains. Only then is this mind designated as "True Suchness" (*tathatā*). Yet "True Suchness" is merely a name. It further states:
"That which is free from the characteristics of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm, wherein there is nothing [to be grasped]."
It is not universal; it is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal *dharmakāya*. Based upon this *dharmakāya*, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*).
Furthermore, it is said that in reality there is no distinction between "initial awakening" (*ādi-awakening*), because the four marks exist simultaneously and none possess independent self-existence;
they are fundamentally equal and identical to a single awakening. It is further said that by being far removed from subtle thoughts, one perceives the nature of the mind. This mind...

This is precisely what is called "constant abiding," which is termed "ultimate awakening. The commentary (*shu*) states that from the passage "not by means of emptiness and stillness" onwards, it is also fully explained as in the sub-commentary (*chao*) within the preface.

The note cites a scripture from the middle of the text, which says: "From Perfect Awakening flow forth all pure *tathatā*, etc. It further says: "Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday.
The commentary (*shu*) states that from the passage "therefore, the *Avataṃsaka*... onwards, there are two citations of scriptural texts. [End of entry]. No.

Regarding the phrase "not all sentient beings possess [it]," the expression "none" (*naika*) is absent. This distinguishes it from the Five-Nature school (*pañca-gotra-vāda*), which asserts that there are three classes of sentient beings who lack Buddha-nature.

The term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) excludes external insentient objects and the physical environment (*bhājana-loka*). Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Those who lack Buddha-nature are what are called the insentient.
The insentient are grasses, trees, tiles, stones, walls, and so forth. There is nothing that does not possess [it].
"Those" refers to the "endowment. Regarding "the wisdom of the Tathāgata," it is as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* concerning the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*):

"knowledge" is wisdom (*jñāna*), and "vision" is insight (*prajñā*). Therefore, that sutra says: "The wisdom I have attained," and further: "The wisdom of the Buddhas is extremely profound and immeasurable," and again:
"It is for the sake of expounding the wisdom of the Buddhas that the Buddhas appear in the world"—all of which is the opening, revealing, awakening, and entering [into that wisdom].
"The Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "However, it is due to deluded thoughts" refers to the ignorance that acts as an obstruction, as explained herein.
"But they do not realize it" means, according to the commentary, that in the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang) school, wisdom must await the severing of obstructions before realizing the truth.

It has only now begun to be newly born. Because of this, ordinary beings have neither severed nor realized anything at all—not even a hair’s breadth. What is meant here by "the delusive thoughts have not been severed" is that they are obstructed;

because they are obstructed, they do not realize [the truth]. This non-realization means they have not realized the Real (the *tathatā*). That which has neither been severed nor realized is inherently possessed from the very beginning.
One immediately knows this to be the ultimate nature of reality (*dharmatā*), thereby establishing the meaning set forth in the commentary.
"To attain what is present before one" refers to the aspect of its manifest appearance; it does not mean that there is some wisdom existing before one's eyes.
Rather, one should know that there is only a distinction between concealment and manifestation, without any difference in essence. The rest is as explained in the annotations.

Regarding the statement that "the commentaries are largely the same with minor differences": the dharmas are fourfold in their commonality (namely, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and those of indeterminate nature), while one is distinct (the fifth nature).

What is referred to there as "the absence of nature" (niḥsvabhāva) is here called "the nature of the non-Buddhists" (tīrthika-gotra). Furthermore, while those [scriptures] treat the two vehicles separately, here they are explained in combination.

Moreover, the doctrine is the same while the phrasing differs. [Commentary: Regarding the second point, "perfuming to form the five natures": these five natures are extremely difficult to discern from the literal meaning of the sūtras; they are merely mentioned incidentally.
There are five types of persons for whom the seeds [of the five natures] have been perfumed in the past and have reached maturity through the teaching of the five natures.

Or, there may be those who, having received the teachings in this present life, give rise to such a resolve and hold such a view, intending to practice in such a manner and hoping to realize such a fruit—these are the very type of persons for whom the Buddha provides instruction on how to practice and realize.
This is shown in the final section of the text; this [present portion] is merely a brief summary, and the Sūtra certainly does not [conclude] with only one [of these].
This is already explained in detail within the *Kō* (commentary). For the most part, this describes his [the opponent's] views and mental state; it is not that the Buddha himself taught it to be so.
However, if one carefully examines the sūtra with this intention, one will not fall into error. Otherwise, it is extremely difficult [to understand].

As for the mention of a single section in the *Shū* (sub-commentary), this is based on the five natures (*pañca-gotra*). There should be five sections in total, but because the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*) are combined into a single category, there are only four.

If one were to simply merge the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*) into a single nature, then taking the immediately preceding passage of the sutra as "no-nature" (*anabhilakṣya-gotra*), these five sections of the sutra would instead constitute five distinct natures.
In that case, they should be stated as: first, no-nature; second, the nature of the two vehicles; third, the nature of a bodhisattva; fourth, the indeterminate nature;
and fifth, the nature of externalists (*tīrthika*). However, since various sutras and treatises consistently treat the two vehicles as two distinct natures, [the former interpretation is untenable].

It accords with the nature of the non-Buddhists; they are identical in their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Therefore, based on various texts, and because "lack of intrinsic nature" does not carry the meaning of being newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*), it is not accepted [here].

The Commentary (*Śū*) excludes only the first defilement. The "obstructions of phenomena" (*vastv-āvaraṇa*) are precisely the six defilements. Regarding these six defilements, according to the Treatise, the two vehicles [are as follows]:

This refers to the severance of the first type of defilement associated with grasping (*parigraha*). This is defined specifically in terms of its capacity to directly initiate karma and perpetuate the cycle of birth-and-death in discrete segments (*bheda-saṃsāra*).
As for the other five types of defilement, they do not obstruct liberation from the three realms; therefore, the Śrāvakas have not severed them.

Regarding the phrase "the rest, provided they are not accompanied by grasping," it is as previously cited in the treatise: "Based on the increasingly deep grasping of ordinary worldlings, they conceive of a self and what belongs to a self."

...up to the increase of views and craving, and so forth. Although one does not yet sever the subtle defilements within the five mental consciousnesses, this is nonetheless different from the grasping and increase of ordinary beings.
Regarding "presently manifesting," as explained in the *Chapter on the Eight Consciousnesses*.

Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), these are precisely the seeds (*bīja*), such as Śāriputra’s habit of anger, as previously described. Although [the text] proceeds down to the section on the elder, the Dharma...
The matter of the impoverished son within the *Avataṃsaka* has already been cited in the Preface.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary on the "Bodhisattva-nature" section that "first, one distinguishes its characteristics," this refers to those who wish to speak of persons possessing the Bodhisattva-nature—

whether through the manifestation of past habitual tendencies or through the arising of understanding upon hearing the teachings in this present life— and the dharmas and meanings they perceive at the outset.
This is because it concerns the mind that practices cultivation. It is manifested by way of the phases of practice prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and upon entering the stages.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary should say 'etc. (*sū*): this merely alters two characters. One should simply read it according to the original text and not alter the characters within the scriptural fascicle.

The reading is: "First, one should resolve to diligently sever the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). Once the two obstacles have been suppressed, one is then able to accord with and enter the realm of the Bodhisattva."
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): herein, one merely first vows to sever obstructions rather than first realizing the mind; thus, one has not yet escaped the mind of saṃsāra.

Since the true nature has not yet been awakened to, and the two obstructions have already been suppressed so that they do not manifest, the mental activities proceed spontaneously, secretly becoming identical to those of a Bodhisattva;
hence it is called "entering in accordance. The commentary’s phrase "merely removing the illness" implies that there is a portion of people who [possess] Bodhisattvas.

One's nature differs from that of the two vehicles and external paths. Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "manifested by fundamental craving" and ending with "not eliminating cultivation and realization," it is logically necessary to make vows to sever hindrances;
however, once one realizes that all phenomena are empty and empty, this is entirely identical to the awakened essence itself.

Although they have not yet awakened their minds, they accord with principle through the darkness [of ignorance]; thus, by practicing gradually, they do not fall into the vehicles of the two śrāvakas or the external paths.

However, when the two obstacles are suppressed, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that they will inevitably encounter the definitive teachings of the One Vehicle’s perfect reality, whereby they immediately attain realization of the Truth and ascend to the stages (*bhūmi*).

This is just as, at the completion of the seventh stage, it is the natural law that one must inevitably encounter the seven exhortations of the Buddhas in order to enter the eighth stage. Thus it concludes.
In the end, one will attain the fulfillment of bodhi and nirvāṇa;

however, this must wait until one encounters the perfect and true teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), at which time one will finally escape the mind of saṃsāra. Before such an encounter, although one’s practices may appear outwardly compliant with the path, the mind remains bound to saṃsāra.

In the commentary on the indeterminate nature, it is divided into two sections. First, there is a general indication of the sudden and gradual approaches; second, from "If one encounters a Tathāgata... onwards, there is a specific explanation of the sudden approach.
Regarding the gradual approach, the phrase "self-awakening" and so forth is as previously explained:

because one body is pure, many bodies are pure. "Encountering a spiritual friend" refers to a teacher of the Three Vehicles. "The dharma-practice of the causal stage" refers to the fundamental mind that marks the intention and conceives the aspiration.

Furthermore, within the first three stages of the causes described in the Mañjuśrī Chapter, the preceding section established that all sentient beings possess the meaning of universal enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
This corresponds to the first stage, "thoroughly realizing the nature of awakening" (*bodhita-svabhāva*). The present section corresponds to the second stage, "arousing the bodhicitta.

However, because their inclinations differ and they encounter the teachings individually, it is said that they "rejoice in and aspire toward" [the goal], which means: rejoicing in renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) and aspiring toward liberation (*mokṣa*), and rejoicing in the fruit of Buddhahood and aspiring toward...

This refers to the stages of practice and so forth. In the commentary, the section beginning with "If one encounters a Tathāgata" provides a specific explanation of the sudden and gradual [teachings]. This section has two parts;

first, it explains the sudden teaching based on the sutras. Regarding the term "the Perfect School (Yuanzong)," this refers to the several dozen texts such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, as explained in the preface to the commentary.

The commentary further clarifies that although [the practitioners] are inferior, the subsequent section of the sutra explains their gradual [progress]. Those of inferior aspiration are so called because, although they believe in Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), they feel weary of birth and death and long for liberation.

Furthermore, encountering teachers and friends of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) who instruct them, they consequently extinguish mental perceptions and concentrate their minds, directing themselves toward liberation.
Following the path of the Two Vehicles, they will ultimately turn their hearts toward the Great Vehicle; this is termed "gradual."

The term "also" (ye) [indicates inclusion]. "Equal" (deng) means equal to the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna. This refers to those whose faculties (*indriya*) are dull but whose aspirations are far-reaching and great;

they delight solely in the fruit of Buddhahood and do not seek the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). However, because their faculties are dull, they are unable to suddenly dissolve the mental states of ordinary beings and sages.

Furthermore, encountering teachers and friends within the provisional Mahāyāna, they are exhorted to cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and to seek realization through the successive stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore...
This is also a gradual process. Regarding the passage beginning with "The missing portions of the sutra text," the text is easy to understand.

In the commentary on the section concerning the nature of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are two parts: first, the explanation of this specific passage; second, the reconciliation with various teachings. Within the first part, there are three sections: the initial, the middle, and the final. It says:

One should understand other cases by analogy with this. However, where the text is abbreviated, it should be stated that those who encounter the provisional teachings have not yet attained sudden enlightenment;

this is what is termed the "nature of the Two Vehicles" and so forth. That teacher’s narrow restriction is not the fault of sentient beings. [End of] Commentary. Now, regarding the section "the rest below," this refers to the subsequent integration of the various teachings.
[End of] Commentary. Regarding the "Four Means of Integration": they are giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation. [End of] Commentary. Regarding "contemplation":

Regarding the thirty-two types of voices: after the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has extensively explained the merits of Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati again asks the Buddha:
"How does Avalokiteśvara roam this Sahā world? How does he preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
What are the matters concerning his power of skillful means? The Buddha says: "If there is a land where sentient beings..."

Śāriputra, for those who are to be liberated by a Buddha-body, he manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma to them. [For those to be liberated by] Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, Brahmā Kings, or Śakras, [he manifests those respective forms and preaches the Dharma].

Maheśvara, Maheśvarī, Mahāsenapati, Vaiśravaṇa, minor kings, elders, householders, officials, brahmins, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, various women, boys and girls, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas,
kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and the Vajrapāṇi deities— each and every one of them initially appeared in the form of a Buddha. It is Avalokiteśvara who, having accomplished such merit,
wanders through all lands in various forms to deliver and liberate sentient beings.
The "flow" refers to those who act as kinsmen and friends; these are favorable conditions (*anuloma*) by which one is led to enter [the path].
Those who act as enemies are adverse conditions (*pratiloma*), used to frighten one into entering. Furthermore, Vāsukī represents the favorable, while King Anala represents the adverse.
These two individuals are the spiritual friends encountered by the youth Sudhana. According to the commentary, one must necessarily resolve to deliver sentient beings;
for compassion, wisdom, and the vow constitute the very essence of the bodhicitta. Thus, those who first generate the bodhicitta must possess these three.
As stated at the very beginning of the *Vajracchedikā*: "May I lead all beings of the four modes of birth and nine classes to enter nirvana."
Recalling one's former vows, at the moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one’s merit was equal to that of a Buddha. Why is it that today the mind and conduct are such as these?
Examine and weigh the principles: is it the aspiration generated in the past that is right, or is it the mental conduct of today? Through this, one will naturally awaken to the truth.
At present, however, it is not as it was at the initial stage of setting forth; one is immediately struck with alarm and shame, and exerts oneself to seek the eternally abiding.
What is done is no longer according to one's whims. To act according to whims means to deliver those one loves and to abandon those one hates.
Therefore, in the section on the mark of self (*ātman*) below, it says: "If there is another person who praises that Dharma, one immediately gives rise to joy and desires to rescue and deliver them."

Furthermore, if one slanders what has been attained, resentment will arise. Now, I act in accordance with the power of my vows and do not move according to the power of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the previous statement that "one follows the five natures," this also carries the meaning of following one's dispositions;
that is, whatever dharma was habituated in past lives constitutes one's nature, and in this life, one spontaneously takes pleasure in that very dharma which was so habituated. Now it is said:

Regarding those who do not follow [the path]: a person who practices this school must first personally investigate and examine the principles, and only after selecting teachers and friends whose teachings and logic are authentic may they give rise to the Great Mind (therefore it is said:
"arouse a superior resolve toward Great Perfect Enlightenment"). Thus, for a long time, they act solely in accordance with the power of the vow originally made.
Suddenly, however, upon encountering various schools or vehicles—whether persons or teachings—they may become attached due to their past habitual tendencies, and then...
Because he wishes to change his resolve and follow that [other path], it is said that he does not conform to the five natures (*pañca-gotra*). "Five natures" is a general term;
in reality, it simply means that he cannot conform to the two types of natures—namely, those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) and external paths (*tīrthika*).

As explained in the section on compassion, although the underlying meaning is the same, the modes of practice differ slightly: whereas previously one universally delivers others upon encountering them regardless of whether they are enemies or kin, here [one does so] in relation to suffering and pleasure.

Regarding their practice: whenever they encounter [conditions], they act accordingly. Although the principle (*li*) is equal for all, the *Buddhāvatamsaka* (The Flower Ornament Sūtra) states: "In principle, there is immediate awakening; through awakening, everything is simultaneously eliminated.
In phenomena (*shi*), there is no immediate removal; they are exhausted through successive stages. The "Pure Dharma Palace" is the place where one constantly dwells.

Since obstructions are exhausted and one always abides in liberation, it is metaphorically likened to a palace. Furthermore, at the beginning of the first fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is also described as a palace.
This is analogous to *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is liberation. As for "adornment": hitherto, one has not realized that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are merely empty and merely provisional.
This Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) transcends both emptiness and the provisional; it stands solitary and detached, and thus is not termed "adornment."
Now my vows are fulfilled. I have fully realized the single realm of the three truths and the single mind of the three contemplations.

Because the contemplation and the truths are non-dual, all phenomena are each and every one fused and identical with perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Perfect enlightenment possesses these immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable all-encompassing dharmas.

This is the meaning of "adornment. As for "territory," it refers to such things as national borders, royal capitals, the three ancient capitals with their cultural artifacts, and the five imperial tombs with their mist and moonlight.

Within the Dharma, the three realms, the ten directions, the human world, and the heavens—everything encountered by the eye is the boundary and domain of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

Furthermore, the majestic domain of the Dharma-palace may also be understood through two distinct metaphors: liberation (*vimukti*) and perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). However, because...

Liberation is the meaning of absolute transcendence; it is not of the same category as ornamental adornments. Perfect Enlightenment (Pariniṣpanna-bodhi) is the complete integration of all phenomena from beginning to end.
It is apart from all phenomena, yet has no separate location and no place where it can abide; therefore, it is [compared to] a palace.
Nor are they of the same category, for each passage of this sutra serves as a metaphor for a single dharma.
Regarding the phrase "that which is severed, long, and separated" and so forth: in the prose commentary (*dīrghapada*), the root and the branches are distinguished and explained separately;

however, in this verse, it simply says "greed, desire, and birth-and-death" without explaining them individually. This is because desire assists in forming causes, leading to successive and mutual dependence.

Because they give rise to various karmic retributions, they are combined and treated briefly. Regarding the exhortation to "attain equality" in the commentary, the points of separation and combination can be understood accordingly.

As for the latter seven phrases which eulogize compassion and wisdom: among them, the first three phrases refer to compassion and the final four phrases refer to wisdom. This concludes the explanation of the Chapter on Maitreya.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Subcommentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Ten (Part Two);

*Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Subcommentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Eleven (Part One). [Containing the sections from "The Chapter on Primordial Pure Wisdom" through "The Chapter on Majestic Virtue," including the "Contemplation of Illusion"].
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.
Chapter on the Brief Classification of the Grounds (The Question of Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati).

The commentary contains three inquiries and explanations: first, the explanation of the name; second, the identification of its essence; third, the discernment of its reason. Regarding the first, "ent" means non-existence, negation, or absence.
Because it is without marks, the mind cannot reach it; therefore, it is inconceivable. Because it is without names, speech cannot reach it.
Therefore, it cannot be discussed [in this context]. As for what Śrīmālā says, it refers to the intended meaning. She states: "The intrinsically pure mind is difficult to comprehend;
that mind being defiled by ignorance is likewise difficult to comprehend. Regarding the phrase "never before heard or seen":
when this sutra was preached, was it prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* or subsequent to it? If it were prior, then it would be a provisional teaching (*upāya-deśanā*).
It is sublated by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If [the latter] were later, then the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* would have already been preached; why then has this [teaching] not yet appeared?

The answer is that the Introduction and the Preliminary Discourse have already clarified that this is a teaching of sudden enlightenment (*tun-jiao*), which does not belong to the teachings of the three periods or five periods. How much more so since it is preached within the Pure Land?
What determines their sequence? Each is according to the superior or inferior capacities of beings; thus, what they see and hear differs, as has been extensively analyzed previously.

This teaching was specifically reserved for the final age for the sake of the hundred thousand great bodhisattvas. As for the statement that it has "never before been seen," this is simply because those who encounter it and hear it—whether through the establishment of characteristics or the refutation of characteristics—are many;
yet this teaching is difficult to hear and rare to encounter, and is therefore manifested as the appropriate response for the final age.
This merely records these words.

Regarding the preceding discussion on saṃsāra and so forth: it is asked, there is a vast disparity between the cultivation and realization of saṃsāra and that which is inverted or correct; [saṃsāra] consists of perverted and deluded attachments.
If one allows for emptiness and non-existence and practices in accordance with principle, why would it be otherwise? Answer:

Since the nature of awakening is neither born, nor moving, nor changing, how could there be any distinction between an initial inversion and a subsequent rectitude? One thus knows that these two—mutually dependent designations—are both devoid of intrinsic nature.

However, inversion is like the deluded grasping of a snake hidden within the appearance of a rope; cultivation is like the manifestation of an image, which does not obscure the clarity of the mirror. Furthermore, the snake is [merely] the whole...

There is none. A reflection possesses a provisional appearance. Furthermore, a rope does not manifest as a snake, whereas a mirror actually manifests a reflection; thus, there is a distinction between the snake and the reflection in terms of being inverted or upright.

△ In the commentary, regarding the phrase "such as the light of the eyes," this meaning was already explained previously in the section on how the light of the eyes attains freedom from aversion and attachment.
However, concerning the term "equal" (*sama*), since there is no discrimination, there is likewise no partiality of aversion or attachment—neither "this much" nor "that much."

This is the meaning of "few. Therefore, it is called "equality" (*samatā*). It does not mean that there is a person with a level mind and clever intelligence who can distribute things evenly so that they are not biased; therefore, it is said that there is no creator.

Regarding the "the former three" and so forth in the commentary: as in the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), awakening to the non-arising of karma is considered extinction, while failing to awaken to delusion is considered non-extinction.

In the stage of the worthy (*satpuruṣa*), awakening to the characteristic of difference (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is extinction, while failing to awaken to the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is non-extinction. In the stage of the sage (*ārya*), awakening to the characteristic of abiding is extinction, while failing to awaken to the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) is non-extinction.

In all these cases, awakening constitutes extinction and non-awakening constitutes non-extinction. If one follows the original text of this sutra, however, it is at the stage of faith that weariness and anxiety are extinguished.

Pure understanding (*viśuddha-adhimukti*) has not yet been extinguished; this is the stage of the noble one (*ārya-bhūmi*). Pure understanding is extinguished, but the awakening of insight (*darśana-bodhi*) has not yet been extinguished;

this is the stage of the sage (*ārya*), wherein illumination and quiescence have not yet been extinguished, because the obstacles have not yet been attained to as awakening. Regarding the commentary on "crossing the river in a dream" (not verified). Regarding the commentary on "perfectly clear realization and awakening" and so forth:

this refers precisely to the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), and thus it is characterized by signlessness (*animitta*) and effortlessness (*anābhoga*). Question: There are three further layers of subtle obstacles that have not yet been exhausted; why [is this so]?
"Attaining perfect clarity (*yuanming*). Answer: This stage is the beginning of perfect realization. Thereafter, the wisdom that accords with the nature (*xing*) flows spontaneously;

subtle afflictions are exhausted of their own accord without the need for further effort. Therefore, it is called "perfect clarity. In reality, however, the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) alone constitutes ultimate perfect clarity.

This explanation is still based on the gate of sequential progression (*xingbu men*). If one speaks from the perspective of the gate of total interpenetration (*yuanrong men*), [it begins] at the very first...
"Abiding is itself [the goal]. Regarding the note attributed to Master Zhi, it says: "The Great Way is not attained through practice;

one speaks of practice only for the sake of the ignorant and foolish (those below the stages [bhūmi] and those in the post-meditative, distracted states of each stage all belong to the category of the ignorant and foolish; therefore, the obstacles they sever are called the twenty-two forms of folly).

Mind (*citta*). (It is luminous. By practicing in this manner, up until the point where one abandons the two kinds of grasper and grasped, one realizes non-apprehension and is able to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Once the emptiness of the perceived has been realized, one is further able to know universally that the perceiving consciousness itself is also devoid of consciousness.

The internal objects are definitely non-existent, and the grasper is likewise empty. One understands that the internal consciousness and its transformed appearances are mutually inseparable, like illusory phenomena and the like. However, as previously stated, when one investigates and finds no object of grasping (*grāhya*), at the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)—the lower level—one suppresses and eliminates it;

at the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*)—the higher level—one suppresses and eliminates it until reaching the stage of "Reality. "Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "storehouse"; for within this, there are contained boundless and rare great merits. The above explanation of the first phrase describes the essence of the state (*pada*).

Inconceivable: This is the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). It transcends the path of discursive thought and verbal expression; it is subtle, wondrous, and profoundly deep because it is personally realized within; it cannot be illustrated by any worldly metaphors. Virtuous:

Furthermore, because it is the nature of one's own dharma, the pure dharma-realm (*viśuddha-dharmadhātu*) is far removed from arising and ceasing and is supremely secure; the mental states and factors of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-cittavastu*) possess wondrous functions that are unrestricted and supremely skillful. Both aspects possess these qualities.

Because it is characterized by conformity and benefit, it is "constant" (nitya), for this fruit has no end, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is unchanging, and the four wisdoms (caturjñāna) are never exhausted. Because there is no boundless affliction, and because all characteristics of the dharma-realm are quiescent, it is "blissful" (sukha).
The Body of Liberation (*vimuktikāya*) is so called because it is eternally free from the harm of afflictions (*kleśa*). The Great Muni is named the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*):

while the two fruits of the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles are merely termed the Body of Liberation, the World-Honored Greatly Awakened One is named the Great Muni because he has accomplished the unsurpassed dharma of silent tranquility; the fruit he attains, being eternally free from the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), is also termed the Dharma-body, as it is adorned with immeasurable and boundless dharmas of great merit.

Therefore, this Dharma-body has five dharmas as its nature; it is not the pure *dharmadhātu* alone that is named the Dharma-body, for both fruits of the twofold transformation of the basis are subsumed within it. Such a Dharma-body has three distinct aspects: first, the Essential Body (*svābhāvikakāya*); second, the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogikakāya*); and third, the Transformation Body (*nairmāṇikakāya*).
It is explained in detail as stated therein. The above constitutes the commentary on this single verse (all of which is based on the root text).
Regarding the second point, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Compendium of the Great Vehicle), in its sixth chapter, the section "Entering the Characteristics of the Knowable," asks: "Where does one enter?

(This question concerns the sphere to be entered and the stage of entry). It states: "That is to say, within that very [sphere], there is the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) of the Mahāyāna, which appears as dharmas and appears as objects."

Born from signs (*nimitta*). (This refers to the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that resembles the dharma and resembles the object, which is born from signs regarding the Mahāyāna teachings; it is able to enter this objective sphere. "Able to enter" is the function; the "objective sphere entered" is the entry and the support.
One gives rise to the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

Within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the ultimate path (*niṣṭhā-mārga*), because one follows what has been heard and resolves upon it, one is able to enter—within this mental verbalization, or while in the stage of practice through resolute belief—into the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) regarding all phenomena; one merely hears and generates resolute belief therein.

Because of understanding, it is because of thorough penetration according to reality (or, because one can enter into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by means of this thorough penetration of mental verbalization).

Because of counteracting all obstacles, it is because one can enter into the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), for by means of this cultivation, one counteracts the afflictive and cognitive obstacles (*kleśa- and jñeyāvaraṇa*). Because of being free from all obstacles, it is because one can enter into the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*), which is supremely pure.

"Because it is free from all obstacles. These four kinds constitute the stage of entry (*praveśāvasthā*). [The] Commentary states: "All that has been annotated above is entirely based on the text of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva.
However, the root treatise consists of four sections: first, the clarification of what is entered; second, the clarification that mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) is the means of entry;

third, from 'resolute belief' (*adhimukti*) onwards, the clarification of the stage of entry; and fourth, from 'regarding all phenomena' (*sarvadharmeṣu*) onwards, the demonstration of the actual entry itself."

Regarding the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*): the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains that because they have not yet realized *tathatā*, they cultivate various superior practices by means of the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

(Resolute conviction has the meaning of definitive determination and mental retention; it refers to the determination of a distracted mind, a conceptual reflection through mental resolve, as one has not yet realized direct comprehension. Thus, within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, this is designated as the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

The two stages of the *saṃbhāra* (provision) and *prayoga* (application) are subsumed [here]. Regarding the remaining three [stages], the commentary (*vṛtti*) states that the two treatises are entirely identical.
