However, upon examining the various texts in detail, it appears that the first stage consists only of the three levels of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Worthies) and does not include the *prayoga* stage. This will be explained extensively below by citing various texts after discussing the *yogācāryabhūmi*.
Furthermore, the other three stages are also not entirely identical; the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* [treats them] from the perspective of the *darśana-mārga* (path of seeing).

In the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it speaks only of "attaining the principle" (*tattva-pratilambha*); this means that the intention applies to each stage (*bhūmi*) because one realizes *tathatā*. In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it speaks only of "remedying obstructions" (*āvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*);

this intention also applies to the initial entry into the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), because one abandons the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstructions through their conceptualization.

If one considers the consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) perspective, then both stages possess both the realization of truth and the abandonment of obstructions; this will be explained further below.

Regarding the phrase "the three yogas, etc. in the commentary: this refers to what is taught in the forty-ninth chapter on the "Stages" (*bhūmi*) as well as in the seventh fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Xianyang lun*), which is why the word "etc.
is used. Furthermore, the thirteen abodes (*vihāra*) mentioned in the forty-seventh [chapter] are also subsumed within these seven stages.
Likewise, the fifty-two positions are also subsumed herein; namely, first, the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) are subsumed, and second—

The first [stage] subsumes the three levels of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). The second subsumes the first stage (*bhūmi*). The fourth extends from the second stage to the seventh stage. The fifth is the eighth stage. The sixth is the ninth stage. The seventh is the tenth stage.
As for what the Buddha calls the "stage of the lineage" (*gotrabhūmi*), this refers to the first of those, the "abiding in the lineage" (*gotrastha*).

According to the *Cien* (Yuan Ce), this is assigned to the "innately abiding lineage" (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, because he follows the system of the five lineages (*pañca-gotra*). However, if one follows the various sūtras...
Treatise: This corresponds to the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). In the text concerning "Abiding" (*vihāra*), it says (the following cases should be understood by analogy):

"The various Bodhisattvas are by nature inherently benevolent and virtuous; they are by nature inherently accomplished in the merits of a Bodhisattva. (If explained according to the Ten Faiths, this means that because of past habitual cultivation, these have now become their inherent nature.

Regarding the numerous wholesome dharmas appropriate for a Bodhisattva, these manifest in practice. Because they are inherently benevolent and virtuous, they are impelled toward skillful means, causing them to turn toward the wholesome. It is not [by external force].
By means of discernment, there is benefit; regarding that which is to be guarded against, one abides therein.
Within this state—within the *ālayavijñāna* as the self-nature and within the basis (the continuum of the body)—all seeds of the Buddha-dharmas are already fully present.
By nature, these are free from coarse defilements; yet they cannot manifest the higher afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) to create [unwholesome karma].
Intermediate karma may sever the roots of goodness (as explained in detail in the *Gotra-paṭala*). Regarding the "Stage of Practice through Resolute Conviction" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*):
this refers to the second stage, the "Abode of Practice through Resolute Conviction. Within the text of this abode, it says:

"All bodhisattva practices performed by bodhisattvas from their initial generation of the mind until they have not yet attained pure intention (*viśuddhāśaya*) are subsumed within this abode. (This concludes the first *kalpa*). Regarding the "Pure Resolute Intention":

The "Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) refers to the third dwelling, the Dwelling of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*), as this is the first of the [ten] stages of supreme joy. Regarding the "Stage of Correct Practice" (*samyak-pratipatti-bhūmi*) mentioned in the commentary, it comprises the six dwellings from the fourth through the ninth.
Because the practice of effortful application (*prayoga-caryā*) based on the noble path has been brought to fulfillment, these are grouped together under a single name:

namely, the fourth, the Dwelling of Higher Ethics (*adhiśīla-vihāra*, the second stage); the fifth, the Dwelling of Higher Mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*, the third stage); and the sixth, the Dwelling Corresponding to the Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-saṃprayukta-vihāra*).
The Abiding in Higher Wisdom (the fourth stage). (5) The Abiding in Higher Wisdom Corresponding to the Seven Truths (the fifth stage).

(6) The Abiding in Higher Wisdom Corresponding to the Arising and Cessation of Dependent Origination (the sixth stage). (7) The Abiding with Effort in the Signless (the seventh stage; these constitute the second aeon).

The fifth, the Stage of Certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*), is so named because it involves effortless and spontaneous progress; it corresponds to the tenth stage, the dwelling of signlessness and effortlessness (*animitta-anābhoga-vihāra*).
The sixth, the Stage of Certain Practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*), is so named because one relies on effortlessness to cultivate practices for the benefit of others;

it corresponds to the eleventh stage, the dwelling of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid-vihāra*). The seventh, the Stage of Reaching the Ultimate (*niṣṭhāgama-bhūmi*), is the tenth [stage].
Second is the Supreme Fulfillment Bodhisattva Abode (the ten stages; these are subsumed within the third aeon). Thirteenth is the Ultimate Tathāgata Abode (the stage of wondrous enlightenment).
This seventh stage subsumes two abodes—namely, those of the bodhisattva and the tathāgata—and establishes them as a single stage for their combined presentation.
"Reaching" means that the position is fulfilled; the ultimate ground of the bodhisattva is precisely that of the tathāgata. As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, [this is] the transformation...

Based on the two fruits, the modes of relinquishing and attaining are explained within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), and are subsequently subsumed within the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*).
The verse says: "This is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), inconceivable, etc. However, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* has already been cited previously.

In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) subsumes both the stage of equipment (*saṃbhāra-avasthā*) and the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*);

this applies equally to the "ground of practice through resolute belief" and the "abiding in practice through resolute belief. The commentary on that [text] explains this abiding as being precisely the two paths of equipment and application.
Among the five verses, the first two verses subsume it, because that treatise states (in the section on the second abiding within the *Yogācārabhūmi*): "From the initial generation..."
Regarding the mind: until one has attained the pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya*), this is the stage of abiding in resolute conviction (*adhimukti-vihāra*).

Since the treatises state that the bodhisattva’s stage of pure superior intention is subsumed under the first bhūmi, it is known that the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) are likewise subsumed within the initial stage of the practice of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*). This being so:
This clearly indicates that it is subsumed within the first *kalpa*, for the treatise states that this stage (*vihāra*) is subsumed within the first *kalpa*. [The author] critiques, saying:

"Now, if we carefully examine the various texts, those who practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-carita*) belong only to the three stages of the worthy ones (*tri-śaikṣa*). Among the four stages of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the thirteen stages (*trayodaśa-vihāra*) of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the seven grounds (*sapta-bhūmi*), and so forth, none establish a stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
This does not mean they are included within the stage of practicing through resolute belief; rather, all these texts assign them accordingly."

This stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā*) is subsumed within the first *kalpa*. If it were the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), such as the roots of goodness beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*), it would not belong to the first *kalpa*.
Regarding this stage, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The Bodhisattva first, during the first incalculable *kalpa*, thoroughly prepares the provisions of merit and wisdom.
Once the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) have been perfected, he further cultivates the stage of application in order to enter the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). Furthermore...
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-śāstra* both state that the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) are cultivated after the first eon has been completed.
Since it is stated that the "provisions" (*sambhāra*) have already reached full completion, one knows that the stage of application (*prayoga*) does not belong to the first eon.

If the stage of application were also cultivated within the first eon, it would be inconsistent for the conclusion of the [preparatory] period to be attributed to the preceding stage. Furthermore, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-ketu-paripṛcchā*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Avataṃsaka* [sūtras]...
In all such sūtras that explain the stages (*bhūmi*), the stage of application (*prayoga*) is not established as a separate stage.
This is because within the ten stages, each stage possesses its own application as a means for entering that stage. As for what is established in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā*:

Using the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the first stage as an illustration, they apply to all subsequent stages; however, the specific characteristics of the phenomena within each respective stage differ slightly in their respective preparatory practices.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* contains textual accounts for every stage, all of which appear in the verses recited at the beginning of the text for that particular stage.

For now, I shall describe the characteristics of the practices prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the first stage, using this as an illustration for all the stages. Since [the first stage]...

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* establishes that the realization of the all-pervading *tathatā* (suchness) has the "wisdom-sun" as its proximate sign (*pūrvanimitta*) and the "Great Path" as its remote sign.
Why should it not be the case that when one seeks to realize the stainless *tathatā* and so forth, there are likewise proximate signs?

To now assign these [signs] exclusively to the practitioner of resolute belief (*adhimukticaryā*) is the view of later Indian and Chinese scholars who failed to exhaust the profound meaning; it is not the original intention of Vasubandhu. Although his commentary on that treatise has been revised several times...

This refutes the ancient criticisms. Since the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the first dhyāna is not included within the desire realm, one should know by analogy that "conduct" (*caryā*) is neither "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*) nor included within the first eon;
this also addresses the criticisms regarding the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Adornments) and the like. These [criticisms] merely cite specific examples.
Ultimately, there is no principle that explains away the preceding objection; moreover, you have not yet reconciled this with texts such as the *Avataṃsaka*.
Now, it would be improper to attempt to rescue this position by means of those several rounds of interrogation and explanation.

Furthermore, we do not cite here that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) does not exist prior to the first bhūmi, for we are discussing the preparatory stage of the first bhūmi, which is admitted to belong to non-āryas. As for the second bhūmi and above, since it has already been stated that [the preparatory stage] also...
If there is preparatory application (*prayoga*), how can one be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)? Answer:

From the second stage (*bhūmi*) onward, when one has not yet realized the *tathatā* (suchness) of one's own stage, what prevents one from being like an ordinary person while emerging from meditative observation within a mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)?

The general principle is the same for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Within each stage, there is a path of seeing; since *tathatā* is realized in every stage, is *tathatā* not indeed that which is seen?

This is the path of the [Buddha] Way. However, because at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) one suddenly perceives *tathatā* (suchness) and suddenly severs the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), and because the characteristics of this initial perception and initial severance are clearly manifest, it is established as a single stage and demonstrated with distinct clarity.

The remaining stages are treated by analogy, as they are all easily understood. Prior to the ten stages of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are twelve verses that collectively explain the realization and severance of the ten stages.
This obstructs the mode of activity; it does not clarify only the first bhūmi. Therefore, there is no stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

This can be understood by analogy with the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* and other texts. Thus, both the stage of application (*prayogamārga*) and the path of seeing proceed with extreme rapidity, unlike other stages which involve a long duration.

The wise deeply illuminate this. Later, when explaining the text on the "Realization of the Path" (*zhengdao*) in this present sutra, this meaning will be further clarified in contrast to the sutra itself.

Regarding the third section of the commentary, which states that the provisional designation of stages and grounds (*bhūmi*) in the Final Teaching is because the "stages" are the true nature (*tathatā*) following conditions, and since conditions lack self-nature, they are fundamentally empty.

The annotation states: "The *Benevolent Kings Sutra* first contemplates emptiness" refers to the "Chapter on Contemplating Emptiness" in the first volume; there, the Buddha knows the ten... [text ends].

The six kings wished to inquire about the causes and conditions for protecting the kingdom. First, he spoke of the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and the causes and conditions for protecting the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
He explained that all things are empty, up to the emptiness of *prajñā*; because the fruit of Buddhahood is empty, and because even the emptiness of emptiness is empty, it is empty.

It exists only because phenomena (*dharma*) have accumulated (through the provisional conjunction of various conditions). It exists because sensation (*vedanā*) has accumulated (this refers to the accumulation of names, the accumulation of causes, and the accumulation of effects—these are two such examples).
If a Bodhisattva perceives phenomena, sentient beings, self, or person, then that person wanders in the world;

even up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the three types of birth—initial, abiding, and final—are unobtainable because they are empty of birth in each stage. Furthermore, it is not the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*). Mahā...
Because [the nature of] the *vaipulya* is emptiness. If a bodhisattva perceives objects, perceives wisdom, perceives speech, or perceives a recipient, this is a non-noble view.
To perceive dharmas with inverted conceptions is the way of ordinary worldlings. The commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* states: "As for 'even up to the three stages of worthies' and so forth:

O Son of the Buddha, it refers to the wisdom of the signless dharma-body in a single thought-moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*), and so on, until the mind and mind-objects are extinguished within the stream of the Dharma."
Above, one does not perceive all Buddha-dharmas or all karmic fruits; below, one does not perceive ignorance, the various views that are to be severed, or sentient beings who are to be transformed.

Rather, within the teachings of provisional transformation according to worldly convention (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one perceives that the Buddha is to be sought, the various views are to be severed, and sentient beings are to be transformed.
Thus, a Son of the Buddha may also be said to cultivate the dharmas of the Three Sages (*traya-ārya*) and enter the stage of a noble one (*ārya*). However, as for the Dharma...
Within the flowing waters, mind after mind is stilled and extinguished, naturally flowing into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment.

Disciple of the Buddha, even the names of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of the bodhisattva grounds are without name and without form; they exist only for the sake of responding to and transforming beings. According to the path and Dharma of the ancient Buddhas, there are the names of the ten stages.
Disciple of the Buddha, you should receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas as being equal and without distinction. *Commentary:*
Regarding the "Five Patiences," as stated in the *Teaching and Transformation* chapter (*śāsanavineya-parivarta*) of that sutra, King Prasenajit asked:

"How does a bodhisattva who guards the practice of the ten stages proceed? How should they act? How do they transform sentient beings? By what characteristics are sentient beings to be transformed? The Buddha said:

"Great King, the five patiences are the dharma of bodhisattvas: the patience of subduing (*kṣānti-vinaya*) in its upper, middle, and lower grades; the patience of faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*) in its upper, middle, and lower grades; and the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*)."

The superior, middling, and inferior levels of patience; the superior, middling, and inferior levels of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and the superior, middling, and inferior levels of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*)—these are called the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā* by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Good son, there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who first give rise to the thought of faith.
Practicing the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), one gives rise within the Three Jewels to the ten minds of the stage of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*):

faith, diligence, mindfulness, wisdom, concentration, giving, precept-keeping, protection, aspiration, and dedication. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to transform sentient beings even slightly and thereby surpass all the wholesome stages of the two vehicles.
All Buddhas and bodhisattvas nurture these ten minds as the "sacred embryo" (*ārya-garbha*). (End of excerpt)

This refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). These constitute ten positions, as they are not further divided into two distinct stages. The verse says: "The thirty persons of the Worthy Embryo (*āryagarbha*) within the Patience of Subjugation (*kṣānti*": the ten faiths, the ten cessations, and the ten steadfast cessations).

Subsequently, one gives rise to the ten wisdoms, the nature-seed-lineage (*gotra*), and the ten minds. These include the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*, such as the impurity of the body), the three roots of goodness (compassion, giving, and wisdom), and the three bases of mental focus (*manasikāra*).

(Regarding the patience with the present causes and effects, etc., which has already resulted from past causes but not yet reached fruition: Furthermore, there are ten stages of the Path of Seed-Nature (*gotrabhūmi*). One contemplates form, consciousness, feeling, and formations, thereby attaining the patience regarding precepts, knowledge-and-vision, concentration, wisdom, and liberation.
One contemplates the causes and effects of the three realms, thereby attaining the patience regarding emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
One contemplates the reality and unreality of the two truths, thereby attaining the patience regarding impermanence, suffering, and non-self. These ten firm minds constitute the turning of the wheel.

O King, (the above refers to the upper, middle, and lower levels of the Patience of Submission). Furthermore, the Bodhisattva of the Patience of Accordance perceives the superior phenomena of the present life and is able to sever the fetters of afflictions such as the mind within the three realms.
The Bodhisattva of the Patience of Non-arising remains far removed from the wisdom of immovable contemplation and also severs the habitual afflictions of both mind and form within the three realms.
The Patience of Quiescent Extinction is that which both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ in common to enter the Vajra Samādhi. Below.
Practicing within patience is called a bodhisattva; practicing within supreme patience is called sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

Together they contemplate the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), severing the mental tendencies of the three realms and exhausting the marks of ignorance; this mark of exhaustion is the diamond-like [samādhi]. This signlessness is sarvajñā.
...and so forth. Great King, I have always told all sentient beings that one who has severed the afflictions of the three realms and exhausted their karmic retribution is called a Buddha.

Innate purity is termed "Awakening" (*bodhi*); it is the nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is the fundamental activity of sentient beings and the primary practice cultivated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Within the five patiences (*kṣānti*), the fourteen patiences are fully perfected. (As the verse says: "The merit of the five patiences..."

This is the wondrous Dharma-gate. Fourteen virtuous men can understand it clearly; those practicing within the patience of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood cannot exhaust its source—only a Buddha alone can do so.
... "Good son, these fourteen Dharma-gates are that which all sentient beings of the three periods of time, all those of the three vehicles, and all Buddhas have practiced and cultivated.
If one does not enter through this gate, one shall not attain Sarvākārajñatā (all-knowing wisdom)."

It is impossible that such a thing could be; for if there were anyone who, upon hearing these various gates of patience— namely, the patience of faith, the patience of cessation, the patience of firmness,

the patience of excellent awakening, the patience of transcendent penetration, the patience of clear wisdom, the patience of blazing wisdom, the patience of supreme wisdom, the patience of contemplating the Dharma,

the patience of far-reaching penetration, the patience of equal awakening, the patience of the light of wisdom, the patience of consecration, and the patience of perfect awakening— were to surpass a hundred or a thousand kalpas [of practice].

Throughout immeasurable eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one undergoes the hardships of birth after birth; yet upon entering this Dharma-gate, one receives the retribution [of enlightenment] in the present body.
*Commentary:* Regarding the six kinds of nature (*ṣaḍ-gotra*), the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, these six natures are the jeweled necklaces of merit for all Bodhisattvas.
They adorn the two kinds of Dharma-bodies of the Bodhisattvas and are what the Bodhisattvas wear—namely, the meritorious practices of a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
“Necklace. If any Bodhisattvas were to enter the stage of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) without entering the merit of the necklace, such a thing is impossible.

Son of the Buddha, the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) are as follows: the lineage of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*), the lineage of nature (*prakṛti-gotra*), the lineage of the path (*mārga-gotra*), the lineage of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*), the nature of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-gotra*), and the nature of wondrous enlightenment (*vibuddha-gotra*).

They are also called the six firmnesses: firmness of faith (*śraddhā-dṛḍha*), firmness of Dharma (*dharma-dṛḍha*), firmness of cultivation (*bhāvanā-dṛḍha*), firmness of virtue (*guṇa-dṛḍha*), and firmness of the summit (*mūrdhan-dṛḍha*).”

Firmness; awakening to firmness. These are also called the six patiences (*kṣānti*): the patience of faith, the patience of the Dharma, the patience of cultivation, the patience of correctness, the stainless patience, and the patience of omniscience.

They are also called the six wisdoms (*prajñā*): the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, the wisdom of cultivation, the wisdom of signlessness, the wisdom of illuminating quiescence, and the wisdom of quiescent illumination.

They are also called the six contemplations (*vipaśyanā*): the contemplation of abiding, the contemplation of practice, the contemplation of orientation, the contemplation of the stages, the contemplation of signlessness, and the contemplation of omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha, there are no Bodhisattvas or Buddhas who do not enter this Dharma-gate of the six kinds of clear contemplation, which is the definitive meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*).
The rest is as explained in other fascicles. △ Regarding the "Six Identities" (*liu ji*) of the Threefold Heaven-Tai school, the *Mohe Zhiguan* states:

"From the beginning as an ordinary person to the end as a sage; because one begins as an ordinary person, doubts and timidity are removed; because one ends as a sage, indolence and arrogance are removed. (Each of these identities is assigned within the [text]).

Furthermore, regarding the "Identity with Principle" (Liri) in the context of the union of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: a single thought-moment is the *tathāgatagarbha*. Because it is as-it-is (*tathatā*), it is emptiness;

because it is the *garbha*, it is the provisional; because it is the principle (*li*), it is the Middle. Thus, the three types of wisdom are fully present within a single thought-moment, which is inconceivable, as explained above.
The three truths are neither three nor one. A single form, a single fragrance—every phenomenon—is called the Identity with Principle, which is the Bodhicitta. It is also...
Principle is itself *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. That which is quiescent is called *śamatha*; that which is illuminating is called *vipaśyanā*. Regarding "identity in name":

although principle is indeed identical [to phenomena], one uses it daily without knowing it, because one has not heard of the three truths and does not recognize the Buddha-dharma at all—like the eyes of an ox or a sheep, unable to discern the directions.
However, having heard from a spiritual teacher or from the scriptures about the aforementioned single reality of Bodhi, one attains thorough penetration and understanding within the context of names.

To know that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma—this is what is called "name-as-enlightenment" (nāma-bodhi). It is also the "cessation-and-contemplation of names. When one has not yet heard [the teaching], one rushes about seeking it everywhere.

Once one has heard it, the mind that clings to and seeks after [objects] ceases; this is called "cessation" (śamatha). One simply trusts in the *dharmatā* and does not trust in various names; this is "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).

As for "practice-as-enlightenment," if one merely hears the names and speaks them aloud, it is like an insect gnawing through wood and accidentally forming characters. This insect does not know whether these are characters or not. Since it is not...

Thorough penetration—how could this alone be bodhi? It must involve the clear understanding of principle through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), such that one's practice accords with one's words, and one's words accord with one's practice.
As the *Huashou jing* says: "Much is said but little is practiced; I do not rely on mere words, but practice bodhi with my mind.

This correspondence between mind and speech is the bodhi of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). (Constantly maintaining this thought is called *vipaśyanā*; the cessation of other thoughts is called *śamatha*.)

Regarding "that which resembles [Bodhi] is itself Bodhi": because as one contemplates further, it becomes increasingly clear, and as one brings the mind to rest further, it becomes increasingly tranquil—like an arrow hitting the bullseye—it is called "resembling contemplative wisdom" (*sādṛśya-prajñā*).
It does not contradict any of the worldly activities of production and livelihood; all thoughts and mental states of equal measure are the seeing of the Buddha.
As stated in the sutras, such as in the section on the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), where it is said that ignorance is completely subdued.

That which is called "stopping" resembles middle-grade wisdom, while that which is called "contemplation" corresponds to the stage of partial realization. Due to the power of this similar contemplation, at the stage of the copper wheel, one first breaks through ignorance, perceives the Buddha-nature, opens the treasury of reality, and manifests true suchness;
this is called the "Abiding in the Resolve" (Prathamacittotpādika). This continues until ignorance becomes thin and subtle.
Wisdom transforms attachment. It is like the moonlight from the first day until the fourteenth day, when it is nearly full yet still slightly waning.
If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the Buddha-body, he manifests the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*aṣṭābhisambodhi*).

If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the bodies of the nine realms of existence, he manifests through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), as explained at length in the sutra. This is called "partial true bodhi" (also known as partial true *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and partial true wisdom).
As for "the ultimate severance is itself Bodhi": through one further turning from Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one enters Subtle Enlightenment (*suviśuddha-bodhi*).

The light of wisdom is fully perfected and can no longer be increased; this is called the fruit of Bodhi. In Great Nirvāṇa, there is nothing further to be severed, which is called the fruit of fruits.
Therefore, it is named Ultimate Bodhi (also known as Ultimate Calm and Contemplation). To illustrate this by analogy: it is like a poor man’s house containing a treasury of jewels...
For those who lack knowledge: (Principle) it is shown through instruction, whereby one immediately attains understanding. (Name) One eradicates weeds and impurities and excavates [the treasure].

(Practice) One gradually draws near. (Similarity) Having drawn near, the storehouse is opened. (Partial Truth) One takes and utilizes it entirely. (Ultimate Truth) These six [stages] may be understood as a unified whole.

In the fourth section on the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*), the commentary states: "Regarding the statement that, in terms of reality, there is no realization or attainment, this refers to the aforementioned passage:

'no grasping, no realization,' and so forth. Regarding the statement that, based on delusion, distinctions are spoken of, this refers to the aforementioned passage: 'Sentient beings are deluded and inverted;
even within the midst of their deluded efforts regarding what is extinguished and what is not yet extinguished, they manifest distinctions.'"
Regarding the "seven stages" in the Commentary: Among all the teachings on the stages (*bhūmi*), none are as complete and clear as those in the *Avataṃsaka*.

The first assembly constitutes the general overview of this entire scripture and therefore does not follow a sequential order of stages. It is only from the second assembly onward that the stages of practice are explained in full according to their sequence.
As for the present mention of "seven," these consist of five stages spanning from the second assembly to the sixth assembly, with the seventh [assembly] being the final one.

Within the assembly, there are two; thus, there are seven. Regarding the commentary on "differentiation and equality": their equality integrates differentiation within cause and effect such that each is equal.
Within this very equality, there exists the aforementioned differentiation, signifying the non-obstruction between these two.

This was also explained in the seventy-first assembly. This same meaning also appears in the latter part of this sutra; it shall be demonstrated when we reach that passage. Regarding the "fifty-two stages" mentioned in the commentary:
while that sutra lists each stage by name, only the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) represent the foundation of all these stages.

Since their functional efficacy is entirely identical to the realm of the Buddha, they belong to the category of general and universal characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, they are not specifically correlated with the other stages.

Ten names are listed; however, they are collectively taken as the substance of faith and understanding through the ten profundities (*daśa-gambhīra*). Regarding the variations in whether these are expanded or condensed:

in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the seven stages expand the ten faiths into the Stage of the Seed-lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), while they condense the ten stages and so forth—along with the Sublime and Wondrous stages—into the seventh stage, the "Mixed" stage.
In the *Ratnakuṇḍala-sūtra*, the six types of lineage condense the ten faiths into the lower level of the Sages (*bhadra*), making it the first, the "Cultivated" lineage.

Regarding the nature (*dhātu*): [the stages] from "Opening" (*kai*) to "Sublime" (*myō*) each constitute a distinct nature. This sutra and the *Awakening of Faith* open up the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and combine them with the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhi*).
Both the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, as well as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, all open them up; therefore, there are fifty-two stages.

The five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*) in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) also describe fifty-two positions according to the subsequent text. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the cause encompasses the fruit," it means that one does not need to wait for its destruction.

Regarding the aspects of practice (*ākāra*): each individual aspect is the entire whole, for they are identical with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, within the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), one possesses the virtues of the Buddha-fruit.

As for "sequential arrangement" (*xingbu*), it is as explained above; it refers to the differentiated cause and effect. "Perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*) refers to the equalized cause and effect, as extensively analyzed in the *Xuantan* (Introductory Discourse).
However, the stages and grounds of the Sudden Teaching and the Perfect Teaching have no fixed reality. "Differentiation" refers to the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Thus, each and every thing is perfectly interfused. In this scripture, while there is a sequential arrangement, each and every thing is free from characteristics.

Regarding the note on "the aforementioned state of non-position": the treatise cited above states, "In reality, there is no distinction between initial enlightenment; it is fundamentally equal, being one single awakening."
This is also the Benevolent Kings’ contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the meaning of the *Ratnavyūha* (Jewel-Necklace) being nameless and signless (*animitta*).

Regarding the four [sections] at the beginning of the commentary (*śāstra*), there are eight textual divisions: first, listing the four stages; second, correlating them with the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);

third, stating the intention and providing a general heading; fourth, specifically explaining the four characteristics; fifth, the general subsumption; sixth, reversing them to establish the four stages; seventh, indicating and explaining.

Meaning. Eighth, the correct explanation of the text. First, regarding the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*): according to the Perfect and Sudden school, this stage is the root of all practices and all virtues.
Because the initial mind is identical to the Buddha, it is only then called "faith. One who does not believe that one's own mind is the *tathāgatagarbha* [does not possess true faith].
Because they are not yet Bodhisattvas. There is no distinction between the initial resolve and the ultimate goal;

since these two states of mind are inseparable from the outset, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* specifically opens a single assembly with six chapters to expound upon them. This sutra and the *Awakening of Faith* both open this as a single stage.

In the provisional and gradual teachings, it is often not so opened because, in those systems, merely having faith in the teaching is termed "faith," and it does not necessarily entail realization and understanding.
Just as light feathers on a road are unstable, shifting with the wind, it takes ten thousand kalpas of cultivation before one enters the stage of the first resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*).

The "two stages of the noble ones" (*pṛthagjana*) comprise both the path of provisions (*sambhāramārga*) and the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*); among these, the characteristics of the path of preparation are primarily emphasized because they pertain to contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanājñāna*).

The "stage of the sages" (*ārya*) refers to those who directly realize *tathatā* (suchness), and are thus called "sages"; this encompasses both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding this single stage: among these, it specifically adopts the aspect of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because the aspect of realizing the truth (*tattva*) extends through all ten stages (*bhūmi*).

As for the four fruits, they refer solely to the state of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is the ultimate stage. [The commentary] states: "This is... and so forth; second, the correlation with the four aspects.

Regarding the "reversal of the sequence": first, the characteristic of cessation; second, the characteristic of difference; third, the characteristic of abiding; and fourth, the characteristic of arising.

These are called a reversal because they run counter to the sequence of arising. This is because arising proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, whereas elimination proceeds from the coarse to the subtle;
the subtle is difficult to eliminate. As for the note concerning the "True Mind" and so forth, it is because in the Dharma-nature school (*Faxing zong*), the four characteristics are identical.
*Kṣaṇa* (moment). Fearing that this term might be confused with it, [the author] now distinguishes between them. The meaning of "following the perfuming" will be explained below.

In the commentary, from the passage beginning "However, as for the nature of the mind," three points are raised to indicate the conceptual intention. Regarding the phrase "precisely because of ignorance (*avidyā*)":

this refers to the principle of ignorance perfuming the *tathatā* (Suchness), as explained in the "Chapter on Samantabhadra. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-nature follows the stream and forms various flavors."

And so forth. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The intrinsically pure mind is moved by the wind of ignorance," and so on, because it is most subtle at the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). The *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are associated with the characteristic of arising when considered from the perspective of the prior limit; they are associated with the characteristic of cessation when considered from the perspective of the posterior limit;
and they are associated with the characteristics of abiding and change when considered from the perspective of the middle limit. [In the commentary,] the initial phrase refers to being "most subtle."

Below: A detailed explanation of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). These four characteristics constitute four sections. Regarding the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*)—which is the characteristic of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*):

it is like a change in sleep wherein one’s own mind suddenly has a dream-thought, yet the pre-dream mind remains entirely unaware. The transformation of the mind by ignorance (*avidyā*), such that a single thought first arises, is also like this.
Although there is the characteristic of arising, the subject and object are not yet differentiated; therefore, it is called "most subtle. Thus, it says further below: "Non-..."
Regarding the consciousness that arises from clarity: this can be known only by a Buddha. It is like how one only knows there was a false dream when waking up, suddenly realizing it arose.
Among these two, that which accords with the preceding birth-phase is due to the power of prior ignorance;

because one does not perceive the movement of the preceding phase, there is no movement. This is like how, when a single thought-moment first arises in a dream, one is entirely unaware of its initial arising.
Furthermore, one reflects that these dreams—which originally did not exist and suddenly appeared—seem as though they have no source yet already exist.
Now, one realizes that the initial thought is likewise so. Because of this, it transforms into the characteristic of the perceiving subject (the *vivartana-lakṣaṇa*).

Moreover, based on that prior perceiving subject’s failure to realize ignorance (*avidyā*), the objective realm is caused to appear falsely (the *pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, due to ignorance, one is deluded regarding what is manifested by one's own mind.

Furthermore, within the objective realm, deluded thoughts arise, discriminating between signs of defilement and purity (this is the *jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Moreover, due to the power of ignorance, one fails to realize that what was previously discriminated is empty and non-existent;

thus, these thoughts correspond with one another in every moment without interruption (this is the *saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*). These four aforementioned types constitute the second stage, the *sthiti-lakṣaṇa*.
It is said that the *pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa* is still subtle because the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self" have not yet arisen. As for the preceding...
Within the two types of fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the latter two constitute the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) within the middle [consciousness].

Among the subtle divisions of consciousness, that which is called "firmly abiding" (*susthita*) refers to a state where various phenomenal characteristics—such as craving, views, greed, and hatred, as well as sharp or dull faculties, ignorance or wisdom, and good or evil—have not yet arisen;

it is merely a single, similar type that continues in succession, remaining unchanged from moment to moment. Therefore, it is named "firmly abiding. The third refers to this very ignorance (*avidyā*).

Deluded regarding the dharmas of defilement and purity, or the inverse and the conformable, one further gives rise to greed, anger, the notion of self and others, craving, views, and grasping at signs (*nimittagrāha*).
One calculates names (*nāmavikalpa*) and clings with ever-deepening attachment. This constitutes the stage of coarse abiding within the functioning consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Here, ignorance (*avidyā*) blends with the characteristics of the preceding stages; (it is simply this lack of awakening that is termed "blending"). It transforms that pure mind, causing it to reach this state. Its mode of activity is as follows:
Whether coarse, or foolish or wise, or good or evil, each is distinct; these prompt the body and speech to engage in the creation of karma, which is termed "distinctive characteristics" (*viśeṣa*).

Among the four [aspects], those who do not understand karmic retribution fail to realize that wholesome and unwholesome karma inevitably bring about the two types of retribution—suffering and pleasure—and thus they extensively create karma.
Because one undergoes retribution based on karma, the preceding [states such as] "distinctive characteristics" and so forth cease. This is...
This is the fifth of the six gross characteristics. Because the retributive fruits one receives are not dharmas that can be severed, the sixth characteristic is not discussed here.
Both the gross and the subtle are subsumed within the characteristic of "entering," which constitutes birth, abiding, change, and cessation.

[Commentary: Therefore, from the passage "the three realms" onwards, there are five general subsumptions. Within this, there are further two parts: first, subsuming [all things] back to their fundamental source; this fundamental source is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is also like this: just as all coarse and subtle thoughts during sleep are dreams, so the Sūtra says, "The power of the ground of abiding ignorance is the greatest.
The Treatise says, "One should know that ignorance can give rise to all defiled dharmas, for all defiled dharmas are the characteristics of non-awakening.
△ [Commentary] "However, although... and below: second, the subsumption into a single thought-moment. This is further divided into two parts: first, the actual subsumption; the previous...
It is said: although there are many diverse distinctions and perceptions of coarseness and subtlety within this single dreaming mind, both are nothing other than dreams;
therefore, it is called "one dreaming mind. Now, when these are subsumed back into the fundamental nature, it is that one state which is devoid of all marks of differentiation.

Therefore, it is called "a single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*). This refers to the very first arising of a thought-moment, when subject and object have not yet been differentiated, and which arises directly dependent upon the true mind.
Thus it is said: "Because it is but the one mind. Furthermore, this single thought-moment pervades all differentiated thoughts; it is not restricted to the characteristic of a single lifetime.
However, because all the pervasive thoughts are merely this one [mind], it is as when it is said regarding a dream:
whether it be one's own body or another's body, or the mind or its objects, these various appearances cannot be said to exist; yet, neither can it be said that it was not a dream.

One simply says, "This is a dream," for it naturally lacks intrinsic substance and constitutes the fundamental consciousness of the mind. Now, it is the same with all phenomena: they cannot be said to exist.
Furthermore, one should not say that there is no deluded thought; rather, one should simply say that deluded thought is naturally without substance and becomes the truly pure mind.

Therefore, it is said: "It is gathered back into a single thought," because there is only this one mind. Thus, the Treatise says: "The four marks exist simultaneously, yet none have independent existence, for they are fundamentally one with awakening.
[Commentary: Now, regarding the section beginning with "However, [if one] has not yet exhausted... (the second part), it serves to dispel potential objections. The objection is as follows:
Since the four characteristics exist simultaneously as a single moment of thought, those who now seek the Way have either not yet attained realization or they have already realized it.

Why, then, would there be gradual stages for the worthy and sages, or a sequence of positions from coarse to subtle, such that one must proceed step by step before finally severing [delusion] completely?
Therefore, this text generally states, "Thus, though not yet exhausting the source," and so forth. It is like seeing a dream within a dream; one simply knows what is being seen.
This is a dream. One does not realize that the one currently seeing [the dream] is also a dream. It is not problematic for these layers to unfold and awaken one another in this way;
all that is awakened is unerring. It is only the subject who awakens that is deluded. Only when one suddenly awakens from sleep and rises does one finally know that it was but a single dream.
Therefore, it is said that "one who reaches the source of the mind knows everything in a single thought. Thus, a sutra says: "The Bodhisattva knows the mark of extinction at the end."

...up to the point of changing states, one does not know the beginning. Only the Buddha-Tathāgata knows both the beginning and the end. Question: The previous commentary stated that this is not based on *kṣaṇas* (moments).
Why, now, do you again subsume the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*)?

Is a single thought-moment not itself a *kṣaṇa*? Answer: As a verse says: "In a dream, one thinks a year has passed; upon waking, it is but a brief instant. Thus, we know that this dream contains [the passage of time].
Regarding the various distinct meanings of the four seasons within a year, they all share the single meaning of being but a brief moment (*muhūrta*).

Now, this thought stirred by ignorance is likewise: there is the sense of arising through successive stages from the subtle to the coarse, and there is the sense that from beginning to end it is but a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*).
As noted previously, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are here treated as four stages, taking them from the coarse to the subtle.
The meaning of "successively reversing and severing" is not taken in the sense of a single *kṣaṇa* (moment). This does not mean that it is not solely a *kṣaṇa*;
rather, because a *kṣaṇa* lacks the sense of a sequential stage (*avasthā*), it is not taken as a "ground" (*bhūmi*). [The] Commentary says: "Since it is due to the following... and so forth.

The sixth [point] reverses these to establish four stages. Since these various dream-like thoughts have already agitated the source of the mind, causing one to sleep long within the three realms and transmigrate through the six paths, now, by virtue of the power of internal and external conditioning, fundamental wisdom is augmented and inverted sentiments are diminished, reaching even to the source of the mind;
thus, the four stages and their gradations are established. It is not that the nature of Perfect Enlightenment possesses these practices and stages.

Separate. ▲ The commentary now proceeds from the treatise below; this is the seventh section, which indicates the heading and explains the meaning. Question: If one composes a commentary on a treatise (*śāstra*), one is explaining that treatise.
Now, in composing a commentary on a sutra (*sūtra*), one should only explain the sutra. Why do you incorporate the treatise, making it difficult to understand? Answer:

The intention here is to explain the dharmas concerning the inversion and rectification of mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*); it is not for the sake of explaining the literal text. If [the treatise] were not contrasted...

Regarding the treatise: it is difficult to thoroughly perceive the mental characteristics (*citta-lakṣaṇa*) of those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Now, this commentary on the treatise intends to make these characteristics manifest;

therefore, it says, "the meaning is clearly seen. Why, then, do you say it is difficult? Furthermore, when the Buddha preached the sūtras, his underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) was difficult to understand.

At that time, however, the capacities of sentient beings were superior, so they could attain realization even while facing him in person. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, times have shifted and eras have changed; the capacities of people have become increasingly inferior. How [can you say it is not difficult]?
Because they have attained understanding, the Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, compose treatises to explain and point the way.
Some take the dharmas and meanings from various sūtras and, organizing them into thematic categories (*arthamukha*), explain them all at once; these are called *śāstra* (treatises on tenets).

Others explain according to the text of a single sūtra or a single section of a work; these are called *vyākhyāna-śāstra* (commentaries). This is as stated in the Mahāyāna-śāstra composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa composed this *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* based upon approximately one hundred Mahāyāna sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Thus, one should know that this treatise provides a comprehensive explanation of the meanings within those hundred sūtras; this very sūtra [in question] is also included among their number.

However, the titles of those sūtras differ slightly from those established in the treatise. If one does not rely on the text revealed by the Bodhisattva, how could doubts and hesitations be resolved? Therefore, it is necessary...

The treatise (*śāstra*) serves as the authoritative standard (*pramāṇa*) for explaining the meaning. There are instances throughout the preceding and following sections where various treatises are extensively employed; the intent in all such cases is the same.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "the treatise concerning the *yoga*," the intent of the treatise is already known. Regarding the sūtra’s discussion of "the superiority or inferiority of awakening and purity":

first, pure understanding (*viśuddha-adhimukti*) transcends weariness and anxiety; second, the understanding of insight (*darśana-adhimukti*) acts as an obstacle. This insight is, in turn, superior to pure understanding. Next, constant awareness...

Abiding. Illumination is also quiescent extinction. The wisdom of non-abiding is further superior to seeing and awakening. Subsequently, when obstacles are awakened to, it is further superior to cessation.

Compared to what precedes them, the awakening regarding obstructions is inferior. Question: Since each is established according to a single meaning and their meanings thus differ, how can the treatise be used to explain them?
Therefore, the subsequent answer says: "Now, by means of equality," etc. This refers to the transformation of defiled characteristics.
Subtle. When the attachment to the aspect of purity transforms, the aspects of defilement are entirely exhausted. This is primordial purity (*ādi-viśuddhi*);

there is no defilement to be exhausted and no obstruction to be removed. Therefore, the treatise concludes: "The four marks all lack independent existence, for they are primordially one with awakening.
This is precisely what the sutra means by "all obstructions are ultimate awakening. It is simply because external awakening exists that there are no separate obstructions.

It can be eliminated; therefore, it is called "immediate awakening. Thus, one knows that the boundaries of the four stages, when compared for their relative depth and shallowness, are identical in each case.

When discussed in terms of these temporal periods, both meanings are simultaneously revealed. However, if the thematic gates being applied were entirely identical, it would be inappropriate to employ them redundantly.
Let the wise reflect upon this. [End of] Commentary: Regarding the section on the Stage of Initial Faith below, eight points correctly explain the text.

Furthermore, regarding the "distinctive objects" (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*), these are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that have already been explained within the section on the eight consciousnesses. Regarding the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, that sutra states:
"What the Buddha calls the view of self and the view of a person is not actually a view of self or a view of a person. This was commented upon in Asaṅga’s treatise.
It says: "As the non-Buddhists speak of a 'self,' the Tathāgata calls it the 'view of self' (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); therefore, he establishes the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Furthermore, because he speaks of the existence of this view of self, he establishes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). The commentary explains:

By using the term "view of self" and so forth, one does not practice the self as it is grasped by those [non-Buddhists] (removing the disease). Furthermore, by using the phrase "is not," one does not practice the view of self and so forth (dispelling the medicine).
The treatise states: "Regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*): 'self' (*ātman*) is that which is to be remedied, while 'phenomena' (*dharma*) are that by which they are remedied.

The term 'phenomena' refers precisely to the view of a person (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*) and so forth; thus, one knows that the view of self belongs to the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). This is the intention of Asanga.

Since the view of self is the mind that performs the grasping, the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with it constitute the clinging to phenomena. The commentary further notes that "deluded thoughts" and so forth refer to the grasping at a self.
This refers to the seventh consciousness. Because these four afflictions exist within this consciousness, they are used to explain the meaning of the four afflictions in the scriptural passage.

This has also been fully explained in the chapter on the eight consciousnesses. As for the phrase "the text follows below," it is explained in the section on the four characteristics within the chapter on the Bodhisattva Pure Deeds (*Śuddhakarmā*).
Furthermore, the faults of clinging to a self have already been explained in the preceding section on the two kinds of emptiness.

[The commentary] concludes: "Since the causes and conditions are complete," the treatise explains that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) has possessed original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) from beginningless time, which perfumes ignorance and causes the deluded mind to give rise to the sense of wearying of suffering and seeking happiness, and so forth. It then poses the question itself:

If this is the meaning, then since all sentient beings equally possess the permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*), why are there immeasurable differences regarding faith and lack of faith, as well as distinctions of before and after?

Why should they not all simultaneously realize for themselves that they possess the Dharma of True Suchness, diligently cultivate skillful means, and equally enter *nirvāṇa*? The answer is: True Suchness is fundamentally one, yet it possesses immeasurable, boundless, and...
It is explained as follows: (up to) the Buddha-dharma has causes and conditions. When causes and conditions are fully assembled, it is then accomplished.
(Original enlightenment internally perfuming serves as the cause; virtuous friends, the arising of activity, and the production of the thought of enlightenment serve as the conditions.

Even though there is the power of the perfuming of the true cause (the cause), if one does not encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends to serve as conditions, one cannot spontaneously sever afflictions and enter nirvana.
"槃" (pan) refers to the absence of such a possibility (this refers to external conditions).

Even if there is the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharmas have not yet acquired the power of perfuming (this refers to the causal condition of activity), one will still be unable to ultimately weary of birth and death and seek nirvana. Regarding the commentary's phrase "like when waking from a dream":
although this meaning is easy to understand, it is difficult for those who do not illuminate the mind to perceive. This means that the presence or absence of a dream is, conversely...

The two explanations regarding "covering" (*paryavasthāna*) are as follows: First, speaking in terms of the characteristics of delusion: during sleep there are no dreams (because one perceives only the waking state;

thus it was said previously that one is never self-aware of the arising and ceasing of every thought-moment), whereas during the waking state there are dreams (because one then perceives the mental objects of the dream-state that occurred throughout the night). Second, speaking in terms of the true nature and characteristics:

during sleep there are dreams (because one is actually dreaming), whereas during the waking state there are no dreams (because each and every mental object of the dream being contemplated is empty). Delusion and awakening.
These views can each be understood through their respective analogies. What is now called "arising" is like the manifestation of dream-objects during the waking state.
"Clarity" means knowing it to be a dream; it means knowing that all things are empty. This is because emptiness does not destroy the appearance of what is being observed.

Next, the phrase "one immediately knows one's toil and anxiety," along with the two subsequent lines, is like the state of dreaming where, because one is merged with the dream, one does not perceive it as a dream.
Furthermore, the two lines concerning "the darkness below" are like being awake and knowing each instance as a dream.
This is truly because, when deluded, one takes the arising and ceasing of delusive thoughts to be the self; thus, the thought cannot see itself, just as the eye cannot see itself.

Now that awakening has been attained, one no longer takes delusive thoughts to be the self; therefore, by means of the wisdom that realizes the dark truth, one illuminates the thoughts of arising and ceasing.
One knows every arising and ceasing in each and every thought-moment, just as nothing can hide from a clear, bright mirror.

Regarding those who follow the gradual school and whose teachings give rise to practitioners of Chan, when a beginner first practices seated meditation, they say to their teacher: "Since I began the practice of stilling the mind..."
His thoughts became increasingly chaotic and numerous; he did not know what kind of evil karma had caused this. The Master said: "It is like a house with cracks in its walls;
when the sun rises outside, a single beam of light shines into the interior of the house. Within that light, there are immeasurable motes of dust."
Chaos and turmoil: yet the entire room is filled with this dust; it is simply not perceived when it is dark, but is seen immediately upon meeting the sun.

Your *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) gives rise to mental conceptions as numerous as dust motes and sands; previously, you were deluded and did not perceive them. Now, because you have calmed these thoughts through sitting meditation (*zazen*) and possess a degree of effortful application (*prayoga*), you become aware of them.
Since there is no real external object, why harbor hatred or love? This is because, as stated before, one does not know one's own thoughts.

Because one is mindful of arising and ceasing, one gives rise to hatred and love, and becomes greedily attached to the five desires. This current explanation follows upon the previous one to clarify this point.

The "real objects" are precisely the five desires. Since these objects of hatred and love now arise from the transformations of one’s own mind and do not exist externally as realities, one knows they are the nature of one’s own mind—the laboring and worrying of its own characteristics.
This nature is characterized by arising and ceasing; it is not the true awakened nature.

The commentary on "stopping delusion and following the truth" consists of two parts. First, the specific explanation of this section: "To sever seeking and cease acting" means not creating various karmas;

although one follows the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and cultivates the auxiliary dharmas of the path, because the mind’s activity is without seeking or fabrication, it is said that one does not "follow" [delusion] and so forth.
Second, from "the preceding is knowing... onwards, is the general correlation with the scriptural text. The Sūtra contains both sudden and gradual enlightenment.
"Quiescence of activity" refers to the mental formations already established; "sudden awakening" refers to the observation of one's views and understanding. In reality, they are one and the same.

Regarding "awakening to delusion," it means knowing that one’s own efforts and anxieties are laborious. Even in this stage, as discussed in the *Zhonglun* (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā), one knows in this way;

however, because it concerns mental formations, it is said that one must "restrain them so they do not arise. Here, saying "severing laborious anxiety" likewise means not following along with its creation.
Because of karma, they appear different when categorized by their specific aspects, yet their fundamental boundaries are identical.

Regarding the distinction between "discriminating" (*vikalpa*) and "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) mentioned above: it refers to being deluded regarding the aforementioned phenomena—such as those that are favorable or unfavorable—and further giving rise to greed and hatred.
"Self and others" refers to the views of self and possession (*ātma-ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*). "Grasping at marks and calculating names" refers to the arousal of body, speech, and so forth.

Therefore, the treatise cited previously states: "Based on the deepening attachment of ordinary persons," and so on. "To contemplate that there are no distinct marks" means that while mental conceptions have not yet been eliminated, one simply perceives that these conceptions lack distinct marks.
The rest is as explained in the commentary. "Gross discrimination" and so forth are precisely what constitutes distinct marks, as it is also like [the previous case].

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as seen in the preceding [sections] of the *Śāstra*," the mindfulness that dwells in pure understanding is likewise a coarse discrimination, as stated in the treatise.
To be able to cognize names and meanings is also ignorance; to feel aversion toward suffering and aspiration for bliss is the deluded mind.

That which is precisely in this stage is the awareness that discerns this distinct thought; it is the seeing-awareness (*darśana-vijñāna*) in which one dwells according to the Sūtra. This awareness...

This is not correct; therefore, it is classified as a "semblance" within the treatise. Regarding the phrase "Buddha-peak" (*buddhā-uṣṇīṣa*) in the commentary: this refers to the passage concerning the "Peak Stage" (*mūrdhan*) among the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).
It is also the preliminary aspect (*pūrva-nimitta*) of that stage, and thus can serve as proof, as has already been explained above.

This sutra primarily concerns the aspects of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), wherein one cultivates the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) during the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*), and cultivates the wholesome roots conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) during the stage of preparation (*prayoga-avasthā*).

The "wholesome factors conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kusala*). Since this sūtra’s primary tenet clarifies the wisdom of contemplation, these are the factors that accord with penetration;

"penetration" (*nirveda*) itself is wisdom. Regarding the commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "A few things are empty" refers to non-abiding in pure understanding; this is also because one realizes that both the defiled and the pure are empty.
Therefore, it does not abide. That which "has something to be attained" is precisely this seeing through awakening. That which is "not real" is identical to what is discussed as being similar.
Hence, it is pointed out next. As for the term "sincerity" (*què*): if one has not yet reached the state of original reality, which is still and quiescent.

In the end, one cannot dissolve the wisdom that perceives; those who are truly concentrated and tranquil immediately enter the stages (*bhūmi*). Here, illumination and the illuminator are both quiescent.

To "brush away and resolve" refers to pure understanding. To "transcend the ordinary" means to pass beyond the stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and the position of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
"Still being constrained" refers to remaining within this very stage.
The *Śāstra* states: "One who is awakened regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)... The subsequent passage in the *Sūtra* says: "Always being awake, one does not abide;

it is precisely because of abiding in awakening that one does not abide. Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra*, "obstructed yet not realized," etc.: the ocean of fruition is perfectly in accord with the *dharmadhātu*.

In the *dharmadhātu*, there is neither interruption nor non-interruption, neither realization nor non-realization, and neither obstruction nor non-obstruction. To speak [of such distinctions] is to contradict its nature. (*Daśabhūmika Sūtra*)

Regarding the phrase "the commentary, although it employs oppositions," etc.: it entrusts itself to various obstructive phenomena and uses their opposites to reveal the characteristics of the fruition (*phala*).

Furthermore, the ten pairs such as mindfulness and forgetfulness are all phenomena of mutual dependence. By relying on these dependencies, both are simultaneously negated and both are simultaneously integrated to reveal the characteristics of the realization of fruition.
Thus, one knows that from the perspective of the essential nature itself, it is beyond reach; therefore, it is said to be "beyond words."

"Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)" refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). "The principle of non-differentiation" refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
"The object [of cognition] merges with [the subject]" explains the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of non-conceptual and undifferentiated [wisdom]. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

Wisdom and suchness are equal and identical. (This is because the mind and its object correspond, and wisdom and [suchness] merge in darkness; both are free from the two grasps and cut off all conceptual proliferation.

This is because they are both free from the characteristics of the grasper (*grāhaka*) (which is non-conceptualization) and the grasped (*grāhya*) (which is non-differentiation). Furthermore, it is said: "Although there is a seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*), it is non-conceptual;

although there is no image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*), it arises bearing the aspect of suchness, for it does not depart from suchness. (This wisdom that takes suchness as its object arises bearing the essence and aspect of suchness; it does not bear that image-division.)

It arises from images; therefore, it is said that they are not separate. This meaning will be analyzed in detail below when we confront the sūtra. Regarding the second point, "the non-duality of subject and object," Master Sheng says:

"Now, the true principle is spontaneous; upon awakening, one is in dark resonance with it. Since the true principle is without differentiation, how could awakening admit of difference? This passage appears in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Regarding the third point, "the simultaneous submergence of both subject and object," there are two interpretations. The first is the interpretation by mutual negation (*hu-duo*).
Regarding "wisdom is identical to principle" (*jñāna eva tattvam*): this means that when wisdom is identical to principle, the totality is entirely the other;

since not even a fraction of the principle remains apart [from it], it is said to be "not wisdom. If one's own portion of wisdom were to remain, what else could there be that is "identical to principle"?

This should be carefully examined and reflected upon. The same applies to "principle is identical to wisdom. Therefore, regarding their mutual sublation (*anyonya-apoha*), at the moment they are mutually identical, they are of a single *kṣaṇa*.
Therefore, they mutually negate one another such that both are absent. Why is this?

If the preceding thought-moment were wisdom and the succeeding thought-moment were principle, then it would not hinder the fact that although the preceding moment lacks principle, wisdom remains; and although the succeeding moment lacks wisdom, principle remains.

This is because it is not a matter of successive moments being alternately real; rather, they are mutually identical within a single thought-moment. Thus, through their mutual negation, both are simultaneously absent.

The commentary continues directly below. This second section is an explanation that defines the fundamental substance. Regarding the phrase "neither subject nor object": to say it is "not the object" means it is not that which is negated as an object;
that is, it is the negation of the object. The same applies to its being "not the subject. Regarding the phrase "not abiding, which is to be free from subject and object":
the sutra states immediately following this, "The illumination and the illuminator are simultaneously extinguished. The former clause refers to the subject and object; the latter clause...
It is a departure. Regarding the commentary’s reference to the "first three gates" and so forth: it is not only that there are times of sequential realization;
there are also sequential aspects within a single moment. This means that what is called "non-arising" is further like the third gate:
if there were no realizing wisdom and no realized principle, how would this differ from the deluded conventional? For even the ignorant and worldly lack such wisdom. This is truly because...
Those at the stage of faith and the stage of worthiness cultivate this contemplation to refine and temper the mind-intellect, thereby seeing the Truth with vivid clarity.

That which is seen is itself the seer; furthermore, one knows that the Principle of Truth is one's own mind. When the self-mind is manifest, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Thus, principle and wisdom are non-dual.
Moreover, awakening is not merely non-duality, nor is it something newly acquired; both principle and wisdom are inherently true.

The mind of true awakening is originally perfect and luminous; what can it do, and what is its object? When both [subject and object] are extinguished through this realization, only then does the prior state of their coexistence become manifest.

That existence and extinction are simultaneous is the meaning of this gate. It is for this reason that it is said: only by means of the "capable of realizing" (*neng zheng*) do the three gates become unimpeded, and only then is the meaning of the three gates established.

Thus it is said: "One must rely on the 'capable of realizing' before one awakens to the fact that the essence of the mind is fundamentally devoid of subject and object. This is like the cutting off of the head.
The "Metaphor" (yù) section is a passage from the *Zhìduàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Severing of Wisdom). As for what is called "Zào [Sengzhào] says," this is a passage from the *Prajñā-śāstra*.
Prajñā is wisdom (*jñāna*), and the True Truth (*satya*) is principle (*tattva*). Since that treatise also speaks of both wisdom and principle, it is cited here as an analogy.

When that text speaks of "function" (*yòng*), it refers to these two aspects: the subjective and the objective (the two gates). Wisdom possesses the function of realizing principle, and principle possesses the function of eliciting wisdom.
"Quiescence" refers to the simultaneous submergence of both [subject and object]. (Third Gate) "Identity" refers to the non-obstruction between existence and submergence.

(Fourth Gate) "Identical yet different" means that while the second [gate] is the non-duality of subject and object, the first [gate] is the distinct clarity of subject and object. "Different yet identical" means that the first is identical to the second.
Because they are identical, there is no mental preoccupation with "self" or "other. This is the third gate, the gate of simultaneous submergence.
Furthermore, "not losing the merit of illumination" refers to the third stage of merging; it does not obstruct the simultaneous existence of the first and second stages.
This constitutes the fourth gate. Moreover, the word "equal" (等) is equivalent to the following phrase: "Thus, that which distinguishes the same is the same as the different;
that which distinguishes the different is different from the same" (the first and second gates are thus mutually inclusive and unobstructed). This, then, cannot be grasped [as a fixed entity].

They are different; they cannot be made the same. (This is the third and fourth gate. Regarding the commentary’s mention of "the first and so forth": if this gate did not exist, one would assume that the fourth [gate] is simply the non-obstruction between existence and cessation (*yu-miṃn*).
This would mean that the preceding four gates—where existence and cessation are distinct—are not permitted.

"Distinct" refers to opening (*kāi*); "non-obstruction" refers to merging (*hé*). This concludes the three preceding gates: the time of opening is precisely the time of merging in the fourth. The fourth...
When they unite, they immediately open; thus it is said that "opening and closing are not different. Only when the wise person creates this realm can it be considered the true realization of the Way.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Constantly aware, one does not abide. The Commentary next establishes the remaining [realms]. The "remaining" refers to the three other dharma-realms:

namely, the dharma-realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*), the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*li-shi wuai fajie*), and the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wuai fajie*). Their meanings are as explained in the *Dharmadhātudarśana* (Contemplation of the Dharma-realm).
This has already been explained within the chapter. All teachings speak only of realizing the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) as principle; none of them speak of realizing these three layers of meaning.
As for the statement regarding "unobstructed wisdom and its object," this refers to being endowed with the threefold *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the phrase "one wisdom is all wisdom":
this explains that realizing one object is called "one wisdom," while realizing all objects is called "all wisdom. It does not mean that [the former] is restricted [to a single object].
Regarding *sarvajñā* (here translated as "all-aspect wisdom," which refers specifically to the wisdom of the Buddha’s fruition).

The commentary on the *Śāstra* states that the "Meaning of the Hundred Gates" refers to the *Huayan Zang Heshang’s* composition, the *Baimen Yihai* (The Ocean of Meaning of the Hundred Gates), in which he explains the meaning of the hundred gates within a single mote of dust; this has already been listed previously.
