Untie the waistband and adjust it so that it remains secure and does not slip off while sitting. Next, one should straighten the legs.

If sitting in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), place the left foot upon the right foot, drawing it close to the body so that the toes of the left foot are level with the right thigh and the toes of the right foot are level with the left thigh.
If one wishes to practice the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), then place the right foot upon the left foot as described above. Next...
Place the palm of the left hand upon the right hand, with the hands stacked facing each other, and rest them atop the right foot.
Pull [the foot] close to the body, then straighten and move the torso along with all the limbs and joints seven or eight times, according to the method for self-massage.
Do not allow the feet to be uneven. Next, straighten the body so that it is upright, ensuring the vertebrae are aligned;
do not slouch and do not arch. Align the head so that the nose is directly opposite the navel; keep it neither biased nor tilted, neither lowered nor raised, but resting level and upright.
Next, expel the foul air from within the chest and above the diaphragm by uttering the sound "ha. As for the method of this expulsion: open [the mouth]...
Exhale the breath from the mouth. Imagine that the blockages in the hundred vessels throughout the body, which are the source of affliction, are all expelled along with the breath.
Close the mouth and nose, then draw in pure air. Do this three times. If the body and breath are harmonized, one session alone will suffice.
Next, close the mouth so that the lips and teeth just barely touch, and press the tongue against the upper palate. Then, close the eyes just enough...
One merely cuts off external light. One should sit upright with the body straightened like a pillar of stone;
one must not allow the body to be "blind" [unaware] or cause the four limbs to move restlessly. This is the method for adjusting the body when first entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

To state the essentials: neither too loose nor too tight—this is the mark of an adjusted body. Regarding "sparse breathing": there are four types of breath; the first three are unadjusted, while the last one is adjusted.
"Wind" (vāyu) refers to the sound produced by the breath as it enters and exits through the nostrils while sitting. "Sighing" (śvāsa) refers to the entry and exit being obstructed and stagnant.

"Breath" (prāṇa) refers to the entry and exit being coarse and violent. "Respiration" (ānāpāna) is without sound, without stagnation, and without coarseness; its entry and exit are continuous, as if existing and yet as if non-existent.
The spirit is supported and at peace; the mind is joyful and content. If one dwells on the wind (*vāyu*), it scatters; if one dwells on the panting (*śvāsa*), it knots;

if one dwells on the vital energy (*prāṇa*), it fatigues; if one dwells on the breath (*āśvāsa*), it becomes settled. When sitting, there may be a sense of presence or absence; one should regulate this by relying on three methods: first, fix the mind.
Second, relax the body. Third, imagine the breath pervading the entire body, entering and exiting through the pores, flowing freely without obstruction.
With the mind refined and subtle, cause the breath to become increasingly faint. When the breath is thus regulated, various afflictions do not arise, and the mind easily attains concentration.
To state the essentials: being neither constricted nor slippery is the characteristic of regulated breath. Regarding "refining the mind," there are two meanings to refining the mind; the first is...
Subdue distracted thoughts so that they do not wander or stray. Second, one should ensure that sinking (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), as well as laxity and tension, are brought into balance.
Regarding sinking: when sitting, the mind becomes dark and obscured, there is nothing to be recorded, and the head tends to droop; this is the sign of sinking.

At that time, one should bind the mindfulness to the tip of the nose, causing the mind to abide within the object of focus without any intention to scatter; this can remedy sinking. [Regarding] agitation...
When sitting, if the mind is prone to wandering and the body is also restless, and one thinks of external, distracting objects, this is the sign of floating (*uddhata*).

At such a time, one should settle the mind by directing it downward and binding the object of focus within the navel; by restraining all scattered thoughts, the mind will become stabilized and tranquil.
To state the essential point: being neither sunken nor floating is the sign of a well-regulated mind. As for agitation, it arises from gripping the mind too tightly while sitting.
By means of mindfulness and aspiration, one enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For this reason, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) moves upward, causing acute pain in the chest.

One should relax the mind and imagine that the breath flows entirely downward; thus, delusion is immediately eliminated. "Relaxation" means perceiving the mind wandering freely within the heart and the body becoming supple and relaxed.

If saliva flows from the mouth, or if one becomes dark and obscured at times, at such moments one should contract the body and recollect with urgency, causing the mind to abide within its object so that the body and [mind] are in harmony;
this serves as the remedy. This is the method for initially entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by regulating the body, regulating the breath, and regulating the mind.
Regarding the phrase "the body and so forth": when wishing to enter meditative concentration, one fundamentally proceeds from the coarse to the subtle; therefore...
The body is coarse; the breath resides within it; and the mind is the most subtle.

To harmonize the coarse and proceed toward the subtle until one attains tranquility—this is precisely what is meant by "harmonizing for application," which refers to harmonizing the body, the breath, and the mind while seated. This is truly understandable.

The above are all the skillful means for first entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). However, during the sitting as well as when wishing to emerge from concentration, there are likewise methods for harmonizing the body and the mind.
There are three matters, as explained in a separate fascicle.

In the commentary on the "Expedient Means," regarding "desire" (*chanda*): it is to be free from all worldly delusions, inversions, and cravings, and to attain the aspiration for the joy found within the Dharma-gate of pure wisdom.
This is also termed "resolve" (*adhimukti*), "vow" (*praṇidhāna*), and "delight" (*ruci*). Resolve...
One should wish to delight in all profound Dharma-gates; thus it is said, "for the sake of desire. As for diligence:

throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one should be single-mindedly devoted and never desist. It is like praising fire—one does not stop until it has become hot. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"All Buddhas attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by being single-minded and diligent in their exertion; how much more so regarding other wholesome dharmas of the Path. As for mindfulness: in the world, it serves as...

Deception is loathsome and contemptible. The various outflows-free (*anāsrava*) states, all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and spiritual faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*) arising from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are venerable and noble.
One who possesses skillful wisdom weighs the gains and losses, and the lightness and gravity, of worldly pleasure versus the pleasure of meditative concentration.

He considers that worldly pleasure brings little joy but much suffering; it is illusory and unreal, a loss and something light. The pleasure of meditative concentration is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), outflows-free, and tranquil.

Secluded and vast; even unto eternal liberation from birth and death, forever parting from suffering. This is what is attained through this profound [practice]. As for "single-mindedness": mindfulness and wisdom are clear and distinct.
One clearly perceives that worldly things are to be endured or loathed, while meditative concentration and wisdom are to be honored and esteemed.
One should practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with single-minded determination. With a mind like a diamond (*vajra*), neither celestial Māras nor external paths can obstruct or discourage one.
It is destroyed. Even if one is empty-handed and gains nothing, or even in the face of death, illness, and the like, one will ultimately not fall away from it.

This is because if one is single-minded, it is like a person who wishes to travel: they must first know the signs of whether the road is passable or obstructed, and only then proceed with determination and a single mind along the path.
Therefore, it is said that skillful wisdom and single-mindedness go together; there is no wisdom without meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and no wisdom without meditative concentration.
The commentary on "recognizing the deeds of Māra" consists of two parts: first, based on the original text; second, supplementing with the *Awakening of Faith*.
Regarding the first part, it is stated in full that *māra* means "the killer" in the language of Qin (Chinese). He seizes the wealth of the practitioner’s merit and kills the life of wisdom.
Why are these called the deeds of Māra? For instance, while the Buddha takes as his task the liberation of sentient beings through merit and wisdom and their entry into nirvāṇa, Māra—
They constantly take it as their business to destroy the roots of goodness in sentient beings and cause them to wander through birth and death.

Because demons flourish when one’s mind is settled in the Way and one’s realization is high, one must skillfully recognize demonic activities. There are four kinds of demons: first, the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*); second, the demon of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu-māra*);

third, the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*); and fourth, the demon of ghosts and spirits (*devaputra-māra*). Furthermore, there are the ten armies, all of which are detailed in a separate fascicle. Now...
Regarding the conceptualization of the forms of spirits, ghosts, and māras, one must know that there are three types: first, *piśācas*; second, *ḍākinīs*;

and third, *māras*. First, as for the *piśācas*: these are beasts of the twelve periods who transform themselves into various shapes and colors, appearing in the forms of young men, young women, or elderly persons, as well as terrifying bodies;
their manifestations are manifold, and they cause confusion and delusion in those who practice.
As for these various *piśācīs* and *yakṣiṇīs* who wish to disturb the practitioner, each arrives at its respective time; one must skillfully discern them.

If they appear most frequently during the hour of the Tiger (*yínshí*), they are surely tigers, rhinoceroses, and the like. If they appear most frequently during the hour of the Rabbit (*mǎoshí*), they are surely hares, deer, and the like.

During the hour of the Dragon (*chénshí*), they are crocodiles, dragons, and the like. During the hour of the Snake (*sìshí*), they are pythons, snakes, and the like. During the hour of the Horse (*wǔshí*), they are horses and donkeys. During the hour of the Sheep (*wèishí*), they are sheep and the like.

At the hour of Shen (15–17), monkeys and the like; at the hour of You (17–19), chickens, birds, and the like; at the hour of Xu (19–21), dogs, wolves, and the like; at the hour of Hai (21–23), pigs, boars, and the like;
at the hour of Zi (23–01), rats and the like; and at the hour of Chou (01–03), oxen and the like.

If a practitioner observes these times, they will know that those who constantly arrive during such hours are specific spirits or demons. By calling out their names and rebuking them, they will immediately apologize and vanish. One should not give rise to fear.
The *jingmei* (spirit-demons) are deities. As for the *duihuiti* ghosts, they also manifest various forms to afflict and disturb practitioners.
Sometimes they appear like insects with human heads and faces, boring and piercing [the body]; sometimes they strike or tickle both armpits; sometimes they suddenly embrace and hold people;
or again, they speak with clamorous voices and assume the forms of various beasts—these are strange and extraordinary manifestations.
First: If a spirit comes to harass a practitioner, one should immediately become aware of it. With single-minded focus, close the eyes and secretly revile it, saying these words:
"I now recognize you! You are the Fire-Eater, Scent-Sniffer, Stealer of Wax, and Kilijika of this Jambudvīpa."
Those of wrong views delight in breaking the precepts, but I now uphold them; you shall never fear me.

If one is an ordained person, one should recite the Preface to the Precepts, the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and so forth; then the ghosts and spirits will retreat and crawl away on their bellies.

Such matters, as well as various obstacles, the signs of those who afflict people, and other methods for severing them, are all explained in the *Dhyāna-sūtra*. [The section on] the Three Māras follows.
As for "Luo" (Rākṣasa), it has been translated and explained as above; they are the followers of Pāpīyas. Although this is a general name, it serves here as a specific designation.
These beings frequently manifest the appearances of the three types of five-sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) to come and destroy people's wholesome minds.
For now, let us explain this in terms of the sense-object of form (*rūpa*). "Contrary" refers to that which contradicts one's emotions.
It may manifest in the forms of tigers, wolves, lions, or rākṣasas—various terrifying images that cause people to feel fear.

"Concordant" refers to [manifesting as] parents, brothers, wives, children, or the forms of various Buddhas, as well as handsome men and women and other lovely objects that cause the mind to become attached. "Neutral" refers to...

"Neutral" means neither contrary nor compliant; it merely takes the form of a neutral category. Yet it agitates the minds of people and causes them to lose meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
therefore, it is called "killing. The other four objects, such as sound and so forth, may be understood by analogy with this:

that is, producing various pleasant and unpleasant sounds, producing various fragrant odors, producing various pleasant and unpleasant tastes, and producing various sensations of suffering and pleasure.
When objects come into contact with the human body, they are all the deeds of Māra. Their manifestations are numerous and cannot be fully described. To state the essentials:
anything that causes people to lose wholesome dharmas and gives rise to afflictions, sorrow, anger, sleep, and so forth, is all Māra.
Regarding the phrase "once the practitioner has become aware," there are two ways to repel them: first, by practicing *śamatha* (calm abiding) to repel them. Whenever one sees...

Regarding all external realms of good and evil demons, one should know them to be false and deceptive; thus, one neither craves nor fears them, nor does one engage in the discrimination of grasping or rejecting.
By calming the mind until it is tranquil and still, those [demons] will naturally vanish. Second, one may repel them by practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

If one perceives the various demonic realms described above and employs cessation (*śamatha*) rather than repelling them, one should instead turn back and contemplate the perceiving mind. When that [perceiving mind] is not perceived, [the demons vanish].
Regarding the locus: when one observes in this way, "What is it that causes affliction? [the affliction] will immediately subside and vanish.

As for the statement from the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā), it serves to establish that one should employ *śamatha* (calm abiding) to perceive reality as it is (*yathābhūta*) and thereby treat the affliction. There are further meanings, as explained in another fascicle.
The phrase "The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* also says" marks the second section. The *Treatise* states:

"There may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness and are thus deluded and disturbed by various māras, heterodox teachers, ghosts, and spirits. While they are sitting [in meditation], these beings manifest forms to terrify them."
Or manifesting as handsome men, women, and so forth—these should be understood as being solely mind; thus, objective spheres cease and ultimately do not cause affliction.

(The treatise is somewhat extensive here, which I shall not include in full; I have merely extracted the essential passages from the commentary. Regarding the manifestation of images such as Buddhas, these refer to devas and bodhisattvas. Regarding the teaching of dharmas such as giving, [it refers to]...
[The perfections are] morality, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom. As for the principle of signlessness (animitta) and so forth:

equality, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, absence of enmity, absence of intimacy, absence of cause, and absence of fruit—this ultimate emptiness and quiescence is true nirvana. Regarding the phrase "able to cause" and so forth in the commentary:
It is further said: it can cause sentient beings to become greedily attached to worldly fame and profit;

it can also cause people to frequently experience anger or joy, and to fluctuate between diligence and indolence—either suddenly exerting great effort and then subsequently abandoning it, or being full of doubt and deliberation, or even forsaking their original superior practices to cultivate other tasks.
Regarding those who obtain food through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the text states that it can also cause people [to act in such ways].
They attain minor semblances of various samādhis, all of which are obtained by non-Buddhists;
these may cause a person to remain in meditative absorption for one day, two days, three, four, five, or even seven days, and to obtain naturally fragrant and delicious food and drink.
"The body and mind are comfortable and joyful; one is neither hungry nor thirsty; people feel affection for them; and their complexion becomes clear.
Regarding the phrase "the complexion changes," the commentary states: "Or it may cause a person to have no moderation in eating—sometimes much, sometimes little—and their complexion undergoes change.

The term "etcetera" (*ādi*) indicates that the preceding and subsequent aspects of the matter are fully encompassed therein. Regarding the phrase "one should always," the commentary states: "For this reason, the practitioner..."
One should observe with wisdom so as not to allow this mind to fall into the net of error. One should apply oneself diligently to right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging;

thus one will be able to escape these various karmic obstacles. Regarding the point that if one sees signs such as auspicious marks—such as seeing images of Buddhas or Bodhisattvas preaching the profound Dharma—one asks:
how does one distinguish whether this has been produced by the roots of goodness from past lives?
To determine what is erroneous and what is correct is truly difficult. Why is this so?
If it is a creation of Māra, yet one perceives it as a sign of goodness and the mind becomes attached to it, one falls into the net of error.

If it is an object manifested by one's own roots of goodness, yet one regards it as the work of Māra and, with a mind of doubt, abandons it, one will lose those roots of goodness and ultimately fail to make progress. Therefore, the distinction between the erroneous and the correct is indeed...
It is difficult to distinguish [the authentic from the spurious]. For now, I shall briefly rely on the oral tradition of the ancient masters and examine it by means of three methods:

first, refining through meditative concentration; second, practicing according to the original source; and third, investigating with wisdom. As the sutra says: "If one wishes to know true gold, one tests it with three methods."
This refers to burning, grinding, and polishing; the practitioner is likewise so difficult to distinguish. If one wishes to distinguish them, one must also undergo three tests:

first, by seeking to engage in joint activities; if one does not know [the practitioner's nature] through joint activities, one should dwell with them for a long time; if one still does not know through long-term cohabitation, one must observe with wisdom.
Now, borrowing this principle to verify what is heterodox or orthodox, it is like when signs and appearances arise within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding that which is difficult to know: one should enter deeply into a concentrated mind. Within that object, neither grasping nor rejecting, but simply abiding in equanimity and concentration.
If it is produced by the power of roots of goodness, the power of concentration will become even deeper and the roots of goodness will further flourish.

If it is the work of Māra, it will naturally collapse before long. Second is relying on the original practice for cultivation; for example, as when one originally practiced the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), now—
One practices the contemplation of impurity based on the original object. If, by practicing in this way, the object becomes increasingly clear and vivid, then it is correct.
If, while treating it according to the original practice, the object gradually diminishes, one should know that it is erroneous. Third is the observation through wisdom.
Observe the characteristics that arise and investigate their source; not seeing a place of origin, one deeply realizes emptiness and stillness.

When the mind no longer dwells in attachment, the false will naturally extinguish and the correct will naturally manifest. It is like smelting true gold, which increases its luster and color; whereas if it were counterfeit gold, [it would be consumed].

It will immediately be consumed and destroyed. One should know that the distinction between the true and the false herein is likewise so. Concentration is likened to grinding; fundamental cultivation is like striking;
wisdom and observation are analogous to burning. By means of these three tests, the heterodox and the orthodox can be discerned.

Regarding the treatment of illness: when a practitioner settles the mind to cultivate the Way, either due to a pre-existing illness or because the current application of the mind causes the breath to strike like a drum, thereby provoking the underlying ailment;

or because at times one cannot properly harmonize the three factors of body, mind, and breath, resulting in internal and external transgressions that cause the illness to manifest and lead to the loss of the method of seated meditation. If one can skillfully apply the mind, then...
The four hundred and four illnesses will naturally be cured. When the mind loses its proper place, it agitates these four hundred and four illnesses.

Therefore, whether practicing for oneself or transforming others, one should skillfully identify the sources of illness and be well-versed in the methods for treating the internal and external minds while seated.
If one does not know the methods for treating illness, should an ailment be provoked at any time, it will not only create obstacles to the practice of the Way, but furthermore—

The Great Life has its concerns. Within the text there are two parts: first, the explanation of illness; second, the explanation of treatment. Regarding the first part, concerning the phrase "the four great elements" (*mahābhūta*):
each character shall be annotated in turn and then correlated with the pathological manifestations of earth, water, fire, and wind.
That is to say, if the earth element increases, there arise swellings, knots, heaviness, emaciation of the body, and so forth—a hundred and one such afflictions. If the water element...
If the element of water increases, there arise over a hundred ailments, such as rapid onset of cold-natured swelling and distension, indigestion, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and so forth.
If the element of fire increases, there arise over a hundred ailments, such as increased chills and high fever, aching in all the limbs and joints, and obstruction of the large and small intestines.
If the element of wind increases, there arise [over a hundred ailments], such as the body feeling empty and suspended, trembling, shaking, and painful distress.
There is oppression, urgent vomiting, coughing, and labored breathing; thus, one hundred and one illnesses arise. Therefore, a sutra says:
"When one of the four great elements is disturbed, one hundred and one illnesses manifest; when all four great elements are disturbed, four hundred and four illnesses manifest simultaneously.

When these illnesses of the four great elements arise, each has its own specific signs; one should observe them during sitting meditation and within dreams (such as seeing water or fire, the body flying, or the body feeling heavy).

[This] immediately reveals which organ is afflicted by disease. Regarding the "commentary on the five viscera," each has its specific correspondence. As for the heart, it is from the heart that ailments arise (the other four are to be understood by this example).
This refers to frequent physical coldness and heat, as well as pain; the mouth becomes parched and so forth, because the heart governs the mouth.

Regarding the lungs, it says "pain in the limbs"; this means aching in the four extremities. Regarding the nose being congested, it is because the lungs govern the nose. As for the liver, there is much sorrow and grief.
Regarding joy, sorrow, anxiety, and anger, there is headache, blurred vision, and so forth; for the liver governs the eyes.
Regarding the spleen, there is the "wandering wind" throughout the body and face, causing frequent itching, numbness, pain, and loss of appetite; for the spleen governs the tongue.
Regarding the kidneys, there is constriction in the throat, abdominal distension, and fullness in the ears; for the kidneys govern the ears. Thus, many ailments arise from the five viscera.

Each has its own characteristic signs; one should examine them while seated or in dreams (dreaming of fire indicates a heart disease; dreaming of water indicates a kidney disease). Regarding "increasing or decreasing":
the four great elements and the five viscera either increase or decrease, thereby resulting in illness. The notes above are all signs of such increase or decrease.
"Contrary to the principle of regulation" refers to the causes of such increase or decrease; that is to say, the mind is filled with excessive sorrow or joy.
The channels of anger and other afflictions lead to disturbances such as those caused by external influences; or it may be due to immoderate diet and lifestyle.

Thus, the ailments of the four elements and five viscera arise from manifold causes, and their symptoms are so numerous that they cannot be fully described here. For now, I shall cite one or two examples to illustrate the many others.
If you wish for a more detailed account, it is found in another volume. Furthermore, these illnesses may be summoned by karma or wrought by malevolent spirits.
These are two matters. Regarding "simultaneously deviating from the principle of integration," there are generally three kinds of causes and conditions for contracting illness:
first, deviation from the principle of integration; second, karmic retribution from past lives; and third, the actions of ghosts and spirits.

Illnesses such as these are easy to treat when first acquired, but difficult to cure after a long duration. [The commentary] states, "Now, to clarify below," which refers to treatment. The text has two parts: first, treating deviation from integration; second, treating the remainder.
II. Regarding the first [of the two parts], there are two sections: 1. The actual exposition of the treatment; 2. Resolving doubts. As for the first:

having understood the origin and manifestation of the illness, one should apply skillful means to treat it. Now, the methods for treating illness do not exceed *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Herein begins *śamatha*.

As for the phrase "the place where the mind rests in peace," this was first explained by a certain master: because the mind is the sovereign of the karmic retribution of this entire life, it is likened to—

Just as wherever a king goes, the bands of thieves disperse; regarding "below the navel," another teacher says that one inch below the navel is called the *udāna*, which is translated here as the *dantian* (elixir field).
If one can still the mind and maintain it there without distraction, after a long time many ailments will be cured.
Regarding "under the feet," another teacher says that one should always settle the mind under the feet, regardless of whether one is walking or not.

Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, one can immediately cure all illnesses. Why is this? Because when the mind-consciousness takes [external objects] as its superior object, it causes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to become unbalanced.
If one settles the mind beneath the soles of the feet, the four great elements will naturally become harmonious and pervasive, and all illnesses will be eliminated.

Alternatively, by realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and so forth—next, another teacher says—one should simply know that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, and not grasp at the characteristics of illness; thus, [the mind] becomes tranquil.
Nevertheless, it remains that there are many things to be treated. Why is this so? It is because the mind’s recollections and imaginings stir up the four great elements, and thus illness arises.
When the mind is stilled and harmonious, all illnesses are immediately cured. Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra asks: "What is called the root of illness?"
What is called "clinging" (*ālambana*)? How does one cling? It means clinging to the three realms (*tridhātu*). How does one cease clinging? It means the mind has nothing to be attained.

Since there are thus various explanations regarding the signs of using the mind to treat illness, one must know that skillfully cultivating the method of *śamatha* (calm abiding) can cure all afflictions.
Below [the section on] "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*), this is the second part. It consists of four sections: first, breath; second, cessation; third...

Regarding the "Visualizations" (xiǎng): In the first of the four observations (*guān*), there is a master who says that one uses six types of breath (*qì*) to treat illnesses through the visualization of the mind.

(As cited in the commentary [shū]), these are all performed by visualizing the mind within the lips and mouth, employing skillful means (*fāngbiàn*) to turn and shift it. When illness occurs, one blows in sequence to remove cold and so forth, as also recorded in the annotations.
However, this differs slightly from the *Qiānjīn fāng* (Thousand-Golden Prescriptions) and various other *Qījīng* (Scriptures on Breath). For example:
The separate fascicle reconciles these points. Regarding the "twelve breaths" mentioned in the commentary: the second is the "cessation breath.

Furthermore, there is a teacher who says that if one can skillfully employ visualization (*vipaśyanā*) and direct the mind to perform twelve types of breath-regulation (*ānāpāna*), they can cure various ailments;

all of these arise from the mind of visualization. First, the upward breath cures heaviness. Second, the downward breath cures emptiness and suspension. Third, the full breath cures emaciation. Fourth, the burning breath...

1. The *śvāsa* (breath) for treating swelling and distension. 2. The *dīrgha-śvāsa* (long breath) for treating emaciation and depletion. 3. The *bhañjana-śvāsa* (breaking breath) for treating increased cold. 4. The *uṣṇa-śvāsa* (warm breath) for treating cold. 5. The *śīta-śvāsa* (cold breath) for treating heat. 6.
The *preraka-śvāsa* (impelling breath)—one version reads *krama-śvāsa*—for treating obstructions and blockages. 7. The *dhāraṇa-śvāsa* (sustaining breath) for treating trembling and agitation. 8.

The *samādhi-śvāsa* (harmonizing breath) for generally treating the disharmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). 9. The *pūraṇa-śvāsa* (filling breath) for providing nourishment and supplementation.

The Four Great Elements. (In the present commentary, whenever the character "xing" (行) appears, it refers to the breath that acts as the remedy; the sub-notes refer to the illnesses that are to be remedied. They may be understood by correlating them accordingly. The commentary continues below with the third section:
"Contemplation of Mental Imagery. This refers to what certain masters say: "One who skillfully employs mental imagery can cure various ailments.

For example, if a person suffers from cold, they imagine a fiery energy arising within their body, and the cold is thereby cured. This is like the method for curing dhyāna [disturbances] found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

The secret methods for treating illness are explained in detail among the seventy-two methods; however, because the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of people today are shallow, they frequently fail to achieve success when performing these visualizations (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, they have not been widely circulated in the world. The commentary further extends [the analysis] to the fourth, the "contemplation of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*).

Next, there is a teacher who says: simply employ *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to examine the mind and subdue the body; then the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the illnesses within them cannot be found, nor can the illness within the mind.
[The afflictions] cannot be found; the various illnesses are immediately stilled. Such various explanations as these employ different methods of treatment through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

If one skillfully grasps their underlying intent, they are all capable of curing illness. One should know that the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for the purpose of treating illness is entirely grounded in principle.
If one can skillfully grasp their intent, there is no illness that cannot be cured. [End of] the commentary on what was stated above. Second, resolving doubts.
This is the spirit [of the practice]. A question was asked: "If one applies the mind while sitting in meditation, will there necessarily be efficacy in curing illness?

The answer was: "If one possesses ten dharmas, there is nothing that will not be beneficial. These ten dharmas are: first, faith; second, application; third, diligence, and so forth (as detailed in the commentary).

Regarding faith: it is believing that this dharma can certainly cure illness. Regarding application: it is using it at all times. Regarding diligence: it is being single-minded and tireless. Regarding constancy...

"Attaining the difference as the measure" means that the one who abides dwells within the middle of conditions. "Subtle mind" refers to moment-to-moment dwelling in accordance with the Dharma without diverging from conditions.

"Discerning the illness" means discerning its causal origin, as explained above. "Expedient means" refers to the skillful accomplishment of breath-regulation (*ānāpāna*), mental application, and visualization, such that they do not lose their appropriateness.
Regarding "long-term practice," although it is beneficial to employ these methods, one does not harbor [calculating] thoughts regarding them.

"Sun and Moon" means practicing constantly without ceasing. "Taking and abandoning" means knowing what to take up and what to abandon: that which is beneficial, one applies diligently; that which is detrimental, one abandons.
"Transforming the mind to achieve order" means guarding [the mind]. "Recognizing obstructions" means identifying those factors that hinder progress.
This refers to not speaking outwardly of the benefits gained, so as to avoid the harm of generating doubt or slander. Furthermore, while the illness has not yet been diminished...
"Do not doubt or slander. In the commentary, the character "sun" (損) is used twice. If one relies on these ten methods, the treatment will certainly be effective.

In the sub-commentary (*shū*), following the section on "prohibitions and mantras," the second part treats the remaining two types of illness. If it is an illness caused by spirits (*bhūta*), one should employ spirit-mantras and the like to empower the treatment.
If it is an illness resulting from karma, one must supplement the practice with the cultivation of merit and repentance. One must simply obtain...

When karma is eliminated, afflictions are naturally extinguished. These two methods for treating illness—if a practitioner can properly attain single-mindedness—can be applied both to oneself and to others;
how much more so if one possesses full mastery and penetration? If one knows nothing at all, then when illness arises there will be no cure.
Not only will the cultivation of the True Dharma be abandoned, but one’s very life and nature may be in peril. How then could one practice this for oneself or teach it to others? This is...
Therefore, those who wish to cultivate the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must have a thorough understanding of the internal methods for treating the mind’s ailments.
These methods possess many gateways; how could they all be fully transmitted in writing? Those who wish to practice and master them must consult in detail as the occasion arises.

Furthermore, they should consult other volumes and seek out those who have attained mastery for detailed examination. If one is merely engaged in ordinary exegesis, it is sufficient to simply explain the literal text.
This merely explains the meaning.

In the eighth section on "Correct Cultivation" (*zhèngxiū*) of the Commentary (*shù*), there are two parts: first, the headings for these two gates; second, the citation and explanation of that dharma.

"That" refers to Tiantai. Regarding the first part: it means that all preceding sections were preparatory skillful means practiced prior to meditative concentration (*dìng*), whereas this gate is the actual [cultivation].

It speaks of the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). That [text] cultivates the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of insight (*vipaśyanā*), which are largely the same as, yet slightly different from, these three insights;
this shall be further distinguished below. For now, following the sequence of its ten gates, I shall briefly set them forth in order.

Furthermore, in contrast to this gate of the sudden cultivation of the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-uttaratantra-śrī-sarvatathāgata-tattvasaṃgraha*), that [text’s] formal cultivation also constitutes a preparatory means (*upāya*); this can be seen by comparing them in detail. There are two modes of cultivation.

"Planting the seed" refers to the exposition and explanation of those dharmas. Within the second section, regarding "cultivation while seated," there are two parts: first, [cultivation] in contrast to coarse distraction; second, in contrast to other dharmas.

Regarding the first, among the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), sitting is specifically prescribed because walking gives rise to much restlessness (*auddhatya*), lying down gives rise to much torpor (*styāna*), and standing or walking for long periods also produces fatigue;
therefore, sitting alone is superior. "Binding the mind to a single point" means guarding the object.
This is *śamatha* (calm abiding). Whether at the tip of the nose, below the navel, or following whatever object arises, the Sūtra says:
"Bind the mind and do not let it wander; it is like a monkey tied with a chain—whenever it moves, immediately restrain it. This is the restraint of the mind through *śamatha*.
That is to say, as soon as the mind arises [in distraction], one immediately restrains it so that it does not scatter. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Of these five faculties, the mind is their master."
Therefore, you should properly restrain the mind. This principle is precisely "stopping by realizing the true nature" (*tattva-śamatha*).

It means that according to whatever the mind contemplates, one knows that all phenomena arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature; thus, the mind does not grasp or cling, and deluded thoughts cease.
For this reason, it is called "stopping. As a verse in a sutra says: "Among all phenomena, causes and conditions are empty and without a master; the mind that rests reaches the fundamental source."
This is the source; therefore, one is called a śramaṇa. Furthermore, the causes and effects of the three realms and all dharmas are created solely by the one mind.
Now that the mind is known to be without intrinsic nature, how could there be any reality to the various dharmas? Thus, one remains tranquil and non-active. Non-action is the source of all dharmas.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The mind does not know the mind; the mind is not known by the mind. When the mind gives rise to conceptualization—

This is delusion. Because there is no perception, it is Nirvana. As for "cessation" (*śamatha*), if one does not descend [into it], it is "insight" (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding "remedies that assist the Path":

these treat specific ailments; they subsequently assist the Right Path, such as the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana-bhāvanā*), which uses the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha*) to remedy lustful desire.

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) remedies ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) remedies discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*) remedies attachment to a self (*ātmasakti*).

Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) remedies ignorance (*avidyā*). "Principle" (*li*) refers to the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpādadarśana*), which is also the contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and is further named the wisdom of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇajñāna*).

That text explains these characteristics by extensively investigating all phenomena; through many layers of enumeration, it establishes the meaning of emptiness and provisionality (*śūnyatā-prajñapti*). This is the meaning.

The meaning is no different from what was stated previously in the chapter on the emptiness of phenomena; therefore, it is not reiterated here. In the commentary, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, one cultivates śamatha...

refers to the second section, which correlates [the practice] with other dharmas. By correlating the four [states] with the mind, one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā. Regarding "floating" and "sinking": these refer to the movement of floating and the movement of sinking.

When there is floating, one cultivates śamatha; when there is sinking, one cultivates vipaśyanā. The characteristics of floating and sinking are no different from those explained previously. As for "according to what is convenient," although the above...

If one cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*) to counteract mental sinking, yet the mind remains unclear and unpurified, and there is no benefit from the Dharma, at that time one should test whether it is appropriate to cultivate calm abiding (*śamatha*) to settle the mind.
If, during the practice of calm abiding, one perceives that body and mind are peaceful and pure, one should know that it is appropriate to rest in calm abiding;

one should then cultivate calm abiding to settle the mind. Even if one cultivates calm abiding to counteract mental agitation, if the mind still does not abide, [one should likewise proceed accordingly].
If [the practitioner] finds that calming meditation (śamatha) does not bring benefit, they should attempt to practice insight (vipaśyanā).

If, during the practice of insight, one perceives that the mind is luminous, pure, tranquil, and peaceful, one should know that insight is appropriate; one should then apply insight to settle the mind. This is called "calming and insight according to what is suitable" (*yathāpratyaya-śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
The three methods of cultivation are fully explained as above. Regarding those with subtle minds who hold fixed views, the arising of views from within meditative concentration is called...
There is fixed vision (*niyata-dṛṣ� craving attachment to this vision is called the subtle mind (*sūkṣma-citta*). Now, one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to counteract and break it.
This means that when coarse and distracted thoughts cease, one perceives the body as empty and tranquil, and experiences this bliss.

Alternatively, if a sharp faculty (*tīkṣṇendriya*) arises, and one does not realize that this fixed vision is deceptive, taking it to be real, one will inevitably give rise to greedy attachment; this then belongs to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*). If these two do not arise, [the subtle mind is transcended].

This is called the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding). If the mind remains deluded and attached to craving and views, and the fetters of karma do not cease, one should cultivate *vipaśyanā* (insight).

Within the vision of meditative concentration, one observes that the subtle mind has no point of origin; thus, one does not cling to that concentrated vision. Because of this non-clinging, craving and views do not arise;
hence it is called "counteracting. Regarding the balancing of concentration and wisdom: it refers to if, during the preceding cultivation of *śamatha*, [the practitioner perceives an imbalance].

Alternatively, one may cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). If the wisdom of contemplation is slight and insufficient, one will be unable to give rise to true wisdom and sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

One should therefore cultivate contemplation to dismantle and break down discursive differentiation, causing wisdom to unfold; when concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium, one can sever the fetters.

Regarding the realization of the various dharma-gates: if, through the practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight) or the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding), the mind suddenly attains a breakthrough and wisdom engages in discernment, yet the power of concentration is slight, the mind will then become restless and scattered, like a lamp in the wind whose light fails to illuminate objects clearly.

One should practice *śamatha*. By practicing *śamatha*, one attains profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because one attains profound meditative concentration, one then knows the equanimity of the concentrated mind;
it is like a lamp in a sealed room, which can dispel darkness and illuminate objects with clarity.

Therefore, it is said that concentration and wisdom are balanced and equal. Thus, one practices *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the second point, "passing through conditions" (*li yuan*), the text has two parts: first, passing through conditions; second, [passing through dharmas].

Regarding the object of focus: first, one must sit with the body upright, as this is the supreme essential for entering the Way. However, if one accumulates days [without practice], the body will inevitably become entangled in worldly affairs.

If one follows conditions and encounters objects without practicing, then cultivation will be interrupted; when cultivation is interrupted, karmic bonds arise again, and one will not be in accord with the Buddha.
If one practices constantly at all times and in all places, one will surely be able to penetrate the One.

Regarding all Buddha-dharmas, as for "passing through conditions," there are six kinds of conditions: first, the four modes of deportment and the performance of activities (the upper character *zuò* is pronounced with the entering tone, the lower character *zuò* is pronounced *zìsù*).
In all these, one should form this thought [as explained below]; the six conditions share the same intent, and their texts are largely identical.
Now, I shall briefly describe the practice during walking to serve as an illustration for the remaining five. When walking, one should form this thought: "For what purpose am I now acting?"
Regarding the intention to act: if one is impelled by afflictions (*kleśa*) or by unwholesome and indeterminate matters, one should not act.

If one is not impelled by afflictions but acts for the sake of benefiting others through matters that accord with the Dharma, then one should act. How does one cultivate tranquility (*śamatha*) within such action?

If, while walking, one realizes that it is because of walking that all phenomena—both wholesome and unwholesome afflictions—arise, and understands that within the state of walking, neither the mind nor any of the phenomena therein can be apprehended, then the deluded mind ceases;

this is called the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) while walking. How does one cultivate *vipaśyanā* (insight) while walking? One should reflect as follows: "It is because the mind moves that the body moves."
That which advances is called "activity" (*saṃskāra*). Because of this activity, there arise all phenomena, whether afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome.
One should then reflect back upon the mind of activity; seeing no marks or characteristics, one should know that the practitioner and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.

This is called the cultivation of contemplation within activity. (The remaining five [aggregates] are not described here where they are the same [as above]; those that differ are summarized and briefly described. Regarding "abiding": by means of the mind...

Regarding standing: when sitting, one should apply the mind to placing the feet and settling the body. Regarding lying down: if it is for the sake of negligence or similar matters, one should not lie down;
however, if one lies down for the purpose of harmonizing the four great elements, one should do so in the manner of a lion king.
As for "acting," this refers to moving the body and performing various tasks with the hands. Regarding speech: if it follows from the afflictions, it is subsequently discussed as unwholesome.

Regarding "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*): it should not be [discussed] in terms of speech and so forth. However, by proceeding through the six internal bases (*āyatana*) and confronting the six external objects, each instance is identical to the meaning of the five previous sections on the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
In those texts, each section likewise refers back to the preceding passage. In the commentary, "confronting objects" is the second [point].
"Knowing form and so forth" fully describes the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* when the eye confronts form; this serves as an analogy for the others.
Regarding the other five, such as the city of the *gandharvas*: one realizes that these are illusory and fundamentally empty; thus, although things are seen, they lack fixed reality.

Because they lack fixed reality, if one sees forms that accord with one's desires, one should not become greedily attached; if one sees forms that oppose one's desires, one should not become angry or distressed.
This is therefore called the cultivation of *śamatha*. As for "realizing the absence of the characteristic of seeing": whatever is seen, it is immediately devoid of the characteristic of seeing.
Why is this so? Within that emptiness and clarity of the sense faculties and their objects, there is no seeing in each instance, nor is there any discrimination.

Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, visual consciousness arises; from the conditions of visual consciousness, mental consciousness is produced. When mental consciousness arises, [it perceives].
One is then able to discern various forms. Because of this, there arise all dharmas, such as afflictions, good, and evil.
One should immediately turn back the mind that contemplates form and not perceive its characteristics; one should know that the seer and all dharmas are ultimately empty and quiescent.
Therefore, this is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the examples of sound and so forth: those whose textual structure is identical have also not been recorded here.
I shall merely briefly describe their differences: sound is like an echo in a valley; fragrance is like the wind; taste is like that which is experienced in a dream.
Furthermore, the nature of the six external objects is devoid of discrimination, and the nature of the internal tongue-faculty likewise possesses no cognition.

Touch is like a shadow or a magical transformation, and the mind is like a dream. Thus it is in all circumstances—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and in all acts of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Regarding those who cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within [this teaching]: because they truly cultivate the Mahāyāna path, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva, when walking, knows that he is walking; when sitting, knows that he is sitting; and even regarding his body, eyes, saṃghāṭī robe, looking, blinking, and the single-mindedness of entering and emerging from meditative concentration—all these he knows.
This is called the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva, because it is non-apprehendable (*anupalambha*)."
Because it can be attained.

Regarding the phrase "the arousal of wholesome roots" (*kuśalamūla*) and so forth, this will be explained below in the section on the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). Within the formal explanation, for one who takes tranquility as their practice, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the intention of the cultivation; second, the actual demonstration beginning with the question "How [is it done]? and so forth; third, a detailed explanation by citing the treatise.

Regarding the two [passages]: "Having already awakened" refers back to what preceded. From "Ultimate stillness" (*zhìjìng*) onwards, this contemplation is pointed out in each of the various wheels, and in every instance it is called "ultimate stillness.

This is consistent throughout the text. In the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the *bodhimaṇḍa*, it also says: "First, one takes up ultimate stillness" (which, according to the commentary, means "settling the mind and abiding herein");

"one does not give rise to thoughts" (which, according to the commentary, means "not grasping at dharmas"); and "when stillness reaches its extreme, one becomes aware" (which corresponds to the subsequent scripture stating that "tranquil wisdom arises").

The commentary states: The terms "ultimate stillness" (*zhi jing*) and "extreme stillness" (*ji jing*) both serve to distinguish [the path] from the practices of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). This means that when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) attain stillness, they merely have no thoughts regarding the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*);
yet, because the myriad phenomena have never been non-existent, they also achieve a state of spiritual stillness.

Furthermore, those of the two vehicles realize the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and thus their minds do not arise; they too abide in stillness. As for the provisional Mahāyāna teachings, they merely awaken to the fact that both mind and objects are empty.

Emptiness. By following this, one settles the mind and likewise attains stillness. (This is stillness because of non-existence; it is the absence of all dharmas. It is like saying that the mere absence of something is called "stillness.

According to this school, awakening to the pure, awakened true mind as being unarisen from dharmas constitutes ultimate stillness. (This is stillness because of existence; it is because the true mind exists. It is like seeing the substance of moisture:

if this substance is not moved by the wind, one designates this moisture as the "substance of stillness"). The commentary below [the character] "▲" provides a detailed explanation. Regarding "dwelling," it refers to the ten spheres of totality (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*).
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are ten [elements], namely: blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
For example, when one practices the contemplation of blue, all places are entirely blue and no other colors remain; the same applies to yellow and the others.

These are provisional and gradual teachings intended for those practicing specific meditative exercises. When cultivating the Samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one does not rely upon these at all. Now...
This sutra does not rely upon that [approach] either. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*nàizhì*) in the commentary, it is an abbreviation for the intermediate portion.

The subsequent passage states: "All conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*) are eliminated along with their recollections; even the thought of 'elimination' is discarded. This is because all phenomena are fundamentally without conceptualization;

they do not arise from moment to moment, nor do they cease from moment to moment. Furthermore, one cannot follow the mind’s outward recollection of objects and subsequently use the mind to eliminate the mind."

"If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately collect it and return it to dwell in right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). As for 'right mindfulness,' one should know that it is nothing but mind," and so forth (as in the commentary).
The phrase "and so forth" refers to the subsequent passage. The subsequent passage states: "In every thought-moment, [the mind] is ungraspable.

Whether rising from one's seat, going or coming, advancing or stopping, or performing any action, at all times one should constantly maintain mindfulness of skillful means and observe in accordance with them."

Through sustained investigation, long practice, and thorough mastery, the mind attains stability. Because the mind is stabilized, one follows [the truth] with fierce intensity and enters the samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Afflictions are deeply subdued, faith increases, and one quickly achieves the stage of non-retrogression—except for those who harbor doubt and uncertainty, lack faith, engage in slander, possess the karmic obstructions of evil deeds, or suffer from pride and indolence; such persons are unable to enter.

"Guests are not the fundamental nature"—these two phrases explain the meaning of "adventitious dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*). Because guests are not the fundamental nature, and the fundamental nature is the host, while deluded thoughts are the guests.

As for "dust," it defiles the self-substance, like dust upon a mirror. Regarding the phrase "distancing oneself from heaviness and rigidity" (*dausthulya*), it means being light, clear, bright, sharp, and at ease.
Being free from heaviness and rigidity is called "lightness"; it refers to the body and mind being harmonious and supple.

It is named "peace" (*praśrabdhi*). This is of two kinds: first, the untainted (*anāsrava*), which removes the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the tainted; heaviness pertains to all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

Second, the tainted (*sāsrava*), which removes the heaviness of the afflictions (*kleśa*); this is exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*). (In this present text, based on the state of being [the path], it refers to the tainted wholesome.

If one follows the tenet of the Sūtras—that tainted phenomena are fundamentally non-existent—these two kinds would not be mentioned. This is the direct antidote to torpor (*styāna*). It is the single dharma that leads toward the Dharma; it removes all obstacles. That [treatise] concerns...
This refers to the specific obstacles. Since lethargy (*styāna*) is the state of being unserviceable (*akarmanyatā*), while pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is serviceability, only the former is excluded;

by means of the latter, one subdues and eliminates it (subduing when there is an agent, eliminating when there is none). These are factors that obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—whether they be attachment to the teachings or anything else that merely hinders concentration.

That is to say, it causes that upon which it depends to become transformed and at ease; furthermore, what is now being discussed is simply *styāna* (sloth), because it causes the body that serves as its basis to be transformed away from its coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and to attain tranquility.
The commentary on the threefold "Response and Induction" has four parts: first, a direct explanation; second, citing examples; third, reconciling the two texts;

and fourth, a specific explanation of the meaning of "manifestation. Regarding the phrase "the mind of true purity": this refers to the pure source-mind upon which both ordinary beings and sages equally rely. As for "it is the Dharma-body":

speaking from the perspective of actual manifestation, at the time when contemplation is perfected, the bodies and minds of the true purity of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are all mutually pervasive and interpenetrating.
As for the mention of "mind" alone: this fundamental source-mind is the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Within it, the two dharmas of body and mind are contained.
Its purity and lack of marks is the True Body (*dharmakāya*); its numinous awareness that is never obscured is the True Mind (*cittatattva*). Therefore, only "mind" is designated.

Therefore, both the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* merely point to the single mind as that which encompasses all things; this is the reason for the statement in the Commentary, "and so forth.
This serves as the primary proof that body and mind are non-dual. The nature of wisdom is the mind; the nature of form is the Dharma-body. Now, let us explain this in detail:
the nature of form is emptiness and quiescence, which is precisely what wisdom knows—namely, that emptiness and quiescence are themselves wisdom. The nature of wisdom is numinous awareness.

That which is form is precisely the numinous clarity; it is this that can directly manifest form. For example, although a mirror possesses both the qualities of purity and clarity, it is precisely the clarity that directly manifests forms.
However, in the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*), the commentary takes the essential meaning of the treatise;

therein, in order to reveal the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it speaks of the two bodies—the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—manifested by the Buddha, as well as matters such as their physical marks and adornments. Only...

It manifests based on the mind, yet it is not mixed with True Suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, it is said that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) has no marks of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*). To this, a question is raised (the full text follows below):
"If the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are free from marks of form, how can they manifest marks of form?

The answer is: "Because this very Dharma-body is the substance of form, it is able to manifest form. (This is the general statement by which the answer is given. What follows specifically clarifies the identity of body and wisdom as the reason for their ability to manifest.)
That is to say: from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual.

Because the nature of form is itself wisdom, the substance of form is formless (just as a shadow is inseparable from light, the substance of the shadow is empty); thus it is called the "Wisdom-body" (the body of wisdom; the luminous essence of wisdom).

Because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the "Dharma-body" (this very numinous and luminous mental wisdom, because it can manifest form and serves as the basis for form, is designated as the Dharma-body; "body" here carries the sense of being the essential substance and the locus). It pervades all places. (Because it can...)

"Because all things are manifested, they return to pervade the very places where they were manifested. Regarding the phrase "to speak according to the actual principle," an ancient master’s verse says: "At twilight, all becomes silent and still."

Body and mind are entirely devoid of substance; the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges enter my body, and my body constantly enters the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—this is the meaning of this passage.
Question: If this is so, why do the sutras state only that the Buddha manifests within the minds of sentient beings?

Therefore, the following section implicitly answers this point by now focusing specifically on the entry into contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and so forth. [The commentary] states: "Therefore, the treatise asks... This constitutes the second part: citing examples.

In the treatise, there are two layers of question and answer. Following the discussion that when a Bodhisattva’s stage is fulfilled and they attain Buddhahood, there naturally arises inconceivable activity capable of manifesting throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings, a question is posed:
"The space of the world and the mental activities of sentient beings are each infinite; how can the Buddha know them all? The answer is: "All objective realms are, from the very beginning..."
With a single mind, free from conceptualization, [the Buddha perceives] that because sentient beings see realms through delusion, their minds have limitations.
The Buddha is free from the marks of seeing and is omnipresent because his mind is true. Thus, his own essence clearly illuminates all deluded phenomena.
Possessing the function of great wisdom and immeasurable skillful means, he is able to reveal various teachings according to what each being should understand.
[This is] the meaning. Therefore, it is named "Omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*). For this reason, he asks again: [This refers to the commentary text.

(The passages cited above and those cited within the commentary are all abridged essential texts and have not been written out in full. As for the statement that "many are unable to see," the text continues:

"If all sentient beings were to see his body, behold his miraculous transformations, or hear his teachings, there would be none who do not derive benefit. Why is it that many in the world do not [see him]?"
"One is able to see. The commentary on the text can be understood accordingly. Regarding the section "The Sūtra says... below, these three points harmonize the two passages.

In the commentary, the term "obstructed" (*ài*) below contains three meanings to explain obstruction and non-obstruction. First, it transcends the two gates of initially grasping stillness and subsequently giving rise to illusions.

Third, causing the transcendence of both illusion and afflictions constitutes one meaning, while combining the grasping of stillness and nirvāṇa constitutes another meaning. This is because...
This constitutes a pair; specifically, the character *shè* (涉) in the first phrase and the character *tóng* (同) in the second phrase convey this meaning. To combine the first phrase means:
to give rise to illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna*) to eliminate illusion, and further, desiring to transform all illusions to open the assembly of illusions.

This involves numerous mental factors (*caitta*), each of which exerts its own volitional activity (*manasikāra*), thereby agitating and disturbing the mind. Although this is contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanājñāna*), it "involves" (*shè*) afflictions (*kleśa*). It is "the same" (*tóng*) [as the preceding].
This is because it is a mode of activity that causes disturbance. This intent takes the arising of illusions as an obstacle to the afflictions;
