One feels weary of birth and death and yearns for nirvana; one becomes addicted to emptiness and stalled in stillness. Since nirvana is a dharma of non-obstruction, taking the aspect of quiescent practice now belongs to this category;

thus it is said they are "the same. This meaning is that one takes the grasping of stillness as the characteristic of nirvana, rather than separately explaining nirvana as the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the extinguishing of the body, the extinction of wisdom, and so forth. Therefore, this one...
Each of these is explained separately from the preceding ones, constituting the third meaning.

Regarding the commentary on the *Vajrasamādhi* and so forth, the phrase "belonging to oneself" (*shushu jiri*) refers to all things one possesses for personal use and enjoyment, including requisites, dwellings, fields, gardens, groves, and pavilions, as well as the territories and districts governed by kings and officials;
all such things are considered the implements for one's own personal use and enjoyment. This...
When the practice of the gate-observation is perfected and the mind merges with the numinous source, these [phenomena] remain exactly as they were before;
yet, there is no longer any thought of grasping or rejecting, nor any conceptualization of existence or non-existence, and so forth.

Regarding those who dwell together in nations and towns, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises state that this trichiliocosm is produced by the collective karma of sentient beings, comprising all varieties of noble and base, human and animal.
Sentient beings dwell together by relying upon this [environment], which is called the "retributive support based on common reliance" (yi bao). As for their own bodies, each follows its own karma;

they differ in status—noble or base—and experience—suffering or pleasure—and are distinguished by species such as those that fly or walk. This is called the "primary retribution of individual karma" (bie ye zheng bao).
My intention here is that since this is easily perceived by ordinary people, I speak directly of "dwelling together in countries and towns," meaning perhaps within one Jambudvīpa or one Aparagoyānī.
Whether it be a single Nih (Nepal), a single Great Tang, or a single Tufan (Tibet), whether broad or narrow, comprehensive or restricted, as long as they share the same suitability of soil and water,
the customs practiced, the products of the mountains and rivers, and the transformation through royal law, they may all be collectively termed a "world" (*loka-dhātu*).

It is not necessarily required that a world consist of a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhatu*), for the scope of the meditative object for one practicing contemplative cultivation is not fixed.
This is because it must pervade the great trichiliocosm. As for the commentary’s mention of those who have seen or heard [it], it briefly cites two consciousnesses as examples for the remaining ones;
furthermore, it cites the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as an example for the mental factors (*caitta*). These modes of perception and deliberation are no different from the ordinary;

they simply lack the intentional mental construction (*vitarka-vicāra*) that occurs when one has not yet cultivated meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the phrase "the realm of sensory objects" (*viṣaya-dhātu*) in the commentary, this refers to the habitual boundaries of the sensory objects of the mind.
Furthermore, "Lingzhao" (Spiritual Illumination) refers to the essence of the spiritual mind; it is so called because its great wisdom-light universally illuminates the Dharma-realm.
Vairocana is the body of the Dharma-realm; in this land [China], his name is translated as "Universal Radiance. As for other terms that are not explained here: [they are omitted].
All may be sought according to one’s inclination.

In the commentary on the metaphors, there are two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of alternative explanations. Regarding the first: as for "the basis of the metaphor," this refers to the physical object upon which the metaphor relies.

The object itself is not the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison), and the *dharma* (the subject) is not the *upameya* (the object of comparison), because these two are entirely distinct. However, upon the object...
The meaning [of the simile] and the meaning of the Dharma are similar. Only when these two meanings are present can there be the analogy and the object of analogy.
For example, if one takes the diamond (*vajra*) as an analogy for *prajñā*, yet grasps them as two distinct entities, then there is no connection between them.
This is because the diamond has a physical form, whereas *prajñā* is formless; *prajñā* is the wisdom of discernment, so how could a diamond possibly discern phenomena? *Prajñā* possesses...

From the myriad virtues up to the wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the *vajra* possesses none of these. Yet, it is taken here as a metaphor solely for the sake of expressing the meanings of "solidity" and "sharpness.
As for the *vajra*: that which no thing in the world can destroy is its solidity; that which can shatter and destroy all things is its sharpness.
One who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* likewise [destroys] the celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, afflictions (*kleśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and all obstacles.
"Immovable" refers to firmness (*dṛḍha*). "Able to sever afflictions and illuminate the emptiness of the five aggregates" refers to sharpness (*tīkṣṇa*).
One need only take these two dharmas—each possessing the respective meanings of firmness and sharpness—and they immediately form a metaphor. A "metaphor" (*upamā*) is that which instructs;

it instructs by means of similarity, leading one to understanding. Now, there are those who wish to examine the holy teachings exhaustively, or who lecture on or listen to their meanings, or who engage in the study of Chan.

Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*): one who investigates and debates the principles of doctrine must necessarily have a thorough understanding of the meaning of comparing the Dharma with its parables. Thus, a sutra says:
"The wise attain understanding through parables," but it does not say this of the foolish. As for the character *huáng* (鍠) being indeterminate, one should seek out its etymological explanations.
This character does not signify sound; nor is it entirely without meaning, for it may be understood through its intended application.

Because the meaning is ambiguous, three interpretations have been preserved. Regarding "gold and so forth": "and so forth" refers to copper, iron, and their like, or those among jade and stone that possess clear and far-reaching sounds.
"Characteristics of sound" refers to the appearance of sound—the resemblance of its clarity, turbidity, pitch, and height.
This is what it means. As for the sound "huang-huang," one can understand it simply by imagining the resonance of striking a bell or a chime.

In the local customs of the region south of Ba, the braying of a donkey is also called the "huang-huang" sound; however, that is heavy and dull, unlike the clear, far-reaching, and resonant quality of bells and chimes.

Those who were somewhat clumsy at this were those who, during the time of translating the scriptures, had Indian monks recite the Sanskrit texts while interpreters proficient in both languages provided the explanation.

To translate [the Indic text] into the language of Tang (Chinese) is called "transcribing" (*bishou*). Because the Indian language and this [Chinese] have inverted word orders, the text must be rearranged;

furthermore, as that language is often plain and direct, the phrasing must be polished. When it is said here that [a sound] is "crude," it is because "sound" (*sheng*) is the essence and "resonance" (*huanghuang*) is its characteristic;
one should properly say "sound" first. The commentary [describes it] as a "great bell" (*da zhong*), which is an explanation cited from the *Qieyun*; it is also synonymous with *yong*.

The same explanation applies. Question: If that is so, then the *karaṇḍa* itself is a material substance. Why does the text not say "like the sound within the *karaṇḍa*," but rather "the *karaṇḍa* within the vessel"?

Therefore, the following response clarifies this point: "These various vessels, etc. This means that among those various vessels, there is one golden vessel (or one made of copper, iron, and so forth) which is called a *karaṇḍa*.
When this *karaṇḍa* is struck, the sound issues forth externally; thus, the phrasing of the text is highly appropriate.
This means that, according to this principle, it accords with the original text and so forth.

However, as for the "pen-receivers" (the scribes), it is truly because the two pronunciations *huáng* and *huáng* are identical, both characters are derived from the "metal" radical, and the two characters *huáng* and *hóng* are likewise homophonous; therefore, they were easily confused.
Regarding the "shu-sheng-huang" (the reed organ): its form is as follows. This four-fold sheng has thirteen pipes; each pipe contains a single reed (*huang*), and they differ in length.
When blown, the air vibrates within the middle [of the pipe], thereby producing sound.

If the sound is not in tune, there is a small piece of tin on the fan-like membrane, about the size of a grain of flour or bran; by shifting it up or down, one adjusts the tonal quality. This is called "tuning" (*diao*).

Regarding "clear" (*qing*), it refers to things such as flutes and reed organs. The *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) by Ci'en states: "Because internal wind arises, there is sound and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Laozi*, Chapter on the Way (*Daode jing*), says: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows; it is empty and yet inexhaustible."

The more it moves, the more it produces [sound]. (The commentary by He Shang states: "The bellows are hollow within; therefore, they can produce sound and breath. There is no time when they are exhausted or depleted; the more they are shaken, the more they produce. Wang Bi’s commentary states: 'The bellows maintain the center, and thus there is no end.

Abandoning the self and entrusting to things, all things find their principle. These two explanations refer to two matters; here we take only the *yè* (flute/reed), as it is the object that produces sound. The *tō* (bellows) refers to types such as bags and bellows for smelting; it is not an object that produces sound.
All such items as pipes, flutes, and *xiāo* flutes accord with the meaning illustrated in the scripture. Regarding the phrase "both commentaries are erroneous," it is because...

The character *huáng* (簧) is [the same as] the character *hóng* (鍠). Taking the phonetic sound of *huáng* (黃) as the phonetic sound of *héng* (橫). Regarding the commentary’s statement “although the three differ”:

*hóng*, *luóng*, and *huáng* are all [types of] bells. Regarding “all are pervasive”: these three objects, as well as body and mind, cannot be confined to where they emerge—[namely, the sound and the luminous spirit (*língmíng*)].

They do not allow one to depart from within oneself, nor can one drive them away. Thus, both the dharma and the metaphor correspond perfectly. [End of] Commentary on the second section below the character *què* (慤).
This introduces an alternative interpretation. A *jūn* (鈞) is thirty *jin* (斤). A *yóng* (鏞) is a large bell. A "star-tower" (*xínglóu*) is a high tower that rivals the stars and the moon.
A "realm" (*huánqū*) refers to the nations and cities within the divisions of the world. [The sound] takes as its basis the hearing of it throughout the four quarters and the eight directions;
it need not necessarily pervade the entire realm. The "self-substance" is the bell; the "other" is the tower. This commentary cannot yet avoid harboring [reservations].

The doubt is now addressed and explained. The word "only" refers to the sound striking the *yong* bell. When we reach the point where the text reiterates and refutes this by providing a counter-explanation, it further adds the *guan* pipe;
thus, one knows that there was also a doubt that the *yong* bell was not the *huang*. Therefore, the *guan* pipe is used to clarify it.

Furthermore, even if one were to disregard the discrepancies in the translation of the scriptures, according to the extant text, the current explanation is also deficient. This is because the scripture states: "Just as when a *huang* [bell] within a vessel, the sound emerges..."
Externally, this refers to the vessel itself, not the clapper; it is the clapper within the vessel. The clapper is not the sound itself, yet it is that which can produce the sound.
Is it not evident, then, that these three elements are each distinct? Now, the commentary explains: "A ten-thousand-jun bronze bell. This refers to the vessel.
He then says, "The sound vibrates throughout the world. Does this not omit the character *huáng* (鍠) by failing one section?

Regarding the phrase "unable to resolve," it further means that he cannot definitively determine the discrepancies in the translations and commentaries of the scriptures. Furthermore, he does not state what the character *huáng* signifies;
should it be *yóng* (a large bell), or should it be *guǎn* (a pipe)? Nor does he say that both are two distinct objects, nor does he say that they are both [the same].
These are the sounds of two objects. Should they not be considered individually as the sound of a *yong* (large bell)? Is it not because they are described in a vague and general manner?
"Vague" (*mian-er*) means to be indistinct and muddled; it refers to containing the general meaning. The *Qieyun Shishi* (Explanations of the Qieyun) states:

This is not a definitive conclusion. Since there is no text that provides a final judgment, if someone were to challenge each of the aforementioned points one by one, with what words could one respond?
My answer is: if you encounter someone who lectures on that commentary (*śāstra*), I request that you treat them with compassion and have them provide a detailed analysis.

However, the author of this commentary is naturally quick-witted and possesses a modest degree of monastic erudition; he has directly recorded his critical judgments (*vibhāga*) upon the scriptural text.
While it is indeed commendable that you have provided an explanation following the text, as for the profound meanings of the sūtras and śāstras, these are by no means captured in your work.

Consequently, in many places your word-by-word commentary is incomplete and omissions abound; every section is sparse and deficient. Furthermore, you do not investigate the underlying intent of the sūtra’s text, how its preceding and succeeding parts are interconnected from beginning to end.
Among these, even the explanation of this particular section is presented with some degree of clarity and explicit instruction, yet the remainder is even more deficient and abbreviated.

However, in each case, whether there were three phrases or two, they were all merely remote [from my own position]. As for the passages from those texts I have cited previously and subsequently, I have only selected those where the principle was just barely compatible;

I did so with the intent of providing corroboration to establish common ground as allies of the school that takes the true nature (*dharmatā*) as its fundamental principle, while also being unwilling to overlook even a fragment of another’s merit.
Yet, I have never added a single new meaning [to their doctrine]; this intention and its underlying logic can be understood thereby.

The intent of the *Shu* (Commentary) is also the same as the former. Because the preceding [text] specifically pointed out errors in the translation of the scriptures, it took the meaning for its own use;

subsequently, when one examines this passage by the Venerable Guan-ke, they instead come into accord. As for "still being consistent with the Dharma" (*fǎhé*) and so forth, it is because the *Shu* provides a formal correspondence between the teaching and the analogy for others that it can be understood in this way.
However, according to the interpretation in that *Chao* (Excerpts) and the explanations of those who lecture and transmit [the teachings], it is also...
There is no such statement.

Regarding the commentary’s remark that it does not accept "illusory transformations" and the like: although illusions and transformations are empty, they do not destroy their illusory appearance; however, one does not grasp at them with attachment.
Since they are fundamentally devoid of an inherently arising self-nature, they are said to be "quiescent. Nevertheless, this merely means not forming intentional grasping, nor...

It obstructs the effortless, vivid perception of things as they appear; therefore, one speaks only of "quiescence" (*śānta*) and not of "extinction" (*nirodha*). As for "quiescence": it is originally not a characteristic (*nimitta*).

It becomes a characteristic of quiescence only because the mind grasps it and takes it as an object of cognition (*ālambana*). When the mind is empty and forgetful of its own illumination, and does not grasp this as an object, the characteristic itself ceases.
This is unlike illusory appearances, which persist effortlessly and vividly. As for "extinction," it merely means the cessation [of the characteristic].
This characteristic of the object of focus (*ālambana*) is not something that can be stilled or extinguished.

"Stilling" (*śānti*) carries the meaning of the cessation of mental activity; it is not the objective realm itself. Therefore, both the Commentary and this [text] do not grasp at illusory transformations (*nirmāṇa*). Illusory transformations are themselves extinction (as previously stated: "Because the illusory body is extinguished, the illusory mind is also extinguished," and also:

"Because the reflected image is extinguished"). One does not grasp at the characteristic of stillness (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*). Stillness is itself quiescence (*śama*). (The non-arising of mental movement is called stillness; however, by not grasping at it, one realizes the essence of true quiescence, for there is no separate characteristic of stillness.)
"Furthermore, they may both be applicable" means that although illusion and stillness exist, one does not take them as objects of contemplation, nor does one grasp them as fixed characteristics;
rather, they are fundamentally and eternally quiescent. The commentary further explains this by defining their essential nature:

"However, within the true mind, there are sands-of-the-Ganges principles, yet all of these are merely phenomenal functions arising in accordance with conditions. Only quiescence is the essential nature."

This is the principle of ultimate reality; hence it is called "real principle" (*satya-artha*). The previous teaching that the two dharmas of illusion and stillness are quiescent was the Middle Way as negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*).
The present teaching that the single mind is quiescent is the Middle Way as affirmation (*vidhi*). This means that the essence of this true mind is inherently quiescent from the beginning;
it is not quiescence defined by the absence of movement or lack of substance, nor is it cessation defined by existing and then disappearing. Therefore, it was previously called "perfect."

Awakening universally illuminates quiescence and non-duality; this is also identical to the "one mind" (*ekacitta*) of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The commentary states "therefore" below to conclude by returning to the intent of the sūtra: all are without intentionality toward that [object], and that itself is quiescent and extinguished. This is not like the aforementioned [state] where one deliberately makes it non-existent or extinguishes it. Therefore, it says "arising within.
