I shall now revert to the initial detailed outline to explain the text. Furthermore, there are two parts. First, the direct explanation. Regarding the phrase "thereby":

this refers within the Sūtra itself to the delusion of the four characteristics, such as the grasping at a self, mentioned in the preceding section. Second, regarding "the false": there are two interpretations.
That is to say, the substance of the aforementioned falsity is one delusion, and the re-grasping [of it] is another delusion; thus they constitute two. Furthermore, attachment and aversion...
The "two dharmas" refers to the two [types of objects]. The commentary states that these two "draw in others. Regarding "of one measure": there is nothing to be selected or measured;
"measure" (kui) here means to gauge. "Agreeable" means what is loved; upon encountering it, one immediately gives rise to karma. "Disagreeable" means what is loathed;
because they run toward each other, resentment increases, and one further creates karma. This master did not wish to repeat the phrasing, and thus simply says "resentment" (ei).
It is merely regrettable. If one does not speak of the creation of karma, how can one reconcile the statement in the sutras that both types of delusion give rise to the path of karma?
Among the ten thousand objects, none transcend the agreeable and the disagreeable; when the deluded person encounters them, both sides constitute karma.
Furthermore, as for the karma of a single lifetime, how could its quantity even be calculated? Alas, alas! Regarding the phrase "a single thought of greed, etc. in the commentary:

Nor is it separate from the two states of hatred and love. "To arise even slightly" means that as soon as the mind begins to stir, it is not yet fully formed—just like the expression "a fleeting thought.
Hell is the general category, while the "blades of swords" is a specific instance; both are instruments for undergoing suffering on the path to the underworld.

The preceding has already been explained. "Hell" is literally translated as "the vessel of suffering. Regarding the commentary on "loving form and so forth," the text is found in the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-sūtra*.

Regarding the commentary on "being entangled in emptiness": it refers to being stuck in the realm of emptiness, as if bound by shackles; this is being "entangled by emptiness," meaning one is ensnared by that object.

Alternatively, emptiness itself is originally without mind, yet it is the minds of the followers of the Two Vehicles that come to be entangled in the transformation into empty quiescence. Regarding the commentary on the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*).

"...this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. And so forth. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "due to recognizing the four marks (*lakṣaṇa*)": this explains the word "this" (*ci*) in the sutra. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "due to taking the beginningless [ignorance]":

this refers to the five dwelling grounds (*pañca-vāsa-bhūmi*) taught in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the original root": this is the fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodhi*) mentioned in the treatise; it is the source.
This refers to the intrinsically pure true mind (*tathatā-citta*). In the treatise, it is stated that non-enlightenment exists based upon fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
Regarding the scriptural citation, it refers to the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*.

As for the commentary’s initial explanation by means of the Dharma, the text is divided into three parts. First is the direct exposition. Within this, the mention of "the golden probe and the color of milk" refers to the commentary.
Regarding "both body and mind are ignorance," the *Śāstra* states: "Because it relies on non-awakening, the mind moves;

when it moves, there is suffering" (suffering being the body of birth-and-death). Thus, the fruit (the fruit of suffering) does not depart from its cause (ignorance). Furthermore, summarizing all three subtle and six coarse [delusions], it says: "All defiled dharmas."

All of these are characteristics of non-awakening (*a-bodha*). [The *Sūtra Commentary* states: "If one is in dark resonance with... and so forth. Second, this is an indirect clarification (*pratiṣedha-vyañjana*).
Since that [Awakening] is perfectly luminous, it reveals the purity of the mind. This continues until the end of the Sūtra, where it says that all is awakening;

thus one knows that this arises from fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), thereby forming the aforementioned successive layers of faults and afflictions, culminating in the final conclusion that all ignorance is overturned.
The categories are similar; the meaning is very clear. In the commentary (*śūtra*), following the phrase "previously obtained," there is an explanation by contrasting three aspects.

Within this, regarding the term "the work of Māra," it also implicitly includes the bodhicitta. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that practicing while forgetting the bodhicitta leads to being captured by Māra.
Regarding the subsequent metaphor in the commentary, the text has four parts: first, explaining non-interruption according to appearances, such as a person with ten million assets...
Wealth. One is stingy and begrudging toward each of these; yet, if one encounters circumstances that threaten life, one is willing to discard them all in order to preserve one's life.

Second, regarding the passage "Furthermore, there is the self" and below: this explains the severing of attachment in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*). Previously, it was only said that one cannot sever [attachment] oneself, which implies that there still remains a self to be severed;
thus, that was explained according to appearances (*lakṣaṇa*). Now, it is clarified that even while grasping, one is not yet aware that there is a self being grasped; this is...

Regarding these faults and afflictions: upon what basis can one speak of severing them? Even if one wishes to sever them, this too is but a delusive thought (*vikalpa*). When such thoughts are exhausted, there remains only the True Self (*ātman*).
Since the True Self is free from affliction, upon what basis could one wish to sever it? Now, we simply take the realization of namelessness as "severance";

thus it is called "intimate severance. Third, regarding the passage on the dream-body below: there are two explanations of the dream analogy, yet in the end, [the practitioner] is unwilling to sever [the body]. The above analogies follow accordingly.

Regarding the "characteristic" (xiàng): it must be understood that the character "awakening" (jué) following "already below" is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng), specifically the *gǎo* rhyme (古効反).
Furthermore, this analogy below also serves as an analogy for the subsequent text, which can be understood accordingly.
The meaning of "the seeds of the latent tendencies manifesting" is as explained previously. Regarding the citation from the *Ratnakūṭa*, it uses attachment as an example for aversion.

As for "falling into the evil destinies," this means not only failing to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood, but actually falling into the evil destinies. This has two implications: first, it is as stated in the third [chapter] regarding the "enmity of future lives";
second, since one already possesses attachment and a deluded mind, and attachment is the root of the six realms of existence, [it leads to further suffering]. Good.
Evil is repeated; suffering and pleasure revolve, continuing until the end of the future, such that one ultimately fails to escape the sufferings of the three miserable realms (*trāya*).

To say that one does not fall into the evil destinies through patience (*kṣānti*) is because one practices in accordance with the principle of non-self (*anātman*) and the meaning that craving is the root of suffering.
Therefore, one will certainly not fall. Regarding "constant" (*nitya*) in the commentary: it refers to the four [types of] delusion regarding consciousness and its objects, as previously explained.

These are the marks (*lakṣaṇa*). As for "the first fruit being excluded," this refers to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), wherein one realizes the true suchness (*tathatā*) of self-emptiness.

Regarding "the Arhat not yet understanding": these four marks obstruct perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). If the Arhat were to understand them, they would immediately awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, Tiantai taught that beyond the three realms there are sands-of-the-Ganges numbers of ignorance (*avidyā*); these attachments are precisely what constitute that number. This is the synthesis.
Regarding the term "Arhat," in the present text, for the sake of brevity and to correspond with the number of characters in the word "greed" (貪), it is explained concisely.

As for the commentary’s statement that "the 'self' is verified by means of phenomena": phenomena are what belong to the self (*ātmīya*). That which belongs to the self refers to all objective spheres and things belonging to one;

these include both sentient and insentient phenomena, all of which can be seen and known. Yet, the self itself cannot, in turn, see or know itself. Therefore, it is by means of objective spheres and phenomena that [the self] is [negated].
By examining what belongs to the self, one realizes that all other things are not the self; thus, one knows that the self is not those others.
The commentary states: "One who merely perceives the existence of mind" means that one knows all phenomena and objects are not the self, and that this very [perception] is called the self.

Regarding the term "in leisure" (*yàn jū*), the character *yàn* is pronounced with the departing tone (fourth tone), sounding like *yàn*. This follows the usage of the character *yàn* in the *Lúnyǔ* (Analects) for the phrase "dwelling in leisure."

Regarding the essence of awakening (*bodhi*): emptiness and stillness are its essence, which is *nirvāṇa*; knowing is its function, which is awakening. Thus, the essence is the function, and *nirvāṇa* is awakening;
the function is the essence, and awakening is *nirvāṇa*. Since essence and function are mutually identical, there is no separate essence that can be realized.
This corresponds to the third stage within the five gates of realizing the Way, wherein both subject and object are extinguished.

...is so. That which is the mark of self (*ātman*) is that which one falsely perceives as the *nirvāṇa* to be realized; what is realized is precisely the self, because "self" carries the meaning of "intrinsic substance.

Furthermore, when one truly realizes the true essence, since that is the *dharmakāya*, the true self, now, when one erroneously realizes a delusive essence, that is precisely the delusive self of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The analogy is quite clear. As for the commentator [Dharma]pāla, "pāla" means "protector," and "pāda" means "foot. Regarding the term "person" (*pudgala*), all...
In the commentaries on the *Śāstra*, the character "person" (人) frequently appears in its essential form. It may refer to one who can realize [the truth], or one who can grasp it;

even when speaking of a person or listening to a person—whether in terms of the real or the false—it is always referred to as such. This is like the Sanskrit term *buddha*, which is translated here as "the awakened one" (覺者).
This refers directly to persons. If one speaks of "bodhi," this merely denotes "awakening" and refers directly to phenomena (dharmas). The analogy is like this;
those who are widely learned should understand it for themselves.

Regarding the phrase "there is nothing that is not exhausted": it means there are no faults or transgressions that are not eliminated; rather, it signifies that all faults and transgressions have already been exhausted.
As for the statement "that emptiness and this wisdom": "that" refers to the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka*);

furthermore, these very grasped and grasper are definitively empty. Since the faults of all grasping have been exhausted, only emptiness remains as the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*). This is...
This is not yet fully understood; therefore, it is called "a small thing. In this state, all faults are exhausted, and only wisdom remains.

Although wisdom and emptiness differ, they both ultimately result in a single realm; thus, this is cited as proof. Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra* (Sūtra Commentary), "traces arise one after another":
since they arise in a continuous succession, these traces are inexhaustible. This means that many arisings occur without interruption, which is also the meaning of "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
Furthermore, according to the commentary following this passage, it explains itself by saying: "Sentient beings" refers to those who do not fixedly cling to a single [identity].

Therefore, it says here, "and so forth. Question: In the previous section on the characteristics of persons (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*), it was already stated that one does not grasp at subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*).
Why, then, at this point, is it said that they all successively become subject and object? Answer: That they all become subject and object refers to this person...

Having understood that these are faults, one does not recognize them as being correct. Among the characteristics of the preceding person, they perceived the mark of a self (*ātman*) as the fault of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*);
they merely perceived a single layer of subject and object, yet did not realize that this very wisdom is also called "subject.

Now, because this realization has become even deeper, one perceives that the infinite succession [of moments] is entirely subject and object. Is this not far superior to the former? Thus, the Sūtra says:
It is said that awakening is beyond reach (where "reach" implies being encompassed by all things). The subheading states: "The traces are realized as arising. The commentary explains:

"Because one realizes these are not fixed, one departs from the aforementioned errors. It further states: "One does not fixate on them as being determinate or singular. All of this is extremely clear.
In the section where the commentary cites an analogy to investigate and explain [the text], it concludes by stating: "Regarding oneself and regarding others, one does not calculate 'self' or 'person.
The following two phrases both state 'not that self. At first glance, these appear to be restatements of the preceding text; therefore, the word "後" (later/after) is used to separate them.

Nevertheless, fearing that this might still be difficult to discern, I shall further analyze it: the phrase "not that self" in the preceding sentence serves to conclude the explanation of the sūtra passage.
The heading states, "neither mine nor his," meaning that it is neither this nor that.
The subsequent phrase, "nor his mine," reiterates and explains the final sentence of the sutra, meaning that it simply speaks of the "mine" belonging to that person.

My name also belongs to that [category], yet this is not explicitly stated. Here, the "that-self" (pī-wo) in the first phrase is a *dvandva* (appositional compound), while the "that-self" in the second phrase is a *karmadhāraya* (descriptive compound).
Although the meaning may be quite simple and straightforward, the phrasing is somewhat obscure;
one must therefore pay close attention to analyze it.
The commentary states: "That which illuminates the mind" refers to the mind itself, one's own original mind.

In the preceding three gates, because they were characterized by specific qualities such as being able to realize, awaken, and comprehend, the term "mind" was not used. Now that all traces [of these distinctions] have ceased, it is called "mind.

This is as in the passage in the *Treatise* concerning the marks of difference and abiding; it simply says: "To be aware of the difference in thoughts is the mark of no-difference in thoughts; to be aware of..."
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) abides in the characteristic of non-abiding. Upon reaching the point where the initial arising-characteristic has already ceased, even subtle mindfulness is absent.

It is stated directly that when the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic; the meaning is entirely the same as this. This point is most profound and subtle; it should be reflected upon with care.

As for "purity" (*viśuddhi*), it also results from being free from the three characteristics previously mentioned—realization, understanding, and so forth—because the mind is simply self-illuminating. Thus it is called "self-."

"Awakening" (jue) means that one's own mind is capable of awakening; it does not mean awakening to a self. However, while the sutras speak of "illumination" (zhao), here we say "awakening" in accordance with the general conventions of commentaries and treatises, which mostly state that one awakens to both self and others.
Regarding terms such as "realization" (zhengwu) and so forth, they are equivalent to the character "comprehension" (liao).

That is to say, the mark of the self is called "realization," the mark of the person is called "awakening," and for sentient beings it is called "comprehension. Herein, because all things are exhausted within the totality, one penetrates the true source.
There is nothing else capable of verifying this and so forth. "This intending wisdom" refers to this illuminating wisdom. Regarding "karmic function":
the former was named according to that which is cultivated; this is named according to the capacity to initiate function. "But awakening to... and below clarifies the essence of this karmic wisdom.

This essence is precisely the "karmic aspect of karmic wisdom" mentioned in the treatise. It merely takes non-awakening as its object; it is the wisdom that recognizes this, wherein subtle thought remains latent.
Therefore, it is called the "characteristic of life-span. It is also called "Equal Enlightenment illuminating stillness. This is the wisdom that fulfills the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

However, because there is still a subtle trace of the characteristic of an "illuminator," it is not yet fully exhausted; thus, it is called the "veil of fine silk" (*paṭala*). This is difficult to perceive, just like the life-span.
Fundamentally, it is also a wisdom of functional capacity. What is referred to as "worldly spontaneous karma" [is this].

"Wisdom" refers to the wisdom that is obstructed by ignorance among those two types of obstructions; this has already been explained in the section on the "Two Obstructions" within the chapter on Maitreya.
As for the "characteristic of inconceivable activity," it is one of the two characteristics produced when fundamental awakening conforms to defilement, as fully described therein.
Because it is the wisdom capable of performing all functional activities, it is pointed out [as such].
As for its essential nature: that which removes delusion consists of the first three [stages]. That which does not remove it itself takes this as being correct;

thus, it becomes a latent recognition that remains unsevered, like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Regarding this single gate, except for those who have long cultivated meditative practice and whose mental application is subtle, there is no way to understand it even if it is revealed repeatedly in this manner.

The Commentary’s general reference to the preceding three aspects is as follows: "Awakening" (*jue*) is the collective name for mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). If these three names are explained individually, they are:

first, realization (*zheng*); second, awakening (*wu*); and third, comprehension (*liao*). If spoken of collectively, they are simply termed "awakening. Regarding the phrase "because the mind has not yet forgotten," this precisely explains the meaning of the name "dust and defilement" (*chen-gou*) in relation to the "illumination of the mind.
That is to say, one knows that if the mind forgets "this and that"—where "that" refers to the three [aspects] and "this" refers to the illumination—[then it is defiled].
The immediate illumination of the mind is precisely the natural wisdom of karma (as annotated above). Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the exhaustion of both self and wisdom":
this refers to the exhaustion of both the four marks of the self (*ātman*) and of wisdom. "Self and wisdom" means the self and wisdom; it does not mean "the wisdom of the self."

"Radiant essence stands alone" is the phrase of Master Daosheng. The *Essentials of Mind* by the Great Master Qingliang also says: "When a single thought does not arise, the past and future limits are severed; radiant essence stands alone; things and self are both thus. If one compares these four lines with the preceding text in detail, they correspond perfectly from beginning to end; therefore, I have taken this single line as representative. If one were to rely on the literal opposition between the beginning and the end of the text, it would instead be appropriate to say: [The text continues: "The mind-ground is originally tranquil and still; the myriad phenomena are all empty and silent. The ten directions are vast and open, like empty space; the six senses are pure and clear, like a mirror. The body of reality is eternally present, without coming or going; the nature of the dharma is inherently complete, without increase or decrease. Thus, the former text speaks of the ultimate principle, while the latter describes the phenomenal manifestation. Although the two differ in their respective expressions, their meaning is identical. This is because the former clarifies the essence, while the latter elucidates its function. Since the essence and function are non-dual, the two texts are mutually complementary. Therefore, although the phrasing differs, the underlying intent is the same. It is for this reason that I have selected the single line [from the *Essentials of Mind*] as the representative expression. It is said: "When water freezes, it becomes ice; when the ice melts, the water remains. When the mind is deluded, it becomes the self; when the self is exhausted, the mind remains.

Now, the two characters for "mind" (心) and "water" (水) both share the common attribute of moisture. This is especially so in light of the phrase "the illuminating essence standing alone," as they correspond to one another in this regard.
This is consistent with the Dharma. That the nature of moisture alone remains is called "the illuminating essence standing independently. Question:

You say that this "illuminating essence standing independently" is the wondrous wisdom that is free from thought and devoid of marks. Yet the Sūtra states that "mental illumination" is a subtle affliction of the mark of life-span (*āyus-saṃskāra*).
How can you use that to correspond to this? Answer: As soon as there is movement within the moisture, it is named "waves. When the waves have ceased, the moisture [remains].

The nature is fundamentally true; it merely arises from illumination, which is then termed the "life-principle" (*jīvātman*). When this life-principle is exhausted, the essence of illumination is revealed as inherently wondrous.
That which arises from illumination is the perception of all-encompassing awareness. Furthermore, the cited passage merely serves to illustrate the analogy between the fundamental and the derivative;
it does not directly explain the sutra itself. Within the sutra, there is originally no mention of "water and moisture," nor is there any reference to "true mind. This is the analogy.
In the middle [section], it simply speaks of "ice-water. In the Dharma, it simply speaks of "illuminating all-encompassing awareness. Ice and water must depend upon water;

the moist nature of water never undergoes change or extinction. Thus, one knows that illuminating awareness must depend upon the true mind, and the illuminating essence of the mind likewise never undergoes change or extinction.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*,
Fascicle Twelve (Part One) and Fascicle Twelve (Part Two).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.
This is the third major section from here on: "Abiding in the Self and Losing the Way. This section has two parts: first, a general indication of losing the way;

second, an extensive explanation through successive stages. Regarding the first: as for the phrase "the six perfections over many kalpas," this was discussed in detail and fully cited previously; one may consult that for reference.
Regarding "one who knows the thief": the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Just as when a person recognizes a thief, the thief can do nothing;
'damage' means gradual depletion, and 'ruin' means sudden destruction. As for the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*), it contains all seeds of both defiled and pure phenomena;
this is the *ālayavijñāna*. The very essence of this consciousness is the *tathāgatagarbha* (the womb of the Tathāgata). The *tathāgatagarbha*...
Thus, it alone contains immeasurable, boundless, and Ganges-sand-like supreme and wondrous merits, all as previously explained.

However, the distinction between the meanings of these two names lies in the difference between the provisional and the ultimate teachings. As the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s pure storehouse..."
The worldly *ālaya* is like gold and a ring; they are mutually indistinguishable. Furthermore, it is said that those of inferior wisdom do not know that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the *ālayavijñāna*.
Regarding "poverty and so forth," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "They are impoverished, lacking both merit and wisdom."
Entering the perilous path of birth and death—now, I shall employ this by taking its essential meaning.
The commentary states: "Even if one recognizes me," the intended meaning is that Nirvana is the true nature of all phenomena; it is my very essence.
This is also *nirvāṇa*. Even if one recognizes it as the realization of a self, what contradiction would there be? What hindrance would it pose to the Path?
The commentary states that while the objects of one’s former attachment remain the same—namely, the five desires and *nirvāṇa*—the mind that feels attachment does not differ;
that is, the very mind that formerly loved the five desires is now once again used to love *nirvāṇa*.
The same applies to hatred by analogy. Regarding "original habituation": it is because the perfuming has matured since beginningless kalpas.

Regarding "craving is the root of birth and death," this was already explained in the Chapter on Maitreya. "Sprouts" refers to the craving for the retribution of karma. Regarding "not knowing craving and so forth," the full text says:
"Not knowing that craving is the true nature of birth and death, one separately hates birth and death; this is called not being liberated."

Regarding the statement "the dharmas of the śāstra do not lead to liberation": because it was previously questioned and explained that "I am not liberated" due to erroneously realizing *nirvāṇa*, it is now questioned again:
How is it known that the *dharma* of the realized *nirvāṇa* is erroneous, is craving, and is the root of saṃsāra, such that one says one is not liberated?
The commentary states, "As for those who have truly realized," which explains this in accordance with the preceding text. Now, however—
Reasoning by way of reductio ad absurdum (prasanga) clarifies that [the claim] is not real. That is to say, once it is verified that anger and joy arise, one knows that there is a self;

knowing there is a self, one knows that [enlightenment] has not yet been realized. To claim realization when it has not been realized is known to be unreal. The point of this verification lies in the text.
The commentary states: "The grasping of self-identity remains firm" refers to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*’s description of this eighth consciousness as follows:
it "appropriates the sense organs and the body, taking them as its internal self. It is subtle and unknowable; its external transformation of the receptacle world is likewise unknowable.

"Latent storage" (*saṃniviṣṭa*) means that it and the defiled phenomena serve as both the container and the contained for one another. "Continuity" (*prabandha*) indicates, as explained in the sūtras, that it has never been interrupted. Wisdom...
Regarding the mobilization of the army: *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* serve as the generals; the myriad practices that aid the Path serve as the soldiers.

As previously mentioned, those of sharp faculties have already entered the Universal Eye Contemplation and the Three Contemplations; however, those of dull faculties, though possessing the two wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*), are obstructed by the four marks (*catvāraḥ lakṣaṇāḥ*).

Thus, their wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) has not yet been aroused. For this reason, the preceding text of this section further states: "Though one undergoes diligent suffering for many kalpas..."

This is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, it is recorded briefly in the commentary. Regarding "the hosts of Māra being repeatedly crushed": this refers to having subdued and attained [mastery over] coarse and superficial delusions, and having ceased all evil karma;
thus, there is the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). The rest is as explained in the commentary.

As for *ālaya*, this is translated as "clinging storehouse" (*zhí-cáng*); all of this has already been explained in the previous main chapter. "City" refers to taking the sense organs, the physical body, the seeds, and the receptacle world as its objects.
This refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect). That which exercises sovereignty is the mark of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*), which corresponds to the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect).

Because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is subtle and difficult to discern, it is hard to assail. When the noble ones of the three vehicles reach the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they sever the heavy residues of afflictions (*kleśa-dausthulya*) within this consciousness;
when these are ultimately exhausted, they no longer grasp the ālayavijñāna as a self, and are thus able to permanently lose [the state of] the ālayavijñāna.

This is a name. It does not mean that the substance of consciousness is abandoned. It is like a powerful minister of a state who does not submit to the imperial transformation, but usurps the title of King for himself.

Later, when imperial troops repeatedly campaign against him, he finally surrenders after a long time. He relinquishes his royal title, and the Emperor grants him amnesty; his life is spared, and he is entrusted once more with the authority of the state.

The "Emperor of Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*) is also like this. The correspondence [between the two] can be understood. (The above is all from the commentary on the text. Firmly grasping and maintaining [it], it remains latent...)

[This refers to] the *ālayavijñāna* as a hidden treasure. The commentary on the verse regarding "the City of Enlightenment" (*Bodhimaṇḍa*) and so forth states: The text says that love and hatred arise in the mind, and thus one cannot enter the City of Enlightenment.

This means that the *ālayavijñāna* and enlightenment are not two separate cities; rather, based on the distinction between the deluded and awakened mind, they are conceptually divided into the two realms of defilement and purity.
Therefore, it is said that [this city] is conceptually equivalent to the inversion of this [present] city. Regarding "conceptually equivalent," in the scriptural text at this point...
There is no word for "city" [in the root text]; however, the commentators established it as a metaphor to correspond with the "city" in the verse.
If we rely on the essence, the two cities are not different; they serve as metaphors just as Chang'an was occupied by Zhu Ci.

At that time, all the ministers and subjects of the empire called it the "City of Rebels," yet from the Xingyuan and Zhenyuan eras onward, everyone called it the "Imperial City. The city itself did not change.
To summarize, this refers to those who govern and lead others. Those who govern and lead are none other than *prajñā* (wisdom) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, it is said that delusion and awakening are divided into two. Consequently, the verse on the City of Awakening (*bodhipura*) that follows states: "If one can return to the land of awakening, how could its manifestation not be evident? Question:
Previously, you yourself raised an analogy, stating that even one who usurps the title of King, after surrendering, has their life and nature preserved.
Now you further say that it is like Zhu Ci; yet Zhu Ci was precisely the one who executed Xian. Is this not a contradiction? Answer:

Previously, the king was used as a metaphor for the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*); since the king’s life remained intact, [the analogy held]. Now, the city is used as a metaphor for the substance of consciousness; the city likewise remains undestroyed. Each has its specific application.
Why suddenly take the previous metaphor of the non-duality of the substance of consciousness to challenge this [distinction between] delusion and awakening, thereby attempting to overturn it?
This is the meaning of "covering" (*nivṛti*). The *manas* is a constant attendant; it may also be called an "inner attendant.

It exclusively takes internal objects as its conditions and constantly clings to the perceived aspect (*dṛṣṭi-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as the self. Because it arises in dependence upon that [eighth consciousness] and constantly takes it as its object, it is said to be a "constant attendant.

Since it possesses the four functional activities of self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and self-pride (*ātma-māna*), it is said to "protect"; that is, it protects the self. As for "firm and strong":

The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)—which is also attained during the stage of training (śaikṣa)—and the supramundane path (lokottaramārga), such as the first fruit (srotāpanna), although they temporarily suppress and extinguish [the afflictions], do not permanently sever them.
It is only upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) within the three vehicles that they are permanently severed and extinguished.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that these afflictions associated with the afflicted manas (kliṣṭamanas) are innate (*sahaja*) and thus are not abandoned through the path of insight (*darśana-heya*). As for "consciousness" (*manovijñāna*), it refers to the sixth [consciousness], which is capable of...
It grasps all phenomena and is capable of creating the karma of the three realms; therefore, it is called the "minister.

It universally takes as its objects the internal and external, the three times, the three natures, and the fifty-one mental factors; therefore, it is called "managing. Furthermore, it pervades the five consciousnesses;

as soon as the five consciousnesses arise abruptly, this manas functions as their simultaneous object-condition; therefore, it is called "supervising. Together with the five generals in their respective positions, it is thus described.

"Six aspects. "The leader of the thieves" refers to the master of the six thieves; because I am the master, and because there are the gateways of the six sense organs, I am able to pass through them and sport.
(This explains "sporting with the various faculties. "The thief's name" refers to what was previously stated as being "for the sake of the Dharma."
Hating that and crossing over this, one does not know that this mind is originally one's own mark of selfhood; thus one immediately knows that one has been robbed by others of the title of "Dharma.

The rest is as explained in the commentary. Regarding the phrase "greed for titles," etc.: greedily craving the city and palace, one governs the assembly of kings (in the departing tone), transforming the noble and the humble, the clergy and the laity, who all flock to him with reverence and offerings.
He himself claims to preach the Dharma out of compassion and pity for sentient beings.
They seek to deliver others, yet they do not realize that it is all the hidden flow of craving that has merely changed its name and appearance.
Sometimes, harboring anger within their hearts toward others, they use various harsh words to scold them, or strike them with clubs, or drive them out.

They claim this is for the sake of the Dharma—to subdue demons, punish evil, and encourage goodness—yet they do not realize that this is again the hidden influence of thoughts such as hatred, resentment, and aversion.
It is a matter of changing names and altering appearances. Thus, Master Zhigong said: "Two heads cannot be distinguished; they mingle within the royal city.
Because of such various transformations of identity, it causes me—the Dharma-preacher and converter—to fail to perceive the thief, instead regarding him as a source of spiritual efficacy.
Being entirely unliberated from the ocean of suffering, they remain complacent, neither startled nor afraid; thus, while still bound themselves, they seek to untie the bonds of others.
Therefore, it is said that they delude the Dharma King. Regarding those who "invade the borders": if one discusses the boundaries of the Dharmakāya, [they are as follows].

Pervading the Dharma-realm and throughout the ten directions, even the realm of sentient beings and the realm of the physical vessel are all identical to the state of true purity; they are entirely a realm free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Defilement and purity originally possess no dual substance. Now, it is only because of delusion regarding the six objects—form and so forth—that one regards them as definitely existing as six external dusts outside the mind;
this is the realm of ignorance and the self-mastering subject. Upon awakening, one realizes that these six dusts and form are themselves emptiness.

Form is not different from emptiness; it merely arises as a transformation of one's own mind. All of it is entirely the form of emptiness. It is the same for the remaining [objects] such as sound, fragrance, and so forth.
This is precisely the samādhi of form and the other [sensory objects], called the six wondrous realms; it is the very sphere of the Prajñā Dharmakāya.
Now, because I have awakened to this realm as belonging to me, I unconsciously give rise to delusion and secretly grasp it as existing;

I secretly generate attachment, which in turn recreates the mundane world of dust. Hence it is said that they "frequently encroach. Viewed from this perspective, it is difficult to clarify and difficult to stabilize.

Therefore, it is said that they "disturb my contemplation of the object. "Contemplation" (guān) refers to contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*), which is insight; it is the practice of contemplation, which is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Object" (*viṣaya*) does not exceed the six sense objects and the realm of *tathatā* (suchness). At whatever time one contemplates, that becomes the object.

As for those who are externally timid, because they possess an awakened mind and constantly desire to remain vigilant, their deluded thoughts appear inferior; thus, they do not dare intentionally give rise to emotions or commit acts of greed or hatred.
Karma waits in ambush; its observation is clear and manifest.

Just as one remains hidden during the daytime, it causes those who investigate the principles of body and mind to see only themselves as a person of clear awakening and understanding, one who does not seek fame or profit, one who acts for the sake of the Dharma and serves as a teacher, and one who is entirely without fault.
Thus it is said that [karma] "hides by day. Yet, when one is personally confronted with circumstances of adversity or favor...
When external circumstances run contrary to one’s sentiments and are utterly displeasing; when deluded habits obscure the mind such that one fails to perceive what is right before one’s face;
and when everything is as dark as a pitch-black night—one then gives rein to arbitrary calculations and various emotions arise.
One may contemplate retreating in defeat, or contravening human ethics and the Dharma, or devising some other form of adjustment, or deliberating upon principles in order to vindicate oneself.
One attributes one's own faults to others; because various [defilements] arise without being recognized as non-virtuous, it is called "wandering at night.

Regarding the phrase "internally harboring" (*neijie*): the meaning of the character *jie* (harbor) is as described in the *Shiji*, where Cao Cao, before ascending to the throne, was styled "Lord Cao" (*Caogong*) and "harbored the Son of Heaven" (*jietianzi*) to command the feudal lords.
Here, this single character is used for rhetorical effect to refer to ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth.

This refers to the objects of the six consciousnesses as described above—whether they be awakened or delusory, dormant or active—as well as the seeds within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) consisting of the three subtle and five coarse [evolutions], along with those of the seventh manas-consciousness and its co-nascent notions of self and so forth; these constitute the fundamental root of the beginningless dwelling-place.
It is never abandoned or separated. Even when a practitioner is engaged in conscious observation and contemplation, this [consciousness] continues to flow secretly;
therefore, it is said that "day and night it is uninterrupted. This precisely explains the scriptural phrase "never interrupted. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"This consciousness, from beginningless time, is a single, continuous stream, always uninterrupted; it is the fundamental basis for the designation of realms, destinies, and births."

Therefore, it is of a nature that firmly maintains its seeds so that they are not lost; thus, it constantly evolves in conjunction with internal habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), external objects of contact, and other such phenomena.
However, the meaning of the eight consciousnesses employed herein has already been fully established in the main body of this treatise, and therefore shall not be explained here.

Regarding the phrase "therefore, it is inferred and examined": the scriptural text explains the case of those who revile [the teaching] by way of contrast, whereas it explains the case of those who preach the Dharma in accordance with it.

If the commentary (*śāstra*) were to explain each case both contrastively and in accordance with the other, and if the scriptural text were likewise to explain each case both contrastively and in accordance with the other, it should have said:
"If one knows that the self is empty, there is no one who can revile the self; yet if there is one who reviles the self, it is because the self is ultimately empty. If one knows the self...
"Empty. [The Buddha] taught the Dharma as being without self; [yet some say] he taught the Dharma as having a self because his own notion of self was not yet severed.

The rest of the text is intelligible. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "each only increases [the fault]": water and soil, when infused with licorice, increase its sweet flavor; when infused with *gegen* (yellow-bitter ginseng), they increase its bitterness.
The bitter taste increases; thus we know it arises from the seed and not from the soil or water.

By this analogy, one knows that while the myriad practices supported by the notion of a self-identity constitute the work of Māra, those supported by awakened wisdom constitute the cause of Buddhahood. Therefore, we know that it depends on the mind and not on the myriad practices.
This point is extremely important and may be made clear.
Regarding "counting the treasures of others": it is said in full, for example, that a poor person spends all day counting the treasures of others, yet has not even half a coin for himself;
so it is with those who are indolent. Regarding "suppressing the high": this refers to claiming that the Buddha’s sphere of understanding and sphere of practice is merely like...
Because his mind operates within the realm of such conduct, it is said that he "descends. As for "galloping," it means he gallops through his own [conceit], claiming:
"I have already realized Bodhi; I have already attained Nirvana; I have already completed the task of becoming a Buddha."

That which is attained through the commentary is the principle; this is *nirvāṇa*. "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to realization. Because one realizes the principle, it is simply called the "body. "Body" means essence;
that is, the very essence of wisdom itself is what is termed "realization," just as there is the "self-verifying portion" (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) among the various consciousnesses.

Regarding the fundamental precepts: for *bhikṣus* there are four grave offenses, while for *bhikṣuṇīs* there are eight. As for the great falsehood, both monks and nuns are identical in this regard. That is to say:
To say of oneself, "I have attained superhuman states," and so forth, even claiming, "I know and I see," constitutes a false and deceptive lie.

This excludes cases of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), which is what that [other text] excludes; therefore, it is said that this is not the intent of the present text. That [other case] constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*), whereas here there is no offense.
In this case, one’s realization and understanding are cumulative; in that case, there is nothing cumulative.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "it may be a realization": even if one attains the non-duality of self and others, rejoices in the excellence and virtue of others, and yet remains personally uncertain—this may be the power of realization, or it may be a delusion unrelated to realization.
For example, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru have a mental disposition of non-self; would this then be considered realization?
Furthermore, how could there be the active manifestation of envy and so forth in the higher realms? Therefore, we know that for oneself—
Examining the traces of the mind, one observes whether they accord with the practice of the Path; yet, this is not yet a definitive conclusion.

If, upon examining the traces of the mind, there are matters such as jealousy, envy, anger, or resentment, then one knows for certain that it is not the Path—excepting the case of a Great Bodhisattva’s practice of "counter-flowing" (pratiloma).

However, regarding the fundamental traces of the mind in relation to what accords with or deviates from the Path, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, those that accord exclusively [with the Path], such as when a Bodhisattva rejoices in the virtues of others...
1. Practicing generosity and so forth is exclusively concordant. 2. Being foolish and ignorant, harboring jealousy and envy, and committing acts such as killing is exclusively discordant. 3.

That which is both concordant and discordant includes, for example, the killing and so forth of a Bodhisattva, where the mind is concordant but the outward trace is discordant; or the generosity and so forth of a foolish person, where the mind is discordant but the outward trace is concordant. 4. That which is neither discordant nor concordant.

This refers to the Buddha (who is unimpeded regarding both defilement and purity because he is entirely without [discursive] mind), as well as the Arhat (who does not conform because he lacks the wisdom, vows, and great compassion; yet he does not oppose [the path] because his afflictions, karma, and suffering have been exhausted).

If one were to establish four propositions based solely on whether the mind conforms to or opposes the path, and whether it is determinate or indeterminate, they would be: first, determinately conforming to the path; second, determinately opposing the path—these correspond to the first two propositions mentioned previously;
third, determinately both opposing and conforming, which refers to when a Bodhisattva has self-knowledge; fourth, indeterminate in both opposing and conforming, which refers to...
Those who are beginners cannot, through practices such as giving, discern [the nature of reality] for themselves; the same applies when observing the goodness of others.
The commentary states that they ultimately cannot enter pure awakening because, in each of the preceding sections, it was concluded that they do not enter awakening.
To speak broadly, this is all rooted in self-love (*ātmasneha*). However, if one were to fully clarify how one enters awakening:

One must find its gateway. In the *Huayan xuanyi zhang* (Profound Meaning of the Avataṃsaka), consisting of fifteen sections (also composed by Master Zang), the tenth section clarifies the Gateway to the Expedient Means for Entering the Path.
It has three parts: first, discerning the mind; second, discerning the object; third, performing the superior practices of cultivation. These are fully cited in a separate volume.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that the *Sūtra* mentions "śrāvakas and others," some say this refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, though I have not yet had the opportunity to verify it;
its general intent can be understood. As for the instruction that one must first "awaken the mind," this means recognizing the true mind that is neither born nor extinguished.

Even if one is partial or dogmatic, having something to rely upon is not an obstacle to seeking out teachers and friends everywhere to investigate and harmonize with their teachings, or to study the sūtras and śāstras.

[This] completes [the discussion]. If there is nothing at all to be acknowledged, and the mind and intentions are in a state of frantic agitation, what benefit is there in hearing [the teachings] in such disorder?
It is like a person born blind hearing others dispute over the characteristics of colors; each person holds to their own word—what could they possibly believe?

Those who merely rely on names and categories are, for the time being, people belonging to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiangzong). This is because the sutras state that "only much learning is beneficial," and [this view] accords with that intent. If one were to refute [this]:

Among those belonging to the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇavāda), namely the principles of the Yogācāra school, although they do not particularly esteem names and categories, none of them strive to reflect upon their own minds.

Such individuals are termed "those who study through wisdom" (prajñā-śikṣā); as this is not the characteristic of one who is "learned in the scriptures" (bahuśruta), it is omitted here and not discussed.

Regarding those who merely increase their sense of self: even if they truly acquire extensive knowledge of names and categories, such that they know everything when questioned, or are skilled in establishing and refuting arguments to dismantle the discourse of others, they nonetheless further increase their signs of selfhood (*ātman*) and deceive or look down upon others. Thus, some say:

"The sūtras and śāstras are the causes for the emergence of sentient beings, yet through understanding them, greed and hatred instead grow longer. This refers to the case of spontaneous pride and arrogance.
Gao: This point is the same for both the schools of the Dharma-character (Faxiang) and the Shattering of Characteristics (Poxiang).

If we rely on the mind of discrimination, those who definitely identify with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and have not yet eliminated the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) are exclusively followers of the Faxiang school, as they increase their views of self. As for the followers of the Poxiang school...

There is no intentional determination [of the view], because they do not establish a fixed doctrine. Question: If one understands the Dharma yet treats others with contempt, saying, "My own characteristics are increasing," since the view they cling to is already fixed, how can it be said that it is "increasing"?
Answer: There is indeed a sense of "increase" here; it refers to those who have not practiced the teachings and merely hold their views spontaneously.
If they hear an interpreter say that something exists or does not exist, or that it is the same as the Buddha or different from the Buddha, [their attachment intensifies].

All are indeterminate as to whether they believe or do not believe. If one who studies the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) were to encounter this, they would certainly not believe that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) lack a self.

Thus we know that their grasping views become increasingly firm; hence it is said that [the afflictions] increase. Regarding the phrase "unable to comprehend one's own mind," the commentary subsequently asks:
"How can one know the right path? It is because of inverted wisdom (*viparyāsa-prajñā*) that all evils increase. As for "all evils," this refers to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Within this, once aversion increases, it is due to not understanding the mind; thus, it is identical to increasing the self.

Since one does not seek awakening, one should know that seeking awakening is what causes one to understand the mind; therefore, this is cited as proof. Furthermore, since inverted wisdom is established through not understanding the mind, one knows that one must first understand the mind.
Based on the textual meaning of this proof, the essential point of the four lines is: "Conditioned by... (pratyaya).

To study [this] yet lack both hearing and wisdom is like an ox among humans; one clearly knows nothing at all. Only by possessing these two qualities can one know the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This is precisely what was previously realized as the pure, perfect *bodhi*: it is identical to the mind of pure awakening.

In the commentary (*śūtra*), regarding the prior section on "severing delusions" (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), there are two parts: first, the provisional assignment of the text to the sūtra; second, from "Now, as for severing delusions," the explicit clarification of the meaning of severance.

Within this [second part], there are three sections, as listed in the commentary. Regarding the phrase "The commentary states," the text has three parts: first, a brief indication of the two treatises (*śāstra*).

Regarding the section "Second, Consciousness-Only" below, the number is indicated in general. Within this, the term "fundamental" (*mūla*) and so forth refers to what is designated as "fundamental" in the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, whereas the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* simply calls them "afflictions" (*kleśa*).
The prose commentary explains them as "fundamental," as cited in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*);

that is to say, the six beginning with greed (*lobha*) are the roots of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Although they are subsequently also termed secondary afflictions, they remain the root...

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that those [factors] subsumed under the root [afflictions] do not receive the name "affliction" (*kleśa*) solely by virtue of being of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*);

they are not called "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*). The seventh chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains that while all afflictions are secondary afflictions, there are secondary afflictions that are not afflictions.

For this reason, even the root afflictions themselves may be designated as "secondary," because they also arise in dependence upon others. Factors such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth are called only "secondary," but are not called "afflictions."

"Affliction (*kleśa*). Because it is not fundamental, the commentary states, "Although they are equal," which serves as a general response to an objection. The objection asks: "The treatise clearly states that these are fundamental afflictions;

how can you previously judge them to be derivative? This is the response to that. "Delusion regarding the truth" refers to the aforementioned fundamental initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) from the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

In the commentary on the chapter on the eight consciousnesses, section three explains the treatise’s interpretation of the scriptural text in six parts: first, the explanation of the root afflictions; second, the explanation of the secondary afflictions;

third, the determination of the presence or absence of numerical categories; fourth, the increase or decrease in the number of afflictions; fifth, the expansion upon the aforementioned numbers; and sixth, the explanation of the underlying intent of the scriptural repetition.
The first section has two parts. First, the analysis of the term *tṛṣṇā* (craving). Although there are four [types] mentioned in the Sūtra, according to the Śāstra, there are only three.
This is because among the six afflictions (*kleśa*) in that treatise, *tṛṣṇā* is not mentioned separately; thus, one knows it is subsumed within *lobha* (greed).

Therefore, in Maitreya’s text, he frequently speaks of "greed and craving" (*lobhatṛṣṇā*) without distinguishing them as two separate entities. If one were to distinguish their differences in detail: *tṛṣṇā* is more subtle and deep-seated, whereas *lobha* is somewhat coarse and violent.
The former takes craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its basis. Furthermore, there are three—craving, greed (*lobha*), and so forth—as well as objects that accord with one's feelings;

these are mutually related as being internal and external. That is to say, first, regarding the internal mind, "craving" is commonly used; regarding sublime objects, "greed" is commonly used. Next, regarding the internal mind, "greed" is used, while regarding sublime objects, "desire" (*kāma*) is used.
Therefore, it is stated in various places that form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates constitute the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). Subsequently, furthermore, "desire" is...
The mind of covetous desire also belongs to the internal; the wondrous object is the desired object, which alone belongs to the external.
Therefore, Śāriputra said: "The wondrous objects of the world are not true desire; true desire is the covetousness that enters into conceptual discrimination.

For this reason, in the texts of Maitreya as well as in various sūtras and teachings, it is sometimes called "covetous craving" (tṛṣṇā) and sometimes called "covetous desire" (rāga); the character for "covetousness" (貪) appears frequently.

This applies to both locations. Regarding the passage "As for those who are greedy... and below, there are two explanations for the remaining three [fetters]. Within the explanation of greed (*rāga*), it says "regarding existence" (*bhava*);

this refers to future existence (*punar-bhava*), which is exclusively the fruit of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*) as maturation (*vipāka*). "Possessors of existence" (*bhavopakarana*) refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), along with afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), because these are the requisites for the three realms of existence.
Alternatively, there are no untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*); as stated in the lower section of the treatise, "untainted [phenomena] do not exist."

Greed (*lobha*) is the desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*). Now, according to the Mahāyāna teaching, attachment to the Buddha and greed that has been extinguished are both defiled (*kliṣṭa*);

therefore, they arise together with views (*dṛṣṭi*). [The commentary] states "regarding existence" (*bhava*) below; this second [section] clarifies the essential nature and function [of greed]. Because it is deluded regarding contaminated existence (*sāsrava-bhava*), even uncontaminated dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) which can nourish and increase existence are also called "instruments of existence" (*bhava-upakaraṇa*).
However, if they accord with the nourishment and growth of the uncontaminated, they are not [such instruments]. [The commentary] states "by means of" (*yena*) below, following...

This is explained by resolving the difficulty: it means that whether it be the initiation of karma (*karmābhinirvṛtti*) or the moistening of rebirth (*janmopabṛṃhaṇa*), both cause the arising of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*).

It does not mean that only the moistening of afflictions (*kleśa*) is intended. In the two upper realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*), because of craving for meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth, the various afflictions increase on this basis, and thus the appropriated aggregates also arise.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 8, also states this; likewise do fascicles 55, 58, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the *Pañcaskandhaka*.
Regarding the Abhidharma, all these have been explained in detail. As for "in relation to suffering," this means that all three types of suffering increase based on hatred (*dveṣa*).
This is because not only do the specific objects of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*) possess it, but hatred also arises based on the loss of pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*).

Regarding "objects of suffering," all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena that can produce suffering are objects of suffering; hatred arises based upon them. Question: Regarding contaminated [phenomena] that are concordant with...
The dharmas of suffering may be called instruments of suffering (*duḥkha-sādhana*). Since the untainted (*anāsrava*) does not accord with suffering, how can it be called an instrument of suffering?

Answer: That which accords with the instruments of suffering is not itself untainted. Because [the mind] gives rise to suffering by taking [something] as its object, the untainted is also [included in this category].

Therefore, those such as wrong views who slander the non-existence of the untainted all invite rebirth in the evil destinies. The rest is as explained in other volumes. Regarding the commentary’s mention of "hatred and so forth": hatred necessarily gives rise to karma; it does not...
It is designated as being comprised within the nature of the wholesome, because that which incites unwholesome karma is necessarily unwholesome. "Unpeaceful" means a lack of tranquility.
The Abhidharma states: "Because one harbors hatred and malice, one dwells frequently in suffering. Thus, this anger serves as the basis for unwholesome conduct and lack of peace.

Regarding "the hindrance of non-conceit" (*anauddhatya-vibandha*): the preceding text of that treatise states that non-conceit is subsumed under one part of faith (*śraddhā*), meaning that because one has faith in that [object], one does not feel conceit toward it;
or it is subsumed under one part of relinquishment (*tyāga*), because one whose mind is equanimous (*samacitta*) is not arrogant;

or it is subsumed under one part of shame (*hrī*), because one who reveres that [object] does not feel conceit toward it. (In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, it is stated that conceit has the function of producing disrespect and suffering. Of these, the third meaning is superior, as reverence is included within shame.)

"Because of [the need to] respect teachers and elders," etc. The Commentary (*śāstra*) states "if there is... and so forth; the treatise simply says "toward virtue and those possessing virtue. Now, this [passage] refers to that.

The Commentary says "toward superior virtuous qualities (*guṇa*) and those possessing virtue"; this is intended to facilitate the understanding of the meaning. "By this... and so forth, reveals the instruction to cultivate revulsion and abandon [pride], lest one continue to transmigrate.
However, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is simply because of the existence of a self (*ātman*) that the mind becomes haughty; in the Commentary...
This refers to that which is associated with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), as well as that which arises from its outflow (*niṣyanda*), or is explained by tracing it back to its root.

In the commentary on the distinctions of pride (*māna*) below, although there are seven types and nine types, they do not exceed arising upon five factors: namely, the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior, along with the self and superior qualities.
Regarding the seven types of pride, they are explained in terms of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); that is, one gives rise to the first [type] toward those who are inferior.
First is pride (*māna*). This refers to considering oneself superior to those who are inferior, or considering oneself equal to those who are equal.

Regarding the middling degree, there arises *adhimāna* (excessive pride), which is considering oneself superior to those who are equal, or considering oneself equal to those who are superior. Regarding the superior degree, there arises *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride), which is considering oneself superior to those who are superior.

Regarding the aggregates of self (*ātma-skandha*), there arises *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"), which is the haughty elevation based on self-reliance. Regarding qualities that have not yet been clearly understood, there arises...
Regarding overweening pride (*adhimāna*): although one has attained only a small portion, one claims to have attained much;

thus, toward those of superior grade, one gives rise to the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), reckoning oneself as slightly inferior to others who are far superior. Regarding the pride of error (*mithyāmāna*): when one has no attainment, one claims to have attained;
this pride of error consists in claiming to possess what is entirely non-existent. As for overweening pride, it is when one has attained only a little, yet claims it to be much and preeminent.

[The distinction between] the two [types of pride] is due to [the difference between] qualities (*guṇa*) and [their] absence. However, regarding the three categories [of objects], four types of pride arise; regarding the self, one type of pride arises; regarding qualities, two types of pride arise;

and regarding the five bases, seven types of pride arise. As for the nine [types of pride]: by cross-referencing and combining the aforementioned three—namely, pride (*māna*), over-pride (*atimāna*), and inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*)—nine are formed.
Thus, while the seven are broad, the nine are narrow; they can simply be understood through the three [categories of] "I," "existence," and "non-existence."

The character "ge" (each) is paired respectively with the three grades of superior, equal, and inferior, thus forming nine [types of pride]. However, these nine types of pride are not seen in the texts of the Mahāyāna.
The first fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* merely states that, as explained in the Sūtras, there are three categories of pride:
the category of "I am superior," "I am equal," and "I am inferior. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (199), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (19), and the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* [also treat this matter].
Twenty. It is said that there are nine types of pride (*māna*), as cited in the commentary. Specifically, *adhimāna*, *mānātimāna*, and *ūnamāna* constitute the first three;
*ūnamāna*, *māna*, and *adhimāna* constitute the middle three; and *māna*, *adhimāna*, and *ūnamāna* constitute the final three.
Regarding the note that these form nine by grouping them in threes: these three types of pride each become three because the objects they relate to are distinct.
Regarding the three types of *māna* (pride): when one faces those who are equal to oneself, it arises in the medium degree (*madhya-mātra*)—that is, [conceiving oneself as] equal to equals.

When one faces those who are not equal to oneself, it arises in the low degree (*mṛdu-mātra*)—that is, [conceiving oneself as] superior to the inferior. Regarding the three types of *atimāna* (excessive pride): when one faces those who are superior to oneself, those who are inferior to oneself, or those who are not equal to oneself, it arises in all cases in the medium degree—that is, [conceiving oneself as] superior to equals.

Regarding the three types of *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride): when one faces those who are inferior to oneself, those who are superior to oneself, or those who are not inferior to oneself, it arises in all cases in the high degree (*adhimātra*).

[The mind] arises. (Regarding the superior, one considers oneself inferior. These nine types of pride (*māna*)—their names and meanings—are cited from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śūtra*.
As the text there is extremely brief, I shall now provide a twofold classification so that their respective states (*avasthā*) become clear.

In the commentary, regarding the phrase "flattery (*śāṭhya*), crookedness (*māyā*), and so forth," this is the second explanation of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Regarding the "minor secondary afflictions" (*parīttakleśabhūmika*): among the twenty secondary afflictions, there are three categories.

The first ten are the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the next two are the intermediate secondary afflictions, and the final eight are the major secondary afflictions, as already explained in the chapter on the eight consciousnesses.
Other meanings are as discussed in separate volumes. Regarding the phrase "but these are [secondary] afflictions" (*kleśānuśaya*):

the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that they are called secondary afflictions because they are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of specific states and distinctions within the coarse manifestations of the root afflictions, such as greed and so forth. Here, two phrases have been omitted; other meanings are as follows.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Eight Consciousnesses" and its commentary in the separate fascicle, the *Śāstra* states that [these afflictions] are for the purpose of "snaring others" and so forth.

Now, although these traits such as flattery (*śāṭhya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*) are all explained by citing the treatises in the "Chapter on the Eight Consciousnesses," I shall provide a more detailed explanation here in relation to the scriptural text.

"Devious" (*khañja*) means unreal; "crooked" (*kuṭila*) means not straight. Thus, one who is "flatteringly crooked" acts to snare and hoodwink others, bending and conforming to the exigencies of the moment, employing artifice and contrivance.
To seize upon the intentions of others, or to conceal one's own faults, because one is incapable of receiving the correct instruction and admonition of teachers and friends.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "It means to deceive others, or to ensnare and oppress them, or to mask one's reputation;

that is, although an action is improper, one complies with what is currently appropriate, employing a deceptive net of artifice and establishing skillful means to enter into what is suitable for them; thus, one deliberately constructs a snare."

The character "zhī" (諂) here signifies adopting the intentions of others. One who looks toward others does so because they desire what is pleasing to them, or to comply with their own requests, or as a skillful means to conceal one's own faults;
thus, it serves as the cause for hiding transgressions. For this reason, such a person is incapable of receiving instruction from teachers or friends.

Regarding the statement that its essence consists of a portion of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*): apart from these two, there is no distinct characteristic or function of flattery (*śāṭhya*). Greed is called "instruction" (*jiao*), and flattery is... [the text continues].
It is due to ignorance that there is guile (*śāṭhya*). The *Pañcaskandhaka* states: "It is because it is comprised of the skillful means for concealing one's own faults.

Guile is followed by concealment (*mrakṣa*); thus, the cause is revealed through its fruit. Fearing that others will speak of one's own evils, one practices guile, hoping that others will speak well of the cause of concealment.
Otherwise, since both concealment and guile conceal transgressions, how would their two characteristics differ? [The text continues: "...devoting oneself to one's own..."

Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the mental state of jealousy regarding merit, reputation, honor, and material gain. It functions as an obstacle to non-envy.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*), fascicle 1, states that its function is to obstruct loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Fascicle 2 states that joy (*muditā*) has non-envy as its fundamental wholesome root.
Regarding "a portion of hatred" (*dveṣa-ekadeśa*): the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that it is a portion of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) equal to hatred.

"Not being envious" (*anīrṣyā*) is simply the absence of hatred; it does not possess a separate substantial entity. As for the note stating "it follows [the root]," this is like how flattery (*māyā*) is a portion of greed (*lobha*); by merely severing greed, flattery is naturally severed.

Therefore, among the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), their stages of subduing and severing are not explained separately. [End of] Commentary: Regarding the section beginning with "However, the fundamental... (Section 3).

This distinguishes between the presence and absence of the enumerations. According to the list provided above, they are absent; yet, upon careful examination of what precedes and follows, they are present. To speak of the "six root afflictions" is to state the total number collectively.
The subsequent two phrases indicate their absence. As for "delusion" (*moha*): its nature is to be obscured and ignorant regarding all principles and phenomena;
its function is to obstruct non-delusion and to serve as the basis for all defilements. That is to say, by means of ignorance (*avidyā*), [the other afflictions] arise.
The afflictions of the fixedly wrong category, such as greed and so forth, along with their attendant karma, have the function of summoning the defilements of future births.

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) has the nature of hesitation regarding the principles of the truths; its function is to obstruct the wholesome qualities that consist in freedom from doubt, because [when it exists] the wholesome does not arise.
Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) has the nature of defiled wisdom that erroneously speculates upon the principles of the truths; its function is to obstruct right view and to summon suffering.
The commentary places the discussion of delusion (*moha*) below the verse, yet it clarifies the possession [of the afflictions]. There are three rounds of interrogation and explanation;

According to this school, once one awakens to and enters pure awakening, all principles are no longer [obstructed].

The purport of the sūtra is that its purpose lies in serving true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and eliminating the subtle ailments of the mind.

Therefore, throughout the first four sections up to the second exposition, these two matters are addressed: first, the teacher is introduced; second, the ailments are pointed out; third, the manner of serving the teacher is explained;

and fourth, the practice for eliminating those ailments is explained. Furthermore, according to the introductory and concluding passages, this also corresponds precisely to the answers given to the questions.

nor, at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, was there truly any dharma by which he attained unexcelled bodhi—how much less so the dream-like and illusion-like realms of the world.

Though he manifests the faults of pride and so forth, even unto those of the hungry ghosts, he is fully endowed with merit. He practices the paths of the form and formless realms without regarding them as superior;
he manifests the practice of desire while remaining free from all defiled attachments; he manifests the practice of anger while harboring no resentment or obstruction toward sentient beings;
he manifests the practice of delusion while subduing his mind with wisdom; and he manifests the practice of stinginess and greed while practicing relinquishment.

Regarding all things internal and external, they do not spare their own bodies or lives; they manifest the practice of violating the precepts, yet they abide securely in the upholding of the precepts.

They harbor great dread even toward minor transgressions. They manifest the practice of anger, yet they are always compassionate and patient. They manifest the practice of indolence, yet they exhort others to cultivate merit and virtue.

They manifest the practice of a distracted mind, yet they are constantly mindful of meditative concentration. They manifest the practice of ignorance, yet they penetrate both the mundane and the supramundane.
In the world, he manifests deceitful conduct, yet through skillful means he accords with the meaning of all sutras;
he manifests arrogance, yet toward sentient beings he is like a bridge; he manifests various afflictions, yet his mind is always pure.

For those whose minds are estranged from defilement and who exert themselves in diligent practice—those who have attained the Way, because they experience both the pleasure of the cause and the pleasure of the fruit—ordinarily, when people of magical arts or those who praise his virtues speak of him, they all say:

Delighting in the Way. What is called the "austere practice" of a Bodhisattva means that while their conduct follows the traces of austerity, their mind delights in the flavor of the Way and is ever joyful.
If it were the mind operated by a deluded person, its entirety would be defiled;

they would merely fear transgressions and crave blessings, or desire the fruit of Buddhahood, thus toiling their body and mind—all of which is the labor of worldly defilement and does not accord with the realization of the Way or the nature of reality. It is not so.

Regarding the citation from the *Catuḥdharma-sūtra*, the *Jiao Shu* states: "However, because one leaves the mundane world through the Dharma, the Dharma serves as a boat and a raft. By means of this...

The Master has realized the Dharma. The Master is the helmsman; without the Master, the boat cannot proceed. Without the boat, there is nothing upon which to rely for crossing over. The boat depends on the Master for its movement.
Therefore, in revering the Dharma, one must revere the Master. Thus, Guanyin rejoiced that he had transcended hearing, and exhorted all ordinary beings to look up to him in the same way.

For this reason, there have been those who sacrificed their entire bodies to repay the Dharma, sold their marrow to requite its grace, cut their own flesh to hear the sutras, and burned their bodies to express gratitude for its virtue.

Alas! Those of later learning steal the Dharma rather than honoring their teachers; they long for the elegant form of a phoenix or crane, yet fail to perceive the ugliness of a mirror reflecting an owl.

Thus, what was intended to flourish instead brings about destruction; seeking enlightenment, one instead falls deeper into delusion. To destroy the Dharma and harm the teacher brings a retribution as constant as that between a shadow and its form.
