I shall now provide a brief indication of their intended meaning: Armor and weapons subdue Māra; ropes and cables pull you out and away from hell; wondrous medicines heal the afflictions of the mind.

He is a physician who severs the net of all cravings with a sharp blade; he is the timely rain that moistens the sprouts of bodhi; he is the bright lamp that destroys the darkness of the five hindrances;

he is the one who skillfully points out the right path; he is the firewood for the flame that ripens the food of nirvāṇa; he is the sharp arrow that shoots the thieves of affliction; he is the valiant general who breaks the army of birth and death;

and it is the Tathāgata who destroys afflictions and reaches nirvāṇa. (Fearing that these would be difficult to memorize, I have merely provided the essential meaning. From this point onward, the commentary proceeds.)
I shall also cite the passage from the *Yìxíng* (義行) that concludes with a eulogy, recording it here in full: "Good son, a virtuous friend possesses such immeasurable merit;

therefore, I now instruct you to draw near to them. (This sutra merely instructs one to draw near and serve, but does not explain the reason why; thus, I cite that scripture to explain the reason for drawing near.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāsa and the great assembly heard the Buddha preach this sublime Dharma and [the qualities of] the virtuous friend.
At these essential points of the profound Dharma, he raised his voice and wailed, tears falling like rain. Weeping and lamenting in distress, he could not compose himself. He thought to himself:
"From time immemorial, this body of mine has been protected by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Therefore, today I have encountered the Tathāgata and am able to hear the profound Dharma. To encounter such a thing is due to the power of the spiritual friend; it is not through my own power."
Reflecting within themselves, they thought, "From the very beginning, we have never repaid our debt of gratitude, nor have we had the intention to draw near.
Having spoken these words, they raised their voices once more: "Regarding 'distant yet intimate' and 'intimate yet near,' there are four permutations. First, those who are intimate but not near:
those whose hearts and minds are one, yet who dwell in different locations. Second, those who are near but not intimate: such as merchants or artisans who work together."
First, those who serve together in government offices and harbor mutual hatred or jealousy, contending for power and profit;

second, those who are both intimate and close, such as compassionate parents, filial children, affectionate spouses, and teachers and disciples bound by a shared path who have no cause for separation;
third, those who are neither intimate nor close, such as strangers on the road; and fourth, those who are distanced by millions of obstacles and follow the three miserable realms.
Regarding the phrase "The Commentary on the *Lunyu* says": "The commentary is like empty space. There are many common metaphors for empty space and the Dharma;
elsewhere, it is often used to illustrate that the Dharma is without arising or ceasing, is all-pervasive, and encompasses all, or to illustrate that the Buddha is without mind (*acitta*).

Here, however, it serves only as a metaphor for the mind being subject to no alteration, and not as a metaphor for being without mind. This means one must always maintain reverence and make offerings, following the teacher's countenance with deference. [Recorded.]
Having received the verbal instructions, how could one remain without a mind? "Sattva" translates here as "sentient being," which refers to living beings.

The concluding statement, "only then does one enter Perfect Enlightenment," serves as a counter-clarification: it indicates that if one does not thus serve the teacher until the end of one's life, one will not be able to enter Perfect Enlightenment.

The commentary states that this is not fixed or restrictive; it does not preclude the possibility of setting aside the illness [of literalism] to speak according to the Dharma through inquiry. This is profound.

Regarding "subtle afflictions": among all the various defilements (*kleśa*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the root. It extends throughout the higher realms; because there is aversion (*dveṣa*) due to craving, both aversion and craving are profound and subtle.
Moreover, since this is the seed [of all afflictions], and as it is not restricted to a single question, this too is the underlying cause of the four types of illness.
When one examines the aforementioned four types of people who practice while carrying these illnesses, it is due to aversion and craving.

Therefore, regarding the seven grades of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the *Śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that those who practice and study the mind of loving-kindness cannot achieve it instantaneously;

they must employ skillful means (*upāya*) to gradually guide the ordinary mind until the practice of loving-kindness is perfected, whereby one attains equanimity toward both enemies and kin. Once loving-kindness...

One is able to bestow happiness. Bestowing happiness must also be impartial. Regarding the "seven grades," these refer to: superior, middling, and inferior relatives; those who are neither enemies nor relatives;

and inferior, middling, and superior enemies, and so forth. This means that when encountering a superior relative, one causes them to receive superior happiness, which clearly accords with their heart.
This refers to exhausting one's strength to serve one’s parents with sweet and delicate foods, or providing one’s wife, children, and brothers with the most excellent things.

Regarding objects: one’s mind is capable of treating those who are moderately close, those who are distantly close, and those who are neutral—whether they harbor resentment or affection—with equal impartiality.

One simply allows things to proceed naturally without bestowing objects upon them. Next, one gives moderate happiness to those who are moderately close; although this is but one degree higher [than the previous stage], it may still be pursued.

This refers to giving moderate happiness to those who are distantly close, rather than inferior happiness to those who are neither resentful nor affectionate. When this state of mind has matured, one further causes those who are...
One gives the highest happiness to one's kin, down to giving the lowest happiness to an inferior enemy.

Then, after another turn, one gives the highest happiness to those who are neither enemies nor kin, and likewise the middle happiness to inferior enemies and the highest happiness to middling enemies.

Proceeding gradually in this manner until one is able to give the highest happiness even to a superior enemy, one achieves the state where enemies and kin are non-dual, identical to the compassion of a Buddha.

Regarding the method of contemplating the mind through the commentaries (*śāstra*) and other texts: the preceding section sets forth the "Sublime Dharma" and concludes with "right contemplation," which appears to answer the question of the dharma upon which one relies.

Within that, it further avoids the "four illnesses"; here, it sets forth "non-liberation" and concludes with "removing illness," which appears to answer the question of which illness is to be removed.

Furthermore, because it causes one to contemplate the dharma therein, it states that this does not hinder the removal of illness; thus, it is explained by synthesizing the teachings according to the Dharma.
The commentary differs from the preceding section in that the former [sections] regard people with an impartial mind (*samacitta*). Regarding the commentary’s response to the fifth point:

while the first four all involve a combination of preceding and following elements, answering them in a manner that allows their thematic momentum to intersect and their meanings to flow continuously, this one alone answers directly regarding the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

The Sūtra speaks thus; "words" here also refers to the "intention. Regarding the phrase "those who, while on the grounds, all make vows," this characteristic is extensively elucidated throughout the *Avataṃsaka* as a whole.

Among these, from beginning to end, the "Chapter on the Merit of the Initial Resolve for Awakening" exclusively reveals the characteristics of this resolve and its practice, providing a detailed comparison of its merits.
A brief summary may be found in the section on the essence, characteristics, and merit of the bodhicitta at the beginning of the "Mañjuśrī Chapter."
It is said: "If there is no aspiration of the mind and so forth. Now, an aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is a vow of the heart, a firm resolve, and a longing within the emotions.
It is the specific desire to perform such and such deeds; when the emotion arises from within, it then takes form through verbal expression.

Yet I see those of shallow understanding in the present day who treat mere words of the mind and characters on paper as the act of making an aspiration, without ever reflecting back [upon its true nature].
To verify how one’s own mind is, one specifically speaks of the "heart's vow" (*cittapraṇidhāna*). As for "encouraging and guiding," it means to exhort and lead.

When Tiantai instructs one to recollect the original aspiration for enlightenment, this is the power of the vow (*praṇidhibala*). Regarding "the practice not being accomplished": a vow is that which gives rise to the mind.
The practitioner is the track; it is the practice upon which one relies. If there is no fundamental goal, it is called a state of sudden, indeterminate mind.
How could such a state accord with bodhi? All the more so when there is no power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*); then the mind advances when vigorous and retreats when weary.
How could it remain unchanging from beginning to end and thereby achieve the supreme fruit? As for the analogy of the chariot and so forth: practice and vows support one another like two [wheels].
The "wheel" refers to the two wings. Regarding the commentary’s statement that it is "the same as the *vajra*," this follows what is cited below.

If one follows the interpretation of Vasubandhu, this answers the question of "how one dwells" by causing one to dwell in the four minds. If one follows the interpretation of Asaṅga, among the eighteen stages of dwelling (*vihāra*), it corresponds to the first, the stage of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*).
Thus, this current passage likewise pertains to the text on the arousal of the mind; it is from the verses of Maitreya.

As for this: originally, the Bodhisattva Asanga entered the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* (Sunlight Samādhi) and ascended to Tuṣita Heaven to inquire about the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* from Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Maitreya expounded eighty verses (*kārikās*) to explain the text of the single fascicle of the sūtra.
Asanga transmitted these to Vasubandhu, who composed three fascicles of prose commentary (*vṛtti*) to explain these verses; therefore, the present commentary cites the original source.

This half-verse of the stanza enumerates four types of mind. The latter half states: "Abiding in the profound mind of benefit. This refers to the fulfillment of the merit of this vehicle through the mind of benefiting others;
it signifies the meaning of universally delivering [beings] and realizing the fruit. The "profound mind" (gambhīra-citta) accords with principle (*yathābhūta*):

there is neither deliverance nor realization, and no beginning or end. The word "abiding" (*sthita*) directly answers the question posed. Therefore, the preceding major section implicitly employs this intent when it speaks of "manifesting the arousal of the resolve" (*cittotpāda*).

"Profound and vast. "Vast" means universally benefiting others; the term "profound" is likewise the same. Among the four [types of mind]: first, the expansive mind, because it universally delivers those within the three realms;
second, the supreme mind, because it causes them to attain the most excellent ultimate fruit;

third, the eternal mind, because sentient beings are fundamentally quiescent, eternally abiding and unchanging, without beginning or end; fourth, the non-perverted mind, because there is no one who can deliver me.

[The mark] of characteristics. Because there is no characteristic of sentient beings to be delivered. If one possesses characteristics such as self or person, one is not a bodhisattva. Regarding the "four modes of birth" in the commentary:
if it refers to egg-birth, this has already been explained in the chapter on Maitreya. Regarding the "nine categories": these are the four [modes of birth] with five added.

If they have form (the fifth), this refers to the four dhyānas; if they are formless (the sixth), this refers to the four emptinesses; if they have perception (the seventh), this excludes those without perception...

The heavens of perception (*saṃjñā*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). All others possess perception. As for "non-perception" (the eighth), the *Guṇadāna-śāstra* states: "Among the four formless absorptions, those with perception are the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness;
those without perception are the sphere of nothingness. As for "neither with perception nor without perception" (the ninth), this refers to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Regarding "nirvāṇa without remainder," this is not the third among the four types of nirvāṇa, as that is shared by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); rather, it is the non-abiding Great Parinirvāṇa.
Because it is free from the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) of the bodhisattvas of the two vehicles and all subtle hindrances, it is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "When one attains Buddhahood, one is endowed with the thirty-two marks; at that time, it can be said that [defilements] are forever extinguished and exhausted without remainder.
As for *nirvāṇa*, the Qin translation renders it as "extinction and transcendence" (*mie-du*). Therefore, the subsequent sūtra says: "and brings about extinction and transcendence. If, by...
The new translation renders this as "perfect stillness" (*parinirvāṇa*). This is explained in detail in the preceding chapter on *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the terms "transverse" and "vertical":

"vertical" refers to the past, which is beginningless (because one does not see a point where it has already been transcended); the future, which is endless (because there is no cessation); and the present, which is non-abiding (because there is nothing that can be transcended).

Thus, there is no temporal limitation or boundary. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: "The two types of birth from eggs and moisture, as well as the two [realms] of the Unconscious and the Peak of Existence..."
Those dwelling in states that cannot be saved must also wait until their retribution is exhausted before being reborn in a place free of difficulties, at which point they are then saved.

One should know that this represents an intention that never ceases. The *Śāstra* says: "The egg-born and moisture-born (the difficulties of animals), the non-percipient beings, and those in the heavens of long life (the difficulties of the heavens)—by principle, these should all be included among the 'difficulties,' though they are omitted in the text for brevity.
Thus, one cannot say that [the bodhisattva] enters everywhere. (This is a hypothetical question posed by the *Śāstra*, to which it answers itself: "There are..."

There are three causes and conditions: first, for those born in difficult circumstances, it is because they must await the proper time; second, for those born in non-difficult circumstances who have not yet matured, it is because they must reach maturity;
third, for those who have already matured, it is because of their liberation. Thus, one knows that [the practice] pervades both horizontally and vertically.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It continues without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future. It further says: "Moment after moment..."
"Continuously" means without interruption. "Transversely" refers to the distinctions of near and far throughout the ten directions.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "As vast as the Dharma-realm; as ultimate as empty space. Regarding "the strong and the soft":

among all sentient beings, there are those who are stubborn and difficult to transform, and those who are gentle and easy to deliver. Now, I make a vow to deliver them both without a second thought. At this time, [the conditions] are difficult.
To find a true and genuine spiritual friend or excellent teacher is a rare occurrence. How is this known?
Whenever I travel and encounter those who transmit the Chan or the Teaching lineages, I have yet to see anyone who has attained self-awakening or whose mind accords with the vow for Bodhi.

It is not that I have encountered no one with whom I could engage in discourse; rather, all see others as different from themselves, like enemies, and view the followers of other schools as mere gaps.

Is this not because they resent others being difficult to convert? Should they not, therefore, turn their hearts toward them instead of setting themselves apart? If one can benefit others according to one's capacity, what limit is there to the skillful means?

As for my own difficulties, I cannot avoid them, yet I am certain that others can understand them; I shall never harbor them within myself, and I have already acted accordingly to the best of my ability.
Practice this. I pray that those who have truly resolved their minds will examine this thoroughly and join me in this aspiration.

Do not let it become like the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi lun), which was privately transmitted within the imperial palace and has been handed down to the present day; people hold it aloft as a supreme achievement, failing to perceive its flaws.

It has been passed down through successive generations, yet they do not understand how to eliminate its traces, using it merely to conceal the errors of their own masters. Furthermore, because some used gold to enter [the lineage],...
[The character] "hall" (tīng) [implies one who serves]. It is already like bribing a gatekeeper; how much more so could one forget their own body to devise schemes and act as an unasked-for friend?
Even in the past, did he not further offer his own person as a servant to skillfully transform others? Therefore, the commentary says "vast and great" (*guǎngdà*).

This follows the force of the meaning of the Sūtra’s explanation and concludes by identifying the name of Maitreya’s first resolve (*prathama-citta-utpāda*) as it is employed in the explanatory text. Thus, it is attributed to him.
This is a passage from the Sūtra. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "it causes one to awaken to equality," the character *jue* (awaken) used above refers to *shijiao* (initial awakening).
"Awakening to the original" intends to clarify the sudden enlightenment of the initial mind; "entering below" intends to clarify the ultimate, final realization. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

"The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two different things. Of these two states of mind, the former is difficult; now, with this initial aspiration, one universally delivers [all beings]."
It is appropriate to initiate this instruction; one need not fear its difficulty. Rather than focusing exclusively on the ripening of the faculties, the Sūtra simply speaks of "entering.

One should understand that what follows encompasses what precedes it, seeking the intended meaning within the spirit of the teaching rather than becoming confused about the Buddha’s intent. Since the Sūtra speaks of "ultimate realization," this constitutes the core content of the Treatise.

Consequently, by employing the terminology of the Treatise regarding the beginning and the foundation, one may perfect the aspects of practice from the outset to the end, thereby further manifesting the vow to deliver sentient beings.
From beginning to end, the distinction is clear; one need only rely on these words to harmonize with the same resonance and discern this essential subtlety.

Furthermore, one must realize that the term "Ultimate Perfect Enlightenment" (*atyanta-pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) within the *Awakening of Faith* (*Juejing*) fully penetrates the meanings found in both the sūtras and the śāstras, thereby establishing the characteristics of the ultimate fruit.

One should know that the noble wisdom functions spontaneously and permeates all things; thus, the stages of the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata are certainly not two separate paths. In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is in truth only...

Regarding the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*): as for the commentary stating it is "the foremost," this is a concluding explanation modeled after the preceding [sections], following the logical momentum of the sūtra’s meaning;
it should be understood that the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood is truly the foremost. However, within the *Vajraśekhara*, it is called "foremost" because it transcends the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

This, moreover, simultaneously surpasses the views of the provisional and gradual teachings; thus it is called "foremost. Furthermore, that [other system] is a school that negates characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), [attaining the foremost] through the exhaustion of karmic burdens.
It is the ultimate; because it takes negation (*paryudāsa*) as the supreme principle, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Yet, it also possesses unsurpassed *bodhi*, for the original question within the inquiry was precisely about those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is the school that reveals the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).
Taking what is originally possessed as the ultimate, and taking that which is expressed through linguistic designation as the definitive meaning, it is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*).
It also accords with *nirvāṇa*; thus, the verse states: "Realizing enlightenment and entering *parinirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the section beginning with "As long as space exists and sentient beings...

universally reveals the characteristics of the arousal of the mind and its practice; therefore, each of the ten types of vows in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* concludes by saying: "Until the realm of space is exhausted, and sentient beings..."

When the realms are exhausted, when the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, and when the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted, my prostrations shall likewise be exhausted. (The first of these is the vow of prostrating to the Buddha;

the remaining sections—from the praise and offerings up to the tenth dedication—are each identical to this. Because the realm of empty space and even the afflictions are inexhaustible, my prostrations and reverence are without end.
May they continue from moment to moment without interruption, such that my actions of body, speech, and mind are never stilled.
Because of weariness and exhaustion, it is said here that "sentient beings in space are without limit," and so forth. The term "sentient beings" includes karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
"The compassionate vow is likewise so" means it is exactly as he said, "I [vow for] these [beings]," and so on.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "by the arousal of this vow, etc.": if one's present mind is still of the nature of past habituation, how could it be otherwise from the past?
Forgetting oneself to save others, one should simply exert and inspire the mind at every moment, taking this object of aspiration as the basis for contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*).
Through long-term cultivation, this naturally becomes one's nature, until one attains the realization of *bodhi* and transforms beings without deliberate intent; such transformation is truly great.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "I enter awakening," it means that there is certainly no separate awakening to be entered.

This is as explained at the beginning of the previous chapter on the Four Characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), and also like the preceding analogy of hot water melting ice. Since I am thus, so too are all sentient beings.

Therefore, the *Treatise by Vasubandhu* states in full: "The Bodhisattva regards all sentient beings as his own body; when his own self attains parinirvāṇa, there is no difference from [the nirvāṇa of] others."

They give rise to the thought of liberation. Thus they take hold of sentient beings as they do their own bodies, never abandoning them; this is called the benefit of the constant mind (*nitya-citta*).
Based on this, one knows that the equality of self and others is precisely what constitutes the constant mind. As for this constant mind, it has existed from time immemorial.

Fundamentally, there are no such characteristics as self or sentient beings; it is only Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti’s *yuanjue*), which is without increase or decrease, without beginning or end, without birth to be saved, and without truth to be realized. That it has been thus from the very beginning is what is called "constant.

If one perceives sentient beings and so forth—meaning if one perceives that "I am saving sentient beings" and that "sentient beings, because of my salvation, shall all enter enlightenment"—then I am [already]... [attached].
[They] enter. Sentient beings enter later. Once they have entered, there is awakening within non-self; yet before they had entered, there was a self without awakening.
Since the end of awakening is identical to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) at its beginning, how could it be called permanent? Therefore, it is said that it is "not permanent.

As for the statement that "there are no sentient beings to be saved," according to the *Dà yún shū* (Great Cloud Commentary) on the *Vajracchedikā*, this accords with the meaning: "In reality, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. Therein lies... [the principle].

There are five kinds. First, because of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Second, because of being of the same essence (*samatā-kāya*). This means that the Bodhisattva’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is free from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and lacks any notion of self.

Subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) attains great compassion of the same essence; outside of one's own person, there are no separate sentient beings, and thus there is no notion of "other.
Consequently, there are no sentient beings to be brought to parinirvāṇa. This citation from Vasubandhu’s commentary is the same as that cited above. [This concludes the section.]

The commentary states: This teaching concerns the practice prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the realization upon the stages; it is the contemplation of great compassion of the same essence (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*). It says, "Because it is fundamentally quiescent. Citing a sutra, it says:

"All sentient beings, from the very beginning, have always been in the state of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-lakṣaṇa*); they do not undergo further extinction. This is because of the four kinds of non-thought (*amanasikāra*).
Since one accords with the *dharmatā*, which is fundamentally without thought, if the mind gives rise to thought, it immediately violates the *dharmatā*. Fifth, the Dharma...
Because of the *dhātu* (element/realm). The verse by Maitreya says: "In the equal and true *dharmadhātu*, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings.

Regarding the commentary's phrase "removing those [notions]": although both oneself and others, in terms of deluded conceptualization, each possess the four [grasping notions] of self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), sentient being (*sattva*), and life-span (*jīva*), for the sake of the flow of the text and linguistic convenience, the "self" is provisionally taken as the deliverer and "sentient beings" are assigned to the delivered.

It is not that those beings who are to be saved do not exist because of the existence of a self; rather, the self that is able to save them likewise exists in relation to sentient beings. This can be clearly seen through careful examination.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "Therefore, Vasubandhu, etc.": "detachment" refers to wisdom. The section beginning with "relying upon" refers to the obstacles to be abandoned.

Within this, "relying upon" is the general category, while the remainder are the specific instances. That is to say, the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is the characteristic of a self, which is precisely that which is able to save.
Furthermore, "sentient beings" refers to others; these are precisely those who are to be saved. Therefore, it concludes by saying "equal characteristics. Regarding the phrase "without attachment":

having already severed the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, this is the abandonment of the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*). "By means of faith and understanding" and below, this is the abandonment of the notion of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃjñā*).

The commentary [states] "in total, according to that sutra," which refers to the correspondence between the two texts as being identical. That non-perverted mind is explained inversely in that sutra, whereas in this sutra it is explained directly.
This is clarified; the details can be understood from the text.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "having realized oneself as equal to ordinary beings," the text says:

"To fully realize that body and mind are ultimately equal and of one essence with all sentient beings without distinction—only by practicing in this way does one enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Regarding "revering the teacher as a Buddha," [the preceding section...]
Regarding the principle of realization: this refers to the arising of practice. Furthermore, by realizing that one is the same as ordinary beings, one loses one's pride;
by looking up to the teacher as a Buddha, one increases one's reverence. Facing the opponent directly, one thereby accomplishes supreme practice.

If one universally observes all sentient beings with universal reverence and universal transformation, there are four permutations regarding the relationship between self and other. The first is observing others from the perspective of principle.

First, regarding one's own state of mind, one contemplates oneself as an ordinary person; thereby, one accomplishes the practice of reverence. Second, regarding the state of mind directed toward others, one contemplates them as ordinary, deluded beings with suffering bodies;
yet, through awakened understanding, one knows that they share the same Buddha-wisdom and can be saved, thereby accomplishing the practice of great compassion.

The third [point] concerns both together in terms of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): one contemplates the Buddha as superior to oneself to increase practices for one's own benefit, and contemplates sentient beings as inferior to oneself to increase practices for the benefit of others.
The fourth concerns both together in terms of the principle of nature (*dharmatā*): thereby one accomplishes the ultimate practice and realization of the equality of non-self.

The commentary (*vṛtti*) only recites that which remedies [the afflictions], whereas the prose section first describes that which is to be remedied; this is because there exists, from time immemorial, hatred and attachment.
Because the seeds [of affliction] remain, one is not yet liberated. Regarding the causes for violating the precepts, the previous section on Maitreya described evil karma as follows:

"When the object of perception turns away from the mind of love, one gives rise to hatred and jealousy, creating various kinds of karma and being born in the realms of hungry ghosts or hell. Thus, at the beginning of the text on the four marks (catur-lakṣaṇa):
Furthermore, through the successive progression of hatred and attachment, up to the point of deluded karma and deluded transmigration, one repeatedly produces fruits from hatred and attachment.
Because these cannot be extensively induced, they oppose the virtue of the precepts. "Precepts" refers to the *Prātimokṣa*, which here means "leading to liberation.

Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) states: "The precepts are correctly aligned with liberation. Therefore, the relationship between that which treats and that which is treated is one of direct opposition.
Conversely, this establishes the meaning of "governance" (*vyavasthāna*). Regarding the commentary’s subsequent explanation of the four types of mind in the verse:

the first two are evident. In the third, "self" and "person" refer to the perceiver. In the fourth, "always relying on wisdom" means being non-perverted. Although the phrasing of the third is identical to the fourth, it excludes terms such as "that self" and "person";
nevertheless, its meaning is comprehensive. Alternatively, the two lines of the third and fourth verses may apply to all three [of the preceding categories].
The four types of mind: the "Vajra-Eternal Mind" states that there are truly no sentient beings; the "Non-Subverting Mind" states that if there were [sentient beings], one would not be a bodhisattva.

Although these differ in being expressed through negation (*pratipakṣa*) or affirmation (*anuloma*), both are characterized by non-self and so forth. Therefore, this does not preclude their application to the verses.
The preceding explanation of the chapter on the Four Illnesses is concluded.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Sub-commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll 12 (Part 2) / Scroll 13 (Part 1).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.

The Chapter on the Preparatory Practices for the Site of Enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This chapter consists of three parts: first, the explanation of the structural outline; second, the indication of the specific sections; and third, the formal explanation of the chapter itself.
Regarding the term "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which refers to the place where the Way is attained, this encompasses both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). As for phenomena:
for example, when the Buddha sat upon grass beneath the Great Tree in the kingdom of Magadha and attained *bodhi*, that place was called the *bodhimaṇḍa*. Its...

The tree is also called the Bodhi tree. The principle is as explained in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*: all myriad practices are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), namely, the direct mind and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* praises the Buddha, saying: "His body constantly and universally sits in all sites of enlightenment. Regarding the term "all":

This means that the Wisdom Body (jñānakāya) sits pervasively within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of the Dharma-nature; the Dharma Body (dharmakāya) does not sit, yet it sits in the site of enlightenment.

The Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) with its physical marks sits peacefully upon the site of enlightenment of the myriad practices. The Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) sits peacefully upon the site of enlightenment of the water-moon.

The phrase "those with heavy obstructions" explains the preparatory application (prayoga); "those with a floating mind" explains the site of enlightenment. Regarding the passage "If one relies on the four divisions," the second point indicates the specific distinctions.
This is a section heading, as has been fully detailed previously. As for those with corroborating evidence, they shall be seen in the relevant passages of the text.
In the fourth part of the sub-commentary (*shu*), there are three sections that open the chapters and provide explanations. Regarding the fact that one may cite the preceding text:

while the names of the various bodhisattvas in the previous inquiry were not to be explained again, this particular case requires a further demonstration because it marks the conclusion of the main body of the scripture and returns to the fundamental source of the teaching.
This is because one must always know [the connection] most essentialy. For this reason, the general outline of the lineage and continuity of a single sutra is presented here.
Since these names of the Bodhisattvas constitute the title of this sutra, the preceding text—in the commentary on the introductory section—states:

"However, within this main body of the teaching, the fundamental intent of the various Bodhisattvas and the Buddha in their dialogue is to reveal Perfect Enlightenment; yet, because the afflictions and obstacles have not been exhausted at every stage," [the subsequent sections follow].

The underlying meaning was not yet complete, and the capacity of those to be guided had not yet been universally encompassed; therefore, the Bodhisattvas who symbolize the Dharma had not yet been designated by the name "Perfect Enlightenment" (Yuanjue).

Now there are three reasons why they receive this name: first, although the afflictions have been exhausted and the principle perfected as previously described, there remains concern that those of inferior faculties might find it difficult to enter.

This further elaborates, through skillful means, the three-period *maṇḍala* for those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities, so that all may universally return to *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (Perfect Enlightenment).

Second, because their preceding gradual practices and understandings have already been perfected, reaching this point is termed "attaining the ultimate. The state of attaining the ultimate has no separate essence;
it is solely *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*. Third, the reason *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* was initially designated as the *dhāraṇī* is that it arises from the fundamental source.
End. Now that the exposition of the meaning has been completed, returning to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) signifies the integration of the derivative with the fundamental.
To represent these three meanings, the Bodhisattva of Perfect Enlightenment poses his question at this juncture.
The commentary follows up on the preceding expressions of joy by describing Great Wisdom; it clarifies the purpose [of the treatise] by describing Great Compassion.
Just as a compassionate father in the world thinks of his child as soon as he attains happiness, so too the mental conduct of a Bodhisattva constantly practices both compassion and wisdom.

Regarding the "Correct Dharma" (*saddharma*) and "Semblance Dharma" (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) periods, their duration in years has already been set forth previously. These two are both spoken of in terms of the number of years they remain in the world only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
If the Buddha were still present, he would be the Master of the Dharma himself, and there would be no further occasion for such discussion;

thus, the text mentions only the "Final Dharma" (*mappo*). Since this refers to the period following the Buddha’s extinction, it thereby encompasses both the Correct and Semblance Dharma periods. [The commentary] definitively distinguishes these from other natures.

As for that, it is said that all five [lineages] possess a fixed nature and are all inherently present (*prakṛtistha*). Among these, those with the nature of the two vehicles or of non-Buddhists are permanently excluded;
only those with the Mahāyāna nature are included. Thus, at the beginning of the account of the five stages, the text says:

"That is to say, one who possesses the two kinds of Mahāyāna nature gradually awakens and enters [the path] through the five stages in brief. First is the *prakṛtistha-gotra* (nature-abiding lineage), which means...

Since beginningless time, it has been dependent upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). It is the cause for uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) obtained through the nature of things (*dharmatā*), and the lineage (*gotra*) formed by two types of cultivation.
That is to say, having heard the teachings that flow forth from the *dharmadhātu*, one is formed by the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of what is produced by hearing and so forth.

Only when one possesses these two types of lineage of the Mahāyāna can one gradually awaken to and enter into Vijñaptimātratā. According to that school which maintains five lineages (*pañcagotra*), there are those who do not [possess this] from the very beginning.
Regarding those who possess the nature of the Mahāyāna, it is said that they "must possess" it. Ci'en’s commentary states:

"The mere mention of 'Mahāyāna' serves to distinguish them from those of the fixed nature of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) as well as those without the spiritual lineage (agotra). Thus, one knows that the remaining two vehicles—those without the lineage—and half of those with indeterminate lineage are 'not possessing' [the Mahāyāna nature];
for them, there is never the sense of possessing it. Based on this, it refers to those like the people nowadays who study the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. (5)

Within their natures, it is not necessarily the case that all are complete; there must be many people who labor in vain through their study and practice, for there would otherwise be no possibility of attaining understanding, conduct, or realization.
Therefore, within this school, one must cultivate [the teachings] thoroughly; if one has never been permeated by them, [realization is impossible].
Those who lack seeds [of awakening] perfume [their minds] so as to form seeds; thus, when they encounter conditions again in this life or in subsequent lives, those seeds will inevitably arise.
However, at present, we focus our resolve upon the site of practice (*dojō*) for those who already possess such seeds; therefore, it is said that they "possess the Mahāyāna nature.

This is because those who do not yet possess seeds from past lives will ultimately never consent to enter the site of practice. Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "the wisdom of hearing first opens": this refers to the third [stage].
This is the first of the three layers of causes. The phrase "the arousal of the bodhicitta" in the Commentary refers to the meaning of the second layer of causes.
"Contemplating according to one's capacity" and "the preparatory practices at the site of enlightenment" refer to the third layer: the cultivation of the bodhisattva path.
These three layers of causal meanings are found in the opening section of the Mañjuśrī chapter, within the passage concerning the original ground of the causal stage (*yuan-di*).

Regarding the "official business" mentioned in the *Sūtra Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, the text states: "For example, suppose a man goes to the house of a close friend and falls asleep after drinking wine.
At that time, the friend has official business to attend to and departs, having tied a priceless jewel inside the man's garment and given it to him.
In this analogy, the Bodhisattva’s work of delivering sentient beings is likened to public service, while his practice for self-benefit is likened to private affairs.

Regarding these matters: just as in the world, the virtuous ministers of a state consider the benefit and salvation of the common people their public duty, while regarding their own family estates as private affairs.
As for the phrase "the perils to the King, the Thieves, and Life," all three contain the character for "peril" (nán).

This refers to the peril of the King, the peril of thieves, and the peril of life; these three collectively are termed the "perils to the Brahma-faring" (brahmacarya-vighna). Circumstances such as water and fire also belong to this category.

This is a matter of destiny. It is not the same as the individual distinctions made within the Vinaya rules. For instance, there may be cases where a king does not believe in the Buddha-dharma and prohibits the conditions for practicing the Dharma;
or where bandits cause unrest, making it difficult to dwell in peace; or where various obstacles arise that involve the threat to one's life and limb.
These are all "external matters. "External" carries the meaning of being generally beyond one's own control. Therefore, one should know that even though such [circumstances] exist...
These obstructive conditions must still be examined and contemplated to some extent; if they were absent, one would be able to apply the full power of one's preparatory practice.
Yet there are those today who lack such obstacles and also lack the conditions for saving sentient beings, yet are still unable even to contemplate these matters.
How much more so regarding the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the *maṇḍala*? Yet they remain complacent and unalarmed, passing their time in indolence; this is truly to be pitied.
As for the determination of a three-month period without further purpose, there are those who speak from mere conjecture regarding the meaning of the number of days for these three periods;
such views are extremely narrow and biased, and must not be accepted as correct. Tiantai once resolved to apply himself with diligent effort, vowing to seek realization within a hundred days.

One will then attain the *svādhisthāna-dhāraṇī*. Regarding the practice of the *Lotus Sūtra* repentance ritual (*lǐchàn*), the ritual site (*daochǎng*) is prescribed for only twenty-one days (*sānqī*).
For the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* ritual site, it is further prescribed for one hundred days. Within the ritual protocols of the *Vaipulya* sūtras, it is also stated:
"The period should be set at seven days; more is not forbidden, but less must not be reduced. Among the various teachings, such are the texts that speak of the ritual site.
They are very numerous; it would be impossible to cite them all in full. Their durations vary, and their rituals likewise differ. How could each one not have its own specific significance?

Regarding the "long period" for those of inferior capacity: because their obstructions are heavy, they are difficult to exhaust. For those of middling capacity, the middle and upper grades follow the same sequence as above, which can be understood accordingly.
Conversely, the "long period" for those of superior capacity refers to those who are capable of diligence and can endure hardship. These are many.

Because they would not regress at that time, [the Buddha] set a later deadline for those of inferior faculties—namely, those who are by nature indolent, unable to endure hardship for long, who can practice easily but regress as soon as it becomes difficult, and who, despite hearing the Way for a long time, are unwilling to cultivate it. Therefore, the Buddha condescends to guide and lead them.

Eighty days is also permitted. This refers to those of middling capacity during the middle period; their progress or decline remains within the mean. One should regulate this according to one's own strength.

If categorized by the sharpness or dullness of faculties, both possibilities apply. Furthermore, regarding those of sharp faculties—meaning those who are clever and quick-witted—and those who are indolent, the latter are assigned the lower limit.

Because they are indolent, they are unwilling to persevere for long; because they are sharp, their obstacles are easily exhausted. Those who are both sharp and diligent are assigned the upper limit; they advance.
Because they are capable of enduring for a long time, hindrances are categorized as coarse or subtle. Until one attains Buddhahood, both the root and its branches are exhausted.

Regarding those of dull faculties: those who are dull yet diligent are assigned to the upper period; those who are dull and indolent are assigned to the lower period. The underlying meaning may be understood by analogy with the above.
As for the middle period, all such cases are taken as being of the "nature of the locus. The Buddha’s intention is manifold; this has been formulated here according to the general outline.

However, the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of sentient beings vary in many ways; therefore, one must act according to what is appropriate for the occasion and cannot be fixed definitively.

One should simply gauge the strength of oneself and others—whether superior, middling, or inferior—and ensure that the ritual procedures and principles are in accord with the situation. Some say that if the mind is pure, one attains [the goal] immediately;
why then must one strictly purify the external features of the *bodhimaṇḍa*? If the mind does not engage in discursive clinging, one attains it; why then restrict [the practice]?
Dwelling in one place is like being in confinement; this is spoken of merely in terms of general principle.
Without closely examining one's own mind, it is difficult to purify and easy to become defiled, or difficult to settle and easy to become restless.

Furthermore, since the arising of a defiled mind necessarily depends upon defiled conditions, how could the accomplishment of a pure mind possibly occur without depending upon pure conditions? Question: Suppose among them there were suddenly someone of the highest, most superior faculties who, through a single realization—
Later, [the practitioner] will always be accompanied by the Way; it becomes easily purified and easily peaceful. How could it be an impediment for others to have such words? Answer:

If one is a person of the highest, sharpest faculties, they must be fully endowed with compassion and wisdom, able to protect the mental conduct of sentient beings and skillfully exhort and restrain them.

Such a person would certainly not speak these words. Those who do speak these words are ultimately not of this class. Question: How could it be an impediment for others to still encounter those of the highest [faculties]?

"Is it an ordinary person who speaks these words? [The Master] replied: "This pertains to the preceding general and specific contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*). Who would prevent others from entering this Dharma hall?
Nevertheless, one must also settle the assembly in quiet rooms for seated meditation.

Whether generally or specifically, one must ultimately cause the arising of mental activity through conditions to correspond with the principle realized. Therefore, it is said that 'phenomenon and principle are in accord,' meaning internally and externally."
Both are purified; body and mind are entirely at peace. Regarding the three sections within the commentary:
the first concerns the aspect of the Buddha’s presence; the second, the aspect of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; and the third, the response and the attainment of benefit.
Within the first section, the phrase "It should be known," etc., consists entirely of the treatise itself; that [treatise] introduces it as "Correctly..."

One who contemplates should know that it is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*). This is because the meanings of "right reflection" (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) and "right mindfulness" (*samyaksmṛti*) are identical; thus, the former is used to explain the latter. Furthermore, the meaning of "mind-only" is the same as the intent of this [teaching].
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one contemplates by means of images, which constitutes "possessing objects.

During the Buddha’s lifetime, however, the faculties and conditions were both superior, such that there was no need for external objects; one directly contemplated the mind and the Buddha. Therefore, it is called "mind-only. Thus it is said:

Regarding the superiority of the faculties (*indriya*) and the conditions (*pratyaya*), the *Śāstra* states: "When the Tathāgata was in the world, [the time] was superior; sentient beings possessed sharp faculties, which is the superiority of the faculties (*indriya-viśeṣa*);

the person capable of preaching possessed excellence in both form and mental karma, which is the superiority of the conditions (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*); and when he uttered a single perfect sound, various classes of beings understood it equally, which manifests the characteristic of the superiority of the faculties."

In the commentary, from "If [the Buddha]... onwards, there are two parts explaining the mode of practice after his parinirvāṇa. These further consist of two sections: first, preparing the necessary conditions; second, clearly explaining the mode of practice.
Within the first section, there are again two parts. First is preparing the primary conditions. Regarding the phrase "not beholding the true countenance" and so forth:
while the Buddha was still in the world, he once ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for three months to preach the Dharma to his mother, Māyā. King Udayana, filled with longing and remembrance...

My feelings are most earnest. If one is still moved to carve sandalwood to create an image of the World-Honored One for worship and offerings, how much more so should one fashion an image to behold after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when his golden countenance can no longer be seen?
Is it that the aspiration for the Way is not equal to Ding Lan’s filial piety?
Moreover, is it not by means of such a representation that one leads the mind into the Dharma? To lead the mind is to rely upon seeing the vermilion...

Upon seeing the blue image, he immediately perceived the World-Honored One as a manifested transformation of his physical body—its eyes possessing a spiritual luster, its hands and body moving with grace, its compassionate countenance and joyful expression, and its speech remaining in tranquil silence.
Standing majestically and dignified amidst the great assembly, it was as if the Buddha were right before one's eyes.

Although his eyes beheld the painted colors, his mind was focused entirely on the Buddha’s form; subsequently, by virtue of seeing this image, he came to know the transformation with absolute certainty.
Manifestation is like an image in a mirror; an image must depend upon a clear and bright surface. The marks of the Buddha must depend upon stillness and illumination.

Just as one beholds the reflected image with the eyes in the metaphor, the mind fully perceives the clear brightness; so too, when beholding the manifested forms within the Dharma, the mind fully perceives the Dharma-body and Reward-body.
Since it is thus for the Dharma and Reward bodies, my own mind is likewise so. My mind is identical to the Buddha-mind; I melt my mind into...
The Buddha: "From this point on, one cultivates the three contemplations. What demons and the like would dare to delude and disturb?
What are these 'flowers in the sky' afflictions that can obstruct the mind? Therefore, it is said next: 'Form is itself formlessness;

thus one sees the Tathāgata. This is where the Vajra-knot [of the teaching] lies. Furthermore, the subsequent passage is a re-explanation of the two lines, 'Returning to the same as the Tathāgata,' which was previously explained."
This means that by focusing the mind upon the manifested signs of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), they appear vividly as if present before one's eyes, as if one were still in the world with him.

This takes the transformations of a single lifetime while he was in the world to be his eternal abiding (*nitya*). Now, as for the interpretation [of the other view], it takes the World-Honored One’s true body of wisdom and principle (*jñāna-dharmatā-kāya*) directly to be the eternally abiding.
Therefore, it says "it may also be" [the case]. Within this, the intended meaning lies in the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body).

The Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), including its eyes, ears, and so forth, each pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Because there is a body that can be spoken of as imperishable and because it is worthy of veneration, [the text states]:
"Below 'Hanging Banners,' second, clarifying the auxiliary conditions. The original intent was to honor the Buddha by establishing images;
consequently, one adorns the site of practice (maṇḍala) and pledges a specific number of days. Regarding "adorned with the altar site," this is as described below in the section on repentance.

Briefly citing the Vaipulya sutras, the commentary (*shu*) omits distinctions regarding their antiquity or recentness when they do not represent anything specific; this intent is as explained above in the discussion of the three periods.

The commentary begins with "I prostrate to all Buddhas," which precisely clarifies the characteristics of mental application and practice. The text of the commentary consists of four parts: first, a general clarification of completeness and deficiency.
Second, a detailed exposition of the eight kinds; third, the sequence of their arising; fourth, a conclusion summarizing the intent of the detailed exposition.
Within the first [section], there are two parts: the initial deficiency and the subsequent completeness. Regarding the deficiency, the commentary states:

"The *Sūtra on Good Precepts*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*, the discourse of King Aśoka, and the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*—these are identical. These five matters are the same; they constitute the practice of faith.
In this section, the former part explains faith and the latter part explains practice. Practice refers to the six perfections, such as giving and so forth.

Within the context of diligence (*vīrya*), there is a passage concerning the gateway of removing obstacles: "If a person has, in previous lives, many grave karmic obstructions and is afflicted by evil spirits and demons...
and so on, up to "...one should be courageous and resolute... (as in the commentary). Since that text occurs within the section on diligence, it is also...
This is the meaning of "added practice" (*prayoga*), which is also consistent with the intent of this sutra. [The commentary] at the very end provides a full exposition.

First, the eight dharmas are listed collectively; subsequently, their text is explained individually. Regarding the phrase "the Sutra on Bowing to the Buddha": it explains the method for bowing to the Buddha.

Since the title of the sutra already specifies "bowing to the Buddha," bowing to the Buddha is the primary principle (*adhikṛta*); the remaining seven [dharmas] are all for the purpose of bowing to the Buddha.

Regarding the conditions: making offerings and praises constitutes the category of paying homage to the Buddha; repentance, exhortation, and sympathetic joy constitute the intent of paying homage to the Buddha.

Because one desires to repent and so forth, one pays respectful homage to express one's earnest resolve. The seventh [point] is the dedication of all merit from such acts as paying homage toward the three objects.
The eighth is the articulation of what one hopes for in one's mind. Since that [text] is titled "Paying Homage to the Buddha," the remaining [sections] are the methods. Now, regarding this sutra...
Next, it says, "I prostrate to the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions," which directly presents the primary object of veneration.
The practitioner generally expresses the intent of the prostration here; logically, this should encompass all ritual methods. The essential doctrine of this sutra lies in its brevity of expression.

Therefore, three [practices] are briefly cited: namely, ritual worship (*li*), repentance (*chan*), and praise (*zan*). As the text says, "names," this refers precisely to praise. △ Regarding the subsequent detailed explanation of the text:

as for the phrase in the commentary, "all are able to remain far removed from [evil]," it means that by single-mindedly and diligently practicing even one matter, all other benefits are fully realized.

Thus, although the various teachings cited previously vary in number—some few, some many—one obtains great benefit from each. The others are all of a similar cause, producing results of equal flow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This is the fruit. To explain the meaning in detail, its benefits become clearly manifest. Regarding the first point, the ordinary text says:

"Vigorously maintain incense and flowers, making offerings according to the Dharma," and so forth; its benefit can be understood from this. Regarding the second point, this is the ordinary text in *Brahma-svara* (Sanskrit) script.
It is the passage in which Queen Śrīmālā praises the Buddha. Furthermore, the *Upādhyāya-viśeṣa-stotra* (Elder’s Special Praise) says: "The Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is like space."

Regarding the "Emptiness" and other [practices], among the three [categories], there are the Seven Buddhas, the Buddhas of the Ten Directions, the Twenty-five Buddhas, the Fifty-three Buddhas, and the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, up to the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*.
According to one's inclination, these may be expanded or abbreviated; for each, there exists a sūtra praising their efficacy.

From four or five [buddhas] downwards, they are all as usual, chanted according to the liturgical rites performed at the appointed times. These may also be either extensive or abbreviated; however, only for the morning...
The morning service is most complete. In the fourth [section], it says: "There is nothing that the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions do not know," and so forth.

The commentary notes: "Regarding the removal of the third and fourth obstacles, the text follows below. As for the "endowment of both the primary and secondary [recompenses]," these were originally incomplete; they were summoned by karma.

Now, because one has washed away and repented of sinful karma until it is exhausted, both the primary and secondary recompenses are fully endowed. In the fifth [section], it says: "The various [Buddhas] of the ten directions..."

Regarding the passage "The Tathāgata manifests his body and attains enlightenment," etc., the commentary notes that this excludes those who slander. This was because their slandering prevented them from speaking or listening;
now, having rectified their past transgressions, they are exhorted to speak for a long time. Since they have requested the teaching of the Dharma, they will certainly hear it themselves;

thus, through extensive learning, their wisdom increases. Among the six [types of people], it says: "In the past, out of jealousy toward others, they did not attract followers to gather around them; now, their retribution for that sin has ended."
One receives the retribution of being solitary for oneself; now, by reversing this and rejoicing [in others' merit], one obtains a retinue.

Regarding the seventh point, it says: "May all the meritorious deeds I have performed be harmonized," and so forth. Because one was previously greedy and restricted one's own merit without dedicating it to others, it was narrow and inferior;
now, by dedicating it toward them, it becomes vast and great. It is like a sound that, when directed into a horn, is heard from afar. Regarding the eighth point...
It says: "May all sentient beings quickly resolve upon bodhicitta," and so forth. This excludes those who would regress from upholding the practice, as previously explained.
The meaning is that if there is no aspiration to urge and guide one forward, the practice will not be accomplished.

Regarding the passage "As for the offerings described in the commentary" below, this section provides a detailed exposition of the eight types of offerings. We shall now address the first type. Furthermore, this is divided into three parts (as found in the commentary).
First, concerning the phrase "internal and external": external wealth refers to money, silk, gold, jewels, clothing, food, and so forth, such as those offered by the Elder Sudatta;
internal wealth refers to one's head, eyes, body, and life, such as those offered by Prince Sattva. Therefore, it is called "substantial offering" (*vastu-dāna*).
There are two reasons why all these can be known: first, they are commonly explained in secular lectures everywhere, so that neither monastics nor laypeople are unaware of them;

second, since these are matters of ritual form (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there is no need to laboriously clarify their underlying principles. Once they are presented, they are understood and practiced immediately—what need is there for arduous discourse?
As for the "Dharma-offering" (*dharmapūjā*) detailed in the commentary, each point is correctly elucidated; thus, it is called "ten."
Regarding "those who practice the Dharma": this refers generally to all the teachings and instructions of various schools; it means that they all receive and uphold the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

Master Huayan Zang’s *Explanation of What Must Be Known Regarding the Receiving and Upholding of Mahāyāna Sūtras* contains five points, as clarified below in the section on the *Pariṇāmanā* (Dedication) chapter.
Among these, regarding the "teachings" (*dharma*), one should first distinguish between principle, fruition, and practice. Regarding "transcribing," [it involves] flaying the skin...

[This refers to] making paper and so forth. Regarding "transferring the gift": seeing another who has resolved to uphold [the teachings] but lacks the power to accomplish it, one then transfers what one possesses to serve as a superior condition for them.
Regarding "listening": listening to another’s exposition oneself, or listening to their recitation.

Regarding "reading": searching through and examining the text. Regarding "upholding": taking it up as the essential core of one's mind. However, ordinary people generally consider mere reading and recitation sufficient.

To treat "upholding" (śrutvā dhārayitavyaḥ) as merely reciting is a great loss of the original intent. This is because one fails to recognize that upholding is distinct from turning over the text for recitation (parivartana-pāṭha), and is also distinct from chanting (svādhyāya).
These—reciting, chanting, and upholding—constitute three types of Dharma practice. Otherwise, there would only be two types.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga’s commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the passage on "upholding, reciting, and chanting" states: "As for 'chanting' (uddeśa)..."
This explains the causes for receiving and upholding [the Dharma]. One reads with the desire to receive it, and one recites with the desire to uphold it. Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

"Receiving and upholding" refers to practicing based on the *dhāraṇī* (total-holding) methods; "reading and reciting" refers to practicing based on the expansion of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

These shall be explained in detail within the section on the dissemination of the teaching. "Expounding" means lecturing; "contemplating" means investigating through the wisdom of observation (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and "cultivating" [refers to the wisdom derived from meditation].
Regarding "practice" (xi): one may rely upon it to take as the object of dhyāna (as stated in Asaṅga’s commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

"when in conjunction with samāpatti"), or one may rely upon it to give rise to the myriad practices; thus, there are ten. In the sub-commentary (*shu*) following the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the second section compares the superiority and inferiority of material wealth versus the Dharma.
"Those who make offerings" refers to internal and external wealth, each of which has various different forms. [The term] "Dharma" [is used here].

Regarding the most excellent form of offering: material giving is limited, while the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible. Material giving comes to an end when much is given; the gift of Dharma increases as it is given more and more.
Material giving yields worldly retribution; the gift of Dharma yields supramundane retribution.

The commentary states that regarding the "seven practices," only four are briefly listed in the text, while the remaining three are included by the term "etc. The full text does not state this explicitly, but it refers to the offering of practicing according to what has been taught.
Nurturing; making offerings to benefit sentient beings; making offerings to gather in sentient beings; making offerings by taking on the suffering of sentient beings;
making offerings by diligently cultivating roots of goodness; making offerings by not abandoning the bodhisattva deeds; making offerings by not departing from the bodhicitta.
The word "equal" (*samā*) includes the three middle types. However, these seven practices encompass two meanings: first, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

Because it is practiced, the relinquishing of material wealth, food, and so forth as an offering is itself called "supreme. The remaining six [perfections] are to be understood by this analogy. Second, practicing in accordance with the Dharma is itself an offering;
it is not necessary to rely on material things and the like to be called an offering. The remaining six are also to be understood by this analogy. [Commentary:

Regarding the passage beginning with "However, when one speaks of the Dharma," the third point clarifies that there is no distinction between material wealth and the Dharma. Thus, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Extensive Text on Bodhisattva Precepts) states: "Wealth..."
The Dharma and material gifts are equal and without distinction. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That which is equal regarding the Dharma is also equal regarding food.

Regarding the expression "material gift corresponding to the Dharma," there are two meanings: first, giving material wealth for the sake of the Dharma is also called a "gift corresponding to the Dharma";

second, it refers to not reckoning the existence of the giver, the object given, or the recipient—such that all three wheels (*tri-maṇḍala*) are empty. (The term "wheel" [maṇḍala] carries the sense of crushing or grinding. Holding...

If there is existence, it destroys the merit of the outflows-free; if one penetrates emptiness, it destroys the obstacles and delusions of ignorance. This accords with the True Dharma and the phenomena of dream-like and illusion-like dependent origination.
Regarding the passage "like the Venerable Sudatta," this refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, wherein the Buddha commands the elder Sudatta to inquire after his illness.
Sudatta says to the Buddha, "I am not capable of this," and then proceeds to recount how he went to his father’s house and established a great assembly of offerings to provide for all.
When the seven days had concluded, there were śramaṇas, brahmins, non-Buddhists, the poor, the lowly, the solitary, and beggars.
Then Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said: "This great sacrificial assembly is not equal to the gift bestowed by you, O virtuous ones; it should be an assembly for the gift of Dharma.
What is the use of this sacrificial assembly of material wealth? An assembly for the gift of Dharma has neither beginning nor end; it is a simultaneous offering."
"All sentient beings"—this is called the assembly for the gift of Dharma. The meaning and intent herein are as explained in a separate fascicle.
Regarding the "joyful vision who burned his body," this refers to what is taught in the tenth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Long ago, when the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa taught the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, that joyful vision...
He practiced asceticism and attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms. Overjoyed, he thought to himself, "This is the power of hearing this sutra.

He entered samādhi, and from the sky there rained down various fragrant flowers as an offering. Having completed the offering, he arose from his concentration and thought, "It would be better to offer my own body.
Thereupon, he consumed various incenses and drank fragrant oils for twelve hundred years. He anointed his body with fragrant oils and [proceeded] before the Buddha.
First, wrapping his body in celestial *tāmbūla* robes and pouring over it various fragrant oils, he used his supernormal powers to spontaneously ignite his own body.
Its radiance shone throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers. The Buddhas therein simultaneously praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! This is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. If one were to use incense, flowers, necklaces, and other such objects—even..."

This is also beyond their reach. The commentary states: "Virtuous merit" refers to external wealth, while "Joyful Vision" refers to internal wealth; because these accord with the Dharma, they are called "Dharma-offering.

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "all accord with ultimate truth": although the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are fundamentally empty and ultimate truth is fundamentally existent, those who cling to the three spheres as being real fall into delusion regarding ultimate truth by claiming it does not exist.
Now, having distanced oneself from the three forms of emptiness, one must accord with ultimate truth.
Ultimate truth is suchness (tathatā) as manifested by the two kinds of emptiness. For example, the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—are not necessarily themselves suchness;

rather, it is that which is manifested by these two kinds of emptiness that constitutes suchness. While various teachings merely speak of the "emptiness of the three wheels," this is done for the purpose of refuting attachments.
Now, to speak directly of "Ultimate Truth" (tattva) is precisely to manifest the nature (dhātu). How much more so when one speaks of "conforming" to it;

herein, the three wheels (trimaṇḍala) do not require destruction, for the entire body [of the practitioner] is vast and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, non-different from Ultimate Truth. It is like a box and its lid fitting perfectly; thus, it is called "conformity.

Only in this way does it become an offering of contemplative practice (bhāvanā-caryā). Therefore, its characteristics and efficacy are far superior to the previous two [offerings], being equal to empty space.
This displays the proportions of that which can be weighed and that which is weighed. "The body of the complete Dharma" is the first wheel;
"weighing the reality of things" is the second wheel; "making offerings to the Buddha" is the third wheel. Regarding the term "equal":
the subsequent text states, "For this reason, the Bodhisattva does not practice their cultivation in vain; they constantly encounter the Buddhas and never miss the proper time."
All ritual implements are constantly accomplished in accordance with principle. Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma accords with the true principle for the sake of the Buddha.
The commentary states: "Based on this, it is said that 'one incense, one flower,' etc., and it is further said that they are 'constantly accomplished in accordance with principle.

From this, we know that all items listed in the sutra are accomplished by being in accord with principle—whether they be one or many, and so forth. Therefore, the practitioner need only settle [the mind]..."
Regarding the practice of mental contemplation: each and every thing is inherently manifold, and all are pervasive as the Buddha.

As for the phrase "The Commentary says that sutra," it refers to the third section on the Extensive Cultivation of Offerings within the *Universal Worthy’s Vows and Practices* (*Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*). It states: "By the power of my Universal Worthy vows and practices"—this refers to the power of the Dharma.
In the preceding text of that sutra, it says: "Arising deep faith and understanding"—this refers to one's own power. Thus, the causes and conditions of one's own power are fully complete.
Therefore, the offerings and so forth are immeasurable. Regarding the commentary’s statement that they are "like Mount Sumeru," this takes the human perception of height and greatness as the limit.
Furthermore, because it is composed of the four jewels and possesses ten virtues, it symbolizes that each individual offering is endowed with virtuous characteristics and wondrous function.

"Like the waters of the ocean" refers to their depth and vastness; they are deep because they accord with principle, and vast because they accord with phenomena. "Clouds of incense and flowers" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Regarding each set of offering implements and so forth, for every single item, it is like a cloud. "Cloud" is a metaphor for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This means that while these offering implements have manifest forms and characteristics, wisdom discerns them as being without intrinsic nature. Arising from the emptiness of the *dharmatā*, they emerge from the dharma of non-arising. They can manifest (through contemplative practice) what is manifested; yet the offerings are utterly without support.
They appear and arrive in response, yet in arriving, they come from nowhere. Their function fades and they depart, yet in departing, they go nowhere. And...
It is able to contain compassion and pour down the rain of the Dharma, benefiting and sustaining all things in inexhaustible succession; thus it possesses the likeness of clouds.
Regarding the phrase "the expression of feelings arises from the middle," this borrows the phrasing from the Preface to the Mao Commentary on the *Shijing*.

Because one's singing and chanting are insufficient, one does not realize the need for hand-dancing and foot-stamping; here, because one's praise and recitation are insufficient, one must offer earnest prayers and prostrations.
Regarding these, the laudatory verses in various sutras include: for instance, the *Nāgī-stotra* says, "Profoundly penetrating that sin and merit are equal in nature";
the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* says, "The wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata, etc."; the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* says, "His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses, etc.";
and regarding the World-Honored One’s stage as a bodhisattva, it is said he praised Buddha Tiṣya by standing on one foot: "Heaven and earth, this world, and the Hall of Much Learning, etc."
"Even unto sovereign and blazing majesty," "The Tathāgata is most wondrous and marvelous," and "In the heavens above and the heavens below, none can equal him.
At the end of the Avataṃsaka section, it says: "The atoms of all lands and the thoughts of every mind may be counted; the waters of the great oceans may be drunk up;
space may be measured and the wind bound; yet no one can fully describe the Buddha’s merits."
Regarding the Tripiṭaka Master Na of Shule, the *Huayan Zuangling Ji* states: The Tripiṭaka Master was a native of India;
having arrived in this land, he was also proficient in the Chinese language. He lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and both monastics and laypeople gathered like clouds.

During the lecture, a man suddenly appeared holding a ceremonial tablet, appearing like a high official, who said, "The Heavenly Emperor has sent me to invite you, Master, to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. [At that time,] the presiding lecturer (Dujiang) and the *Venerable*...
The *brahman* chants and all requisites for the Dharma service must be fully prepared. When the assembly of monks at the lecture hall all saw this together, he vanished upon finishing his speech.
At that moment, the Tripitaka Master, the *dujiang*, and the *vinaya-dhara* suddenly passed away on their Dharma seats.
