if one lacks detachment from characteristics, one is identical to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). This section below [of the commentary] explains these three reasons. The "object" (*suǒ*)...

Because there are three [aspects]: being endowed with compassion and wisdom while remaining free from signs. That is to say, great compassion involves downward transformation, which is dedication toward sentient beings;

great wisdom involves upward seeking, which is directed toward bodhi; and being free from these two refers to direction toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Furthermore, regarding these three below:
Second, because they mutually support one another. To say that "one is identical to the three" means: in order to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one must turn toward sentient beings;
for if one realizes emptiness apart from form, it is not the true limit of reality. Therefore, one must turn toward *bodhi*;

by swiftly realizing *bodhi*, one accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and severs the two obstacles, thereby exhausting the ultimate reality. Furthermore, in order to save sentient beings, one must realize the limit of reality regarding delusions.
Only when one possesses mastery can one transform others; for if one is bound by oneself, one cannot untie the bonds of others.

Therefore, one must turn toward Bodhi, for it is only through wisdom that one can extensively benefit others. Furthermore, in order to dedicate merit toward Bodhi, one must turn toward sentient beings;

for if one does not act for the sake of sentient beings, one will never realize the great fruit. Thus, one must turn toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); yet, if one were to realize the limit of reality, that would not be Bodhi.

Regarding the four great vows (*catvāri mahāpraṇidhānāni*), they may be understood as usual. They are formulated in correspondence with the Four Noble Truths, as explained in the section on the meaning of generating the bodhicitta.

Nevertheless, I shall now briefly restate them: because one contemplates the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one vows to deliver sentient beings; because one contemplates the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), one severs afflictions (*kleśa*);

because one contemplates the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), one studies the dharma-gates that are free from fault; and because one contemplates the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), one vows to realize *bodhi*.
This is the realization of true quiescence (*śānti*). As for the five vows, they are also as previously described;
that is, rather than merely severing afflictions, one adds the foundation of the Tathāgata’s boundless vows and the vow to gather merit and wisdom without exception.
The commentary states: "From the eighth section above, this is the third major heading: the sequence of arising. (1) First, one must generate the mind of awakening to perform offerings;

(2) verbal praise (the custom of India is to speak words of praise upon seeing [the object of veneration], for when emotion arises within, it spontaneously issues forth in speech); (3) physical prostration (one prostrates immediately following the verbal praise;

it is not necessary to remain standing rigidly). Next is the cleansing of the ritual vessel (4), which is repentance; by purifying body and mind, one prepares to seek the Dharma). This is followed by joyfully seeking the rain of Dharma (5), which is the exhortation [for the turning of the wheel of Dharma]."

"Requesting the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma" means to gather others into oneself (sixth). "Dedication" refers to the three points (seventh; all practices are now directed toward these three points).

"Vowing that all may attain Buddhahood" (eighth; the affairs of self and others are perfected). As for the ten types: first, prostration to the Buddha; second, praise; third, making offerings; fourth, repentance of karma; fifth, sympathetic joy; sixth, requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma;
seventh, requesting the Buddha to remain in the world (this is divided into two parts within the category of "requesting," while the other [part] is combined with the preceding).

1) Constantly following and learning from the Buddha (this is the dedication toward Bodhi); 2) Always complying with sentient beings (this is the dedication toward sentient beings); 3) Universally dedicating all [merit] (the meaning corresponds to the *bhūtakoṭi*;
the preceding three were expanded within the category of dedication, whereas here they are combined into one). Regarding the distinct meanings of these, each is as noted in the marginal glosses.
As for the statement that those [practitioners] lack conduct and vows, it is because all ten gates are, in fact, the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra.

The Commentary: If [the response] does not descend, this is the fourth point, which concludes the intent. Regarding the three sections on "Response and Induction" (*ganying*), the first briefly explains the text.

As for the phrase "or sees," etc., it means that what is seen is without fixed standard—whether it be the Buddha stroking the crown of the head, or various flowers and lights preaching the Dharma, and so forth; hence the word "or."
As for "seeing": either within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one may suddenly see it while the mind has forgotten the characteristics of its physical location;

or within contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one sees the true nature (*tathatā*) manifesting such appearances in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*). Although these are established according to the principles of meaning, they do not exclusively consist of these appearances alone.
Nevertheless, at that time, it corresponds with this; or perhaps one sees such things within sleep or dreams. This collectively clarifies encountering a wholesome environment.

Regarding the phrase "not conceiving a holy mind": in the *Buddhāvatamsaka Sūtra* (specifically the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*), when describing various superior signs, it concludes each by stating, "Not conceiving a holy mind is called a wholesome environment;
if one forms a holy interpretation, one will immediately be possessed by various demons. The present usage employs this very expression.
The meaning of *praśrabdhi* (lightness-and-ease) is as explained previously; here it merely clarifies the mental and physical modes of activity at that time.

[In the] commentary, following the phrase "as stated below," there are two parts: first, the citation of examples to provide proof; second, the separate explanation of various dhyānas, beginning with the section on the Tiantai *Zhiguan*.
Regarding the "signs of the arising of wholesome roots" within the ninth gate—since the eight gates have already been explained as before, this constitutes the ninth.
Some feel heavy, as if weighed down by objects; others feel light, as if their bodies were about to fly. The rest can all be understood, though the text is brief;

The commentary below the sutra-text provides a twofold reconciliation. Regarding "eliminating delusions" and so forth: delusions and karma reside within the mind, like silt and mud in water;

Thus, it is said that for those whose minds are agitated by excessive discursive thought, the remedy is the contemplation of counting the breath. This is because when the mind is distracted by various objects, it becomes difficult to concentrate; therefore, one must rely on the method of counting the breath to pacify the mind. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the mind is not yet settled": this means that although the mind has been brought under control through the aforementioned methods, it has not yet attained the state of being fully settled. ...and so forth. Regarding "or realizing equality": there are two kinds of this realization and purity (*pratisaṃvid*). First is similar realization, which refers to the five preparatory stages where a semblance of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) arises.
Second is true realization, which refers to the true untainted wisdom from the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* up to the ninth path of non-obstruction (the thirty-four moments of mind).
Because the defilements of the three realms are exhausted therein, it is called realization and purity. *Commentary:* "According to what is convenient" means:
This is the second section. Those who wish to attain profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom must first skillfully settle the mind (*citta*).
One must thoroughly understand and study all six methods to regulate the mind, employing whichever is most suitable for long-term practice.
Why is this? If the mind is not made comfortable, forceful cultivation is of no benefit; therefore, one should study all six to test oneself and apply whichever is appropriate. Following...
"To employ them as occasion demands" means that one does not select a fixed sequence.

"Various meditative concentrations" refers to attaining the maintenance of the body (*dhāraṇī-kāya*), coarse abiding (*sthūla-sthiti*), subtle abiding (*sūkṣma-sthiti*), the preparatory stage of the desire realm (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), the first dhyāna, and so forth. The commentary states: "Counteracting" refers to the third section.

However, regarding the six afflictions to be remedied, it is taught that they all arise during the midst of sitting while practicing various forms of concentration. This passage has two parts; the first is as follows:

To provide the formal explanation of this section: When the mind takes various objects as its conditions, it becomes restless and sharp (making those objects difficult to forget). The mind wanders aimlessly in all directions and is difficult to restrain or record.
Therefore, one must practice the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) to control it. Because the mind is focused exclusively on counting, it forgets external objects.

Thus, the Buddha said that for those with excessive *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), he taught them to count the breath. As for "dullness and distraction": dullness means a lack of...
Commentary: When the mind is obscured by sleep, it becomes distracted and floats upward into restlessness. This "restlessness" refers to a state of dazed confusion where there is no fixed direction;

it is also characterized by the mind’s discursive thoughts and clinging to objects. These are all signs of instability while sitting in meditation. Therefore, one should regulate the mind by following the breath, clearly observing the inhalation and exhalation.

This clear observation of the inhalation and exhalation remedies the dullness and sleep of the indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta*), while the mind’s reliance upon the breath remedies the clinging to discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Regarding coarse breath: it arises because the mind is applied with excessive urgency, or because it is shortened and unsettled due to external circumstances, causing the spirit and mind to become restless and vexed;
thus the breath becomes coarse. This pertains to the body. When the mind is scattered and in motion, it pertains to the mind. Therefore, the gate of cessation (*śamatha*) is employed.
Relax the body and release the breath; settle the mind in profound stillness to bring all sensory objects to rest—this should be used as the remedy. As for those who harbor greed and anger:

while sitting, if one suddenly thinks of something desirable—be it fame and profit, sensual desire, or the memory of an enemy who previously committed such-and-such an offense against us—greed and anger will immediately arise.
These are coarse hindrances that are difficult to suppress; one must...
One contemplates the impurity and various defects of one's own body and the bodies of others to counteract greed.

One practices the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, feeling pity for all beings and forgiving their ignorance and afflictions, in order to counteract hatred; thus it is said, "one contemplates immediately. Regarding the phrase "when delusion and false obstructions arise, one returns":
this delusion is not like that of cattle or sheep; rather, it is a lack of faith in the causes and conditions of karmic retribution, or like planting [seeds]...

Thus, various differing views arise. Therefore, it is further said: "The heterodox must be reflected upon through inversion. One contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in reverse order from birth and death back to their mutual causality, even unto ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since [ignorance] arises horizontally from emptiness, one returns to the original source; hence, it is called "returning" (*huan*).

Thus, all commentaries and treatises regard contemplation in the forward order as the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti-dvāra*) and contemplation in the reverse order as the gate of cessation (*nivṛtti-dvāra*), which is precisely returning to the root.

"Source" (*yuan*) means the extinction of all deluded thoughts. Regarding "evil thoughts and the like": this refers to when, while sitting in meditation, evil thoughts suddenly arise in one's contemplation, wishing to commit various evil deeds;
or when various kinds of evil objects appear, even to the point of distressing the body and mind.
One should know that these are all the manifestation of past karmic obstacles of evil. One should employ the gateway of purity and maintain mindfulness of the Dharma.
The body is fundamentally pure, neither arising nor ceasing; its intrinsic nature is pure. It is treated as empty in order to counteract various defilements and to destroy adverse conditions.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, etc. (*shōran jō*) in the commentary: this consists of two parts analyzing the sequence, which are further divided into two: first, the preceding [analysis], and second, the subsequent [analysis]. Within the preceding analysis, there are again two parts:
first, the formal analysis, and second, the reconciliation with the sutra. Now, for the first: it says "it is common" (*tsū*). This refers to the six [perfections] that are practiced.
As for the gates: whether by sequential order, by what is appropriate, or by the mode of counteractive practice (*pratipakṣa*).

As for their distinctions: each has its own views and tenets, and each has its own pursuit. These are roughly assigned as in the commentary; now they shall be further explained, first by way of several categories.
Those who seek pleasure refer to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Because their faculties are dull, they rely solely on the teacher’s instructions.
When practicing the counting of breaths, they know only to count from one to ten to stabilize the mind, desiring through this dhyāna to experience various pleasures.

This is the arising of demonic activity (*mārakarma*) through counting the breaths, because they crave birth and death. Or it is like those among the followers of the Daoist teachings here in this land, who likewise practice such regulation.
The breath nurtures the life-force; one seeks the bliss of longevity. Although there is no formal teaching on counting the breaths, mental visualization is no different from following the breath;
thus the commentary states, "seeking bliss. As for those with [wrong] views—namely, non-Buddhist practitioners of sharp faculties—their views are intense and vigorous.
When they count the breaths from one to ten, desiring to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are likewise able to discern the present.
There are four propositions regarding the existence and non-existence of breath, as explained in other fascicles.

Following what the mind perceives, one reckons it to be real and gives rise to various wrong practices, severing wholesome states of mind and even going so far as to explain them to others; thus, they are said to "possess views.

Those who seek *nirvāṇa* refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), who desire to exit the triple world and seek *nirvāṇa* for themselves; therefore, they count the breaths to regulate the mind. Regarding this counting:

At the time of cessation, one does not depart from the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth. That the text specifically clarifies the Bodhisattva is also evident; by examining it closely, this can be understood.
Since this is the case for counting the breaths (*ānāpāna*), the same applies to the other five methods: following, stopping, contemplation, returning, and purification.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "Now, in this sutra," it refers to the second assembly of the sutra. This is the intended meaning: to distinguish [the practitioner] from ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the Two Vehicles, in order to cultivate the Perfect [Teaching].

The great causes and conditions have been frequently clarified in the preceding text. The arousal of the mind and the cultivation of thought do not go beyond seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.
The commentary states that what follows below serves to distinguish the latter [from the former]. Regarding "the One Vehicle alone," within this there are further distinctions of sudden and gradual.
As for the "Gate of Revolving," it refers to the *Svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* (Revolutionary Dhāraṇī) attained by Tiantai; through it, one understands all phenomena within a single phenomenon.
Each and every one is thus; they revolve without obstruction. This is attained through the perfection of gradual cultivation.

This is the core teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*, known as the "Gradual Gate. Therefore, it is said: "The preceding gates involve entering emptiness from the conventional and attaining the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*);

this is the dharma practiced in common by those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas. Now, entering the conventional from emptiness constitutes the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*). That is to say, entering the conventional from emptiness involves revolving...

One turns forth the merits of all dharmas and conditioned activities; that is, one first understands how [the bodhisattva] was identical to the two vehicles in entering emptiness from the conventional.
Once the contemplation of emptiness is perfected, one subsequently does not abide in this wisdom of emptiness, but uses it to enter the conventional. Only then can one revolve all dharmas.

Is this not the case where the merit of gradual cultivation culminates in perfect realization? As for the Gate of Contemplating the Mind, one directly proceeds from the source of the fundamental mind to comprehend all phenomena;
thus, it belongs to the Sudden Teaching. It is said therein: "One illuminates the source of all phenomena from afar, and that source is the mind of sentient beings.
Although there are slight differences between the sudden and gradual methods regarding the ritual of setting forth on the path, both share the same essential tenet of the One Vehicle’s true teaching.
△ Regarding "revolving," this is the fourth section. Its general meaning has already been explained above. As for what was stated above regarding "entering the provisional from emptiness":
while counting the breaths, one should give rise to a great vow out of compassion for sentient beings.

Although one knows that sentient beings are empty and the buddha-fields are empty, one desires to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the buddha-fields throughout the future eons. One makes this vow in this manner.
Once this is done, one should immediately realize that the breath being counted is neither arising nor ceasing, its nature being empty and quiescent.

It is the breath itself that is empty; it is not that the breath is extinguished to become empty. The nature of the breath is inherently empty, and one is able to do so because one has previously entered the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
That "emptiness is the breath" means that one is now entering the provisional (*prajñapti*) from emptiness. As for "neither true nor provisional,"...
Only by relying on the dharma-nature of the Middle Way can one transform all phenomena.

"Neither mundane nor supramundane" means that because this cessation lacks the nature of being either mundane or supramundane, it accomplishes both the mundane and the supramundane. "Like a dream or an illusion" means that although no reality can be found therein, one still performs various activities through conceptualization;
the realization of cessation is likewise: although no nature of cessation can be found, it nevertheless accomplishes [its purpose].
Regarding the mindfulness of breathing: from one to ten, one knows it with complete clarity.

As for those who have accomplished the characteristics of this breath and enter this gate, they achieve mastery over all phenomena through a single phenomenon. Therefore, the breath is the root of all things.
If one grasps it, all worldly dharmas are accomplished; if one penetrates it, all supramundane dharmas are accomplished.
Within this, each and every dharma-gate and its mode of practice should be extensively expounded, as described in other fascicles.

Regarding the phrase "cannot be exhausted," it means that although the cultivation of the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* within the gate of counting the breath has been briefly explained, the practices of the Bodhisattva are inexhaustible.
Only then is one a Bodhisattva. If one enters this gate and speaks directly of counting the breaths to harmonize the mind, it would not be exhausted even in an entire kalpa;

how much less so for the five gates of following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and equanimity, the various types of dhyāna, wisdom, supernormal powers, the four analytical knowledges, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the practices and vows of the stages, the knowledge of all modes, and all inexhaustible merits—how could these be fully described? They revolve [in infinite ways].
This concludes [the preceding section]. Therefore, it is said that "each and every one is thus. △ Regarding the "Contemplation of the Mind," this is the fifth gate.

It is intended for those of superior faculties—namely, beginners with sudden-capacity roots. If one has practiced for a long time before being able to fully comprehend the mind, they are not termed "superior faculty."

Therefore, what was previously stated as "entering the provisional from emptiness" and what is here stated as "illuminating the source of dharmas directly without following a gradual sequence" should be understood as indicating the difference between the sudden and the gradual approaches.
Regarding the "source" or the "mind," that text states: "The source of all dharmas is precisely the mind of sentient beings.
By means of the power of cultivation, when one's practice and realization are perfected, one penetrates the emptiness of all dharmas, such that neither the mind nor mental objects can be apprehended.
Only upon its attainment is it called "fundamentally pure. Regarding suffering, this is spoken solely in terms of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*); sentient beings possess this fundamentally.
This pure mind does not depend upon the emptiness of all delusive defilements. As the text on the Minor *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "One then penetrates the Middle Way within the nature of the mind.
If one perceives the Middle Way and the Two Truths within one's own mind, then one perceives the Middle Way and the Two Truths of all phenomena."
Furthermore, the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states: "All Buddhas attain liberation through the mind; the mind is pure and is called 'stainless.
It is pristine within the five realms of existence and does not receive form. Those who study this shall achieve the Great Way.
In that treatise, the essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma is identified as follows: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind is able to encompass all worlds."

The supramundane dharmas rely upon this mind to manifest the meaning of the Mahāyāna; now, likewise relying upon this mind, the six subtle gates—such as counting and so forth—are manifested for cultivation.
Regarding the contemplation that the mind is without marks (*animitta*), it refers to all phenomena.
It arises from the mind. If one can reflect back upon the source of the mind, the nature of the mind cannot be apprehended;

thus one knows that all phenomena (dharmas) are without root, and thereby attains unimpeded penetration into all phenomena. As for "the mind as the gate of counting," it refers to counting all phenomena.
All are governed by the mind; thus, the mind is the gateway of conformity. This means that all phenomena, whether in number or measure, entirely follow the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
If there were no mind-king, there would be no mental factors (*caitasika*; "number" here refers to mental factors). Because the mind-king moves, the mental factors also move.

When observing in this way, one immediately knows that the mind is the gateway of following. Regarding "the mind being tranquil is cessation": when contemplating the mind, one knows that the nature of the mind is eternally tranquil;
thus, all phenomena are also tranquil. Because they are tranquil, there is no thought of movement; because there is no thought of movement, it is called cessation.
One should know that the mind itself is the gateway of cessation. Regarding "awakening to the mind": when contemplating the mind, one clearly realizes the nature of the mind. Just as...
Like space, it opens the storehouse of ignorance and reveals the true nature; because one attains non-attached wisdom, the mind itself is the gate of contemplation.

Regarding that which is without subject or object: when contemplating the mind, since the mind that is contemplated cannot be found, nor can the wisdom that contemplates be found, both subject and object are unobtainable.
This is precisely the gate of returning to the source. As for "delusions being unable to defile": [it means that]...
When contemplating the mind, although one discriminates all phenomena, one does not cling to the discrimination of all phenomena;
for its intrinsic nature is pure and has never, from the very beginning, been defiled by the delusions of ignorance. As the Sūtra says:
"The mind is not defiled by afflictions, nor are afflictions defiled by the mind. Because the practitioner penetrates this intrinsically pure mind, they enter into the stains.
Dharma is not defiled by defiled dharmas; therefore, one knows that the mind is a gateway to purity. Regarding "directly observing" and so forth, the text is clear for all to understand.
[In the] Commentary, from "Now, as for this sutra" onwards is the third section, which correlates [the text] with the sutra. As for "applying the mind here in the fifth," it refers to contemplation.

This is the gateway of the mind (*cittadvāra*). Regarding what is called "applying the mind": it means awakening to and understanding the principles, directing the mind to form intentions, and ensuring that every thought-moment corresponds with the pure mind (*viśuddhacitta*).

Furthermore, one does not obstruct phenomena such as the defiled or the pure, but follows their characteristics and modes of activity, thereby remaining perpetually within the gateway of contemplating the mind.
If one is to counteract past habitual tendencies and regulate deluded thoughts so that they accord with rational knowledge, one then relies upon the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
These are the auxiliary skillful means for supporting *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This first points to the application of the mind, followed by the citation of scriptural evidence.

Regarding the phrase "as previously stated," this occurs at the beginning of each of the texts on the three fundamental contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). The full text reads: "To awaken to pure, perfect *bodhi* is precisely sudden awakening."

"To employ the mind of pure awakening is precisely to employ the mind. Here, "to employ" (yi) means "to use" (yong). This refers exactly to what was previously stated regarding the contemplation of the mind as fundamentally pure.
Within the mind, one clearly knows—and likewise realizes—the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the objects of knowledge, as well as the mental factors (*caitasika*) and other such phenomena.
One does not know them outside of the mind; rather, each and every thing is understood solely within one's own mind. Therefore, it is said thus. That is to say, one knows.

The mind itself is not birth, abiding, change, or cessation; yet it can discern birth, abiding, change, and cessation as previously described. The mind is not the same as the mental factors (saṃskāra) and so forth, yet these mental factors are not separate from the single mind;
thus, this serves as proof. Regarding the commentary’s statement that "cultivation occurs in the first gate":

by relying on external conditions as skillful means, one cultivates according to the characteristics, such as counting the breaths, to regulate the deluded mind and thereby accomplish this contemplation of the Middle Way of quiescent extinction (śamatha-vipaśyanā).
The cited proof states: "First, regarding those who grasp the number," this means one already knows [the sequence] and practices according to it;
"and those who progress gradually" refers to the latter section which says, "gradually increasing until one attains knowledge," etc.

This indicates that by following the numbers and so forth, one gradually proceeds through the stages, successively increasing and advancing toward the subsequent positions. Thus, it is known that this is the gate of sequential progression. Among the two or three [sections],...

The Commentary states: Regarding "first taking up the gate of counting," it refers to a question such as this: "The second [gate] is 'convenience' and the third is 'remedy,' both of which do not follow the sequential order.
Now, why does the Sūtra first mention the gate of counting? Since the gate of counting is primary, it follows the sequential order."

How is it that one says "sometimes two or three"? The answer is that this cites one case as an illustration for all others. An illustration does not preclude saying, for instance, that one first takes up the "gate of following" (*anugama*) or the "gate of cessation" (*nirodha*).
This means that whichever numerical gate is more convenient, one first takes up that number; or, if there is much discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one may do so accordingly.

One may also first take up a specific number [of gates], or take whichever gate is convenient according to one's disposition; or if one is suddenly drowsy or distracted, one likewise takes whichever gate is suitable. This applies to all four remaining cases as well.
As for the sutra citing only one case as an illustration for the others—how could it be restricted to the literal text? Furthermore, a question is raised:

based on two or three gates, if one practices whichever is most convenient or serves as an antidote, one can still attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without hindrance. Because of the remaining...
Because the gates are not expedient means, and because there is no illness to be treated, since they do not obstruct the single [practice], how can one speak of "first"?

If one speaks of "first," would that not imply a continuity that further entails a middle and a subsequent stage? Answer: This refers to the "first" in relation to the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) of the fundamental sutra.
This is because prior to this contemplation, one first practices counting and following, and so forth; it does not refer to the Six Sublime Gates (*ṣaḍ-mukha*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "the sequence is established in the fourth [chapter]," that school asserts that practitioners of the three vehicles collectively cultivate *śamatha* (calm abiding), *vipaśyanā* (insight), and so forth—whether by way of sequence, convenience, or as antidotes—and when they have exhausted all obstacles such as applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), they achieve the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
From emptiness, they enter into the provisional (*prajñapti*), revolving through all phenomena with unimpeded mastery. Now, in this sutra...
Regarding numbers and so forth, one may practice the six [perfections] in sequence, or follow one or two practices.

Once coarse obstacles have been exhausted, one realizes the quantity of mental states, even coming to know the affairs of hundreds of thousands of worlds. Although the text specifically mentions raindrops, the intent is to illustrate all phenomena by analogy.
Otherwise, how could one rotate through immeasurable Dharma gates, knowing the locus of each and every one?

Therefore, it is said that "accomplishment occurs in the fourth. Regarding the phrase "or beginning and end, etc. in the commentary: the sutra text originally contains no character for "cessation" (*xi*); it simply speaks of the "gates of counting" (*shumen*).
Furthermore, regarding the numerical categories of the dharmas to be known, it does not mention the counting of breaths, their length, or their inhalation and exhalation;
it only mentions arising, abiding, ceasing, and mindfulness. Since the fifth gate likewise does not speak of employing the breath, [this refers to] the first among the Six Sublime Gates.

One interpretation states that the mind itself is not an obstacle; this is the intended meaning of this sutra. Since it fundamentally teaches the dharma-gates within the observation of mental factors (*caitasika*), it does not necessarily require the counting of breaths.
Therefore, it is said thus: while the path of counting breaths from one to ten is also called "counting," the arising, abiding, and ceasing of thoughts within the mind are likewise called "counting.
Why must one necessarily count the breaths for them to be termed the "gate of counting"? Thus, it says "not necessarily. Question:

Since this sutra is entirely identical to the fifth gate, "Contemplating the Mind," why not simply use this alone to explain the scriptural text, rather than taking the trouble to cite the meanings of the various gates?
Answer: The Sage’s intention is manifold and does not restrict itself to a single aspect. Sentient beings have faculties that are either sharp and sudden or dull and gradual;
the Buddha’s intent secretly encompasses them all, so that each may enter according to their own inclinations. Thus, the ancient masters all said: "The Sūtra..."
One must seek the meaning within the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*); why then restrict oneself to a single path? Therefore, the text in the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Concluding Chapter) states:

"This sutra is the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, yet it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice through gradual cultivation; it is like the asuras, mosquitoes, and gnats drinking from the ocean until they are all filled.
The various meanings discussed above are all for the purpose of explaining the phrase "first taking the numerical categories" from the opening section of the sutra.

In the commentary, from "clearly knowing within the mind" onwards, the text has three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the corroboration by parallel texts; third, the differentiation from other systems.

From "due to the preceding" up to "the mind becomes pure" explains the sūtra’s phrase "first taking the counting method. This refers back to the preceding cause of counting the breaths and entering the mental counts.
The phrase "merely entering the mental counts" introduces the subsequent passage on the mindfulness of arising, abiding, and ceasing. All these references to the preceding [text] are based upon...
One may practice the meditation on the breath (*ānāpāna*) by means of the three gates, such as "successively," "at will," and "as an antidote.

Alternatively, one may not rely on the latter two phrases, but instead apply only the fifth gate to cultivate the six subtle wonders of the mind. Therefore, the phrase "clearly knowing" below encompasses both meanings;
once cultivation is perfected, one is able to know both. Question: The Sūtra says "clearly knowing within the mind. How can it be said here that one "clearly knows the mind"?
[Question: Is this not, then, an inversion? [Answer: It possesses both meanings. That is to say, it is simply that which is known within my own mind; there is no separate wisdom that knows it.
Furthermore, it is merely the knowing of the thoughts of arising and ceasing within my own mind;

it is not the knowing of some fixed phenomena existing as real entities outside the mind. Therefore, it should be explained in this way. How could this be an inversion? [Regarding] coarse and subtle...

Regarding this, according to the treatise, the [four phases of] arising, abiding, change, and cessation are expanded into the three subtleties and five coarsenesses (five only, because the fruit of karma is excluded) in order to distinguish between the coarse and the subtle.
These are to be assigned accordingly within the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) below: the "coarse" refers to the five coarse [evolutions], and the "subtle" refers to the three subtle [evolutions].

Furthermore, the coarsest among the coarse consists of the two characteristics of differentiation and cessation; the subtlest among the subtle is exclusively the characteristic of arising; the coarsest among the subtle consists of the first two [characteristics] within the characteristic of duration;

and the subtlest among the coarse consists of the latter two [characteristics] within the characteristic of duration. "Distracted thought" (*vikalpa*) is a general designation. "Fundamental" (*mūla*) refers to the three [subtle evolutions].

The subtle consists of the five coarse [factors]. Furthermore, the three characteristics beginning with abiding (*sthiti*) are all derivative, while the characteristic of arising (*utpāda*) is the root.

Moreover, the four characteristics beginning with arising are all derivative, while fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is the root. As for their respective limits, they are contained within the first two of the characteristics of arising and abiding.

Within the *ālayavijñāna*, all other [factors] reside within the *pravṛttivijñāna*. Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned coarse and subtle [aspects], each has its own root and branches, and each has its own distinct boundaries and limits.
Thus, the treatise states: "The characteristics of arising and ceasing are of two kinds:

first, the coarse, which is associated with the mind (that is, mental factors are associated with the mind-king, or objects are associated with the mind); second, the subtle, which is not associated with the mind (because there is no mind-king or mental factors)."

...these characteristics can correspond [to one another]. Furthermore, the coarsest among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The subtle among the coarse and the coarse among the subtle is the realm of bodhisattvas.
The subtle among the subtle is the realm of Buddhas. "Realm" (*dhātu*) here carries the meaning of a boundary or limit.

Regarding the "headings and quantities," this summarizes what precedes; it means that the four characteristics are like heads or leaders, and within each individual characteristic, there are [further divisions].

There are numerous phenomena such as arising and ceasing that arise through mutual dependence and causality, each possessing its own thread [of continuity] without becoming confused with others, even up to eighty-four thousand [dharmas], because they do not deviate from the four characteristics. Regarding the clear enumeration of these threads, to explain them individually:

among those of arising, the first is the "characteristic of karma" (karma-lakṣaṇa); among those of ceasing, the first is the "characteristic of initiating karma" (karma-utthāna-lakṣaṇa); and there are four [characteristics] of abiding.
The characteristics of transformation (*pariṇāma*), manifestation (*prādurbhāva*), cognition (*jñāna*), and continuity (*saṃtati*) differ from the [other] two.

The characteristic of grasping (*udgraha*) and the characteristic of conceptualizing names (*nāman-vikalpa*) have both been repeatedly cited and explained as in the preceding text. Furthermore, regarding conformity with the three periods of time: the prior, middle, and subsequent moments of a single *kṣaṇa* constitute the three periods.

Cessation (*nirodha*) is the past; abiding (*sthiti*) is the present; and arising (*utpāda*) is the future (as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts: "the past has already ceased," etc.).
Alternatively, once having arisen, it abides; thus, arising is the past and abiding is the present. Once having abided, it ceases; thus, cessation is the future.
Therefore, in the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, they either fully explain four characteristics or briefly explain three.

This is because the two characteristics of abiding and change (sthiti-anyathātva) are both of the present and are therefore combined into one. (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Change indicates that this dharma is not static; abiding indicates that this dharma has existed.")

[This] is used [to show that] that which exists only temporarily is not immutable; therefore, they are combined as one. Thus, the verse of Maitreya explains the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*’s statement that "the marks of the body are themselves no marks of the body" because the three marks have distinct natures.
Vasubandhu’s prose commentary further establishes four marks. The text says: "The marks are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), namely arising, abiding, change, and cessation.

It should be known that such persons have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas (this is an indirect indication); rather, it is because they have [planted them] under immeasurable [Buddhas]."
Having planted various roots of goodness before hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, he is by no means an ordinary person.

As for the scriptural passage cited from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: those who "delight in birth and death" are those who are attached to wealth and pleasure, who rely on their own power and strength, and who constantly take pleasure in surpassing others;
these are the karmas of saṃsāra. Those who "adhere to various views" possess false wisdom. Therefore, [the text] cites this.

As proof, regarding those who focus on right and wrong or victory and defeat, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "To delight in the practice of victory and defeat is the conduct of the celestial Māras;
to delight in seeing right and wrong is the conduct of the external paths."
Regarding the person who acts as the petitioner for the commentary (*śāstra*), it is as explained in the first gate of the *Xuántán* (Prolegomena), citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
As for the "one *yojana*" mentioned in the commentary, the old translation states it is forty *li*, while the new translation states it is sixteen *li*.

From the phrase "I, the commentator, reflect upon... onwards is the fourth major section: the Celebration and Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This section has three parts: first, celebration; second, praise; third, dedication.

Within the first (celebration), there are two sub-sections: first, lamenting the past; second, rejoicing in the present. Regarding the first (lamenting the past): the term "delusion" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Ocean of mind" is a metaphor where "mind" is the actual phenomenon (*dharma*) and "ocean" is the simile. This corresponds to the phrase "within the waves of birth and death" in the subsequent section, where "birth and death" is the actual phenomenon.
The waves serve as a metaphor. Just as wind blows upon the ocean to produce waves, so too does ignorance delude the mind to produce birth and death. Thus, the Treatise says:

"Just as the water of the great ocean is stirred by the wind into waves, the nature of the water and the nature of the wind do not separate from one another; yet the water itself is not of a moving nature.
If the wind ceases, the appearance of movement is extinguished, though the moist nature remains unimpaired. Such is the intrinsic nature of sentient beings."
The pure mind, stirred by the wind of ignorance, is such that the mind and ignorance are both devoid of form and are never separated from one another;
yet the mind is not of a nature to move. If ignorance ceases, the continuity [of movement] ceases as well, for the nature of wisdom is indestructible.

According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the wind is used as a metaphor for objective conditions (*viṣaya*). The text states: "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) abides eternally, [disturbed] by the winds of objective conditions."

"Movement. The vast waves surge through the depths of the ocean abyss with no end in sight. The *Śāstra* speaks of "ignorance," referring to the cause; the *Sūtra* speaks of "objects," referring to the conditions.
When cause and condition are fully present, they cause the pure mind to stir and move, forming the waves of birth and death.
As for "floating and sinking": the realms of humans and devas are "floating," while the three miserable paths are "sinking. It is like a person falling into the swirling eddies of water.
Once it sinks to the bottom, it floats to the surface for a moment, but upon emerging from the water, it cannot stay and sinks back down again;
each instance may be understood through this analogy. Regarding the phrase "the various Buddhas emerge from the dust and sand": since beginningless time, the compassion of all Buddhas has been thus.
Out of compassion for sentient beings who are deluded and fallen, he appears in the human world.
If one were to calculate their number, it would be like the number of atoms produced by grinding this world to dust, or like all the sands within the Ganges River;

even if there were as many such Ganges Rivers as there are grains of fine sand in each individual Ganges, [the number of those Buddhas] would still be vast. Alas, I have no affinity with the Buddha, even though the Buddha has appeared in this world.
When a Buddha appears in other worlds, I am born in this world; or when a Buddha appears, I am in the three miserable realms or in all such difficult places as the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*).
Even if I briefly obtain a human body, the Buddha and his teachings have already ceased to exist.
Or, even if the Dharma has not yet ceased, I neither hear it nor believe it, and am unable to resolve my mind toward enlightenment—just like one who is blind.
A tortoise has fallen into the ocean; it seeks to emerge but cannot. In the sea there is a floating log with a hole large enough to accommodate the tortoise’s body.

If the tortoise could enter within it, it would drift to the shore and thus escape the sea. Yet, for hundreds of thousands of blind tortoises and such a floating log, it is impossible for them to meet by chance.
I am like the blind tortoise, and the Buddha is like the hole in the floating log; because we have not met, [this opportunity is lost].

Regarding ordinary beings today, both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* contain this metaphor. When it says that the Buddha appears among humans, it is because he is especially concerned for those in whom the illness is most severe.
The retributions of the six realms of existence are mostly acquired through the human body of Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, the arousal of the mind to cultivate the untainted karma of the Three Vehicles likewise occurs within the human body, as the power of discernment is strongest among humans.

Because there is much deliberation [regarding the Dharma], the suffering of the six heavens is slight; yet they are separated by the conditions of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). Those capable of receiving transformation are found only among human beings.
[Regarding the phrase] "How fortunate" and below: second, this is the celebration of the present.

If one were to rely on the teachings of the definitive teaching encountered here, there are several sections of the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras and śāstras of the perfect and sudden [teachings] that reveal the nature. However, for now, we primarily celebrate this very sūtra. Regarding the "thousandfold doubts": I, [the author], previously...

Within the teachings on the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, I have spent several years developing the aspiration for enlightenment and engaging in study; yet, I could not resolve my countless doubts.

Later, upon meeting a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the Southern School of Chan, my doubts were severed regarding the fundamental path of delusion and awakening, and of rising and sinking from beginning to end.
As for the various distinct gateways—the mind and its objects, their origin and culmination, and the practices of cultivation and realization—[my doubts were likewise resolved].
Regarding the various stages, the immeasurable gates of meaning, and the provisional and ultimate teachings, they have not yet been fully resolved.

Whenever I engage in contemplative observation, or when I peruse the various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, I encounter passages that appear contradictory, convoluted intentions, and points of confusion and doubt.

Wisdom then becomes obstructed and stagnant, just as when water flows along it is frozen by the wind into ice, whereby it can no longer flow freely; the depression and distress of the mind and heart are likewise like this.
By personally practicing these teachings, each [obstruction] is dissolved and released, just like ice in the sunlight or like frost and snow drenched with hot water;
hence it is said that they "melt like ice. As for "investigation and reflection" and so forth, one examines past causes through reverse inference; if it were not...

Having encountered various spiritual friends over successive lifetimes and having been perfumed by the teachings of definitive meaning within the *ālayavijñāna*, how could one attain awakening and understanding merely upon seeing this wondrous scripture now?
Could it be that after hearing and believing it for only one, two, three, four, or five lifetimes, one is able to enter into realization?

Such is the unimpeded nature and characteristics, the harmonious integration of the real and the false, and the mutual penetration of the ordinary and the sagely, wherein the fundamental and the derivative are naturally...
It stands without confusion or disorder; its myriad gates and ten thousand meanings are each perfectly accomplished. Is there any doubt or obstruction?

You should know that it is only by having accumulated the permeation of hearing over successive lifetimes and having encountered virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) throughout many births that one can penetrate such profound meanings as these—wherein the words diverge yet the intent is unified, and so forth. Indeed, I have frequently investigated and contemplated this.
I reflect that whether it be through a whole night in stillness, a full day in leisurely repose, or walking alone for the duration of an entire journey, I have harbored these thoughts in my heart.
I am deeply grateful that, throughout many lifetimes, various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) have opened my mind, guided me, and exhorted me until I have reached this point.

Furthermore, I have carefully contemplated the period several lifetimes prior; when I first encountered a virtuous friend, I must have found it difficult to believe and incline toward the path, as there were all manner of firm [obstacles].
He persisted in uttering various irrational words, displaying his skill and eloquence with the sole intent of resistance.

Fortunately, through the compassionate mindfulness and awakening of a virtuous friend—who feared he was treading upon the destruction of the Teaching and feared he would fall into ruin—he exerted every effort and applied skillful means to rescue and deliver him.
After such a number of births, they finally consented to believe and accept [the teaching]. Although they were able to believe and comply, they had not yet attained realization.

Furthermore, virtuous friends exhausted various skillful means and parables to instruct them so that they might achieve thorough understanding. After another such number of births, although they understood immediately upon hearing the words, afterwards they merely followed along as before;
they still did not give rise to the thought that this was difficult to encounter, nor did they maintain it moment by moment.
In seeking learning, one constantly merely exhausts the strength of heart and mind of virtuous friends; only through long-term exhortation and encouragement can one gradually progress.
Furthermore, for several lifetimes, one may vainly delight in studying the principles of verbal teachings, yet fail to examine the mind in the face of sensory objects.

One does not perceive or investigate deluded thoughts to subdue emotional inclinations. Whenever hearing virtuous friends explain profound meanings, one listens with joy and receives them; yet one also hears...
Pointing to those instances where one’s application of the mind deviates from the Way, one feels no joy;
instead, one suspects one’s spiritual friends, perhaps thinking they lack compassion or that one trusts the words of others, or harbors other ulterior motives.

Such various gateways that obstruct the Way—from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the present life—should be reflected upon in detail, contemplating their categories and varieties, which number in the thousands, tens of thousands, and millions.
I must have been protected by the compassionate pity of a virtuous friend who did not abandon me, employing hundreds of schemes and thousands of examinations to gradually guide and lead me;
only thus could I, in this present life, transcend so many such obstacles and critical junctures on the path.

On several occasions during my leisure time, while in secluded places, I reflected upon the events of many lifetimes; my tears flowed down to my neck, and my heart-throat constricted to my chest, often becoming faint.

He wept aloud, lamenting that he would not easily meet many virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) again. He remembered each one clearly and paid them respectful thanks with the utmost sincerity, pledging to repay their kindness in various ways.
Consequently, he made a vow in every thought-moment, wishing that in a future life he might encounter each of them once more and, moreover, attain the knowledge of past lives (pūrvajātismara).
He vowed to remain fully conscious of each encounter and to exhaust his body and mind in making offerings to repay their benevolence with sincere devotion.

Thus it is; not knowing what to do, I have briefly written this to show my fellow practitioners, so that they may know my former carriage has already overturned, and that those in their subsequent carriages should change their course.
The commentary states: "The Superior One’s compassion extends downward. This is the second [section], the eulogy.

Regarding "lamenting for the末世 (final age)," among the individual inquiries of the twelve bodhisattvas, each says, "May you act for the sake of bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age. As for the sequence from beginning to end:

the beginning refers to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the fundamental ground of the causal stage; the end refers to the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment’s inquiry regarding the cultivation and realization of the three contemplations. If one were to correlate them...
For those of the highest faculties, the first cycle of teaching—the Chapter on Pure Wisdom—is sufficient;

it concludes by explaining the characteristics of how ordinary and sagely beings accord with the nature of awakening through the causes and effects of their practice. As for the sequential approach, this refers to those who resolve their minds upon hearing the teachings and proceed directly toward the Mahāyāna.
For such individuals, one must first ask: "Upon what dharma do they initially rely to resolve their minds? What serves as the fundamental cause? Therefore...
Mañjuśrī questioned based on this; therefore, the Buddha expounded for him the pure mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*).

This primordially existing *dhāraṇī* is the source of all phenomena, both defiled and pure. Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one falsely identifies this body and mind as the self, and thus there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, ignorance is fundamentally non-existent, and likewise, there is no one who attains awakening. One returns to the Tathāgatagarbha, reaching ultimate consummation.
This concludes the section. Having now awakened to this realm, it is naturally fitting to understand the principle of practicing based on the locus of that awakening.
However, pure awareness is inherently complete, with neither increase nor decrease; ignorance is fundamentally non-existent, with nothing to be removed or severed.

Thus, there would be no need for cultivation. Yet, if one does not practice, one will perpetually dwell within illusion. The meaning of "cultivating" versus "not cultivating" is such that words may seem contrary while their implications are consistent; one must certainly comprehend this. Therefore:
Samantabhadra questioned based on this. The Buddha taught that the body, mind, and the wisdom of practice are all like illusions;
yet, although they are like illusions, it is not precluded that illusory wisdom cultivates the illusory body and mind. When the body and mind are exhausted, illusory wisdom also ceases.

The nature of awakening is perfect and complete, without arising or ceasing. Having realized this principle, one must naturally know the skillful means for its cultivation. How should one conceive the creative intention?
"How should one direct the mind so that contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) may be accomplished? Thus, Samantacakṣus asked this,

and the Buddha replied that taking right mindfulness to transcend illusion as the preliminary means (*pūrvaprayoga*), one should cease all conditions (*śamatha*, here translated as "stopping"), firmly maintain the prohibitive precepts,

dwell peacefully among the assembly, sit in quietude in a secluded room, and constantly contemplate by analytically deconstructing each of the four great elements, the sense faculties, consciousness, and sense objects.

Within this objective realm (*viṣaya*), both the attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) are entirely non-existent. Thus, one realizes the true nature manifested by the two kinds of emptiness.

Furthermore, the marks of cultivation and awakening are extinguished; even mental images (*pratibimba*) cease. The awakened mind is pure, and all things are likewise so. There is no self and no other;
it is equal, immovable, and pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. Toward all dualistic objects, there is neither love nor hatred, and so on, even unto the multitude...
[The Bodhisattva] Vajragarbha was born having already attained the Buddha-way. Upon hearing this teaching, those whose faculties were somewhat inferior naturally felt doubt:

how could that which had originally attained the Way now appear to differ from the Buddha in its superiority and inferiority, separated by such a vast gulf? Thus, Vajragarbha, knowing the capacities of the assembly, questioned [the Buddha] based on this.
The Buddha’s explanation arose from observing the perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) through the lens of the sentient beings’ cyclic mind, wherein there appears to be transmigration.
In truth, Awakened Nature is unmoving; it is like seeing both banks of a river move because a boat is traveling, whereas in reality, the banks do not move at all.
Once this doubt is resolved, one will know that it is due to the mind of saṃsāra that one perceives Perfect Awakening as being subject to flux.
It is natural that this mind must be severed. However, this mind of saṃsāra and its appearances flow on spontaneously, beyond one's own control.
Knowing that which is the root of saṃsāra, and seeing that it continues without interruption or cessation, Maitreya questioned based on this.
The Buddha taught that because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is transformed into the root, one creates karma and undergoes retribution in an endless succession.

Even if one relies on the teachings of the Three Vehicles for cultivation, if the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is not eliminated, it will ultimately be difficult to enter awakening. Next, having understood how to eliminate it—
Free from craving, give rise to the supreme mind and make pure vows. Abiding in the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, seek out virtuous friends;

thus you will not follow false views, but cultivate true stillness and eliminate delusion. This principle is all-encompassing and must be understood as it naturally is; practice in accordance with this.

Having proceeded from the initial resolve to the fruit of Buddhahood, one must always rely upon Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi). Whatever one does or undertakes must constantly be in accord with it, following and conforming to Perfect Enlightenment.
Since there is no distinction between ordinary beings and sages, nor any gradations of difference, how can there be distinct stages and levels?

All are in accord with non-discriminating awakening; therefore, Pure Wisdom (Vimalamati) relies upon this to inquire. The Buddha taught the ten levels of faith, the three stages of worthiness, the ten grounds, and the fruit of Buddhahood;
these follow the nature of awakening and each possesses its own characteristic mode of practice. This constitutes the complete cycle of the Dharma’s meaning from beginning to end.
However, the faculties and natures of sentient beings are diverse and not uniform—whether superior, middling, or inferior; whether active, moving, or still and quiescent; or...
One may appropriately accord with the Way through spontaneous effort, or one may appropriately realize the principle through focused concentration and restraint.

It is like a city with four gates, each entered from its respective direction. By what skillful means can [the teaching] universally reach all capacities? Therefore, the Bodhisattva Majestic Virtue (Vaiśravaṇa) inquired based on this.
The Buddha taught that among all practices there is truly no duality; yet, the number of conforming skillful means is immeasurable. Perfect...
Regarding the subsumption of what is to be attained, there are three types according to the distinctions of individual capacities, namely: śamatha and so forth.

Having heard that these three contemplations are the gateways for entry suited to the specific faculties of individuals, it is natural that one must know whether a single person practices all three collectively, or whether three people each practice one, two, or three, or whether they practice them singly or in combination. Thus, Bhadrapāla arose [to inquire].

Question: The Buddha taught the twenty-five wheels, all of which are permitted. Having understood the gateways of the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) to be cultivated, it is natural that some individuals may realize them for themselves and practice according to the Dharma.

Yet, if their mental attention does not cease and the contemplative practice fails to be accomplished, they may doubt that their own awakened nature (*buddhadhātu*) is fundamentally pure, thinking that this is due to delusion and inversion and thus inconsistent with reality. Now, having attained sudden awakening, they again rely upon and follow [the teachings].
One enters through the gateway and cultivates therein; why then is one unable to realize entry? Thus, Pure Karma (Viśuddhakarma) raises this question.

The Buddha explains that it is because of the continuous succession of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time—consisting of attachments to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life span—that one does not enter awakening.

It is not that awakening rejects those who seek to enter. Next, since one knows that the mark of selfhood (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) lies latent, being difficult to discern and difficult to eliminate, one must rely upon a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This is the gateway to the accumulation of practice. One must resolve to diligently sever [afflictions]. By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one must know:
what kind of person is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) worthy of being relied upon?

Furthermore, by the very nature of things, there is a class of persons who, because they have resolved to practice and sever [afflictions] with diligence, may either engage in various activities, striving to realize [the goal] early, or fear that the arising of such thoughts constitutes a failure, and thus remain solely in a state of indifference.

Fate. Or perhaps they merely cease their deluded thoughts, or seek to extinguish the faculties and their objects; thus the Bodhisattva Pujue (Universal Awakening) recognizes this and directs his efforts toward them.
This is the method taught by the Buddha for relying upon an enlightened master to eliminate subtle afflictions.

Next, regarding those of middling capacity, the Dharma gates have been fully explained. Furthermore, there is another class—those of inferior capacity—who nevertheless possess great resolve and are determined to [attain liberation].
Those who seek realization must employ formal practices and methods of restraint; only then can they fulfill their aspirations and achieve success.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva of Perfect Enlightenment questioned [the Buddha] based on this intent. The Buddha taught the method of the three-period *dharmakṣetra* (meditation hall), the application of effort and practice, and the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
Whether these are practiced individually, collectively, or alternately, if one is unable to succeed through such cultivation, he further instructed the performance of repentance rituals (*li-chan*).
...and so forth. Next, regarding the three categories of the main body of the teaching (*samyak-artha*), all are perfectly complete.
It is naturally necessary to know the methods for upholding and practicing these verbal instructions, so as to ensure that this teaching circulates without interruption.

Therefore, the Venerable Subhūti raises a question, and the Buddha provides the name of the sutra, the Buddhas who preach and protect the sutra, a comparison of the merit of upholding the teaching, and [the account] up to the various devas.
Because they protect and serve the great assembly, it is called "sequential order. Regarding the term "inquiry" (*xúnzī*) in the commentary:

this refers to the Buddha’s praise of Mañjuśrī, stating that he is able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the practices for attaining the ground of enlightenment for all bodhisattvas, and so forth. As for "the Able One" (*Néng rén*):
In the Sanskrit language it is *Śākya*; here it is translated as "The Capable One" (*Nengren*). Regarding "those who respond to the resonance":

the assembly of Bodhisattvas who pose the questions are the "resonators," while the Buddha is the "resonated. The Buddha is the "one who responds," and the Bodhisattvas are the "responded-to. Regarding "that which accords with the source of the mind":
the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*Yuanjue*) is the source of all phenomena (*dharmas*). The mind itself is the source; thus it is called the "source of the mind. Alternatively, the mind...
This is that which can sever the defiled and pure minds that are to be severed; its source is the awakened nature, the true mind.

This is the source of the mind, termed the "source of the mind" (*cittasrota*). The former [etymological analysis] is a *karmadhāraya* (attributive) compound, while the latter is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound; both interpretations are valid.
From the beginning to the end of this sutra, all the various distinct dharmas and meanings taught therein are each based upon the purity of *pariniṣpanna-avabodha* (perfectly realized enlightenment).
It is distinguished by the mind; hence it is called "designation" (*saṃjñā*). Regarding "no obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative":

among the various Mahāyāna teachings, some exclusively expound the principle of empty quiescence—true thusness and cessation where there is nothing to cultivate and nothing to realize, neither subject nor object, inconceivable by cognition, cut off from the path of language, and extinguished as the sphere of mental activity.
This is to speak only of the fundamental while obstructing the derivative. Or, [some]... one.
As previously stated, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have relied upon the eight consciousnesses; through their mutual perfuming, they give rise to all phenomena, both defiled and pure.
Whether sentient or insentient, because of ignorance, they give rise to delusions and create karma, undergoing endless retribution.

Had they not encountered the Buddha, they would certainly remain ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) with no means of attaining perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). However, if they encounter the Buddha and his teachings...

They give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and develop faith, practicing the six perfections and myriad deeds, or the practices of the two vehicles, gradually entering [the path] and each relying upon their own vehicle to attain Buddhahood after three lifetimes, sixty kalpas, or three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

This merely describes the branches while obscuring the root. Now, this sutra is complete, definitive, and clear, revealing both the root and the branches. The Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses great...
Perfect Enlightenment. Furthermore, ignorance is fundamentally non-existent; moreover, even the knowledge that it is non-existent is like a flower in the sky.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no arising or ceasing of cognition or vision. Even within the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind, there is fundamentally no bodhi nor nirvāṇa;
there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the failure to attain it; there is neither deluded saṃsāra nor the absence of saṃsāra. Examples of this kind are beyond [reckoning].

All that has been fully set forth is the root. Furthermore, the various manifestations of deluded conduct, the various manifestations of spiritual practice, the stages and levels of the path, the distinctions among contemplative practices, and the rules for the site of enlightenment—examples such as these are also difficult to cite in their entirety;
they are all the branches. All that is described as branches are precisely the branches of the root, never obscuring the root. All that is described as the root is... [the root].

This is the root of the branches; it has never obstructed the branches. Therefore, it is said that "the root and the branches are without obstruction. These words regarding "non-obstruction" were requested by Vajragarbha, who said:
"I only pray that you will not abandon your unobstructed great compassion, but for the sake of all bodhisattvas, reveal the secret treasury."
It is like holding a great *vaiśvadeva* feast (*asaṃgapūjā*), where monastics and nuns from near and far come and are provided for without any obstruction;
even practitioners, children, the poor, and the sick—all are admitted without hindrance. This is called an "unrestricted feast" (*asaṃgapūjā*). The present sutra is likewise so:

it includes all great bodhisattvas, those on the stages (*bhūmi*) and those prior to the stages, as well as those in the final age, whether they are beginners entering the gateway or those who have cultivated its intent.

It encompasses both the deep and the shallow, just as the waters of the great ocean do not refuse even small streams; whether asuras, mosquitoes, or gadflies drink from it, they are all fully satisfied.
Therefore, it is called "unrestricted" (*asaṃvara*). "Sudden" (*ton*) refers to the suddenness of the pedagogical method (*vyavahāra*).

This means that if one were merely to speak of the effacement of traces and the departure from signs, it would still not be called "sudden. Thus, the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* states: "All sūtras on emptiness are teachings with remainder; their principle is not yet [complete]."
Because [the conventional] is exhausted. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states that emptiness is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna.

If one were to speak merely of the stages of practice regarding phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), this would not be "sudden" either, as it would not yet have fathomed the true source. This present sutra, however, explains both the beginning and the end together;
since phenomena are themselves unimpeded, it is called the "sudden exposition."

The commentary has already been excerpted below; this is the third dedication. Regarding "the various expositions": these refer to the various sūtras and vinayas, the various treatises and commentaries, and the various essential and wondrous secret instructions.
Regarding "striking at true stillness": this means turning back to observe one's own mind and illuminate the principle.

Based upon the place of awakening and the place of vision, I have composed this commentary. Within this, there are two intentions: first, because I have excerpted from the various expositions, it is not of a single uniform type.
The Chan school merely takes the delusion of the mind as its focus and does not examine the principles [of doctrine] to take the holy teachings as a definitive standard.

Second, because it involves "knocking at the silence," it differs from those who study literary commentaries—such scholars who merely collect and compile old phrases from various treatises and commentaries, altering the beginning and changing the end, yet claim, "I have composed this commentary.
Now, we take the holy teachings as a clear mirror to illuminate and see.
One’s own mind: taking one’s own mind as the lamp of wisdom to illuminate the profound purport of the scriptures; hence it is said, "to gather the exegesis and strike at the silence," and so forth.
The phrase "striking at silence" refers to what is stated in the *Zi shu*: "to strike at the silent void in order to seek the underlying meaning. Regarding "responding to the Sage’s intent":

although one may have perused all the various teachings, one does not employ them exhaustively, nor does one simply select and use those areas with which one is already familiar. Rather, [one employs that which accords with] the Sage...
When one speaks this sutra, its meaning and intent correspond to its application; thus it is said that "it accords with the sacred intent.
"This text" refers to this sutra. Regarding the dedication of merit toward sentient beings: there are three aspects to the locus of such dedication.

This refers to the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) of the enlightenment of sentient beings. Now, according to the intent of the sutra, since every gate pertains to sentient beings of the final age, I follow the sutra by designating "sentient beings.
Furthermore, among those who practice the Mahāyāna, there are those in whom great compassion predominates and those in whom great wisdom predominates;
as for me, my faculties are dull and weak, so I take pity on those of inferior capacity and thus dedicate this merit toward sentient beings so that we may enter together.

The Treasury of Light (*prabhā-kośa*). The Treasury of Light is precisely the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). It lacks only the word "bodhi," which is implicitly contained within the character "entering" (*ru*).
Since that which is able to enter is wisdom (*jñāna*), it corresponds to bodhi.
*Commentary on the Great Sub-commentary to the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Thirteen (Part Two) [End].
According to the manuscript:
Residing in Yang’ao Village, Chusheng County, Pingjiang Prefecture, Jiangzhe; the devoted disciple Liu Hua.
Together with my family and dependents, I have respectfully commissioned artisans to open this secret edict.

May it serve above to bless the enlightened and the worthy, and below to support all movement and growth. It is my hope that those who hear and receive it will forget the mental activities of birth and extinction, and that those who lecture upon it...
Free from the noble understanding and ordinary sentiments, every phrase flows as pure *tathatā*, and every word enters the ocean-nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

It opens the sun of wisdom for all sentient beings and awakens the wondrous mind of all Buddhas. When consciousness is shattered, wisdom becomes bright; when consciousness is forgotten, wisdom is revealed.

Thereafter, whether moving horizontally or vertically, with the heart-mind and consciousness sealing off emotional attachments, one departs together from the source of delusion and all ascend to the true ferry.

On the fourteenth day of the eleventh month in the ninth year of the Shaoxing era, I respectfully vow that, as compared to the summer of the fourth year of Kenchō, this manuscript—having been entrusted to another for transcription using the original from Katsura-oe—is indeed a new crossing [of the sea].
This is a single copy belonging to our temple; it should be revered and honored.
In the tenth month of the same year, this was completed by collating it against one manuscript copy.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Shi Xinhai (aged thirty-two; sixteen years since receiving the precepts).
